q: Maple Syrup Urine Disease, management?

q: A 3-day-old infant is brought to the Paediatrics Clinic with refusal to feed, vomiting and inactivity. The infant was born at term with no perinatal problems. The infant's urine smells ilk bumed sugar. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

q: Patient with glycosuria and aminoaciduria. What is the diagnosis? It was a long case

n: Answer B, galactosemia (aminoaciduria plus glycosuria).

q: 3 days (not sure but age was in days)with abdominal pain ketone in urin with odour ABG Acidosis Low ph not remember the exact number What is the diagnosis

q: Newborn developed seizure, the urine have a distinct odor[ no mention of sweet or any description] and there is ketone in the urine, what is the diagnosis?

q: 2 week old boy product of uneventful delivery discharged in generally good condition. the mother noticed hes less active with poor feeding and yellow discoloration of his skin that gets deeper with time. she came to pediatric er where he developed fever labs: ph 7.26 glucose 2.1 bicarb 19.5 full septic screen e coli sepsis urine analysis shows aminoglycosurea and glucosurea (urine analysis was this or similar words) what's the diagnosis?

q: 5 year kid with bilateral hydronephrosis and thick bladder what's the investigation?
k: Pediatric renal imaging: match the question to the tool.
r: Thick walled bladder plus bilateral hydronephrosis = bladder outlet problem (posterior urethral valves in a boy), and the confirming test is a voiding study, not a scan of the kidneys.
n: Answer MCUG (unlettered options lettered by position). Compiler approach (over-simplified): renal scarring -> DMSA; first febrile UTI in children <6 months (NICE) -> renal US; recurrent UTI in children -> renal US; unilateral or bilateral hydronephrosis -> MCU

q: Neonate diagnosed during pregnancy with bilateral hydronephrosis. Now US shows bilateral hydronephrosis and thickened bladder wall. Which of the following imaging modalities has the highest diagnostic yield?
k: Bilateral hydronephrosis + thick-walled bladder in a newborn = bladder outlet obstruction (PUV) until proven otherwise: confirm with MCUG.
r: Unilateral hydronephrosis with a normal bladder points to PUJ obstruction (MAG3); bilateral with a thick bladder points to PUV (MCUG).

q: 6 month old come with UTI her parents are concerned, what investigation you will do?
k: Imaging after a childhood UTI is stepwise.
r: First UTI in a child: ultrasound first; MCUG for reflux and DMSA for scarring only in selected cases.
n: Answer A, renal US.

q: Pediatric patient with recurrent UTI. Mother says she does not remember if any investigations were done. Came with dysuria, Investigations showed positive nitrate, leukocytes. What is the most indicated investigation?

q: I forgot the exact wording of the question, but it was approximately like this: A 2-year-old child gets recurrent UTIs. The mother is asking for UTI prevention.

q: A 7-year-old girl is diagnosed with nephrotic syndrome. Laboratory investigations reveal hypoalbuminemia and heavy proteinuria. Which of the following is most commonly associated with this condition?

q: A 6 years old boy with increasing lethargy, edema he had severe gastroenteritis with bloody diarrhea 1 week ago some other symptoms as well i can't recall them No fever not sure about BP Labs show: High creatinine Many many labs Glucose not mentioned Urinalysis: +Protein +Ketones +Blood Nitrites not mentioned in the urinalysis Which culture will help establish the diagnosis?

q: 12-week-old child with Beckwith Wiedemann syndrome with the mother concerned about increased risk for liver lesion. What tumor marker will you use ?

q: 12 years old with dysurea found to have klebsella colony 100000 from mid urine culture ??

q: Parent's brought their child to the hospital for inability to move his arm X-ray showed a fracture at both distal ulna and radial bone. The child looks healthy and dressed well, and has good hygiene they recall that 2 days ago the mom. dropped a plate on the child's arm and noticed he couldn't move his arm and after 2nd day the child couldn't move his arm they didn't notice any bruising so they thought it's just a strain. Which of the following is indicative of child abuse?
k: Red flags for child abuse on history and examination: Delay in seeking medical care after an obvious injury; History inconsistent, changing, or not matching the injury or developmental stage; Multiple fractures of different ages; posterior rib or metaphyseal corner fractures
r: A tidy, well kept child does not exclude abuse; the delay in presentation is the flag.
n: Printed answer B: delayed presentation (2 days before seeking care) is the red flag for non-accidental injury.

o: Do further workup (Bone profile, CBC, Ua/C)
Reassurance, as he will catch up to adult hight eventually
k: Bone age + growth velocity sort short stature: Normal bone age, normal velocity: familial short stature (short final height, matches mid parental target); Delayed bone age, normal velocity: constitutional delay, reassure, normal final height; Delayed bone age, slow velocity: pathological (GH deficie
r: Delayed bone age with normal velocity = reassure; it is a slow or falling velocity that triggers workup.
n: Delayed bone age with normal growth velocity = constitutional growth delay; reassure.

q: 6 y.o child came complaining of mild hip and thigh pain, examination: he is febrile, mild-moderate tenderness of hip joint, child has mild pain when walking apart from that the child is looking good US of hip: Joint effusion WBC: 11 Whats the diagnosis?
k: Irritable hip in a child: transient synovitis vs septic arthritis (Kocher criteria).
r: Same effusion, but a child who refuses to bear weight with high WBC flips the answer to septic arthritis and urgent aspiration.
n: Printed answer A, toxic synovitis (well looking child, WBC 11); another group (Monsters) also answered A. Recaller: Option C not fully remembered.

q: Child with fever that comes daily, with arthritis and arthralgia, and salmon-colored rash. ESR and CRP are elevated.

r: Salmon rash that comes and goes with a once-daily fever spike = systemic JIA; erythema marginatum (rings) = rheumatic fever.
n: Quotidian fever + arthritis + salmon rash = systemic JIA.

q: Defenitve treatment for severe combined immuno deficiency
o: Life long or long term steroid
k: Match the defect to the definitive treatment.
r: 'X-linked' does not mean immunoglobulin: X-linked SCID still needs a transplant; only X-linked agammaglobulinemia gets lifelong IVIG.
n: Option A was actually 'Lifelong Immunoglobulin'. X-linked agammaglobulinemia is treated with lifelong immunoglobulin; X-linked SCID is treated with bone marrow transplant. Don't get fooled by 'X-linked': SCID is commonly X-linked.

q: 8 years old child with lax joints and fingers Arachnodactyly what is the investigation that will protect him from a life threatening condition?
k: Marfan = tall, lax, long fingers: echo for the aortic root.
r: The killer in Marfan is the aorta, so the protective test images the aortic root.
n: Marfan syndrome: echo to screen for aortic root dilatation and prevent aortic dissection.

q: A 5 year Pedia patient comes with fever 37.9 for 6 weeks associated with joint pain With salmon color rash especially trunk and hepatomegaly and bilateral wrist swelling with is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Fever + arthritis + salmon rash = systemic JIA.
r: Salmon rash that appears with the fever is systemic JIA; cytopenias or night bone pain should make you think ALL.
n: Better recall. Prolonged fever, arthritis, salmon-colored rash and hepatomegaly: systemic JIA. Other version of this recall in Part 4: SWR-4316 → D. systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis

q: a child has gastroenteritis 2 weeks ago treated with supportive treatment presents with bilateral knee pain and 3 interphalangeal pain there is edema around the knees and reduce range of motion temperature 36.6 wbc 8 X ray knees shows no soft tissue enlargement what is the most appropriate management
k: Post-infectious arthritis = sterile, treat symptoms.
r: A recent gut infection with afebrile, multi joint arthritis = NSAIDs; a single hot joint with fever = tap it.
n: Reactive arthritis after gastroenteritis, afebrile with normal WBC; treat with NSAIDs (ibuprofen).

q: 36- 10yr polyarthritis and fever, small joint stiffness. Rheumatoid factor 100 (N < 58). First line:
k: JIA: arthritis lasting at least 6 weeks with onset before 16 years, after excluding other causes.
r: RF-positive polyarticular JIA is 'childhood RA': start methotrexate, do not rely on NSAIDs.
n: Methotrexate as first line; handwritten note 'Evidence Wing confirmed'.

q: Child with sore throat came with complaint of left knee pain then the pain resolved and become in right knee then right ankle and skin rash after hot shower:
k: Jones criteria: evidence of preceding group A strep plus 2 major, or 1 major + 2 minor.
r: Migratory arthritis that dramatically responds to aspirin = rheumatic fever; fixed arthritis for 6 weeks or more = JIA.

q: 3 months old baby with SCID. Oral thrush, chronic diarrhea, pneumonia. What is the definitive treatment?
k: Primary immunodeficiency: treatment depends on the defective line.
r: "Definitive" means curative: in SCID that is always HSCT, even though IVIG is given first.
n: Compiler marks 'Oral thrush' in red. Recaller: Option D not recalled.

q: Pt (forgot the age but was a teenager male) came for routine visit, asymptomatic he is taller than his classmates, he's very accomplished and leads the basketball team, on examination he has high arched palate, mild scoliosis, hyperextended joints and thin, what could be the cause ?
k: Tall + thin + hypermobile + scoliosis/pectus + high arched palate = Marfan.
r: Hypermobility alone does not separate them; tall stature favours Marfan, stretchy skin and bruising favour Ehlers-Danlos.
n: Tall stature, high arched palate, scoliosis and joint hypermobility point to Marfan syndrome.

q: A young girl presents with a weakness and heliotrope rash around the eyes and Her laboratory investigations show negative ANA and anti-dsDNA antibodies. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Weakness + heliotrope rash = dermatomyositis; in a child, juvenile dermatomyositis.
r: Heliotrope rash plus weakness is dermatomyositis even if ANA is negative; a negative ANA makes SLE very unlikely but does not exclude JDM.
n: Recaller: Arabic recaller notes: does not remember the age but thinks 7; does not remember where exactly the weakness was; remembers something on her fingers (nodules or similar) and on her hands. Option B not remembered (printed in Arabic).

q: An 11-month-old child was brought to the emergency department by his parents with a history of falling onto an outstretched hand 2 days earlier. There was no bruising or other evidence of external injury. The following day, the parents noticed that the child was not moving the affected arm, so they brought him to the emergency department. The child appeared well nourished and was up to date with his vaccinations and routine follow-up appointments. There were no concerning features in the family or social history. An X-ray showed mid-shaft fractures of both the radius and ulna. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Contact the police and report suspected child abuse
Believe the parents' history and treat the fracture
Admit the child for full work up and perform a non-contrast CT scan of the head
k: Suspicion of abuse is enough to report; proof is not required.
r: A well-looking family and up-to-date vaccines do not cancel red flags; the injury-mechanism mismatch in an infant decides it.
n: Mid-shaft radius and ulna fractures in a non-ambulatory 11-month-old with a fall history are suspicious for non-accidental injury -> contact Child Protective Services.

q: A 6-year-old child presents with daytime and nighttime anuresis and chronic constipation. Examination reveals a sacral dimple. What is the most appropriate next step in management?

q: Parents brought their 3 y old child concerning about blood with the stool , everything was normal except the main complaint, after examination and investigation the pediatrician said : don't worry it's a common preventable condition what's the dx:

q: 9 year old child presents with 2 months history of epigastric pain that wakes him up at night, mother mentioned a hx of PUD, what is the confirmatory test?

q: Neonate with ambigioua genitalia, have hyopnatremia and hyperkalemia

q: 125 - A child presents with vomiting and diarrhea about seven times a day, has very dry skin and mucous membranes, sunken eyes, delayed capillary refill of 4 seconds, lethargy, and hypotension, What type of dehydration does this child have?
k: Dehydration grading: Mild (<5%): alert, thirsty, normal signs; Moderate (6 to 9%): irritable, sunken eyes, dry tongue, slow skin pinch, tachycardia; Severe (≥10%): drowsy, very sunken eyes, very slow skin pinch, weak thready pulse, scanty urine
r: Hypotension in a child is a late sign: once BP falls, call it shock, not just severe dehydration.
n: Highlighted answer: C (hypotension and delayed capillary refill = hypovolemic shock).

q: A 10-year-old boy presents to the clinic complaining of abdominal pain, frequent diarrhoea that is sometimes bloody, and pain usually accompanying defecation. On examination, he looks ill, pale, with a so> abdomen, no tenderness or organomegaly (see lab results). Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? Patient had low albumin levels

q: 14 YO male presented to ER with history of diarrhea for 3 months. Associated with abdominal bloating and loss of subcutaneous fat. What is the best treatment?

q: Child presenting with vomiting crying and red currant jelly stool, what is the origin of this pathology?
k: Intussusception: ileocolic in most children.
r: Typical toddler intussusception = ileocolic; HSP-related = ileoileal.
n: Intussusception, most commonly ileocecal (ileocolic).

q: Mother brought Child who is choking. They cannot speak, cry or respond. What to do?

k: Choking algorithm (conscious): Effective cough (crying, talking): encourage coughing and watch.; Ineffective cough, child over 1 year: 5 back blows, then 5 abdominal thrusts, repeat.; Infant under 1 year: 5 back blows, then 5 CHEST thrusts (no abdominal thrusts).
r: Can cry or talk: encourage cough; cannot make a sound: back blows and thrusts.
n: Severe airway obstruction in a conscious child: back blows and abdominal thrusts; if unconscious, CPR. Following pages show the UpToDate FB airway obstruction algorithm and the choking child figure (child: 5 back slaps + 5 abdominal thrusts; infant: back blows

q: 2years child previously healthy, suddenly develops a cough during a family gathering. She is now in severe respiratory distress and cyanotic. What to do?
o: Give antibiotics and order chest X-ray
Perform 5 back blows and 5 abdominal thrusts
k: Foreign body aspiration in children: Peak age about 1 to 3 years; nuts, seeds and small toys.; Sudden choking or coughing while eating or playing, without fever.; Severe (cyanosis, silent cough): back blows and abdominal thrusts (chest thrusts under 1 year).
r: Under 1 year swap abdominal thrusts for chest thrusts; over 1 year it is back blows plus abdominal thrusts.
n: Severe foreign body airway obstruction in a child over 1 year: back blows and abdominal thrusts.

q: baby press with greenish vomiting, irritabilty. What is the most appropriate management?
k: Infant vomiting, colour decides the test: Bilious vomiting: malrotation or volvulus until proven otherwise; Initial: abdominal X-ray; most appropriate or diagnostic: upper GI contrast study; Unstable or peritonitic: straight to laparotomy (Ladd procedure)
r: 'Initial investigation' in bilious vomiting is the X-ray; 'most appropriate' or 'diagnostic' is the upper GI study.
n: Bilious vomiting: initial -> X-ray; most appropriate -> upper GI study.

q: Pediatric patient with Henoch-Schönlein Purpura (HSP). Which clinical feature represents a potentially life-threatening complication requiring immediate urgent evaluation?
o: Mild joint pain getting better with rest
New onset of bloody stool and severe abdominal pain
k: HSP tetrad: palpable purpura (normal platelets), abdominal pain, arthritis, renal involvement.
r: Purpura is the diagnosis, not the danger; in HSP the acute danger is the gut (intussusception), the long-term danger is the kidney.
n: Printed answer D; no compiler commentary.

q: A child presents with tea-colored urine and jaundice, preceded by nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. The same issue was reported in the kindergarten, with some other children also affected. Liver enzymes were elevated: ALT: 500 AST: 400 What is the most appropriate treatment?
k: Hepatitis A in children: supportive care.
r: Jaundice after a GI prodrome in a daycare cluster = hepatitis A; the answer is supportive unless the stem shows liver failure.
n: Answer C Hydration and rest; diagnosis HAV (hepatitis A outbreak in kindergarten), supportive care.

q: a child with vomiting and diharreah for 2 days presents now with jaundince and dark color urine, he attend daycare and there are similar episodes in children there AST 600 ALT 500 what is the next step
k: Acute viral hepatitis in a child from daycare = hepatitis A.
r: Liver transplant becomes the answer only if the stem adds encephalopathy or severe coagulopathy.
n: Answer B rest and rehydration (hepatitis A in daycare outbreak, supportive management).

q: child with recurrent diarrhea feeling full after eating only a small snack Physical examination reveals perianal fistula
k: Perianal fistula in a child with chronic diarrhoea = Crohn's disease.
r: Bloody diarrhoea with tenesmus points to UC; fistula, perianal disease or skip lesions point to Crohn's.

q: 3m FTT bilateral cataract hepatomegaly Rbc 3 Keton present Which investigation to confirm dx
k: Metabolic hepatomegaly in an infant: imaging describes, tissue or enzyme or gene testing confirms.

n: Athar answered liver biopsy. Alhomrani: not sure this is the same recall Athar answered 'B', but maybe yes; he did not search it.

q: 5 months with failure to thrive, has Bilateral cataract with hepatomegaly, positive ketones and high UA and trigelycride with RBC 3, What is best to confirm diagnosis" not sure"

n: Handwritten red 'Athar: C' = liver biopsy (same answer as the previous version, mapped to C here).

q: 7 year-old boy who has recently visited his grandfather's farm, now presents to you with diarrhea, miosis, vomiting, lacrimation, salivation, excessive urination, bronchospasm, and a garlic odor in his mouth. Which of the following should be administered?
k: Organophosphate = cholinergic excess (DUMBBELSS).
r: Pinpoint pupils with WET secretions = organophosphate (atropine); pinpoint pupils with a DRY, slow breathing patient = opioid (naloxone).
n: Organophosphate poisoning (cholinergic toxidrome, garlic odor); give atropine.

q: 5 years old boy presented complain of fecal incontinence and there is history of concitipation and passage of hard stool 3 times per week on DRE ther is dilated rectum and brownish soiling what is your managment??
k: Functional constipation with overflow soiling in children: Clues: hard infrequent stools, withholding, soiling, large rectum full of stool; Step 1: disimpaction, oral PEG first line (enema if oral fails); Step 2: maintenance PEG for months, scheduled toilet sitting, fiber and fluids
r: Dilated rectum full of stool = functional impaction; empty rectum with explosive stool on finger withdrawal = Hirschsprung.

q: A child is brought to the emergency department after accidentally swallowing a coin. He is asymptomatic. A plain X-ray shows that the coin has passed into the stomach What is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: Discharge the child and advise the parents to monitor for passage of the coin in the stool
k: Swallowed foreign body: decide by object risk, position on X-ray and symptoms.
r: Same coin picture but a button battery in the oesophagus, or a child drooling and unable to swallow, flips the answer to urgent endoscopic removal.

q: A Child with greenish vomiting and abdominal pain. What is the most appropriate investigation?
k: Bilious vomiting in a child = malrotation with volvulus until proven otherwise.
r: Bilious vomiting points above the colon, so the contrast goes in from above (upper GI series), not from below.

q: Baby with fever, abdominal pain and cramps, diarrhea with mucus and blood, what is the likely cause?
o: Rota virus (or adenovirus not sure which one)

r: Bloody stool plus a seizure points to Shigella; bloody stool alone among viral and protozoal options points to Campylobacter.

q: A child with chronic epigastric pain for the past year with retrosternal burning sensation. His mother complains of chronic abdominal pain. His stool has mucous and blood. How to CONFIRM the diagnosis:

q: Scenario about intussusception, examination confirmed child ill looking - i think they mentioned something about him being drowsy or confused- most appropriate management

n: Ill looking, drowsy child with intussusception: compiler considers him septic/peritonitic, so surgery rather than enema reduction.

q: Neonate, immediately after feeding starts drooling and bubbling from mouth and nose. Dx?

q: A 4 day old infant, parents complain of him vomiting green substance, irritable and uncomfortable something like that, what is the test with the most diagnostic value or most valuable test?

q: A 2 year old presented with Sudden jaundice and fever for 3 days after flu like illness Family hx of brother with severe neonatal jaundice treated with exchange Hb is 90 What medication is contraindicated?

q: A term infant delivered by cesarean section has respiratory distress but is not desaturating. fluid in lung fissures. What is the most important management?

q: A child older than 3 or 3 years old has constipation and nothing else

q: 3 y/o boy, presented with hard stool 3-4 times per week with fecal soiling, what is the most likely cause? (he was growing well with no other symptoms)

q: A child presented with weight loss, diarrhea, can't remember all signs, but they were traveling and drank from water, what's the management?

q: Child with inhalation of alkaline fluid 3 h ago presented with oropharyngeal pain, difficulty swallowing, Drooling Of Saliva. Vitally stable, O/E orohpharngeal redness, mild tenderness.

q: A Child with inhalation of alkaline fluid 3h ago presented with oropharyngeal pain, difficulty swallowing, Drooling Of Saliva. Vitally stable, O/E oropharyngeal redness, mild tenderness. What to do?

q: Child with non bloody diarrhea with megaloblastic anemia in lab + B12 low

q: 9y Child with enuresis in the bedtime 3 times a week. not get dry ever, and he doesn't has dysurea, or incontinence next step?

n: Mild jaundice on day 4 in a well-feeding baby: benign (breast milk) jaundice.

q: A 6-month-old infant presents to the Emergency Room with sudden apnea and color change. The mother gave history of recurrent vomiting and multiple chest infection. Inappropriate relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter

q: A 7 years old girl came to the ER after she ingested 20 tablets of iron 3 hours ago, she presented with abdominal pain ,nausea, and vomiting Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

q: A 10-year-old patient presents with a 3-day history of yellow discoloration of the sclera, anorexia and abdominal pain (see lab results). Test Result Normal Values Indirect bilirubin 140 <19 mol/L Total bilirubin 260 <20.5 mol/L Albumin 40 36-52 g/L Total Proteins 76 56-80 g/L Alanine aminotransferase 878 10-35 U/L Aspartate aminotransferase 1005 12-40 IU/L Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

r: Transaminases in the thousands put the answer in the hepatitis group, whatever the bilirubin split.

q: A child diagnosed with epilepsy and his mother is concerned to have another attack and she give antipyretic every four hour and we have jaundice this and right Upper quadrant pain on investigation AST and ALT is high what is the diagnose?

q: A four-year-old child presented to the pediatric ER with a four-day history of dark urine and jaundice preceded by diarrhea, nausea, and vomiting. q: A 4-year-old girl is brought to the clinic with a 4-day history of dark urine, jaundice, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. She attends a daycare center where several children have developed similar symptoms. Laboratory tests show ALT 600 IU/L. What is the most appropriate initial management?

r: High transaminases alone do not mean liver failure; check INR and mental status before thinking of transplant.
n: Printed answer B; embedded 'Full recall' inset is the same version with Answer: B. Rehydration and rest (hepatitis A outbreak, supportive care).

q: Child with 2 days of vomiting and diarrhea, now with jaundice and dark urine; attends daycare where others had similar episodes. AST 600, ALT 500. Next step?
k: Hepatitis A: fecal-oral, outbreaks in daycares and schools, self-limited; treatment is supportive.
r: Very high transaminases alone do not mean liver failure; it is the INR and mental status that decide escalation.
n: Hepatitis A outbreak in daycare: supportive care, rest and rehydration.

q: Same scenario of Wilson (without mention diagnosis).. need gold standard test :
k: Wilson disease diagnosis ladder: Clinical: liver disease, neuro/psychiatric signs (tremor, dysarthria, school decline), Kayser-Fleischer rings, Coombs-negative hemolysis; Initial: low serum ceruloplasmin, high 24 h urine copper, slit-lamp for KF rings; Low total serum copper but high free copper
r: "Initial / screening" = ceruloplasmin and 24 h urine copper; "gold standard" = liver biopsy with copper quantification.
n: Gold standard for diagnosing Wilson disease is liver biopsy with hepatic copper quantification; 24 h urine copper is a screening test. Inset versions agree (liver biopsy).

q: A child that is presenting with what looks like wilson disease and (jundice an neuro) asking about the gold standard for the dx?

q: 4 weeks old infant, uncircumcised had progressive jaundice for the last 4 days, poor eater, and fever started today so his mom brought him to the ER Vitally stable except T: 39 , Urine analysis: + nitrates, Leukocyts, and erythrocytes Sepsis workup: coli septicemia What's the diagnosis?

q: Child is scheduled for routine preschool vaccinations. He has been on long-term oral corticosteroid therapy for nephrotic syndrome. What is the most appropriate next step in this patient?
o: Remove pertussis component, give DT only
Avoid live vaccines, delay MMR and OPV
Replace OPV with iPV, give MMR and Tdap
k: Steroid immunosuppression stops live vaccines only; non-live vaccines (Tdap/DTaP, IPV) go ahead on time.
r: If asked what to do with the live vaccines (MMR, OPV, varicella), the answer is to defer them; if asked about Tdap, give it.
n: Same concept as the previous version: long duration and high dose steroids are contraindications for live vaccines; nephrotic syndrome is high dose steroid by definition, so you do not need to know the steroid dose. Compiler highlights both A and C in red as t

q: Case of pedia pt with nephrotic syndrome on high dose of prednisolone 4 weeks ago and came for preschool vaccine
o: delay all vaccines until he is off treatment
give dtap and mmr but no varicella or OPV
don't give Dtap but give varicella

r: Read the timing: if the stem says he STOPPED steroids 4 or more weeks ago, the answer flips to giving all vaccines.
n: Keep in mind: if he is off steroids for 4 weeks, then you can give ALL vaccines. Pre-school vaccines = 6 years = MOVD.

q: An unvaccinated child presents with symptoms of Haemophilus influenzae infection. What is the appropriate next step?
k: Epiglottitis (Hib, unvaccinated child): airway first, in a controlled setting, then cultures and antibiotics.
r: If PICU is not offered but "intubate in the OR" is, that is the best answer; ER intubation is the trap.
n: Epiglottitis-type scenario. Compiler (Alhomrani) answers B. Transfer to PICU; the Fay-Avengers group answers C. Intubate in the ER.

q: 3 years old boy came with fever, mu led sound, and drooling of saliva on exam he looks acutely ill, sit on his mother's lap with his neck extended. Fever 39 What is the next step?
k: Epiglottitis = airway emergency: intubate in the OR first, then antibiotics.
r: Barking cough with a non-toxic child flips the answer to dexamethasone (croup); drooling and toxicity mean airway in the OR.
n: Epiglottitis: secure the airway by intubation in the OR (OR emphasized in red).

q: 5 months old came with her mother her brother has (symptoms of rash not reacalling sorry) and she had only her birth vaccination (sure of this written like this) and the family are all living together what to give?
o: no need to give vaccine as the child less than 6 months
k: Measles post-exposure prophylaxis by age: Under 6 months: immunoglobulin (within 6 days); 6 to 12 months: MMR within 72 h, or immunoglobulin within 6 days; Over 12 months, non-immune: MMR within 72 h
r: Measles contact under 6 months = immunoglobulin; 6 months or older within 72 h = MMR.
n: Original recall had symptoms of measles according to the examinee. Measles exposure -> A. immunoglobulin (vaccine if 6 months). If VZV -> reassure till 12 months.

q: two years old child came with generalized tonic clonic seizure that lasted for three minute then stopped. Patient is drowsy but responsive fever 38 with runny nose and cough, family history of febrile seizure. no focal neurological sign or symptoms no neck stiffness. what's the most appropriate next step?
o: parent salary, reassurance and assessment for the source of fever
k: Simple febrile seizure = reassure + treat the fever source.
r: Neck stiffness or a focal sign flips the answer to LP or imaging; a stopped short generalized seizure does not.
n: Simple febrile seizure: reassurance and look for the source of fever; no EEG, CT or prophylactic antiepileptics.

q: A 7-year-old asymptomatic child has a father with active pulmonary TB. CXR is normal and TST is 14 mm. What is the next step?
o: Start treatment for latent TB infection
k: TB contact: TST/IGRA tells infection, symptoms + CXR tell active vs latent.
r: Add cough, weight loss or a hilar node on CXR and the answer flips to full anti TB treatment.
n: Positive TST with normal CXR in an asymptomatic contact = latent TB; treat LTBI.

q: Child with progressive neck swelling for 3 WEEKS, there were also reported subjective or low grade fever “can’t remember “ , multiple lymph node enlargement, hepatomegaly , and weight loss for 4 weeks Asking about investigation :
k: Lymphoma vs leukemia in a child with nodes and organomegaly.
r: Add pallor or petechiae to this stem and the answer flips to leukemia: blood film first, bone marrow to confirm.
n: This is lymphoma, not leukemia, so lymph node biopsy. If pallor or petechiae (signs of bone marrow failure) were present the diagnosis would be leukemia (anemia can occur in both but more in leukemia). Leukemia: initial = blood film, confirm = bone marrow exam

q: 2 months old with poor oral intake and vomiting brought by mother Lab : positive nitrate esterase What u will do
o: send them to hospital to initiate Iv antibiotics
k: Infant UTI: young age, ill appearance or inability to take orally = admit for IV antibiotics.
r: Vomiting with poor intake is an admission criterion on its own, even before considering the infant's age.

q: vaccinated baby 6 y Has injured rusty nail What is next step in addition to antibiotics
k: Tetanus-prone wound: always clean; booster depends on vaccine history.
r: The red word is 'vaccinated': it removes the booster and leaves wound irrigation as the step.
n: Printed answer Irrigation and cleaning; compiler flags 'vaccinated' in red (fully vaccinated child, so no tetanus booster needed; wound care is the step).

q: 9 months never immunized what to give
o: BCG Hep B OPV-1 Dtap-1 Measles
k: Catch-up rule: give every missed vaccine due for age at the same visit; never restart a series.
r: A fully immunised 9-month-old gets measles + MCV4 only; "never immunised" flips it to the full catch-up list with BCG and Hep B.
n: Rule of thumb: look for the longest option that contains HBV and BCG (catch-up for a never-immunized infant).

q: A 9-month-old healthy boy is brought to the clinic. The child has received no vaccinations since birth due to the mother's previous concerns. The mother now consents to vaccinate her child. Which of the following sets of vaccines should be administered at today's visit?
k: Unvaccinated child: give all missed, age-appropriate vaccines at one visit (simultaneous administration is safe).
r: Look for the option containing BCG + Hep B and the most other vaccines; an option without the birth vaccines is wrong for a never-immunised child.
n: Another version (Question 18) of the never-immunized 9-month-old recall; answer is the longest option containing BCG and HepB.

q: 2 years baby brought by his mother child to opd concern about high fever, difficulty in sollowing abnormal jerky movement last for 2 minutes,her brother complain from nasal discharge , and the same happen for her older sister Fever: 40

q: A 2-year-old girl started chemotherapy for ALL two days ago and now presents with a history of exposure to a child who has chickenpox, or varicella infection. The child is asymptomatic. What do we do?
k: Varicella exposure: who gets what.
r: Asymptomatic immunocompromised contact = passive immunity (VZIG); symptomatic = acyclovir; healthy contact = vaccine.

q: A child's mother had TB a year ago. Her kid now presents with signs and symptoms of TB; chest X-ray is positive. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

INH, rifampin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol for 2 months, then continue INH and rifampin for 4 months.

r: Positive chest X-ray = active disease = four drugs; normal chest X-ray with positive test = latent = single or dual-drug prophylaxis.
n: Recaller: 100% sure of the choices.

q: An 18-month-old child came for routine vaccination. Mother mentions he had Kawasaki disease and was managed with IVIG 2 months ago. Which of the following vaccines is safe to administer at this visit?
k: Passive antibodies (IVIG, blood products) interfere with LIVE injected vaccines, not inactivated ones.
r: Recent IVIG = postpone live vaccines; killed vaccines continue on schedule.
n: Avoid live vaccines in those receiving IVIG.

q: A 5-year-old child will receive pre-school vaccine. What do you have to know before giving the vaccine?

q: A child with ALL received chemotherapy 2 days ago. She had contact with someone infected with chickenpox. What is the best next step?
k: Varicella exposure in an immunocompromised child.
r: Exposure only = immunoglobulin; actual rash = IV acyclovir.
n: Compiler: if the child developed the disease give IV acyclovir (oral if IV unavailable); if not developed (post-exposure only), give varicella immunoglobulin. This scenario did not develop the disease, so D.

q: A 3-month-old boy presented to the Emergency Room with history paroxysmal episodes of cough followed by whoopi sounds at the end of each episode. It is associated with perioral cyanosis and posttussive vomiting. There is no history of diarrhea. This illness has been preceded by runny nose a few days ago. History revealed he did not receive his 2-month vaccine yet. On examination, the child looks unwell and tachypneic. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Paroxysmal cough in a young infant: the extra features decide.
r: Whoop + coryza + missed vaccine = pertussis; diagnose by nasopharyngeal PCR or culture and treat patient and contacts with a macrolide.
n: Whoop, coryzal prodrome and unvaccinated infant -> pertussis. Compiler rule for this cluster: not vaccinated -> pertussis; diarrhea present -> adenovirus; staccato cough and conjunctivitis present -> Chlamydia. Other versions of this recall in this deck: SWR-0

q: A 3-month-old boy presented to the Emergency Room with history paroxysmal episodes of cough associated with an inspiratory whoop and possessive emesis. It is associated with fever, conjunctival redness and diarrhea. His immunization is up to date. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Paroxysmal cough in a young infant: the extra features decide.
r: A whoop does not always mean pertussis: fever + conjunctivitis + diarrhea in a vaccinated infant = adenovirus.
n: Despite the whoop, fever with conjunctivitis and diarrhea in a vaccinated infant -> adenovirus. Compiler rule for this cluster: not vaccinated -> pertussis; diarrhea present -> adenovirus; staccato cough and conjunctivitis present -> Chlamydia.

q: Kid with chills and fever just returned from Africa. Blood culture confirms the diagnosis (diagnosis not stated). Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

r: "Blood film" = malaria; "blood culture" = bacteremia (typhoid): one word flips the answer.

q: Paediatric after flu 2 days he develop papules in face and trunk and limps no lymphadinopathy and other symptoms
k: Viral exanthems by pattern: Measles: high fever, cough, coryza, conjunctivitis, Koplik spots, face to body confluent rash, may desquamate; Rubella: low fever, posterior auricular/occipital nodes, discrete pink rash fades in about 3 days, no desquamation; Roseola (HHV 6/7): high fever, rash appears a
r: Lymph nodes behind the ear tip the face to trunk rash to rubella; their absence is what keys this card to measles.
n: Compiler picks Measles just because the stem says no lymphadenopathy, but notes other features are needed to be sure. Option D refers to fifth disease (parvovirus): rash typically on cheeks plus joint pains. Explanation page: both rubella and measles have rash

q: I think 8 years Child with runny nose and general symptoms had maculopapular rash from face to trunk but supsided after 3rd day with no squamation and post auricular involvement
k: Measles vs rubella (both cephalocaudal): Fever: measles high; rubella low grade; Prodrome: measles cough, coryza, conjunctivitis plus Koplik spots; rubella mild; Nodes: rubella posterior auricular and suboccipital
r: Desquamation = measles; a rash gone by day 3 without peeling = rubella.

q: A Child with Kawasaki disease, already received IVIG and IV aspirin, his symptoms are still not improving, what will you do next ?
k: Refractory Kawasaki (persistent or recurrent fever 36 hours or more after IVIG): Initial: IVIG single infusion plus aspirin, ideally within 10 days of illness; No carditis: 1) second dose IVIG, 2) infliximab or tapering oral prednisolone, 3) pulse IV methylprednisolone; Carditis/coronary involvement
r: No carditis = second IVIG; carditis present = infliximab or oral steroid instead.
n: Textbook excerpt shown: up to 10% of KD children fail to respond to IVIG; most respond to retreatment with IVIG. Corticosteroids or infliximab are used less frequently, with a role if active carditis is apparent or for persistent fever after two doses of IVIG.

q: Child with Kawasaki and received aspirin but still very sick with cardiac involvement in ECHO report. What to give?
k: Refractory Kawasaki (persistent or recurrent fever 36 hours or more after IVIG): Initial: IVIG single infusion plus aspirin, ideally within 10 days of illness; No carditis: 1) second dose IVIG, 2) infliximab or tapering oral prednisolone, 3) pulse IV methylprednisolone; Carditis/coronary involvement
r: If IVIG has not yet been given at all, IVIG is the answer; this card has no IVIG option, and carditis pushes to steroids.
n: Printed answer B; should ideally be oral not IV steroid but it is the best option. Oral steroid and infliximab are better than IV steroid if present and are both first line for carditis. Refractory Kawasaki management (choose whichever present in order): cardi

q: 4 years old boy is diagnosed with Kawasaki disease (diagnosis is mentioned) and was treated by IVIG and high-dose aspirin and after 3 days child was not responding. His symptoms: Fever and cardiac symptoms On echocardiogram left coronary artery dilation. What is the appropriate initial treatment regimen? (What is most appropriate treatment in this case?)
k: Refractory Kawasaki (persistent or recurrent fever 36 hours or more after IVIG): Initial: IVIG single infusion plus aspirin, ideally within 10 days of illness; No carditis: 1) second dose IVIG, 2) infliximab or tapering oral prednisolone, 3) pulse IV methylprednisolone; Carditis/coronary involvement
r: Another recall of this scenario is keyed to a second IVIG dose; with coronary involvement and no IVIG option, steroids are the answer.
n: Answer by exclusion since all other options are nonsense. Carditis (if present) should be treated with oral steroid or infliximab.

q: A 7-year-old patient presents with abnormal jerky movements, sore throat, and fever. His brother and sister had similar symptoms with fever. What is the most appropriate action?

Perform throat culture and start penicillin
Obtain brain imaging and lumbar puncture

r: Concurrent fever and sore throat with jerks = febrile illness; chorea that starts weeks AFTER the sore throat = rheumatic fever.

q: two years old child came with generalized tonic clonic seizure that lasted for three minute then stopped. Patient is drowsy but responsive fever 38° with runny nose and cough, no family history of febrile seizure. no focal neurological sign or symptoms no neck stiffness. what’s the most appropriate next step?

q: Child with cold symptoms, high fever and runny nose and cough. Was discharged with conservative management. Came back to the ER with fever 38.5. Examination showed erythamatous pharynx. What is most concerning?

q: Child came from Africa (Region Not Specified , Just Africa) with his family, complaining of cyclic fever, fatigue and sweating, the diagnosis is confirmed by blood film (Diagnosis Not Mentioned, Just "Diagnosis Confirmed") what is the management?

q: A 7-year-old child was bitten and scratched by a bat. Which of the following conditions can result from such an exposure?

n: Presented by the compiler as 'See this recall' after an earlier answer 'A. Rabies'; handwritten pen mark A.

q: Pediatric pt with bronchiolitis treated conservatively with hydration and suction then develop fever 38 and loss of appetite and red pharynx. What will require further investigations?

r: Low grade fever and red throat are expected in bronchiolitis; a high fever that persists is the clue to look for a bacterial complication.

q: A child has abdominal cramps, diarrhea, and a large amount of foul-smelling green stool. Which of the following is the most likely cause?

q: Boy with fever and sore throat in examination : congested throat no follicular, tender lymph node bilateral and around 0.5 or 1.5 the throat culture swab was positive what of the following decrease the complications?

n: Positive strep throat culture: a full 10-day course of penicillin V prevents complications such as rheumatic fever.

q: Suspected immune issue patient is 3 month referred to immunologist what to stop for now until they investigate him?

q: A 1-year-old boy is brought to the clinic for failure to thrive, recurrent oral thrush and hepatosplenomegaly. He had a brother who died at the age of 3 years with severe infection and septic shock. Which of the following vaccines must be avoided until a diagnosis is made?

q: 1-year-old child received the MMR (measles, mumps, rubella) vaccine three days ago. The child now presents with a low-grade fever and a generalized maculopapular rash. There are no other significant symptoms, and the child appears well overall. What is the most likely explanation for these symptoms?

Early onset of measles due to vaccine failure
k: Live vaccine reaction timeline.

n: Alharshan and Fay-Avengers: B. Vaccine-related rash and fever after MMR occurs 1-2 weeks after vaccination; a rash before that period is most likely another viral infection unrelated to the vaccine.

q: A 6-month-old girl is brought for routine vaccination. Her mother reports that after the previous vaccination she developed fever with local redness and swelling. What modification, if any, should be made to the vaccination schedule?

n: Fever and local redness/swelling are common side effects of DTaP given at 2 and 4 months and are not contraindications.

q: 5 year old child presented with 2 days history of fever 38.9 with confusion and drowsiness. the mother also described occasional vomiting and one seizure what is the most important investigation to be done?

q: A 1-year-old infant presents to Vaccina9on Clinic with normal exam and growth What are the recommended vaccines according according to Saudi national program?

q: the child was on leukemia treatment and then was exposed to child with chickenpox. the child is asymptomatic?

q: Child 6 year old fully vaccinated injured or cut by rusty nail what to give?
k: Tetanus-prone wound in a fully vaccinated child: Last dose under 5 years ago: wound care only (irrigation); Last dose more than 5 years ago: booster (DTaP under 7 years, Tdap/Td at 7 and older); Unknown or incomplete history: vaccine plus TIG

r: Symptoms plus consolidation = active disease = 4 drugs; the word "latent" or a normal CXR = 1 or 2 drugs.
n: Printed answer D (active TB: RIPE 2 months then INH + rifampin 4 months); embedded inset of same version also answers D. Recaller: Inset recaller: 100% sure of the choices.

Do Interferon Gamma Release Assay (IGRA) and start him on 4 TB medication

q: A mother brings her 2-year-old child to the clinic because she is concerned about TB infection. q: Conjunctivitis in Two Siblings A 5-year-old child presents with bilateral conjunctival redness, fever, headache, and sore throat. Examination reveals bilateral conjunctivitis and pharyngeal inflammation. His 2-year-old brother developed similar symptoms two days earlier. What is the most likely causative organism?
k: Conjunctivitis plus pharyngitis plus fever = adenovirus (pharyngoconjunctival fever).
r: Conjunctivitis argues AGAINST strep pharyngitis; a sick sibling argues against Kawasaki.
n: Pharyngoconjunctival fever = adenovirus. GAS pharyngitis does not cause conjunctivitis; viral pharyngitis can also cause exudate/petechiae, so assess the full picture, not only Centor features.

q: 10 year old boy with frontal headache, fever, and stuffed nose. 2 days prior he had runny nose and sore throat. On examination, he had left cheek tenderness. What is the next best management?
k: Acute bacterial sinusitis in children is diagnosed clinically by one of three patterns.
r: Imaging is never the answer for uncomplicated sinusitis; complications (orbital swelling, neuro signs) call for CT.
n: Embedded older lookalike of the 'frontal tenderness what next?' recall. URTI symptoms followed by fever, headache and sinus (cheek) tenderness indicate acute bacterial sinusitis (severe onset with fever), so treat with amoxicillin-clavulanate for 10 days; imag

q: An 8-year-old boy presented to the emergency department with fever, headache and sore throat for 2 days. On examination, there was enlarged tonsils with exudate and pharyngeal petechiae. He had enlargement of anterior and posterior cervical and submandibular lymph nodes, spleen is palpable 3cm below the costal margin. Blood film shows atypical lymphocytes. What is the diagnosis?
k: Exudate plus petechiae fits both strep and EBV; splenomegaly, posterior nodes or atypical lymphocytes settle it as EBV.
r: Do not diagnose strep on exudate alone; the spleen and the blood film decide.
n: Embedded inset (same version, option C Celiac) answers A. Compiler: viral pharyngitis can cause exudate/petechiae like bacterial; assess full picture, not only Centor. Atypical lymphocytes, splenomegaly and/or raised ALT/AST favour mononucleosis.

q: A child with fever (39) and Sore throat with yellow exudate and petechiae and the hard palate. Negative antigen test. What's the management
k: Suspected GAS pharyngitis in a child: RADT first; negative RADT, confirm with throat culture.
r: Not done RADT: do RADT. RADT negative in a child: culture. Only treat after a positive test.
n: In a child with suspected strep pharyngitis: if RADT not done, do it; if RADT done and negative, send throat culture.

q: 10 years old with high grade fever , ant and post LN enlargement with tonsillitis and purelent exudate, fast strep is negative ?
k: Child with suspected strep: rapid antigen test; if negative, throat culture; treat only when positive.
r: In children a negative rapid strep test is not the end; culture it before deciding on antibiotics.
n: Embedded 20 October recall. Negative rapid strep test in a child should be followed by throat culture.

q: 2 years old presented with brassy cough and low grade fever what is the management
k: Croup = barking cough, inspiratory stridor, low-grade fever after a URTI; caused by parainfluenza.
r: Every croup gets dexamethasone; epinephrine is only added when there is stridor at rest.
n: Croup: dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg.

q: A 3 year old male patient who had fever, sore throat and malaise for 3 days presents to the ER with congested mouth, difficulty swallowing, acutely ill, looking unwell, setting on mothers lap with his neck extended, which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
k: Epiglottitis = airway first, in a controlled setting.
r: Croup gets racemic epinephrine; epiglottitis gets the operating room.
n: Epiglottitis: intubate in a controlled environment (OR or PICU), not the ER.

q: Child came to ER before 12hours with fever and SOB, yesterday he had sore throat and dysphasia, on exam he looks toxic immobile in a chair opens his mouth with drooling of saliva, tachycardic tackypnic and fever 40 what's the next step?
k: Compiler's rule for this topic: Intubate in the OR > Admit to the PICU.
r: No OR in the options: PICU, not intubation in the ER.
n: Similar recall (by Nai) of the epiglottitis question with no answer printed for it. The compiler's updated answer for the topic is 'Intubate in the OR > Admit to the PICU'; with no OR option here, PICU (controlled airway setting in OR/ICU per the textbook exce

q: A 4-year-old child presents with high fever, severe sore throat, difficulty swallowing, and excessive drooling of saliva. The child appears distressed and has inspiratory stridor. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Examine the throat using a tongue depressor
Arrange urgent airway management and transfer to PICU
k: Drooling plus stridor plus high fever = epiglottitis: airway first, then cultures and IV antibiotics.
r: Any option that touches the throat before the airway is secured is wrong in epiglottitis.
n: Note on slide: airway stabilization by an experienced team must take priority over transfer.

q: A 3-year-old unimmunized child is brought to the Emergency Department in severe respiratory distress. His parents report a 12-hour history of high-grade fever, sore throat, and difficulty swallowing. On examination, the child looks toxic, is sitting upright, leaning forward with his hands on his knees, and is drooling saliva with his mouth open. His temperature is 39.8oC. Which of the following is the most likely causative organism?
k: Upper airway infections in children: Croup: parainfluenza, barking cough, steeple sign, low-grade fever; Epiglottitis: Hib (unimmunized), abrupt, toxic, drooling, tripod, thumb sign; Bacterial tracheitis: S. aureus, viral prodrome then toxic, purulent secretions
r: 'Unimmunized' plus drooling and tripod position = Hib epiglottitis; the same picture after a croup prodrome in a vaccinated child = S. aureus tracheitis.
n: Slide titled (epiglottitis organism); embedded 21-23 July recall. Answer tagged (MG). Unimmunized child with epiglottitis: Hib.

q: 5-year-old child presents with a prolonged history of fever (37.9C) for 6 weeks, associated with joint pain, a salmon-colored rash predominantly over the trunk, hepatomegaly, and bilateral wrist swelling. The rash appears during fever episodes and disappears when the fever subsides. What is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Prolonged fever + evanescent salmon rash with fever spikes + arthritis = systemic JIA.
r: Rash that appears with the fever and disappears with it = systemic JIA; a 6-week fever rules out Kawasaki on duration alone.
n: Printed answer B. Jia (systemic JIA). Embedded 'Better recall' inset gives fuller options. 19 October update ↻ Printed again later in this 19 October file (p.755) with the same answer; author's note there: Printed answer B: systemic onset JIA (Still disease) w

q: A 2-year-old child presented to the clinic with high-fever of 5-day duration. Examination showed ill child, with mild conjunctivitis, a rash, cervical lymphadenopathy and cracked red lips (see lab results), Blood pressure 110/70 mmHg Heart rate 120 /min Respiratory rate 24 /min Temperature 39.2 C Test Result Normal Values RBC 5 4.8-7.1 x 1012/L (Newborn) 4.6-4.8 x 1012/L (Child) Hb 115 165-195 g/L (Newborn) 112-165 g/L (Child) Platelets count 550 150-400 x 109/L ESR 125 2-10 mm/h WBC 18 4.5-13.5 x 109/L (2-10 years) 4.5-11.1 x 109/L (11 years-older adult) C-reactive peptide 135 0-0.5 mg/dl Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Kawasaki: fever ≥5 days + 4 of 5 principal features (CRASH).
r: Thrombocytosis and very high ESR/CRP in a febrile toddler with mucocutaneous signs favour Kawasaki over viral exanthems.
n: Printed answer D (Kawasaki: fever 5 days with conjunctivitis, rash, cervical LAP, cracked lips, thrombocytosis). 19 October update Other version of this recall in 19 October: OCT-2314 → A. Aspirin. 20 October update Other version of this recall in 20 October:

q: A 2-year-old child presented to the clinic with high-fever of 5-day duration. Examination showed ill child with mild conjunctivitis, a rash, cervical lymphadenopathy, and cracked red lips (see lab results), Blood pressure 110/70 mmHg Heart rate 115 /min Respiratory rate 22 /min Temperature 39.5 C Test Result Normal Values C-reactive peptide 135 0-0.5 mg/di RBC 4 4.8-7.1 x 1012/L (Newborn) 4.6-4.8 x 1012/L (Child) Hb 115 165-195 g/L (Newborn) 112-165 g/L (Child) Platelets count 550 150-400 x 109/L ESR 125 2-10 mm/h WBC 15 4.5-13.5 x 109/L. (2-10 years) 4.5-11.1 x 109/L. (11 years-older adult) Which of the following is the best management?
k: Kawasaki disease: fever 5 days or more plus 4 of 5 principal features.
r: If IVIG is listed, IVIG is the best answer; if it is missing, choose aspirin.
n: Embedded inset: same Kawasaki vignette but asks for management; inset prints 'Answer: A' (aspirin, with IVIG not among options). Other versions of this recall in this deck: OCT-0703 → D. Kawasaki disease Other version of this recall earlier in October: OCT-070

q: 5-year-old with high fever for 6 days (38 C), cracked red lips, rash, cervical lymphadenopathy and red eyes. Diagnosis?
k: Kawasaki disease = fever for 5 days or more plus at least 4 of 5 principal features: Bilateral non-exudative conjunctival injection; Oral changes: red cracked lips, strawberry tongue, red pharynx; Polymorphous rash
r: Fever of 5 days or more with non-purulent red eyes and cracked lips = Kawasaki; purulent eye discharge, exudative tonsils or tick exposure point elsewhere.
n: Fever 5 days or more plus mucosal changes, rash, cervical lymphadenopathy, conjunctivitis: Kawasaki disease. Other versions of this recall in this deck: OCT-1391 → B. Kawasaki disease October By Similar update Other version of this recall in 21 October: OCT-76

q: Year old child with high fever i think (38) for 6 days, cracked red lips, rash, cervical lymphadenopathy, red eyes What is the diagnosis?
k: Kawasaki disease = fever for 5 days or more plus at least 4 of 5 principal features: Bilateral non-exudative conjunctival injection; Oral changes: red cracked lips, strawberry tongue, red pharynx; Polymorphous rash
r: Duration of fever (5 days or more) is the criterion, not the height of the temperature; with 4 features the diagnosis stands.
n: Embedded older recall (17 September). Printed B. Recaller: Recaller unsure of temperature ('i think (38)'). Other versions of this recall in this deck: OCT-1390 → B. Kawasaki disease October By Similar update Other version of this recall in 21 October: OCT-760

q: A child presents with conjunctival injection, dry cracked lips, cervical lymphadenopathy and a skin rash. What is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Kawasaki = fever 5 days or more + 4 of CREAM: C: conjunctivitis (bilateral, non exudative); R: rash (polymorphous); E: extremity changes (edema, erythema, later desquamation)
r: Exudative conjunctivitis or exudative tonsillitis points away from Kawasaki toward adenovirus or strep.
n: Printed answer A) Kawasaki disease [Complete]; compiler answer line A. Kawasaki disease. Source tag [q08887 Pediatrics Paediatric infectious disease]. Only three options printed. Other version of this recall earlier in October: OCT-0703 → D. Kawasaki disease.

q: Child with a rash that started in the jaw then spread to the trunk for three days before disappearing. Findings include postauricular and suboccipital lymphadenopathy with no desquamation.
k: Rubella = mild illness, 3-day cephalocaudal rash, posterior (postauricular, suboccipital) nodes.
r: Postauricular and suboccipital nodes point to rubella; Koplik spots and the 3 Cs point to measles.

q: Suspected rheumatic fever , whats the most echo finding ?
k: Acute rheumatic fever = regurgitation; chronic rheumatic heart disease = stenosis.
r: "Acute" or "suspected rheumatic fever" = MR; "long-standing rheumatic heart disease" in an adult = MS.
n: Acute rheumatic fever: mitral regurgitation is the most common echo finding. Other versions of this recall in this deck: OCT-0154 → B. Mitral regurgitation

q: A patient presents with multiple swollen joints and multiple subcutaneous nodules. Acute rheumatic fever is suspected. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
k: ARF management: Eradicate strep: single IM benzathine penicillin (or 10 days oral penicillin/amoxicillin); Arthritis and mild carditis: high-dose aspirin (NSAID alternatives); Moderate to severe carditis: add corticosteroids
r: 'Management' of active ARF = aspirin; 'prevent recurrence' = monthly benzathine penicillin.
n: Other versions of this recall in this deck: OCT-8022 → A. High dose acetylsalicylic acid; OCT-8022 → A. High dose acetylsalicylic acid; OCT-8022 → A. High dose acetylsalicylic acid Printed again later in this file (p.4992). Printed again later in this file (p.

q: Child with fever, subcutaneous nodule and arthralgia; acute rheumatic fever suspected. Most appropriate next step?
k: ARF treatment by component: Arthritis / arthralgia, mild carditis: high-dose aspirin (or NSAID); Severe carditis with heart failure: corticosteroids + diuretics; Strep eradication: oral penicillin or single IM benzathine penicillin
r: Steroids only if severe carditis; joints and mild disease get aspirin.
n: Printed answer B (high-dose aspirin for ARF arthritis). Options were printed unlettered and lettered by position. Slide cites p. 172.

q: Persistent fever with mucocutaneous findings including a strawberry tongue and generalized rash. If the intended diagnosis is Kawasaki disease, what is the initial treatment?
k: Kawasaki: fever ≥5 days + 4 of 5 principal features → IVIG + aspirin.
r: Infliximab, cyclosporine and repeat IVIG are for IVIG-resistant Kawasaki; the standard first regimen is IVIG plus aspirin (steroids are added up front only in high-risk cases).
n: Embedded inset of the same version also answers B.

q: A patient with known Kawasaki disease was started on IVIG and high-dose aspirin. After 3 days, the patient continues to have persistent fever and a maculopapular rash, with no improvement. Echocardiography shows right coronary artery dilation. Which medication should be added?
k: Kawasaki treatment ladder: Initial: IVIG single infusion plus aspirin (higher dose in acute phase); Afebrile: switch to low-dose aspirin until echo is normal (or long term if aneurysms); IVIG resistance (fever persisting over 36 hours after IVIG): second IVIG dose or corticosteroids
r: If 'second dose of IVIG' appears among the options it competes with steroids; here, with no repeat IVIG listed and coronary involvement, methylprednisolone is the add-on.
n: Embedded inset of the same version prints Answer: A. IV methylprednisolone (IVIG resistant Kawasaki with coronary involvement). Printed again later in this file (p.4998).

q: A child has a persistent infection despite several days of treatment. Which finding is most concerning?
k: Treatment failure in a child with infection: persistent fever after 48 to 72 hours of appropriate antibiotics is the trigger to re-evaluate.
r: Residual cough after treatment is normal; residual fever is not.
n: Embedded 15 September inset of the same version also answers B. Persistent fever.

q: Child with fever, cough, rash and (koplik spots) How to manage?
k: Measles = supportive care + vitamin A.
r: Vaccine is for the contact, vitamin A and supportive care are for the patient.

q: Pediatric came with headache runny nose, continues fever for 2 days and generelized bodyache, mild tonsils erythema with no exudative
k: Sore throat: viral vs strep.
r: Runny nose in a sore throat stem is the clue that it is viral.

q: 8 years old child presented to emergency department with high grade fever , arthralgia, myalgia and Erythmatous Rash , no abdominal pain , history of Mosquito bites hg 12.9 Plt 160 What is appropriate management
o: Supportive treatment with good oral hydration
k: Dengue triage by warning signs.
r: No abdominal pain and normal platelets means no warning signs, so oral fluids, not IV.
n: Dengue without warning signs: supportive with oral hydration. Embedded 19-20 September inset of the same version gives the same answer.

q: 11-Child with high grade fever, arthralgia , erythematous rash with hx of mosquito multiple bite Vitals : normal Bp (i'm sure)
o: Abx ( i think was impirical abx)
k: Suspected dengue: fluids and paracetamol, no NSAIDs, watch for warning signs.
r: Normal blood pressure is the clue against aggressive IV fluids; the fever drug in dengue is paracetamol, not ibuprofen.

q: Kid with chills and fever just returned from Africa. Blood film confirms the diagnosis (diagnosis not stated). Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
k: Traveller from an endemic area + fever and chills + blood film positive = malaria.
r: The test named decides the drug: blood FILM = malaria (antimalarial); blood CULTURE = bacterial (ceftriaxone).
n: Printed answer A. Chloroquine (malaria). Compiler: it was blood FILM, not culture; only if the recall really said culture would the answer be Ceftriaxone by exclusion. Other versions of this recall in this deck: OCT-1746 → A. Chloroquine 19 October update ↻ Pr

q: Pediatric pt w low grade fever, lower left limb redness swelling and increasing in size No hx of trauma or bite What is the most apro initial management
k: Cellulitis severity decides the route.
r: Fever plus an expanding red area is the switch from oral to IV antibiotics.
n: Printed answer B. Iv abx (cellulitis with fever -> IV antibiotics per IDSA).

q: -10 years old presented with tender, warmth, and red swelling on the left leg, Then it increased gradually. No history of trauma or insect bite (only low grade fever) otherwise normal, What is the initial step in management?
k: Cellulitis: purulent vs nonpurulent, then mild vs moderate vs severe.
r: Same leg, no fever = oral antibiotics; add even a low-grade fever = IV.
n: IV antibiotic (IDSA guidelines and Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics). IDSA: fever (T >38, considered low grade fever) is an indication for IV antibiotics in nonpurulent SSTI (moderate infection with systemic signs). IDSA guidelines apply to both adults and pediat

q: Q5. A 6-year-old boy presents with a low-grade fever and progressively increasing swelling over the affected area. There is no history of trauma or insect bite. On examination, there is localized erythema, warmth, swelling, and tenderness of the surrounding soft tissue. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
k: Cellulitis severity decides the route.
r: The phrase "low-grade fever" is the trap: any fever with cellulitis counts as a systemic sign and means IV antibiotics on this exam.
n: Printed answer A. Compiler rule: 'Fever = IV (EVEN If LOW Grade)'; cellulitis with systemic features (fever) gets IV antibiotics. 'Low-grade fever' highlighted in red.

q: Child had injury, penetrating the knee. Started on oral antibiotics. Came back to hospital with worsening fever and pain only, what is the most likely cause of worsening symptoms:
k: Infection worsening despite appropriate antibiotics = look for a collection that needs drainage.
r: Antibiotics do not sterilize pus; persistent fever and pain on treatment means find and drain the collection.
n: Worsening despite antibiotics after penetrating injury suggests abscess formation. October By Similar update The same question reappears in 15-18 October as OCT-8106 → no answer marked.

q: 5 year old patient presented with pain in the shaft of his lower leg. Had h/o penetrating injury. Has subjective fever and pain in the lower limb. Redness and swelling. Started on parenteral antibiotics. After few days still no improvement and pain increased. What is the cause of no improvement?
k: Cellulitis or pyelonephritis not responding to empirical antibiotics: First: rule out anatomical complication (abscess, osteomyelitis, obstruction for pyelonephritis); Then: resistant organism; IV therapy in hospital makes non-compliance very unlikely
r: Inpatient IV antibiotics remove compliance from the list; failing therapy then means pus first, resistance second.
n: Embedded inset: cellulitis/pyelonephritis not responding to empirical management -> R/O anatomical complications (abscess, osteomyelitis); if abscess is ruled out, the most likely cause is resistance.

q: Pedia patient with non-Hodgkin lymphoma was started on chemotherapy and has completed four cycles. One week after completing chemotherapy, he developed a fever and presented to the emergency department. On physical examination, there was no obvious source of infection. Laboratory investigations showed LOW WBC (3.0 i think) and his neutrophil count was 70% (within the normal range, at the upper end of the normal range). What is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: Start IV antibiotics and admit the patient to the hospital.
Obtain blood cultures and "WAIT" for antibiotic sensitivity testing.
k: Febrile neutropenia = medical emergency.
r: The word "WAIT" is the trap: cultures yes, but never hold antibiotics for results in neutropenic fever.
n: Treat as febrile neutropenia (functional neutropenia in hematologic malignancy despite a normal neutrophil count). In neutropenic fever, culture BEFORE antibiotics, then IMMEDIATE empiric antibiotics; this version says WAIT for sensitivity, so A (admit, IV ant

q: A 20-day-old infant presents with fever and decreased activity. Physical examination ^shows no focus on infection^.( it was written like this) BP: 60/42 mmHg Temperature: 38.2°C RR: 35/min HR: 120/min (This all the stem and 100% accurate the vitals) What is the most appropriate management?
o: Discharge and follow up after 2 weeks
Administer IV antibiotics after obtaining blood, urine, and CSF cultures
Tell the mother to return if the infant does not tolerate oral intake
Admit for fever observation ( i think they said for 24 h not sure)
k: Fever ≥38 C under 28 days = admit, full septic screen including LP, IV antibiotics.
r: Obtain cultures before the first dose, but never let waiting for results delay antibiotics.
n: Printed answer B: febrile neonate (under 28 days) needs full sepsis workup (blood, urine, CSF cultures) then IV antibiotics. Recaller: Recaller says the stem and vitals are 100% accurate; unsure whether option D said 24 h.

q: 7Y girl came with abdominal pain , Fever and vomiting. She looks unwell In Examination there is suprpubic tenderness , -ve rebound tenderness T: 39 Urin dipstick: Wbc: +ve Nitrate: +ve Rbc: +ve (+3) What is the most appropriate next step in management ?
k: Pediatric febrile UTI: route depends on how sick the child is.
r: "Looks unwell" plus vomiting is the phrase that turns oral treatment into IV.
n: Printed answer A: febrile UTI in an unwell, vomiting child is treated with IV antibiotics. Recaller: Arabic note from recaller: many compiled questions in the exam, not new, but details may differ.

q: Pediatric with slight fever leg warmth and redness and swelling
k: Cellulitis treatment depends on severity: well and localized = oral; systemic signs or high risk = IV.
r: "Slight fever" is the word that pushes the key from oral to IV; an afebrile well child with the same leg goes home on oral antibiotics.

q: 2month of poor feeding, vomiting and lethargy. Urine analysis + Nitrate. What's the management ?
o: Refer to hospital for Iv antibiotic
k: Febrile or ill UTI in a young infant: admit and give IV antibiotics.
r: Any one of age below 3 months, vomiting or toxic look switches the answer from oral to IV.
n: Age below 3 months OR vomiting OR toxic appearance, any one is an indication for IV antibiotics in UTI. Recaller: Only 3 options recalled.

q: A 2-month-child presents with fever, vomiting, poor feeding and lethargy, urine dipstick shows positive leukocytes esterase and nitrates. What the most initial management?
o: Do chest x-ray to rule out pneumonia
Refer to the hospital for intravenous antibiotic
k: Young or toxic infant with UTI: hospital and IV antibiotics.
r: Contrast with a well, feeding 4 month old with a UTI: that child gets oral antibiotics.
n: Embedded earlier version. Age below 3 months OR vomiting OR toxic appearance, any is an indication for IV antibiotics.

q: 4-Pediatric patient came with leg swelling, fever and expanding swelling → case of cellulitis. What to give?
k: Cellulitis: mild = oral, systemic signs = IV, toxic or rapidly necrotizing = surgery.
r: Fever is the systemic sign that moves cellulitis from oral to IV antibiotics.
n: Printed answer IV antibiotics: febrile child with expanding cellulitis gets IV antibiotics.

q: A 7-year-old girl presents with fever, flank pain, vomiting and urinary symptoms. Urinalysis shows pyuria and urine culture is positive. What is the most appropriate treatment?
k: Pediatric UTI route: oral if well and tolerating orals; IV if toxic, vomiting or very young.
r: Same picture without vomiting in a well looking child flips the answer to oral antibiotics.
n: Printed answer C. IV antibiotics: pyelonephritis with vomiting needs IV antibiotics. Other versions of this recall in this deck: OCT-8130 → B. IV Ab

q: 3 cases of UTI 10 years old Have dysurea+ fever flank pain + looking unwell What's ttt
k: In pediatric UTI the general appearance decides the route.
r: Flank pain alone does not force IV; it is the toxic look (or vomiting) that does.
n: Printed answer A. IV antibiotic. Compiler: Unwell (Toxic) then IV.

k: Pediatric UTI treatment route: Well, tolerating orally: oral antibiotics (amoxicillin if susceptible, amoxicillin clavulanate, cefixime, cephalexin, TMP SMX); Toxic, vomiting, dehydrated or young infant (under about 2 to 3 months): admit for IV antibiotics; Always send a urine culture before startin

q: A 13-month-old child presents to the ER with fever and painful micturition. What medication will you give?
k: Pediatric UTI: route depends on how sick the child is, not on fever alone.

n: Embedded inset: older version (13-month-old, oral ciprofloxacin option). Printed answer A. Compiler: unless child has vomiting or toxic appearance, I am not choosing IV antibiotics. October By Similar update

q: A 7-month-old infant presents with signs of UTI, Stable not dehydrated. Alert and feeding. Urinalysis : + Nitrite, +leukocytes. Fever: 39.1 What's the appropriate empirical antibiotic to be started?
k: Pediatric UTI: oral if well and tolerating orals, IV if young infant, toxic or vomiting.
r: High fever alone does not mandate IV antibiotics; the switch to IV is toxicity, vomiting/oral intolerance or very young age (under about 2 months).
n: Embedded inset: 2nd recall from 17 July compilation; well, non-dehydrated infant with UTI can be treated with oral antibiotic.
