r: Spasms in an infant who has STOPPED smiling or interacting = West syndrome; do not confuse with colic or reflux (Sandifer posturing).
n: Infantile spasms (West syndrome) with developmental regression; EEG shows hypsarrhythmia (chaotic multifocal spikes and slow waves). Compiler notes the word 'Hypsarrhythmia' was NOT written in the exam option.

q: Pediatric with sever headech, and 3 times vomiting, sensety to light and stays in dark room( gave multiple symptoms suggesting migraine) Whats more worrisome something like that?
o: Sever headache waking her from sleep
k: Pediatric headache red flags point to a secondary cause and need imaging.
r: Migraine is relieved by sleep; a headache that wakes the child from sleep is a red flag.
n: No commentary; printed answer: headache waking from sleep is the red flag.

q: Mother brought her 2 month old baby bc of squinting (not mentioned persistent or not) What is the most appropriate ASESSMENT?
k: Infant squint: check red reflex first; refer if abnormal reflex, constant squint, or squint after 4 months.
r: Same squint at 4 months or older, or any abnormal red reflex, flips the answer to referral.
n: No printed answer for this version; compiler (Alhomrani) answer in the boxed 15-16 September version is B. Red reflex test, while Almajhadi-Avengers chose A (refer, if type of squint not specified). Refer if at 4 months (when type of squint is not specified).

q: A mother brought her 2-month-old infant who has a squint. What is the most appropriate action?
k: Squint under 4 months: red reflex first; reassure if normal and intermittent; refer if abnormal, constant or persistent.
r: A 4 month old (not 2) with the same squint is a referral answer.
n: Almajhadi-Avengers: A. Refer for ophthalmology (if type of squint not specified, refer for evaluation). Alhomrani: B. Red reflex test. If 4 months, refer (if type of squint not specified).

q: 2- child came to ER complaining of sudden convergent squint and double vision he has no hx of trauma or surgery:
o: refer to pediatric ophthalmology next day
full septic work up including LP
CT scan to rule out space occupying lesion
k: Sudden-onset squint, especially convergent, in a child = image the brain.
r: Congenital or gradual squint goes to ophthalmology; sudden squint goes to the scanner.
n: Older version answered d. CT scan (Abdulmajeed Pediatric and Surgery). Sudden onset squint is ominous, especially convergent: likely 6th nerve palsy from raised intracranial pressure (e.g. tumors). If MRI is an option it is the better answer for brain tumors.

q: 5-years old boy came with his mother concerned sudden squint of the left eye. Upon examination, abnormal in the left eye. What is the most appropriate next step?
k: Acquired, sudden squint in a child = exclude intracranial lesion.
r: Gradual or congenital squint goes to ophthalmology; a sudden new squint in a child is a neurological red flag that needs brain imaging.
n: Sudden-onset squint in a child needs brain imaging to rule out a space occupying lesion. Other version of this recall in Part 3: SWR-2466 → C. Refer to ophthalmology

q: mother brings her 2-month-old infant because she is concerned that the baby may have a squint. What is the most appropriate assessment?
k: Squint in infancy: examine first (red reflex), then decide reassure or refer.
r: Retinoblastoma presents with leukocoria first and strabismus second, so a squint question in a young infant often wants the red reflex.
n: Printed answer C: red reflex test.

q: 10 year old presented with ptosis and double vision's n that worsens toward the end of the day, he has difficulty chewing and speaking in the evining, but in the morning he is fine. He has no limb weakness, sensory deficit, or absent relfexes, apon neuro exam he has fatiguable ptosis and dysarthria: What is the most appripriate next investigation to confirm the diagnosis:
k: Fatigable ocular and bulbar weakness, normal reflexes and sensation = myasthenia gravis; confirm with AChR antibodies.
r: Areflexia and sensory loss push you to GBS and nerve conduction studies; preserved reflexes with fatigability keep you on MG.
n: Printed answer D: myasthenia gravis confirmed with acetylcholine receptor antibody test.

q: 15 month old with an attack tonic clonic seizure he was febrile after that recovered well and no complications, which of the following predicts developing epilepsy in the future:
k: Predictors of epilepsy after febrile seizure: complex seizure, abnormal neurodevelopment, family history of epilepsy.
r: Family history of febrile seizures predicts more febrile seizures; family history of epilepsy and complex features predict epilepsy.
n: Printed answer C: complex febrile seizure is a risk factor for later epilepsy.

q: A 4 years-old child with a worsening history of N/V, headache, and visual disturbances for the last 6 weeks. The symptoms worsen at the morning and at night and decrease with walking. What is the most appropriate investigation?
k: Red flag headache in a child: image the brain.
r: Headache worse on lying down with morning vomiting is raised ICP, not migraine: MRI first.

q: Mother came to you complaining that his 7 months old boy have constant convergent squint, what is the most appropriate assessment?
k: Squint in infants: decide by constancy and age.
r: 'Constant' is the word that removes the option of waiting: refer, because amblyopia is time sensitive.
n: Constant squint (highlighted in red) beyond early infancy warrants ophthalmology referral.

q: A child presents with progressive muscle weakness and difficulty chewing. The weakness is worse toward the end of the day and improves after rest, with symptoms being least severe in the morning. Which of the following is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the diagnosis?
k: Myasthenia gravis: fatigable weakness, normal reflexes and sensation.
r: Worse in the evening, better in the morning = MG; the confirm question wants AChR antibodies, not CK.
n: Fatigable weakness suggests myasthenia gravis; printed answer is AChR antibodies to confirm.

q: 4 month EMG : myopathy pattern CK : normal ( just normal bo values ) Weak antigravity movement Hypotonia Preseved but reduced reflexes Diagnosis?
k: Myopathic EMG + normal CK = congenital myopathy; myopathic EMG + high CK = dystrophy.
r: CK is the one test that separates congenital myopathy from congenital muscular dystrophy when the EMG is myopathic in both.
n: Embedded inset: 16-17 February recall with different options. CK normal and very young age, this cannot be muscular dystrophy, so congenital myopathy.

q: جاني النونو اللي فجأة يسير احول (a baby who suddenly started squinting)
o: CT to role out occupat space
k: Squint in a child: onset and associated signs decide the step.
r: Sudden squint is neurological until proven otherwise: image before you refer.
n: Sudden-onset squint in a baby: image to rule out space-occupying lesion. Recaller notes there was no MRI option ('MRI مافي'). Recaller: Stem recalled in Arabic; MRI was not among the options

q: Five year-old child present to the emergency department and this mother concern of squint and there is no history of trauma and normal red reflex test and on examination there was convergent squint what is the next most appropriate?
o: CT scan to exclude space occupying
k: Sudden or acquired squint in a child = rule out raised ICP first.
r: Normal red reflex removes retinoblastoma from the picture, which pushes the answer toward brain imaging for a new squint.
n: Sudden onset squint, especially convergent, is ominous: likely 6th nerve palsy from raised ICP (e.g. tumors), so image to rule out space-occupying lesion; MRI would be better if offered. Sudden squint or squint after trauma -> imaging.

q: Child came to ER complaining of sudden convergent squint and double vision he has no hx of trauma or surgery:
o: full septic work up including LP
CT scan to rule out space occupying lesion
k: Sudden or acquired squint in a child = rule out raised ICP first.
r: Image before LP: a 6th nerve palsy may be the first sign of raised ICP.
n: Embedded inset: older version with eye photos (convergent vs divergent squint); answer d per Abdulmajeed Pediatric & Surgery. Sudden convergent squint = likely 6th nerve palsy from high ICP, image to exclude SOL.

q: Mother brought her daughter to the clinic because she had developed a sudden-onset squint. On examination, the girl had squint with blurred vision. What is the most appropriate next step in management? Options:
o: CT scan of the brain to rule out a space-occupying lesion (SOL)
k: Sudden or acquired squint in a child = rule out raised ICP first.
r: "Sudden" is the word that converts a squint question from ophthalmology referral to brain imaging.
n: Sudden-onset squint: brain CT to rule out SOL.

q: Child (don't remember the age) came with a squint, and the eye doesn't move and has an absent red reflex ->
k: Any infant or child with an abnormal red reflex needs urgent ophthalmology referral.
r: An absent red reflex outranks the squint. It is the finding that makes referral urgent.
n: Absent red reflex -> refer to ophthalmology.

q: 8 month-old girl brought to the Well Baby Clinic by her mother who notes a squint. During examination, she has an absent red reflex Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
k: Any infant or child with an abnormal red reflex needs urgent ophthalmology referral.
r: For imaging options: no CT in retinoblastoma, and MRI comes only after the ophthalmologist confirms the tumor.
n: Indications for referral: constant strabismus at any age; intermittent strabismus after 6 months (6 is okay, 7 is bad); abnormal corneal reflex / red reflex / cover-uncover. Inset (9-month-old, CT eye / MRI eye options) is the same version with Answer: D.

q: A 9-month-old girl brought to the Well Baby Clinic by her mother which notes a squint, during examination she has absent red reflex. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
k: Strabismus referral rules plus red reflex.
r: Imaging options in a red reflex question are distractors; the next step is the ophthalmologist.
n: Embedded inset: 9-month-old version with CT eye / MRI eye options; printed Answer: D. Compiler lists indications for referral: constant strabismus at any age, intermittent strabismus after age 6 months (6 is okay, 7 is bad), abnormal corneal reflex / red refle

q: Infant with convergent squint in right eye since birth.
k: Constant squint at any age means referral; intermittent squint is normal only in early infancy.
r: The words 'since birth' or 'constant' turn a reassurance question into a referral question.
n: Constant squint since birth -> refer to ophthalmology.

q: جا اظن طفل صغير جابته امه معه squint وش تسوي له؟ (I think a small child brought by his mother with squint, what do you do?)
k: For an infant with suspected squint: examine first, then decide.
r: If the options include both red reflex and light reflex, the red reflex is the 'rule out cancer' answer and the light reflex is the 'screen alignment' answer. Read which one the version is asking for.
n: Printed answer C, red reflex. Recaller: Stem recalled in Arabic; option B not recalled

q: A mother brings her 2-month-old infant because she is concerned that the baby may have a squint. What is the most appropriate assessment?
k: Infant with suspected squint: examine first, refer if abnormal.
r: If the stem shows or says the red reflex is absent or white, the answer flips to immediate ophthalmology referral.
n: Screenshot from an external compilation (SMLE First Aid, October 2026, q11161); answer C red reflex test, key source past recall, key checked. October By Similar update ↻ Printed again later in the October By Similar file (p.291) with the same answer; note the

q: 4 Months old baby his mother is concerned about squint?
k: For an infant with suspected squint: examine first, then decide.
r: Concern only, no findings given: examine (red reflex). An abnormal finding in the stem: refer.
n: Telegram screenshot; red handwritten check mark next to C. Red reflex test.

q: 2 months boy brought by mother concerned about squint what to do ?
k: For a young infant whose mother is worried about squint, examine first.
r: Reassurance is tempting at 2 months, but in exam logic it comes only after a normal red reflex.
n: Confirmed red reflex test. Chat screenshot confirms 2 months and mother only concerned. Recaller: Recaller: chose C, not sure if correct

q: Child with squint mom is worried what to do?
k: Hirschberg (corneal light reflex) = the screening test for strabismus.
r: 'Screen for strabismus' points to the light reflex; 'rule out retinoblastoma' points to the red reflex. Other versions of this recall are keyed to the red reflex.
n: Printed answer light reflex (Hirschberg corneal light reflex test).

q: 2 mo. Mother worried about inward squint that happens sometimes when the child tries ro focus closely. He has a symmetric red reflex and normal corneal light reflexes. What to do?
k: Intermittent squint in early infancy with normal reflexes is normal.
r: 'Sometimes', '2 months' and normal reflexes mean reassure. 'Since birth', 'constant' or an absent red reflex mean refer.
n: Intermittent squint at 2 months with normal red and corneal reflexes -> reassure.

q: A mother brings her infant (5-week-old) because she is concerned about hypotonia. On examination, the infant has decreased/absent lower-limb reflexes [ tonqe facciculation?]What is the most appropriate advice/management?
o: The condition will improve with time.
Perform a muscle biopsy to establish the diagnosis and treat accordingly.
Reassure, the condition will resolve during adolescence.
New modality to treat or mangment this case or somthing like this
k: Floppy infant + areflexia + tongue fasciculation = SMA.
r: Reflexes separate the two floppy infants: absent reflexes and fasciculations = peripheral (SMA); normal reflexes = central cause.
n: Printed answer D (new treatment modality), consistent with SMA (hypotonia, areflexia, tongue fasciculation) now having new disease modifying therapies.

q: Child with history of three infections this year, presented now with pneumonia; his older brother died with a similar condition; his sisters (3 and 5 years) are normal and well. Workup shows low B cells and normal T cells. What is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Low B cells, normal T cells, affected boy with an affected brother = X-linked agammaglobulinemia.
r: Normal B cell count with low IgG and high IgM is hyper IgM, not Bruton; count the B cells.
n: Embedded inset: question bank item 8, fuller version of the main recall with complete options; its own answer line (partly cropped, legible as A) gives X-linked agammaglobulinemia (affected males only, low B cells, normal T cells). October By Similar update

q: A 12-year-old girl has typical symptoms of migraine and was diagnosed with migraine. She was treated with first-line therapy but has had no improvement, and symptoms have persisted for 3 weeks. What is the most appropriate second-line treatment?
k: Pediatric migraine: NSAID/paracetamol acute, triptan if they fail, prophylaxis if attacks are frequent, disabling or refractory.
r: If a triptan is listed for failure of acute NSAID, pick the triptan; with no triptan and persistent symptoms, pick prophylaxis.
n: Printed answer A (inset also A). Compiler: 'No Triptan' among options. Answer depends on what first line is: Nelson says NSAID first line, UpToDate says paracetamol > NSAIDs (ignore UTD, follow Nelson); NSAID is the stronger analgesic so if no response to NSAI

q: 12 year old girl presented to emergency department after blood withdrawal with transient loss of consciousness and quickly awake previously healthy
k: Typical trigger + brief LOC + rapid full recovery + normal history = vasovagal syncope: reassure.
r: Syncope during exercise is cardiac until proven otherwise; syncope at the sight of a needle is vasovagal.
n: Vasovagal syncope: reassurance. Older version shown with the same answer.

q: A girl had a brief episode of loss of consciousness after standing for a prolonged period in the sun. She regained consciousness immediately. Which of the following findings would be considered a red flag?
k: In syncope questions, trigger + prodrome = benign; red flags point to the heart.
r: Options describing the trigger or the prodrome are reassuring distractors; pick the one that hints at inherited cardiac disease.
n: Printed answer C.

q: Regarding febrile convulsions in children, which of the following statements is correct?
o: There is a 2% chance to develop epilepsy
If it is a complex febrile seizure, it is more likely to progress to epilepsy
If parents had febrile seizures, it will increase the chance to progress to epilepsy
Using antipyretics will decrease the chance of febrile convulsions
k: Febrile seizure: age about 6 months to 5 or 6 years, fever, no CNS infection.
r: Family history of febrile seizures predicts RECURRENCE; complex features and family history of epilepsy predict EPILEPSY.
n: Embedded inset: 'Other Updates In Examiner 6 Part' version; printed B. Compiler: if option B says complex febrile seizure is more likely to progress to epilepsy, go for it as the 'more' correct answer. Other versions of this recall in this deck: OCT-1721 → A.

q: A 2 year old child develops tonic-clonic convulsions for 3 minutes, he is drowsy but responsive. Temperature of 39, sore throat and runny nose. Parents reported no past medical history. He has a positive family history of febrile convulsions. Parents are asking for consultation:
o: Reassurance, and find the source of fever
k: Febrile seizure: age about 6 months to 5 or 6 years, fever, no CNS infection.
r: Drowsy but responsive after a short febrile seizure is postictal; prolonged unresponsiveness or meningism would change the plan to LP and further workup.
n: Embedded inset: 'Last Days Of Feb, Part 3' version; boxed answer A. October By Similar update ↻ Printed again later in the October By Similar file (p.3178) with the same answer; note there: Embedded inset: older version with different option order; Answer A. S

q: Case of febrile seizure. The mother is concerned about future convulsions and already giving antipyrites for fever. What would be the consultation for her?
o: Perform EEG to predict future seizures
Start antipyrites when fever is present
Educate the family about how to deal with future seizures
k: Simple febrile seizure: benign, counsel and educate, no tests or prophylaxis.
r: "Worried about future seizures" = educate on what to do during a seizure; antipyretics and EEG do not change recurrence.
n: Printed answer D. 15-18 October update Other version of this recall in 15-18 October: OCT-0786 → A. There is 2% chance to develop epilepsy. 19 October update 20 October update

q: The question about febrile seizure consultation choices were
o: There is 2% chance to develop epilepsy
anti epileptic medication daily will reduce the risk
anti pyretic during fever will reduce the risk of future epilepsy
the child will have intellectual disability
k: Febrile seizure: seizure with fever at 6 months to 6 years, no CNS infection or prior afebrile seizure.
r: Another version of this recall lists 'educate the family how to deal with future seizures' as the answer; pick that when it is offered.
n: Printed answer A: counselling after febrile seizure, small (about 2%) risk of later epilepsy; neither daily antiepileptics nor antipyretics reduce future epilepsy risk, and no intellectual disability. Other version of this recall earlier in October: OCT-0529 →

q: A 2-year-old boy is brought to the ER after a generalized seizure during a fever of 39 C. He has no past medical history and his development is normal. His parents are worried and ask whether he is at risk of or not. Which of the following increases his risk of developing epilepsy?
k: Febrile seizure: age about 6 months to 5 or 6 years, fever, no CNS infection.
r: Read the lead-in: 'recurrence' points to family history of febrile seizures and young age; 'epilepsy' points to complex seizure, developmental delay and family history of epilepsy.
n: Printed answer A.

q: A 7-year-old girl suddenly collapses in front of her family. fell down the floor with head nodding (popping) and when she regains consciousness, she has no memory of the event. Her family takes her to the hospital. What is the most likely type of seizure?
k: Match the motor feature to the seizure type.
r: Falls limp with a head drop = atonic; falls stiff = tonic; stares without falling = absence.
n: Printed answer D (Atonic). Embedded 21-23 September recalls: one recaller said the case had a weird description but was an atonic seizure (options tonic-clonic, atonic, myoclonic); another version, 11-year-old girl with multiple LOC episodes who fell to the fl

q: Pedia with sudden loss of awareness of the environment EEG 3hz spikes
k: EEG patterns decide pediatric seizure questions.
r: 3 Hz spike and wave = absence; hypsarrhythmia = infantile spasms. Hyperventilation in clinic provokes the absence.

q: A 17 year old complaining of sudden movement stop without falling for 15 seconds while Lip smacking EEG : 3 Hz spike. What is the management ?
k: Absence seizure treatment.
r: Ethosuximide covers ONLY absences; if a teenager with absences also has tonic-clonic seizures, a broad-spectrum drug such as valproate or lamotrigine is preferred.
n: Embedded inset: management version; printed Answer A with note 'A case of absence seizure'. Ethosuximide treats absence seizures; phenytoin may worsen them.

q: Long Case last line ( 3Hz ) What is the diagnosis ?
k: EEG patterns to recognize: 3 Hz generalized spike and wave: absence seizures (first line ethosuximide; valproate if GTC seizures also occur); Hypsarrhythmia: infantile spasms (West syndrome); Centrotemporal spikes: benign rolandic epilepsy
r: Carbamazepine and phenytoin can worsen absence seizures; do not pick them for a 3 Hz pattern.
n: Printed answer A (3 Hz spike-and-wave = absence seizure). Embedded inset (19-20 August) of a fuller version also answers Absence seizure.

q: 6 years old was brought by his parents with history of sudden A abrupt loss of environmental awarness with lip smacking followed sudden return to normal baseline. by Brain Imaging= Normal, EEG 3-Hz spikes Which of the following is the most appropriate diagnosis?
k: Brief staring + immediate recovery + 3 Hz spike and wave = absence seizure.
r: Automatisms like lip smacking do not exclude absence; the lack of postictal confusion and the 3 Hz EEG decide it.
n: Printed answer B; the embedded identical older recall also prints Answer: B. Brief loss of awareness with abrupt return to baseline and 3 Hz spike-and-wave = absence seizure. Other versions of this recall in this deck: OCT-6587 → B. Absence seizure

q: A 6-year-old presents with sudden abrupt loss of environmental awareness with lip- smacking, followed by a sudden return to normal baseline. Brain imaging is normal and EEG shows 3-Hz spike-and-wave discharges. What is the most appropriate diagnosis?
k: EEG pattern decides the diagnosis.
r: Brief staring with abrupt return to normal and no postictal confusion = absence; postictal confusion suggests a focal seizure.
n: Printed answer B. 3 Hz spike-and-wave with brief absences in a school-age child = childhood absence seizure. Other versions of this recall in this deck: OCT-6586 → B. Absence seizure

q: 5 months old, mother noted decreased activity and not smiling. He presented with multiple bouts of volatile flexion of extensors that lasts for 1-2 s with 20 bouts occurring (i believe infantile spasms). EEG ordered, what finding is expected in EEG?
k: EEG by syndrome: West = hypsarrhythmia; Lennox-Gastaut = slow spike-and-wave; absence = 3 Hz spike-and-wave.
r: Regression (stopped smiling) in an infant with spasms is the clue that makes this West syndrome, not benign infant movements.
n: Embedded inset: earlier version with 3 options; answer A (hypsarrhythmia).

q: An 8-year-old girl is brought by her mother due to abnormal movements during sleep. The episodes consist of brief tonic- clonic movements associated with deviation of the mouth, lasting a few seconds and resolving spontaneously. The mother also reports similar symptoms occurring in the morning when the child uses her hand to comb her hair. Neurological examination is normal. Electroencephalography (EEG) shows sharp spikes in the centrotemporal region. What is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Match the EEG pattern to the syndrome.
r: Morning jerks while combing hair in a TEENAGER with generalized polyspikes = juvenile myoclonic epilepsy; the centrotemporal spikes and facial involvement here make it Rolandic.

q: A child's EEG shows sharp spikes in the centrotemporal region. What is the diagnosis?
k: EEG pattern = syndrome. Centrotemporal spikes: Rolandic epilepsy; 3 Hz spike-and-wave: childhood absence epilepsy; Hypsarrhythmia: West syndrome
r: Rolandic epilepsy often needs no antiseizure drug at all if seizures are infrequent and nocturnal, because it is self-limited.
n: Printed answer A; embedded card (Q46 Neurology, EEG) agrees: Rolandic epilepsy = nocturnal focal facial seizures with drooling in school-age children, good prognosis; closest wrong answer absence epilepsy shows 3 Hz spike-and-wave instead. Recaller: Other opti

q: 7 months old pt. His mother noticed that he stopped smiling, low activity, fatigue. While examining the pt. he had multiple movements of neck flexion followed by extension of body & limbs lasting for 1-2 seconds in a repetitive pattern. EEG showed slow wave & multifocal spikes chaotic What's the diagnosis?
k: West syndrome = infantile spasms + hypsarrhythmia + developmental regression.
r: Infant age plus hypsarrhythmia means West; the same picture in a preschooler with slow spike and wave means Lennox-Gastaut.
n: Printed answer B; embedded identical recall prints Answer: B. Infantile spasms (West syndrome). Developmental regression, flexor/extensor spasms in clusters and chaotic hypsarrhythmia EEG = West syndrome. Printed again later in this file (p.3206).

q: 10 years old girl come to ER she has abnormal movement when sleeping in her face and limbs she has history of seizure other wise she is normal EEG showed frontotemporal spike What's the diagnosis?
k: Normal child + nocturnal facial seizures + centrotemporal spikes = Rolandic epilepsy.

q: Girl presents with joint pain, malar rash, and photosensitivity, followed by headache, confusion, and a generalized tonic-clonic seizure. IV methylprednisolone is started. Anti-dsDNA is positive, renal function is normal, and complement levels are low. Which drug should be added to her treatment?
k: Severe organ-threatening SLE = steroids plus an induction immunosuppressant.
r: Kidney flare: cyclophosphamide OR mycophenolate; brain flare (seizure, psychosis): cyclophosphamide.
n: Printed answer B. Embedded 18 Feb recall of the same version also prints Answer: B. Neuropsychiatric lupus -> cyclophosphamide. Recaller: Case was long, but clear neuropsychiatric lupus; I think ANA was negative while dsDNA positive.

q: A 10-year-old boy fell from a tree and hit his head. He had a brief LOSS OF CONSCIOUSNESS followed by a SEIZURE lasting one minute which resolved completely. On arrival he is post-ictal but arousable, conscious and oriented, with equal reactive pupils and NO focal neurological deficit. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Observe in the emergency department for 2 hours
k: Paediatric head injury: decide CT by risk tier.
r: Isolated vomiting or brief LOC with a normal exam = observe; add a post-traumatic seizure and it becomes urgent CT.
n: Bank q06961 (Pediatrics, Paediatric emergency & trauma, REPEAT); key tagged [Review]. Post-traumatic seizure with LOC is an indication for urgent CT head. ↻ Repeated recall (originally from REPEAT ★).

q: 8 months old baby, exclusively breastfeeding came with reduction in weight at birth he was 50th percentile now after month she is at 10th percentile, his height and head circumference still in 50thpercentile. Metabolic disorder
k: Which parameter falls first tells the cause.
r: Weight crossing two or more major centile lines downward is faltering growth, not 'reassure', even while still inside the normal range.
n: Printed answer A: increase calorie intake (weight alone dropping with preserved height and head circumference suggests inadequate caloric intake).

q: A 10-year-old boy, known case of chronic kidney disease (CKD) stage 4, presents with bone pain and hyperparathyroidism. Which of the following laboratory findings is most likely to be present?
k: CKD mineral bone disease: phosphate up, calcium down, calcitriol down, PTH up.
r: Phosphate is the one that goes UP in renal secondary hyperparathyroidism; if calcium is high too, think tertiary or primary.
n: Compiler notes option D should read LOW 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (in CKD it is low).

q: mother of 2 came to clinic, she mentions her older child recently got diagnosed with celiac disease and asks if theres anything to be done for the baby (maybe 5 to 6 months?) baby has normal weight gain and feeding, no changes in bowel habits and no other symptoms
k: Celiac screening in at-risk relatives needs gluten exposure (partial recall; other options were forgotten, baby's age uncertain).
r: A well infant who has not yet eaten gluten cannot be screened meaningfully; reassure now, screen later or if symptoms appear.

q: 9 month old baby brought to clinic, mother mentions that he cannot sit on his own yet, he can roll from prone to supine position, props himself up on his hands, doesnt have any syndromic features, no signs of failure to thrive, good weight and feeding next step?
o: emg study (some electric muscle test im not sure of the name)
k: Missed milestone: is it expected yet? If overdue, refer.
r: Reassure only when the missing skill belongs to an older age; an overdue milestone means referral.
n: Not sitting by 9 months is a red-flag motor delay: refer for further testing. Recaller: Recaller unsure of the name of option D.

q: child who can identify colors and articulate words, age in years:
k: Colors ladder: point to a color 3 y, name colors 4 y.
r: If the stem adds opposites to colors, the version is keyed to 5 years, not 4.
n: Nelson milestones: names colors at 4 years (highlighted in the table). This is the version solved as 4 years.

q: Child with difficulty swallowing and congested throat, febrile, no cough, she is ill and sitting silently in her mother's but with her neck extended?
k: Epiglottitis: airway first, everything else after.
r: Barking cough with stridor in a non-toxic child flips the diagnosis to croup and the answer to dexamethasone (plus nebulised epinephrine if severe).
n: Toxic, silent child with neck extended and dysphagia suggests epiglottitis; secure the airway by intubation in the OR.

q: Child 7 years old came for short stature, everything is normal but Delayed bone age but normal velocity. What you will do?
o: do basic lab such ( CBC , U&E ..)
reassure it will catch the adult height

q: 8-month-old exclusively breastfed infant whose weight fell from the 50th to the 10th percentile over a month; height and head circumference remain at the 50th.

q: 15-year-old (not mentioned male or female) for a check-up. Labs: RBC: 5.8 WBC: 68 Hb: 89 MCV: 69 MCHC: 261, I think (it's in the normal range anyway) Reticulocyte: 1% Diagnosis:

q: 10 y/o boy, came to clinic because mother is concerned his boy not growing well compared to his siblings Weight above 95% Examination normal except looks pale Labs: LDL high 5, Cholesterol high, Triglycerides high, No other lab What most appropriate action?

q: 3 months old boy Mother reported baby has recurrent viral and fungal infection Chronic diarrhea Labs: LOW T cell Low immunoglobulin What is the most likely diagnosis?

q: A full-term neonate presented with spontaneous soft tissue bleeding and joint swelling suggestive of hemarthrosis. Laboratory investigations showed a normal platelet count and a normal prothrombin time (PT), but the activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) was prolonged. A mixing study was performed, and the aPTT failed to correct after mixing with normal plasma. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

k: Mixing study: corrects = factor deficiency; fails to correct = inhibitor.
r: Same lab pattern as hemophilia A; the failure to correct on mixing is the only clue that flips it to an inhibitor.
n: Failure of aPTT to correct on mixing indicates an inhibitor, so maternal autoantibodies (acquired hemophilia) rather than factor deficiency.

q: A patient presents with a huge abdominal mass, hematuria, and a blood pressure of 150/100 mmHg. Which disease needs to be excluded?
k: Pediatric abdominal mass: Wilms vs neuroblastoma.
r: Hematuria points to a renal origin: even if neuroblastoma is offered, mass + hematuria + hypertension = Wilms.
n: Abdominal mass with hematuria and hypertension -> Wilms tumor; even if neuroblastoma is in the options, don't choose it.

q: A child whose mother mentions that his maternal uncle was diagnosed with leukemia at age 12 and his sister has retinoblastoma presents for evaluation. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Refer the child to an ophthalmologist to screen for retinoblastoma
Order a complete blood count (CBC) to look for anemia
k: Family history of retinoblastoma = ophthalmology screening of at risk relatives.

n: Compiler endorses referral to ophthalmology for retinoblastoma (option D in the sibling Telegram version, mapped here to A by meaning): retinoblastoma has high rate of inheritance (up to 40%), could be late onset even at 10 years, other options nonsense.

q: 10 years old male child come to clinic with mild URTI , his mother cncern because he has family history of malignancy. his uncle diagnosed with leukemia at the age of 10 , and his brother have hx of rtinoblastoma , she concern about the condition What is the appropriate management?

k: Neonatal thrombocytopenia: check the mother's platelets first.

n: Same recall as the previous versions with different options; alloimmune thrombocytopenia (normal maternal platelets, can occur in first pregnancy). 'Alloimmune' and 'Congenital' shown in red as the discriminating pair.

q: A child's parents notice a white pupillary reflex when taking a photograph with a camera flash. What is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Leukocoria: age is the tie breaker in recalls.
r: Same stem, different age, different answer: 6 weeks = cataract; 1 to 2 years = retinoblastoma.

q: "Pediatrics pt 2 yr come to clinic complaint of white reflex on his right eye after photo with flash, no pain or change in vision What's the diagnosis:
k: Leukocoria in a child = retinoblastoma until proven otherwise.
r: Heritable retinoblastoma carries a later risk of osteosarcoma.

q: A child presents with pallor agression and a strong craving to eat non-food substances such as paper and wall paint. What is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Pica + pallor in a child = iron deficiency anemia.
r: Lead poisoning and iron deficiency often coexist; neuro or GI features tip the answer to lead, pica with pallor to IDA.

q: A child with hemolytic anemia and splenomegaly has a peripheral smear showing microspherocytes and anisocytosis. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Spherocytes on smear: HS vs warm AIHA.
r: A positive direct Coombs test in the stem (especially after a recent infection) flips the answer to autoimmune hemolytic anemia.
n: Splenomegaly can occur in AIHA but is more suggestive of HS (chronicity); child age also favors HS over AIHA; spherocytes are present in both and are not differentiating.

q: A child is brought to the clinic for poor nutrition and pallor. The diet consists mainly of biscuits and milk. Hemoglobin is approximately 6 g/dL with microcytosis. What is the most appropriate management?
o: Oral ferrous sulfate plus dietary education
k: Stable iron deficiency anemia: oral iron first, fix the diet.
r: Do not transfuse a stable child with chronic IDA just because Hb is around 6; treat the patient, not the number.
n: Other options from a different recall: transfusion, IV iron. Rule: Hb 7 transfusion threshold is for hemorrhage, not for iron deficiency anemia; stable IDA is treated with oral iron and dietary education.

q: Child bleeds after umbilical stump His mother has SLE THE child has normal PTt and pt with PLT 18000 what is the TREATMENT?
k: Neonatal umbilical bleeding: read platelets vs PT/PTT.
r: Normal PT/PTT rules out vitamin K deficiency; a low platelet count with maternal SLE means antibodies, so IVIG.
n: Printed answer A: neonatal immune thrombocytopenia from maternal autoimmune disease treated with platelets and IVIG.

q: A 2-year-old girl brought to Primary Clinic because the mother noticed she is pale. History of drinking 3 pints of cow's milk daily and is a very picky eater. The mother gave history of similar presentation on 2 of her brother (see lab results). Test Result Normal Values RBC 3 4.8-7.1 x 1012/L (Newborn) 4.6-4.8 x 1012/L (Child) Hb 4 165-195 g/L (Newborn) 112-165 g/L (Child) MCH 18 28-33 pg/cell MCV 62 80-95 fl Reticulocyte 3 0.2-1.2 % Platelets count 480 150-400 x 109/L Ferritin 9 20-200 ug/L Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Microcytic anemia: ferritin decides.
r: Low ferritin with reactive thrombocytosis in a toddler on excess cow's milk = iron deficiency; the 'similar anemia in brothers' is the distractor.
n: Pints version: printed answer C (iron deficiency anemia) attributed to MG. Cow's milk excess, picky eating, microcytosis and low ferritin point to IDA. Sibling versions (glasses wording) carry answer A per MEDGARD and are debated. Other versions of this recall

q: 3 y Child came to the clinic with his mother to treat something.. In examination you the doctor notice multiple aged bruises and fracture also the doctor noticed bruises in mother hand or arm, when he asked the mother she said she was trying to catch him when he was falling and denied any abuse, What should you do?
o: Take consent from father to treat child
Treat and focus in child and ignore the finding in mother arm
Tell the mother to report to the police
Treat the child and report to child authority
k: Suspected child abuse: treat, protect, report.
r: Never hand the reporting duty to the family; the physician reports suspected abuse himself.
n: Suspected child abuse (multiple bruises of different ages plus fracture): treat the child and report to child protection authority.

q: A 4 years old complaining of recurrent infections ( 6 sinopulmonary and recurrent gastroenteritis and more than 4 giardiasis upon and his brother died 5 months due to sepsis upon examination all lymph nodes are not palpable. Which of the following is the diagnosis?
k: Recurrent bacterial infections plus giardia plus affected brother plus no lymph nodes or tonsils: XLA.

n: Printed answer only. Recurrent sinopulmonary infections plus giardiasis, affected male sibling and absent lymph nodes = X-linked agammaglobulinemia. A sibling version follows on the next page.

q: Child for Preschool screening RDW 20 PLT 450 LOW Hb and MCV diagnosis ?
k: Microcytic anemia: RDW separates IDA from thalassemia trait.
r: Normal RDW with microcytosis that fails iron therapy flips the answer to thalassemia (Hb electrophoresis).
n: IDA: raised RDW. Normal RDW is below about 14 (memorize this number); exam usually gives reference ranges but some recalls came without one for RDW.

q: 6 years old known case of bronchial asthma and recurrent acute asthma exacerbation. Which of the following is most helpful teaching points for prevention of his exacerbation?
o: Patient Skills using peak flow rate
k: Recurrent asthma exacerbations, check before stepping up: General scenario: trigger avoidance and environmental control; On ICS and still exacerbating: check inhaler or spacer technique and adherence first; Then step up controller therapy (low dose ICS, then ICS plus LABA)
r: If the stem says he is already on an ICS inhaler, the answer flips to spacer technique and adherence.
n: If the scenario clearly mentions he is on ICS, prevention is via C (ICS compliance and technique). If the scenario is general, like this recall, the preventive teaching point is environmental control measures.

q: 18 months old with painless left flank mass. (Neuroblastoma) X ray: internal calcifications What is most appropriate to diagnose:
k: Neuroblastoma versus Wilms tumour: Neuroblastoma: younger child, crosses the midline, fixed, calcification common, unwell child, raised urinary catecholamines (VMA, HVA), opsoclonus myoclonus.; Wilms: well child, mobile mass, usually does not cross the midline, hematuria, hypertension, WAGR or Beckw
r: Calcification in a toddler's abdominal mass points to neuroblastoma, and neuroblastoma is diagnosed on tissue.
n: Neuroblastoma requires tissue biopsy, unlike Wilms tumor. Approach: Wilms: next US > CT, most appropriate CT, diagnostic CT, confirmatory biopsy. Neuroblastoma: next US > CT, most appropriate biopsy, diagnostic biopsy, confirmatory biopsy.

q: A 3-day-old infant is brought to the clinic with yellowish discoloration of the skin and sclera. Which laboratory finding would indicate that the jaundice is due to hemolytic anemia?
k: Neonatal jaundice: first split by bilirubin fraction.
r: "Conjugated" jaundice in a baby never means hemolysis; it means think biliary atresia, especially with pale stools.
n: Hemolysis floods the liver with bilirubin faster than it can be conjugated, so the indirect fraction rises; expect a high reticulocyte count. Conjugated jaundice means cholestasis or biliary atresia.

q: A 6 years old boy came to the clinic with ecchymosis post viral URTI two weeks ago. He has no hepatosplenomegaly. Labs showed low platelets. What is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the diagnosis?
k: Childhood ITP. Picture: well child, petechiae/bruising/mucosal bleeding 1 to 4 weeks after a viral illness.; CBC: isolated thrombocytopenia; film: large platelets, otherwise normal.; Marrow (if done): increased megakaryocytes.
r: Add pallor, bone pain, hepatosplenomegaly or a high WBC and the answer becomes bone marrow aspiration for leukemia.
n: This is ITP; blood film confirms (if CBC is among the options, choose it). 'Same above'.

q: A child with asthma was prescribed inhaler but is not using it, misses 2-3x per week. Family has cats at home. How should you manage this patient?
o: Tell them to remove cats from the environment
k: Uncontrolled asthma: fix the basics before stepping up.

q: An 18 month old boy, came to the clinic for review. The child is always hungry, drinks 1 liter of milk daily and eats dirt. Poor solid food intake. On exam He is underweight & has pale conjunctiva. Which is the most appropriate investigation?
k: Cow's milk anemia: lead-in verb decides CBC vs ferritin.
r: "Most appropriate investigation" = CBC with smear; "diagnostic test" = ferritin.
n: Printed answer b (CBC with blood smear) for 'most appropriate' investigation. Compiler: if the question asks for the DIAGNOSTIC test, the answer is d. Ferritin level. Other version of this recall in Part 4: SWR-3562 → B. CBC with blood smear

q: Child pale, eats non-food such as soil and chalk. Labs show microcytic anemia and low ferritin.

r: Pica plus microcytosis with LOW ferritin = iron deficiency; with normal ferritin and stippling = lead.
n: Printed answer D; no compiler commentary. Recaller: Not exactly the same but similar idea

q: Pregnant lady just delivered a baby. O/E: of the newborn: -multiple petechial rash on skin. Labs (baby): Hb was low, plt 8, WBC 5 US head of baby: grade 1 intraventricular hemorrhage. Mother plt (also low not 315). What is the Dx?
k: Neonatal thrombocytopenia: check the mother's platelet count.

q: A 1-year-old boy has markedly elevated HbF and elevated HbA2.
k: Hb electrophoresis patterns.
r: Raised HbA2 = beta-thalassemia; iron deficiency can falsely lower HbA2 and mask trait, so correct iron first.
n: Printed answer B (raised HbF and HbA2 = beta-thalassemia).

q: Child pale eat non-food such as soil, chalk microsytic ferttine low

r: Low ferritin settles it: microcytosis with normal ferritin should make you think lead or thalassaemia.

q: 6 y old boy present with convulsions, pallor hepatosplenomegaly and lymphadenopathy Hb and plt low WBCs 25 What is the line of management for his CNS should be involved ?
k: ALL: the CNS and testes are sanctuary sites, so CNS prophylaxis or treatment is given intrathecally.
r: "CNS involved" in leukemia = intrathecal chemotherapy; systemic chemotherapy is the trap because it does not cross the blood brain barrier well.
n: Handwritten B; no further compiler commentary.

q: A physician advises a mother during a well-baby visit to start an iron supplement for her exclusively breastfed infant one month from today. How old is the infant at the time of this visit?
k: Iron in infancy depends on feeding type and gestation.
r: Term breastfed baby: iron at 4 months; preterm: from 1 month; the question works backwards from 4 months.
n: Compiler (Athar): B. 3 months. He thinks this is a poor recall, but assuming it is written like this the answer is B, because iron supplements for exclusively breastfed infants start from 4 to 6 months (4 months is one month after the visit).

q: 18 month child present by her mother who report that her baby is hungry almost of time , baby drink about 1 liter of milk daily , eats dirty and solid food sporadic On examination she appears mildly pale , no organomegaly Which of the following has highest diagnostic value ??
o: full blood count and blood smear
k: Same scenario, different lead in: Next or initial step: CBC and blood smear; Highest diagnostic value: iron studies (ferritin); Most appropriate management in a stable child: trial of oral iron and follow up

n: Handwritten A; compiler underlined 'highest diagnostic value'. Three recalls about IDA: 'next' is C, 'most appropriate' is C, but 'HIGHEST DIAGNOSTIC VALUE' is A (iron studies). Recaller: Recaller (Arabic): written literally like this, I added nothing.

q: A 6 Year Old child with asthma has frequent exacerbation, what is the best way to reduce the frequency of exacerbation? (that's it no mention of any environmental factors or medications or spacer use)

q: A full term girl with growth restriction is admitted to the NICU. What is the most important abnormality that needs monitoring?

q: patient complains of recurrent infections, labs show absent T cells and low serum immunoglobulins + RECURRENT FUNGAL INFECTION AND DIARRHEA?

r: T cells absent with Ig low = SCID; B cells absent with T cells normal = Bruton.

q: 7 month old with febrile illness and multiple episodes of diarrhea and vomiting upon examination ill looking and dehydrated patient. What is the earliest sign of early compensated shock

r: Children keep a normal blood pressure until late; a normotensive child with cold peripheries and tachycardia is already in shock.

q: 13 year old with medulloblastoma was treated with chemotherapy and radiotherapy but relapsed and was found to have metastasis to bone and chest and no curative treatment, palliative care and DNR were discussed with parents, singed and completed What is the management?
k: Palliative care in incurable childhood cancer: comfort is the goal.
r: Do not resuscitate never means do not treat: symptom relief with morphine is still expected.

q: Baby had a delayed separation of his umbilical cords and start bleeding from the site which the same thing happened with his older brother. Labs of coagulation normal PT, PTT and platelets count and function normal. There is delay in clot Time only take 5 hours. Which factors is affected ?

r: Delayed cord separation with omphalitis and high neutrophils but no bleeding is leukocyte adhesion deficiency; umbilical stump bleeding with normal coagulation tests is factor XIII deficiency.

q: Preschool Child came for routine assessment (this is the stem nothing more) : Hb:9 MCV: 60 something Reticulocytes: 1.1 RDW: 20 Platelet: 450~ RBCs: 5 MCH&MCHC: low

q: A 16 y.o boy presented to ED complaining of chest pain and SOB, happened multiple times before Cardiopumo exam was normal Abdominal exam: there was tenderness Labs: Hg 80 Reticulocyte 2.5 Platelets 430 WBC 12 ESR10 What is the best investigation to establish diagnosis?
k: Hemoglobinopathy (sickle cell, thalassemia) = hemoglobin electrophoresis to confirm.
r: Chest pain plus new infiltrate and fever in a known sickle patient is acute chest syndrome; the question then asks for management, not electrophoresis.

q: 4 yeras girle old known case of ALL after 2 day of chemotherapy she spent the morning with playmate that has developed chicken pox now, what she give?

q: 2 years old child presented with his mother his hemoglobin was 10.6 was started on ferrous sulfate, after 6 months his hemoglobin became 10.3 , mother continued to give him iron , after 3 months she returned to the clinic, doctor ordered labs Hemoglobin was 9.1 MCV 63 Everything else normal How to get the definitive diagnosis?
k: Microcytic anemia not responding to iron: think beyond iron deficiency.
r: Iron trial failed + normal everything else = electrophoresis; iron trial failed + low ferritin = look for malabsorption (celiac).
n: Answer D, Hb electrophoresis. Microcytic anemia refractory to iron supplements: suspect thalassemia or celiac. Options C and D were shown in red as the main contenders.

q: 8 years old girl brought to primary healthcare clinic by her mother, complaining of poor concentration and hyperactivity at school. Her teacher noticed that she has difficulty staying seated at her place. The mother reported that her daughter only sleeps 5 hours per night from 1 AM to 6 AM. What's the most appropriate step in management?

q: Five years old with poorly controlled asthma, and sweat chloride of 77 ( high ) which of the following is the most frequent complication? ( this is the full recall)

q: A 4 year old boy with jaundice and fatigue, look pale Labs show : Hb low MCV low low MCH low RBC count high (or relatively high) RDW normal/slightly high Ferritin normal/high Serum iron normal/high HbA2 high -> key finding HbF high What is the diagnosis ?

q: After dilvery, hematoma, easy bleeding and brosing, diagnosed Hemophilia A First next step in management?

q: I had a question in my exam with a pediatric that had jaundice, scleral icterus, and he came with right hypochondriac pain, splenomegaly. Ultrasound showed calculous cholecystitis. Blood film: he had hypochromic microcytic anemia, hypochromic microcytic anemia with reticulocytes of 2%. And they had a picture of a blood film. my description : They all looked like similar cells. There was one big cell with a nucleus in the middle. All cells were a bit pale. They were not spheres. They were normally shaped. No schistocytes. No pencil-shaped cells. ( picture attached very similar ) And then they asked what kind of anemia does he have?

q: a 4 yrs old girl with flank pain, no other symptoms? Erythrocyte 40 Protein +3 ? Dignosis?
k: Wilms vs neuroblastoma: well child + hematuria = Wilms; sick child + midline-crossing mass = neuroblastoma.
r: Add fever, weight loss or bone pain to the same flank mass and the answer flips to neuroblastoma.

q: Young age came with symptoms of PICA (eating weird things) and symptoms of anemia Labs : Digoxin within normal range ( I think so) HB Low Leads HIGH ( 2 ) Ferritin normal ( I think ) X RAY : I remember there is dense or tenses Metaphyseal bands or line What is the appropriate management? q: A 1-year-old boy is being investigated for pallor, jaundice, lethargy and delayed growth. On examination, found to be short for his age, with prominent forehead and splenomegaly (see lab results). Test Result Normal Values HB 40 112-165 RDW 14 11.5-14.5% MCV 70 80-95f Reticulocyte 2.4 0.2-1.2% WBC 5.5 4.5-10.5 x 109/L RBC 5.8 4.6-4.8 x 1012/L HB electrophoresis Hb A2 30 2-3% Hb F 50 1-2% Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

q: A preschool child presents for his routine preschool-entry examination (see lab results). q: There was also a very very long case describing how a pediatric patient would get recurrent chest pains that would result in repetitive hospitalizations and blood transfusions. Essentially the entire case has features of sickle cell disease (they do not provide you with the diagnosis). The stem at the end asks: absence of which of the following confirms the diagnosis?
k: Hemoglobin electrophoresis is the confirmatory test for hemoglobinopathies; read it by what is present and what is missing.
r: Trait vs disease: HbA alongside HbS means trait (or S/beta+ thalassemia), unless the child was recently transfused, since donor blood adds HbA; untransfused HbSS has none.
n: Absence of HbA on electrophoresis confirms sickle cell disease (HbSS).

q: A 6-year-old girl presents to the Emergency Department with a history of feeling unwell and redness over the last 10 hours. On examination, she looks pale, had a palpable liver and her spleen was 6 cm below the costal margin (see lab results). Blood pressure 93/55 mmH Heart rate 169 /min Respiratory rate 28 /min Temperature 37.5 C Test Result Normal Values Hb 58 112-165 g/L Platelet count 98 150-400 x 109/L Sickle cell screen Positive Which of the following is the most useful investigation?
k: Acute anemia in sickle cell disease: check the spleen and the reticulocytes.
r: Big spleen with high retics = sequestration; normal spleen with no retics = parvovirus aplastic crisis.
n: Source cited: Medgard. Reticulocyte count differentiates aplastic crisis from hemolytic and sequestration crisis.

q: A Baby delayed separation of umbilical cords and bleeding from the site. Labs of coagulation prolonged PT PTT. platelets count normal. There is delay in clot time.
k: Read PT and PTT together.
r: Delayed cord separation on its own (no bleeding, normal coagulation, omphalitis) points to leukocyte adhesion deficiency, not a coagulation defect.
n: Prolonged PT and PTT with normal platelets and umbilical bleeding: vitamin K deficiency.

q: 10-year-old boy with mild URTI; mother concerned due to family history of malignancy - uncle had leukemia at age 10, brother has history of retinoblastoma. Most appropriate management?
o: Refer to ophthalmology to assess for retinoblastoma
k: Screen for the cancer that runs in a heritable pattern in close relatives, not for every cancer mentioned.
r: A brother with retinoblastoma means refer to ophthalmology; family leukemia alone does not justify a CBC.
n: Printed answer C. A screenshot of another recall version (options CXR to exclude leukemia, BRCA 1&2, CBC, refer to ophtha) shows the refer-to-ophthalmology answer as '#Confirmed'.

q: A baby was delivered by vacuum-assisted delivery and developed a scalp hematoma that crosses the suture lines. Hb is 7.5 g/dL. What is the most appropriate management?
k: Scalp swelling after delivery: sutures plus Hb decide.
r: Both caput and subgaleal hemorrhage cross sutures; anemia or shock after vacuum makes it subgaleal.
n: Subgaleal hemorrhage after vacuum delivery (crosses suture lines) with significant anemia; printed answer is blood transfusion.

q: Newborn 2 days old came with lethargy, hypotension and pallor. History of vacuum (ventouse) used during delivery. Had head swelling that crosses the suture lines. Hemoglobin 7.5. Normal platelets, normal PTT and PT. What is the most appropriate management?
k: Subgaleal hemorrhage with shock = resuscitate with blood and volume now.
r: Normal coagulation removes vitamin K from the picture; hypotension makes observation unsafe.
n: Subgaleal hemorrhage with hemodynamic compromise and normal coagulation; printed answer is transfusion and fluid resuscitation.

q: 6 months old exclusively breastfeeding came to the well health clinic, child is asymptomatic, Physical exam normal, mother ask for supplementes?
k: Exclusively breastfed infant: supplement the baby, not the mother.
r: "Give the mother iron" is the trap: maternal supplements do not fix low iron in breast milk.
n: Compiler says 'See Below': the next page cites AAP (via Makrami): exclusively breastfed term infants should receive iron supplementation 1 mg/kg/d by 4 months of age, or alternatively start at 6 months when iron containing complementary foods are introduced. R

q: A 5-year-old child presented with acute petechiae and ecchymoses. Two weeks ago, he had flu-like symptoms and was treated. On examination, the child is well and has scattered petechiae. Laboratory investigations: White blood cell count: 8 Platelet count: 22 Hemoglobin: 125 What is the most appropriate diagnostic test?
k: Childhood ITP: well child, post-viral, petechiae, isolated low platelets.
r: Hb 125 g/L is normal: isolated thrombocytopenia means smear, not marrow.
n: Printed answer D: typical post-viral ITP with isolated thrombocytopenia; peripheral smear is the appropriate test. Compiler notes Hb 125 is not low (no other cytopenia, so no bone marrow needed).

q: A 14-year-old boy presents to the clinic with his parents due to asymmetrical breast enlargement (one breast is noticeably larger than the other). He feels self-conscious and embarrassed at school. On examination, a smooth, tender subareolar mass is palpated on the right side, with a smaller soft disc on the left. Secondary sexual characteristics are appropriate for his Tanner stage. What is the most appropriate management/counselling step?
o: Reassure him that this is a common condition in pubertal males that usually resolves spontaneously.
Refer him immediately for surgical excision (mastectomy).
Order a comprehensive endocrine panel (testosterone, oestrogen, LH, FSH).
k: Pubertal gynecomastia: reassure unless red flags.
r: Normal Tanner stage plus tender subareolar disc in a teenage boy = reassure; abnormal development or testicular findings flip it to investigation.
n: Printed answer A: physiological pubertal gynecomastia with normal pubertal development is managed with reassurance.

q: 3 days old with yellowish skin Which of the following suggest hemolysis?
k: Classify jaundice first by which bilirubin is raised.
r: Hemolysis raises UNCONJUGATED bilirubin with high reticulocytes; a raised CONJUGATED level in a neonate points to cholestasis (biliary atresia, hepatitis) and needs urgent workup.
n: Printed answer B. Compiler: what indicates hemolytic anemia is increased unconjugated bilirubin. He also says he does not think this question comes anymore.

q: Child with recurrent chest infection and poorly controlled bronchial asthma and foul-smelling stool. Positive sweat chloride test (66 i think). What most frequent complication?
k: Cystic fibrosis = CFTR defect causing thick secretions in lungs, pancreas, gut and sweat glands.
r: "Asthma" that never gets controlled plus fatty foul stools in a child = think CF, and the classic lung complication is bronchiectasis.
n: Earlier recall version shown as a screenshot; printed answer B (bronchiectasis).

q: Paediatric patient presented with jaundice, splenomegaly, and forehead enlargement very low haemoglobin and high reticulocytes Hb A2 30% and Hb F 50% What is the diagnosis:
k: Raised HbA2 = beta thalassaemia; very high HbF with absent or markedly reduced HbA = major.
r: HbA2 rises only in beta thalassaemia; in alpha thalassaemia and iron deficiency it is normal or low.
n: Printed answer B (raised HbA2 and HbF with frontal bossing point to beta thalassemia); no further commentary.

q: An 11-year-old child presents with failure to thrive, pallor, and hepatosplenomegaly. Laboratory investigations show: Hemoglobin: 6 g/dL MCV: 78 fL Peripheral blood smear shows target cells and nucleated red blood cells. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Microcytic anemia + target cells + nucleated RBCs + hepatosplenomegaly/growth failure = β-thalassemia major.
r: Organomegaly with nucleated RBCs means ineffective erythropoiesis, which separates thalassemia major from iron deficiency.
n: Printed answer C; no further commentary.

q: A 6-week-old infant, known to have G6PD deficiency, presents to the outpatient clinic for evaluation of anemia. Examination is normal. Hemoglobin is 90 g/L. Platelets are normal. Bilirubin is normal. Urine is clear. What is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Isolated mild anemia in a well term infant at about 2 months = physiological anemia of infancy; reassure.
r: A known G6PD label does not mean hemolysis; without jaundice, dark urine or a trigger, think age first.
n: Bilirubin normal in a 6-week-old with mild anemia: physiological anemia of infancy rather than hemolysis.

q: A 53-day-old boy is referred to the Paediatric Clinic for investigation of anemia. He was born at full term and he is a known case of G6PD deficiency. On examination, both height and weight are in the 10th percentile, the rest of the examination is normal (see lab results). Test Result Normal Values Hb 70 112-165 g/L Platelet count 350 150-400 x 109/L Total bilirubin 25.1 <20.5 mol/L Urinalysis Result Normal Values Color Clear Clear or light yellow Leukocytes 0 0-3 per high power field Erythrocytes 0 0-2 per high power field Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Well term infant at about 8 weeks with isolated anemia, normal exam and clear urine = physiological (not hemolytic) process; reassure.
r: Known G6PD deficiency is the distractor; with no trigger and clear urine, the answer is the physiological option.
n: Original Medgard question screenshot with C marked (**).

q: 10 years old with marked upper respiratory tract infection mother concerned due to family history of malignancy, uncle had leukemia at 10, brother had retinoblastoma, most appropriate management
o: chest X-ray annually for rule out leukemia
k: Screen relatives for the cancer syndrome the family history actually points to.
r: Ignore the distracting complaint (URTI) and the distant relative; the first-degree relative with retinoblastoma decides the answer.
n: Athar: C, referral to ophthalmology (sibling with retinoblastoma, screen for hereditary retinoblastoma). Alhomrani: confirmed 120. The Telegram screenshot of another version shows the same answer as confirmed.

q: A 10 y/o child (aprox.) pale with lymphodonpathy, hepatosplenomegaly, (with or without convulsions) lap: 60 platelets, 9 hg, 25000 wbc Csf cytology: lymphoblast How to protect CNS?
k: ALL: every child gets CNS directed therapy because the CNS is a sanctuary site.
r: "Systemic chemo" treats the marrow but not the CNS sanctuary; the CNS answer is always intrathecal.
n: ALL with CNS involvement; CNS prophylaxis/treatment is intrathecal chemotherapy.

q: Preschool age came for routine, cbc shows low hemoglobin, low mcv, but RDW is 20 (don't remember normal range but upper limit was 16) and rbc 5 (normal 3.8-4.7). Whats the most likely diagnosis:
k: Microcytic anemia: IDA versus thalassemia trait.
r: High RDW points to IDA; a normal RDW with a high RBC count points to thalassemia trait.
n: High RDW with microcytosis points to iron deficiency anemia.

q: New born to known SLE mother have very low platelets I think 18 and normal APTT and PTT ask about ttt?
k: Neonatal thrombocytopenia with normal PT/APTT: think immune (maternal ITP or SLE, alloimmune) or sepsis.
r: Plasma is for factors, not platelets: if PT and APTT are normal, FFP has no role.
n: Recaller: His platelets were between 10 to 20 but definitely less than 20. Option B was actually 'Iv steroids + plasma'.

q: Child in preschool came for preschool check up Hb 90 Rdw 20 Mch mcv mchc all low Reticulocyte 1.1 Rbc 5 Other labs were normal ( ferritin wasn't mentioned) What is the diagnosis
k: Microcytic anemia: RDW splits IDA from thalassemia trait.
r: Microcytosis with a HIGH RDW = iron deficiency; microcytosis with a normal RDW and high RBC count = thalassemia trait.
n: Printed answer C: microcytic anemia with high RDW favors iron deficiency anemia.

q: Child came to the clinic regarding poor nutrition, he is always eating biscuits and milk and not eating well. On examination there is mild conjunctival pallor, Hb is 6.2 mg/dl with low MCV. What is the most appropriate management for this child?
o: Give oral iron and advise diet modification
k: Stable child + dietary history + microcytic anemia = trial of oral iron and diet change.
r: A very low Hb alone does not mean transfusion: judge the child's stability; chronic, well compensated IDA gets oral iron.
n: Recaller: Marked '(confirmed) 17jul'.

q: A 10-day-old infant is brought in due to 5 hours of continuous bleeding post-circumcision. INR 1.1 (normal), aPTT 70 (high), platelets ~200 (normal). Best next step?
k: Read the coagulation screen to locate the defect: Isolated high aPTT: intrinsic pathway (VIII, IX, XI) or von Willebrand disease; Isolated high PT/INR: factor VII (or early vitamin K deficiency); Both high: common pathway (X, V, II, fibrinogen), vitamin K deficiency, liver disease or DIC
r: Isolated prolonged aPTT plus circumcision bleeding in a boy = hemophilia; press the wound, do not explore it.
n: Options printed without letters; lettered by position.

q: Peditatric come after URTI with ecchymosis Normal pt and ptt Which is impaired in this child ?
k: Platelets vs factors: match the test to the defect.
r: Petechiae and ecchymosis with normal PT/PTT point to platelets; hemarthrosis with a long PTT points to factors.
n: Printed answer B; post-viral ITP (platelet problem) prolongs bleeding time with normal PT/PTT. Recaller: It was a one-line, direct question.

q: Pedia Pt with RBC Containing chromatin (or smth like this) and target sign, with low Hb and low MCV , doagnosis?
k: Microcytic anemia in a child: read the film and the severity.
r: Target cells plus nucleated or inclusion bearing RBCs in a severely anemic microcytic child = thalassemia major, not iron deficiency.
n: Target cells with microcytic anemia in a child: printed answer beta thalassemia major. Recaller: Unsure of RBC inclusion wording; forgot other options.

q: A child is brought to the clinic by his mother with complaints of generalized fatigue and constipation. Full laboratory tests were done. Lab results show: Hb 8.1, MCV 65, MCH 19, Total Iron-Binding Capacity 700. What is the recommended supplement/treatment for this patient?
k: Microcytic anemia + high TIBC = iron deficiency anemia, treat with oral iron.
r: High TIBC points to iron deficiency; a LOW TIBC with microcytosis suggests anemia of chronic disease instead.
n: Microcytic hypochromic anemia with high TIBC is iron deficiency; treat with iron.

q: 2 years old child presented to the clinic for mild pallor. He eats a lot of biscuits and drinks a lot of milk. (See labs) Hgb: 62!!! MCV: 63 MCH: 60ish What is the most appropriate management of his condition?
k: Microcytic anemia + excess cow's milk in a toddler = IDA = oral iron trial + limit milk.
r: A very low Hb does not mean transfusion; the deciding clue is the clinical state ("mild pallor", clinic visit = stable).
n: Iron deficiency anemia from excess cow's milk in a hemodynamically stable toddler: oral iron, not transfusion. Inset of an older recall (Hb 6.2, low MCV, mild pallor) answered B. Give oral iron and advise diet modification (confirmed). Recaller: (EXACT RECALL)

q: -pic of spherocytosis .. a child has diarrea or a GIT related infection and pallor with spleen 3 cm below costal margin .. lab results shows anemia with positive direct and indirect coombs test
o: A child I believe with chronic kidney disease ask about the stage eGFR=18
k: Spherocytes on smear: hereditary spherocytosis vs warm AIHA; the Coombs test separates them.
r: A picture of spherocytes tempts you to pick spherocytosis, but a positive Coombs test always moves the answer to AIHA.
n: Positive Coombs test with spherocytes points to AIHA rather than hereditary spherocytosis. Compiler questions the diarrhea detail ('Why Diarrhea????'). Attached older bank version: pediatric blood disorder, blood film, no family history, spleen palpable 2 cm,

q: 1 year old boy with a mass coming from the paravertebral sympathetic chain. What is the diagnosis?
k: Neuroblastoma vs Wilms: Neuroblastoma: adrenal or sympathetic chain, crosses midline, fixed, calcified, unwell child, raised urinary catecholamines; Associations: opsoclonus myoclonus, periorbital bruising, cord compression from paraspinal spread; Wilms: kidney, rarely crosses midline, mobile, well
r: "Sympathetic chain" or "adrenal" in the stem means neuroblastoma; "arising from the kidney" means Wilms.
n: Mass from the paravertebral sympathetic chain in an infant = neuroblastoma (neural crest). Other versions of this recall in this deck: OCT-4221 → A. Neuroblastoma

q: 1 years old presented with lower weakness, noted by the mother. The abdominal and pelvic CT showed mass coming from the paravertebral sympathetic chain. What is the diagnosis?
k: Neuroblastoma: neural crest tumour of adrenal medulla or sympathetic chain.
r: Leg weakness plus an abdominal or paraspinal mass in an infant is neuroblastoma with cord compression, an emergency.
n: Embedded inset: older version with lower limb weakness and CT finding; answer neuroblastoma. Other versions of this recall in this deck: OCT-4220 → B. Neuroblastoma

q: 2-year-old with a white reflex in the right eye after a flash photograph; no pain or change in vision. Diagnosis?
k: Leukocoria (white pupillary reflex) in a child: retinoblastoma until proven otherwise.
r: Painless and normal vision does not reassure: retinoblastoma is painless early; the next step question asks for urgent ophthalmology, not imaging.
n: Leukocoria in a toddler: retinoblastoma until proven otherwise.

q: A 2-month-old girl brought to the Well Baby Clinic. On examination, she has absent red reflex in her left eye. She is otherwise healthy and growing well with no concerns from her parents. Which of the following is the most likely tumour in such patient?
k: Leukocoria = retinoblastoma until proven otherwise.
r: Absent red reflex at a well baby visit is never a normal variant; refer the same day.
n: Absent red reflex (leukocoria) in an infant: the tumour to suspect is retinoblastoma.

q: A 6-month-old infant presents with recurrent pneumonia, chronic diarrhea, and otitis media. Laboratory evaluation reveals normal T-cell counts and undetectable levels of IgG, IgM, and IgA. What is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Read the T cell count first.
r: Normal T cells exclude SCID; bacterial infections after 6 months fit a pure B cell defect.
n: Printed B; same-version inset prints Answer: B. XLA is a B-cell disease (manifestations of B-cell disease described above).

q: A 8 month child presents with recurrent infections including pneumonia, upper respiratory tract infections, and his month confirmed he had episodes of diarrhea. Which of the following investigations is the most appropriate next step?
k: Match the infection pattern to the immune arm.
r: Diarrhea in a child with recurrent chest infections does not mean celiac; think antibody deficiency with Giardia.
n: Embedded inset: five-option version; printed answer D. Serum immunoglobulin levels. Suspected diagnosis is XLA -> measure immunoglobulin count (low). Platelet count useful only if Wiskott-Aldrich suspected. 20 October update ↻ Printed again later in this 20 Oc

q: Month year old infant came with recurrent pyogenic infection and otitis media the mother said he had chronic diarrhea also. What is the most appropriate investigation?
k: Match the infection pattern to the immune test.
r: Pyogenic bacteria plus otitis plus chronic diarrhea = check the antibodies first; Neisseria alone = check complement.
n: Embedded inset: older version with different option order; answer immunoglobulin level. October By Similar update

q: 6 weeks baby - follow up in clinic- dx G6PD what u will do?
k: Well 6 to 12 week old term infant with Hb around 9 to 11 = physiological nadir: reassure.
r: The G6PD label is a distractor: with no hemolysis features, the age (about 2 months) points to physiological anemia, not a G6PD crisis.
n: Answer points to the possible recall below: reassurance (Hb 9 at 6 weeks is physiologic nadir in an asymptomatic infant).

q: 36- 6 weeks old child know case of G6PD. Came to the clinic for anemia screening. (No symptoms) Hgb 9 Platelet normal No MCV or any thing else) What you will do?
k: Asymptomatic infant at about 2 months with mild isolated anemia = physiological anemia: reassure and follow.
r: If the stem adds jaundice, dark urine or a trigger (fava beans, drugs, infection), think G6PD hemolysis, not physiological anemia.
n: Answer: reassurance.

q: Peds developed DIC due to sepsis What to give?
o: FFP and platelets (both together in the option)
k: DIC management: Treat the cause (sepsis: antibiotics, support).; Bleeding: FFP for prolonged PT/aPTT, platelets for low count, cryoprecipitate for low fibrinogen.; If forced to choose one: FFP/cryo (factor replacement) over platelets.
r: DIC is a consumptive multi-factor problem; single-factor concentrates are for hemophilia.
n: Printed answer A. Compiler teaching: DIC is mainly a clotting factor disease; if forced to choose FFP/cryo vs platelets choose FFP/cryo. Warfarin toxicity: PCC > FFP > cryo > factor 7 plus vitamin K; if choosing one, factor replacement first. Recaller: Recalle

q: Pre term infant diagnosed with DIC (Diagnosis Mentioned) Prolonged PT and PTT and thrombocytopenia Initial Management?
k: Neonatal bleeding, read the platelets: PT and aPTT prolonged, platelets normal: vitamin K deficiency, give vitamin K.; PT and aPTT prolonged, platelets low: DIC, give FFP and platelets (cryo if fibrinogen low) and treat cause.; Isolated aPTT prolonged: hemophilia A or B.
r: Low platelets with prolonged PT/aPTT = DIC, not vitamin K deficiency.
n: Embedded inset: older version, answer A; compiler: This Is DIC, Management Is FFP.

q: Child with recurrent URTIs , eczema and thrombocytopenia both brother and uncle have the same condition?
k: Primary immunodeficiency recognition by triad: WAS: eczema + thrombocytopenia (small platelets) + infections; X-linked (boys, maternal male relatives).; Hyper-IgE: eczema + cold staph abscesses + pneumatoceles + high IgE.; CGD: catalase-positive abscesses, granulomas; DHR test.
r: Eczema + infections is not enough; the thrombocytopenia is what makes it Wiskott-Aldrich rather than Hyper-IgE.
n: Embedded inset: Telegram screenshot of a related recall with a green check mark on A. Wiskott aldrich (X-linked: eczema, thrombocytopenia, recurrent infections).

q: Children have rach face shoulder with itching some time and cheek erythema. hx Of Recurrent Infections. Labs: Low platelet (No Other Labs)
k: Rash plus labs: when a 'skin' question adds infections and low platelets, think immunodeficiency.
r: The low platelet count is the clue that converts 'atopic dermatitis' into Wiskott-Aldrich.
n: Embedded older lookalike (Q33); printed answer D. Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome (eczema, thrombocytopenia, recurrent infections). 20 October update October By Similar update

q: A child presents with a rash that spreads over the face and the abdomen and spares the diaper area. Peripheral smear shows small platelets. What is the diagnosis?
k: Eczema + thrombocytopenia with SMALL platelets + recurrent infections = Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome.
r: Small platelets = Wiskott-Aldrich; giant platelets = Bernard-Soulier.
n: 19 October update October By Similar update

q: Baby has rash and itcheness in his scalp, flexors, sparing the diper area, and history of multiple revurrent infections. Small sized platelets
k: Wiskott-Aldrich triad: eczema + thrombocytopenia with small platelets + recurrent infections.
r: Eczema alone = atopic dermatitis; add infections and SMALL platelets = Wiskott-Aldrich.
n: Eczema plus recurrent infections plus small platelets (microthrombocytopenia) = Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome. Embedded lookalike inset also answers Wiskott-Aldrich.

q: Rash on face extensor scalp, sparing the dippers Repeated infection Blood film showed small platelet What is the diagnosis?
k: Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome (X-linked recessive, WAS gene): Triad: eczema + thrombocytopenia with SMALL platelets + recurrent infections (encapsulated bacteria).; Usually boys; bleeding, petechiae, bloody diarrhea.; Risk of autoimmunity and lymphoma.
r: Small platelets = Wiskott-Aldrich; large platelets with low count = Bernard-Soulier or consumption (ITP).
n: Printed answer B. Eczema + recurrent infections + small platelets = Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome.

q: 18 months symptoms of atopic dermatitis, low hemoglobin, low platelet, and recurrent infection.
k: Wiskott Aldrich = WATER: Wiskott, Aldrich, Thrombocytopenia, Eczema, Recurrent infections.
r: Eczema in a boy with bruising or bleeding: check the platelet count and size; small platelets = Wiskott Aldrich.
n: Printed answer A (Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome). Classic triad: eczema, thrombocytopenia, recurrent infections.

q: A Child with Dry, scaly skin with erythematous patches over the cheeks, scalp, and extensor surfaces of both upper and lower limbs, without diaper are (i'm sure) and “low platelets count” What is the diagnosis?
k: Eczema + extra finding: + low (small) platelets ± recurrent infections: Wiskott-Aldrich.; + high IgE, cold abscesses, coarse face: hyper-IgE (Job) syndrome.; + honey-coloured crusts: secondary impetigo.
r: The rash distribution fits both options; the platelet count decides.
n: Printed answer B. Eczematous rash sparing the diaper area plus low platelets = Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome. Recaller: Recaller sure about diaper area sparing.

q: Preterm infant was admitted to the ICU with DIC. Platelets were low, and PT and PTT were prolonged. What is the most appropriate treatment?
k: Neonatal DIC: treat the cause, then replace what is consumed.
r: Prolonged PT and PTT with LOW platelets = consumption (DIC); with NORMAL platelets in a newborn = vitamin K deficiency.
n: Printed answer A (recaller's own choice); recaller unsure whether FFP was among choices. Recaller: Sorry for poor recall, maybe mixing; thinks FFP may have been in choices; chose PCC + PLTs.

q: A 12 year old came to the er after transient loss of conciousness after standing for a long time under the sun. She is medically free physical exam unremarkable What is the redflag for this patient
o: Hx of unexplained / early family death
k: Pediatric syncope red flags (suggest cardiac cause): Syncope during exercise or exertion; Syncope triggered by loud noise or startle, or while supine; No prodrome, or chest pain/palpitations before the event
r: Prodrome plus trigger (standing, heat) = reflex syncope; family history of young sudden death = get an ECG.

q: A child presents with pallor. He eats a lot, drinks one liter of milk a day and even eats dirt. Labs show low hemoglobin, low MCV, high total iron-binding capacity and low ferritin. What is the most likely cause of his symptoms?

q: A2-year-old child with sickle cell disease had an upper respiratory tract infection, which was followed by shortness of breath, and pallor. On examination, looked pale, sick and had a splenomegaly (see lab results). Blood pressure 90/60 mmHg Heart rate 110 /min Respiratory rate 25 min temperature 38.6 C Test Result Normal Values Hb 34 112-165 g/L WBC 3.1 4.5-10.5 x 109/L Lymphocytes 52 20-40 % Neutrophils 58 40-60% Platelets count 166 150-400 x 109/L Reticulocyte 0.1 0.2-1.2 % ESR 25 2-10 mm/h Which of the following is the best immediate management?

q: Child presents with pallor, [irritability/aggression - word unclear in the scan] and a strong craving to eat non-food substances such as paper and wall paint. Most likely diagnosis?
