q: A girl brought to Clinic because the mother noticed she is pale. Drinking HIGH INTAKE of milk daily and is a very picky eater. NOT EATING SOLID FOOD AS MUCH, no history of family problems or organomegaly Hb 80 MCV 68 WBC 5.2 No rbc mentioned Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

r: No RBC count and no family history: the diet decides, so choose IDA.

q: 11-month-old boy presents with right ulnar and radial fractures, 2 days after a reported fall on an outstretched hand. The parents delayed seeking medical care, stating that they did not notice any bruising and initially believed the injury was just a strain. The child is well-nourished, well-dressed, and has attended regular well-baby visits. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Believe the parents and treat the child
Admit the child for further evaluation and order a head CT
k: Suspected child abuse: protect the child and report.
r: A well dressed, well nourished child with regular visits can still be abused; the injury pattern decides.
n: Embedded inset: version without the consistent-parental-answers clause and with reworded options (C. Admit... head CT). Prints answer A. Call child protective services, matching the main recall's answer.

q: An 11-month-old is brought to the clinic. The Parent reports that he has a 1-day history of passing bright red blood mixed with foul smelling, dark brownish-black stool. The child is pale. Coagulation tests are normal (see lab result). Blood pressure 118/56 mmHg Heart rate 160 /min Respiratory rate 26 /min Temperature 36.6 C Test Result Normal Value Hb 70 112-165 g/L Which of the following investigations is most likely to confirm the source of bleeding?
k: Localise first, then pick the matching test.
r: Normal coagulation is given to exclude vitamin K deficiency and bleeding disorders, pushing you to a structural source.
n: Printed answer D. Barium meal for this version.

q: Child with mass in the abdomen in the left flank Xray abdomen: Confirmed a mass with internal calcification Which of the following is the most appropriate next step to reach diagnosis
k: Pediatric abdominal mass: image first, then define, then tissue.
r: Calcification on X-ray = think neuroblastoma; next imaging to define it = CT.
n: Embedded inset: similar recall with X-ray showing calcification; printed answer B. CT. Other versions of this recall in this deck: OCT-9571 → C. refer for biopsy

q: 18 month old with painless left flank mass otherwise well X ray: internal calcifications What is most appropriate to diagnose:
k: Pediatric flank mass: neuroblastoma vs Wilms.
r: Read the verb: next step / initial = ultrasound; to diagnose / confirm = biopsy.
n: Options were unlettered (lettered by position). Definitive diagnosis (likely neuroblastoma) is tissue biopsy; compiler: if the question asks next step, US then CT.

q: Child with mass in the abdomen in the left flank Ultrasound: Confirmed a mass with internal calcification What is the Most Appropriate test to reach the diagnosis (The Word "Next" Not Present , I Am SURE 100%)
k: Pediatric abdominal mass: separate the steps by the lead-in.
r: The calcification wording is the switch: with it the recall is keyed to biopsy, without it to CT.
n: Embedded inset: older ultrasound version; answer C refer for biopsy. If calcification not mentioned, most appropriate is CT; biopsy rarely needed for Wilms (tumor seeding). Other versions of this recall in this deck: OCT-9569 → B. CT

q: A young boy presents with a palpable rash on his legs extending up to his buttocks, with abdominal and knee pain. He had one bout of bloody diarrhea. Urinalysis shows moderate proteinuria. What is the most likely diagnosis?
k: HSP (IgA vasculitis) tetrad, normal platelet count.
r: Bloody diarrhea plus kidney involvement tempts HUS, but palpable purpura with arthralgia and normal platelets means HSP.
n: Printed answer A. HSP.

q: A 5-year-old child presents with drowsiness, abdominal pain, nausea and bloody diarrhea after ingesting an unknown number of iron tablets several hours before (see lab result). Test Result Normal Value Iron 94 9-21.5 umol/L Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
k: Iron poisoning: supportive care plus IV deferoxamine when systemic toxicity is present.
r: Charcoal does not bind iron: in symptomatic iron poisoning the answer is IV deferoxamine, not decontamination.
n: Second of 2 iron poisoning recalls: symptomatic iron toxicity with markedly high serum iron is treated with IV deferoxamine. Printed answer credited (MG). October By Similar update

q: A 2-year-old presented with sudden jaundice and fever for 3 days after flu-like illness. Family history of brother with severe neonatal jaundice treated with exchange. Hb is 90 (I think) What medication is contraindicated?
k: G6PD deficiency: X-linked, oxidant stress triggers intravascular hemolysis.
r: In a 'contraindicated drug' question with G6PD clues, aspirin beats paracetamol and ibuprofen.
n: Printed answer A: G6PD deficiency hemolysis (Mediterranean origin in the older recall); aspirin precipitates hemolysis. Inset is the older full version (same options, different order, with lab table) without its own answer line.

q: 12 yrs old girl. the child presented with pallor, lethargy, and fatigue, the family are strict vegetarians. She has decreased appetite. See this picture (exactly same pic) Hb: 9
k: Nutritional IDA in a child with an intact gut: start oral ferrous sulfate, correct the diet.
r: Switch to IV iron only when the story gives a reason oral iron cannot work (celiac, IBD, intolerance, failed adequate trial).

q: 12 week old child with beckwith-wiedemann syndrome with the mother concerned about increased risk for malignancy? (didn't mention liver). what tumor marker should be tested ?
o: Urine Homovanillic acid (HVA) and vanillylmandelic acid (VMA)
k: Beckwith-Wiedemann surveillance.
r: BWS + 'tumor marker' = AFP (hepatoblastoma); BWS + 'imaging' = abdominal ultrasound (Wilms).
n: Printed answer B. AFP (hepatoblastoma screening in Beckwith-Wiedemann). October By Similar update

q: 3 or 4 years Child came to ER before 12hours with fever and SOB, yesterday he had sore throat and dysphasia, on exam he looks toxic immobile in a chair opens his mouth with drooling of saliva. Vital singns: Tachycardic Tackypnic Tempreture 39 Oxygen sat 88% What's the Most appropriat next step or Next step (not sure)?
k: Toxic + drooling + tripod/open mouth posture + rapid onset = epiglottitis: secure the airway in a controlled setting.

q: babys mother came complaining of noisy breathing in her 2-4 months old child, theres no episdoes of distress or apnea monophasic wheezing?? + inspiratory stridor, weight gain and feeding is normal, the stridor disappears when baby is lying prone whats the management?
k: Positional stridor in infancy: diagnose by position, manage by growth and red flags.
r: Same diagnosis, different answer: add failure to thrive or apneic episodes and the answer flips to surgical management.
n: Laryngomalacia with normal growth and feeding: reassure and observe. Recaller: Recaller unsure of option C.

q: 2 hour newborn with TTN, placed on 30% oxygen which indicated the need for escalation of care

k: TTN should improve; a baby who needs more support is not behaving like TTN.
r: In neonatal distress the trend matters more than the label: increasing oxygen need = escalate.

q: school-aged child with asthma came to the ER with acute asthma exacerbation, SpO2 95%, peak flow meter at best 60, can complete ful sentences, took two pufs of salbutamol at home, mild wheeze on auscultation. Which is the most appropriate management?
o: Give salbutamol by spacer then reassess
k: Pediatric acute asthma: grade severity, then treat.
r: Full sentences and SpO2 above 92% = mild/moderate; spacer then reassess, not admission or ipratropium.
n: Mild exacerbation: salbutamol via spacer then reassess.

q: 7 Years old complains of chronic clear thin nasal discharge and easy nasal itching, o/e there is periorbital dark swollen and pale turbinates mucosa. What is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Allergic rhinitis: itch, sneeze, clear rhinorrhea, congestion.
r: Unilateral foul-smelling discharge = foreign body; bilateral clear itchy discharge with pale turbinates = allergic.
n: Clear rhinorrhea, itching, allergic shiners and pale boggy turbinates = allergic rhinitis. Recaller: Recaller: option B was written 'foreign body'.

q: A 5 y/o boy known case of cystic fibrosis. Presented with cough and SOB with green sputum recently (No period mention) and clubbing., Vitals: All stable (temperature is 37.3) Physical: Crackles all over Sputum culture: Positive for MSSA What’s the most appropriate next step in management?
k: CF exacerbation: treat the organism on sputum culture.
r: Stable child + known sputum organism = treat it now; tests that do not change management are distractors.
n: Stable CF child with MSSA on sputum: treat with oral anti-staphylococcal antibiotic (amoxicillin clavulanate).

q: An eight-month-old infant presented to the clinic with a history of multiple pyogenic infections with Streptococcus pneumoniae, along with recurrent otitis media and pneumonia. The mother also gave a history of chronic diarrhea. Which of the following investigation is required to reach the diagnosis?
k: Match the infection pattern to the immune arm: Encapsulated bacteria, sinopulmonary infections, onset after 6 months, Giardia: B-cell/antibody defect, test immunoglobulins.; Viral, fungal, opportunistic infections, failure to thrive from early infancy: T-cell or combined defect (SCID), test lymphocy
r: Infections that start only after 6 months of age point to antibody deficiency, because maternal IgG protected the first months.

q: A 6-hour-old newborn delivered by cesarean section because of sever fetal deceleration and meconium stained fluid. He required intubation and ventilation with iontropic support. Few hours later, he started to have low saturation with increase oxygen requirement. The pre ducal saturation is 92 while the post ductal saturation is 81. Chest X-ray done and showed no pneumothorax. Which of the following is the next step in the management?

r: Gap between pre- and post-ductal saturation in a ventilated neonate = PPHN = inhaled nitric oxide.
n: Reference question screenshot shown next to the 13a recall; option C is starred (**) and 'Nitric' highlighted. Differential pre/post ductal saturation indicates PPHN, treated with inhaled nitric oxide.

q: Boy with bacterial sinusitis, started on amoxicillin, didn’t improve after 3 days. What to do?
k: Pediatric acute bacterial sinusitis ladder.
r: The 72-hour mark is the decision point: no improvement on amoxicillin means add clavulanate, not wait or refer.
n: Printed answer C: failure of amoxicillin in bacterial sinusitis, escalate to amoxicillin-clavulanate.

q: 3-month-old boy presented to the ER with paroxysmal episodes of staccato cough, with inspiration between each cough. Associated with perioral cyanosis and post-tussive vomiting. No history of diarrhea. Illness preceded by conjunctivitis a few days ago. On examination, the child looks unwell and tachypneic with auscultatory crackles. Normal WBC count with elevated eosinophils. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Paroxysmal cough in a young infant: the extra features decide.
r: Staccato cough + conjunctivitis + eosinophilia = Chlamydia; add diarrhea and fever and it flips to adenovirus.
n: Staccato cough, preceding conjunctivitis, eosinophilia, afebrile infant -> Chlamydia trachomatis pneumonia. Compiler rule for this cluster: not vaccinated -> pertussis; diarrhea present -> adenovirus; staccato cough and conjunctivitis present -> Chlamydia. Oth

q: A 3-month-old boy presented to the Emergency Room with history paroxysmal episodes of staccato cough, inspiration between each cough. It is associated with perioral cyanosis and post-tussive vomiting. There is no history of diarrhea. This illness has been preceded by conjunctivitis few days ago. On examination, the child looks unwell and tachypneic with auscultatory crackles. He has normal white blood cell count with elevated eosinophils on laboratory evaluation. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Paroxysmal cough in a young infant: the extra features decide.
r: Read the prodrome: conjunctivitis before the cough = Chlamydia; runny nose before a whoop = pertussis.
n: Staccato cough, conjunctivitis, eosinophilia -> Chlamydia trachomatis pneumonia. Compiler rule for this cluster: not vaccinated -> pertussis; diarrhea present -> adenovirus; staccato cough and conjunctivitis present -> Chlamydia. Other versions of this recall

q: 5-year-old child has red eye, headache, sore throat, and fever. On examination the patient has bilateral conjunctivitis and tonsillitis with exudates. His 2-year-old brother had the same symptoms 2 days ago. What IS the likely cause? (No lymph node, no cough, no hepatosplenomegaly. no Gl symptoms were mentioned) (I Said Not Mentioned , Didn't Say Absent)
k: Sore throat + red eyes: think adenovirus.
r: Exudate does not mean strep: add conjunctivitis and a sick sibling and it is adenovirus.
n: Viral pharyngitis can also cause pharyngeal exudate and/or petechiae like bacterial; assess the full clinical picture, not only Centor features. GAS pharyngitis does NOT cause conjunctivitis; that is a feature of pharyngoconjunctival fever (adenovirus).

q: year-old boy presents with a barky cough, appears cyanotic, and has spells of breath holding. On auscultation, you hear a monophasic wheeze. There is no inspiratory stridor noted. What is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Noisy breathing in a child: the phase of the noise localises the lesion.
r: Barky cough does not always mean croup: barky cough + inspiratory stridor = croup or laryngomalacia; barky cough + monophonic wheeze and NO stridor = tracheomalacia.
n: Barky cough with monophonic wheeze, cyanotic spells and no inspiratory stridor: tracheomalacia (laryngomalacia gives inspiratory stridor). Recaller: Age missing from the start of the stem.

q: 4 year old boy came with barking cough and on auscultation there was monophonic wheeze and he was cyanotic with no inspiratory stridor?
k: Noisy breathing in a child: the phase of the noise localises the lesion.
r: Barky cough does not always mean croup: barky cough + inspiratory stridor = croup or laryngomalacia; barky cough + monophonic wheeze and NO stridor = tracheomalacia.
n: Compiler notes the age is just not right for this diagnosis, but all answers point one way: tracheomalacia. A different recall (3 year old) follows on the next page with the same answer. Other versions of this recall in this deck: SWR-0393 → B. Tracheomalacia

q: A mother is worried about her son who has asthma. What is the most appropriate counseling?
o: He will develop chronic lung disorder
Childhood asthma will disappear by adolescence
He will have asthma for the rest of his life
No correlation between childhood and adulthood asthma
k: Childhood asthma prognosis.
r: 'Most grow out of it' is the counselling answer; 'no correlation' sounds reassuring but is false.
n: Printed answer B; no further commentary.

q: child presents with symptoms suggestive of bronchial asthma, with episodes that worsen during upper respiratory tract infections. At this visit, the chest X-ray is normal. What is the best information to give the parents regarding this case?
o: Bronchial asthma increases the risk of upper respiratory tract infections.
k: Childhood asthma: clinical diagnosis with typical triggers.

q: Pedia developed sudden onset of cough and shortness of breath, the child had a history of eating cereal, the family denied any history of lever or choke, xray was given. Which of the following is the most likely the cause ?

r: Absence of a witnessed choking episode or a normal X-ray does not rule out aspiration; strong history still goes to bronchoscopy.
n: Labelled 'Full recall'. Answer B foreign body: initial investigation is CXR (already done); most appropriate is bronchoscopy.

q: A 10-year-old child inhales an alkaline substance and subsequently develops throat erythema, excessive salivation, and stridor. What is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Caustic (alkali) exposure with stridor = airway burn: secure the airway first.
r: Drooling plus stridor is not always epiglottitis; a caustic exposure history points to airway burn.
n: Compiler notes we need to know the other options.

q: A full-term newborn delivered by cesarean section develops tachypnea with mild chest retractions shortly after birth. The baby is placed on a nasal cannula for oxygen support. Chest X-ray shows prominent/interstitial lung markings etc I don't remember What is the most appropriate management?
o: Continue oxygen therapy and observe/support the infant
k: Neonatal respiratory distress by the vignette: TTN: term, cesarean, perihilar streaks and fluid in the fissures; resolves with support.; RDS: preterm, surfactant deficiency, ground-glass (reticulogranular) X-ray; surfactant and CPAP.; Meconium aspiration: meconium-stained fluid, patchy infiltrates a
r: Term plus cesarean plus fluid in the fissure = TTN: oxygen and observation, not antibiotics.
n: Not every respiratory distress requires antibiotics, especially when explained by an alternative cause (X-ray showing TTN). Term + C-section (not vaginal) means the risk of neonatal sepsis is very low.

q: Pediatric patient diagnosed with pneumonia and treated as an outpatient with oral antibiotics. He returns to the ER after 4 days with deterioration. O2 saturation: 85% despite oxygen face mask Drowsy Bilateral crepitations Moderate to severe respiratory distress What is the next management?
k: Escalation of respiratory support: Hypoxia, alert: escalate oxygen (nasal, face mask, non-rebreather, high flow); Failing but alert and cooperative: NIV (CPAP/BiPAP); Drowsy/reduced GCS, cannot protect airway, poor gag, copious secretions: intubate
r: Reduced consciousness is a contraindication to NIV: go straight to intubation.
n: Hypoxia + drowsy = invasive ventilation (altered consciousness contraindicates NIV).

q: 3ys boy Pharyngitis case, throat fast swab positive, What to do to prevent complications?
k: Strep throat: what each step achieves.
r: Stopping antibiotics when the child feels better is the error; the full 10 days is what prevents rheumatic fever.
n: Another version of GAS pharyngitis: 10 days of penicillin prevents rheumatic fever.

q: pedia has barking cough and inspiratory stridor and suprasternal retraction vital signs RR 25 temperature i think was below than 38 oxygen what i remembered was above 90% what you will give
k: Croup: viral (parainfluenza) subglottic narrowing; treat by severity.
r: Toxic, drooling child with no barking cough = epiglottitis, airway in the OR; barking cough in a stable child = dexamethasone.
n: Croup without severe features: dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg. Compiler says the options are meant to confuse; intubation in the OR is for epiglottitis (or severe life-threatening/refractory croup).

q: 8 yrs old came with Cough and fever (sign of croup).. the child look WELL setting in his mother lap .. on examination there is retraction of suprasternal and stridor .. best next step or initial (im not sure):
k: Croup: viral (parainfluenza) subglottic narrowing; treat by severity.
r: "Looks well" is the clue: steroid only; add epinephrine only for stridor at rest with distress.
n: Well-looking child with croup: dexamethasone. Compiler: even if epinephrine is among the options, do not choose it. Recaller: Recaller unsure whether lead-in was best next step or initial.

q: A pediatric patient presents with a barking cough, inspiratory stridor, and suprasternal retractions. The respiratory rate is 25 breaths/minute, temperature is 37.8 C, and oxygen saturation is above 90%. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

q: 2 years old male patient came in the morning Co low grade fever ,brassy cough and inspiratory stridor , just like that , what is the most appropriate management?

r: Low-grade fever + stridor = croup; high fever + toxic + drooling = epiglottitis.
n: Toddler with low-grade fever and acute stridor, no drooling: croup is the most common cause.

q: Peds chocked on peanut he had something in his right lower lung on imaging
k: Foreign body aspiration in children: History of choking is the key clue; often a toddler with nuts or seeds.; Signs: sudden cough, unilateral wheeze or reduced air entry.; CXR: ipsilateral hyperinflation with mediastinal shift away (check-valve air trapping), better seen on expiratory or decubitus f
r: A normal chest X-ray does not exclude an aspirated peanut; a convincing choking history still goes to bronchoscopy.
n: Bronchoscope based on the available information; approach to foreign body explained elsewhere.

q: 2 year old child with a history of recurrent ear infection found to have a dull retracted tympanic membrane with visible fluid level, but there is no fever, pain. What is the most likely diagnosis

q: A child presents with of respiratory infection attacks, complains of dry cough, particularly at night. Used a short-acting b2-agonist inhaler without significant improvement. What is the most appropriate treatment?
k: Uncontrolled on SABA alone (night symptoms, frequent reliever use) → add inhaled corticosteroid.
r: Nocturnal dry cough in a child is asthma until proven otherwise; night symptoms signal poor control and the need for ICS.
n: Uncontrolled asthma on SABA (nocturnal cough): step up to inhaled corticosteroid. Inset sibling (28 year old woman) also answers inhaled corticosteroid (MG).

q: Child presented with fever, pharyngeal erythema, and inflamed tonsils with white exudate, lymphadenopathy, or enlarged cervical lymph nodes, something like that. The ASO titer was high, maybe 700 or 800. What is the most likely organism?
k: Exudative tonsillitis + tender anterior cervical nodes + fever, no cough = GAS until proven otherwise.
r: ASO is a retrospective marker used mainly to support post-streptococcal disease (rheumatic fever, PSGN); for acute pharyngitis the test of choice is the rapid strep test or throat culture.
n: Printed answer B: exudative tonsillitis with high ASO titer indicates group A streptococcus.

q: A term newborn develops respiratory distress shortly after birth. Chest X-ray shows prominent pulmonary vascular markings with fluid fissures, What is the most appropriate initial management?
o: was either intubation or observe for hypoxia (I forgot what it was exactly)
k: Neonatal respiratory distress by gestation and CXR: Term, CS, fluid in fissures/perihilar streaks: TTN, supportive O2; Preterm, ground glass/air bronchograms: RDS, CPAP and surfactant; Meconium-stained, post term, patchy hyperinflation: meconium aspiration
r: TTN worsening or lasting beyond about 72 hours is not TTN; rethink RDS, pneumonia or heart disease.
n: Printed answer A: transient tachypnea of the newborn is managed supportively with supplemental oxygen. Other version of this recall in Part 1: SWR-0452 → D. NGT

q: An infant has required CPAP at 6 cm H2O for 2 months. When he is switched to nasal cannula, he develops respiratory distress and cyanosis, which improve when CPAP is restarted. What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Tracheomalacia secondary to prolonged mechanical ventilation
k: Dynamic airway collapse improves with positive pressure; fixed stenosis does not.
r: Bronchopulmonary dysplasia causes oxygen dependence in an ex-preterm; failing only when CPAP pressure is removed suggests an airway that collapses.
n: Printed answer B. Compiler notes that option A in the actual exam was Bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD), not Tracheomalacia.

q: 5 years old child presented with persistent shortness of breath. He's a past history of pneumonia 4 days ago for which he received oral Antibiotics. On physical examination, there's bilateral coarse crackles & moderate to severe respiratory distress. Vitals : HR : 110 (?) RR: 60 O2 saturation :: 85% BP isn't mentioned. Investigations: pCO2 : 70 pO2 : 45 pH: 7.2 which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Respiratory failure is defined by the blood gas.
r: When the stem hands you an ABG with high CO2 and low pH, the label is respiratory failure; ARDS needs a chest X-ray and P/F ratio.
n: Hypoxemia with hypercapnia and acidosis = (type 2) respiratory failure. Recaller: Recall accuracy +95%, recaller reorganized the information to memorize it.

q: A 3 years old child with persistent wheezing. His mother reported that he had choking attack 4 months ago. Evaluation of his past Serial CXR showed persistent right lower atelectasis and pneumonia. What is the best modality to establish diagnosis?
k: Foreign body aspiration: history of choking plus focal signs = bronchoscopy.
r: Recurrent pneumonia in the same lobe in a toddler points to a mechanical obstruction, not asthma.
n: Suspected retained foreign body aspiration: bronchoscopy establishes the diagnosis (and is therapeutic).

q: A child is diagnosed with tracheomalacia and has recurrent respiratory infections, pneumonia, and a weight below the 3rd percentile. What is the most appropriate management?
k: Rule: mild tracheomalacia = observe (self-resolves); severe (recurrent pneumonia, FTT, apneic spells) = surgical referral.
r: The word 'failure to thrive' or 'recurrent pneumonia' turns tracheomalacia from observation into surgery.
n: Severe tracheomalacia with recurrent infections and failure to thrive warrants surgical referral.

q: A pediatric patient on two inhalers presents by his mother with asthma with histrory of multiple exacerbations and hospitalization and the doctor was too busy to refer him to the education clinic to teach him how to use the spacer and inhaler what is the most likely consequence of this action ?
k: Before stepping up asthma treatment, check technique and adherence first.
r: "Doctor too busy to educate" questions always end in worse outcomes: more adverse events, not fewer.
n: Printed C: failing to provide inhaler technique education leads to poor control and more adverse events.

q: A 3-year-old alert and oriented girl presents to the Pediatric Emergency Department. with breathing difficulties and a barking cough. There is inspiratory stridor and. The girl has been suffering from a viral upper airway infection for the past two days. A physical examination shows moderate chest wall retractions.
k: Croup severity decides treatment.
r: Stridor at rest or retractions = add nebulized epinephrine to the steroid; salbutamol has no role in croup.
n: Moderate croup: printed answer is inhaled epinephrine and steroids; no further commentary.

q: A 3-year-old child presents with a nocturnal cough after recently recovering from an upper respiratory tract infection. His mother reports that he had a similar nocturnal cough following a previous upper respiratory tract infection. The doctor asks what treatment he used during the previous episode, and the mother replies, "an inhaler medication." Which of the following is the most crucial point to address during this consultation?
o: His symptoms will likely improve by preschool age
Antibiotic use can lead to long-term complications
k: Episodic cough/wheeze only with colds in a preschool child = viral-induced wheeze; counsel on good prognosis.
r: Symptoms only with colds and normal in between = transient viral wheeze, likely outgrown; interval or multi-trigger symptoms point to asthma instead.
n: Printed answer B (viral-induced wheeze/post-viral cough usually improves by preschool age).

q: Child, post tracheoesophageal fistula repair, mild respiratory symptoms No brassy cough, not toxic Bilateral expiratory wheez diagnosis?
k: Wheeze or noisy breathing after TEF repair = think tracheomalacia first.
r: Stridor that is INSPIRATORY points above the thoracic inlet (larynx, subglottis); EXPIRATORY wheeze points to the intrathoracic airway, as in tracheomalacia.
n: Printed answer B. Tracheomalacia (classic association after TEF repair). Compiler thinks the examinee mixed up recalls (e.g. 'no brassy cough' does not fit tracheomalacia).

q: pediatric patient developed fever and cough post urti, stony dulness on percussion what would you find on xray
k: Percussion note localizes the lesion: Stony dull: pleural effusion; Dull + bronchial breathing: consolidation; Dull + trachea pulled toward the side: collapse
r: Dull with bronchial breathing = consolidation; stony dull with reduced air entry = pleural effusion.
n: Stony dullness on percussion after a URTI indicates pleural effusion on X-ray.

q: Pedia Eating corn “or cereals” started to cough and went out but came to ER on examination right main bronchus wheezing X ray expiratory film was done and showed increased area in right lung Next:
k: Suspected paediatric foreign body aspiration with supportive history or imaging = rigid bronchoscopy (diagnostic and therapeutic).
r: A normal chest X-ray does not exclude aspiration; a convincing choking history alone is enough to proceed to rigid bronchoscopy.
n: Foreign body aspiration is managed via RIGID bronchoscope.

q: A 5 month old presents to the emergency department with a 3-day history of coryza and flu-like symptoms( sneezing cough and runny nose) . He develops respiratory distress with bilateral decreased air entry and diffuse crackles. There are marked subcostal and intercostal retractions. The skin is pale and peripheral pulses are week. Vital signs: BP: 100/70 mmHg; HR: 130 bpm; RR: 70/min; SpO2: 80% despite receiving 100% oxygen via a non-rebreather mask. What is the your immediate action?
k: Respiratory failure despite maximal oxygen = intubate.
r: Same infant with mild distress and SpO2 that corrects with oxygen: the answer is oxygen, not intubation.

q: 10 yo boy using inhaled steroid for treating asthma came complaining of whitish discoloration in the oral mucosa and white buccal with thrush What is the most appropriate management?
k: Oral candidiasis: topical first, systemic only if severe.
r: Thrush plus dysphagia or odynophagia suggests esophageal candidiasis, which needs systemic fluconazole, not nystatin.

q: An 18-month-old vaccinated child presents with fever and cough. The child looks well on examination, but crackles are heard over the right lower lobe. What is the most likely cause? (No other information were given)
k: Pediatric CAP organism by age.
r: Change the age to a school-age child with gradual cough and headache and the answer flips to Mycoplasma.
n: Printed answer: Streptococcus pneumoniae (lobar pneumonia in a vaccinated toddler).

q: A child with allergic rhinitis continues to experience frequent sneezing and prominent nasal congestion despite taking an antihistamine regularly. (allergic rhinitis) What is the most appropriate next step in pharmacotherapy?
k: Allergic rhinitis step-up: Allergen avoidance and saline irrigation throughout.; Mild or intermittent: oral second-generation antihistamine or intranasal steroid.; Congestion-predominant, moderate to severe, or failure of antihistamine: intranasal corticosteroid.
r: Congestion is the clue: antihistamines help sneezing and itch, intranasal steroids fix the blocked nose.
n: Printed answer intranasal corticosteroid. Compiler: if he has asthma WITH rhinitis, then B. Montelukast.

q: 7 years old child with cough and chest pain with sob. There is pleural effusion (stated in the question) X ray showed right lower consolidation What is the causative organism?
k: Pediatric pneumonia organism by age and picture.
r: Effusion alone does not mean Staph; lobar consolidation with effusion is still pneumococcus unless the stem adds post-flu or pneumatoceles.
n: No compiler commentary; printed answer line only.

q: 4 years old with asthma, he is responding to inhaled thereby, whats the most appropriate to confirm the diagnosis ?
k: Asthma is confirmed by spirometry with bronchodilator reversibility.
r: If the options include "trial of therapy" for a child under 5, that becomes the more age appropriate answer.
n: Spirometry, although it is not used below 4 to 5 years, but this is a general question.

q: 10-year-old pediatric patient presents with respiratory symptoms and a history of recurrent choking and aspirated foreign body On physical examination, right lower lobe consolidation is found. What is the diagnostic investigation?
k: Suspected foreign body aspiration: CXR first (inspiratory and expiratory), bronchoscopy to diagnose and remove.
r: 'Initial' = chest X-ray; 'diagnostic' or 'confirm' = bronchoscopy.
n: Initial/next investigation is CXR, but diagnostic is bronchoscopy (foreign body).

q: family brought their kid who has a fever, cough, and runny nose. Symptoms started after hx of choking after he ingested some seed. Chest exam: dec RT side breathing sound X ray pictures was shown What is the next thing to do?
o: Send home with antipyretic and nasal fluid
k: A choking episode plus unilateral chest signs = foreign body aspiration; remove it by rigid bronchoscopy.
r: When the X-ray is already shown in the stem, the 'next step' moves on to bronchoscopy.
n: Next is normally X-ray, but X-ray is already done, so next is bronchoscopy. Sequence: CXR then rigid bronchoscopy.

q: 5-week-old infant presents with paroxysmal coughing episodes associated with cyanosis and posttussive vomiting. The infant has mild tachypnea and is afebrile. Temperature: 36.9C Laboratory investigations: WBC: 27 x 10^9/L Lymphocytes: 80% What is the most appropriate management?
k: Paroxysmal cough + whoop or posttussive vomiting + lymphocytosis = pertussis, treat with a macrolide.
r: In infants under 1 month, choose azithromycin over erythromycin because erythromycin is linked to infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis.
n: Pertussis: treat with azithromycin.

q: 6-month-old infant presents with a history of recurrent cough and upper respiratory tract infections (URTI) about 7-8 episodes over the past year. What should we do?
o: Refer to ENT for tonsillectomy and adenoidectomy
k: Frequent colds in an otherwise well child = normal; look for red flags before investigating.
r: Seven episodes of TONSILLITIS suggests surgery; seven common colds just means a normal child who needs hand hygiene.
n: Printed answer hand hygiene (compiler finds it odd for a 6 month old). All answers make little sense anyway; tonsillectomy is for recurrent tonsillitis, not for cold/URTI.

q: m baby presented with cough and nasal congestion low oral intake Bilateral wheeze Tachypnic but alert O2 89%
o: high flow nasal o2 with iv fluid
iv antibiotic with xray to rule out pnemona
low oxgyen , frequent nasal suctioning , facilitate prober feeding
k: Bronchiolitis = supportive care only.
r: Wheeze in an infant tempts you to give salbutamol; in bronchiolitis the answer is oxygen, suction and fluids.
n: Bronchiolitis: supportive care with low flow oxygen, nasal suctioning and feeding support.

q: child had an URTI for 4 days (he has clear nasal discharge, fever, sneezing) , 3 days after resolving of the symptoms he presented with purulent nasal discharge and frontal tenderness. What's the diagnosis
k: Acute bacterial sinusitis in children: three clinical patterns.
r: Improvement then relapse = bacterial; steady improvement, even with colored mucus, = still viral.
n: Double worsening after initial improvement: acute bacterial rhinosinusitis (ABRS).

q: A child presents with wheezing that worsens during feeding and crying. On examination, there is monophasic bilateral expiratory wheezing. What is the most appropriate way to advise the parents?
o: Reassurance that it will mostly resolve spontaneously
k: Monophasic (homophonic) wheeze = large central airway; polyphonic wheeze = diffuse small airways.
r: Monophasic expiratory wheeze worse with crying/feeding = tracheomalacia; inspiratory stridor = laryngomalacia; both usually resolve, so reassure.
n: Tracheomalacia: reassure, mostly resolves spontaneously.

q: child presents with suspected airway foreign body aspiration (popcorn). What is the most appropriate
k: Suspected foreign body aspiration in a child: history decides, rigid bronchoscopy treats.
r: A normal chest X-ray does not exclude aspiration; a convincing choking history still goes to rigid bronchoscopy.
n: Printed answer B. Rigid bronchoscopy. Supporting screenshot of a similar question (choking history, CXR unilateral hyperinflation) with answer rigid bronchoscopy.

q: Term baby was a product of planned CS after delivery he was healthy cry immediately pink in color with good other parameters and good sucking reflex developed increases work of breathing and they put him on nasal prong Normal vital What is the next thing to do now:
k: Well term CS baby with mild early distress: think TTN and confirm with CXR.
r: Normal vitals in a well CS baby = investigate (CXR), not escalate.
n: Printed answer A. CXR (suspected transient tachypnea of the newborn after elective CS). Other version of this recall in Part 2: SWR-1551 → A. CXR

q: A full-term male infant is born to a 28-year-old primigravida via uncomplicated scheduled Cesarean section at 39 weeks of gestation. At 2 hours of life, the neonate develops tachypnea, nasal flaring, and mild intercostal retractions Most next step
k: Elective CS + term + mild distress in first hours = TTN; CXR is the next step.
r: No labour and intact membranes means sepsis is unlikely; image the chest before reaching for antibiotics.
n: Options B and C marked red; printed answer B. Term baby born via scheduled elective C-section has extremely low risk of neonatal sepsis, so option C (antibiotics) is wrong; CXR for suspected TTN.

q: A newborn is suspected to have meconium aspiration syndrome at birth and presents with respiratory distress. What is the appropriate initial management?
o: Suction the airway before stimulating the baby
k: Meconium stained newborn: treat like any other baby; no routine suctioning.
r: If the baby is apnoeic or HR <100, the answer becomes positive pressure ventilation, not oxygen alone.
n: Printed answer B (routine suctioning before stimulation is no longer recommended).

q: A child with a history of otitis media underwent tympanostomy tube insertion, which remained in place for a certain period. The child loves to swim. After some time, purulent ear discharge was noted coming through the tympanostomy tube. Which of the following bacteria is the most likely causative organism?
k: Ear infection organism depends on the route: nasopharynx vs water.
r: The words 'swimming' or 'water' turn an ear-infection organism question into Pseudomonas.
n: Tube otorrhea with water exposure (swimming, red hint) is classically Pseudomonas aeruginosa.

q: A preterm newborn, 27 or 29 weeks (not sure), suddenly developed bradycardia and apnea, then responded after stimulation. What is the most likely cause?
o: Immaturity of the central respiratory center
k: Apnea of prematurity is a diagnosis of exclusion in a preterm with recurrent apneas.
r: Sudden apnea that responds to stimulation in a very preterm baby = apnea of prematurity; progressive distress from birth = RDS.
n: Apnea of prematurity: immaturity of the central respiratory center, responds to stimulation. Recaller: Option C printed in Arabic as 'forgot the rest'; gestational age not sure.

q: Pediatric Pt had pneumonia with fever , Respiratory rate of 44 , cough, sob Whichis most sensitive for the diagnosis in this case ?
k: Pediatric pneumonia: tachypnea is the most sensitive sign.
r: Most SENSITIVE = tachypnea; signs of SEVERITY are hypoxia and chest indrawing, which a "severity" lead in would ask for.
n: Tachypnea (respiratory rate) is the most sensitive sign of pneumonia in children (red hint on 'most sensitive').

q: A 5-year-old child presents with recurrent upper respiratory tract infections. The mother reports that the child frequently complains of sore throat, nasal congestion, and fever. The child has a history of asthma, and the mother states that she uses a metered-dose inhaler with a spacer as prescribed. On examination, there is mild wheeze, sore throat, and erythema. What is the most important educational advice to give the mother?
o: Ensure proper use of the inhaler as prescribed
Advise giving the child vitamin C-containing juices
k: Pediatric asthma education: correct inhaler use and adherence come first.
r: When an asthma question asks for the "most important advice", the answer is almost always proper inhaler technique and adherence, not a new drug or restriction.
n: No commentary; printed answer C with the word Ensure highlighted in red.

q: 10 year child has severe uncontrolled bronchial asthma. he has nighttime cough almost every night and is on an inhaler. the child's room is well ventilated and sunny. the family has 2 cats at the house. the child is not compliant on inhaler and misses his medication 1 or 2 days every week. what is the most important step in management?
k: Persistent asthma: daily ICS is the foundation; LABA, LTRA and oral steroids are add-ons.
r: Never give a LABA without an ICS in asthma; if a LABA option looks attractive, look for the ICS option.
n: Compiler questions whether there was no prior exacerbation, but still chooses B, ICS. Recaller: Examinee: the question was exactly like this with the poor grammar; it asked most important step (not next step) and did not mention what inhaler he was on.

q: A mother came with her 13 yo son complaining of dry cough on and off and she mentioned a weird smell on his clothes. In a private interview with him he said that he was experimenting with smoking in school breaks with a group of his friends.
o: Inform school to take disciplinary measures
Counsel him about the risks of smoking
k: Adolescent risk behavior: interview privately, keep confidentiality, counsel first.
r: The doctor's job is to counsel, not to punish or over-refer: a teen experimenting with cigarettes gets brief counseling first.
n: Adolescent experimenting with smoking: counsel him on the risks (brief intervention) rather than referral or disciplinary measures.

q: Inspiratory stridor + low grade fever + cough, not distressed, what is the management:
k: Croup: severity decides treatment.
r: Steroid for every croup; add epinephrine only when there is stridor at rest or distress.
n: Printed answer B (dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg) for mild croup; no further commentary.

q: A 3-year-old boy presents with recurrent wheezing. His mother reports a choking episode 4 months ago. Serial chest radiographs have repeatedly shown right lower lobe pneumonia and atelectasis. Which diagnostic test has the highest diagnostic value?
k: Recurrent pneumonia in the same lobe + choking history = retained foreign body.
r: A suggestive choking history needs bronchoscopy even with normal X-rays; recurrent pneumonia in one lobe is the clue.
n: Retained foreign body aspiration; bronchoscopy is diagnostic (and therapeutic).

q: 8 yo boy came with knee sweeling and redness and so on, pain was limitng his movement he cries as soon as he walks on that limb What to do next important step
k: Hot swollen joint + refusal to bear weight in a child = septic arthritis: tap the joint first.
r: Fever + hot joint + pain on any movement = aspirate before antibiotics; a transient synovitis child looks well and walks with a limp.
n: Rule: aspirate (joint fluid) before antibiotics in suspected septic arthritis. Recaller: Recaller (Arabic): the question had odd wording so I forgot what it was.

q: A 5-month-old infant is growing normally, but his mother is concerned about a harsh inspiratory sound (stridor). It increases with playing, feeding, and illness, and decreases when he is relaxed and in the prone position. What is the next step?
o: CT of the head and upper chest
k: Laryngomalacia: most common cause of chronic stridor in infants; positional and benign.
r: Normal growth = reassure; poor weight gain or apnea flips the answer to laryngoscopy and surgical referral.
n: Laryngomalacia with normal growth: reassurance.

q: Newborn With TTN Not Decanting. X-Ray Showed Fluid In The Fissures. Something Like This N What Should You Do?
k: TTN: term or near-term baby, often C-section, tachypnea soon after birth, fissure fluid on X-ray, resolves on its own; treat with oxygen and support.
r: Fluid in the fissures = TTN = oxygen and wait; ground glass in a preterm = RDS = surfactant.
n: Transient tachypnea of the newborn is managed supportively with oxygen.

q: 10 years old boy fully immunized came to the emergency department complain of sore throat, runny nose, examination he has enlarged tonsil with yellow exudate interior. anterior Cervical lymph nodes was large and tender to touch, other examam were unremarkable strep rapid test was positive. What is the next step management?
k: Sore throat ladder in children.
r: Positive rapid strep = treat now; only a NEGATIVE rapid test in a child needs a throat culture.
n: Positive rapid strep test with exudative tonsillitis = treat GAS pharyngitis with oral penicillin V. Inset version also answers penicillin V.

q: 10 years old boy presented to the emergency department with fever, headache and sore throat for 2 days, in examination there were enlarged tonsils with exudate and pharyngeal petechiae. He had enlargement of anterior and posterior cervical lymph nodes. The rapid strep test was positive . BP: 100/65 T: 39 Others normal What's the most appropriate next step in management?
k: GAS pharyngitis versus infectious mononucleosis.
r: Read the test result first: positive rapid strep = treat with penicillin; negative test plus posterior nodes and splenomegaly = mononucleosis.
n: Older recall version in inset; positive rapid strep test needs no confirmatory culture, treat with oral penicillin V. Other version of this recall in Part 3: SWR-2685 → A. infectious mononucleosis

q: 18 months old with 7-8 episode of cold in one year, otherwise healthy, his parents asking about anything that could prevent these episodes, what's your advice?
o: Reassure and tell them about Hand Hygiene
Refer to ENT for possible Tonsillectomy or Adenoidectomy
k: Frequent colds in a thriving young child = normal immune maturation; reassure and advise hand hygiene.
r: The number of colds alone is not a red flag; growth failure or severe, unusual infections are.
n: 6 to 8 uncomplicated colds a year is normal in young children; reassure and advise hand hygiene. Inset version also answers reassurance and hand hygiene.

q: Healthy Child got cold 7-8 times last year, that lasts for a few days and resolves with no complications, (everything else was normal in the case) The parents are asking about how to prevent?
o: Referral to ENT for possible adenotonsillectomy
k: Recurrent uncomplicated colds in a thriving child: reassure and advise hand hygiene.
r: "Resolves with no complications" plus "everything else normal" means reassure; do not confuse colds with recurrent tonsillitis.
n: Older recall version in inset; normal frequency of colds, reassure and advise hand hygiene.

q: 18months fully vaccinated with URTI and right lower (crepitations?) in the lung. Which of the following is most likely causative organism?
k: Pediatric CAP organism by age: Neonate: GBS, E. coli, Listeria.; 1 to 3 months afebrile with staccato cough, conjunctivitis: Chlamydia trachomatis.; 3 months to 5 years: viruses (RSV) most common overall; S. pneumoniae most common bacterium.
r: Focal (lobar) crackles + toddler = pneumococcus; diffuse signs + school-age child + dry cough = Mycoplasma.
n: Printed answer: Streptococcus pneumoniae (most common cause of lobar community acquired pneumonia in a vaccinated toddler).

q: Baby 3 months old Wheezing, respiratory distress, low grade fever. Saturation is 89% and has retraction of chest. Management:
o: High flow oxygen and IV fluid
Low flow oxygen and suction of nose with appropriate feeding care
Chest X-ray to rule out pneumonia
k: Bronchiolitis = supportive care only.
r: Low saturation means oxygen, not antibiotics or steroids; start with low-flow and escalate only if it fails.
n: Printed answer B: supportive care for bronchiolitis (oxygen when saturation is low, nasal suction, feeding support).

q: Newborn with grunting with no desaturation (stated like this) what to add to add to the management? (No other vitals mentioned)
k: Grunting, flaring, retractions or tachypnea in a newborn = respiratory distress; support breathing first, then find the cause.
r: In a newborn, grunting is a distress sign even when saturation is still normal.
n: Printed answer B. Oxygen; no further commentary. Recaller: Only two options recalled; no other vitals mentioned.

q: Child with red membrane , exudate ASO 700 or 500
k: Bacterial vs viral pharyngitis.
r: Exudate plus raised ASO = streptococcal; cough and coryza = viral.
n: Embedded 15-16 September recall; printed answer A.

q: Child came to ER before 12hours with fever and SOB, yesterday he had sore throat and dysphasia, on exam he looks toxic with drooling of saliva , tachycardic tachypneic Fever 40 What's the next step?
k: Epiglottitis: airway first, then antibiotics.
r: Toxic drooling child: never send to X-ray or examine the throat; go to the OR to secure the airway.
n: Printed answer C: suspected epiglottitis, secure the airway with laryngoscopy in the operating room.

q: Child with recurrent infection, recurrent hospitalization due to pneumonia respiratory distress they did rigid broncoscopy and found trachea to be collapsaple 95% of lower part of trachea What to do with tracheostomy?
k: Tracheomalacia = dynamic airway collapse; treat by splinting with positive pressure.
r: If "positive pressure ventilation" is an option, choose it. Otherwise choose the option that still delivers positive pressure (NIV).
n: Answer A. Tracheomalacia: management is tracheostomy with positive pressure ventilation; if a 'positive pressure' option is present, go for it (new). Here there was no PPV option, so non invasive ventilation. Recaller: No PPV option.

q: A 5-month-old child came complaining of cough and sneezing for 3 days. On examination, there is decreased breath sounds bilaterally and bilateral crepitations. He is on O2 100% non-rebreather mask, and his O2 is still 80%. BP: 100/70 RR: 70 Heart rate: 130 O2: 80% Temp: 38.4 What is the most appropriate immediate action?
k: Infant respiratory distress ladder: oxygen, then non-invasive support, then intubation.
r: Saturation still low on a non-rebreather = oxygen has failed; the answer moves to the airway, not to drugs.
n: Printed answer D. Persistent hypoxemia (80%) despite 100% non-rebreather in an infant with bronchiolitis/pneumonia indicates respiratory failure requiring intubation and ventilation.

q: 2 years child presents with fever , cough, shortness of brith , and he breath 50 breaths per minute he appears lethargic. on auscultation there is coarse crackles in the right lower lobe . What is the most clinical finding suggest the presence of pneumonia?
k: Pediatric pneumonia: tachypnea is the most sensitive sign; absence of tachypnea makes pneumonia unlikely.
r: Sensitive sign of pneumonia = tachypnea; judge it against the age specific cut off, not adult numbers.
n: Tachypnea is the most sensitive sign for pneumonia (illustrated).

q: A 3-year-old child presents with fever, shortness of breath, and cough. On examination, the respiratory rate is 50 breaths per minute. Chest examination reveals crackles in the right lower lobe. What is the most sensitive clinical finding suggestive of pneumonia in this child?
k: Tachypnea is the single most sensitive sign of pneumonia in children.
r: Most sensitive = tachypnea; do not be pulled to fever, which is the commonest but nonspecific feature.
n: Embedded earlier recall (#50). Illustrated: tachypnea is the most sensitive sign for pneumonia.

q: previously healthy 13-month-old girl has a 2-day history of fever and increasing cough. She is fully immunized, alert, mildly ill, with crackles over the right lung base, no grunting or retractions, and oxygen saturation 95%. Which organism is most likely?
k: Pediatric CAP organisms by age.
r: Fully immunized removes Hib; under 5 with focal crackles = S. pneumoniae, at 5 years or older think Mycoplasma.

q: Rr 50 fever cough Which clinical finding is the most sensitive for pneumonia?
k: Tachypnea = most sensitive clinical sign of childhood pneumonia.
r: Most sensitive = respiratory rate; most specific findings are focal signs such as crackles or bronchial breathing.
n: Tachypnea (respiratory rate) is the most sensitive clinical finding for pneumonia.

q: 3 years old toxic child with saliva drooling down the chin immobile sittings up temp 40 respiratory rate 36 heart rate 133 which organism responsible ?
k: Upper airway infection in children: match picture to organism.
r: Barking cough means croup (parainfluenza); drooling with a toxic child and no cough means epiglottitis (Hib).
n: Epiglottitis picture: Haemophilus influenzae type B.

q: Child (idk exact age) has severe uncontrolled bronchial asthma. He has cough, especially at night (DESPITE) using inhaler frequently. The child's room is well ventilated and sunny. The family has 2 cats at the house. (Did not mention anything regarding compliance, only mentioned that uncontrolled despite frequent use of inhaler.) What is the most important step in management (not sure)?
k: Uncontrolled on reliever alone = step up by adding an inhaled corticosteroid.
r: If the stem says he is already on an ICS with good adherence and technique, trigger control (the cats) or a step up becomes the answer; on reliever only, start the ICS.
n: Printed answer A: uncontrolled asthma with frequent reliever use needs a controller (inhaled corticosteroid) despite the cat exposure distractor. Recaller: These are the only medications mentioned 100%. Other options did not make sense, I do not remember them

q: A premature infant required CPAP/oxygen support for a prolonged period. After transition off CPAP, the infant develops a monophasic expiratory wheeze. What is the complication?
o: Tracheomalacia due to prolonged airway support
k: Site of the noise localizes the airway lesion.

q: 5-year-old with persistent shortness of breath; pneumonia 4 days ago treated with oral antibiotics; bilateral coarse crackles and moderate-to-severe respiratory distress. HR 110, RR 60, SpO2 85%; pCO2 70, pO2 45, pH 7.2. Most likely diagnosis?

r: When the stem hands you a full blood gas with low pO2, high pCO2 and low pH, the question is testing respiratory failure, not the underlying lung pathology.
n: Printed answer B. Hypoxemia with hypercapnia and acidosis (pO2 45, pCO2 70, pH 7.2) defines respiratory failure. Source inset 21-23 September recall (31-September-Without-Repetition-Part-4 p. 664) also answers B. Slide cites p. 123.

q: 3y old, 89% on room air, moderate to severe respiratory distress RR:60

n: RF is on room air; ARDS must be on oxygen. Berlin criteria for ARDS in adults are the same in pediatrics (except some modifications).

n: Printed answer B. Oral amoxicillin (acute bacterial sinusitis, symptoms over 10 days).

q: A 3-year-old child presents with a cough and wheezing that worsen after upper respiratory tract infections (URTIs)The child has previously experienced similar episodes and improved after using inhaled medication( not written what it is) Consulnig parents ?
o: Symtombs of wheez will subside preschool ( exactly like this )
Subtamol inhaler reduce or stop developing of asthma

Episodic viral wheeze: only with colds, well between: usually outgrown by school age; SABA during episodes; Multiple-trigger wheeze: also with exercise, laughter, allergens: higher asthma risk; consider ICS trial; Predictors of persistent asthma: eczema, allergic rhinitis, pa
r: Bronchodilators treat the episode; they never prevent asthma.
n: Printed answer A (viral-induced wheeze usually subsides by preschool/school age).

q: A 3 years old, hx of URTI, complaining of wheezing, no hx atopy within family, no allergies, takes inhaler(?), Family concerned about wheezing What is the appropriate counseling
o: Salbutamol improves developing asthma or wheeze
k: Preschool wheeze phenotypes: Transient/viral wheeze: only with colds, no atopy, usually outgrown; Persistent/atopic: eczema, allergies, parental asthma, wheeze between colds: likely asthma; Most children with mild, viral triggered wheeze become symptom free
r: Atopy (eczema, allergy, parental asthma) is what predicts persistence; its absence here makes reassurance correct.
n: Printed answer A (transient viral wheeze, no atopy, resolves with age).

q: 3 year old child came with nocturnal cough and wheezing that preceded by URTI 1 week ago, she had a previous history of extended respiratory symptoms after URTI. The mother is concerned about the wheezing, what is the best counseling advice for her?
o: Inhaled Salbutamol will prevent develop asthma
Wheezing will disappear at preschool age
k: Viral triggered wheeze in preschoolers: Wheeze only with colds, symptom free between; Usually outgrown with airway growth; Relief with SABA during episodes
r: Counseling questions on preschool wheeze reward reassurance about natural history, not drug myths.
n: Printed answer B.

q: A. mother brings her child, who has asthma, to the clinic. She explains that she finds it difficult to take her child outdoors because the child requires a nebulizer. She must carry the nebulizer equipment and medication whenever they leave home. She asks the physician for a more convenient way to administer the child's treatment. What is the most appropriate recommendation?
o: Advise the mother to keep her child indoors and avoid outdoor activities.
Educate the mother on using a metered-dose inhaler with an appropriate spacer instead of the nebulizer.
Change the child's medication to an alternative drug.
k: Inhaler device choice in children: MDI + spacer = nebulizer in effectiveness, and portable; Under about 4 years: MDI + spacer with face mask; Older children: spacer with mouthpiece
r: Poor control or device complaints: fix technique and device before changing the drug.
n: Printed answer B: switch to MDI with spacer instead of nebulizer.

q: 6ys old Child with Bronchial asthma on ventoiln nebulizer. Family is stressed and can't go out because the nebulizer needs electric supply. What do you counsel?
o: Adding Oral treatment to improve situation
Teach how to use inhaler and advise stopping nebulizer
Staying home because asthma control is top priority
k: Asthma device choice in children.
r: Spacer equals nebuliser for salbutamol, so the inhaler wins on practicality.
n: Printed answer C. Teach how to use inhaler and advise stopping nebulizer.

q: A 3-year-old child with bronchial asthma on ventolin nebulizer at home as per needs. The mother expresses concern that the family cannot go out of the home most of the time because the nebulizer machine need electricity power source. Which of the following is the most appropriate counselling should be given?
o: Agree and support their decision as the priority is asthma control
Find someone to take care of asthmatic child if family goes out of the home
Educate with clear instructions inhaler usage and advice to stop nebulizer
Find out nebulizer machine with portability feature
k: Device choice in childhood asthma: Under about 4 years: MDI plus spacer plus face mask; About 4 years and older: MDI plus spacer with mouthpiece; Older children/adolescents may use dry powder inhalers
r: MDI with spacer is as good as a nebuliser, so "portable nebuliser" is the tempting but wrong answer.
n: Embedded inset: question bank version with 4 options; answer educate on inhaler use and stop the nebulizer. October By Similar update

q: A 4 years old male patient who is a known asthmatic is on ventolin nebuliser at home AS NEEDED. The mother states that due to the nebuliser requiring electrical output, her and the family are unable to leave the house? How do you council her regarding the situation?
o: Advise her to stay at home as the nebuliser is more important
Advise her on the use of inhaler and advise her to stop the nebuliser
k: Inhaler with spacer = nebuliser for salbutamol delivery in children, and more practical.
r: The barrier is the device, not the disease: change the device, not the family's life.
n: Switch to MDI with spacer and stop the nebuliser; older inset version also answers C. Recaller: Recaller (Arabic): I was devastated trying to remember this question.

q: Child with asthma is using a Ventolin nebulizer. His mother says she cannot take him outside because the nebulizer requires an electrical power source. What is the most appropriate advice?
o: Educate how to use a the inhaler and Advise to stop the nebulizer
Advise the child to stay at home
Prescribe a portable nebulizer for outdoor use
k: MDI + spacer is as effective as a nebulizer for salbutamol in children.
r: A device that limits the child's life is a reason to change the device to an inhaler, not to change the child's life or the drug.
n: Printed answer A. Educate on inhaler use and advise stopping the nebulizer.

q: Asthmatic child not going outside because he was on nebulizer device that needs electricity his mother came for counsling i forgot the rest.
o: Forget but i think was adding medication
Advice him on spacer and educate him on it
not going outside is better because asthma is a priority
k: MDI + spacer = nebulizer for bronchodilator delivery in children.
r: When the barrier is the device, change the device to an inhaler with spacer, not the drug or the child's lifestyle.
n: Printed answer C with source tag (MG).

q: Asthmatic patient came with exacerbation , he uses a nebulizer in his home with electrical machine and he's most of the time outside what to do for him
o: Switch to another nebulizer that he can use outside
k: Reliever must be with the patient at all times.
r: Equal efficacy plus portability is why the inhaler beats any nebulizer for daily life.
n: Printed answer 'Give him inhaler' with source tag (MG); options were unlettered and lettered by position.

q: A 6-year-old child with asthma is now complaining of cough, increased asthma attacks, and more frequent use of his inhaler. The mother reports that the father smokes one pack per day inside the house, and the mother uses shisha on weekends. What should be done to prevent worsening of the child's symptoms?
o: Tell the mother to stop using shisha or reduce it
Advise the parents to reduce the child's exposure to smoking
k: Before stepping up asthma therapy, check: adherence, inhaler technique, triggers (smoke, allergens), comorbidities.
r: When two answers both reduce smoke, choose the one that removes ALL exposure, not one smoker's habit.
n: Printed answer C; embedded inset (same version) prints the same answer. Compiler notes: Similar recall: 11 Feb, Athar's Code.

q: Child diagnosed with asthma and mother still give medium inhealer as percsribe when exam patient found sore throat and nasal congestion, what is correct according to education or something
o: Tell mother not to use inhealer in cold
Educat mother about how to use inhealer
k: Inhaler education points for parents.
r: Throat symptoms in a child on an inhaled steroid point to technique (no spacer, no mouth rinse), not to stopping the medicine.
n: Recaller: Only 2 options recalled

q: A 5-year-old girl with asthma has recurrent respiratory infections, low-grade fever, and cough. She uses her inhaler with a spacer as needed. What is the most important thing to educate the mother about?
o: Advise the mother to use the inhaler as prescribed
Do not use the inhaler when she has a cold
k: Asthma education core: correct use of the prescribed inhalers, adherence, technique, written action plan, trigger avoidance.
r: A cold is a reason to use the inhaler, never a reason to stop it.

q: 6 years old In asthmatic with frequent exacerbation, what is the preventative teaching point?
k: Uncontrolled or frequently exacerbating asthma: check technique, adherence and triggers before escalating.
r: Word swap trap: "how to use inhaler" = answer; per the author, "how to use spacer" flips the answer to environmental control.
n: Compiler (Telegram screenshot): if option C was 'Teach how to use inhaler' it is correct; if it was 'Teach how to use spacer' it is wrong and choose D. Environmental control. The slide prints 'inhaler' in red, so C.

q: Pediatric Asthma: Inhaler Technique A child with bronchial asthma presents with frequent exacerbations. Further history reveals that the child does not use the prescribed inhaler correctly. What is the most appropriate preventive intervention?
k: Uncontrolled asthma checklist before escalation: technique, adherence, environment.
r: Recurrent exacerbation prevention recalls with no other fix offered are keyed to environmental control; check how each version words the technique clue.

q: Year old Boy known case of asthma on inhaled steroid presented in the clinic white discoloration toung. Examination relieved white toung with witesh plaques on buccal mucosa. Which of the following medication is the best choice ?
k: ICS side effects: oral candidiasis and dysphonia.
r: Continue the inhaled steroid; treat the thrush topically and teach mouth rinsing.

q: A 10-year-old boy with a history of asthma presents with whitish patches on his tongue and inner cheeks. He has been using his inhaled corticosteroid regularly. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
k: Oral thrush from inhaled steroids: topical antifungal + mouth rinse, keep the ICS.
r: Do not stop or step down a controlling ICS because of thrush; treat topically and teach mouth rinsing.
n: Compiler answer line A. Nystatin; bank tag [Review]. ICS-related oral candidiasis is treated with topical nystatin (and mouth rinsing after inhaler use).

q: A 5-year-old child with bronchial asthma under control with inhalers. Mother concerned about the future of her child's asthma during adulthood. the most likely prognosis?
o: Most of the children grow out of it
No correlation between childhood and adulthood asthma
k: Childhood asthma prognosis.
r: Reassure the mother: most grow out of it, but mild relapse in adulthood can happen.
n: Similar recall: 12-14 Feb, 21-23 Jul, MedGard.

q: A 5-year-old child with asthma is brought by his mother. She is worried about his asthma in adulthood. Which of the following best describes the prognosis?
o: Childhood asthma is unrelated to adult asthma.
Childhood asthma will disappear in adulthood.
Childhood asthma will become worse in adulthood.
Childhood asthma will persist into adulthood
k: Childhood asthma prognosis: Most children grow out of it, often by adolescence; Persistence more likely with: severe or frequent symptoms, atopy/eczema, parental asthma, early sensitization, female sex, smoke exposure; Remission may be followed by relapse in adulthood
r: For the worried parent, the exam answer is reassurance: most children grow out of asthma.
n: Embedded inset of the same version from 15-16 August prints B. Childhood asthma will disappear in adulthood. Printed again later in this file (p.5217).

q: A mother is worried about her son who has asthma. Most appropriate counseling?
o: He will develop a chronic lung disorder
Childhood asthma will disappear by adolescence
He will have asthma for the rest of his life
There is no correlation between childhood and adult asthma
k: Prognosis of childhood asthma: most children improve or become symptom free by adolescence.
r: "Most grow out of it" is the counseling answer; reserve lifelong persistence for severe, atopic, female or parental asthma cases.
n: Printed B: many children outgrow childhood asthma by adolescence. Other versions of this recall in this deck: OCT-1381 → B. Childhood asthma will disappear by adolescence October By Similar update

q: A child with asthma complaining of night time cough and (not sure if it exacerbation also present) he have 2 cat at home, his room is well ventilated, he is not complaints to inhalers miss 2-3 days per week How should you manage this patients?
k: Persistent symptoms (night cough) = needs a daily controller, and the first controller is ICS.
r: LABA without ICS is never correct in asthma; if LABA appears as an option, it is a distractor unless ICS is already on board.
n: Printed answer C (inhaled corticosteroids). Compared with the 21-23 September inset, where the compiler questions 'No prior exacerbation?' but still chooses ICS. Recaller: Recaller unsure whether exacerbation was present; option D not recalled.

q: A 10-year-old with severe uncontrolled asthma has night cough almost every night. His room is ventilated and sunny; the family has 2 cats. He misses his inhaler 1–2 days a week. What is the most important step?
k: Persistent symptoms (night waking, frequent reliever use) = needs ICS.
