q: Child presented to the ER with acute asthma excerbation, had similar attacks preceded by viral infections, there is no cyanosis only subcostal retractions What is the first line for his acute exacerbation?
k: Acute asthma sequence: O2 if hypoxic, then SABA, then ipratropium (SAMA), then systemic steroid, then reassess, then IV MgSO4, then intubation.
r: Viral triggered wheeze history does not change the acute step: bronchodilator (SABA) first, steroid second.
n: Printed answer D. Inhaled short-acting beta2 agonist; first line for acute asthma exacerbation is SABA. Embedded older version also answers inhaled SABA. Recaller: recaller kept original letters A and D only; B and C were irrelevant

q: Case about asthmatic child with acute asthma presented to ER asking about first line ttt?
o: IV corticosteroids or MgSo4 can't exactly remember
k: Acute asthma ladder: O2, then SABA, then SAMA, then systemic steroid, then reassess / ICU, then IV MgSO4, then intubation.
r: If the lead in is "not improving after SABA, ipratropium and steroid", the answer moves to IV magnesium sulfate.
n: Embedded inset: older version with different options; printed Answer: C. Inhaled short acting beta2 agonist.

q: A child-presented with tracheomalacia s/s ماذكر التشخيص presents with bilateral monophasic wheezing. The child shows no severe respiratory distress. What is the most appropriate management?
k: Tracheomalacia vs asthma wheeze: Tracheomalacia: monophasic, central, expiratory; present since early infancy; no bronchodilator response; Asthma: polyphonic, diffuse; responds to salbutamol; Diagnosis: bronchoscopy
r: Monophasic wheeze + no distress = reassure; reserve surgery for cyanotic or apneic spells.
n: Lookalike printed under 'See below' for Q21. Mild tracheomalacia without severe distress is managed with reassurance (most outgrow it). Recaller: Arabic note in stem: the diagnosis was not mentioned (only signs/symptoms). October By Similar update

q: A patient presents with a monophasic wheeze, hinting towards tracheomalacia. The patient's weight is in the 50th percentile with stable growth. What is the management?
k: Tracheomalacia / laryngomalacia: noisy breathing, expiratory wheeze or stridor, self-limiting.
r: Normal growth is the clue that converts a structural airway diagnosis into reassurance.
n: Embedded inset (21-23 July): different option order and adds normal growth; printed Answer: C. Reassure.

q: ولد عمره 7 سنين جاء في سؤال exacerbation of asthma .. وصح عشان اخد 2 puffs of salbutamol ... لكن كل حاجة حرفيا كويسة فيه لماذا؟ عشان ... ف ايش دورك تعمل؟
o: give him salbutamol w spacer and reassess
k: Mild to moderate acute asthma in children: SABA via MDI + spacer, then reassess.
r: An exacerbation that looks fine after 2 puffs still needs bronchodilator via spacer and reassessment, not discharge and not antibiotics.
n: Printed answer B (salbutamol with spacer and reassess). Recaller: Arabic stem, roughly: a 7-year-old boy with asthma exacerbation who took 2 puffs of salbutamol, but everything is literally fine on assessment; what is your role? Only 3 options recalled.

q: 9-school-aged child with asthma came to the ER with acute asthma exacerbation, Sp02 95%, peak flow meter at best 60, can complete ful sentences, took two pufs of salbutamol at home, mild wheeze on auscultation. Which is the most appropriate management?
o: Give salbutamol by spacer then reassess
k: Acute asthma: grade severity first, then SABA and reassess; escalate only with severe features or poor response.
r: Full sentences with normal saturation = mild; give salbutamol by spacer and reassess before any admission decision.
n: Printed answer D; embedded inset of the same version also prints 'Answer : D'. Mild exacerbation (full sentences, SpO2 95%) is managed with inhaled salbutamol via spacer and reassessment. 19 October update ↻ Printed again later in this 19 October file (p.876)

q: 3-year-old child presented to the ER with 3 days history of coughing and noisy breathing. His symptoms started after choking on some seeds. His past medical history is unremarkable. The patient was irritable and coughing upon arrival to the ER. Examination revealed decreased air entry on the right side with expiratory wheeze mainly on the right side. Dx?
k: Toddler + choking history + unilateral wheeze or reduced air entry = foreign body aspiration.
r: Unilateral wheeze in a toddler is a foreign body, not asthma.
n: Printed answer B (Foreign body).

q: A young child presents to the emergency department with a sudden-onset cough and shortness of breath shortly after eating cereal. The family denies any history of fever or witnessed choking episodes. A chest X-ray is obtained and provided. What is the most likely cause of the child's symptoms?
k: Sudden cough/choke + eating or playing with small objects + unilateral signs = foreign body aspiration.
r: Absence of witnessed choking does not exclude aspiration; a normal CXR does not exclude it either.
n: Sudden cough after eating with unilateral hyperinflation on CXR = foreign body aspiration. Embedded 21-23 July inset (same version) prints 'Answer: B. Foreign body' and adds: initial investigation is CXR (already done), most appropriate is bronchoscopy.

q: Patient With Low-Grade Fever, Acute Onset Stridor, What Is The Most Common Cause Of This Presentation?
k: Acute stridor by clues: Low-grade fever, barking cough, no drooling: viral croup (parainfluenza); Drooling present: tracheitis more common than epiglottitis (epiglottitis rare unless unvaccinated); No fever, sudden: foreign body
r: 'Most common cause' plus low-grade fever = croup; switch only if drooling or toxicity appears.
n: Embedded inset: low-grade fever version answered A. Viral Croup. Most common causes of stridor: drooling absent/not mentioned -> croup; drooling present -> tracheitis > epiglottitis (epiglottitis rare unless unvaccinated).

q: Pediatric patient came with barky cough worse when spine with inspiratory stridor and spells of cyanosis and shortness of breath What is the management?
k: Laryngomalacia severity ladder: Mild (stridor only, feeding and growth fine): reassure, resolves by about 1 to 2 years; Moderate (feeding issues, reflux): treat reflux, monitor; Severe (cyanosis, apnea, failure to thrive, cor pulmonale): supraglottoplasty
r: Cyanotic spells, apnea or failure to thrive turn laryngomalacia from 'reassure' to 'supraglottoplasty'.
n: Lookalike version offered by the compiler for the laryngomalacia recall. Severe laryngomalacia (cyanotic spells) warrants supraglottoplasty rather than reassurance.

q: Child with hoarseness of voice, runny nose, on his mother lab with Stridor and barky cough Temperature: was not so high maybe 37.8 Most likely diagnosis?
k: Croup vs epiglottitis. Croup: URTI prodrome, barking cough, hoarse voice, low-grade fever, well looking; Epiglottitis: abrupt high fever, toxic, drooling, muffled voice, no bark; Croup is a clinical diagnosis; no imaging needed
r: Bark plus hoarse voice plus low fever = croup; drooling plus toxic = epiglottitis.
n: Printed answer A. Croup.

q: Peds complaining of cough ,URT symptoms, *hoarseness of voice*, barking cough, sitting on mother's lap looking well not in resp distress. What is the Diagnosis?
k: Croup = laryngotracheobronchitis, subglottic narrowing.
r: Hoarseness is shared by laryngitis and croup; the bark makes it croup.
n: Embedded inset: older version with laryngitis as an option; printed 'Ans: Croup'.

q: An 18-month-old child presents with stridor and a barking cough for 2 days after flu-like symptoms. Examination reveals an active, well-looking child. Blood pressure 100/70 mmHg, heart rate 102/min, respiratory rate 20/min, temperature 37.6 C, oxygen saturation 95%. What is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Barking cough + inspiratory stridor + viral prodrome in a well child (6 months to 3 years) = croup.
r: Well looking + barking = croup; toxic looking + drooling = epiglottitis; toxic + barking not improving = tracheitis.
n: Printed answer A with source tag (MG); inset (same version) prints Answer: A.

q: A child develops shortness of breath, wheezing and cough with infections or when playing at school and is otherwise well. He takes no medications and is medically free. Which finding supports the diagnosis of asthma?
k: Wheeze character localizes the obstruction.
r: A finding that is merely compatible (normal CXR) is not one that supports the diagnosis; pick the positive feature.

q: Child presents with symptoms suggestive of bronchial asthma, with episodes that worsen during upper respiratory tract infections And After Playing (Something Like This). At this visit, the chest X-ray is normal. Which Of The Following Indicates Asthma?
o: Bronchial asthma increases the risk of upper respiratory tract infections.
Polyphonic wheeze occurs on exertion (not exercise)
Between attacks, the chest X-ray is normal.
k: Pick the POSITIVE typical feature, not the normal test.
r: Viral infections trigger asthma attacks; asthma does not cause more infections.
n: Embedded inset: older recall with different options; answer polyphonic wheeze on exertion. Recaller: Almost exactly like this, if anyone in the comments can add please. 19 October update ↻ Printed again later in this 19 October file (p.1056) with the same answ

q: Child with asthma, has upper respiratory tract infection, on examination he has wheeze. What support the diagnosis of asthma?
o: Normal chest x ray between episodes
k: Features that support asthma in a child: Recurrent wheeze with triggers: exercise, viral infection, cold air, allergens; Polyphonic expiratory wheeze, symptoms worse at night or early morning; Atopy: eczema, allergic rhinitis, family history
r: Recurrent infections point away from asthma toward CF or immunodeficiency.
n: Printed answer A, bottom line A. Polyphonic wheeze with exertion. Recaller note: it is a case then a general question. Embedded 15 February inset of the same topic (options A URTI risk, B polyphonic wheeze on exertion, C normal CXR between attacks) answered B.

q: Pedia with asthma what support the diagnosis?
o: Normal chest x ray between episodes
k: Asthma in children = recurrent variable wheeze/cough/breathlessness with triggers and reversibility.
r: A normal finding (normal CXR) never "supports" a diagnosis; pick the positive typical feature, and polyphonic means asthma while monophonic means a focal obstruction.
n: Polyphonic wheeze on exertion supports asthma; the older inset version gives the same answer. 19 October update ↻ Printed again later in this 19 October file (p.1056) with the same answer; author's note there: Polyphonic wheeze on exertion supports asthma diag

q: 3-year-old post-tracheoesophageal repair came with a brassy cough. He had a runny nose 2 days ago. Vitals: T: 37.4C HR: 120 bpm RR: 28/min SpO2: 94% i think Chest : Normal, except bilateral expiratory wheezing.
k: Where the airway narrows decides the noise.
r: Brassy cough + expiratory wheeze after TEF repair = tracheomalacia, not asthma.
n: Printed answer B. Prolonged ventilation and TEF repair are risk factors for acquired tracheomalacia. Recaller: Recaller (Arabic): this question came to him, he memorized and wrote it; will check what else came and send. 19 October update ↻ Printed again later

q: Child came after tracheoesophageal fistula repair with Brassy cough , no family history of asthma and no history of atopy In chest examination bilateral air entry with expiratory wheezing What is your diagnosis?
k: TEF repair + brassy cough + expiratory wheeze = tracheomalacia.
r: "No atopy, no family history" is the stem telling you it is not asthma.
n: Embedded inset: older version; printed B, 'Prolonged Ventilation & TEF Repair Are Risk Factors For Acquired Tracheomalacia'.

q: A child presents with reduced oral intake, expiratory wheeze, nasal discharge and mild respiratory distress, with no fever. What is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Infant + coryza + then wheeze/crackles + distress = bronchiolitis.
r: Afebrile does not exclude bronchiolitis; the URTI then LRTI sequence decides it.
n: Embedded 12-14 Aug inset of the same recall (options Pneumonia/Bronchiolitis) also answered Bronchiolitis.

q: A child presents with a history of reduced oral intake, an expiratory wheeze, nasal discharge, and mild respiratory distress. The patient has no fever. What is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Bronchiolitis = infant under 2 years + viral prodrome (coryza) + wheeze and/or crackles + increased work of breathing.
r: Coryza then wheeze in an infant is bronchiolitis; stridor and barking cough is croup.
n: Embedded inset (12-14 Aug recall): 2-option version; printed answer B. Bronchiolitis (main 4-option version answers C. Bronchiolitis).

q: Bronchiolitis vs. Pneumonia A 7-month-old infant presents to the Emergency Department with fever and cough. On examination, the infant has moderate respiratory distress and bilateral rhonchi during inspiration and expiration, without obvious wheezing. What is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Bronchiolitis vs pneumonia in an infant: Bronchiolitis: under 1 to 2 years, coryza first, diffuse bilateral wheeze, rhonchi or fine crackles, hyperinflation; Pneumonia: higher fever, focal signs, lobar consolidation on X-ray; Both cause fever, cough and distress, so the distribution of signs decides
r: Bilateral diffuse signs = bronchiolitis; focal signs = pneumonia.

q: 7 month old coming with cough, fever, wheezing on physical exam he is in respiratory distress and there is inspiratory creptations and expiratory ronchi
k: First wheeze with URTI features under 1 year = bronchiolitis.
r: Acute presentation = bronchiolitis; persistent for weeks after a severe infection = bronchiolitis obliterans.
n: Compiler highlights 7 month old in red. Recaller: Recaller (Arabic): there is a question I remember; notes two bronchiolitis options appeared.

q: 7 months old came with fever sneezing and something else i forgot on examination there was Inspiratory rhonchi and crackles
k: URTI symptoms (sneezing, coryza, cough) then LRTI signs (rhonchi, crackles, wheeze, tachypnea) in an infant = bronchiolitis.
r: Sneezing first, chest signs later, under 1 year: think bronchiolitis.

q: A 7-month-old infant presents with wheezing, rhonchi, cough, and tachypnea. What is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Infant wheeze ladder: First acute wheeze with coryza, under 1 year: bronchiolitis; Persistent wheeze and crackles after severe infection: bronchiolitis obliterans; Recurrent wheeze with triggers and atopy, older child: asthma
r: The word obliterans means chronic; an acute wheezy infant is plain bronchiolitis.

q: 7 months have signs of bronchiolitis Wheezing , rhonchi , cough , tachypnea, What is the diagnosis:
k: Infant wheeze: First episode, under 2 years, coryza then wheeze/crackles: bronchiolitis (RSV); Management: supportive; oxygen if SpO2 low, fluids, suction; No routine bronchodilators, steroids, or antibiotics
r: First wheezy episode in an infant is bronchiolitis, not asthma.

q: A child with normal everything except wheeze and RR of 65
k: Wheeze vs stridor localizes the airway.
r: Under 2 with wheeze and tachypnea is bronchiolitis; if the option says "bronchitis" and no bronchiolitis is offered, the exam is likely using a typo.
n: Compiler: answer is B; says this is a typo from the SMLE exam and the question itself is wrong (likely meant bronchiolitis).

q: Wheeze Pediatric patient with inspiratory stridor, everything else is normal
k: Phase of the noise localizes the lesion.
r: Inspiratory = laryngomalacia, expiratory = tracheomalacia.
n: Compiler table: laryngomalacia gives inspiratory stridor; tracheomalacia gives expiratory (monophasic wheeze). Recaller: Recaller (Arabic): got a question similar to the compilations but it did not have [the rest].

q: Child presenting with croup and received the usual treatment with no improvement. What is the MOST APPROPRIATE NEXT investigation to be done?

r: Croup not responding to steroids and epinephrine: scope the airway.

q: Pediatric patient diagnosed with croup in the ER, given the proper management, but after 1 hour he did not improve. What is the appropriate management?
k: Croup that fails standard treatment = think alternative diagnosis and look directly.
r: Croup is a clinical diagnosis; imaging is not needed in typical croup, and failure to improve points to endoscopy, not more films.
n: Approach to refractory croup: per Athar, next step is neck X-ray and most appropriate is laryngoscope; per Alhomrani, initial, next and most appropriate are all laryngoscope.

q: Child presents with brassy cough and inspiratory stridor, suspected to have croup and managed as croup, but he did not improve. What is the most appropriate initial next step?
k: Croup that fails standard treatment is no longer simple croup: look directly at the airway.
r: Failed croup therapy = wrong or complicated diagnosis; visualize the airway in theatre.
n: Athar: next = lateral neck X-ray, most appropriate = direct visualization. Alhomrani: next and most appropriate are BOTH C, direct visualization with laryngoscope. Refractory croup -> laryngoscope in OR (same as epiglottitis).

q: Patient complaining of inspiratory stridor and brassy cough was diagnosed as croup and given the full management, but no improvement Whats the most appropriate next step
k: Croup that fails standard treatment is no longer simple croup: look directly at the airway.
r: Persistent stridor after croup treatment: scope, do not just image.
n: Embedded inset: small 17 September slide with only two remembered options and a handwritten red B (visualization scope); consistent with compiler's laryngoscope answer.

q: Child presents with foul-smelling breath, nasal congestion, and facial tenderness. The symptoms have worsened after 14 weeks, despite multiple courses of antibiotics. What is the highest diagnostic value?
o: Radiograph of the Sinus (I think sinus XRAY)
k: Chronic nasal symptoms failing antibiotics in a child: look for the cause.
r: Foul smell plus antibiotic failure in a child = foreign body; scope the nose.
n: Embedded inset of same recall (lead-in 'most appropriate next step in management') notes No CT; Answer: C, nasal foreign body.

q: Child present with chronic rhinorrhea, nasal itching and sneezing with dark circles under the eyes and pale and buggy nasal mucus What is the diagnosis
k: Chronic childhood rhinitis: look at sides, smell and mucosa.
r: Unilateral foul discharge flips the answer to foreign body; itching and pale boggy mucosa keep it allergic.
n: Allergic shiners and pale boggy mucosa point to allergic rhinitis. Recaller: Only two options recalled

q: 5 years old girl came with black circles below both eyes, complains of chronic rhinorrhea and nasal itching darkening under the eyes & pale Boggy Nasal mucosa. What is the most likely diagnosis?

n: Embedded inset: older version with four options; answer A. Allergic rhinitis.

q: Child has history of allergic rhinitis Presented with congested nose not responding to anti histamines What to give?
k: Allergic rhinitis ladder: allergen avoidance, then antihistamine or intranasal steroid, then combinations, then immunotherapy.
r: Nasal congestion not responding to antihistamine is the classic cue for an intranasal steroid; montelukast only wins when asthma coexists.
n: Rule: rhinitis alone -> intranasal steroid; asthma alone -> inhaled steroid; rhinitis and asthma -> montelukast.

q: Child with allergic rhinitis still sneezing and nasal cognition even after take antihistamine:

r: Congestion is the symptom antihistamines treat worst; intranasal steroid fixes it.

q: A 4-year-old boy with cystic fibrosis attends the well-child clinic. He has had no recent respiratory problems but complains of foul-smelling, greasy stools and abdominal pain after meals rich in fat and protein. His weight has stayed at the 3rd percentile for several months despite adequate nutritional intake. Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation for his nutritional status?
k: CF nutrition rules: Pancreatic insufficiency in most patients: steatorrhea, failure to thrive; Pancreatic enzymes with every meal and snack; High-calorie, high-fat, salt-supplemented diet
r: In CF never restrict fat; give enzymes so the fat can be absorbed.
n: Embedded 21-23 September inset of the same recall answered B (pancreatic enzyme supplements).

q: Case of cystic fibrosis with Upeer respiratoy tract symptoms and greenish sputum Spurum culture: Methicillin sensitive staphylococcus aureus What is the most appropriate management?
k: CF organisms by age and the matching drug: Early childhood: S. aureus and H. influenzae, treat MSSA with flucloxacillin or amoxicillin-clavulanate; MRSA: vancomycin, linezolid or other anti-MRSA agents; Later: Pseudomonas aeruginosa, anti-pseudomonal therapy (inhaled tobramycin for eradication)
r: Culture already in hand: treat the organism, do not re-sample.
n: Handwritten red check mark on Amoxicillin clavulanate. Recaller: Other choices irrelevant Printed again later in this file (p.5342).

q: Pedia pt with cystic fibrosis came with cough with greenish purulent sputum ( typical sx of pneumonia) Culture with Methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus They give also radilogical description but I forget Mx?
k: CF exacerbation: treat the organism grown on sputum culture.
r: Pseudomonas or a toxic child moves you to IV double antipseudomonal cover; MSSA in a stable child stays oral.
n: CF exacerbation with MSSA on sputum culture: oral anti-staphylococcal antibiotic such as amoxicillin-clavulanate. Embedded older recall gives A- amoxicillin-clavulanate. Recaller: Radiological description forgotten; only two options recalled.

q: Pediatric known case of Cystic fibrosis came with productive cough greenish, no fever Sputum culture showed MSSA , next step ?

k: Known organism + stable child = treat, do not re-investigate.
r: Fever, hypoxia or toxic appearance would make admission and IV antibiotics (with blood culture) the answer.
n: Embedded inset: older recall with different options; answer A- amoxicillin-clavulanate.

q: A child with known cystic fibrosis presents with fever and a productive cough. Chest X-ray shows hyperinflation and other Unrecalled findings. Blood culture grows methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus (MSSA). What is the most appropriate next step in management?
k: CF infection with a known organism: treat it.
r: Identified organism + sick patient = start antibiotics, do not re-investigate.

q: A child presents with difficult-to-treat asthma and a history of hard, foul-smelling stools. What is the most appropriate investigation?
k: Uncontrolled asthma: rule out a mimic before escalating.
r: Asthma that will not settle plus greasy, offensive stools = think CF and order a sweat test, not imaging.
n: Options printed unlettered, lettered by position. Compiler: in people with uncontrolled asthma make sure to rule out mimicking conditions (eg CF, GERD, vocal cord paralysis).

q: Child with uncontrolled asthma and frequent foul smelling stool Initial test to do? No other details
k: Lung + gut symptoms in a child = CF screen first.
r: The stool clue is what turns 'difficult asthma' into a CF question; without it, think technique, adherence and triggers first.
n: Embedded inset: older version with different options (CXR instead of CT). Compiler: in uncontrolled asthma rule out mimicking conditions (CF, GERD, vocal cord paralysis).

q: Pediatric with positive cystic fibrosis test what is the most common respiratory complication ?
k: CF lung disease = mucus plugging, infection, bronchiectasis.
r: Chronic infection plus destroyed, dilated airways = bronchiectasis; emphysema belongs to smokers and alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency.
n: Printed Answer: A. Bronchiectasis is the most common respiratory complication of cystic fibrosis. Recaller: Only two options recalled

q: Peds pt w uncontrolled asthma chlorine sweat test is 78 what is long term complications

r: The stem says 'asthma' but the sweat test says CF; answer the CF question.

q: Child with Sx of pneumonia.. Whats Most sensitive to pneumonia at this child ?
k: Pediatric pneumonia: tachypnea is the most sensitive sign; absence of tachypnea makes pneumonia unlikely.
r: Sensitive = best to rule out = tachypnea; do not pick fever just because it is common.

q: A. pediatric patient presents with cough, fever, and respiratory symptoms following a suspected aspiration event. Chest X-ray reveals scattered patchy infiltrates. What is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Aspiration event + fever + patchy infiltrate = aspiration pneumonia.
r: Patchy infiltrate after aspiration = pneumonia; a hyperlucent, overinflated lung after choking = retained foreign body.
n: Printed answer B. Aspiration pneumonia.

Blood pressure 98/65 mmHg Heart rate 105 /min Respiratory rate 22 /min Temperature 38.6 C Oxygen saturation 95 % Which of the following is the expected finding in chest X-ray match child's chest finding?

q: Pediatric stony fullness choices :

q: Cough , fevere developed SOB , on examination the child looks well basal crackles on rt lower chest auscaltation , stony dullness on percussion , T 38.5 ?

q: Patient with cough and sob. on PE there is stony dullness. What is the diagnosis

q: Amily brought their kid who has a fever, cough, and runny nose. Symptoms started after hx of choking after he ingested some seed. Chest exam: dec RT side breathing sound X ray pictures was shown What is the next thing to do?

k: Choking history + unilateral signs = FB aspiration: CXR first, then bronchoscopy.

q: Kid is fine but he coughed earlier or something basically he choked on popcorn brought by family. CXR shows hyperinflation of right middle lobe. What's the best?

r: A well looking child after a choking episode can still have a bronchial FB; the quiet interval is a trap, not reassurance.
n: Option D is wrong for two reasons: it says flexible (should be rigid) and laryngoscope (should be bronchoscope, this is a bronchial FB).

q: 2 years old child came to ER due to Cyanosis during crying, and he has Hx of recurrent pneumonia, they did for him flexible bronchoscopy and they found 90% occlusion (Not sure if it was in the epiglottis or trachea). Tracheostomy done, what is additional thing you will add:

r: Collapsing airway + 'negative pressure' option = the trap; always pick positive pressure.

q: A 2-year-old child presents with cyanosis during crying and recurrent hospital admissions due to pneumonia. Bronchoscopy reveals a 90% narrowing of the lower third of the trachea during expiration. After performing a tracheostomy, what is the most appropriate next management?
k: Expiratory collapse of the intrathoracic trachea = tracheomalacia.
r: Collapse 'during expiration' in the lower trachea is malacia, not a fixed stenosis; treat with positive pressure.
n: Embedded inset: fuller version with different option order; answer C. Non-invasive ventilation (CONFIRMED). If there is 'POSITIVE' pressure then go for it; 'Negative' highlighted red as the distractor.

q: 3 months old patient brought by family to ER due to cyanosis with crying, hx of pt he has multiple previous pneumonia admissions now pt has respiratory distress and tachypnea (written pike this) he has intercostal and substernal retractions + RR Was 60 and has monophasic expiratory wheeze, otherwise NORMAL (no vitals were mentioned, so i assumed he is vitally normal based on this) what is the highest diagnostic test?

q: 5-month-old child admitted many times with pneumonia, now with cough and monophasic bilateral expiratory wheezing. Diagnostic test?

q: 3 years old boy with barky cough, cyanotics, holding spill, no inspiratory stridor, positive monophasic wheeze in auscultation, dx:
k: Sound localises the lesion.
r: Barky/brassy cough with a monophasic wheeze and NO inspiratory stridor points below the larynx: think tracheomalacia, not laryngomalacia or croup.
n: Embedded inset: related recall asking the diagnosis; answer B. Tracheomalacia (monophasic expiratory wheeze, no inspiratory stridor).

q: A child was choking with a popcorn and then was removed by coughing. After that he has hyperinflation of the right lower lobe and crackles ig or crepitations what to do next?

q: A patient presents with a history of choking. A chest X-ray shows unilateral hyperinflation. What is the most appropriate next step in management?

q: Child with fever, cough and runny nose; symptoms began after choking on a seed. Chest exam: decreased breath sounds on the right; X-ray shown. Next step?

q: Pt pediatric c history of cough & DOB not response to salbutamol in examine there is wheez in the area of lower zoon & there absent air entry what is the most appropriate next step:
k: Unilateral wheeze not responding to bronchodilators = think focal obstruction (foreign body).
r: Asthma wheeze is diffuse and bilateral and responds to salbutamol; a localized wheeze with absent air entry that does not respond is obstruction.
n: Printed answer PA and lateral X-ray ('next' in red in the stem: investigate before bronchoscopy). Only two options recalled.

q: Child came with wheezing the mother stated that he had a URTI couple of days ago. On examination wheezing and crackles heard on the right lung Initial next step?
k: Unilateral wheeze in a child: think foreign body.
r: The wording decides it: 'initial' with a weak history usually favours CXR; 'establish diagnosis' or a choking history favours bronchoscopy.

q: Child with the one day of cough and shortness of breath, the mother gave him inhaled sad bit them all I think but it did not help. There is wheezing at the lower right zone, and there is diminished air entry or breath Sounds one of them. What's the next step?
k: Suspected foreign body in a stable child: CXR, then bronchoscopy.
r: Unilateral wheeze that ignores salbutamol is a foreign body, not asthma.
n: Suspected foreign body aspiration; initial/next step is AP and lateral chest X-ray. 'next' in red.

q: CHILD 1 day sob gave him salbutamol not affective Localized wheezing and absent breath sound Whats intitial ?
k: Suspected bronchial foreign body in a child: Clues: choking episode, sudden cough or SOB, unilateral wheeze or reduced breath sounds, no response to bronchodilator; Initial: chest X-ray (most foreign bodies are radiolucent, so look for hyperinflation or collapse); Definitive: rigid bronchoscopy for
r: Initial = chest X-ray; best or definitive = rigid bronchoscopy; unstable or complete obstruction = act immediately without imaging.
n: Suspected foreign body aspiration; initial investigation is chest X-ray (AP and lateral), bronchoscopy follows for diagnosis and removal.

q: A child is brought to the emergency department by his parents with shortness of breath (SOB). His parents report that they gave him a salbutamol inhaler at home, but there was no improvement. On examination, he has wheezing and absent breath sounds in the left lower lung. What is the next step?
k: Unilateral absent breath sounds + wheeze after failed salbutamol = foreign body until proven otherwise.
r: Left-sided signs do not exclude a foreign body; right is commoner, not exclusive.
n: Suspected foreign body: next step chest X-ray. Printed again later in this file (p.5575).

q: A 28 weeks old preterm baby was put in the NICU. The baby then experienced periods of stopped breathing (for 15-20 seconds) several times in an hour. What is the type of apnea?

r: Most common type = mixed; underlying mechanism = central (immature brainstem).

q: 1-preterm newborn, 27 weeks, suddenly developed bradycardia and apnea, then responded after stimulation. What is the most likely cause?

q: A 5-day-old cyanotic infant with a diagnosis of Tricuspid Atresia. Which of the following is the most important issue to consider during the discussion with parents?
o: Make sure that you have left no question unanswered
Make sure the parents understand the dismal prognosis
Make sure the parents understand that you are doing everything you can
Make sure you leave the parents with a follow-up plan and provide them cardiac consultation
k: Breaking bad news (SPIKES): end with Strategy and summary, a concrete plan and follow-up.
r: In communication questions about a serious but treatable diagnosis, pick the option that gives a concrete plan and referral, not false hope or doom.
n: Printed answer D (follow-up plan plus cardiac consultation). No further commentary.

q: Q:The type of heart anomaly that causes a delayed pulse in the lower extremities
k: Coarctation of the aorta: the pulses tell the story.
r: Arm hypertension with weak or delayed femoral pulses is coarctation until proved otherwise.
n: Radio-femoral delay points to coarctation of the aorta.

q: A 9-year-old presents with weakness, fatigue, and hypertension in upper limbs. Examination confirms delayed pulses in lower extremities. Which of the following is the most likely etiology?
k: Hypertensive child: always feel the femoral pulses.
r: Strong radial plus weak or delayed femoral pulse equals coarctation, whatever distractors (obesity, family history) appear.
n: Similar recall: upper limb hypertension with delayed lower limb pulses is coarctation of the aorta (MG).

q: Newborn with Down syndrome presenting with Ejection Systolic Murmur:
k: Murmur character points to the lesion.
r: 'Systolic' in a Down baby with superior axis = AVSD; isolated 'ejection systolic' = ASD per this recall.
n: Both ASD and AVSD can cause ejection systolic murmur and AVSD is more common in Down, but AVSD should be accompanied by other murmurs (holosystolic). Since the only finding is an isolated ejection systolic murmur, best answer is ASD (always choose the most com

q: A 4-month-old boy with down syndrome exhibits poor weight gain, tachypnea, a low-pitched grade 2 systolic murmur and a fixed splitting of S2. Chest X-ray reveals cardiomegaly and increased pulmonary vascularity. Electrocardiography documents biventricular hypertrophy and a superior frontal plane QRS axis. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
k: AVSD (endocardial cushion defect): ASD + VSD + common AV valve.
r: Fixed split S2 with a SUPERIOR axis = AVSD; with RIGHT axis deviation = secundum ASD.
n: MG recall referenced from the previous page: systolic murmur (not specified as ejection) with fixed S2 splitting, biventricular hypertrophy and superior axis in Down syndrome -> AVSD. Textbook excerpt: complete ECD (AV canal) is about 50% of CHD in Down syndro

q: جاني سؤال طفل عمره ٦ أسابيع عنده VSD ال RR 47, HR 174 في ال X.ray كان cardiothorasic ratio 65 وفي increase vascularity الخيارات
k: VSD management by size and symptoms: Small, asymptomatic: observe; many close spontaneously.; Large: tachypnea, poor feeding, sweating with feeds, failure to thrive, recurrent chest infections.; Large with heart failure: diuretics first (furosemide), plus optimized calories.
r: VSD + cardiomegaly + increased vascularity = heart failure: treat with diuretics, never reassure.
n: VSD with heart failure (cardiomegaly, increased vascularity): diuretics. Compiler refers to the fuller version on the next page (medical treatment with diuretics, MEDGARD).

q: Pediatric patient has T1DM and dyslepedima his blood pressure is high Which diet is best to reduce cardiovascular risk?
k: Diet for cardiovascular risk: pick the one that targets the stated risk.
r: High blood pressure in the stem is the clue that points to DASH.
n: DASH, as long as there is no Mediterranean diet among the options. Asked what to choose if both are present, compiler said he will not search it unless he sees both in the same recall.

q: 2 month infant healthy with unremarkable PE except for low femoral BP 86/50 and upper limb PB 102/70 Which of the following modalities will support your diagnosis
k: Coarctation of the aorta: Clues: arm BP higher than leg BP, weak or delayed femoral pulses, radio-femoral delay, differential cyanosis in neonates.; Murmur: systolic, may be heard in the left interscapular area.; Confirm: echocardiography; CT or MRI angiography for detailed anatomy.
r: Rib notching is a late sign in older children; in infants the confirming test is echo.
n: Printed answer B, echo (coarctation of the aorta picture with upper vs lower limb BP gradient). No further commentary.

q: A 10 yearold girl experienced a brief episode of blackout while running then recovers completely. Examination unremarkable except for an ejection systolic murmur. What is the most appropriate next investigation?
k: Syncope with exertion = cardiac until proven otherwise: ECG first, then echo.
r: "Next" = ECG; "confirm/diagnose" = echocardiography; vasovagal with normal ECG = reassurance.
n: Printed answer ECG as the next investigation (compiler highlights 'next' in red); no further commentary.

q: A 2-year-old girl, a known case of valvular aortic stenosis, develops new exertional dyspnea and has an ejection systolic murmur. What is the most appropriate management?
k: Valvular AS: symptoms decide the timing of intervention.
r: Same symptomatic AS in an elderly adult = valve replacement, not balloon dilation.
n: Symptomatic congenital valvular AS in a child: transcatheter balloon dilation.

q: An 8-year-old child presents to the emergency department complaining of chest pain and a "pounding" sensation in his heart for the past two hours. On physical examination, the child looks well and is hemodynamically stable. There are no murmurs heard on auscultation. Vitals reveal a heart rate of 242 bpm. What is the most appropriate next step in the management of this patient?
k: Any tachycardia: ECG first, then treat by stability.
r: If the stem says hypotensive, mottled or drowsy, the answer jumps straight to synchronized cardioversion; 'stable' means ECG first.

q: A girl was running & had an episode of LOC then immediately regained consciousness. No previous episodes/hx of chronic disease. Physical examination unremarkable except for systolic ejection murmur What is the most appropriate investigation?
k: Syncope red flags: exertional, no prodrome, murmur, family history of sudden death, abnormal ECG.
r: Syncope while running, not after, is cardiac until proven otherwise.
n: Options A (Echocardiogram) and B (ECG) both shown in red; 'most appropriate' in red; printed answer A (exertional syncope with systolic ejection murmur suggests structural cause such as HCM).

q: Male patient born with hypotonia, murmur on examination Found to have Low set ears Pectus extravum Hypertelorism Webbed neck Confirmed to be pulmonary stenosis on echo Parents are worried this is part of a syndromic condition. What is the best counseling advice and what to do regarding it could be part of syndromic?
o: refer to gastroenterology for metabolic causes
endocrine referral and order liver function test
Treat heart failure and then refer to cardiology
k: Dysmorphism + congenital heart lesion = think syndrome, confirm genetically.
r: Turner-like features in a boy with pulmonary stenosis = Noonan; Turner itself pairs with coarctation or bicuspid aortic valve.
n: Answer A even when option D is present; confirmed. As explained earlier, there is no symptom treatment for pulmonary stenosis, so cardiac referral plus genetic testing (Noonan picture) rather than treating heart failure. Options A and D highlighted in red.

q: A child with dilated cardiomyopathy and CHF presented to ED with SOB and excersice intolerance. no meds,no vitals nothing.
o: reassurance as its part of the illness
k: Acute decompensated heart failure: relieve congestion first.
r: Wheeze in a cardiac patient can be cardiac asthma: treat the fluid with furosemide, not with salbutamol and steroids.
n: Printed answer: furosemide stat. Recaller: I couldn't find the CXR, but quite sure it had bilateral pulmonary edema? The markings were prominent and hazy. Something like this maybeee? (no image shown on page)

q: Two years old came for evaluation for murmur She is asymptomatic echo Shows left to right shunt in the atrium with bulging membrane ( this is the full recall)
k: Name the defect by where the echo puts the shunt.
r: "Shunt in the atrium" = ASD whatever the extra description; AVSD needs ventricular involvement and is usually symptomatic early.
n: Atrial level left to right shunt with bulging (aneurysmal) septal membrane = ASD. Recaller: Recaller: this is the full recall.

q: 2 y/o known valvular heart disease. Presents with new onset of shortness of breath on moderate? Exertion. Echo: Moderate aortic stenosis with LVH [Arabic: exactly like this] Most appropriate management ?
k: Aortic stenosis: asymptomatic means follow-up, symptomatic means intervene; the method depends on age.
r: Adult AS questions key valve replacement; in a young child the same picture is keyed to balloon valvuloplasty.
n: Printed answer D. Compiler pasted an older recall (161-Pedia: 6y known aortic stenosis, new SOB on exertion, echo moderate AS; options follow up 3-6m, reassurance, medical symptomatic treatment, transvalvular balloon dilatation). Symptomatic congenital AS in a

q: A 2-month-old infant presents with persistent central cyanosis and poor feeding. Chest X-ray is shown. What is the most appropriate next step? ( picture of x-ray )
k: Persistent central cyanosis in an infant = cyanotic CHD → cardiology and echocardiography.
r: A cyanotic infant who is not acutely unstable needs cardiology referral, not antibiotics or reassurance.
n: Printed answer B. Persistent central cyanosis in an infant suggests cyanotic congenital heart disease; refer to pediatric cardiology. Compiler notes the picture is needed.

q: 18 month child presented with his mother for progressive dyspnea for 1 week. Preceded by upper respiratory tract infection. On examination, there's hepatomegaly, hyperactive pericardium & gallop rhythm but no murmur. Vitals : BP: 75/ (55?) HR : 170 RR : (50?) I think that there's no lab investigations (maybe other examinees can confirm that) CXR picture: I'm sure that there's cardiomegaly, I appreciated some shadows over the lung but I cannot describe them. What's the most appropriate diagnostic test?
k: Child with new heart failure signs after a viral illness: think myocarditis, confirm dysfunction with echo.
r: No murmur plus heart failure after a viral illness = myocardium, not valves or shunt; get an echo.
n: Post-viral heart failure picture (likely viral myocarditis) -> echocardiography. Recaller: Recaller unsure about lab investigations and CXR shadows; asks other examinees to confirm.

q: A new born with Flat nasal bridge, Upward-slanting palpebral fissures and Single transverse palmar crease , with ejection murmur, what is the possible cardiac effect?
k: Down syndrome heart: most common lesion is AVSD, but read the murmur clue.
r: "Most common heart defect in Down" = AVSD; a specific "ejection murmur" clue was used here to key ASD.
n: Printed A. ASD and compiler stresses 'this is NOT a typo': an ejection (flow) murmur fits ASD rather than AV canal, although AV septal defect is the commonest Down syndrome lesion (both A and C highlighted). Compiler doubts this is the full recall.

q: 4 month baby with SOB and intermittent feeding.examination show signs of congestive heart and murmur (literally written like this) what is the heart lesion?
k: Infant (weeks to months) with heart failure + murmur, no cyanosis = large VSD until proven otherwise.
r: Heart failure in infancy points to a large left-to-right shunt (VSD); cyanosis with spells points to TOF, which does not cause heart failure.
n: Printed answer B. VSD (most common cause of heart failure in an infant at a few months of age).

q: A child presents with migratory polyarthritis involving large joints and fever, with a history of sore throat a few weeks earlier. Acute rheumatic fever is suspected. What is the most appropriate treatment for her joint symptoms? (Cardiac examination is unremarkable)
k: ARF management has three separate goals.
r: If Jones criteria are not yet met, the author's other version prefers paracetamol so the migratory pattern and fever are not masked before the diagnosis is secured.
n: Printed answer high-dose aspirin for ARF arthritis. Note: on the 21-23 September version of this question (next page) the compiler says the answer should be paracetamol when Jones criteria are not met, aspirin only when met. Other versions of this recall in th

q: 6-week infant. Suspected pyloric stenosis. Next step (100% It Said Next, NOT Initial)
k: Compiler's lead-in rule for suspected pyloric stenosis with NPO / NGT / saline options: "Next", "initial" or "most appropriate next" → NPO.; "Most appropriate" (without "next") → normal saline (resuscitation is the mainstay).; Then correct electrolytes; add K only after urine output.
r: Read the lead-in: "next" here = NPO, plain "most appropriate" = normal saline.
n: Athar: Normal saline; Alhomrani (compiler): NPO. Next, initial, or most appropriate next are all NPO, unless it says 'most appropriate' without 'next'.

q: 6-week infant. Suspected pyloric stenosis. What is most appropriate next step? (not initial)
k: Pyloric stenosis sequence: NPO → IV normal saline → correct Cl and K → ultrasound confirms → pyloromyotomy.
r: "Most appropriate NEXT" still contains "next": per this compiler that is NPO, not saline.
n: Alhomrani (compiler): next, initial, or most appropriate [next] are all NPO. Athar: Normal Saline.

q: Term baby after birth he was plethoric with tachypnea and irritability. Echo showed hypertrophic cardiomyopathy What was the maternal condition during pregnancy?
k: Infant of diabetic mother: fetal hyperinsulinemia explains almost every feature.
r: Maternal disease and the neonatal heart: diabetes gives septal hypertrophy, SLE gives congenital heart block.
n: Infant of diabetic mother: polycythemia (plethora) and hypertrophic (septal) cardiomyopathy.

q: Child complaining with no weight gain. Mother noticed prolonged feeding, perioral cyanosis, and sweating while feeding. Systolic murmurs found on auscult. What to do regarding child thrive?
k: Failure to thrive: find and treat the organic cause first.
r: Sweating during feeds in an infant is a heart failure sign until proven otherwise.
n: Failure to thrive from a cardiac cause: refer to cardiology.

q: month old child was found to have an ejection systolic murmur on clinical examination. The mother reports SOB on exertion with physical activity. There is no history of chest pain nor syncope. ECHO confirmed aortic stenosis with good left ventricular systolic function. Aortic valve gradient of 60 mmH. BP and HR are normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate management option?
k: Aortic stenosis: symptoms trigger intervention; age picks the procedure.
r: Same AS stem, different patient: child = balloon valvuloplasty, adult = valve replacement, asymptomatic = follow-up (see SWR-3495).
n: Symptomatic child with aortic stenosis gradient 60: balloon valvuloplasty. Contrast with the older adult version shown on the page (asymptomatic, gradient 40): follow up. Other versions of this recall in this deck: SWR-3495 → A. Follow-up

q: Long case describing Down syndrome. What is the most common congenital heart disease?
k: Syndrome to heart lesion pairs: Down syndrome: AVSD (endocardial cushion defect), then VSD, ASD; Turner: coarctation, bicuspid aortic valve; Williams: supravalvular aortic stenosis
r: "Most common CHD" alone = VSD; "most common CHD in Down syndrome" = AV canal.
n: Most common congenital heart defect in Down syndrome is AV canal (endocardial cushion defect).

q: 3 m infant has SOB and interrupted feeding , O/E CHF signs with murmur what is dx?
k: Infant with heart failure and a murmur at 6 weeks to 3 months = large VSD until proven otherwise.
r: Heart failure points to a left to right shunt (VSD); cyanosis with feeding points to TOF.
n: Type of murmur is not mentioned (compiler stresses this is the full recall, not a poor recall); answer is VSD since it is the most common lesion presenting with heart failure at this age.

q: New onset of murmur after signs and symptoms like persistent vomiting, diarrhea, and cough for three days on examination the patient had murmur and right lung (consolidation or sounds basically what I understood is that there's pneumonia). Her previous pediatrician visit had an unremarkable examination.
o: To reassess after dealing with the underlying cause
k: New murmur during febrile illness with prior normal cardiac exams = innocent flow murmur; treat the illness, then re-examine.
r: A murmur heard only while the child is sick is re-checked after recovery before any cardiac work-up.
n: Likely a flow (physiologic) murmur from the acute illness; reassess after treating the cause.

q: A boy presents with arthralgia, subcutaneous nodules, and chest pain. He is suspected for acute rheumatic fever What is the most appropriate management?
o: Intramuscular benzathine penicillin G every month
k: ARF: treat the inflammation, eradicate the strep, then prevent recurrence.
r: "Every month" = prophylaxis, not treatment of the current attack.
n: High-dose aspirin is treatment of ARF; the monthly penicillin option is to prevent recurrence of ARF (compiler wrote 'B' for prevention, likely meaning the benzathine penicillin option).

q: Three day old newborn came with skin lesion that looks like erythmatuse macule is on erythmatuse base vital sign blood pressure 85/55 saturation 99% temperature 36.6 heart rate 110 what is this next step in management?
k: Benign newborn rashes = reassure; an unwell baby with a rash = sepsis or HSV workup.
r: Look at the baby, not the rash: a well, afebrile neonate with a red-based rash in the first days is erythema toxicum, so reassure.
n: Erythema toxicum neonatorum in a well afebrile 3-day-old: benign, reassure. Inset version also answers reassurance.

q: 4 day old preterm baby devolved frequent (or intermittent apnea), clinical examination found machinery murmur and wide pulse pressure CXR: Wit lung bilateraly Which of the following most appropriate next step
k: Preterm + machinery murmur + bounding pulses / wide pulse pressure = PDA.
r: NSAIDs close the duct; prostaglandin E1 keeps it open. Do not mix them up.
n: Recaller: Option D recalled as NSAIDs, described (Arabic) by its effect on prostaglandin.

q: 12 year old dx with acute rheumatic fever ( diagnosis mentioned ) what is the most likely to be found in echo
k: Acute rheumatic fever = regurgitation; chronic rheumatic heart disease = stenosis.
r: Read the time word: 'acute' rheumatic fever → MR; 'rheumatic heart disease' years later → MS.
n: Printed answer A. Mitral regurgitation is the most common echo finding in acute rheumatic carditis.

q: An 8-year-old boy presents to the Emergency Department. He is alert, with a blood pressure of 75/50 mmg and a heart rate of 130 beats per minute. His ECG is shown below. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
k: Tachycardia with a pulse: stability decides the path.
r: Hypotension makes it unstable, even in an alert patient; "synchronized" because there is a pulse.
n: Hypotensive (unstable) tachyarrhythmia: synchronized electrical cardioversion. Recaller: Stem refers to an ECG that is not reproduced on the slide.

q: Child had pharyngitis 3 weeks ago. Three days ago, he developed pain and swelling in the left knee. On examination, a cardiac murmur is heard. Highest diagnostic test ?
k: Rheumatic fever = evidence of preceding GAS infection + 2 major OR 1 major + 2 minor criteria.
r: Jones criteria are not enough without proof of strep; ASO is that proof, echo is for the heart.
n: Acute rheumatic fever after streptococcal pharyngitis: ASO titer documents preceding strep infection.

q: 3 months down syndrome , mother came complaining that the baby suffers respiratory distress and other things that I can't recall when he is being fed and I think he has ejection systolic murmur and does not have cyanosis ?
k: Down syndrome heart: think AVSD first.
r: An ejection murmur alone suggests ASD, but symptoms in early infancy in a child with Down syndrome point to AVSD.
n: Old Answer: ASD (based solely on the ejection murmur). New Answer: AVSD, because the infant has SOB and ASD is rarely symptomatic in infancy; AVSD is the most common CHD in Down syndrome and can cause an ejection murmur.

q: 10 days old neonate presented with respiratory distress and lethargy, on examination: absent femoral pulse (no vitals mentioned) What of the following is the most appropriate initial management?
k: Neonate in shock or distress in the first 2 weeks with absent or weak femoral pulses = duct dependent lesion: start PGE1.
r: Absent femoral pulses in a newborn need immediate action; give prostaglandin before confirming the lesion, not surgery first.
n: Duct-dependent coarctation of the aorta in a neonate: initial management is prostaglandin infusion to keep the ductus open.

q: A child presents with hypotonia, a flat facial profile, upslanting palpebral fissures, epicanthal folds, small low-set ears, and a single transverse palmar crease. On examination, a cardiac murmur is heard. Which of the following is the most common congenital anomaly associated with this condition?
k: Syndrome to heart lesion pairs.
r: Most common CHD overall = VSD; most common in Down syndrome = AV canal.
n: Down syndrome: the most common congenital heart defect is the atrioventricular canal (AVSD).

q: A child has delayed/weak lower-extremity pulses compared with the upper extremities. Which congenital heart lesion is most likely?
k: Coarctation of the aorta: acyanotic, upper > lower limb BP and weak/delayed femoral pulses.
r: Hypertension in a child or a young Turner girl plus radio-femoral delay = coarctation; check femoral pulses before calling it essential hypertension.
n: Recaller: Terse recall line: 'Delayed pulse in L.L ,,,coarctation of aorta'.

q: A term baby develops respiratory distress 2 hours after birth. What is the most appropriate next step?
k: Neonatal respiratory distress: X-ray pattern names the cause.
r: If the baby stays cyanosed despite oxygen with little distress, think heart and go to echo, not X-ray.
n: Printed answer A: chest X-ray.

q: 2 years old has Aortic stenosis his parents brought him due to new progressive SOB during moderate exercise, ECHO: Moderate AS Most appropriate management?
k: Aortic stenosis: symptoms decide intervention.
r: In AS, symptoms outweigh the echo grade; in a child the procedure is the balloon, in an adult the new valve.

q: Down syndrome (Dx not mentioned they gave me features) most common CHD?
o: Atrioventricular CANAL (they did not write AVSD)
k: Syndrome and classic heart lesion: Down: AVSD (endocardial cushion defect), then VSD; Turner: bicuspid aortic valve, coarctation; Williams: supravalvular aortic stenosis
r: Most common CHD overall is VSD, but in Down syndrome it is AVSD: read whether the stem gives Down features.
n: Most common CHD in Down syndrome: atrioventricular canal (AVSD). Recaller: Diagnosis not named; features given.

q: 2- Child diagnosed with dilated cardiomyopathy presents with fever and worsening shortness of breath on examination liver span is 5 cm below the coastal margin with gallop rhythm on auscultation CXR (pic provided) was showing cardiomegaly and pulmonary edema What would you start along with the ABCD?
k: Acute decompensated HF: decide "wet or dry" and "warm or cold".
r: Add hypotension and cold peripheries to the same stem and the answer moves to an inotrope or epinephrine.
n: Printed answer C: decompensated heart failure with pulmonary edema and congestion; start loop diuretic (furosemide).

q: A patient presents with a illness and fever... On examination, a heart murmur is heard, with decreased air entry. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Reassess the patient after the illness resolves
k: Innocent vs pathological murmur in children: Innocent: soft systolic, varies with position, no symptoms, louder with fever, anemia, exercise; Pathological: any diastolic, pansystolic, grade 3 or more, thrill, fixed split S2, symptoms; Febrile child with a new soft murmur: re-examine when well
r: Fever-associated murmur = re-examine when afebrile; a diastolic murmur is never innocent.
n: Printed answer B: murmur during a febrile illness may be a flow (innocent) murmur; reassess after the illness resolves.

q: A 12 year old boy with Type 1 Diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and dyslipidemia, What is the most effective method of hypertension control? Blood pressure 142/98
k: Lifestyle BP reduction, largest to smaller effect: DASH diet, then weight loss, sodium restriction, exercise, alcohol moderation.
r: If the question asks for drug therapy in a diabetic child or adult with hypertension, choose an ACE inhibitor; if it asks for lifestyle, choose DASH.
n: DASH diet is the most effective lifestyle measure for BP control. Inset of an older recall (95-) answered B. Dash diet in its own order.

q: A pic of heart block Mobtiz 2 and ask about prognosis?
k: Read the strip yourself; the prognosis follows the true rhythm, not the recaller's label.
r: Asymptomatic child with normal growth and an irregular pulse: think sinus arrhythmia and answer normal development.
n: No answer line under options. Compiler: the picture was NOT Mobitz 2 (recaller misidentified it) and the answer is C. Normal development, per Medgard. Compiler flags it as a question needing a better recall ('Bring The Better Recall'). October By Similar updat

q: 14 year old boy came in for pre-sport screening he had a murmur, his dad died at 40 years old ECG shows long QT:
o: continue sport and do annual ECG
give beta blocker and only do sports that require low effort
don't do sport and consider pacemaker

r: Newer guidelines allow some treated LQTS athletes back to sport after shared decision making, but exam keys still favour beta blocker plus low intensity sport only.
n: Embedded unrelated Telegram-screenshot recall inside the same inset; option B is highlighted in yellow (taken as the marked answer). No printed answer line.

q: A 13 yo hx of joint pain and not tolerate activity with CHEST PAIN ASO 800 He took benzathine penicillin When to discontinue?
k: Secondary prophylaxis = monthly benzathine penicillin; always take the LONGER of the two limits.
r: Add the years to the current age and compare with the age cut off; pick the later date.
n: Printed answer A, until 23 years (rheumatic fever with carditis features).

q: Same Q: with the pic (they say in the case that it's an egg on a string but know what it looks like) Next step in management?
k: TGA management ladder: 1. IV PGE1 to keep the PDA open; 2. Balloon atrial septostomy if mixing is still inadequate; 3. Arterial switch operation, usually in the first weeks of life
r: Duct-dependent cyanotic baby: open the duct with prostaglandin; indomethacin closes it and is the trap.
n: TGA (egg on a string): next step is IV prostaglandin (PGE1) to keep the ductus open before surgical repair. Recaller: Students say the stem mentions egg on a string; know what it looks like.

q: 2 weeks newborn came with SOB and cyanosis, on PE there was [delayed pulse] in the lower limbs, what is the diagnosis?
k: Pulse discrepancy between arms and legs = coarctation of the aorta.

q: Neonate who has different upper from lower blood pressure. diagnose?
k: Upper limb BP greater than lower limb BP or radiofemoral delay = coarctation of the aorta.

n: No answer line for the main version; compiler pairs it with a 21-23 September inset headed 'Delayed pulse in L.L = coarctation of aorta' (Answer: B), endorsing coarctation for upper/lower discrepancy.

q: A 2-day-old neonate presents to the Emergency Department with sudden sever cyanosis. On examination, he looks cyanotic, lethargic; with cardiac exam reveals no murmur and normal pulses (see report). Chest X-Ray: Showed egg on side appearance of the cardiac shadow and increased pulmonary vascular marking. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Cyanotic CHD chest X-ray patterns: Egg on a string (side), increased lung markings: TGA; Boot-shaped heart, reduced lung markings: tetralogy of Fallot; Snowman (figure of 8): supracardiac TAPVR
r: Early neonatal severe cyanosis with no murmur and plethoric lungs is TGA; oligaemic lungs with a murmur is TOF.
n: Answer tagged (MG). Egg-on-a-string cardiac shadow with increased pulmonary vascular markings and early severe cyanosis = TGA. Slide shows example chest X-rays.

q: (Image-Based Question) A preterm neonate presents with cyanosis and tachypnea (accompanying image is suggestive of transposition of the great arteries (TGA).) What is the most appropriate next step in management?

n: TGA initial management is prostaglandin to keep the ductus open; surgery is definitive. Embedded file version (Q144) also answers prostaglandin infusion. Recaller: Recaller (exam 20 October): expect images because the files show the egg sign, but in the exam i

q: Picture of transposition of Great vessels 20 hour old baby came with respiratory distress , cyanosis What is the most appropriate next step
k: Neonate with cyanotic duct-dependent CHD: start prostaglandin E1 first.
r: Any duct-dependent neonatal heart lesion: prostaglandin before surgery.
n: Embedded inset: file version (Image-based MCQ Q144) with different options; printed Answer: C. Prostaglandin infusion.

q: 5 day old infant has respiratory distress and absent femoral pulse (cyanosis NOT MENTIONED), what we will do?
k: Critical coarctation in a neonate: open the duct, support the heart, then operate.
r: Absent femoral pulses in a newborn is an emergency sign; a sick neonate gets prostaglandin before any procedure.
n: Embedded inset: older version with options; Answer A. Same concept: even if cyanosis is not mentioned, neonatal CoA is a ductus-dependent lesion, so start prostaglandin.

q: Neonate diagnosed with transposition of great arteries (Xray was provided, egg on a string with lung vascular prominence) they said the Apgar score was good. I don't remember the word 'cyanosis' the baby was almost asymptomatic as far as I remember. 02 sat was in the 70s What is the initial step?
k: Duct dependent cyanotic CHD: prostaglandin E1 first, definitive repair later.
r: Indomethacin closes the duct, PGE1 keeps it open; in TGA you want it open.
n: Answer A. prostaglandin E1; same-version inset (Q 142) agrees and notes definitive treatment is heart surgery. October By Similar update

q: Newborn came with perioral cyanosis and different Pulse oximetry between upper and lower extremities what is the best next step in management?
k: Differential SpO2 (upper > lower) in a newborn = right to left flow through the PDA to the lower body: think ductus dependent arch lesion and start PGE1.
r: Septostomy belongs to TGA; prostaglandin belongs to any ductus dependent lesion, so it is the safe first step here.

q: 14 years old male with dyslipidemia and stage one hypertension and taking antihypertensive Which of the following will help him most (not written like this)

q: Peds 4 weeks discovered he had coarctation of aorta upon blood pressure examination Which of the following anaomalies has this defect

q: Exertional Syncope A 14-year-old patient experiences sudden loss of consciousness while running and regains consciousness spontaneously shortly afterward. There are no preceding symptoms or other associated complaints. Physical examination is unremarkable, with no cardiac murmur. What is the most appropriate next step?

r: Syncope DURING exercise is cardiac until proven otherwise; syncope just AFTER exercise or after prolonged standing is usually vasovagal.
n: Printed answer C (ECG) as the first step in exertional syncope.

q: A 12 years old girl previously healthy brought to emergency after loss of consciousness with immediate recovery, that's happened while taking blood sample for lab investigation, she had normal developmental and had no previous history. Which of the following it is most appropriate next management?

q: A 5-month-old infant is brought by his mother, who has noticed decreased activity and that he no longer smiles. He has repeated clusters of sudden brief flexion-extension spasms, each lasting 1-2 seconds, with about 20 spasms per cluster. An EEG is ordered. Which finding is expected?

r: Brief spasms in clusters plus "no longer smiles" in an infant = West syndrome; do not dismiss the spasms as Moro reflex or colic.
n: Printed answer A (infantile spasms / West syndrome -> hypsarrhythmia). 19 October update ↻ Printed again later in this 19 October file (p.834) with the same answer; author's note there: Printed answer A (infantile spasms / West syndrome).

q: 14-month-old presents to Primary Clinic with recurrent syncopal attack, associated with worsening heart failure manifestation and poor growth. q: A child presents with unconsciousness. ECG image shows (SVT). What is the most appropriate next step in management?
k: SVT management depends on stability.
r: Check consciousness and BP first: unstable SVT means synchronized cardioversion, and drugs or vagal maneuvers must never delay it.
n: Unstable SVT (unconscious) needs synchronized cardioversion.

q: down syndrome young patient came with no cyanosis only some abnormal breathing and mild symptoms Which of the following heart defects is expected

q: A 2-year-old child is referred to a pediatric cardiologist for evaluation of a heart murmur detected during a routine examination. Echocardiography reveals a left-to-right shunt between the atria, with a bulging membrane noted at the interatrial septum. What is the most likely diagnosis?

q: In cardiology clinic 2-year-old child came with heart murmur and child is asymptomatic (see report). Echocardiogram: Left-to-right atrial shunt with bulging membrane.

r: Fixed split S2 or an interatrial shunt on echo = ASD; add Down syndrome and a superior axis = AVSD.
n: Left-to-right shunt between the atria with a bulging membrane = ASD. 15-18 October update

q: Pediatric cardiologist is evaluating child for murmur, echo report: left to right shunt btw atria with bulging membrane, dx?
