k: Stages of shock in children: compensated, then decompensated, then irreversible.
r: "Earliest sign" = tachycardia; "decompensated" = failing perfusion (cold, cyanosed peripheries, then hypotension).
n: Printed answer C.

q: Case of baby with VSD who have poor feeding, SOB, diaphoresis, CXR show cardio megaly cardiothoracic ratio >60% + bilateral infiltration What is the most appropriate?
k: VSD + cardiomegaly + bilateral infiltrates = congestive heart failure, not primary pneumonia.
r: Bilateral patches in a VSD infant are read as congestion; only clear infection features move the answer to antibiotics.
n: Embedded lookalike version of the VSD heart failure question: CXR cardiomegaly with bilateral infiltrates indicates pulmonary congestion, so stabilization and diuretics. Marked 'Need better recall'. Recaller: I only remember options; Need better recall

q: A 7-year-old girl presents with development of secondary sexual characteristics, including breast development and pubic hair. Her bone age is advanced to 9 years. TSH, FSH and LH are within the normal range, while estradiol is elevated. What is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Central vs peripheral precocious puberty is decided by LH and FSH.
r: High sex steroid with LH/FSH not raised = peripheral; another version of this recall is keyed central, so read the gonadotropin result carefully.
n: High estradiol with normal (non-elevated) gonadotropins = gonadotropin independent, peripheral precocious puberty. Other version of this recall in Part 2: SWR-1936 → B. Central precocious puberty.

q: A 3 week old Infant presented with lethargy and hypotonia, glusose measurement was 38 (low), β-hydroxybutyrate (0.1)- normally greater than 15 during fasting, insulin was 40 (reference range 10-110), 4pm cortisol 550 (upper limit 440), urine analysis all absent except for trace protein, what is the likely diagnosis?
k: Critical sample at the time of hypoglycemia sorts the cause: Low ketones + detectable insulin = hyperinsulinism.; Low ketones + suppressed insulin = fatty acid oxidation defect (high free fatty acids).; High ketones + low cortisol or GH = adrenal insufficiency or GH deficiency/hypopituitarism.
r: Do not be reassured by an insulin value inside the reference range: during hypoglycemia it should be undetectable.
n: Recaller: Recaller unsure of the exact wording of option C ("I think").

q: A pediatric patient was diagnosed with phenylketonuria (PKU). What is the most appropriate dietary management?
k: Each metabolic disease restricts its own offending substrate.
r: Diet is lifelong and strictest before and during pregnancy, because maternal PKU harms the fetus (microcephaly, heart defects).
n: Other versions of this recall in this deck: SWR-0326 → A. Restrict phenylalanine

q: What is the appropriate diet for a patient with phenylketonuria (PKU)?
k: PKU diet = low phenylalanine, not low protein overall.
r: Options that list several sugars or "protein" in general are distractors; PKU restricts one amino acid.
n: Other versions of this recall in this deck: SWR-0325 → A. Restrict phenylalanine

q: 7 years old girl present with enlarged breast and pubic hair, height above 95th percentile, bone age of 9 years, tanner stage for breast 3 and pubic hair 2 FSH, LH and TSH: normal Estradiol: high ( no numbers) What is most likely the cause?
k: Central vs peripheral precocious puberty is decided by gonadotropins.
r: Normal pubertal sequence suggests central, but high sex steroid with low or normal LH/FSH overrides it and means peripheral.
n: Printed answer D: high estradiol with normal (not raised) FSH/LH indicates peripheral (gonadotropin-independent) precocious puberty.

q: Girl newborn with ambiguous genitalia. Chromosomal studies done & it was 46 XX with uterus & ovary (mature). What's the cause of ambiguous genitalia?
k: Ambiguous genitalia: karyotype + gonads + uterus sort it.
r: XX + ovaries + virilization = CAH; check electrolytes urgently because salt-wasting crisis can kill in the first weeks.
n: 46,XX virilized newborn with normal uterus and ovaries: congenital adrenal hyperplasia.

q: A 12-year-old boy has joint hyperextensibility and is taller than his classmates (1.78m). No systemic abnormalities noted. What is the likely diagnosis?
k: Tall + hypermobile = Marfan; hypermobile + stretchy fragile skin = Ehlers-Danlos.
r: Height is the tiebreaker: hypermobility alone cannot separate Marfan from EDS, tall stature can.
n: Hyperextensibility is common to both Marfan and EDS; tall stature favors Marfan, absence of eye disease favors EDS (classic distinguishing feature). If you consider 'no systemic abnormalities' equivalent to 'no eye disease' then EDS; if not, then Marfan. It de

q: child did neurosurgery and now having polydpsia, polyuria Na 177 K normal
k: Polyuria after brain injury or surgery: check sodium.
r: DI = high sodium with dilute urine; SIADH = low sodium with concentrated urine.
n: Polyuria, polydipsia and hypernatremia after neurosurgery indicates central diabetes insipidus.

q: Child came with 3 days hx of headache and neck stiffness.. he denised photophobia .. Serum glucose: 4.4 CSf analysis show : Glucose 3.8 Prominent lemphocytes Protien 450 (normal limit was up to 450) What is the diagnosis?
k: Read the CSF by glucose first, then the cell type.
r: Lymphocytes alone do not mean viral: lymphocytes plus LOW glucose is TB until proven otherwise.
n: CSF:serum glucose ratio >0.4 (actually >0.6) -> viral.

q: A previously healthy 4-month-old uncircumcised boy is brought to the Emergency Department with a 2-day history of fever. He has not had vomiting, diarrhea, cough, or nasal congestion. There has been no known contact with ill persons. He has continued to breastfeed and has not had a decrease in the number wet diapers. He is mildly ill appearing but alert and interactive. Examination shows no focus of infection. Urinary catheterization is performed (see lab results). Temperature 39.1 C Test Result Normal Values pH 7.5 4.3-8 Specific gravity 1010 1001-1030 Protein Absent Absent Glucose Absent Absent Ketones Absent Absent Nitrite Positive Absent Leukocytes 30-40 0-3 per high power field Erythrocytes 5-10 0-2 per high power field which of the following is the most appropriate empirical therapy?
k: Febrile infant UTI: the route depends on age and how sick the child looks.
r: 'Alert, interactive, feeding, normal wet diapers' is the stem telling you to go oral.
n: Well-appearing, feeding infant over 2 months with febrile UTI can be treated with oral antibiotics (cephalexin). Source: Medgard (MG). Other version of this recall in Part 2: SWR-1469 → A. Oral Amoxicillin

q: 10-year-old boy presents to the Emergency Department with polyuria, polydipsia, abdominal pain, and vomiting. He is diagnosed with diabetic ketoacidosis DKA) and is started on IV fluids and IV insulin infusion. After 2 hours of treatment, the child becomes confused and drowsy, with a decreased level of consciousness. Vital signs are stable, and blood glucose is declining steadily. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
k: Falling consciousness during pediatric DKA treatment = cerebral edema.
r: Cerebral edema is a clinical diagnosis: give mannitol before the CT.
n: Decreased consciousness during DKA treatment in a child suggests cerebral edema: give IV mannitol.

q: A previously healthy 11-year-old child presents with a 2-day history of vomiting, diarrhea, and lethargy. On examination, he is drowsy and his breath has a fruity odor. Laboratory results show random blood sugar (RBS) of 8.9 mmol/L and bicarbonate of 15 mmol/L. What is the most likely diagnosis?
k: DKA = hyperglycaemia + metabolic acidosis + ketosis.
r: Fruity breath and low bicarbonate mean ketoacidosis; HHS has neither.
n: Printed answer DKA (fruity breath and low bicarbonate despite only mildly raised glucose). No further commentary.

q: 15 years old Turner ( 45X) , she presented with no breast development and High FSH and LH and low estradiol. What do we give her?
k: Delayed puberty: FSH/LH tell you the level of failure.
r: Watch for 'only' in an option: GH alone ignores the estrogen deficiency.
n: Compiler and both other contributors (Naif-KSAU-Avengers, Eithar-Avengers) answer A. Estrogen replacement therapy; the word 'ONLY' in option B makes it wrong. Recaller: They didn't mention Turner, only the karyotype; option B literally said 'only'.

q: A child is brought to the clinic for genetic screening. The physician explains that the child has a 25% chance of inheriting the disease from both parents. Which pattern of inheritance is most likely?
k: Recurrence risk by inheritance pattern.
r: An XLR carrier mother also gives an affected child in 1 of 4 pregnancies overall, but that comes from the mother alone; "from both parents" = autosomal recessive.
n: Printed answer B, autosomal recessive (25% risk when both parents are carriers). No further commentary.

q: A child with a known fatty acid oxidation defect develops fatigue and hypoglycemia following a viral illness. Which of the following measures is most effective in preventing metabolic decompensation during future illness episodes?
k: Fatty acid oxidation defects (e.g. MCAD): avoid fasting, give carbohydrate.
r: Hypoglycemia with LOW or absent ketones after fasting = think fatty acid oxidation defect.
n: Printed answer A, continuous glucose infusion during illness to prevent decompensation in fatty acid oxidation defects. No further commentary.

q: 10-year-old male, known case of decompensated cirrhosis, developed confusion and asterixis. Serum ammonia level is 150 µmol/L (normal < 50). What is the first line of management?
k: Hepatic encephalopathy in cirrhosis.
r: Fever or abdominal pain with encephalopathy in cirrhosis: tap the ascites, because SBP is the precipitant to treat alongside lactulose.
n: Printed answer B: hepatic encephalopathy is treated first line with lactulose (plus rifaximin). Recaller: No Dialysis In Options

q: A child is being followed up for tall stature. He has easy bruising, an arm span greater than his height and long fingers, and is followed by ophthalmology for eye problems. He has no intellectual disability. What is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Tall child differential. Marfan (AD, FBN1): arachnodactyly, arm span > height, ectopia lentis (up), aortic root dilatation, MVP, pectus, normal IQ.; Homocystinuria (AR): Marfanoid, lens down, intellectual disability, thrombosis.; Klinefelter: tall, small testes, gynecomastia, hypogonadism.
r: Marfanoid + intellectual disability or thrombosis = homocystinuria; Marfanoid + normal IQ + aortic root = Marfan.
n: Marfanoid habitus with lens problems and normal intelligence is Marfan syndrome (fibrillin-1). Homocystinuria adds intellectual disability and thromboembolism; Klinefelter has no arachnodactyly or eye involvement. The compiler circled 'easy bruising' with '???

q: A previously healthy 11-year-old with 2 days of vomiting and diarrhea, decreased oral intake, increasing lethargy, fruity breath odor, mild hypotension. Labs: RBS 8.9 mmol/L, Na 131 mmol/L, HCO3 15 mmol/L. Most likely cause?
k: DKA = 2 of 3: hyperglycemia, metabolic acidosis (pH < 7.3, HCO3 < 15), ketosis.
r: Fruity breath plus low bicarbonate means DKA even when the glucose looks unimpressive.

q: 6 day old child, feeds well, presents with jaundice, hepatosplenomegaly, and bilateral cataract. He has positive urine reducing substance test.
k: Neonatal jaundice + hepatomegaly + cataracts + urine reducing substances = galactosemia.
r: Cataracts plus liver disease in a milk-fed neonate = galactosemia; E. coli sepsis is its classic complication.
n: Printed answer A; no compiler commentary.

q: A 6 years old child.... with a father being hypertensive at 30 years old, NO systemic manifestations. Low aldosterone Low renin Labs sent for (SCNN1A, SCNN1B, or SCNN1G) Asked about dx?
k: Hypertension + hypokalaemia: read renin and aldosterone together.
r: Low renin AND low aldosterone with early familial hypertension = Liddle; Conn has low renin but high aldosterone.
n: Liddle syndrome: early familial hypertension with low renin and low aldosterone due to ENaC gene (SCNN1A/B/G) mutations. Compiler praises the recall.

q: How should patients with cystic fibrosis be screened for diabetes mellitus, and how often should screening be performed?
k: CFRD screening = annual OGTT.
r: In CF, a normal HbA1c or fasting glucose does not exclude diabetes; only the OGTT is the recommended screen.

q: 7 year-old pediatric male pt diagnosed with type 2 DM. Which of the following will DELAY the INCIDENCE of type 2 diabetes Mellitus?
k: Read the lead-in exactly (the stem mixes "diagnosed" with "delay incidence"; the recaller confirmed the wording).
r: "Incidence" means prevention, so metformin; "progression" flips the answer to liraglutide.
n: Rule: prevents type 2 DM (delays incidence) -> metformin; delays progression of type 2 DM -> liraglutide. Recaller: Recaller confirmed the wording: 'yes, it's delay the incidence'.

q: A child with type 1 diabetes experiences recurrent hypoglycemia at night, on basal- bolus insulin regimen:
o: Reduce basal insulin dose at night
Add a meal at 3 at night
k: Match the timing of the low to the insulin that acts then.
r: Treat an acute low with juice, but prevent recurrent night lows by cutting the basal insulin.

q: Newborn of diabetic mother with Jitteriness movements. What to check for?
k: Infant of diabetic mother: think glucose first.
r: Jittery newborn: glucose first; if it is normal, go on to calcium, then magnesium.

q: 5 month old boy with fatigue poor weight gain and hypotonia Labs: low glucose 2.1 (slightly below reference range) B-hydroxybutyrate low (0.001) Cortisol 4 pm 552 (range up to 400s) Fasting insulin 40.8 (range up to 110 i think) Most likely diagnosis?
k: Hypoglycemia workup: draw the critical sample at the time of low glucose.
r: Any measurable insulin during hypoglycemia is inappropriate; the reference range applies only to a normal glucose.
n: Handwritten B; no further compiler commentary. Recaller: Option A not recalled; insulin reference range uncertain

q: A child is brought in for genetic screening. The physician explains the child has a 25% chance of inheriting the disease from both parents. Which pattern of inheritance is most likely?
k: Recurrence risk by inheritance pattern: Autosomal recessive: two carriers give a 25% risk in each pregnancy (examples: cystic fibrosis, CAH, sickle cell, thalassemia); Autosomal dominant: 50% in each pregnancy (example: NF1); X-linked recessive: 50% of sons of a carrier mother affected (example: hem
r: In X-linked recessive, 25% of all children of a carrier mother are affected boys, but the risk is quoted as 50% per son and it is never 'from both parents'.

q: A 4-year-old girl presents to the clinic with breast development at Tanner stage III and pubic hair at Tanner stage II. Laboratory evaluation shows normal FSH and LH with elevated estradiol. What is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Precocious puberty in girls: signs before age 8; LH decides the type.
r: "Normal" gonadotropins in a young child are pubertal for her age; "low" or "suppressed" means peripheral.
n: Compiler: he used to answer C (peripheral), but the correct answer is B (central), not C. Other version of this recall in Part 1: SWR-0137 → B. Peripheral precocious puberty

q: Male pediatric patient has referral from the village with wide- set nipples short neck, often with extra folds of skin (webbed neck) or prominent neck muscles (unusual facial characteristics, short stature, heart defects present at birth, bleeding problems, developmental delays, and malformations of the bones of the rib cage)
k: Webbed neck: Turner in girls, Noonan in either sex.
r: Turner features in a BOY (or a girl with normal karyotype and pulmonary stenosis) = Noonan.

q: 173- 7 yrs old girl with type 1 dm, recently with loss of weight, glucose 250mg/dl. what is the something advice best *approach* for her?
o: educate the family on how to use insulin..
give her pamphlet and for follow up
Postpone Education Till Glucose Is Controlled
k: New or poorly controlled T1DM in a child.
r: Postponing education is only right when the child is in DKA; otherwise teach the family now.
n: She had polyuria, polydipsia and weight loss, but did not meet the other criteria for DKA (no acidosis, no ketosis), so the compiler did not choose D (postpone education till glucose is controlled); educate the family on insulin use.

q: Child first developed fever then within 2 days had Headache photophoipa and neck stiffness and vomiting, later he developed altered mental status, what to expect to find in the CSF?
o: leukocytosis with mainly lymphocytes and normal glucose and protein
leukocytosis with mainly lymphocytes and low glucose and high protein
leukocytosis with mainly polymorphic and low glucose and high protein
k: CSF by cause: read the cell type and glucose together.
r: Normal glucose plus lymphocytes = viral; once glucose drops with lymphocytes, think TB or fungal.
n: Compiler's final answer A: the closest answer (HSV/viral meningoencephalitis), i.e. lymphocytic pleocytosis with normal glucose. Following pages show the related recall and references: viral CSF typically shows lymphocytic pleocytosis, normal glucose and norma

q: Meningitis Case About Child Got All Signs Of Meningitis: Neck Stiffness, Photophobia, Altered Consciousness After URTI. What Would You See In Lumbar Puncture?
o: Elevated Leukocytes, Predominant Neutrophils, High Protein, Low Glucose
Elevated Leukocytes, Predominant Lymphocytes, Normal Protein, Normal Glucose
Elevated Leukocytes, Predominant Lymphocytes, High Protein, Low Gluco
k: Viral meningitis CSF: clear, lymphocytes, normal glucose, protein normal or mildly raised.
r: Glucose is the switch: lymphocytes with normal glucose is viral, with low glucose is TB or fungal.

q: 3 (weeks old or days old baby) presented to the ER with lethargy poor feeding, hypotonia, irritability (i think), his bedside glucose was 35 mg/dl. Critical labs was drown before glucose correction. Lab results: beta-hydroxybutyrate levels 0.1 (Normal >1.5) Glucose 2.2 mmol/l (low) Fasting insulin 44 (i think normal) Cortisol 4 hours above normal (i think slightly high) Other labs normal
k: Neonatal hypoglycemia: read the critical sample (ketones first, then insulin).
r: In hypoglycemia there is no such thing as a normal insulin: any measurable insulin with absent ketones points to hyperinsulinism.
n: Recaller: Recaller unsure of several values ('i think', 'not sure').

q: A newborn baby is diagnosed with panhypopituitarism. Laboratory investigations show low levels of all pituitary-dependent hormones: Cortisol: low ACTH: low Free T4: low TSH: low Growth hormone: low LH: low FSH: low What is the most appropriate next step in management?
k: Hypopituitarism replacement order: cortisol before thyroxine.
r: Thyroxine before steroids in combined deficiency can unmask an adrenal crisis; always replace cortisol first.
n: In panhypopituitarism, replace cortisol first (hydrocortisone) before thyroxine. Inset shows the terser 17 September version with the same options and a handwritten A.

q: A patient is taller than the rest of his classmates and playing basketball. On examination, he has a high arched palate and thin. Which of the following syndromes is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Tall + thin + long limbs = Marfan; stretchy skin + hypermobile joints = Ehlers-Danlos.
r: A high arched palate alone is shared by several syndromes (including Turner); tall stature is what makes it Marfan.
n: Printed answer: Marfan syndrome.

q: 6 years old girl her mother noted 8 abnormal movements in the form of tonic colonic some time associated with mouth deviation and last few seconds and resolved without intervention and in the morning. she noticed the same movements when the patient comb her hair and resolve, systemicreview and examination unremarkable EEG-show Focal sharp spick in the cenrto-temporal area, What is the DX?
k: Childhood epilepsy syndromes are decided by age, seizure type and EEG.
r: Morning jerks in a teenager is juvenile myoclonic epilepsy; morning or nocturnal facial seizures with centrotemporal spikes in a school child is Rolandic.
n: Centrotemporal spikes indicate benign Rolandic epilepsy.

q: 7 yo girl with enlarged breast and public hair Normal FSH ,TSH HIGH estradiol Bone age 9 No hyperpigmentation no cafe alu Diagnosis?
k: Precocious puberty = puberty before 8 years in girls (9 in boys). Central vs peripheral: Central: pubertal LH/FSH, gonads make the steroids, normal sequence, always isosexual; Peripheral: suppressed LH/FSH, steroid source is gonad, adrenal, ectopic or exogenous, sequence may be abnormal; Workup: LH,
r: High sex steroid with non-suppressed gonadotropins = central; high steroid with suppressed LH/FSH = peripheral.
n: Printed answer central precocious puberty; no cafe au lait spots argues against McCune-Albright. No further commentary.

q: Male patient with features of wide neck, a low hairline a (broad or flat) chest low set ears, what is the syndrome?
k: Turner-like features: girl = Turner (45,X); boy (or girl with normal karyotype) = Noonan.
r: The sex of the patient flips the answer: same webbed neck and shield chest, male = Noonan, female = Turner.

q: Infant > 6 months, presented with jaundice. Upon taking history his mother revealed that when she introduced fruits at 6 months, he started having N/V and other symptoms. You examine him and he has jaundice, and organomegaly Urine Reducing substance test = + Diagnosis??
k: Link the trigger food to the enzyme defect.
r: Jaundice and vomiting starting with breast milk or formula = galactosemia; starting with fruit = fructose intolerance.

q: 2 days boy present with poor feeding and vomiting then developed decreases consciousness and intermittent apnea ( glucose normal and markedly high ammonia 420 ) urea cycle disorder is suspected Next step in Management?
o: Oral lactuluse and monitor for ammonia for 24 hours
Urgent dialysis after stabilization and hydration
Administer Sodium benzoate and continue protein intake
k: Neonatal hyperammonemia with encephalopathy: stop protein, give glucose, start scavengers and arrange dialysis.
r: Lactulose belongs to cirrhosis; in a neonate with a urea cycle disorder and coma, the answer is dialysis.
n: Compiler highlights apnea and 'Next' step: severe hyperammonemia with encephalopathy in a neonate with suspected urea cycle disorder needs urgent dialysis.

q: New born of diabetic mother have 71% hematocrit and plethora what is next step
k: Neonatal polycythemia = venous hematocrit >65%; infant of a diabetic mother is a classic cause (fetal hypoxia drives erythropoietin).
r: Symptoms decide the step: asymptomatic plethoric baby → fluids/observe; any hyperviscosity symptoms → partial exchange transfusion.
n: Compiler's answer is IV fluid (not among the recalled options); if IV fluid is not an option, answer is A. no intervention needed. Page also notes 'Trust Me, I Saw Option B' (someone insisting option B appeared). Recaller: Trust Me, I Saw Option "B"

q: A 7-year-old girl presents with breast enlargement and pubic hair. She is taller than the 97th percentile, with an advanced bone age. There are no cafe-au-lait skin lesions, no abdominal mass, and no signs of virilization. LH, FSH, and TSH are within the normal range (exact values not provided). Estradiol is elevated. Brain MRI is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Precocious puberty: decide central vs peripheral by the gonadotropins.
r: High estradiol with suppressed LH/FSH flips the answer to peripheral; non-suppressed gonadotropins plus normal sequence means central.
n: Printed answer central precocious puberty; no further commentary.

q: 6 years old girl with pubic and axillary hair Normal testosterone & fsh & lh Except high estradiol what is the diagnosis ?
k: Central vs peripheral precocious puberty (girls: signs before 8 years): Central: pubertal LH/FSH, gonads make the steroids, normal sequence, always isosexual; Peripheral: prepubertal/suppressed LH/FSH, steroid source is gonad tumour/cyst, adrenal or exogenous; sequence may be abnormal; Work-up: LH,
r: High estradiol with LOW LH/FSH = peripheral; high estradiol with pubertal LH/FSH = central. 'Normal' for a 6-year-old is ambiguous.

q: Adolescent present with history of diarrhea for few days what acid-base and electrolyte abnormality
k: Diarrhea loses bicarbonate and potassium: hypokalemic (normal anion gap, hyperchloremic) metabolic acidosis.
r: Vomiting and diarrhea both cause hypokalemia; they differ in pH: vomiting alkalosis, diarrhea acidosis.
n: Printed answer B. Compiler (Alhomrani): careful, it is diarrhea not vomiting. Acidosis can cause hyperkalemia, but diarrhea gives both acidosis AND hypokalemia (diarrhea is directly and indirectly hypokalemic).

q: 10-year-old boy came to the clinic, (he is the tallest student in his school + one sentence about his basketball team) Physical examination: thin body, high-arched palate, scoliosis, and joint hyperextensibility What is the diagnosis?
k: Tall child differential: Marfan: tall thin, arachnodactyly, high-arched palate, pectus, scoliosis, upward lens dislocation, aortic root dilatation, MVP; Homocystinuria: marfanoid + intellectual disability, downward lens dislocation, thrombosis; Klinefelter: tall, small testes, gynecomastia, infertil
r: Joint laxity alone does not mean Ehlers-Danlos; tall thin habitus plus palate and spine findings is Marfan.
n: Printed answer: Marfan syndrome (tall, thin habitus, high-arched palate, scoliosis, joint laxity).

q: A 6-year-old child presents with a 2-day history of fever, photophobia, and confusion. He now develops neck stiffness. CSF analysis is performed. Which of the following CSF findings is most likely?
o: Neutrophil predominance, low glucose, normal protein
Neutrophils with very high protein and low glucose
k: CSF by cause: look at glucose first, then cell type.
r: Normal glucose + lymphocytes = viral; low glucose + neutrophils = bacterial.
n: Printed answer B (viral meningitis CSF picture).

q: Child came for follow up her mother noticed pigmentation on her back and neck, she had low activity and family history of type 2 DM . On examination she is overweight What is the most appropriate for prevention
o: Refere her for dermatology for her skin pigmentation
k: Acanthosis nigricans in an overweight child = insulin resistance: screen for type 2 DM and prediabetes, then lifestyle first.
r: Pigmented neck folds in an obese child are a metabolic sign, not a skin referral: screen glucose and treat with lifestyle.
n: Printed answer A (acanthosis nigricans with risk factors: screen with HbA1c and lifestyle modification).

q: A 2-day-old boy presents with poor feeding and vomiting then developed decreased consciousness and intermittent apnea (glucose normal and markedly high ammonia 420). Urea cycle disorder is suspected. Next step in management?
o: Oral lactulose and monitor ammonia for 24 hours
Urgent dialysis after stabilization and hydration
Administer sodium benzoate and continue protein intake
k: Urea cycle disorder crisis = emergency ammonia removal.
r: Any option that 'continues protein' or 'monitors for 24 hours' in a comatose hyperammonemic neonate is wrong.
n: Embedded related version; printed answer C. Compiler circles 'Next' to contrast lead-ins.

q: Down syndrome child with constipation and decreased inactivity (written like this could be misspelled idk) for 4 months what should be ordered ?
k: Down syndrome + constipation/lethargy/weight gain = check thyroid.
r: Down syndrome with constipation since birth (delayed meconium) is Hirschsprung; new constipation with lethargy is hypothyroidism.
n: Down syndrome with constipation and lethargy: check for hypothyroidism.

q: a 10-year-old child is admitted to PICU after extensive head trauma. Soon afterward urine output rises to about 100 mL/h. Serum osmolality is 326 mOsm/kg and urine osmolality is 90 mOsm/kg.
k: Serum osmolality high + urine inappropriately dilute = DI; serum low + urine inappropriately concentrated = SIADH.
r: Head injury can cause both DI and SIADH; the urine and serum osmolality, not the trigger, decide which.

q: Patient child on insulin dependent diabetes or smth like this But the main question is How to check for Diabetic nephropathy
k: Diabetic nephropathy screening = urine albumin (spot albumin/creatinine ratio).
r: If both "urine microalbumin" and "albumin/creatinine ratio" appear, pick the ratio; it corrects for urine concentration.

q: A 13-year-old patient presents with fatigue and decreased appetite. His BMI is 31 kg/m2, and he has dark discoloration of the neck. He has a family history of type 2 diabetes mellitus. What is the most appropriate preventive care?
o: Check HbA1c and recommend lifestyle modifications
k: Youth T2DM screening: overweight/obese after puberty or from age 10, plus risk factors.
r: Acanthosis nigricans in an obese teen = insulin resistance; screen first, do not treat a diagnosis you have not made.
n: Printed answer B: screen with HbA1c and recommend lifestyle modification (obese adolescent with acanthosis nigricans and family history of T2DM).

q: 12 y.o k/c of DM1 presented to ER with n/v and abdominal pain. Assessment reveled moderate DKA. Pt was transferred to PICU and started on DKA management protocol. After an hour, it become disoriented and GCS went down to 13. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
o: Infuse normal saline 20 ml/kg over 15 mins
k: Pediatric DKA cerebral edema: recognize clinically, treat immediately.
r: In DKA, a dropping GCS after treatment starts is cerebral edema: give mannitol before the CT.

q: A 6-year-old girl presents with accelerated growth, advanced bone age (9 years), Tanner stage 3 breast development, and Tanner stage 2 pubic hair. Her laboratory results show: LH and FSH: Normal (not elevated) Estradiol: Elevated
k: Precocious puberty: gonadotropins decide central vs peripheral.
r: 'Normal' LH/FSH in a young child with high estrogen is not reassuring: it is inappropriately unsuppressed, so think central; 'low/suppressed' LH/FSH flips the answer to peripheral.
n: Even low LH/FSH cannot rule out central puberty; here they are normal, not low (inappropriately normal, i.e. higher than expected). Also stage 3 breast with stage 2 pubic hair 'favors' (not 100%) central over peripheral.

q: 12 y.o k/c of DM1 presented to ER with n/v and abdominal pain. Assessment revealed moderate DKA. Pt was transferred to PICU and started on DKA management protocol. After an hour, it became disoriented and GCS went down to 13. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
o: Infuse normal saline 20 ml/kg over 15 mins
k: Neurological decline during DKA treatment = cerebral edema: treat first, image later.

q: 9-year-old child with bedwetting for 3 months, associated with weight loss and polydipsia. Next investigation?
k: Secondary enuresis (wet again after at least 6 months dry) needs a cause search: Polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss = type 1 diabetes: check blood glucose; Dysuria, frequency, fever = UTI: urinalysis and culture; Polyuria with dilute urine and normal glucose = diabetes insipidus
r: Enuresis plus weight loss and thirst = diabetes until proven otherwise; once glucose is high, check ketones to exclude DKA.

q: A 9-year-old child presents to Emergency Department with hypovolemic shock. Parents gave history of recent brain surgery and the child has polyurea and increased thirst since then (see lab results). Blood pressure 70/40 mmg Heart rate 136 /min Respiratory rate 18 /min Temperature 36.6 C Oxygen saturation 95 % Test Result Normal Values ABG HCO3- 20 13-22 mmol/L ABG PCO2 35 27-40 mmHg pH 7.37 7.36-7.45 ABG PO2 88 8-24 mmHg (Newborn) 55-80 mmg (Child) Base access -6 -2 to 2 mmol/L Sodium 177 134-146 mol/L Potassium 4 3.5-5.1 mol/L Chloride 140 97-108 mmol/L Bicarbonate 20 21-28 mmol/L Blood urea nitrogen 8 0.7-6.7 mmol/L (Newborn) 1.8 to 6.4 mmol/L (Child) Creatinine 60 27-88 mol/L. (Newborn) 27-62 mol/L. (Child) Glucose 4.5 2.8-5 mmol/L (Newborn) 3.3 -5.5 mmol/L (Child) Color colorless clear or light yellow Appearance Clear clear Specific gravity 1003 1001-1030 Ketones absent Absent Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion

n: Printed answer B. Compiler highlights in red sodium 177, glucose 4.5 and ketones absent (pointing away from DKA toward DI after brain surgery); comments 'I Also Can't Read This' about the garbled lab table. Option A carries '**' as printed. October By Similar

q: A 9-year-old child presents to the Emergency Department with hypovolemic shock. He had recent brain surgery and has had polyuria and increased thirst since then. BP 70/40 mmHg, HR 136/min, RR 18/min, temperature 36.6 C, oxygen saturation 95%. ABG: pH 7.37, PCO2 35 mmHg, PO2 88 mmHg, HCO3 20 mmol/L, base excess -6. Sodium 177 mmol/L, potassium 4 mmol/L, chloride 140 mmol/L, BUN 8 mmol/L, creatinine 60 micromol/L, glucose 4.5 mmol/L. Urine: colorless, clear, specific gravity 1003, ketones absent. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion

q: 1 old boy with polyuria and polypepsia and not gaining weight. other boys in the family had the same complain
k: Polyuria + polydipsia + failure to thrive + affected male relatives = X-linked nephrogenic DI.
r: A family history in boys turns DI from central into nephrogenic (X-linked); a head injury or neurosurgery turns it into central.
n: Printed answer line reads 'A. Diabetes insipidus' but Diabetes Insipidus is option C; mapped by meaning to C. X-linked pattern (affected boys in family) suggests nephrogenic DI.

q: 14-year-old boy presents with polyuria, polydipsia, polyphagia, and weight loss. Which of the following is the best intervention to delay the development of type 2 diabetes?
k: Delaying type 2 diabetes: lifestyle first (weight loss, exercise); metformin is the drug of choice when a drug is asked.
r: The verb 'delay' turns a diabetes stem into a prevention question; if lifestyle modification were listed it would beat any drug.
n: Printed answer A. Metformin (compiler highlights 'delay' and 'type 2' in red). 19 October update ↻ Printed again later in this 19 October file (p.653) with the same answer; author's note there: Metformin is the intervention (besides lifestyle) to delay type 2

q: A 7-year-old boy is diagnosed with type 2 diabetes mellitus. Which of the following will delay the incidence of type 2 diabetes mellitus?
k: Pediatric type 2 DM: lifestyle + metformin; insulin if decompensated.
r: If the stem adds ketoacidosis or a very high HbA1c, the answer flips to insulin.
n: Printed answer C) Metformin [Complete], option bold; compiler answer line C. Metformin. Source tag [q10600 Pediatrics Paediatric endocrine].

q: 6-year-old with type 1 DM he is take long-acting insulin before bedtime and rapid acting insulin before meals, he gets frequent hypoglycemia attacks late at night what is the most appropriate management?
k: Match the timing of hypoglycemia to the insulin acting at that time.
r: Night lows on bedtime basal insulin: cut the basal, do not add snacks.
n: Rule: post-prandial hypoglycemia -> decrease short acting (bolus/rapid) insulin; fasting hypoglycemia -> decrease long acting (basal); hypoglycemia at night/throughout the day -> decrease long acting (basal).

q: 6 or 4 years old child with DM type 1 complaining of repeated hypoglycemia at night, his current medication's are rapid acting insulin before meal and basal insulin at night what is the most appropriate modification on his current regimen:
o: decrease the dose of basal insulin
k: Basal-bolus troubleshooting by timing.
r: Treat a single low with sugar; prevent recurring lows by adjusting the insulin acting at that time.
n: Embedded inset: older version with different option order; answer decrease basal insulin. Night hypoglycemia -> decrease long acting (basal) insulin; post-prandial -> decrease rapid insulin.

q: 6 hours old infant, shortly after C-Section he started to have respiratory distress. What is the Most Important Next step investigation ?
k: Respiratory distress after C-section: Most likely TTN (fetal lung fluid not cleared).; Most important investigation: CXR.; Management: oxygen, supportive care.
r: "Most important investigation" for neonatal distress = the one that shows the cause: CXR.
n: Embedded inset: older lookalike recall; '6' and 'C-Section' circled in red, handwritten A, answer A- Chest radiograph.

q: 10-year-old male, known case of decompensated cirrhosis, developed confusion and asterixis. Serum ammonia level is 150 umol/L (normal < 50). What is the first line of management?
k: Asterixis + confusion in cirrhosis = hepatic encephalopathy.
r: Ammonia level does not decide the treatment here; the clinical encephalopathy does, and lactulose is the backbone.
n: Embedded inset: older recall with 3 numbered options (lettered by position); compiler notes 'No Dialysis In Options'. Answer 2 = B. Oral lactulose with rifaximin.

q: Neonate after delivery had jitteriness, hypotonia and developed convulsion that aborted spontaneously. Labs: Glucose: 2.4 (2.8-3.5) Hb: 210 Hct: 0.70 WBC: Low (number was mentioned i think) What is the most appropriate management?
k: Symptomatic neonatal hypoglycemia (seizure, jitteriness, lethargy) = IV dextrose bolus then continuous glucose infusion.
r: A seizing neonate with a low glucose gets dextrose first, whatever else is abnormal on the labs.
n: October By Similar update

q: Full-term infant. presents with episodes of jitteriness and brief seizures lasting a few seconds and resolve spontaneously. I believe his blood glucose was low, 2.(something)

q: A child presents with a band-like headache that has been occurring for the past 2 weeks. He has been spending several hours playing electronic games for the past 3 weeks. There are no other concerning symptoms or neurological abnormalities. What is the most appropriate next step?

q: 2 y Pediatric patient presented in ER with low grade fever and (brassy cough!) not barky. What is the appropriate initial management?
k: Croup: viral (parainfluenza) subglottic narrowing; treat by severity.
r: No stridor at rest = mild = dexamethasone; stridor at rest with distress = epinephrine plus steroid.

q: 7-year-old boy visited grandfather's farm, presents with diarrhea, miosis, vomiting, lacrimation, salivation, excessive urination, bronchospasm, garlic odor. Administer?
k: Organophosphate poisoning: stabilize airway, decontaminate, atropine then pralidoxime.
r: Asked 'diagnosis' the answer is organophosphate poisoning; asked 'administer first' it is atropine, never pralidoxime alone.
n: Organophosphate poisoning: atropine before pralidoxime. UpToDate excerpt: pralidoxime should not be given without concurrent atropine, and an atropine response should be established before pralidoxime.

q: Pediatric KC of febrile seizure, 4days ago had Febrile viral illness, NOW presnted with lathergy, vomiting, no change in bowel habits, his mother said she was worried about him developing seizure so she was giving him ANTIPYRETIC every 4 hours, examination revealed jundice, palpable liver, what is the cause? No labs
k: Repeated supratherapeutic paracetamol in children causes delayed liver injury.
r: Look for the drug in the history: "giving antipyretic every 4 hours" plus jaundice is paracetamol toxicity, not viral hepatitis.
n: Printed answer B: repeated antipyretic (paracetamol) dosing every 4 hours followed by vomiting, lethargy, jaundice and hepatomegaly points to paracetamol hepatotoxicity.

q: An 11-month-old boy presents with right ulnar and radial fractures, 2 days after a reported fall on an outstretched hand. Parents delayed seeking care, stating they didn't notice bruising. The child is well-nourished, well-dressed, and has had regular well-baby visits. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Treat the child and inform the authorities
Believe the parents and treat the child
Treat the child and order head CT
k: Red flags for non-accidental injury in children.
r: A tidy, well-nourished child with regular check-ups is the distractor: the mismatch between age, injury and delay is what matters.
n: Suspected non-accidental injury (fracture in a non-ambulatory infant with delayed presentation): treat and report to authorities.

q: Case of febrile seizure in a child, the mother is frightened about it happening again so she give the child paracetamol each 4 hrs, now presenting with AST 3200, ALT 2000, ALP 300, jaundice, direct Bilirubin 20, total bilirubin 25. Which of the following is the most likely cause of child presentation?
k: Transaminases in the thousands = acute hepatocellular injury: toxin (paracetamol), viral hepatitis or ischemic liver.
r: Antipyretics do not prevent febrile seizure recurrence; a frightened parent giving them every 4 hours is the classic route to chronic paracetamol toxicity.
n: Printed answer A. Paracetamol induced hepatotoxicity.

q: 18 months old boy, came to clinic for review. The child is always hungry, drinks 1 Liter of milk daily and eats dirt. Poor solid food intake. On exam He is underweight & has pale conjunctiva. What is the highest diagnostic test ?
k: Toddler + excess cow's milk + pica + pallor = iron deficiency anemia.
r: If ferritin or an iron profile appears in the options, it beats CBC as the diagnostic test.
n: Iron deficiency anemia from excess cow milk with pica. No ferritin or TIBC in the choices, so CBC with smear; if an iron profile had been offered it would be the correct answer as the highest diagnostic test. Other version of this recall in Part 2: SWR-1412 →

q: 3 year old child presents 2 days later with right forearm pain. X-ray shows fractures of the right radius and ulna. The parents delayed seeking care. There is no bruising on examination. The child is well-nourished, well-dressed, and has had regular well-child visits with no previous concerns noted. What is the most appropriate next step?

Admit for further workup and order head CT

q: Parents smokers came with 13 months child with a lot of problems tachycardia tachypnea failure to thrive other consultant suggests DNR What's your next step in management?

Ask opinion of another consultant And 3 referral physicians
k: Saudi DNR order essentials: Decided by 3 consultants (including the most responsible one) based on futility.; Family is informed; their consent is not what makes the order valid.; Order is documented and reviewed according to the patient's condition.
r: One consultant's suggestion is not a DNR; it needs three consultants first.
n: Embedded inset: different lead in (next step); answer A, ask the opinion of 3 trustworthy consultants.

q: Q74. A 13-year-old boy diagnosed with medulloblastoma has received chemotherapy and radiotherapy. Despite treatment, his disease has relapsed, with metastases to the bones and lungs. The oncology team determines that no further curative treatment options are available. q: A 10 months old baby with hf and ejection fraction of 10%. DNR status was discussed with his family but not completed, now he is in cardiac arrest. What to do next?
o: Start CPR on order of primary consultant
Start CPR and discuss with family about their decision
k: DNR at arrest: Completed DNR: no CPR.; Incomplete DNR: start CPR immediately.; Then discuss with the family to complete or revise the decision.
r: No one waits for a consultant to start CPR.
n: Embedded inset: 15 September Alhomrani recall with 4 options; answer D.

q: Child, DNR discussed but never completed, now he deteriorated, what to do?
o: Do resuscitation and discuss with parents their decision
k: No completed, documented DNR = full resuscitation by default.
r: "Discussed but never completed" means the order does not exist: resuscitate fully.
n: Printed answer A: resuscitate fully because the DNR was never completed.

q: A 15-month-old child with spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) is brought to the emergency department. The physician starts treatment, then discovers that the patient has a DNR order from another facility. What is the correct statement?
o: DNR orders from other facilities are not acceptable
DNR orders from other facilities are not acceptable after 24 hours
The DNR order needs to be verified by the family
The DNR order needs to be verified by identification of the patient by any team member
k: DNR from another facility (as keyed): Honoured up to 24 hours.; After that, must be re-issued by the receiving hospital's consultants.; Family is informed but does not validate the order.
r: "Not acceptable" alone is the trap; the time limit is the point.
n: Options printed unlettered, lettered by position. Printed answer is option 2 (not acceptable after 24 hours, i.e. valid for 24 hours). '(Question)' printed under it.

q: A 5 month patient with brain disease in private hospital then they send him to teratry hospital. They do CPR to the patient and after that they found there is a signed DNR. what is the right to do for signed DNR
o: DNR from the facilities is not valid
DNR from other facilities is valid for 24 hours.
Verify the identity of DNR must be by family responsibility
Verify the identity of DNR must be by a member of the team.
k: Inherited DNR order: verify first (by the team), then assess applicability, then document.
r: If an option says the DNR must be verified, pick it over any option about how many hours it stays valid.

q: 15 months pediatric patient come to er and doctor start treatment and after that know that there is DNR. What to do?
o: DNR from other facility are not acceptable
DNR from other facilities are not acceptable after 24 hours
DNR need to be verified by family
DNR need to be verified by team member

q: Pediatric pt white matter degenerative dis on recurrent chest infx , pts DNR , ask about DNT

k: DNR review: Reviewed whenever the patient's condition changes (and on each admission).; Not lifelong, not fixed intervals.; Decision by 3 consultants; family informed.
r: Any fixed time interval in a DNR review option is the distractor.

q: DNR in pediatric pateint

q: Child have permenant neurological disease and something else and DNR signed - what about DNR in this case?

r: "Who decides" = 3 consultants; "how long" = reviewed by condition.

q: A child presents with a band-like headache for the past 2 weeks. He has been spending several hours a day playing electronic games for the past 3 weeks. There are no other concerning symptoms and no neurological abnormalities. What is the most appropriate next step?

q: 21/10 case of child ingested medicine complain of abdominal pain hematemisis and melena and liver functions weren't normal after 6 hours which medicine he ingested ?
k: Iron poisoning runs in stages: Stage 1 (first hours): vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain, hematemesis and melena from direct corrosive injury to the gut; Stage 2: latent, apparent improvement; Stage 3: shock and metabolic acidosis
r: GI bleeding plus liver injury after a child's ingestion = iron; tinnitus and tachypnea = aspirin; delayed RUQ pain with no bleeding = paracetamol.
n: Answer B: iron (ferrous sulfate) toxicity causes GI bleeding (hematemesis, melena) followed by hepatotoxicity.

q: Mother bring her child after ingestion of unknown drug melena upper abd pain and other symptoms what is the most likely the cause
k: Iron poisoning runs in stages: Stage 1 (first hours): vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain, hematemesis and melena from direct corrosive injury to the gut; Stage 2: latent, apparent improvement; Stage 3: shock and metabolic acidosis
r: Think iron in any toddler with GI bleeding after an ingestion, especially with a pregnant or postpartum mother at home.
n: Answer: ferrous sulfate (unlettered options lettered by position). Supported by the embedded lookalike answered A. Ferrous sulfate.

q: Patient presents to the emergency department with vomiting and diarrhea shortly after ingesting an overdose of tablets. A few hours later; the patient develops melena, hematemesis, and shortness of breath. Laboratory investigations reveal elevated liver enzymes. Which of the following is the most likely substance ingested?
k: Iron poisoning runs in stages: Stage 1 (first hours): vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain, hematemesis and melena from direct corrosive injury to the gut; Stage 2: latent, apparent improvement; Stage 3: shock and metabolic acidosis
r: Early GI bleeding plus later liver injury = iron; tinnitus with hyperventilation = aspirin.
n: Embedded inset: Answer A. Ferrous sulfate. Almakrami note: he previously answered this as B in July, which was a typo.

q: Child for Preschool screening RDW 20 PLT 450 LOW Hb and MCV AND HIGH LEAD diagnosis ?
k: Microcytic anemia causes (TAILS): Thalassemia, Anemia of chronic disease, Iron deficiency, Lead, Sideroblastic.
r: Read the stem for the lead level: the same CBC is IDA when lead is not mentioned and lead poisoning when a high lead is given.

q: 3-year-old with fever 39 C, muffled voice and drooling; acutely ill, sitting on his mother's lap with the neck extended. Next step?
k: Epiglottitis vs croup: Epiglottitis: high fever, toxic, drooling, muffled voice, no barking cough, tripod/neck extended; Croup: barking cough, inspiratory stridor, low-grade fever, URTI prodrome; Epiglottitis: do not lie down, do not examine throat or cannulate; airway in OR first
r: Drooling + toxic + no cough = epiglottitis: airway first, antibiotics second.
n: Epiglottitis: secure the airway, intubate in the OR. Other versions of this recall in this deck: OCT-1365 → C. Intubate in the OR October By Similar update

q: A 3-year-old came in with fever, muffled sound, no swallowing with saliva drooling, and no cough. On exam, he looked acutely ill, sitting on his mother's lap with his neck extended (temperature 39^\circ\text{C}). What is the next step?
k: Epiglottitis: the 4 Ds (drooling, dysphagia, dysphonia, distress) plus high fever and toxicity.
r: "No cough" in a drooling febrile child is the clue that rules out croup.
n: Embedded older recall (15-16 September). Printed C, intubate in the OR. Other versions of this recall in this deck: OCT-1364 → C. Intubate in the OR 20 October update October By Similar update

q: A child presents to the ER with drooling, toxic appearance and extended neck. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
k: Epiglottitis = airway first, in a controlled setting.
r: Barking cough with stridor and no drooling is croup (steroids), not epiglottitis.
n: Printed answer B: suspected epiglottitis; avoid agitating the child, secure the airway in a controlled setting (PICU/OR) rather than intubating in the ER. 15-18 October update

q: Child presents to the ER with drooling, toxic appearance and extended neck. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: Intubate in the ER ( not OR )

q: A 3-year-old child presents to the Paediatric Emergency Department a half hour after ingesting a caustic material. The child is crying, drooling, and does not look well. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management?

q: A child is brought to the Emergency Department because he has not used his right arm since the previous day. Imaging reveals fractures of the radius and ulna. Which of the following findings most strongly raises suspicion of physical abuse?

An isolated radius and ulna fracture

q: 10 year old came to clinic complaining of headache feels like a band around the head, he spends 3 hours daily on video games and sleeps late. What is next step in management?
