n: Tension type headache related to lifestyle (video games, late sleep): advise lifestyle change. Older screenshot of same version gives the same answer. NN: they mentioned in the exam that it's not affecting his sleep.

q: 14 year old pt with ulcerative colitis failed to respond to many medical therapies . Patient has fulminant disease complicated by toxic megacolon , which of the following is the most appropriate URGENT treatment?
k: Acute severe UC ladder: IV steroids → rescue (infliximab or ciclosporin) → surgery if no response.
r: Fulminant UC + toxic megacolon + failed medical therapy = colectomy now; supportive measures only buy time.
n: Printed answer A, colectomy; the embedded older recall (Last Days Of Feb, Part 3, same version) also shows boxed answer A.

q: An 8-year-old girl presents to the Emergency Room by her mother after ingestion of large amount of acetaminophen tablets. According to the mother, she ingested full 2 packs, containing 20 tablets, 1 day ago after she had fight with her. On examination, she has right upper quadrant abdominal pain, with nausea and vomiting. Blood pressure 95/55 mmHg Heart rate 130 /min Respiratory rate 25 /min Temperature 36.6 C Oxygen saturation 96 % Which of the following is the most important antidote according to her stage of toxicity?
o: Antidote is not indicated at this stage
k: Acetaminophen toxicity stages: Stage 1 (first 24 h): nausea, vomiting, malaise, normal labs; Stage 2 (days 2 to 3): RUQ pain, hepatic tenderness, rising transaminases; Stage 3 (days 3 to 4): hepatic failure, encephalopathy, jaundice, coagulopathy, renal failure
r: A sibling version asks which phase (answer: phase 2); this one asks the antidote, which is NAC regardless of the late timing.
n: Printed answer C. N-acetylcysteine (stage 2 hepatic injury at 24 h, beyond charcoal window). Embedded inset is the same version with no answer line visible for it. Other version of this recall earlier in October: OCT-0882 → B. Phase 2.

q: The 8-year-old girl ingested 2 full packs of paracetamol, each one containing 10 tablets (total 20), came to the ER complaining of right abdominal quadrant pain, nausea, and vomiting. BP 95/50 HR 136 RR 25 T 37.6 Which current stage of acetaminophen toxicity is this?
k: Stage paracetamol toxicity by time and liver signs: RUQ pain = stage 2.
r: Vomiting alone = stage 1; vomiting plus RUQ pain = stage 2; jaundice or confusion = stage 3.
n: Answer tagged MG (Medgard). RUQ pain with nausea/vomiting about 1 day after ingestion is stage 2. Recaller: Only 3 options recalled.

q: A 8 year old girl presented to the Emergency department with her mother after ingestion 2 full packs each one containing 20 tablets after one day of disagreement with her mother BP 95/50 HR 135 RR 25 Temperature 36 C O2 saturation 95% What is the level of acetaminophen toxicity in this patient ?
k: Acetaminophen toxicity stages by time: Stage 1 (0 to 24 h): GI upset, normal labs; Stage 2 (24 to 72 h): GI symptoms may ease, RUQ pain, rising transaminases; Stage 3 (72 to 96 h): peak hepatotoxicity, jaundice, INR rise, encephalopathy
r: Count the hours from ingestion: one day later = stage 2, and NAC is still indicated.
n: Printed answer B. Two (phase 2).

q: A child ingested 20 tablets of an unknown drug came with his mother to the ER. He is anxious and had hematemesis and melena a few hours later his LFTs rise. What is the medication that he ingested?
k: Iron poisoning stages: GI, latent, shock/acidosis, hepatotoxicity, late strictures.
r: Early GI bleeding then liver failure = iron; well first then liver failure = paracetamol.
n: Compiler presents this as one of 2 recalls on iron poisoning (GI bleeding then hepatotoxicity); answer Ferrous sulfate.

q: A 12-year-old ingests an unknown amount of high-strength paracetamol four hours ago. Her level is above the Rumack-Matthew treatment line. What is the most appropriate management?
k: Paracetamol overdose management.
r: The nomogram is only valid from 4 hours after a single ingestion; a level before 4 hours cannot be interpreted.
n: Printed A. N-acetylcysteine. Printed again later in this file (p.6986). Printed again later in this file (p.6987).

q: A child (not sure about the age) was playing on a farm and presented with excessive salivation, lacrimation, and sweating. (Not sure about the rest of the stem or pupil size.) What is the most appropriate to give?
k: Organophosphate poisoning: DUMBBELSS (diarrhea, urination, miosis, bronchorrhea, bradycardia, emesis, lacrimation, salivation, sweating).
r: Atropine endpoint is dry chest secretions, not pupil size or heart rate.
n: Printed A. Atropine (organophosphate poisoning).

q: Pedia in a farm, came to the er with salivation, sweating, miosis, bronchocostriction.
k: Organophosphate poisoning = DUMBBELSS (diarrhea, urination, miosis, bronchorrhea or bronchospasm, bradycardia, emesis, lacrimation, salivation, sweating).
r: Farm exposure plus wet secretions and small pupils is organophosphate poisoning until proven otherwise.
n: Printed A. Organophosphate poisoning.

q: A neonate with MAS is on maximum oxygenation mechanical ventilation but is still hypoxic. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
k: Escalation in hypoxic respiratory failure of the term newborn (MAS, PPHN): Optimise ventilation, oxygen, sedation, correct acidosis.; Support systemic blood pressure (fluids, inotropes) to reduce right-to-left shunting.; Surfactant and high-frequency ventilation for parenchymal disease.
r: MAS still hypoxic despite maximal ventilation = think PPHN, give inhaled nitric oxide rather than more pressure or volume.
n: Recaller reported two separate MAS next-step questions (13a and 13b). Compiler: we need to re-evaluate why not A; his answer is C till proven by better evidence, but thinks we need to avoid lung injury (argues against increasing tidal volume). A reference bank

q: Newborn came to ER with abdominal distention, tenderness upon palpation, absent bowel sound, No meconium passage for 48hrs Most appropriate next step?
k: Neonate with delayed meconium (beyond 24 to 48 hours).
r: Tenderness and absent bowel sounds turn a diagnostic workup question into a surgical referral question.
n: Printed answer B: a newborn with an acute (tender, silent) abdomen and delayed meconium needs pediatric surgical referral first.

q: A 37-week gestation baby on delivery has a heart rate below 100 beats per minute, blue extremities, a weak cry with grimace, and little flexion. What is the most accurate APGAR score?
k: APGAR: 5 signs, each scored 0 to 2, total out of 10.
r: Blue EXTREMITIES scores 1, not 0; only a baby blue or pale all over scores 0 for appearance.
n: Printed answer B (APGAR 5).

q: Concerned mom with her newborn ask about when is the time for screening for IDA:
k: Well-baby screening ages.
r: If the options give 12 months instead of 10, it is still the answer because it falls inside the 9 to 12 month window.
n: Handwritten: screening window 9-12 months, so C (10 months).

q: A term newborn is delivered to a healthy mother. Shortly after birth, the newborn develops tachypnea and peripheral cyanosis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Neonatal respiratory distress: sort by gestation and risk factors.
r: Prematurity plus severe hypoxia overrides the CS clue and points to RDS, not TTN.

q: A 2-week-old infant is seen in the clinic. Rubbing the side of the mouth with the tip of the little finger elicits one of the primitive reflexes (image shown). Which of the following is the name of this reflex?
k: Primitive reflex = stimulus + response + disappearance age.
r: If the question shows the same rooting picture but asks WHEN it disappears, the answer is about 4 months.
n: Printed answer B. No further commentary.

q: Newborn vaginal delivery has prolonged PT and PTT and normal platelet
k: Read the coagulation pattern: PT and PTT prolonged, platelets normal: vitamin K deficiency (or liver disease, warfarin); PT and PTT prolonged, platelets low: DIC; Isolated PTT prolonged: hemophilia A or B (or heparin)
r: Add platelets to the picture: normal platelets = vitamin K deficiency, low platelets = DIC.
n: Prolonged PT and PTT with normal platelets: vitamin K deficiency; prolonged PT and PTT with low platelets: DIC.

q: Which of the following is the most sugges5ve of hemolysis as a cause for neonatal hyperbilirubinemia?
k: Neonatal jaundice: split by bilirubin type first.
r: Every option here is the opposite of a hemolysis marker except unconjugated bilirubin.
n: MG (Medgard) recall: printed C, compiler says this is a wrong answer by Medgard and endorses D (increased unconjugated bilirubin indicates hemolysis). Compiler doesn't think this question comes anymore. Other versions of this recall in this deck: SWR-0834 → D.

q: A 3 DAYS (Not Years) Old Child With Yellow Skin Which Of The Following Is. Which of the following is the most sugges5ve of hemolysis as a cause for (neonatal hyperbilirubinemia?)
k: Markers that suggest hemolysis in neonatal jaundice.
r: 'Conjugated' and 'unconjugated' look alike; hemolysis is always the UNconjugated one.
n: Compiler's own recall (modified Medgard). Headline recall: hemolytic anemia is indicated by increased unconjugated bilirubin. Recaller: Not sure if last word was neonatal jaundice or hyper-bili. Other versions of this recall in this deck: SWR-0833 → D. Increas

q: 9-month-old, came for general peds clinic. He is growing well and feeds well, born at 28 weeks GA (extremely premature). He can lift his hands up on his head, he can roll around, and no head lag. However, he cannot sit alone fully, requires assistance . What is the best response?
o: reassure, as his corrected age is 6 months
k: Corrected age = chronological age minus weeks born early.
r: Milestones use corrected age; vaccines use chronological age.
n: Preterm infants are expected to have delayed milestones and should be assessed according to corrected gestational age. Milestones: use corrected (gestational) age; vaccines: use chronological age. Contrast with the term version on page 998 (answer: admit for w

q: ARDS in neonate. Newborn at 33 weeks has fetal pulse/heart rate 66/min:
k: Neonatal respiratory distress: the vignette points to the cause.
r: Preterm suggests RDS and cesarean at term suggests TTN.
n: Answer based on the available information (preterm 33 weeks favors RDS).

q: A 4 day old baby brought to the clinic. The physician noticed that he is mildly jaundiced. He is feeding well (short case like this)
k: Neonatal jaundice timing: <24 h = pathological (hemolysis); day 2 to 3 onward in a well baby = physiological; after the first week in a thriving breastfed baby = breast milk jaundice.
r: Well baby + feeding well + mild jaundice = benign answer; first-day jaundice or a sick baby = hemolysis.
n: Printed answer breast milk jaundice. Compiler says it is not a new recall: it came in his own 14 May exam and he wrote it afterwards. Recaller: Labelled 'New recall?' by recaller; short case.

q: A hypotonic newborn had tongue fasciculations. EMG showed denervation. The parents were concerned about the child's condition. What is the appropriate counseling?
o: Muscle biopsy is needed to determine management
There is a new therapy that is more effective if started early
k: Floppy infant plus tongue fasciculations = SMA until proven otherwise.
r: Tongue fasciculations separate SMA from central causes of hypotonia; the counselling key is "treat early", not reassurance.
n: Compiler (SMA): new therapy more effective if started early, even if symptomatic, unless severe symptoms (e.g. intubated or NG-fed child); if severe symptoms -> symptom treatment and quality of life (palliative care).

q: A 10 days old (not sure about gender)went for the first neonatal check up. Which of the following need an immediate action?
k: Newborn check: what is urgent vs benign.
r: A deep sacral dimple, high above the gluteal cleft or with a hair tuft, needs spinal imaging, but it is still not as urgent as absent femoral pulses.
n: Absent femoral pulse in a neonate suggests coarctation of the aorta and needs immediate action.

q: 2 month old at routine neonatal care, the mother complain of right eye inward deviation when focusing in an object while breatfeeding, red reflix is symmetrical and coreal reflex is symmetrical what is the most appropriate next step
k: Infant eye screen: red reflex + corneal light reflex.
r: Symmetric light reflexes in a young infant = reassure; an abnormal red reflex = urgent referral.
n: Intermittent deviation in a 2 month old with symmetrical red and corneal reflexes is normal (pseudostrabismus/immature alignment); reassure.

q: An infant of a diabetic mother (IDM): what is the most common complication they may experience?
k: Infant of diabetic mother: think "everything high goes low" except size and red cells.
r: Every metabolic option is reversed in the distractors (hyper vs hypo); if hypoglycemia were listed it would compete strongly with RDS.
n: Handwritten D. Compiler notes it is called RDS, not ARDS.

q: A neontologist examining a post term neonate, what sign he will mostly find (it was longer question but that is the idea)?
k: Post term (postmaturity) neonate: Dry, cracked, desquamating skin; little vernix; Long nails, plenty of scalp hair, little lanugo; Thin, wasted look (reduced subcutaneous fat), alert face
r: Lanugo, short nails and thin translucent skin mean preterm; dry peeling skin and long nails mean post term.
n: Recaller: It was a longer question but that is the idea.

q: term baby delivered by cesarean section started to be tachypneic with nasal flaring and expiratory grunting. A chest X-ray showed fluid in the horizontal fissure. The baby's blood pressure is 60/35 mmHg, heart rate is 140/min, respiratory rate is 65/min, and temperature is 36.6 C, with an oxygensaturation of 92%. Which of the following is the most likelydiagnosis?
k: Neonatal respiratory distress by clues.
r: Fluid in the horizontal fissure in a term caesarean baby is TTN; the same distress in a 28-week baby is RDS.

q: 5 years old female with chronic productive cough, was admitted to hospital multiple times with wheezing and received antibiotics, neonatal admission for jaundice and treatment with phototherapy, ((clubbing)) Brother has same condition What is the investigation:
k: CF: chronic suppurative lung disease plus clubbing in a child = sweat test.
r: Clubbing is NOT a feature of asthma: a 'wheezy' child with clubbing needs a sweat test.

q: newborn delivered to a diabetic mother presents with respiratory distress and desaturation shortly after birth. Physical examination is unremarkable except for signs of respiratory distress and macrosomia. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: NICU admission, glucose monitoring, and observation
k: IDM complications: think metabolic + respiratory.
r: In any distressed IDM, check the glucose: hypoglycemia is the most common and most treatable problem.
n: Answer attributed to the 'Monsters' answer source: B, NICU admission with glucose monitoring and observation (infant of diabetic mother).

q: Preterm 29 weeks of gestation developed tachypnia, grunting, nasal flare immediately after birth What is the Most appropriate management?
k: Neonatal respiratory distress: gestation and timing decide the cause.
r: Any option pairing preterm support with 100% oxygen is a trap; the cause-targeted answer for RDS is surfactant.
n: Answer A, surfactant therapy. B and C are correct as initial steps until RDS is diagnosed, but most appropriate is endotracheal surfactant. Not D because 100% O2 is not used in RDS unless low dose O2 fails. Compiler notes this is the first time he sees this re

q: 10 year old girl with rash, fatigue, joint pain She has direct hyperbillirubinemia, elevated ALT and IgG with positive autoantibodies, tx?
k: Autoimmune hepatitis: young female, raised transaminases, high IgG, autoantibodies, treat with steroids plus azathioprine.
r: High IgG plus autoantibodies plus hepatitis = autoimmune hepatitis; phototherapy and exchange transfusion belong to neonatal unconjugated jaundice.
n: Handwritten B: autoimmune hepatitis is treated with steroids and azathioprine.

q: A newborn of a 34 weeks pregnancy addmitted to NICU Patient have several episodes of apnea per hour everyone last from 15 to 20 seconds What is the type of apnea?
k: Apnea of prematurity: most often MIXED type; inversely related to gestational age.
r: If the question asks the most common type of apnea in a premature baby, answer mixed, not central.
n: Apnea of prematurity is most commonly mixed type.

q: Term neonate delivered by cesarean, has retractions and was given oxygen Xray shows hyperareation and interstitial infiltrates Whats the next step in the management?
k: Newborn respiratory distress: match the X-ray and risk factors to the cause.
r: Hyperinflation plus interstitial streaking after an elective C-section is TTN; a preterm baby with low lung volumes and ground-glass is RDS.
n: Transient tachypnea of the newborn picture. Not every respiratory distress requires antibiotics, especially when explained by an alternative cause (X-ray showing TTN). Term plus C-section (not vaginal) means risk of neonatal sepsis is very low.

q: Neonate born at 28 weeks in NICU, has brief moments of (choking/ gasping? Honestly I’m not sure) (Apnea) (apnea was mentioned in brackets in the question) lasting 15-20 seconds multiple times an hour. Stem of the question what is the type of apnea
k: Apnea of prematurity: the more preterm the baby, the more frequent; most episodes are mixed.
r: Preterm apnea = mixed (most common); "no chest movement at all" points to central, and a pause with bradycardia or desaturation counts as apnea even if under 20 seconds.
n: Inset of an earlier recall (Q102): preterm newborn with multiple episodes of apnea, stops breathing for 15-20 seconds multiple times in one hour; options Mixed/Central/Obstructive, answer A (Mixed). Recaller: Recaller unsure whether the stem said choking or ga

q: 7 or 9 month old came with his mother to the clinic, he is able to sit on his own, transfer objects, his mom was worried because he was premature and was in the nicu after birth, what do you tell her? (no mention what ga he was born or anything)
o: Need time to decide (written like this)
This is normal for his age (or similar to this)
k: Developmental assessment: compare achieved skills with expected age, using corrected age for prematurity.
r: Prematurity is a reason to correct the age downward, so a preterm baby who already meets milestones for his actual age is doing well.
n: Compiler: actually, he is well developed. Recaller: Recaller (in Arabic): got a strange milestone question, first time seeing it.

q: There was also an image for a newborn. It was very confusing, honestly, but he was born at 33 weeks and had a diabetic mother. What is the diagnosis?
k: Neonatal respiratory distress: match the risk factor to the diagnosis.
r: Maternal diabetes delays lung maturity, so an infant of a diabetic mother can still have RDS at a gestation where a normal baby would not.
n: Printed answer RDS: prematurity (33 weeks) plus maternal diabetes (delayed surfactant maturation) favour RDS. Recaller: Image was very confusing.

q: A mother came to the clinic with her 9 months child, she state that he can’t sit without support, he born as a preterm infant at 28 weeks
o: Reassure as his chronological age is 6 months
Evaluate him with his chorological age
k: Corrected age = chronological age minus weeks born early (40 minus gestational age).
r: Vaccines follow chronological age, but milestones follow corrected age; mixing them up turns a normal preterm baby into a 'delayed' one.
n: Printed answer A: correct for prematurity (corrected age about 6 months), so reassure.

q: Newborn, during assessment they found small left inguinal mass olive size, empty left hemiscrotum when to do surgery?
k: Undescended testis: wait for spontaneous descent, then orchidopexy in infancy.
r: If the groin mass is a hernia with a normally descended testis, repair soon after diagnosis (incarceration risk is high in infants); only the undescended testis waits a few months.
n: Undescended (inguinal) testis in a newborn: orchidopexy after a few months (typically by 6 to 18 months).

q: Preterm diagnosed with bronchopulmonary displasia (BPD) having difficulty getting off mechanical ventilation What is the most appropriate mangenent?
o: increase tidal volume and inspiratory something
start long term high dose corticosteroids
start short course low dose corticosteroids
k: BPD (chronic lung disease of prematurity): oxygen need beyond 28 days or at 36 weeks corrected age, from ventilator and oxygen injury to immature lungs.
r: Postnatal steroids in BPD are justified only as a SHORT, LOW dose course for ventilator dependence; "long term high dose" is the trap.

q: Preterm after delivery start to have tachypnea and TTN suspected Which of the following is the cause of TTN?
k: Neonatal tachypnoea: cause determines the diagnosis.
r: Fluid in the horizontal fissure after a CS = TTN (fluid clearance); ground-glass lungs in a very preterm baby = RDS (surfactant).
n: TTN is caused by delayed clearance/absorption of fetal lung fluid.

q: Term delivary with meconium stain fluid , vigorous, cryning and good muscle tone What is the most appropriate management?
k: Meconium + vigorous baby = routine care; meconium does not change the resuscitation algorithm.
r: The word 'vigorous' decides it: no suction, no drugs, just routine care.
n: Compiler flags it as '(Question) (For Revision)'.

q: A preterm newborn presents with respiratory distress. Chest X-ray shows a flattened diaphragm and increased AP diameter. What is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Neonatal distress: read the gestation first, then the CXR.
r: Hyperinflation rules out RDS (low volumes); then preterm = TTN, term/post-term = MAS.
n: Printed answer A because the baby is preterm; if he was term/post-term the answer would be MAS (meconium aspiration syndrome).

q: A newborn is suspected to have meconium aspiration syndrome at birth and presents with respiratory distress. What is radio findings ?
o: hyper inflated lung and lung infiltration
k: Neonatal respiratory distress by chest X-ray.
r: Big lungs with patches = meconium; small ground glass lungs = RDS; fluid in the fissure = TTN.
n: Meconium aspiration on CXR: hyperinflated lungs with patchy infiltrates (ground glass suggests RDS).

q: A post-term newborn develops respiratory distress immediately after birth, with tachypnea, grunting, and nasal flaring. Chest X-ray shows patchy infiltrates with hyperinflation and flattening of the diaphragm. What is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Neonatal respiratory distress: match gestation and birth history to the CXR.
r: Post-term baby with patchy infiltrates plus hyperinflation = meconium; TTN can also look hyperinflated but shows perihilar streaks and fissure fluid in a term cesarean baby and clears within 2 to 3 days.
n: Post-term infant with hyperinflation and patchy infiltrates on CXR = meconium aspiration syndrome.

q: 40 week gestation newborn who has respiratory distress came with cyanosis and tachycpenia intercostal retraction. There was meconium in amniotic fluid during labor Which of the following expected to seen in Radiograph:
k: Neonatal CXR patterns by diagnosis: RDS (preterm): low volumes, reticulogranular ground glass, air bronchograms; TTN (term, cesarean section): perihilar streaks, fluid in fissures; MAS (term or post-term, meconium): hyperinflation, patchy coarse infiltrates, flat diaphragm
r: Low volumes = RDS; high volumes with patches = meconium.
n: Meconium aspiration syndrome classically shows hyperinflation with patchy infiltrates on CXR.

q: Neonate in the NICU experience repeated attacks of appnea, it last for 10-20 seconds and dissapper, it happens several times per hour What is the type of appnea?
k: Apnea of prematurity: frequency of types.
r: Asked for the most common type of apnea in a preterm neonate: mixed, not central.
n: Printed answer mixed apnea (most common type in preterm neonates); no further commentary.

q: 38 week neonate with macrosomia 4.5 kg born via vaginal delivery Has absent Moro reflex on right side What is the most appropriate initial management
o: immobilize the affected side with supportive care
k: Asymmetric Moro in a newborn = look at the arm, not the brain.
r: One sided absent Moro = local injury (plexus or clavicle); a symmetric loss of reflexes points to a central or metabolic cause.
n: Answer line attributed to SMLE-GOATs: D. Asymmetric Moro after macrosomic vaginal delivery suggests brachial plexus injury or clavicle fracture, managed initially conservatively with immobilization.

q: typical hirschnburg case (newborn 48h no meconium pass) What is the most appropriate next to diagnose?
k: Hirschsprung disease: aganglionic distal colon causing functional obstruction.
r: "Initial" test = contrast enema; "diagnose / confirm" = rectal biopsy.
n: Printed answer B: surgical referral and (rectal) biopsy for a typical Hirschsprung presentation.

q: A 5-day-old neonate(not sure but less than 1 week) presents to the emergency department with severe jaundice requiring exchange transfusion. His older siblings had similar episodes. Which history is most important to obtain?
k: Recurrent severe neonatal jaundice in siblings = isoimmune hemolytic disease until proven otherwise; ask the maternal blood group.
r: 'Siblings had the same' is the clue: recurrent hemolysis across pregnancies means alloimmunization, so ask the mother's blood group.
n: Printed answer B (mother's blood group). Recurrent severe neonatal jaundice in siblings suggests hemolytic disease of the newborn (Rh/ABO isoimmunization); earlier version shown answered maternal blood group.

q: A 5-day-old girl brought to Emergency Room with lethargy and poor feeding. On examination, she was irritable, deeply jaundiced and dehydrated. The mother gave history of previous babies' required admission and exchange transfusion (see lab results). Which of the following is important to be obtained in the history? Blood pressure 90/55 mmHg, Heart rate 95 /min, Respiratory rate 18 /min, Temperature 36.6 C, Oxygen saturation 94 % Weight 3 kg. Hb 95 (165-195 g/L newborn), Reticulocyte 3 (0.2-1.2 %), Total bilirubin 360 (<274 mol/L preterm 3-5 days, <205 mol/L term 3-5 days)
k: Recurrent severe neonatal jaundice in siblings = isoimmune hemolytic disease until proven otherwise; ask the maternal blood group.
r: Anemia plus reticulocytosis plus high bilirubin = hemolysis; add affected siblings and the answer is maternal blood group.
n: Earlier recall version shown as a screenshot with a lab table; printed answer D (maternal blood group).

q: A 3-Day-Old Neonate Starts To Develop Skin Lesions That Look Like Erythematous Macules On An Erythematous Base, Over The Upper Chest And The Back (See Lab Results) Blood Pressure: 85/55 mmHg Heart Rate: 110 /min Respiratory Rate: 18 /min Temperature: 36.6 C Oxygen Saturation: 99 % Test Result / Normal Values: RBC: 5 (4.8-7.1 x 10^12/L Newborn / 4.6-4.8 x 10^12/L Child) Hb: 145 (165-195 g/L Newborn / 112-165 g/L Child) Platelets Count: 250 (150-400 x 10^9/L) WBC: 9 (9.1-30.1 x 10^9/L Birth / 6.1-17.5 x 10^9/L 1-23 Months) Which Of The Following Is The Best Management Approach?
o: Reassurance As It Is A Benign Condition
Full Sepsis Work Up And Oral Antibiotics For 7 Days
k: Benign newborn rashes = reassure; sepsis is judged on the baby's condition.
r: Borderline lab values are a distractor: a well, afebrile 3-day-old with a red-based truncal rash is erythema toxicum, so reassure.
n: Older recall version (MG source) in inset with labs; erythema toxicum neonatorum is benign, reassure. Option C bolded.

q: Preterm 2 months old ( chronological age ) The mom ask when to give him vaccines
k: Preterm infants: two clocks.
r: Milestones are corrected for prematurity; vaccines are not.
n: Milestones are assessed by gestational (corrected) age, vaccines are given by chronological age. Recaller: Options were written inline after the stem.

q: Pre term infant diagnosed with Broncho-Pulmonary dysplasia is having difficulty weaning from mechanical ventilation. What's the most appropriate next step in management?
o: increase Tidal volume and inspiratory pressure
Administer low dose course of corticosteroids
k: BPD with ventilator dependence: low dose, short course steroids to help extubation.
r: Steroids in BPD: yes if low dose and short course; no if high dose or long term.
n: Printed answer D. Compiler attaches an older version (infant with BPD, difficulty weaning) answered short term low dose steroid, with evidence in 15-17 October Question 32; increasing tidal volume is wrong and increases lung injury.

q: newborn weighing 4.5 kg (macrosomic) is delivered after a difficult delivery. On examination, the baby has a weak Moro reflex on the affected side. What is the most appropriate initial management?
o: Immediate surgical repair of the brachial plexus
Immobilization of the affected arm and supportive care
k: Unilateral weak or absent Moro after a traumatic delivery = brachial plexus injury (or clavicle fracture).
r: Asymmetric Moro is a local (nerve or bone) problem; symmetric depression is systemic or central.
n: Answer line credited to SMLE-GOATs: D (brachial plexus birth injury managed conservatively initially).

q: A preterm infant born at 29 weeks presents with tachypnea, grunting, and nasal flaring. What is the most appropriate management?)
k: Neonatal respiratory distress: gestational age and delivery route point to the cause.
r: Preterm plus grunting = surfactant deficiency; never give premature babies 100% oxygen as a fixed setting.
n: Respiratory distress syndrome of prematurity: intratracheal surfactant.

q: A term/post-term or full-term macrosomic newborn of a mother with diabetes/GDM develops respiratory distress and desaturation shortly after delivery. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Wait and reassess without higher-level monitoring
k: Rule: IDM with distress → NICU, check glucose early, support breathing, then find the cause.
r: Never manage a distressed IDM without a glucose check: hypoglycemia can mimic or worsen respiratory distress.
n: Printed answer B: infant of diabetic mother with respiratory distress needs NICU admission, glucose monitoring and supportive care.

q: Newborn of diabetic mother has hematocrit 71% and plethora. What is the next step?
k: Asymptomatic polycythemia = observe and support; symptomatic polycythemia = partial exchange transfusion.
r: Read the stem for symptoms: plethora alone = no intervention; add lethargy, seizures or hypoglycemia and the answer flips to exchange transfusion.
n: Printed answer A for this second version: no intervention needed in the asymptomatic polycythemic infant of a diabetic mother (partial exchange transfusion only if symptomatic).

q: A 9-month-old term infant is unable to sit independently. He has no dysmorphic features or other abnormalities on examination. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Reassure the parents that this is normal for his age
k: Missed red flag milestone = refer; skill not yet due = reassure.
r: Decide by whether the milestone is overdue, not by whether the exam is normal: overdue + normal exam is still a referral.
n: Printed answer B: refer for developmental evaluation (not sitting by 9 months is a red flag).

q: A full-term infant developed bilateral conjunctivitis at 2 weeks of age. The conjunctivitis is followed by severe coughing but the infant remained febrile. q: Patient had an accident, then picked up by the Red Crescent. He was hypotensive, then after the fluid he became stable. He has lower abdominal pain and back pain. FAST was positive. What is the next step?

q: MVA with Right Pupil dilated , Bp: 90/60 Initial Examiner: HR 102 , BP EXACTLY 90/60

n: MAP is 70; assuming ICP of at least 15, CPP would be 55. Low CPP so avoid head elevation (and hypotension argues against mannitol); hyperventilation chosen as the initial measure for herniation. Recaller: Examiner confirmed HR 102 and BP exactly 90/60.

q: 26yo male MVA blunt maxillofacial trauma with SEVERE OROPHARYNGEAL BLEEDING which of the following is the most appropriate regarding airway management?

q: Vitality stable MVA ( vitals was written) What is the most appropriate next step :

q: A 45 year old woman presented to the Emergency Department after a motor vehicle accident with confusion, headache, and left-sided weakness. GCS is 14/15. CT brain showed a subdural hematoma. What is the most appropriate next step?
k: Traumatic subdural hematoma with a focal neurological deficit = surgical lesion: call neurosurgery for evacuation now.
r: The decisive word is weakness: a focal deficit converts a subdural from 'observe and rescan' to 'neurosurgery now'.

q: Patient had had MVA was stable, (I think after 2 days), had shortness of breath, chest examination: decreased breath sounds and dullness on percussion on one side of the chest diagnosis?
k: Chest trauma: read the percussion note first.
r: Same reduced breath sounds, opposite percussion: dull = blood (hemothorax), hyperresonant = air (pneumothorax).
n: Printed answer A (hemothorax). Dullness with decreased breath sounds after chest trauma in a stable patient = hemothorax; earlier version shown agrees.

q: A patient presents to the emergency department after sustaining chest trauma. He is hemodynamically stable. On examination, there is decreased breath sounds and dullness to percussion over the affected side of the chest. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Unilateral reduced breath sounds after trauma: percussion decides.
r: Distended neck veins push you to tension or tamponade; flat neck veins with a dull chest point to hemothorax.
n: Earlier recall version shown as a screenshot; printed answer A (hemothorax).

q: Adult male (forget his age) involved in trauma with facial fractures and had gurgling of blood in his mouth. What is the next step to do?
k: Trauma airway: indication for a definitive airway, then choose the route.
r: Same airway indication flips with the injury: no facial injury = orotracheal tube; facial fractures = cricothyroidotomy.
n: Printed answer C (cricothyroidotomy). Severe facial fractures with blood in the airway: surgical airway (cricothyroidotomy); nasotracheal intubation is contraindicated. Compiler highlights 'blood in his mouth' in red; earlier version shown agrees.

q: Adult pt involved in RTA presented to ED. Perisplenic fluid in FAST, bruises in periumbilical and epigastric regions. BP 99/70 HR 107 RR 24 What to do
k: Blunt abdominal trauma pathway by FAST and stability: Stable + positive FAST: CT abdomen with contrast; Stable + negative FAST: observe, serial exams; Unstable + positive FAST: laparotomy
r: Positive FAST does not mean surgery: stability decides; a stable patient gets CT, an unstable one goes to theatre.
n: Printed answer B (CT abdomen with contrast). BP 99/70 is treated as hemodynamically stable, so CT rather than laparotomy; earlier version shown also answered CT.

q: Young male after a fight had multiple stab wounds in trunk and lower limb When he arrived was Conscious and oriented his Clothes and bed sheet soaked in blood BP: 60/40 HR: tachy 02 sat: 88% (No fast, ct, any labs) What to do next?
k: Primary survey order (ABCDE), treat each problem as found: A: conscious and talking = airway patent; intubate if SpO2 < 88%, GCS 8 or less, or aspiration risk; B: oxygen; treat tension pneumothorax; C: stop external bleeding, two large bore IVs, fluids or blood
r: SpO2 below 88% = intubate; SpO2 around 88% in a talking patient = give oxygen first.
n: Printed answer B (O2 supplementation), following ABC order with SpO2 88% (highlighted in red). Earlier version shown answered oxygenation.

q: 125-Trauma patient with multiple stab wounds He is conscious and his clothes are soaked in blood. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step? BP:90/60 SpO2: 88%
k: Trauma priorities: treat the first broken letter of ABC first.
r: Hypotension tempts you to answer fluids, but hypoxia (B) outranks shock (C) in the sequence.
n: Earlier recall version shown as a screenshot; printed answer C (oxygenation).

q: presented with trouble breathing, one week ago had mva, 2 days difficulty breathing, picture showing very clear right sided hemothorax what to do next o2 90% dont remeber rest of vitals hemoglobin maybe 8
k: Traumatic hemothorax: ABCDE, then chest tube; thoracotomy only on output criteria.
r: Hemothorax on imaging = chest tube first; the chest tube output, not the X-ray, decides whether he goes to thoracotomy.
n: Traumatic hemothorax: drain with a chest tube. Inset version also answers chest tube.

q: A patient has a history of trauma 1 week ago and presents with dyspnea. Physical examination reveals decreased breath sounds over the right chest and dullness on percussion. The patient is vitally stable, with slight anemia on labs. What is the most important next step?
k: Percussion note decides the chest trauma diagnosis.
r: Dullness after trauma means blood, not air: drain it with a chest tube; the needle is only for tension pneumothorax.
n: Older recall version in inset; stable post-traumatic hemothorax is drained with a chest tube.

q: Pt had a gunshot wound, they operated on him and did a distal pancreatectomy and splenectomy and some kind of partial colonectomy. He presented 1 week later with left upper quadrant pain. Next step?

r: Post-splenectomy LUQ pain with fever is an abscess until proven otherwise; CT, not US, in the left upper quadrant.
n: Left subphrenic abscess after splenectomy/distal pancreatectomy: CT preferred over US.

q: Pt had multiple stab wounds with bleeding all over his clothes and pants. His BP was Low (88/51 mmHg?) and his O2 stat was 88%. Next step?

q: Pt after MVA with GCS 9, and BP of 80/51 mmHg Next Step?

q: Pt after a MVA has severe pain in the pelvis and lower back, FAST showed fluid in the lower abdomen. Pt was vitally stable. Next imagine method?
k: Blunt trauma imaging is driven by stability.

q: A young man was involved in a road traffic accident / fall, sustaining a blow to the temporal region of the head. He was initially conscious and talking normally at the scene, then a short while later he became drowsy, confused, and rapidly deteriorated in consciousness. X ray head shows a fracture in the temporal bone. What is the most likely cause?
k: Extradural vs subdural: Extradural: middle meningeal artery, temporal fracture, lucid interval, biconvex (lens) on CT; Subdural: bridging veins, elderly/alcoholics, crescent (banana) on CT; Ipsilateral blown pupil = uncal herniation compressing CN III
r: Lucid interval + temporal fracture = extradural; a crescent clot in an elderly faller = subdural.
n: Printed answer A: lucid interval with temporal bone fracture (middle meningeal artery) indicates extradural hematoma.

k: Burns follow ABC: airway first, then breathing, circulation (Parkland), then secondary survey.
r: SpO2 can look falsely normal in CO poisoning; a high COHb never delays airway control, and intubation with 100% oxygen treats both.

q: Patient with trauma to the thigh about 4cm with visible underline tissues and bone. What is the initial treatment?

q: Patient came with hemo thorax and chest tube was inserted which of the following will indicate the need for chest thoracotomy?
o: initial fluid came out of chest tube is 500
k: Emergency thoracotomy after chest tube for hemothorax: Initial drainage more than 1500 ml of blood (most tested).; Persistent drainage of 200 ml/hr or more for 2 to 4 hours.; Persistent hemodynamic instability or decompensation after initial stabilization.
r: Thoracotomy numbers: 1500 ml at once or 200 ml/hr continuing; 500 ml initially is not enough.

q: Adult male after MVA came unconscious with large laceration in his right leg, manual blood pressure undetectable. What would be found in his examination?
k: Shock type by heart rate and skin: Hypovolemic/hemorrhagic: tachycardia, weak thready pulse, cold clammy skin, low CVP; Cardiogenic: tachycardia, cold peripheries, raised JVP/PCWP, crackles; Septic (early): tachycardia, warm skin, bounding pulses, low SVR
r: Trauma + hypotension + bradycardia = think neurogenic shock; trauma + hypotension + tachycardia = bleeding.

q: Child fell. CT showed subdural hematoma. Best step in management?
k: Head trauma with bleed on CT: stabilise and involve neurosurgery.
r: Subdural hematoma in an infant or toddler after a trivial fall: consider non-accidental injury (shaken baby) and look for retinal hemorrhages.

q: child fells from 2 meters now he is vomiting multiple times and sleepy. He has left side weakness, CT shows extradural hemorrhage. BEST MANAGEMENT?
k: EDH: middle meningeal artery bleed under the pterion; lens shaped (biconvex), does not cross sutures.
r: EDH plus vomiting, drowsiness and a focal deficit = evacuate now; observation is only for small, asymptomatic clots.
n: Printed answer A; symptomatic epidural hematoma with focal deficit requires surgical evacuation.

r: Do not be distracted by imaging or a second tube: the volume number (>1.5 L at once) alone makes the decision.
n: Option A was not printed (list starts at B). Massive hemothorax (2 L via chest tube) indicates thoracotomy. Full MG recall shown below: '2 L in 15 minutes | MG Surgery, p. 98'.

Blood pressure 90/60 mmHg Heart rate 120 /min Respiratory rate 22/min Temperature 36.6 C Oxygen saturation 90 % Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

r: Hypotension plus >1.5 L chest tube output = operating room, never CT or angiography.
n: Embedded full MG recall (printed as MG question 7; 'Full MG recall: 2 L in 15 minutes | MG Surgery, p. 98'). Answer Thoracotomy. 19 October update

q: Short case: RTA (i think) dullness in the right 78/55 (not sure) most appropriate next step?

q: Hx of trauma (2 days or 1 week), patient presents with dyspnea, physical examination (decreased breath sounds over the right chest + dullness on percussion), vitally stable, slight anemia on labs X-ray: Pleural effusion of the right hemithorax most appropriate?

q: 35 years old male patient presented to the ER after road traffic accident, the patient presented unconscious the GCS was less than 6 , the patient had multiple injuries and he had pelvic fracture with significant instability BP 88/50 HR 120 RR 28 What is the most appropriate next step in management

r: If intubation is an option in a patient with GCS 8 or less, it beats the binder.
n: Embedded lookalike. Compiler: if intubation is among the options go for it first (GCS 8 = intubation); laparotomy is inappropriate in the absence of indications for surgery.

q: Patient with RTA. He is stable and conscious with a patent airway. His blood pressure is 105/90 mmHg. His GCS score is 15. What is the most appropriate next step?
k: Read the pulse pressure, not only the systolic.
r: A "normal" BP with a narrow pulse pressure after trauma is hidden shock.
n: Embedded inset: Normal BP does not mean do not give IV fluids; all trauma patients should receive IV fluids as routine part of ABC (ATLS). By the time hypotension occurs it is too late and end organ damage may not be reversed.

q: Pt mva unresponsive glascow 8 blood pressure is low around 80/40 . Inital step
k: ATLS primary survey order: A (airway with c-spine protection), B, C, D, E.

q: After accident a patient came with warm lower extremities with normal chest exam , BP was low, HR70 what kind of shock?
k: Warm extremities = distributive shock (neurogenic or septic); pulse and context separate them.
r: Relative bradycardia counts: in a hypotensive trauma patient, any 'normal' pulse should make you think neurogenic.
n: Even if not truly bradycardic (<60), HR 70 is relative bradycardia; heart rate would be much higher in hemorrhagic shock, so neurogenic shock.

q: Case of hypovolomic shock after accident, which of the following is the sign of compensation?
k: Compensated vs decompensated shock.
r: If tachycardia is listed it is always the earliest compensation sign; altered mental status means decompensation.
n: Compensated shock: tachycardia > tachypnea > cold pale skin and decreased pulse pressure. Decompensated: confusion and decreasing BP > oliguria > hypotension > anuria. Recaller: There is no tachycardia among the options, 100% sure; fourth option not remembered

q: A 45-year-old male presents with signs and symptoms of intestinal obstruction, including abdominal distension and diffuse abdominal pain. His vital signs are stable. An abdominal X-ray shows: Multiple air-fluid levels; A dense/opaque area in the right lower quadrant; Pneumobilia (air within the biliary tract). What is the next step in management?
k: Pneumobilia + small bowel obstruction + ectopic stone (Rigler's triad) = gallstone ileus, treated by laparotomy and enterolithotomy.
r: 'Ileus' is a misnomer: gallstone ileus is a mechanical obstruction, so the answer is surgery, not conservative management.
n: Gallstone ileus: X-ray feature pneumobilia, best investigation CT, treatment exploratory laparotomy. If both CT and laparotomy are offered, X-ray findings are enough for diagnosis, so do laparotomy, not CT.

q: A 7-year-old child presents with abdominal pain for the past 2 weeks. He is currently stable. On examination, there is right lower abdominal tenderness and a palpable swelling. His WBC count is 20,000/mm3. Which of the following is the most appropriate diagnostic test to definitively diagnose this patient?
k: RLQ mass after days to weeks of pain = appendicular abscess or phlegmon: CT regardless of age.
r: Age alone does not decide the scan: a child with a palpable RLQ mass gets CT, not ultrasound.
n: Printed answer B (suspected appendiceal mass/abscess; CT is definitive).

q: 48 Female Came 4 days after surgery, bowel resection surgery after ischemic colitis. She was on Total Parenteral Feeding by central line. 12 onset of Temperature 39.6 WBC 27.8 what is the cause?
k: Postoperative fever: match the cause to the timing and the clue in the stem.
r: When a stem goes out of its way to mention TPN through a central line, the line is usually the intended source of the fever.
n: No answer printed; embedded older version shown for reference. Recaller: Recaller remembered only option A.

q: old patient underwent laparotomy and adhenolysis. On 4th of post op developed abdominal distension and can’t pass stool or gas. on exam pt had absent bowel sounds. no fever or high Wbc. Vitally stable. What is the most appropriate initial management?
k: Paralytic ileus: recent surgery, diffuse distension, absent bowel sounds, no transition point.
r: Absent bowel sounds a few days after surgery in a well, afebrile patient who is not vomiting is ileus: NPO and IV fluids, no routine NGT, no laxatives, no rush back to theatre.
n: Embedded 'Last Days Of Feb, Part 2' version; boxed answer B. Recaller: Recaller not sure if vitally stable was written but sure there were no other abnormalities.

q: A 91-year-old male resident of a nursing home presents with hyperactive bowel sounds, severe abdominal distension, and severe left lower quadrant pain. He remains hemodynamically stable. What is the most appropriate next step in management? Options:
k: Rule: elderly or institutionalized patient with distension and constipation: examine the rectum first.
r: If the stem adds a coffee bean X-ray, the answer moves to sigmoidoscopy; if fever, peritonism or high WBC, to surgery.
n: Suspected fecal impaction in an elderly nursing home resident: digital rectal examination.

q: A 90-year-old woman presents with a 1-2 day (forget exact duration) history of constipation, abdominal distension, generalized abdominal pain and tenderness, and hyperactive bowel sounds. Her vital signs normal (as I remember). What is the most appropriate next step in management?
k: Rule: in the frail elderly with constipation and distension, DRE first to exclude fecal impaction.
r: Impaction can present with overflow diarrhea; a DRE is still the first step.
n: Embedded 17 September version; handwritten 'C, fecal impaction'.

q: A 50-year-old woman presents with nausea, vomiting, and muscle aches. She is 6 days post-operative and is unable to pass stool, and has abdominal distension (see lab results) (hypokalemia) . Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
k: Symptomatic electrolyte disturbance (K): protect the heart first, then replace, then find the cause.
r: Post-op ileus plus low K: ECG first; urine K is for the cause, not for safety.
n: Hypokalemia (post-op ileus): first get an ECG to assess cardiac effects. Recaller: Lab results were not reproduced in the recall.

q: typical intestinal obstruction , air fluid , distinction abdomen, BP normal 110/70, what is the initial step?
k: Bowel obstruction: resuscitate and decompress first, operate on indication.
r: Stable and no peritonism = NGT first; any sign of strangulation (constant pain, fever, tachycardia, guarding) = straight to laparotomy.

q: 45 y women come to ER complain of abdominal pain and nausea . She has rt iguinal hernia and Alwyes is reduced. Now it become constant On PE : Redish with erythma and Mild tender What is the diagnosis:
k: Hernia states, from least to most severe.
r: Skin redness or discoloration over a hernia = strangulation until proven otherwise; do not try to reduce it.
n: Previously reducible hernia now constant with overlying redness/erythema -> strangulated.

q: Post mesenteric ischemia surgery 5 days unable to tolerate enteral feeding What the most appropriate nutritional management?
o: feeding through NGT and oral if possible
k: Route of feeding: if the gut works, use it; if it does not, go parenteral.
r: The deciding words are ‘unable to tolerate enteral feeding’; without them, early enteral feeding (NGT or oral) would be preferred after surgery.
n: Unable to tolerate enteral feeding after mesenteric ischemia surgery -> parenteral nutrition. Recaller: Options B and C forgotten.

q: Which is most commonly presents with large painless bright per rectal bleeding in elderly patient that looks pale
k: Massive painless lower GI bleeding in the elderly: diverticular disease first, angiodysplasia second.
r: Painless + massive + elderly = diverticular; add painful + vascular risk factors and it flips to ischemic colitis.
n: Printed 'A > B': diverticular disease is favored over angiodysplasia as the most common cause of massive painless lower GI bleeding in the elderly. Related version on p1230. Recaller: Unfortunately I don't remember if there is heart disease or not.

q: An older man has acute diverticulitis with localized left-lower-quadrant findings. CT demonstrates a small sigmoid collection, approximately 2 x 2 cm / ~20 mL. What is the next step?
k: Diverticular abscess management depends on size and peritonitis: Small abscess (under about 3 to 4 cm): IV antibiotics and observation; Larger abscess: CT-guided percutaneous drainage plus antibiotics; Generalized peritonitis or free perforation: emergency laparotomy (resection or washout)
r: Size flips the answer: small abscess = antibiotics; large abscess = percutaneous drainage; peritonitis = theatre.
n: Printed answer B: small (<3 to 4 cm) diverticular abscess is treated with IV antibiotics and observation.

q: An older man (about 60-68 years) presents with massive lower gastrointestinal bleeding. Which is the most likely cause?
k: Rule: elderly + painless + massive hematochezia = diverticulosis first.
r: Massive = diverticulosis; chronic slow bleeding with anemia = angiodysplasia.
n: Printed answer B: diverticulosis is the most common cause of massive lower GI bleeding in older adults. Related version on p1204.

q: A 42-year-old woman underwent an uncomplicated laparoscopic cholecystectomy. Two weeks later, she presented to the Emergency Department with vague abdominal pain. CT scan showed a large collection in the subhepatic area. What is the most appropriate next step?
k: Rule: post-op intra-abdominal collection: small → antibiotics; large single → percutaneous drainage; multiple → laparoscopy; unstable → laparotomy.
r: If ERCP with stent is offered, the version may be testing leak control rather than drainage of the collection; read the options.

q: case about UC with toxic mega colon asking about Mx :
k: UC + toxic megacolon: medical rescue first, colectomy if no response, perforation or deterioration.
r: If steroids appear as an option and the patient is new to treatment, IV steroids may be first; if medical treatment has failed, colectomy.
n: Short highlighted recall printed above a fuller version; the answer line 'A- colectomy' under the fuller version is mapped to this version by meaning. Recaller: I don't remember if steroids was in stem or in choices.

q: 14 year old pt with ulcerative colitis failed to respond to many medical therapies. Patient has fulminant disease complicated by toxic megacolon, which of the following is the most appropriate URGENT treatment?
k: Fulminant UC / toxic megacolon refractory to medical therapy = urgent colectomy.
r: 'Failed medical therapy' plus 'urgent' in a toxic megacolon stem ends the medical options: choose colectomy.

q: An elderly patient presents with left lower quadrant abdominal pain, fever (38.6°C), and marked leukocytosis (WBC 25,000/µL). On examination, there is no guarding or rigidity. ( the q is paraphrased) What is the most appropriate next step in management?
k: Suspected acute diverticulitis: CT abdomen with contrast first; colonoscopy only after the acute episode settles.
r: 'Acute LLQ pain + fever' = CT, not colonoscopy; colonoscopy becomes the answer only in the stem asking about follow up after recovery.
n: Recaller: Recaller notes the question is paraphrased; only 2 options recalled.

q: A 32 years old female presented with severe pelvic pain after MVA. CT showed multiple pelvic injury with severe hematoma. BP 88/55. What Is Most Appropriate NEXT management?
k: Unstable pelvic fracture: bind, transfuse, then stop the bleeding.
r: Hypotension plus pelvic hematoma means blood and angiography, not laparotomy, unless FAST shows free intraperitoneal fluid.
n: Printed answer D: hypotensive pelvic trauma with hematoma needs blood product resuscitation next.

q: 11-year-old boy with sudden vomiting and right lower-quadrant pain. Urine dipstick is negative and WBC is slightly elevated. What is the most appropriate diagnostic step?
k: Appendicitis imaging by patient group.
r: A child with a tender RLQ mass after days to weeks of pain switches the answer to CT.
n: Printed answer C: suspected appendicitis in a child; ultrasound is the first-line imaging (avoid radiation).

q: 70 year old poor historian lady, presented to ER with abdominal pain/distention associated with vomiting and obstipation for 2 days. She is tachycardic and dehydrated. Abdomen is distended, no scars nor signs of peritonism. Xray done, showed dilated small bowel loops, RLQ opacity, and pneumobilia. What is your next step in management?
k: Gallstone ileus: stone passes through a cholecystoenteric fistula and obstructs the small bowel, classically in elderly women.
r: Pneumobilia + SBO in an elderly woman with no scars = gallstone ileus, a surgical obstruction, not a conservative one.
n: Printed answer D: Rigler triad (SBO, ectopic gallstone opacity, pneumobilia) = gallstone ileus, managed with laparotomy. Compiler colors both B (CT scan) and D red; printed line is D.

q: A patient has ischemic colitis with abdominal rigidity. What is the next step?
k: Ischemic colitis: conservative unless peritonitis, perforation or gangrene.
r: Peritoneal signs override the diagnosis: whatever the cause, rigidity in an ischemic bowel goes to theatre.
n: Printed answer B: exploratory laparotomy (peritonitis signs in ischemic colitis).

q: 65-year-old woman underwent elective colon resection. On postoperative day 5, she complained of abdominal pain and distension. While preparing for CT, fresh blood and coffee-ground material appeared in her NGT bag. Her vital signs and hemoglobin were normal. What is the most appropriate diagnostic test?
k: Blood or coffee grounds in the NGT = upper GI bleed: resuscitate, start a PPI, then upper GI endoscopy.
r: Do not let the planned CT distract you: once the NGT shows blood, the question becomes an upper GI bleed workup.
n: Printed answer C: upper GI endoscopy for upper GI bleeding (likely stress ulcer) in a stable patient.

q: patient with a history of appendectomy 10 years ago presents abdominal pain, vomiting, and constipation ( tenderness NO RIGIDITY No sign of peritonitis) Xray small bowel distended or dilated with Mulitble air floud level What is the next step ?
k: Small bowel obstruction: confirm and grade with CT unless there is a clear operative indication.
r: Peritonitis or strangulation is what sends SBO to theatre; without them, image first.
n: No answer printed under this version; the sibling version below on the same page is answered Abdominal CT.

q: A patient presents 5 days after an appendectomy with fever, abdominal distension, feculent discharge from the surgical wound, and no passage of stool or flatus. On examination, he has (signs of peritonitis) (recaller: mentioned like this, not something I inferred), but he is hemodynamically stable. Abdominal ultrasound shows ascites and dilated bowel measuring up to 8 cm. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
k: Post-appendectomy complications by picture: Wound red, purulent discharge, soft abdomen: wound infection, open drainage; Fever, localized pain, no peritonitis: CT for abscess, then percutaneous drainage; Feculent discharge or generalized peritonitis: exploratory laparotomy
r: Stable vitals tempt you toward CT, but peritonitis is a clinical indication for surgery on its own.
n: Compiler red-highlights the feculent discharge from the wound. Recaller: Arabic note in stem: signs of peritonitis were explicitly mentioned like this, not inferred by the recaller.

q: 65 year old women present with abdominal pain and distention. X-ray shows colon lobe distention 9cm and perihaustral gas. What is the diagnostic step?
k: Suspected bowel obstruction: plain films first, then CT with IV contrast to confirm.
r: Stable patient with X-ray-proven colonic dilatation = CT with contrast next; signs of peritonitis or free air flip the answer to laparotomy.

q: An elderly patient with AFib presented with severe abdominal pain. What is the initial step?
k: Old age + AF (or recent MI, valve disease) + severe abdominal pain = acute mesenteric ischemia.
r: AF + abdominal pain out of proportion = CT angiography first; formal angiography is the therapeutic second step.

q: An elderly patient presents to the emergency department with an irreducable hernia in that extends into the scrotum. On examination, negitive cough test. What is the most appropriate next step in management (not sure) ?
k: Irreducible hernia = emergency surgery; delay risks bowel ischemia.
r: A reducible hernia with a cough impulse is repaired electively; once it becomes irreducible and painful, it is an emergency operation.
n: Recaller: Recaller not sure of the lead-in.

q: Typical scenario of divirticulitis (LLQ pain, fever ...) On CT there was 910 cm collection with thick edema of the sigmoid wall and multiple diverticula
k: Diverticulitis management follows Hinchey stage.
r: Abscess size decides: small = antibiotics, large = percutaneous drainage, free perforation/peritonitis = surgery.
n: Diverticular abscess (large collection) is managed with percutaneous drainage.

q: Post appendectomy 5 days present with erythema and pain and tenderness and there was fluctuance at site What is the most appropriate next step?
k: Post-op collection: match the site and size to the procedure.
r: Fluctuance = pus = drain; antibiotics alone are the answer only when there is no collection.
n: Wound abscess after appendectomy: open the wound and drain.

q: A 20-year-old patient underwent emergency appendectomy for a perforated appendix. Five days later, he presented with pain and appeared unwell. He was febrile, and the wound showed redness, tenderness, and foul-smelling discharge. On examination, there was a fluctuant mass at the wound site. What is the most appropriate management?
k: Post-appendectomy collections are managed by where the pus is and how sick the patient is: Wound abscess (red, tender, pus, fluctuance, fever): open drainage / incision and drainage; Seroma (non-inflamed, afebrile, serous fluid): open, irrigate, dressings; Small intra-abdominal collection: antibioti
r: Fluctuance at the wound means pus that needs draining; antibiotics only become the answer when there is no collection or it is a small deep collection.
n: Second recall version: wound abscess, open drainage (listed as A here).

q: A pediatric patient presented with sudden pain and redness of the scrotum with no history of trauma. On examination it was severely tender and red (only these two signs and symptoms). What is the most appropriate next step?
k: Acute scrotum in a child: Torsion: sudden severe pain, high riding horizontal testis, absent cremasteric reflex: exploration; Torsion of appendix testis: localized upper pole tenderness, blue dot sign: analgesia; Epididymitis: gradual onset, fever, dysuria, positive Prehn sign: antibiotics
r: Sudden painful scrotum in a boy: explore first, image only when in doubt.
n: Suspected testicular torsion: urgent surgical exploration.

q: patient with Hx of A.fib presented with sudden severe abdominal pain that is out of proportion and reduce abdominal sound, there is no guarding Hb low CT ANGIO report: Superior mesentric artery occulted with lucent mesenteric thickness What is the most appropriate management?
o: iv fluid, ABX, heparin then reassesses
k: Acute mesenteric ischemia: AF or recent MI + pain out of proportion + soft abdomen; confirm with CT angiography.
r: Add guarding, rigidity or free gas and the answer moves to exploratory laparotomy.
n: Printed answer C: embolic acute mesenteric ischemia without peritonitis; mesenteric angiography with embolectomy. Other version of this recall in Part 2: SWR-1838 → B. thrombolysis and embolectomy

q: A 65 year old woman complain of abdominal pain and distension X-ray findings: Dilation large colon (9 cm) with gas in Haustral wall -No vital signs- What is the most appropriate diagnostic?
k: Acute dilated bowel: X-ray first, CT with contrast to confirm and characterize.
r: If the stem adds peritonitis or shock, skip imaging and go to laparotomy; if it says pregnant, think MRI.
n: Printed answer A: CT abdomen with contrast is the diagnostic study for dilated colon with gas in the wall (pneumatosis/ischemia, obstruction).

q: 68 years old man smoker present with above umbilical abdominal pain during examination found to have pulsating abdomen and decrease lower limb blood pressure 89/60 (not sure about 60) Upper limb blood pressure was 139/86 ( not sure about 86 ) Not sure about the stem but most probably they ask about next step of assessment
k: AAA: ultrasound to screen or for the unstable patient at the bedside; CT angiography to confirm in the stable symptomatic patient.
r: If ultrasound is among the options and the lead-in says 'initial', choose it; if the patient is stable and symptomatic or the lead-in says 'confirm/most appropriate', choose CT angiography.
n: Printed answer C. CT for suspected abdominal aortic aneurysm; ultrasound was not among the options (NO US). Recaller: Recaller unsure of the exact BP values and of the lead-in.

q: A young woman presents with right lower abdominal pain. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial investigation?

n: Severe hypokalemia (K 2.5) with ileus: get ECG first for arrhythmia risk (printed).

q: A 37-year-old man presented to the Emergency Department with vomiting blood after attacks of excessive vomiting (see lab results). q: Pt with diverticulitis and collection on ultra sound did not mention size. Inital step
k: Diverticulitis management by severity: Uncomplicated: antibiotics (outpatient if well); Small abscess (about <3 to 4 cm): IV antibiotics; Large abscess: CT-guided percutaneous drainage plus antibiotics

q: 60y left lower pain, no mass, Diverticulitis and localized left colon collection confirmed by CT (no details mentioned)
k: Diverticulitis management by severity (Hinchey): Uncomplicated: antibiotics (or observation in selected patients), outpatient if well; Small pericolic abscess (Hinchey I): IV antibiotics; Larger abscess (roughly over 3 to 4 cm) or pelvic/distant abscess (Hinchey II): CT guided percutaneous drainage
r: If the stem gives a large abscess, the answer shifts to percutaneous drainage; if it gives generalized peritonitis, surgery.
n: Printed again later in this file (p.5004).

q: 65 years old patient presented with fever 38.3 and abdominal left lower quadrant tenderness Imaging shows: left colon diverticula and pre-colonic ( some recall paracollic ) collection 1x1, what is next?
