o: Conservative (is this justified because of the small size even tho it's symptomatic?)
k: Diverticular abscess: size decides.
r: Whether 1x1 is mm or cm does not matter: either way it is a small collection for antibiotics.
n: Printed answer B conservative: small (1x1) pericolic collection is managed conservatively rather than drained.

q: A 24-year-old man with a known history of Crohn's disease presents to the emergency department with right lower quadrant abdominal pain, fever, nausea, and tenderness over McBurney's point. Laboratory investigations reveal leukocytosis and elevated CRP. CT abdomen with contrast shows a large, 8 x 7 cm right lower quadrant intra-abdominal collection. The appendix cannot be visualized separately from the inflammatory changes. There is no generalized peritonitis, and the patient is hemodynamically stable. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
k: Intra-abdominal collection: decide by size, number and stability.
r: Instability or generalized peritonitis changes the answer to laparotomy; a stable large abscess = percutaneous drain.
n: Printed answer B. percutaneous drain for a large abscess in a stable patient.

q: A 65-year-old man presents with severe left lower quadrant abdominal pain and fever. A CT scan reveals diverticulitis with a 1 x 1 cm pericolic fluid collection. He is hemodynamically stable. What is the best management for this patient?
k: Diverticulitis management by CT finding: Uncomplicated or small abscess (under about 4 cm), stable: antibiotics (conservative); Abscess about 4 cm or larger: CT guided percutaneous drainage plus antibiotics; Perforation with generalized peritonitis or instability: surgery (laparotomy, Hartmann's)
r: Size of the collection decides: 1 cm is antibiotics, 5 cm is percutaneous drainage.
n: Printed answer A. Compiler (inset): ideal management for a febrile patient is antibiotics; since no antibiotic option is listed, the best answer is Conservative; if 'Abx' appears, choose it. Other versions of this recall in this deck: OCT-9405 → (no/undecided

q: A 45-year-old man with no history of surgery presents with diffused abdominal pain for 3 days. An X-ray shows an oblique right iliac fossa mass with pneumobilia. What is the most appropriate management?
k: Gallstone ileus (Rigler triad: pneumobilia, ectopic gallstone, small bowel obstruction).
r: Pneumobilia without previous ERCP or biliary surgery plus obstruction means gallstone ileus.
n: Printed C (Exploratory laparoscopy), but compiler comments 'it should be laparotomy' (gallstone ileus picture: pneumobilia + obstruction), which is not among the options; C is the closest option.

q: Patient with right iliac fossa pain for 7 days on examination: palpable mass at the iliac fossa WBC high US done showing appendiceal mass with NO collection What to do:
k: Late appendicitis with a RIF mass: Phlegmon (no collection): conservative, IV antibiotics; Abscess (collection): percutaneous drainage plus IV antibiotics, then interval appendectomy; Uncomplicated early appendicitis: laparoscopic appendectomy
r: "No collection" means nothing to drain, so the answer is conservative; a collection would make it percutaneous drainage.
n: Printed answer A; embedded inset of the same version from 12-14 Aug also answers A non interventional (appendiceal phlegmon without collection managed conservatively).

q: A 21 year old man present to emergency department with pain in right iliac fossa with 3 episodes of vomiting. Examinations reveal mass in right iliac fossa. CT abdomen: Mass without collection
k: Appendiceal mass: what the CT shows decides.
r: 'Without collection' means phlegmon: nothing to drain and too inflamed to operate.
n: Printed answer C. Compiler rule: age <40 -> non-intervention for phlegmon, drain for abscess; age >40 -> colonoscopy. Recaller: (Arabic) Recaller forgot the question wording but remembered the options.

q: 24 year old complain of RLQ pain examination show right iliac fossa mass CT SCAN. Shows periappendicular collection 10x12 of abscess
o: IV antibiotics and us guided drainage
k: Appendiceal mass on CT: No mass: appendectomy; Phlegmon (no collection): IV antibiotics only; Abscess: IV antibiotics plus percutaneous drainage, then interval appendectomy if indicated
r: Collection present means drain it; collection absent means antibiotics alone.
n: Handwritten red D marks the answer: appendiceal abscess is managed with IV antibiotics and image-guided drainage.

q: Patient presented with weight loss , fever, anorexia, cachectic, abdominal pain, no mention of pmh or anything. On PE abdominal tenderness over the right intercoastal region. On US findings of Liver lesion with No septation and thick perihepatic enhancement. What's the most appropriate management?
k: Liver abscess: identify the type, then drain or treat medically.
r: Amoebic = metronidazole; pyogenic = drain it.
n: Liver abscess (thick enhancing wall, unseptated) in a febrile cachectic patient; printed answer is percutaneous drainage.

q: Elderly known case of left-sided diverticulosis presents LLQ pain, imaging shows 8*9 cm collection Most appropriate management?
k: Other options were not recalled; alternatives to weigh: IV antibiotics alone: small abscess (under about 4 cm); Percutaneous drainage: large abscess, no generalized peritonitis; Laparotomy/Hartmann: generalized peritonitis, free perforation, instability
r: 'No signs of peritonitis' plus a big collection: drain it, do not operate.
n: Large diverticular abscess without peritonitis: percutaneous drainage. Recaller: dont remember rest choices, but it was like this and no signs of peritonitis

q: A patient presents with a 7-day history of right lower quadrant (RLQ) abdominal pain, fever, and leukocytosis. Abdominal CT scan demonstrates an appendiceal mass (... obscured ...). What is the most appropriate management?
k: Late appendicitis with a mass: CT tells you which arm.
r: Mass after ≥5 days = do not rush to the theatre; drain if there is pus, antibiotics if there is only phlegmon.
n: Screenshot of a 'Question 12, General Surgery' card; part of the parenthetical after 'appendiceal mass' is obscured. No answer printed on the page.

q: Patient with RLQ pain, fever, and leukocytosis. CT shows a 14x10 cm abscess with fecolith, and the abscess reaches the left flank. Management?
k: Appendiceal mass algorithm: Uncomplicated appendicitis: laparoscopic appendectomy; Phlegmon: IV antibiotics; Abscess: percutaneous drainage + IV antibiotics + interval appendectomy
r: A huge abscess still means drain first; size alone does not send a stable patient to theatre.
n: Large appendiceal abscess: percutaneous drainage. Printed again later in this file (p.6796).

q: An elderly patient presents with severe left iliac fossa pain, constipation and tenderness. CT shows a 9 x 10 cm collection with colonic wall thickening, enhanced lining, multiple diverticula and surrounding inflammation. What is the next step in management?
k: Diverticulitis by Hinchey stage: Uncomplicated: antibiotics (or supportive in selected cases); Small abscess (<3 to 4 cm): antibiotics alone; Larger abscess (I to II): percutaneous drainage + antibiotics
r: Aspiration and percutaneous drainage are not the same: large abscess needs a catheter drain.
n: Embedded 4-7 September version of the same question: Old Answer B. Aspiration and antibiotic, New Answer C. Percutaneous drainage. Majd Alkhateeb: it should be PC drain WITH antibiotics; aspiration (needle) is not the same as PC drain (catheter). Alhomrani agr

q: Male presented with RLQ pain, progressive for 3 days, with guarding and tenderness at the iliac fossa, localized, and fever and vomiting. US showed perforated appendix with a 6 x 5 cm periappendiceal abscess. What is the management?
k: Perforated appendix: localized abscess vs generalized peritonitis.
r: 'Localized' tenderness plus a measured abscess on imaging = drain, not operate.
n: Slide is an embedded 21-23 September recall; printed answer C. Highlights on the stem are recaller text highlighting. Printed again later in this file (p.6799).

q: 62 years old male presents with left lower abdominal pain for 5 days temp 38 CT: Perforated diverticulitis, 6.2 cm localized abscess what is the most appropriate management?
k: Complicated diverticulitis is managed by Hinchey stage and abscess size.
r: 'Perforated' does not automatically mean surgery: a contained abscess on CT is drained; generalized peritonitis goes to theatre.
n: Printed answer D. Older 15 September version (6.5 cm abscess) gives the same answer (percutaneous drainage with IV antibiotics) under letter C. Other versions of this recall in this deck: OCT-1465 → C. percutaneous drainage with iv antibiotics

q: Patient was admitted with right lower quadrant pain. The diagnosis was made as ruptured appendicitis with a localized abscess. WBC ~13.6 x10^9/L. What is the most appropriate initial management?
k: Appendiceal abscess sequence: drain plus antibiotics now, interval appendectomy later.
r: 'Initial' picks drainage; 'interval' appendectomy is the follow-up, not the first step.
n: Embedded 18 September version (same question, size not specified, only said localized) prints D. Drainage and antibiotics. Other versions of this recall in this deck: OCT-9437 → D. Percutaneous drainage and antibiotics

q: A patient admitted with RLQ pain is diagnosed with ruptured appendicitis with a localized abscess. WBC 13.6. What is the most appropriate initial management?
k: Appendiceal abscess: drain + antibiotics now, consider appendectomy later.
r: "Initial" management of an abscess is drainage; interval appendectomy is a tempting but later step.
n: Embedded app card (Q3 Appendiceal abscess) gives correct answer D: a contained appendiceal abscess in a stable patient is treated with IV antibiotics plus image-guided percutaneous drainage; interval appendectomy may follow. Emergency appendectomy in abscess/p

q: 15 months old boy with empty right hemiscrotum. On examination confirmed right empty hemiscrotum and groin but the left side is normal. What to do?
k: Non-palpable testis: look with the laparoscope.
r: Empty groin as well as scrotum = non-palpable; laparoscopy beats waiting or laparotomy.
n: Embedded inset: older version with different options; answer D. Diagnostic laparoscopy. Compiler: unilateral not palpable -> localize via diagnostic laparoscopy (algorithm figure: unilateral palpable / unilateral nonpalpable / bilateral nonpalpable).

q: A patient presents with multiple fistulas and abscesses, raising suspicion for Crohn's disease. What is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the diagnosis?
k: Perianal fistula workup: confirm the disease vs map the tract.
r: "Confirm Crohn's" = biopsy via colonoscopy; "define the fistula anatomy" = pelvic MRI.
n: Printed answer A. An embedded note from another recaller ('Same as below patient who have diarrhea and abdominal pain and multiple fistula... it was about diagnostic', MRI or colonoscopy with biopsy) gives Answer: Colonoscopy with biopsy.

q: Same as below patient who have diarrhea and abdominal pain and multiple fistula. Answers was different a little bit and it was about diagnostic
k: Crohn's with perianal disease: Diagnosis: ileocolonoscopy with biopsy; Fistula anatomy: MRI pelvis; Abscess: drain first; complex fistula: antibiotics, seton, then anti-TNF if refractory
r: Bowel symptoms + fistulas = scope and biopsy; isolated fistula mapping = MRI.
n: Embedded inset: another recaller's version with Crohn's symptoms (diarrhea, abdominal pain) and options MRI or colonoscopy with biopsy; answer colonoscopy with biopsy.

q: 20 somthing male came with perianal pain he has history of recurrence . examination fluctuation mass with skin tag and fistula. What its the appropite next step.
k: Complex (recurrent or multiple) fistula: known Crohn's = MRI pelvis; not known = colonoscopy with biopsy to confirm Crohn's.
r: The deciding word is "known Crohn's": if Crohn's is already diagnosed, image the tract (MRI); if not, prove the disease (colonoscopy).
n: No answer printed; marked For Future Revision. Compiler: skin tags along with young age MIGHT hint towards Crohn's (favouring colonoscopy with biopsy, as in the 21-23 September lookalike), but future recalls must clarify abdominal pain, weight loss or change i

q: Pt young male they had recurrent abdominal pain and diarrhea with multiple peranal fistula, fissure and skin tags. What is the most diagnostic
k: Crohn's disease workup by question: Diagnosis: colonoscopy with ileal intubation and biopsy (non caseating granulomas, skip lesions); Perianal fistula/abscess mapping: MRI pelvis (or endoanal US / EUA); Small bowel extent: MR or CT enterography
r: "Most diagnostic" for the disease = colonoscopy with biopsy; "best to assess the fistula" = MRI pelvis.

q: 28-year-old patient presented to the clinic complaining of perianal discharge. He reported history of on-off abdominal pain. He reported family history of Crohn's disease. On examination, three fistula openings at 3, 7 and 9 o'clock. What is the most appropriate next step?
k: Multiple perianal fistulas: first decide whether Crohn's is suspected.
r: The flip clue is the history: "on-off abdominal pain" or family history of Crohn's sends you to colonoscopy; no bowel symptoms sends you to MRI.
n: iPad screenshot of a 15-16 August page (412 of 1223); compiler red text on 'on-off abdominal pain'. Printed answer A. Colonoscopy (yellow highlight is recaller highlighting). Crohn's features -> colonoscopy.

q: Male(30s to 40s) presented with perianal discharge for months He denied history of bowel changes On examination he had 3 perianal sinuses at 3,5 and 7 Proctoscopic exam was normal Next step? (forgot)
k: Multiple perianal fistulas: first decide whether Crohn's is suspected.
r: Multiple fistulas + no bowel symptoms + normal proctoscopy = MRI, not colonoscopy.
n: No bowel symptoms with multiple perianal sinuses and normal proctoscopy -> MRI. Options were unlettered and lettered by position.

q: 19? years old, complaining of perineal pain with discharge, but no abdominal pain or diarrhea or blood in stool, exam revealed perineal fistula openings at 3, 5, 7 o'clock, underwent Proctoscopy and was normal "literally stated" , what is the next step:
k: Multiple perianal fistulas: first decide whether Crohn's is suspected.
r: The stem lists negatives (no pain, diarrhea or blood) on purpose: they rule out Crohn's features and point to MRI.
n: Embedded inset: older version (B and C in red as the debated pair); answer C. Perineum MRI. Compiler: 'I Don't Care His Age' (age does not change the answer).

q: 34 YO patient presented to the clinic complaining only of perianal discharge no abdominal pain or diarrhea(was written like this) , on examination three sinuses were noted at the 3 5 7 o'clock positions. Proctoscopy was clear. What is the most appropriate next step?
k: Multiple perianal fistulas: first decide whether Crohn's is suspected.
r: "Only" perianal discharge is the clue: no bowel symptoms = MRI.
n: Embedded inset: older 34 YO version (A and B in red as the debated pair); answer B. MRI. Compiler: 'Same Concept'. Other versions of this recall in this deck: OCT-9454 → B. PELVIC MRI Printed again later in this file (p.6822).

q: Man in his 20s came after a MVA and with examination he is alert but he have abdominal distention. BP: ~ 88/54 FAST: free intra abdominal fluid What is the appropriate management
k: FAST pathway in blunt abdominal trauma: Unstable + FAST positive: laparotomy; Unstable + FAST negative: DPL; Stable + FAST positive: CT
r: Same scenario, different verb: "most appropriate management" = laparotomy, "initial/next" = transfusion.
n: Embedded inset (19-20 September): printed B. Massive transfusion protocol crossed out and A written in pen. Compiler: blunt trauma + hypotensive + FAST +ve: Next ==> transfusion > laparotomy; Most appropriate ==> 50/50 but somewhat more into laparotomy. Origin

q: A trauma patient arrives in the emergency department. Initial fluid resuscitation was given, but the patient remained unstable with very low blood pressure. Then FAST exam was performed and showed moderate free fluid. What is the next step in management?
k: Trauma with positive FAST: hemodynamic status decides.
r: Look for 'despite fluids' or persistent hypotension: that removes CT and laparoscopy and makes it laparotomy.
n: Printed answer B: positive FAST in an unstable patient after fluid resuscitation -> immediate laparotomy.

q: A 25-year-old man brought to the Emergency Department after he was involved in motor vehicle crash, which was driving at a speed of 130 km/hour. Patient was wearing seat belt. On arrival to the Emergency Department, he was conscious, and alert (see report). Chest X-ray: Normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
k: Abdominal trauma: stability first.
r: "Conscious and alert" after a high-speed crash = stable = CT, even with a normal chest X-ray and no abdominal findings.
n: Embedded inset: different version (25-year-old, 130 km/h, seat belt, report not shown); printed Answer: B. Printed again later in this file (p.6856). Printed again later in this file (p.6857).

q: A patient is brought to the emergency department following a motorcycle accident. Airway, breathing, and circulation are maintained. On examination, the patient has generalized abdominal tenderness and guarding, with a blood pressure of 90/40 mmHg. What is the most appropriate next step?
k: Laparotomy indications in abdominal trauma.
r: Unstable with a soft or equivocal abdomen: FAST first; unstable with peritonitis: straight to laparotomy.
n: Printed answer B. laparotomy (unstable with peritonitis). Embedded 15-16 September version also answers exploratory laparotomy.

q: 20 something YO male presented to the ER after MVA, airway is managed,2 large bore IV inserted, 2 L of fluid given. He has GENERALIZED abdominal rigidity and tenderness BP: 90/40 I believe this is the only vital sign given What is the most appropriate (no next) step in management?
k: Read the stage of the scenario.
r: If the stem has not yet given fluids, the answer is resuscitation; once 2 L are in and BP is still low, it is laparotomy.
n: Embedded inset (15-16 September): different version (fluids already given, 'most appropriate (no next)'); printed answer B. Exploratory laparotomy. Compiler: just remember, in septic abdomen, ALWAYS fluid BEFORE surgery.

q: 55-year-old man underwent an open appendectomy for a perforated appendix. He presented to the Emergency Department on the 6th postoperative day complaining of severe abdominal pain, distension and an inability to pass stool. On examination, there is feculent discharge from the wound site with signs of peritonitis (see lab results and report). Blood pressure 110/70 mmH Heart rate 120 /min Respiratory rate 18 /min Temperature 38 C Oxygen saturation 95 % Test Result Normal Values ABG HCO3- 10 22-28 mmol/L ABG PCO2 4.8 4.7-6.0 kPa pH 7.25 7.36-7.45 ABG PO2 11 10.6-14.2 kPa Base excess - 12 -2 to 2 mmol/L Ultrasound abdomen: Moderate ascites with echoes and septations. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
k: Post-appendectomy complications ladder: Seroma (no inflammation): dressings; Wound abscess (purulent discharge, soft abdomen): open drainage; Small intra-abdominal collection: antibiotics
r: 'Feculent' plus peritonitis = laparotomy; 'purulent' with a soft abdomen = open the wound.
n: Printed answer D: feculent wound discharge with peritonitis and metabolic acidosis (stump leak/fecal peritonitis) needs exploratory laparotomy. A small inset of the same question keyed 'D (MG)' with 'feculent' highlighted is shown. 'See below look alike' point

q: A 55-year-old man known case of liver cirrhosis with ascites presented to the Emergency Department complaining of progressive non- specific abdominal pain for 6 days, which was associated with vomiting. Examination confirmed generalized abdominal tendemess (see lab result and report). Blood pressure 100/55 mmH Test Result Normal Values WBC 23.3 4.5-10.5 x 109/L. CT scan abdomen: Moderate ascites with cirrhotic liver. Which of the following is the most appropriate step in treatment?
k: SBP in cirrhosis with ascites: Suspect with any pain, fever, encephalopathy or deterioration; Diagnosis: ascitic fluid neutrophils above 250 cells/mm3; Treat: IV ceftriaxone (third generation cephalosporin), plus IV albumin
r: Cirrhosis plus ascites plus abdominal pain = SBP = antibiotics, not the operating room.
n: Answer A printed both on the phone-screenshot copy and the enlarged copy (presumed SBP in cirrhotic with ascites). Printed again later in this file (p.6871).

q: A 36-year-old man was stabbed in the right lower quadrant of his abdomen 1 hour back. He complained of pain at the wound site. Local wound exploration revealed penetration of the anterior abdominal fascia. Blood pressure 110/62 mmHg Heart rate 87 /min Temperature 37.2 C Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
k: Anterior abdominal stab, local wound exploration: Fascia intact: wound care and discharge; Fascia breached, stable: CT (or serial exams); Hard signs (shock, peritonitis, evisceration): laparotomy
r: Fascial penetration changes the plan from discharge to CT, not to laparotomy.
n: Printed answer A with source tags (Medgard) (Sabiston): stable patient with fascial penetration on local wound exploration goes to CT. CT scan and observation highlighted in red as key options.

q: 40 Guy w suspected intestinal obstruction minimal tenderness
k: Bowel obstruction workup.
r: Add rigidity, fever, tachycardia or CT signs of ischemia and the answer flips to laparotomy.
n: Printed again later in this file (p.6875).

q: 68 y.o. patient with persistent atrial fibrillation, hypertension, and diabetes mellitus presents with abdominal pain out of proportion to the findings on physical examination. CT angiography shows an occlusion of the superior mesenteric artery (SMA). DURING EXAMINATION, THERE IS MILD TENDERNESS BUT NO RIGIDITY. BP/HR: I can't remember, but both were normal. What is the most appropriate management?
k: Acute mesenteric ischemia (embolic SMA occlusion): decide by peritonitis and bowel viability.
r: Read the lead-in: "initial" means fluids, antibiotics and heparin; "most appropriate" without peritonitis means embolectomy; with peritonitis it means laparotomy.
n: Printed B. Compiler rule (inset): no peritonitis -> initial IV fluids/abx/heparin, most appropriate angiography with embolectomy; with peritonitis -> initial resuscitation +/- heparin, most appropriate laparotomy. UpToDate prefers open over catheter embolectom

q: A patient with persistent atrial fibrillation, hypertension, and diabetes mellitus (recaller unsure about the diabetes) presents with abdominal pain out of proportion to the findings on physical examination. CT angiography shows an occlusion of the superior mesenteric artery (SMA). What is the most appropriate management?
k: Acute mesenteric ischemia (embolic SMA occlusion): decide by peritonitis and bowel viability.
r: Once CT angiography confirms SMA occlusion, never choose more imaging; choose revascularization or, with peritonitis, laparotomy.
n: Other versions of this recall in this deck: OCT-9504 → B. Mesenteric angiography with embolectomy Other version of this recall earlier in October: OCT-3031 → A. Mesenteric angiography with embolectomy. October By Similar update ↻ Printed again later in the Oct

q: (Possible new recall?) patient with Hx of A fib presented with sudden severe abdominal pain that is out of proportion and reduce abdominal sound, there is diffuse abdominal guarding and tenderness. CT ANGIO report: Superior mesentric artery occlusion with reduced bowel wall enhancement BP: 90/55 What is the most appropriate initial management?
k: Acute mesenteric ischemia (embolic SMA occlusion): decide by peritonitis and bowel viability.
r: The fork in mesenteric ischemia is peritonitis and bowel viability: stable and soft goes to revascularization, guarding, shock or poor wall enhancement goes to resuscitation then laparotomy.
n: Bare printed answer B with no commentary; diffuse guarding/tenderness highlighted in red. Other versions of this recall in this deck: OCT-9505 → B. thrombolysis and embolectomy

q: A 60-year-old man with a known history of atrial fibrillation presents with severe abdominal pain out of proportion to the physical examination findings. There is minimal abdominal tenderness and no guarding. His vital signs are stable. CT imaging shows superior mesenteric artery (SMA) occlusion with reduced bowel wall enhancement. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
k: Acute mesenteric ischemia: heparin first, then revascularise; laparotomy if peritonitis.
r: Peritoneal signs or instability flip the answer from angiography/embolectomy to emergency laparotomy.
n: Compiler: next should be heparin, but this option is not present, so answer is C (angiography and embolectomy). Other versions of this recall in this deck: OCT-3031 → A. Mesenteric angiography with embolectomy Other version of this recall earlier in October: O

q: Elderly came with signs and symptoms of bowel obstruction Xray done : Air fluid level , dilated small bowel loops, pneumobilia Management ?
k: Gallstone ileus: elderly patient, SBO, no previous surgery.
r: Pneumobilia plus SBO in an elderly patient: think gallstone ileus and choose surgery, not drip and suck.

q: A 70 year old lady, presented to the ER with abdominal pain/distention associated with vomiting and obstipation for 2 days. She is tachycardic and dehydrated. Abdomen is distended, no scars nor signs of peritonism. Xray done, showed dilated small bowel loops, RLQ opacity, and pneumobilia. What is your next step in management?
k: Gallstone ileus: elderly patient, SBO, no previous surgery.
r: No scars plus pneumobilia plus RLQ opacity: skip the CT and go to laparotomy.
n: Rigler triad (RLQ opacity, bowel obstruction, pneumobilia) of gallstone ileus; presence of 2 of 3 on X-ray confirms the diagnosis, so CT is not needed and proceed to laparotomy. Inset of same recall prints Answer: D. CT scan option is shown in red as the tempt

q: Pt after splenectomy surgery presented with multiple episodes of intestinal obstruction Now complaining of abdominal destination pain rigidity sluggish bowel sounds. Initial management?
k: Bowel obstruction management: Uncomplicated (soft abdomen, stable): IV fluids, electrolytes, NG decompression, then treat the cause; Laparotomy indications: peritonitis (rigidity, rebound), strangulation (fever, tachycardia, constant pain, fat stranding on CT), failure of conservative care; Prior su
r: Rigidity is the word that flips obstruction from drip and suck to the operating room.
n: Printed answer C, compiler stresses 'It's NOT A Typo'. Rigidity means peritonitis, which needs surgery even if stable; NGT alone could be accepted, but NGT plus bowel rest is wrong because you do not rest a patient with peritonitis. Other versions of this reca

q: Pt after splenectomy surgery presented with with multiple episodes of intestinal obstruction Now compliaing of abdominal destination pain rigidity sluggish bowel sounds Vitality stable X ray air fluid level What is the [[[[[[INITIAL]]]]]] management?
k: Bowel obstruction: conservative vs operate depends on signs of strangulation or peritonitis, not on vitals alone.
r: "Stable vitals" is the trap: peritonism (rigidity) alone mandates laparotomy; a soft non-tender abdomen would flip the answer to NGT and drip.
n: Embedded older 15-16 September recall inset (26-September-Without-Repetition-Part-2-1, p. 939). Compiler: NGT alone is wrong even without bowel rest, and here it is NGT AND bowel rest, telling you not to choose it. Examiner objection 'patient is stable' answer

q: Pt came with previous splenectomy with 6 admissions due to adhesions came same complaint hypotensive RIGIDITY
k: Adhesive SBO: conservative first, unless peritonitis/strangulation.
r: Recurrent admissions tempt you to "drip and suck" again, but rigidity with hypotension means strangulation or perforation until proven otherwise.
n: Embedded inset: terse older recall numbered 49; no answer line of its own.

q: 62-year-old man, diabetic, previous history of PCI, atrial fibrillation. Presents with sudden severe generalized abdominal pain, 10/10. Examination reveals generalized tenderness, absent bowel sounds, and rigidity. Labs: acidotic pH and high lactate. What is the most appropriate next step?
k: Acute mesenteric ischemia: anticoagulate first in all; the rest depends on the abdomen.
r: Heparin is never wrong in AMI, but rigidity means dead bowel: in a version with 'heparin + laparotomy' or no heparin option, pick surgery.
n: Printed answer A (anticoagulation first for suspected acute mesenteric ischemia from AF embolism). 'rigidity' printed in red by the compiler; note that peritonitis/rigidity would usually push toward laparotomy, so this key may be worth reviewing. 7-10 October

q: A patient presents to the emergency department with severe abdominal pain. He is a known case of atrial fibrillation. His vital signs are stable. What is the most appropriate next step?
k: AF + sudden severe abdominal pain (pain out of proportion to the exam) = embolic acute mesenteric ischemia until proven otherwise.
r: The fork is the abdomen, not the AF: soft abdomen and stable = heparin; rigid abdomen or shock = laparotomy.
n: No answer printed; 'See Below' points to the lookalike on page 16 (AF with acute mesenteric ischemia, printed answer LMWH). 19 October update Other version of this recall in 19 October: OCT-2772 → no answer. 20 October update Other version of this recall in 20

q: A patient with a history of Atrial fibrillation presents to the emergency department with sudden, severe abdominal pain out of proportion. Physical examination reveals generalized abdominal tenderness, guarding, and rigidity. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: NPO, IV fluids and heparin then reassess
k: Acute mesenteric ischemia: peritonitis decides the route.
r: Same AF patient with pain out of proportion but a SOFT abdomen = CT angiography/embolectomy; add guarding and rigidity = laparotomy.
n: Printed answer A: AF with acute mesenteric ischemia and peritoneal signs (guarding, rigidity) means peritonitis, so emergency laparotomy. Option C left blank by recaller. Same question earlier in October: OCT-2772 → no answer. Other version of this recall earl

q: A patient with a history of atrial fibrillation presents to the emergency department with sudden, severe abdominal pain out of proportion to the physical examination findings. Physical examination reveals generalized abdominal distension and guarding with rigidity in left upper quadrant What is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: Keep the patient NPO, administer IV fluids and IV heparin, and reassess
k: Acute mesenteric ischemia: management forks on peritonitis.
r: Early AMI has a soft abdomen; once rigidity appears the bowel is dead and the answer flips to laparotomy.
n: Rigidity = peritonitis, so surgery now (compiler's keyword rule from the inset). Other version of this recall earlier in October: OCT-2772 → no answer.

q: A 78-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with a 2-day history of intermittent, crampy, colicky abdominal pain, nausea and multiple episodes of bilious vomiting. Her last bowel movement was 3 days ago and she has not passed flatus since yesterday. She has known gallbladder stones but never pursued surgery. Temperature is 37.4 C, HR 98/min, BP 128/76 mmHg and RR 18/min. There is diffuse abdominal tenderness without rebound or guarding. Imaging reveals pneumobilia. What is the most appropriate management?
k: Gallstone ileus = mechanical SBO from a gallstone via cholecystoenteric fistula.
r: Pneumobilia with bowel obstruction is not cholangitis; do not reach for ERCP.

q: Patient came after some sort of surgery with fever, anorexia, abdominal pain with tenderness and rebound tenderness. And CT show multiple air fluids. What is the management?
k: Postoperative intra-abdominal sepsis: localized vs generalized.
r: The word that flips drainage to laparotomy is generalized peritonism (rebound, rigidity), not the presence of a collection.
n: Recaller: Im so sorry it was long case that all I can remember

q: A patient presents with abdominal pain. An abdominal X-ray shows pneumobilia, and the stone has passed into the right lower quadrant. What is the most appropriate next step in management?

q: A woman presents with a rapidly enlarging 5 cm breast mass. Imaging shows a well-defined solid lesion. Biopsy shows stromal cells with increased mitotic figures. What is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Phyllodes tumour vs fibroadenoma: Phyllodes: rapid growth, large (often > 5 cm), skin thinning from pressure, stromal hypercellularity and mitoses; Fibroadenoma: small, slow, mobile, bland stroma; US: solid mass with cystic spaces suggests phyllodes
r: "Stromal" + "mitotic figures" + "rapidly enlarging" = phyllodes, never fibroadenoma.
n: Printed answer D; embedded older recall (21-23 September) answered B (Phyllodes tumor in its own list). Other versions of this recall in this deck: OCT-5420 → B. Phyllodes tumor

q: -on histology Breast Phyllodes tumor: Next step or management. ?
k: Phyllodes tumour after tissue diagnosis: Benign / small (e.g. 3 cm, 4 x 5 cm) → wide local excision, ≥ 1 cm margin; Larger than 8 cm or tumour too big for breast size → simple mastectomy; Malignant phyllodes → stage first: contrast CT chest (hematogenous spread to lung), then surgery
r: The histology grade flips the step: benign → wide local excision; malignant → stage with contrast CT chest first.
n: No answer printed for this recall; compiler shows two lookalikes (benign cystosarcoma phyllodes -> WLE; malignant phyllodes -> contrast CT chest).

q: A 40-year-old presents with a right breast lump that has been present for 2 years. On examination, there is firm lump about 4 x 5 cm in the inner quadrant, overlying skin is normal and no palpable axillary nodes (see report) Trucut biopsy: Cystosarcoma Phyllodes. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
k: Phyllodes treatment by size and grade: "Cystosarcoma phyllodes" = phyllodes tumour, despite the name usually benign; Small (≤ ~8 cm) → wide local excision, ≥ 1 cm margins; > 8 cm → simple mastectomy
r: Do not let the word "sarcoma" push you to mastectomy or chemotherapy: size decides.
n: Embedded inset (look alike): Cystosarcoma is a misnomer; cystosarcoma phyllodes is the same as benign phyllodes, managed by WLE (wide local excision with clear margin).

q: A 25-year-old woman presented with a right breast lump, which has been increasing in size over the past year. Physical examination confirmed a 10x12 cm firm, mobile mass involving the upper halve of the right breast with no palpable axillary lymph nodes (see report). Core needle biopsy: Malignant phyllodes tumour. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
k: Malignant tumour approach: diagnose → stage → treat.
r: "Malignant" on biopsy + "next step" = stage first, operate second.
n: Embedded inset (look alike): malignant phyllodes; option C marked with ** (staging CT chest for lung metastasis).

q: Women came with breast asymmetry due to rapid growing mass in the middle of the right breast Well defined mass mobile Biopse show stromal hyperplasia withe mitotic figuer Most appropriate mangment ?
k: Phyllodes surgery: Small or moderate → WLE with ≥ 1 cm margin; > 8 cm → simple mastectomy; Never routine axillary dissection (hematogenous spread)
r: If the stem gives a size above 8 cm, the answer switches to simple mastectomy, not MRM.

q: An 18 years old female patient (I'm 100% sure of the age) has had a huge growth of one of the breasts in a short period of time (I can't remember if it was weeks or months), upon examination there was a 8.3-8.5 cms (I'm 100% sure of the 8 cms) mass in one of the breasts. What is the INITIAL step in management?
o: Excisional biopsy (not sure if both types of biopsies were there, but I'm sure one of them was)

r: "Initial" step for a breast mass = imaging chosen by age, even when the story screams phyllodes.
n: Compiler: 'Answer Is A. Breast ultrasound; Don't Jump'. Triple assessment of breast mass: history and physical, then imaging, then histology. Likely giant fibroadenoma/phyllodes but imaging comes first. Recaller: Recaller sure of age and 8 cm size; unsure whet

q: Breast Adenocarcinoma question: Spiculated with micro-calcifications on imaging BiradsIV or V Options:

r: Even BI-RADS 5 is biopsied before any surgery.

q: Spiculated breast mass A 40-year-old woman presents with a breast lump. Mammography reveals a spiculated mass. What is the next step?
k: Triple assessment = clinical exam + imaging + core needle biopsy.
r: Spiculated = suspicious = core biopsy, not excision.
n: Embedded lookalike (54-year-old, BI-RADS V) also Answer: B.

q: A 54-year-old woman complains of a left breast mass that has been present for 9 months. Physical examination confirmed a 3 x 3 cm firm fixed mass at the left retro-areolar area with associated nipple retraction (see report). Bilateral breast mammogram: Speculated mass at left retro-areolar region associated with suspicious clustered microcalcifications. There are multiple pathological left axillary lymph nodes. Findings coded as BI-RADS V (Probably Malignant). Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
k: Sequence for suspected breast cancer: diagnose → stage → treat.
r: However obvious the cancer looks, the next step is still a needle, not a scan or a knife.
n: Embedded inset: lookalike question bank version; Answer: B.

q: A 40-year-old woman presented for her first screening mammography. She has no past medical history, and no family history of cancer (see reports; the report was not captured in the recall). Bilateral breast mammogram: Bilateral dense breast with multiple fibro glandular opacities, no suspicious microcalcifications or spiculated lesions. Breast ultrasound: Bilateral multiple variable sizes cysts. Findings coded as BI-RADS III (Probably benign). Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
k: BI-RADS category decides the next step: 0: incomplete, recall for additional imaging; 1 negative / 2 benign: routine screening; 3 probably benign: short interval follow-up (about 6 months)
r: Simple cysts alone would usually be BI-RADS 2 (routine screening); answer by the category the question gives you, not by your own reading of the images.
n: Printed answer C; same-version inset (Q20, 3 options) also prints Answer: C, with the compiler unsure whether it was in the surgery or gyn section. BI-RADS III means short interval follow-up.

q: 42-year-old woman presents with a firm, partially movable right breast mass that has been present for 3 months. Physical examination and imaging reveal an ill-defined lobulated hypoechoic mass measuring 2 x 2 cm, which is coded as BI-RADS IV (4). What is the most appropriate next step in management?
k: BI-RADS category decides the next step.
r: BI-RADS 3 means follow up; BI-RADS 4 or 5 means core biopsy, however benign the patient's age or exam looks.
n: BI-RADS 4 requires tissue diagnosis by core needle biopsy. Embedded inset is the same version with BI-RADS IV in red and 'Answer: B. Needle core biopsy'.

q: Female in her 30s with breast cancer Investigation shows 4cm fibroadenoma What is the most high risk ?
k: Benign breast lesions by future cancer risk: Non-proliferative (cysts, simple fibroadenoma, fibrocystic change): no meaningful increase; Proliferative without atypia (usual hyperplasia, complex fibroadenoma, sclerosing adenosis, papilloma): slight increase; Atypical hyperplasia (ADH, ALH): marked in
r: Atypia is the word that raises the risk: "hyperplasia" alone is a distractor, and fibroadenoma size never is the answer for cancer risk.
n: Printed answer D (atypical hyperplasia is the most significant risk factor). October By Similar update

q: ... Year-Old Female Present With 4 Cm Fibroadenoma With Hyperplasia And Atypia. What Is The Most Significant Risk Factor For Breast Cancer?
k: Risk ladder of benign breast histology: Non-proliferative: no meaningful increase; Proliferative without atypia: slight increase; Atypical ductal or lobular hyperplasia: marked increase
r: When both "hyperplasia" and "atypia" are options, atypia is the risk factor; this is the older version of the "hyperplasia with atypia" card.
n: Embedded inset: older version (numbered 58 in another compilation) with different options; Answer C. Atypia. Compiler box: this could be surgery (even if it comes in the second section) but could be gyn. October By Similar update

q: Normal TSH, US showed 2.4 solid nodule. Next step ?
k: Rule: thyroid nodule = TSH + ultrasound first; TSH decides scan vs FNA, ultrasound decides whether FNA is needed.
r: A nodule under 1 cm with normal TSH gets follow-up imaging, not FNA; size and ultrasound features decide.
n: Solid nodule >1-1.5 cm with normal TSH: FNA. Options C and D were left blank by the recaller.

q: A young girl (i think she they mentioned that it was after puberty or something) having unilateral breast enlargement of 8 cm, what to do?
k: Young female with a breast mass: image with ultrasound first, then tissue diagnosis, then excision if large or growing.
r: "Initial" in a young girl = ultrasound, never mammogram; "definitive" for a big solid mass = excision after biopsy.
n: Recaller: C and D were biopsy and excision but i don't remember the exact wording.

q: Lactating woman presents with a 2 weeks history of a tender breast swelling measuring 2 x 3 cm. Breast ultrasound shows a deep cystic lesion measuring 3 x 4 cm. The differential diagnosis includes a suspected breast abscess or galactocele. She has been started on flucloxacillin. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
k: Lactational breast collection: Under 5 cm, single, healthy skin: aspiration (repeat as needed) plus antibiotics; 5 cm or more, multiple, or skin thinning: incision and drainage; Continue breastfeeding or expressing from the affected side
r: A deep lesion is still aspirated under ultrasound guidance; depth alone does not mandate incision.
n: Printed answer aspiration. Inset note: less than 5 cm with no skin thinning favours aspiration over incision and drainage.

q: 24 month old boy came with flaming red right hemi scrotum us: hyper vascular with normal vascularity of testicle what's the diagnosis?
k: Acute scrotum by Doppler and clinical clues: Absent testicular flow, high horizontal testis, no cremasteric reflex: torsion (surgery); Increased flow, thick edematous cord: epididymo-orchitis (antibiotics + NSAID); Upper pole tenderness, blue dot, normal testis: appendage torsion (NSAID, conservativ
r: Hyperemia on Doppler = inflammation (epididymo-orchitis); absent flow = torsion.
n: Printed answer is epididymo-orchitis; compiler reacts with disbelief ('The Hell?') at the recall but gives no alternative answer.

q: An elderly patient with metastatic prostate cancer presents with acute urinary retention. Multiple attempts of catheterization have failed. What is the most appropriate next step?
k: Acute urinary retention ladder: decompress first, treat the cause later.
r: Failed urethral catheterization or suspected urethral injury = suprapubic catheter, not repeated forceful attempts.
n: Failed urethral catheterization in acute retention -> suprapubic catheterization.

q: 50 pt painless hematuria for 3 days no urinary symptoms: initial:
k: Hematuria ladder: confirm, then image the upper tract, then look in the bladder.
r: "Initial" means confirm with urinalysis; "most diagnostic" or "definitive" for painless hematuria at 50 means cystoscopy.

q: Pt child with scrotal tenderness typical torsion s/s Golden time to do surgery
k: Torsion is a clinical diagnosis; time is testis.
r: Never delay exploration for ultrasound when the picture is classic; the clock started at pain onset, not at arrival.

q: A patient is involved in a motor vehicle accident and sustains a pelvic fracture with a perineal hematoma and suspected urethral injury. There is blood at the urethral meatus. What is the most appropriate next investigation?
k: Urethral injury work up: image the urethra from below before anything goes in.
r: Hematuria after pelvic fracture WITHOUT blood at the meatus points to the bladder, so the test becomes CT cystogram, not RUG.
n: Terse recall 'RTA blood from urethral meatus: CT pelvis, retrograde urthrogram' restated as the fuller version; options A and B shown in red as the two contenders; printed answer A, retrograde urethrography.

q: A 12-year-old presents with left-sided lower abdominal pain. Examination confirms a slightly elevated, tender left testis with redness and edema of the scrotum. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Acute scrotum in a boy. Torsion: sudden severe pain, high-riding horizontal testis, absent cremasteric reflex; explore immediately (Doppler only if unsure); Appendage torsion: upper pole tenderness, blue dot sign, testis normal lie; supportive; Epididymo-orchitis: gradual, fever, urinary symptoms, P
r: 'Elevated' or 'high riding' testis means torsion; 'tender upper pole with normal lie' means appendage torsion.
n: Printed answer A. Testicular torsion; compiler highlights 'slightly elevated' testis as the clue. No further commentary.

q: question about testicular torsion, they want initial investigation
k: Acute scrotum: clinical diagnosis first, Doppler US only if it does not delay surgery.
r: If the options include surgical exploration and the picture is classic torsion, exploration beats any imaging; US wins only when an imaging test is asked for.
n: Compiler answer: US. Recaller described two questions on testicular torsion (initial investigation and most diagnostic) sharing the options US/MRI/CT; a single answer 'US' is given. Recaller: Arabic note: two questions on testicular torsion, one asking initial

q: second question about testicular torsion, they want most diagnostic

r: 'Most diagnostic' for torsion is still Doppler US among imaging tests; only if 'surgical exploration' appears would it outrank imaging.
n: Same options as the initial investigation question; compiler gives the single answer 'US' for the testicular torsion recall. Recaller: Arabic note: second question asking most diagnostic. Other versions of this recall in this deck: SWR-1172 → A. US

q: 32 y male with red urine for 1 week with burning micturition and can't urinate for 24H Urinalysis normal Culture no growth PR enlarged tender prostate What is the diagnosis
k: Prostate on DRE: what the gland feels like gives the diagnosis.
r: Retention plus a TENDER prostate in a young man = prostatitis; a non tender gland in an old man = BPH.
n: BPH is unlikely at this age. Acute prostatitis causes rapid enlargement of the prostate causing acute urinary retention, and is severely tender to palpation. Although prostatitis is a subtype of UTI, prostatitis is the more accurate phrase; normal urinalysis w

q: A pediatric patient presents with a 1h history of testicular pain and swelling. On examination, the cremasteric reflex is absent and transillumination is negative. What is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Acute scrotum in a child: torsion first.
r: Absent cremasteric reflex + acute pain = torsion; do not let an ultrasound delay theatre.
n: Printed answer A. Testicular torsion.

q: Neonate came with swilling scrotal edema the surgeon want to do immediate surgery Best time to do it
k: Testicular torsion: time is testis.
r: The magic number for torsion is 6 hours; painless bilateral redness spreading to the groin in a toddler is idiopathic scrotal edema, not torsion.
n: Printed answer A (6 hours), consistent with the testicular salvage window for torsion.

q: patient in 60s diagnosed with prostate cancer presenting with back pain, urine retention and maybe lower limb weakness What is the Appropriate Next Step?
o: Oral analgesia and reassess after 24 hours
k: Malignant spinal cord compression: suspect in any cancer patient with back pain plus neuro or sphincter signs.
r: Cancer plus back pain plus retention or weakness: steroids now, MRI today, never outpatient.

q: A patient presents with severe loin pain that radiates to the scrotum. The patient is rolling on the ground due to the severity of the pain, but there is no fever. What is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Renal colic. Pain: loin to groin, colicky, patient restless; Urinalysis: hematuria; Imaging: non contrast CT KUB (ultrasound in pregnancy and children)
r: Rolling in pain = colic (stone); lying motionless = peritonitis; add fever to a stone and it becomes an emergency.

q: A man presents with flank pain and tea-colored urine, with no other symptoms. Urinalysis shows blood as the only abnormality. What is the most appropriate investigation?
o: A kidney, ureter, and bladder (KUB) X-ray.
k: Hematuria work-up: confirm, then image the upper tract and look in the bladder.
r: Hematuria + flank pain = CT (non contrast for stone); painless gross hematuria in a smoker = cystoscopy plus CT urography.
n: Answer CT. In his 13 August recall it said 'CT KUB'; CT KUB means NON contrast CT, and he still chose it because the patient had flank pain (and got 100 in surgery). Options A and B highlighted in red.

q: ~50 old male age came to the clinic concerned seeing blood in his urine. While obtaining history the patient complained of Right Flank pain. No history of trauma or History Of Prior stones. On examination there's right flank tenderness and enlarged prostate On DRE. Urinalysis : 20 RBC What is The most appropriate investigation
k: Hematuria work-up: confirm, then image the upper tract and look in the bladder.
r: An incidental enlarged prostate does not change the work-up: flank pain plus hematuria still means CT.
n: Answer B CT KUB, confirmed. Enlarged prostate is an incidental finding; the patient could have a stone or RCC, both of which require CT for diagnosis.

q: > 52 year old male medically free came to the clinic complaining of red urine for 2 days associated with right flank pain, no dysuria no fever no other symptoms On examination: right flank tenderness and palpable rectal prostate ( written like this) Urine culture : negative Urine analysis: + erythrocyte Nitrate: absent WBC: absent What is the most appropriate next investigation :
k: Hematuria work-up: confirm, then image the upper tract and look in the bladder.
r: Negative culture and nitrite exclude UTI; the remaining flank pain plus hematuria means CT KUB.
n: Likely answer B CT-KUB (same theme as the preceding flank pain plus hematuria recalls: suspect stone, non contrast CT KUB).

q: A 50 years old patient came for painless hematuria for 3 days Which of the following is the INITIAL investigation:

Cystoscopy+ CT Urography (both in the same answer)

cystogram + CT urogram (both in the same answer)

q: 50 year old patient with painless gross hematuria Most appropriate next step?
k: Hematuria work-up: confirm, then image the upper tract and look in the bladder.

q: 65y old dietetic male with scrotal pain and crepitus Most appropriate inital step?
k: Fournier gangrene is a surgical emergency; imaging must not delay theatre.

q: case about a four-year-old child presenting with a palpable olive like mass in his lower abdomen and empty scrotum asking about the management
o: Do surgery in a few years
k: Undescended testis timing: Birth to 6 months: observe (spontaneous descent possible); Refer by 6 months; orchiopexy at 6 to 18 months; Older child at diagnosis: orchiopexy as soon as possible
r: An 'olive' mass with empty scrotum in a child is the testis; an olive in the epigastrium of a vomiting infant is pyloric stenosis.
n: Undescended testis in a 4 year old (beyond the ideal 6-18 month window): orchiopexy now.

q: A patient with BPH presents to the OPD with urinary frequency, urgency, hesitancy, weak urinary stream, and a feeling of incomplete bladder emptying. He is already taking an a-blocker, What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Adjust the dose of the a-blocker
k: BPH treatment ladder. Mild symptoms: watchful waiting, lifestyle (reduce evening fluids, caffeine, alcohol); Bothersome LUTS: alpha blocker (tamsulosin), fast acting; Large prostate: add 5 alpha reductase inhibitor (finasteride), takes months, shrinks the gland
r: 'Already on an alpha blocker' with persistent symptoms = move up the ladder to TURP, not a dose tweak.

q: A 20 years old patient presents with (NO fever) , flank pain and hematuria. Urinalysis is normal. What is the next investigation?
k: Flank pain with hematuria: workup.
r: Same symptoms, two recalls: the author keys CT for the dysuria and nausea version and renal profile for the no fever and hematuria version.
n: Compiler thinks this and the previous page are different recalls: first recall (dysuria, flank pain, nausea) answer is CT; this second recall answer is Renal Profile. Other version of this recall in Part 4: SWR-4566 → C. Renal profile

q: Case of signs and symptoms of testicular torsion (testicular pain, red...). What confirms the diagnosis?
k: Acute scrotum: torsion is a surgical emergency; do not delay exploration for imaging when the picture is classic.
r: If the options include surgical exploration, pick it over US for a classic torsion: imaging must never delay detorsion.
n: Printed answer B (US); compiler says the answer should be surgical exploration, but this option is not present, so US is the best available.

q: A female patient went to ICU (I don't remember why) and NGT and urinary catheter inserted, after some days (I think 3) she developed fever 38.9, RR: 21,( other vitals normal) she was alert and communicating with the staff, chest x ray normal, what is next?
k: ICU or postoperative fever: think devices and timing.
r: In a febrile ICU patient with a urinary catheter and a normal chest film, the catheter is guilty until proven innocent.
n: Check catheters to exclude catheter related UTI.

q: Man known case of benign prostatic hyperplasia presented with difficulty of voiding,I can't remember the rest What is the appropriate next step?
k: BPH ladder: drain acute retention, start alpha blocker for symptoms, TURP when medical therapy fails.
r: The deciding words are 'already on alpha blocker without improvement' (TURP) versus 'unable to pass urine, distended bladder' (catheter).
n: Compiler (Arabic): the full recall stated he was already on an alpha blocker without improvement, so the answer there was C; but this seems to be a different recall. Rules: chronic symptoms not responding to medical therapy -> TURP; acute urinary retention ->

q: A child suffers from scrotal trauma while he was trying to intercept a pass in a football game, on examination there was (I think right) scrotal swelling not reducible, and the testes can’t be felt (I don’t remember if there was pain or erythema) what is the next step?
k: Irreducible groin or scrotal swelling = hernia until proven otherwise; it is a surgical problem, not an observation one.
r: If the stem gave a painful, tender swelling with a palpable testis after trauma, think hematocele or testicular rupture and get a scrotal ultrasound; a non-reducible swelling hiding the testis points to hernia.
n: Printed answer A. Surgical fixation of hernia. No further commentary. Recaller: Recaller unsure of side and whether there was pain or erythema.

q: A 75-year-old man presents to the emergency department with a 2-day history of inability to pass urine. He reports a history of difficulty starting urination, weak urinary stream, increased urinary frequency, and dysuria. Laboratory investigations show an elevated PSA level. What is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Elderly man with LUTS: let the PSA and associated features separate BPH from cancer.
r: Both BPH and cancer cause the same urinary symptoms; a markedly high PSA (or back pain) is what tips it to cancer.
n: Printed answer prostate cancer; compiler adds that the PSA was in the 70s.

q: A patient known case of BPH presents with inability to void, urgency and frequency for 2 weeks, he is on alpha blocker, what is the next step?
o: increase the dose of alpha blocker
k: BPH ladder: alpha blocker, catheter for retention, then TURP when medical therapy fails.
r: Retention despite an alpha blocker means medical therapy has failed: decompress the bladder first, then surgery (TURP) becomes the definitive step.
n: No answer given; compiler questions the duration in the recall (2 weeks? or 2 days? or 2 years?).

q: 41 old male presents with lower abdominal distended after hernia repair under spinal anesthesia, he unable to void? What is management
k: Postoperative inability to void with a palpable bladder = urinary retention; treat by catheter decompression.
r: Low urine output with a full bladder is an outflow problem (catheter); low output with an empty bladder is a volume problem (fluids).
n: Corrected version of the mix-up AAA recall on the previous page: post-operative urinary retention after spinal anesthesia, manage with urinary catheterization.

q: A 25-year-old woman presents with loin pain and is diagnosed with a 4-mm renal/ureteric stone. She is afebrile and has no other concerning symptoms or complications. What is the most appropriate management?
k: Ureteric stone management depends on size and on red flags.
r: Add fever to the same stone and the answer flips from conservative care to urgent drainage (stent or nephrostomy).
n: Printed answer A: small uncomplicated stone (<5 mm) passes spontaneously, so conservative management. Older inset version (Last Days Of Feb, Part 3) also answered A.

q: Female Pt (can't remember her age) came with a complain Lt loin pain by PE, she has Lt loin pain, the rest of examination is normal (there was no anu lab or imaging in the Q), then said she has 4mm Lt ureteric stone What is the most appropriate management? By this order
o: Something about surgical Insertion of J Y stent (not sure but something like that)
k: Small uncomplicated ureteric stone = conservative with medication; intervene only for size, failure to pass, or red flags.
r: Stone size alone never justifies a stent; a stent answers obstruction plus infection or kidney injury.
n: Inset older version (Last Days Of Feb, Part 3) with boxed answer A: 4 mm stone, conservative with medication.

q: A 30-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after a motor vehicle accident. Examination shows an obvious pelvic fracture and blood at the urethral meatus. What is the most appropriate next step?
k: Pelvic fracture + blood at meatus = image the urethra before any urethral catheter.
r: If the stem already says the RUG shows a urethral injury, the answer flips to suprapubic catheter.

q: A 34-year-old male presents to the emergency department after a high-speed motor vehicle accident. He is found to have a pelvic fracture described as an "open-book" injury. On examination, there is blood at the urethral meatus and a high-riding prostate on digital rectal exam. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
k: Blood at meatus, high-riding prostate, perineal hematoma or inability to void = suspect urethral injury: RUG before Foley.
r: In any pelvic trauma with blood at the meatus, the wrong answer is the Foley: image the urethra first.
n: Suspected urethral injury: do retrograde urethrogram before any Foley insertion.

q: A 60-year-old man is suffering from urinary hesitancy (difficulty initiating urination). He has had diabetes for ten years, his Body Mass Index (BMI) is 41 and ultrasound showed Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia (BPH). What is the risk factor that led to this complaint?
k: Rule: BPH risk factor = age (plus intact testes/androgens).
r: Asked for THE risk factor of BPH: pick age, even when diabetes or obesity is in the stem.
n: Age is the main risk factor for BPH.

q: A kid brought to the ER with tender, right hemiscrotum, high-riding testis, and reducible inguinal hernia. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
o: Refer to surgery for surgical exploration.
Try manual detorsion in the ER, and if succeed, follow up in outpatient.
k: Acute scrotum with high-riding tender testis = torsion = explore now.
r: A reducible hernia is a red herring; it cannot cause a tender high-riding testis.

q: Patient underwent major abdominal surgery after 72hr 87% o2 38 fever What most likely diagnosis

k: Pressure ulcer staging drives management: Stage 1: intact skin, non-blanchable erythema → offload: reposition (about every 2 h), pressure-redistributing mattress/cushion, skin care, nutrition; Stage 2: partial-thickness loss (shallow ulcer, blister) → moist dressing + offloading; Stage 3-4: full thi
r: Intact skin with redness = stage 1 = offload; the moment the skin breaks or tissue dies, the answer moves to dressings or debridement.
n: Stage 1 pressure ulcer (non-blanching erythema) is managed by offloading/repositioning.

q: New q? Eledrly pt with acute aschemic limb symptoms Absent distal pulses Afib on ecg What is the most apr initial management or assessment?
k: ALI ladder: heparin first → imaging (duplex / CT angiography) if the limb is not immediately threatened → revascularize.
r: "Initial" = heparin; "most appropriate management" in AF = embolectomy; "confirmatory investigation" = CT angiography.
n: Initial management of acute limb ischemia (embolic, AF) is heparin. Recaller: Recaller wrote 'New q?'

q: Soup spel on child he is in pain and more in touch , skin erythema,red, moist with bluster?

r: Moist = superficial partial; dry with blisters and reduced pain = deep partial.
n: Blisters and pain can exist in both superficial and deep partial thickness (favor superficial); moist favors superficial partial because deep partial is dry. Options were unlettered, lettered by position.

k: Goodsall rule: draw a transverse line across the anus (3 to 9 o'clock).
r: If the stem gives an opening behind the 3 to 9 o'clock line, the answer is posterior midline whatever its side.

q: Case of hemorrids That was reduced spontaneously Which grade is it?
k: Internal hemorrhoid grading (by prolapse): Grade 1: no prolapse; Grade 2: prolapse, reduces spontaneously; Grade 3: prolapse, needs manual reduction
r: The word to watch is who reduces it: by itself = 2, by the patient's finger = 3, not at all = 4.

q: Patient with a history of constipation presents with bright red rectal bleeding. The haemorrhoids prolapse on straining but reduce spontaneously. What is the grade?
k: Internal hemorrhoid grades and treatment: I: no prolapse; conservative; II: prolapse, reduces spontaneously; conservative, or band ligation if persistent; III: prolapse, needs manual reduction; band ligation, sclerotherapy, infrared coagulation
r: Spontaneous reduction = II; push back with a finger = III.
n: Printed answer B. Grade II (prolapse reducing spontaneously).

q: 20 y/o Rectal bleeding, weight loss Abdominal Tenderness 3 symptoms only Same In mother and siblings Positive Giuac Test
k: Young patient + GI bleeding + affected parent AND siblings = think autosomal dominant polyposis.
r: The family pattern (mother plus siblings) is the decisive clue; IBD does not follow a dominant pedigree.
n: 19 October update The same question reappears in 19 October as OCT-2596 → no answer marked.

q: 20 y/o Rectal bleeding, Weight loss Abdominal Tenderness 3 symptoms only Same In mother and siblings Positive Guaiac Test most likely diagnosis ?

r: 'Same in mother and siblings' is the inheritance clue that tips toward FAP over IBD.
n: No answer printed on the slide; only two options recalled. Same question in this file: OCT-2066 → B. FAP.

q: Question about old pt hospitalized developed coffee ground emesis and blood from NGT how to confirm
k: Upper GI bleed pathway: Resuscitate first (IV access, crystalloid, transfuse if Hb <7); IV PPI; Upper endoscopy within 24 hours: diagnostic and therapeutic
r: Hematemesis or coffee ground NG aspirate: endoscopy is both the diagnostic and therapeutic test; barium is never used in active bleeding.

q: Carcinoid tumor found after appendectomy: 2 cm, at the base of the appendix. Management? (p. 74)
k: Appendiceal carcinoid (neuroendocrine tumor) after appendectomy: Under 2 cm + at the tip + no mesoappendix or node invasion: appendectomy alone, observe; Over 2 cm OR at the base OR mesoappendix / lymph node invasion: right hemicolectomy; Any one high-risk feature is enough to need hemicolectomy
r: Tip and under 2 cm = appendectomy alone; base involvement or over 2 cm = right hemicolectomy.
n: Printed answer A (right hemicolectomy); the embedded 10 September recall gives the same answer. Other versions of this recall in this deck: OCT-1249 → A. Right hemicolectomy 19 October update

q: (Translated from Arabic) In the question on the 21st, he gave the definition of rovesing sign and asked what is the sign; the options were Psoas sign, Rovesing sign, Obturator sign

q: Child fall after 10 days there's discoloration in the abdomen What is the most appropriate next step
