n: Answer printed as 'not verified'. Option D is Arabic for 'I don't remember'. See the 18-day version on the same page (abdominal CT).

q: In GS block 20-30s married women is having gave history of RIF pain and nausea and she has tenderness ( NO fever , No leukocytosis , No rebound) What is the most appropriate next step ?
k: RIF pain in a woman of reproductive age: ultrasound first.
r: Obesity or a long history pushes the choice from ultrasound to CT.
n: Printed answer A. Recaller noted options C and D were not pregnancy test. Recaller: C&D was not pregnancy test

q: A surgeon is performing a back lipoma excision under local anesthesia using lidocaine. During the procedure, he suspects that an excessive dose of lidocaine may have been administered. What is the earliest sign of lidocaine toxicity?
k: LAST progresses CNS first, then cardiovascular.
r: If tinnitus is not among the options, the author picks drowsiness as the next earliest sign.
n: Early local anesthetic toxicity presents with CNS prodrome (tinnitus, perioral numbness) before seizures and cardiovascular collapse. Recaller: Same exact question.

q: Long but clear case of Necrotizing fasciitis (Pain out of proportion, Bulle, Crepitus…). I think there was discharge? And weak pulse or no pulse? What to do next?
k: Necrotizing fasciitis: clinical diagnosis, operate now.
r: "Local" debridement or "imaging first" is the trap; necrotizing fasciitis needs aggressive, repeated surgery.
n: Necrotizing fasciitis needs aggressive surgical debridement (repeated), not local debridement; 'LOCAL' in option A is highlighted as the trap. Recaller: Recaller unsure about discharge and pulse; option D not clearly remembered.

q: 50 years old male came c/o painless hematuria (literally written) started 3 day ago. What most appropriate INITIAL investigation?
o: KUB (literally written without mentioning xray nor CT)
k: Hematuria: confirm with urinalysis first, then investigate the cause.
r: "Initial" picks urinalysis; if the question asks for the most appropriate or definitive investigation of painless hematuria in an older man, pick cystoscopy plus CT urography.

q: Adult after MVC with IIIa fracture of the femur with open contaminated wound. X-ray shows comminuted mid-femur fracture with mild displacement. What is the most appropriate management?
o: Debridement, external fixation with delayed wound closure
k: Open fracture pathway: IV antibiotics and tetanus, then debridement and irrigation, then fixation, then delayed closure or coverage.
r: Any option with "primary closure" or no debridement is wrong for a contaminated open fracture.
n: Compiler: A and B make no sense for a contaminated open IIIa fracture, so it is C by exclusion, until option D is known. Other versions of this recall in this deck: SWR-0243 → C. Debridement , Extramedullary fixation with delayed wound

q: Large open fracture, most appropriate management
o: Debridement external fixation , delay wound closure
k: Large or contaminated open wound: debride, external fixator, leave open.
r: "Large" or "contaminated" open fracture: delayed closure and external fixation, never primary closure.
n: Short sibling recall of the open femur fracture question; compiler's answer for this topic is debridement, external fixation with delayed wound closure (mapped here to B by meaning).

q: Most appropriate initial treatment for liver amoebic abscess?
k: Amoebic liver abscess = medical disease; pyogenic liver abscess = drainage disease.
r: Do not be pulled to drainage by the word "abscess" or by a big size: amoebic still starts with metronidazole; only a pyogenic (toxic, biliary source) abscess goes straight to percutaneous drainage.
n: Initial treatment of amoebic liver abscess is metronidazole; drainage is not first line. Other versions of this recall in this deck: SWR-0389 → A. Metronidazole

q: 25-year-old male came recently from India, presented to ER with RUQ pain, Night sweats, malaise, fever. US showed: right lobe Liver collection, Hypoechoic CT Finding: Thick walled abscess without septations. Which of the following is the diagnosis?
k: Liver abscess / cyst: identify it from the patient, not the picture.
r: Travel from India or Mexico in a young man with a single liver abscess = amoebic; switch to pyogenic only if biliary disease, diabetes or a toxic, jaundiced picture is described.
n: Young man from an endemic area (India) with RUQ pain, fever and a liver collection: amoebic liver abscess.

q: Male patient came from India RUQ pain.. on and off fever for 3 weeks. raised LFT, high WBC (Neurtrophol 70% Lymphocytes 20%) . image showed homogenous hypoechoic mass in the liver.
k: Amoebic vs pyogenic: imaging is similar, so use the clinical table.
r: High bilirubin or a biliary history = pyogenic; travel to a developing country = amoebic. The ultrasound appearance will not break the tie.
n: High bilirubin points to pyogenic; travel to a developing country points to amebic. There is NO radiologic feature that differentiates the two. Attached table: pyogenic favours older adults, left shift, elevated bilirubin, gallstones/DM history; amebic favours

q: Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment for a liver amoebic abscess?
k: Amoebic liver abscess = medical disease; pyogenic liver abscess = drainage disease.
r: Do not be pulled to drainage by the word "abscess" or by a big size: amoebic still starts with metronidazole; only a pyogenic (toxic, biliary source) abscess goes straight to percutaneous drainage.
n: Answer A per Medgard: metronidazole is initial treatment of amoebic liver abscess. Other versions of this recall in this deck: SWR-0381 → A. Metronidazole

q: A 36-year-old male presents to the emergency room with right abdominal pain. On examination, he is febrile, toxic, and has tenderness in the right upper quadrant and lower intercostal margins. He reports anorexia and weight loss. Laboratory findings: Elevated temperature (~37.9C) High WBC count Elevated bilirubin Ultrasound: cystic lesion with thick wall in the liver What is the most appropriate management?
k: Pyogenic liver abscess = drain + antibiotics.
r: Toxic + high bilirubin + no travel = pyogenic = percutaneous drainage; the same lesion in a young traveller from India = amoebic = metronidazole.
n: Toxic febrile patient with high WBC, elevated bilirubin and a thick-walled liver lesion (pyogenic picture): percutaneous drainage is the most appropriate management.

q: Came with diabetic foot, foul smelling of the wound, how to manage?
k: Diabetic foot ulcer management: Assess: pulses/ABI (ischemia), probe to bone (osteomyelitis), X-ray/MRI; Infected or necrotic (foul smell, pus, slough): surgical debridement + culture-guided antibiotics; Ischemic: revascularization before major debridement
r: Foul smell means dead tissue; debridement, not dressing, is the treatment.
n: Answer C: surgical debridement for a foul smelling (infected) diabetic foot wound.

q: 67 years old male complaining of painless hematuria, He is medically free and no dysuria , frequency , discharge , no fever Vitally stable Which is the diagnostic test?
k: Painless gross haematuria in an older adult = urothelial cancer work-up.
r: Painful haematuria points to stone or infection; painless haematuria in an older smoker points to bladder cancer and cystoscopy.
n: Handwritten pen mark A (cystoscopy). Compiler's Arabic header: this recall dates from about 2021, repeats over the years, and is incomplete.

q: 59 YO male post colostomy came after 10 days, during examination the wound is 10 cm, clean with healthy granulation tissue, without oozing pus or any discharge What is the most appropriate next step in management?
k: Open wound management depends on wound bed.
r: Healthy granulation and no discharge mean no antibiotics and no debridement; size is what pushes you to VAC.
n: Answer from the compiler's team (Al-Harshan-Avengers): B. vacuum-assisted wound dressing. Alhomrani himself declines to weigh in ('This Question Is None Of My Business').

q: A patient presents with painless hematuria. What is the most appropriate investigation to evaluate the cause?
k: Painless hematuria in an adult: think malignancy; look at the bladder and the upper tracts.
r: Read the verb: "initial" investigation = urinalysis; "evaluate the cause" / most appropriate = cystoscopy.
n: Options A and B both in red. Answer A (cystoscopy) to evaluate the cause; the initial investigation is B (urinalysis). Other version of this recall in Part 2: SWR-1509 → B. Urinalysis Other version of this recall in Part 2: SWR-1827 → B. Urinalysis

q: Patient developed a circumferential right forearm burn. Saturation in right digit is 86%, absent pulse. What is the appropriate action?
k: Circumferential burns: escharotomy vs fasciotomy.
r: Pulse already lost = act now (escharotomy); measuring pressure is for doubtful cases.
n: Circumferential burn with distal ischemia (low saturation, absent pulse) needs immediate escharotomy; no need to measure compartment pressure.

q: A 37-year-old patient suffered a circumferential right forearm burn with weak distal pulsation and oxygen saturation of 86% in the right arm. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: IV fluids, burn dressing and limb elevation
k: Burned limb monitoring ladder.
r: "Circumferential" plus any sign of distal compromise = escharotomy; vasodilators and observation are the traps.
n: Fuller version of the circumferential forearm burn recall: compromised distal perfusion means immediate escharotomy.

q: Perforated diverticulitis , 6.5 cm abscess
k: Diverticulitis: manage by complication (Hinchey).
r: Contained abscess = drain percutaneously; generalized peritonitis from free perforation = laparotomy.
n: Diverticular abscess larger than 3 to 4 cm needs antibiotics plus percutaneous (PC) drainage.

q: A patient presents with a perianal abscess for the first time. What is the most appropriate management?
k: Abscess anywhere = drain it; antibiotics are adjuncts.
r: Recurrent abscess or chronic discharge after drainage changes the answer to fistula workup (MRI or examination under anaesthesia), not repeated antibiotics.
n: Printed answer A. No further commentary. Other versions of this recall in this deck: SWR-0673 → C. Conservative management; SWR-0678 → C. Urgent surgical management; SWR-0683 → B. Low-molecular-weight heparin; SWR-0694 → A. CBT and lifestyle measures

q: 60 yr old male underwent appendectomy, he presented 6 days post open appendectomy with red, swollen and tender wound site. What's the most appropriate Management? (Or NEXT????) ?
k: Postoperative wound problems.
r: Antibiotics are tempting, but pus or an infected wound is a source-control problem: open it.
n: Surgical site infection: next and most appropriate step is wound exploration (opening the wound). Options A and D shown in red; lead-in may have been 'most appropriate' or 'next'.

q: Mild swelling and redness with increased pain and tenderness at the site of surgical wound
k: Wound findings and the matching step.
r: Increasing pain and tenderness separate infection from a harmless seroma.
n: Compiler insists this is not a defective recall: it is literally the full recall with no additional information. SMLE later modified this recall and made it better (see following pages).

q: Pt with perineal swelling with crepitus and foul smelling discharge, from scrotum to perineal area , what's diagnosis
k: Fournier gangrene. Clues: severe pain out of proportion, swelling, crepitus, foul discharge, dusky or necrotic skin, systemic toxicity; Risk factors: diabetes, immunosuppression, alcohol, perineal or urological source; Organisms: polymicrobial (aerobes + anaerobes)
r: Crepitus is the word that converts an abscess into necrotizing fasciitis: debride, do not just drain.
n: Perineal/scrotal swelling with crepitus and foul discharge: Fournier gangrene.

q: A guy with severe perineal pain and swelling, discoloration that is expanding with crepitus, what is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Perineal pain + swelling + spreading discoloration + crepitus = Fournier's gangrene (perineal necrotizing fasciitis).
r: Crepitus in a soft tissue infection is never simple cellulitis: think necrotizing infection and go to the operating room.
n: Another recall version of Fournier's gangrene diagnosis.

q: Frourniers Gangrene DM crepitus and anal cellulitis initial investigation
k: Fournier's gangrene is a clinical diagnosis; imaging must never delay surgery.
r: Read the options first: when surgical debridement is listed it beats every investigation.
n: CT is the initial investigation for Fournier's gangrene when debridement is not among options. Compiler wondered whether it was CT abdomen or pelvis; a later recall said CT PELVIS. Recaller: *examiner* no debridment in options

q: 56-year-old patient presents with a wound sustained while gardening. The nurse confirms that the patient received a tetanus vaccine 12 years ago. What is the best next step?
k: Fully vaccinated (3 or more doses): Clean minor wound: booster if more than 10 years since last dose; Tetanus-prone wound (soil, rust, puncture, burn, crush): booster if more than 5 years; No TIG when fully vaccinated
r: Garden soil makes the wound tetanus-prone, so use the 5-year rule, not the 10-year rule.
n: For fully vaccinated individuals: clean wound -> no vaccine unless last dose >10 years ago; tetanus-prone wound -> no vaccine unless last dose >5 years ago. Garden = tetanus-prone wound.

q: A child presented to the Emergency Department with a 3rd degree scald burn involving the genitalia. The total body surface area (TBSA) affected is 1%. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
k: Burn unit referral does not depend on size alone.
r: Small TBSA is a trap: location and depth (genitalia, full thickness) earn the burn unit.
n: Burns involving the genitalia (and full-thickness burns) meet burn unit referral criteria regardless of the small TBSA.

q: A Case Of Diverticulitis With Abscess 13x17 cm, Management:
o: IV Abx WITH PC Drain (Both In Same Option)
k: Diverticulitis: manage by complication (Hinchey).
r: Absence of fever does not downgrade a big abscess; size decides the drain.
n: Large diverticular abscess: IV antibiotics with percutaneous drainage. Recaller: Recaller: 100% sure the patient did not have fever or any SIRS criteria in the stem; IV antibiotics and PC drain were in the same option.

q: Case of left leg redness and tenderness after minor trauma, fever spiking. He finish full Course of antibiotic but still there is pain and tenderness What is the cause
k: Infection not responding to antibiotics: look for a collection.
r: Spiking fever after a full antibiotic course = undrained pus; the answer is a collection, not a stronger antibiotic.

q: Child with 3rd degree burn on his genitalia 1% of body mass what to do?
k: Burn unit referral is decided by TYPE and SITE, not only by size.
r: A small % TBSA tempts outpatient care; the words "3rd degree" or "genitalia" each mandate referral on their own.
n: Genital burn of any degree OR 3rd degree burn of any location and surface area are BOTH independent indications for burn unit referral.

q: A 25 year old woman underwent laparoscopic cholecystectomy. In the next morning she started to have Productive cough. Respiratory rate: 23 O2 sat: 94% Temperature: 37.9 BMI: 41 What is the most appropriate management?
k: Postoperative fever by day (the 5 W's): Day 1 to 2: wind, atelectasis; treat with chest physiotherapy and incentive spirometry.; Day 2 to 3: pneumonia, UTI, line or thrombophlebitis.; Day 4 to 5: wound infection, DVT.
r: Fever on day 1 after surgery is atelectasis; treat the lung, not with antibiotics.
n: Postoperative day 1 productive cough with low grade fever (atelectasis) in an obese patient: chest physiotherapy. Compiler points from the terse recall to this fuller version ('See Below'). Recaller: Terse recall: 'Patient post cholecystectomy (1 day i think)

q: A patient presents with a small pinna lesion requiring excision. What is the most appropriate local anesthetic approach?
o: Local infiltration with an alternative agent containing adrenaline
k: Local anaesthetic choice: Plain lidocaine: small, short procedures; classic choice for end-artery sites.; Lidocaine with adrenaline: vascular areas (scalp, face) for less bleeding and longer action; maximum dose is higher than plain lidocaine.; Bupivacaine: long-acting, but more cardiotoxic.
r: For exam purposes: end-artery site plus adrenaline option = choose the plain agent.
n: Printed 'See Below': defers to the fuller recall on the same page, answered A. Local infiltration with 1% lidocaine (Athar). Pinna is an end-artery area, so avoid adrenaline.

q: A patient diagnosed with acute pancreatitis 2 weeks ago now presents with mild abdominal pain and tenderness; cyst measures 4 cm. Most appropriate management?
k: Post-pancreatitis collections.
r: Fever and leukocytosis make percutaneous drainage right at any stage; a mature, large, symptomatic cyst makes internal drainage right.
n: Printed answer C, external drainage. Another recall said 'persistent mild abdominal pain'; compiler unsure whether these are 1 or 2 recalls and treats them the same.

q: Painless gross hematura, 30 pack year. Stable. Next step?
o: Observation and repeat urinalysis in 2 weeks
k: Gross hematuria in an adult with risk factors = cystoscopy plus CT urography.
r: Painless plus smoker = cancer workup; painful plus colic = non contrast CT for stones.
n: Compiler comment: 'NEXT Step Is CT Urography, Not ...' (line cut off at page bottom). 'NONE CONTRAST' in option C and 'Next' in the lead-in are in red. CT urography is not among the options; printed answer A is not changed.

q: 14-year-old presents with a painless midline neck swelling that moves up and down with swallowing. What is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Neck masses by position. Midline, moves with swallowing and tongue protrusion: thyroglossal cyst; Midline, moves with swallowing only: thyroid nodule or goiter; Midline, fixed to skin: dermoid
r: Moves with tongue protrusion separates thyroglossal cyst from a thyroid nodule.
n: Other version of this recall in Part 1: SWR-0679 → B. Thyroglossal cyst

q: A 14-year-old presents with a painless midline neck swelling that moves up and down with swallowing. What is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Neck masses by position. Midline, moves with swallowing and tongue protrusion: thyroglossal cyst; Midline, moves with swallowing only: thyroid nodule or goiter; Midline, fixed to skin: dermoid
r: Moves with tongue protrusion separates thyroglossal cyst from a thyroid nodule.

q: A woman presents with clear nipple discharge. Mammography showed bilateral cystic lesions categorized as BI-RADS 3. What is the most appropriate management?
k: BI-RADS decides the next step.

q: A 14-year-old patient presented with a painless neck swelling. Examination confirmed a midline neck swelling below the hyoid bone that moves up and down with swallowing. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Neck lumps by position: Midline, moves with swallowing and tongue protrusion: thyroglossal cyst; Midline, moves with swallowing only: thyroid nodule/goiter; Midline (often submental), no movement with swallowing or tongue: dermoid
r: Movement with tongue protrusion separates a thyroglossal cyst from a thyroid nodule.
n: Midline neck swelling that moves with swallowing is a thyroglossal cyst. Other version of this recall in Part 1: SWR-0679 → B. Thyroglossal cyst

q: Presents with a painless midline neck swelling that moves up and down with swallowing. (They mentioned that on biopsy there was mucoid fluid) What is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Neck lumps by position: Midline, moves with swallowing and tongue protrusion: thyroglossal cyst; Midline submental, does not move: dermoid cyst; Anterior to sternocleidomastoid, lateral: branchial cyst
r: Moving with swallowing alone fits any thyroid related mass; moving with tongue protrusion is specific to a thyroglossal cyst.
n: Answer A Thyroglossal duct cyst (midline neck swelling moving with swallowing, mucoid fluid on aspiration). Other version of this recall in Part 1: SWR-0679 → B. Thyroglossal cyst

q: A man presents with a right-sided neck swelling that moves with swallowing. He has no red flag features for malignancy. Ultrasound of the thyroid shows a mixed solid and cystic nodule measuring 2 x 3 cm, with the solid component measuring1.8 cm. What is the most appropriate next step in investigation?
o: Fine needle aspiration of the solid component
Fine needle aspiration of the cystic or fluid component.
k: Thyroid nodule workup: TSH plus ultrasound, then FNA criteria.
r: If TSH is low, the next step is a thyroid scan, not FNA; here no hyperthyroid clue is given, so FNA of the solid part.
n: In another recall D was FNA from both; we aspirate only the solid component. Other versions of this recall in this deck: SWR-1706 → B. Fine needle aspiration of the solid component

q: patient post surgery presenting with a fever of 38 and extreme pain at the wound site Won't examination showed erythema , swelling, tenderness, and oozing of fluid from the corner of the wound what is the most appropriate management? Answers where
o: take a culture from the wound
k: Postoperative wound problems and their first move: Cellulitis only (no collection): antibiotics; Wound abscess or infected collection: open the wound, drain, irrigate, dress; Seroma (no pain, no fever): explore and irrigate, leave open, dressing
r: Antibiotics or a culture alone never treat pus; open the wound.
n: Infected postoperative wound with collection: open and explore the wound.

q: 10 years old boy pulled by the fire man from burnt building he was alert oriented Gcs 15/15 presented with hoarseness and stridor and black sputum (carbonaceous sputum) And facial burn his oxygen saturation was 88% on room air and 97 in 2 L O2 what's the diagnosis?
o: sorry I forgot but it was something im sure irrelevant sorry for the half sleeve
k: Inhalation injury: clues and airway action.

n: Hoarseness, stridor, carbonaceous sputum and facial burns after a building fire indicate inhalation injury. Recaller: Recaller said 'carbonaceous sputum' was literally written; forgot whether O2 was nasal or face mask; option D forgotten.

q: Patient presented with difficulty in urinating, he has history of gonorrhea infection few months or years ago, tried foley catheter but failed, what is the most appropriate management?
k: Urethral stricture: think it when there is prior urethritis (gonorrhea), instrumentation/catheterisation or pelvic trauma.
r: Past gonorrhea + failed catheter = stricture, not BPH, so endoscopic dilatation beats alpha blockers.
n: Handwritten B; no further compiler commentary.

q: Male burned his hand while cooking. Total surface area of burn is 4%. Burn with erythema, moist, swelling, blisters. Type of burn:
k: Burn depth by look, feel and pain.
r: Burns of the hands, face, feet, genitalia, perineum or major joints merit burn centre referral even when the TBSA is small.
n: Moist, erythematous, blistering burn = superficial partial thickness (second degree).

q: A 55-year-old woman complained of difficulty in breathing 6-hour post total thyroidectomy. Examination confirmed the presence of large neck swelling. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: Open the wound sutures in the ward
k: Post-thyroidectomy complications by timing.
r: Swelling plus breathlessness after thyroid surgery = open the wound now, in the ward.
n: Neck hematoma post thyroidectomy: evacuate by opening the wound at the bedside (source Medgard). Recaller: Recaller: option D was 're-open bedside'; doesn't remember if options A to C were the same.

q: after appendectomy the wound has mild discharge what type of dressing?
k: Choose the dressing by exudate level.
r: Pus with pain, redness or fever is a wound abscess: open and drain it; a dressing choice question assumes clean exudate.
n: Almakrami answers A assuming the discharge is exudate. Alhomrani: hydrocolloid is used in mild exudate, alginate in moderate to severe exudate, so mild discharge points to hydrocolloid.

q: Diabetic patient, came with a pain that is out proportion, Bulle, Crepitus, pain extends further than the erythema I think there was discharge? weak pulse What to do next?
o: X ray? Or something irrelevant (not sure )
k: Necrotizing fasciitis = clinical diagnosis, go straight to theatre.
r: Cellulitis has pain matching the redness; pain beyond the erythema plus crepitus flips it to necrotizing fasciitis and surgery.
n: Necrotizing fasciitis picture: debridement should be aggressive/extensive; local debridement (option A, LOCAL underlined) is wrong. Recaller: Recaller unsure of option D (X ray? or something irrelevant). Other version of this recall in Part 3: SWR-2182 → A. De

q: Patient presented after RTA 6 hours ago with open laceration on the scalp. What is the most appropriate?
o: Leave it to heal by granulation
Debridement and leave it to heal by granulation
k: Wound closure choice depends on time, contamination and tissue loss.
r: The scalp and face are the exceptions where even a few hours old trauma wound is closed primarily, because of the rich blood supply.

q: A 7-year-old boy is brought by his mother after falling while playing in a playground. He has a 1 x 2 cm superficial laceration on his leg. q: A 62-year-old woman with known left-sided diverticulosis presents with worsening left lower quadrant abdominal pain and fever. r: Localized abscess in a stable patient = drain percutaneously; generalized peritonitis = theatre.

q: Patient with open scalp wound, presented after 6 hours
k: Choosing wound closure. Clean or fresh wound, well vascularized (scalp, face): debride, then primary closure; Tendon or nerve injury: primary repair of the injured structures; Contaminated or late wound: leave open, delayed primary or secondary closure

n: Printed answer A; Alhomrani questions who put this answer (Naif or Almakrami) and flags it as a question, without endorsing another option.

q: A 45-year-old man has a 5-year history of a recurrent right inguinal hernia that is usually painful but easily reducible manually. q: 75-year-old patient presents with an irreducible inguinal hernia. What's the management?

q: A 24-year-old man complains of groin and scrotal swelling when coughing and when standing for a long time. Examination shows an inguinoscrotal swelling that can be reduced manually. What is the most likely type?

r: Irreducible + tender + warm/red skin + fever = strangulation: operate, never force it back.

q: 5-- A middle-aged man with chronic liver disease and ascites presents to the emergency department with a large umbilical swelling. What is the most appropriate management?

r: The word "elective" plus "reducible" decides it: control ascites first. If the skin ulcerates or leaks, it is no longer elective.

q: 80 years old women presented to the emergency department with confusion. Her daughter says she is having fever, diarrhea, and vomiting and she has not been eating or drinking for 3 days. q: 46 years old women came with dysphagia to solid and liquid for 6 months, ill defined chest uncomfortable sensation especially at night, no anemia, no weight loss and labs are normal Dx ?

q: A 30-year-old woman presents with chronic intermittent diarrhea and abdominal pain for several months. There is no history of blood in her stool. q: A 30-year-old woman has chronic intermittent diarrhea and abdominal pain for months, no blood in stool. Hb 95 g/L, MCV 108 fL, vitamin B12 low, folate low. Most likely diagnosis?

n: Printed answer B. Calcitriol (active vitamin D bypasses impaired renal activation).

q: A 65-year-old woman with long-standing chronic renal failure presents with aches and pains for 1 month. Physical examination is unremarkable apart from general pallor (see lab results): Hight PTH Low Calcium Low Vitamin D Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

q: Patient presents after 30 minutes of slurred speech that resolved, no trauma or drug use or fever. Carotid shows stenosis 48% Best management besides controlling risk factors?

q: patient had high grade fever and malaise ( other symptoms not recalling). the features are cyclic and has history of travel to africa what is the diagnostic test?

q: A 45 man presented to ED complaining of low grade fever and wight loss for 6 months Chest examination reduced chest movement stony dullness in percution in the right lung The Next management

q: diabetic patient came presenting with signs of cellulitis with erythema, not well demarked and fever, and they're asking about the management.

r: Clindamycin wins only because no penicillin or cephalosporin is offered; if cefazolin, cephalexin or flucloxacillin appears, pick it instead.

r: Prior pneumococcal pneumonia is not protection: there are many serotypes, so vaccinate after recovery.
n: All adults aged 65 and above should receive pneumococcal vaccine; prior infection does not give immunity because pneumococcus has over 100 strains (PPSV23 covers 23).

q: 65 years old male k/c of DM came with pneumonia and was admitted and treated with abx . And now got better and will be discharged. What would you give as a preventive of this presentation?

r: Discharge after pneumonia in a 65-year-old or diabetic = vaccinate (pneumococcal plus influenza).
n: Embedded inset: older version with different options. Answer C; all adults 65 and above should receive pneumococcal vaccine; prior infection gives immunity to only one strain (over 100 strains; PPSV23 has 23).

q: 32-year-old man with HIV, doing well; Mantoux (PPD) at 48 h is 6 mm; CXR unremarkable. Best preventive measure? (p. 140)

q: A 55-year-old man with rheumatoid arthritis for 6 years (on methotrexate 15 weekly and prednisone 5 daily) presented with a 2-day history of left knee pain and swelling. r: One hot joint out of proportion to the rest of the RA, with fever = infection, not a flare; never inject steroid into it.
n: Septic arthritis in an immunosuppressed RA patient: start IV antibiotics while culture is pending.

n: Malaria is diagnosed via blood film: thick smear for initial diagnosis, thin smear for quantification/species.

q: A patient with atrial fibrillation and hypertension is taking warfarin for stroke prevention. During routine follow-up, The patient has no active bleeding, all laboratory results are normal except for an INR of 4.2 . What is the most appropriate management?
o: Withhold warfarin and administer IV vitamin K.
withhold warfarin and resume at a lower dose when the INR therapeutic range.
Withhold warfarin and administer fresh frozen plasma (FFP).
k: Supratherapeutic INR on warfarin: INR above range but below 4, no bleeding: reduce or omit a dose; INR 4 to 10, no bleeding: hold warfarin, consider oral vitamin K 1 to 2.5 mg, restart at lower dose; INR above 10, no bleeding: hold, oral vitamin K 2.5 to 5 mg
r: The deciding question is bleeding, not the INR number: no bleeding = hold and adjust, never FFP.
n: Printed answer B: supratherapeutic INR without bleeding is managed by holding warfarin and resuming at a lower dose; no vitamin K or FFP.

q: A patient in the ICU has been intubated and mechanically ventilated for 5 days. He develops a fever and is suspected of having ventilator-associated pneumonia , something like this. Which of the following is an appropriate measure to prevent the complication ? ( not same order of answers )

q: A 45-year-old male, smoker for around 15 years, approximately 20 pack-years, came to the clinic concerned because his father had lung cancer at around the age of 60. What is the most appropriate management?

Take sputum and send it for cytology
k: LDCT lung screening = age 50 to 80 + ≥20 pack-years + current smoker or quit within 15 years.
r: The trap is the father's lung cancer: unlike colon or breast cancer, family history does not bring lung screening forward; age 50 is the gate.
n: Lung cancer screening (LDCT) starts at age 50 with 20 pack-years; at 45 no screening is needed now, family history does not change this.

q: COPD patient presented with exacerbation he was fully conscious, he was started on high flow oxygen then he started to deteriorate with decreased level of consciousness. PH:7.18 PaO2:15 kpa PaCO2 was high what is the initial thing you would do?

q: An HIV-positive patient has a positive skin test measuring 6 mm. Chest X-ray is normal. What is the most appropriate treatment?

r: 6 mm is negative in a healthy person but positive in HIV; read the risk group before the number.

q: A 45-year-old man is diagnosed to have pulmonary tuberculosis for which he was started on 4 anti-tuberculous drugs 2 months ago. During routine follow up, his blood work shows hyperuricemia (see lab result). Test Result Normal Values Uric acid 600 200-410 mol/L (Male) 140-360 mol/L (Female) What anti-TB drug is responsible for this finding?
k: One drug, one signature side effect: Pyrazinamide: hyperuricemia / gout; Isoniazid: neuropathy (give pyridoxine); Rifampicin: orange-red fluids
r: If both ethambutol and pyrazinamide are offered for high urate, pick pyrazinamide.
n: Embedded lookalike recall. High uric acid is pyrazinamide: it is converted into pyrazinoic acid, and organic acids compete with uric acid excretion. Neuropathy is isoniazid; orange/red body fluids is rifampicin. October By Similar update

q: A 45-year-old male treated for Pulmonary Tuberculosis presents with red discoloration of his urine and tears two weeks after starting therapy. He has no other complaints, and his lab results are normal. Which of the following medications is responsible for this finding?

q: A 49-year-old woman is evaluated for a 4-month history of dry cough, which began 4 months ago when she noted a paroxysmal onset of persistent coughing spells that make it difficult to carry on a conversation. q: A 17-year-old man presented to the Emergency Department with severe asthma exacerbation that began 12 hours ago. q: 65-year-old heavy smoker with HTN and COPD on Ventolin, Anoro Ellipta and lisinopril; worsening SOB for 4 months, no change in sputum, no fever, no admission for >1 year; decreased breath sounds. q: Which of the following features is most likely to indicate a life-threatening attack?

r: Low Na with HIGH K points to Addison; low Na with NORMAL K and concentrated urine points to SIADH.
n: Printed answer D: hyponatremia with low serum osmolality, normal potassium and inappropriately concentrated urine indicates SIADH.

q: 65-year-old patient presented with a single episode of seizure. Labs: Na+ approx 112 mmol/L K+: Normal Urine osmolality: Forgotten Possible diagnoses:

r: Normal potassium is the clue that removes Addison's; mineralocorticoid excess states (Conn, Cushing) drop potassium, not sodium.

q: A young patient presents with episodic hypertension, presyncope, sweating, and palpitations. Which of the following is the most appropriate investigation?
k: Pheochromocytoma workup. Spells: headache, sweating, palpitations, paroxysmal hypertension; Screen: plasma free or 24-h urinary fractionated metanephrines; Then localize: adrenal CT/MRI (MIBG if not found)
r: Never start a beta blocker before alpha blockade in pheochromocytoma: unopposed alpha stimulation can cause a hypertensive crisis.
n: Older recall (24 September) inset; printed answer B.

q: After receiving 3L of isotonic saline still hypotensive (70/40) HR 130 blood culture and piperacillin tazobacram started but lactate is raising Lactate was 4 and then raised to 5.8
k: Septic shock bundle order: Lactate, blood cultures, broad-spectrum antibiotics within the first hour; Crystalloid 30 mL/kg for hypotension or lactate of 4 or more; Still hypotensive after fluids: norepinephrine (first-line vasopressor), target MAP 65 or more
r: Persistent hypotension after an adequate fluid bolus = septic shock: give norepinephrine, not more fluid.
n: Printed answer C. Norepinephrine: fluid-refractory septic shock needs vasopressor.

q: 65 female complain of back pain for 3 months she takes NSAIDS with no improvement Hb 6 ESR 120 Creatinine 260 Bone marrow aspiration : 20% plasma cells Whats the cause for her deteriorated renal function ?
k: Myeloma kidney: light chain (Bence Jones) cast nephropathy is the commonest cause of renal failure in myeloma.
r: NSAIDs failing for back pain in an elderly anemic patient with high ESR = myeloma until proven otherwise.

q: 60-Year-Old Male Presents With Persistent Back Pain For 3 Months, Unresponsive To NSAIDs. Laboratory Findings: Electrolytes: Normal, Creatinine: Elevated. Bone Marrow Biopsy: 20% Plasma Cells. What is The Most Likely Cause Of This Patient's Deterioration In Kidney Function?
k: Multiple myeloma = CRAB: hyperCalcemia, Renal failure, Anemia, Bone lesions (lytic, back pain).
r: Elderly + back pain + anemia/high creatinine = myeloma; the kidney is injured by light chains, not by the IgM of Waldenström.
n: October By Similar update

q: A patient started on amoxicillin for a respiratory tract infection develops a skin rash after several days of treatment. Investigations show peripheral EOSINOPHILIA and a rising serum creatinine. Urinalysis shows STERILE PYURIA and WHITE CELL CASTS, with no significant proteinuria. What is the most likely renal pathology?
k: Urine sediment points to the lesion.
r: White cell casts with no infection after an antibiotic means AIN, not pyelonephritis.
n: Drug, rash, eosinophilia, sterile pyuria and white cell casts with only modest proteinuria = acute interstitial nephritis; stop the drug. Muddy-brown granular casts = ATN, red cell casts = glomerulonephritis, heavy proteinuria = nephrotic lesion. Source tag: q

q: 8- Patient started on amoxicillin for a respiratory tract infection develops a skin rash after several days of treatment. Labs: peripheral eosinophilia and a rising serum creatinine. Urinalysis: sterile pyuria and white cell casts, no significant proteinuria. What is the most likely renal pathology?
k: Drug + rash + eosinophilia + sterile pyuria/WBC casts + rising creatinine = acute interstitial nephritis.
r: White cell casts with a STERILE urine and a new drug means AIN, not pyelonephritis.
n: Printed answer B (AIN). Other versions of this recall in this deck: OCT-7465 → B. Acute interstitial nephritis

q: An 18-year-old man is evaluated because of acute kidney injury 3 days after an upper respiratory tract infection. Examination reveals lower limb pitting edema up to the knee levels. His laboratory investigations were normal 3 days ago but are repeated today (see lab results). Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Post-infectious hematuria: the latency picks the diagnosis.
r: Same URTI story, different answers: days later = IgA nephropathy, weeks later = PSGN.
n: AKI/hematuria within 1-3 days of URI (synpharyngitic) is classic for IgA nephropathy; post-streptococcal GN has a longer latency of 1-3 weeks. AIN is usually drug induced. October By Similar update

q: 28- Mom came with elevated creat. & urea from two weeks he took ttt for pyelonephritis & still he have symptoms, what's the cause?
k: AKI after an antibiotic course = think drug-induced tubulointerstitial nephritis.
r: Do not blame persisting symptoms on the infection when creatinine rises after treatment; suspect the antibiotic.
n: Embedded inset: older version with its own options; slide answer 'A' (tubulointerstitial nephritis, drug-induced after antibiotic treatment).

q: A patient was treated for a urinary tract infection (UTI) with amoxicillin. Three weeks later, the patient reports fever and feeling generally unwell. Laboratory tests are within normal ranges except for an elevated eosinophil count of 8% / neutrophil were normal I think WBC were high not sure
k: Recent drug + fever + eosinophilia (+ rash, rising creatinine) = acute tubulointerstitial nephritis.
r: Eosinophilia after an antibiotic is a drug reaction until proven otherwise; asthma and polyps are needed before thinking EGPA.
n: Printed answer D (drug-induced ATIN after amoxicillin with eosinophilia). Recaller: Recaller unsure: 'neutrophil were normal I think WBC were high not sure'.

q: A middle-aged woman presents with a one-week history of feeling unwell and fatigued. She was recently treated with amoxicillin for a urinary tract infection. Laboratory investigations reveal: Elevated serum creatinine Hyperkalemia Eosinophils: 8% Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
k: AKI + eosinophilia after a new drug = acute tubulointerstitial nephritis.
r: Hyperkalemia and rising creatinine after an antibiotic course point to the kidney interstitium, not to the original infection.
n: Printed answer B. Only 3 options recalled.

q: A 70-year-old man presented to Emergency Department with generalized fatigability. 2 days ago, he had CT brain with contrast for possible transient ischemic attack. Physical examination is unremarkable (see lab results). Blood pressure 130/70 mmHg Heart rate 76 /min Test Result Normal Values Hb 170 130-170 g/L (Male) 120-160 q/L (Female) Urea 30.4 2.75-7.4 mmol/L Creatinine 378 44-115 mol/L Which of the following is the most likely mechanism for the renal impairment?

n: Option B is starred and highlighted with a pink hand marking. Side notes: no pre-renal history (no dehydration, hypotension, hemorrhage, vomiting/diarrhea), no AIN features (drugs, fever, rash, eosinophilia, WBCs); creatinine rising 24-72 h after contrast = co

q: A 70-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with generalized fatigability. Two days ago, he underwent a contrast-enhanced CT brain scan for suspected transient ischemic attack. Physical examination is unremarkable. Vital signs show blood pressure of 130/70 mmHg and heart rate of 76/min. Laboratory investigations reveal: Hb: 170 g/L (normal) Urea: 30.4 mmol/L (elevated) Creatinine: 378 umol/L (elevated) What is the most likely mechanism for the renal impairment?
k: Rule: AKI 48 to 72 h after iodinated contrast = contrast nephropathy = ATN.
r: Timing gives it away: days after contrast = ATN; days after URTI = IgA; 1 to 2 weeks after = PSGN.
n: Printed answer B. Acute tubular necrosis (contrast induced nephropathy). Embedded insets are the same version (option D reads 'Acute glomerular nephritis'), no answer printed there. 19 October update ↻ Printed again later in this 19 October file (p.759) with t

q: A 28-year-old man who recently joined military service and underwent excessive military training presents to the Emergency Department with lightheadedness on standing, muscle cramping, and fatigue. Physical examination reveals postural hypotension, otherwise unremarkable. A diagnosis of acute kidney injury due to hypovolemia is established. Which of the following is the most expected laboratory abnormality?
o: Blood urea nitrogen/creatinine ratio is elevated > 20
Presence of dysmorphic red blood cell (RBC) and RBC cast
k: Prerenal vs intrinsic (ATN) AKI indices: BUN/Cr: prerenal >20; ATN <15; FENa: prerenal <1%; ATN >2%; Urine Na: prerenal <20; ATN >40
r: Each wrong option here describes intrinsic renal disease; only the high BUN/Cr ratio fits intact tubules saving volume.
n: Answer C (GB); embedded inset 0051 same version with 'Answer: C'. Prerenal AKI raises BUN/Cr ratio above 20. Other versions of this recall in this deck: OCT-3214 → A. Pre-renal azotemia; OCT-3214 → A. Pre-renal azotemia; OCT-3214 → A. Pre-renal azotemia Printe

q: A 28-year-old man who recently joined military service and underwent excessive military training presents to the Emergency Department with lightheadedness on standing and fatigue. Physical examination reveals postural hypotension, otherwise unremarkable. Urine osmolality is elevated > 500 mosmol/L (see lab results). What is the most likely etiology for his acute kidney injury?
k: Concentrated urine = working tubules = pre-renal.
r: Same military recruit with dark cola urine, myalgia and high CK flips the answer to rhabdomyolysis / ATN.
n: Recall 0050. Embedded inset (11 August, same version) prints 'Answer: A. Pre-renal azotemia (GB)' with Arabic note that the soldier question came as pre-renal azotemia. Urine osm >500 means intact concentrating ability (prerenal). October By Similar update

q: Diabetic patient how to check for kidney damage
k: Diabetic kidney disease screening: spot urine albumin/creatinine ratio + eGFR, yearly.
r: Earliest marker = albuminuria (ACR), not creatinine; first abnormal ACR = repeat it.
n: Recaller: Recaller prefaced in Arabic: 'there was a question about'. 15-18 October update

q: A 41-year-old woman presents to the outpatient clinic for routine follow-up. She has a BMI of 31 kg/m2 and a blood pressure of 140/90 mmHg. Laboratory investigations reveal an HbA1c of 8%, with mildly elevated blood urea nitrogen (BUN) and serum creatinine levels. Which of the following interventions is most important to prevent further deterioration of renal function?
k: Diabetic nephropathy: control glucose and blood pressure to slow decline.
r: If an ACE inhibitor or blood pressure control is offered as an option, that usually becomes the best answer for slowing established diabetic nephropathy.
n: Printed answer D. Embedded copies (same version, incl. 21-23 July recall) also give Answer: D. Glycemic control.

q: A 45-year-old man diagnosed with type 2 diabetes 3 months ago, started on metformin 500 TDS, comes for his first follow-up. Blood pressure 125/75 mmHg, Heart rate 80/min. Glucose fasting 7.4, Creatinine 125 (mildly high), HbA1c 6.8%. Which of the following investigations is recommended to assess his renal function/diabetic kidney disease annually?
k: Diabetic kidney disease screening.
r: If both "urine microalbumin" and "urine albumin/creatinine ratio" are offered, pick the ratio; it corrects for urine concentration.
n: Printed answer B. Urine microalbumin; 'annually' in red as the key word. October By Similar update

q: A 55 year old male with dysuria, frequency urgency, otherwise medically free Urinalysis shows erythrocytes of 100 What increases the risk of complication?
k: Complicated UTI = UTI in a host or tract that predisposes to treatment failure.
r: Any UTI in a man is treated as complicated: send a culture and think prostate/obstruction.
n: UTI in a male is by definition complicated; male sex is the risk factor. Compiler attaches the 21-23 September recall (41-year-old male) with the same answer A. 7-10 October update 15-18 October update Other version of this recall in 15-18 October: OCT-0987 →

q: Adult female with recurrent UTI, best way to prevent it?
k: Recurrent UTI prevention ladder.
r: If a prophylactic or postcoital antibiotic appears among the options, it beats cranberry.
n: Embedded 15 September inset of the same version notes no prophylactic antibiotics among the options and answers B. cranberry juice.

q: A case of 56 dm HTN male who has UTI asking about what indicates poor prognosis
k: Complicated UTI risk factors (host factors): Male sex; Diabetes, immunosuppression; Pregnancy
r: Decide by the lead-in: if it asks what makes the UTI complicated or high risk, host factors such as male sex outweigh the degree of hematuria.
n: No answer given; page only marked '(Question)'. Recaller: Only two options recalled.

q: A young man who is sexually active is evaluated in the clinic for clinical features that suggest gonorrhea. Which of the following tests is the most appropriate to establish the diagnosis?
k: Gonorrhea diagnosis = NAAT from the infected site.
r: Same question in a woman: the answer becomes endocervical swab.
n: GB source (0111 inset) prints Answer: C.

q: Q2. A 67-year-old male is hospitalized for a severe bacterial infection and is receiving intravenous aminoglycoside therapy. After several days of treatment, his clinical condition progressively deteriorates. Laboratory investigations reveal an increase in serum creatinine from 1.0 to 2.8 mg/dL and a reduction in urine output. His serum potassium is 4.6 mmol/L, and he is hemodynamically stable. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
k: Drug induced AKI: stop or replace the offending drug first, then supportive care.
r: Normal potassium and stable vitals mean no dialysis: remove the cause.
n: Printed answer A: aminoglycoside nephrotoxicity (AKI) with normal potassium and stable hemodynamics, so stop the offending drug; no dialysis indication. 'Stable' highlighted in red. Embedded same-version inset also prints Answer: A.

q: -Plura effusion after symptms of panceritits 6 days ,how to diagnose
k: Late pancreatitis (several days): serum amylase may be normal; urine amylase and serum lipase remain raised longer.
r: Days into pancreatitis with a normal serum amylase: confirm with urine amylase (or lipase), not by repeating serum amylase.
n: Printed answer A. Urine amylase; an embedded similar recall on the same slide gives the same answer.

q: Patient with SLE came for routine follow up and done renal biopsy that showed class 1 (minimal change) Bp: 150/?? Most appropriate management?
k: Lupus nephritis treatment follows the biopsy class.
r: Class I or II lupus nephritis: no steroids, control BP; class III or IV: steroid plus MMF.
n: Answer B, control BP. Compiler (inset): class 1 and 2 lupus nephritis do not need steroids; just treatment of lupus plus control BP; if not on HCQ she should be started on HCQ. Printed again later in this file (p.4508).

q: SLE unsymptomaic high cr
k: SLE with renal signs: biopsy to confirm and classify lupus nephritis.
r: 'Asymptomatic' does not mean 'watch': raised creatinine in SLE goes to biopsy, not to repeat tests or imaging.
n: Answer A, renal biopsy. Printed again later in this file (p.4510).

q: A 45-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus comes for routine follow-up visit. She was asymptomatic and currently on no medications. Her condition is stable for several years (see lab results). Blood pressure 140/90 mmH Test Result Normal Values 24 hr urine protein 35 0.8-14 mg/di (Male) 2.5-11 mg/di (Female) Protein 500 0-150 mg/24 hr RBC 5000 up to 4,000 in 1 ml Urea 20 2.75-7.4 mmol/L Creatinine 160 44-115 mol/L Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: Repeat urine analysis in next visit
k: SLE plus proteinuria, hematuria or rising creatinine: renal biopsy.
r: Lupus nephritis is clinically silent; lab changes alone in a 'well' SLE patient are enough to biopsy.
n: Embedded inset: full older version with lab table; answer B, renal biopsy.

q: A 26 years old female presented with high BP 150/I don't remember diastolic. She has symptoms of renal artery stenosis (they mentioned left renal bruit). Medical history is unremarkable except for obesity Which of the following is the most appropriate diagnostic imaging?
k: Young woman + hypertension + renal bruit = fibromuscular dysplasia until proven otherwise.
r: 'Most appropriate diagnostic' is the lead in that pushes past ultrasound screening to CT angiography.
n: Answer B, CT of the kidneys. Compiler highlights 'most appropriate diagnostic' in red.

q: Patient has hypertension and renal/flank bruit. Which imaging test is most appropriate to confirm the suspected diagnosis?
k: Renal artery stenosis work-up ladder: Screening / initial: renal duplex Doppler ultrasound; Confirmation: CT angiography (or MR angiography if contrast must be avoided); Gold standard: catheter renal angiography, done when intervention is planned
r: "Initial / screening" = Doppler ultrasound; "confirm" = CT angiography; "gold standard" = catheter angiography.
n: Lookalike recall (renal artery stenosis): to confirm, CT angiography. A recaller reports getting the same question with option B Renal CT.

q: Case of renal artery stenosis abdominal bruit. Young female with hypertension how to confirm
k: Renal artery stenosis: screen with duplex ultrasound, confirm with angiographic imaging.
r: Initial or screening = duplex ultrasound; confirm = CT or MR angiography; gold standard and treatment = catheter angiography with angioplasty (FMD responds well).

q: Hypertensive patient, found to have right abdominal bruit, what is the definitive diagnostic test?
k: Renal artery stenosis: most common cause of secondary hypertension.
r: "Initial" pick US; "definitive/confirm" pick CT angiography.
n: Printed answer option 4 (= D) Renal CT angiography as definitive test for renal artery stenosis.

q: Case of renal bruit heard on the right while doing examination, what is the confirmatory test for renal stenosis
k: Renal artery stenosis imaging by lead-in: Initial/screening: Doppler ultrasound; Confirm/definitive: CT angiography (or MR angiography); If CT angiography not listed: plain "renal CT" over US
r: When CT angiography is missing, the CT option still beats ultrasound for "confirm".
n: Printed answer Renal CT scan (= C). Compiler: no Doppler and no CT angiography in options, so choose CT over US. Recaller insisted option was worded like this ('Sure it was like this'). Recaller: Sure it was like this (re: Renal CT scan option).

q: A patient develops tumor lysis syndrome following chemotherapy. Which electrolyte abnormalities are expected?
k: TLS: three HIGH and one LOW.
r: Calcium goes DOWN in TLS (bound by phosphate); hypercalcemia in a cancer patient points to PTHrP or bone metastases instead.
n: Printed answer A. Only one option recalled. Other version of this recall earlier in October: OCT-3277 → D. Hypocalcemia and hyperkalemia.

q: 23-year-old man with Hodgkin's lymphoma on chemotherapy develops tumor lysis syndrome. Expected disturbance? (p. 134)
k: Tumor lysis syndrome: cell contents spill out.
r: Everything goes UP in TLS except calcium, which goes DOWN.
n: Printed answer C. TLS: hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, hyperuricemia, hypocalcemia. Embedded 21-23 September recall gives the same (listed there as A).

q: Q4. A 45-year-old male with lymphoma develops nausea, vomiting, generalized weakness, and decreased urine output shortly after initiating chemotherapy. Tumor lysis syndrome is suspected. Which of the following electrolyte abnormalities is most likely to be found?
k: TLS: three highs and one low.
r: In TLS everything released from the cell goes up; calcium is the only one that goes down.
n: Printed answer D. TLS causes hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, hyperuricemia and secondary hypocalcemia. Other version of this recall earlier in October: OCT-1213 → A. Hyperkalemia + hypocalcemia. October By Similar update Other version of this recall in 22 Oct

q: Pt with TLS presents with muscle weakness, fatigue, nausea, palpitations K:6.2, Ca: 1.7) Which of the following is attributed to his symptoms?
k: TLS = hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, hyperuricemia, hypocalcemia: Hyperkalemia: weakness, palpitations, arrhythmia (peaked T, wide QRS); Hypocalcemia: tingling, cramps, twitching, tetany, seizures, long QT; Hyperphosphatemia: drives hypocalcemia and calcium phosphate nephropathy
r: Weakness + palpitations = potassium; cramps, twitching or tingling = calcium.
n: Muscle weakness and palpitations point to hyperkalemia. Rule of thumb: if the stem gives muscle pain/aches/twitches, the answer is hypocalcemia. 15-18 October update 19 October update 20 October update Other version of this recall in 20 October: OCT-3057 → A.

q: Pt with TLS presents with muscle weakness, fatigue, nausea, palpitations Which of the following is attributed to his symptoms?
k: TLS: hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, hyperuricemia, hypocalcemia. Match the symptom to the ion: Weakness, palpitations, arrhythmia: hyperkalemia; Tetany, cramps, aches, seizures, long QT: hypocalcemia; Oliguria, AKI: uric acid and phosphate deposition
r: If the stem adds cramps, aches or tetany, the answer flips to hypocalcemia.
n: Inset of the same version from the 15-16 September recall (adds K 6.2, Ca 1.9 'I think') answers Hyperkalemia; if the stem mentions ache/pain then hypocalcemia. The inset carries a '(New)' stamp from its original September compilation. Other version of this re

q: A. patient presents with palpitations and an abnormal cardiac rhythm. Laboratory investigations reveal elevated serum potassium. What is the most likely electrolyte abnormality responsible for the patient's symptoms?
k: Hyperkalemia: the electrolyte that kills through the heart.
r: When the stem states the abnormal lab, answer with that lab; do not overthink calcium or magnesium.
n: Printed answer B. Hyperkalemia.

q: TLS case, patient has palpitations and weakness, what electrolyte abnormality is most likely to be responsible?
k: Match the TLS symptom to the electrolyte.
r: Weakness (flaccid) = potassium; spasm (tetany) = calcium.
n: Printed answer A. hyperkalemia.

q: TLS patient with nausea vomiting and palpitations and muscle WEAKNESS, what's causing it?
k: TLS symptom map. Hyperkalemia: nausea, vomiting, palpitations, muscle weakness, arrhythmia.; Hypocalcemia: tetany, cramps, seizures, long QT.; Hyperuricemia and hyperphosphatemia: AKI, oliguria.
r: In TLS, 'weakness + palpitations' is potassium even if calcium is also abnormal.
n: Embedded inset: older four-option version (adds hypomagnesemia, 'muscle WEAKNESS' in red); printed answer A. Hyperkalemia.

q: A patient with a history of diabetes mellitus (Not sure) presents with an acute gout attack. Laboratory investigations: Serum uric acid: 600 umol/L Serum creatinine: 200 umol/L (reference range: 44-115 umol/L) Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
k: Acute gout: choose by comorbidity.
r: Gout + high creatinine = no NSAID; with colchicine absent from the options, steroids win.
n: Printed answer B. Corticosteroids: high creatinine (renal impairment) makes NSAIDs unsuitable, so steroids. Recaller (Arabic) says it was literally like this and is sure of the labs. Recaller: Literally like this and sure of the labs (Arabic note)

q: Symtoms of TLS How to prevent:
k: TLS prevention: hydration first, then a uric acid drug by risk.
r: No rasburicase in the choices: allopurinol; rasburicase offered and the tumor is bulky: rasburicase.
n: Printed answer A. Allopurinol; no rasburicase in choices. TLS prevention: first line hydration, second line allopurinol or rasburicase if indicated (bulky or stage III/IV DLBCL/Burkitt, venetoclax, AML with WBC 100,000). Recaller: No rasbirucase in choices

q: A lymph node biopsy is consistent with non-Hodgkin lymphoma. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
k: New lymphoma: the step tested depends on the missing clue (TLS prevention before chemotherapy vs hypercalcemia).

q: A 50-year-old man newly diagnosed with bulky diffuse large B-cell lymphoma presents to the emergency department with nausea, vomiting and decreased urine output for 24 hours after his first cycle of R-CHOP chemotherapy. Labs show potassium 6 mmol/L phosphate 3 mmol/L calcium 1.2 mmol/L uric acid is not reported. In addition to hydration, what should be given?
k: Established TLS in a high risk tumor: hydration plus a drug that removes existing uric acid.
r: Fork: uric acid high or AKI in a high risk tumor, rasburicase listed and G6PD normal: rasburicase fits; rasburicase absent, G6PD deficient or lower risk: allopurinol.
n: Options C (Furosemide) and D (Rasburicase) shown in red; compiler: 'No Comment, Choose Whatever'. No final endorsement for this version.

q: جاني كيس طويل وبالاخير قالك عنده TLS, what medication to prevent?
k: TLS = hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, hyperuricemia, hypocalcemia.

q: Long case ends with a patient who has tumor lysis syndrome. What medication prevents it?
k: TLS prevention ladder by risk: Low risk: monitoring and hydration; Intermediate risk: IV hydration + allopurinol; High risk or established TLS: IV hydration + rasburicase
r: Allopurinol stops new urate; rasburicase destroys urate already there, so it wins once risk is high or TLS has started.
n: Printed answer A (Rasburicase). Embedded inset of a fuller ALL version answers B. Rasburicase.

q: Patient with Tumor lysis syndrome and reduced renal output with elevated potassium 6.6, after initial hydration what is the next step
k: TLS with oliguria and hyperkalemia: First: IV hydration to restore volume; Hydrated but still oliguric: loop diuretic (avoid in hypovolemia or obstruction); K ≥ 6.5 or ECG changes: calcium gluconate, insulin with dextrose as for any hyperkalemia
r: Diuretics come only after hydration; giving Lasix to a dry patient worsens AKI.
n: Screenshot of a recall: printed answer C is crossed out with a red X and a red handwritten A written beside it; potassium 6.6 circled. Correction wins: A. Lasix. Printed again later in this file (p.4577). October By Similar update ↻ Printed again later in the

q: A 63-year-old man has chronic lymphocytic leukemia started on chemotherapy. His initial lymphocyte count was 73,000. 2 days after chemotherapy, he presents with fatigue and dry mouth (see lab results). Test Result Normal Values WBC 5.7 4.5-10.5 x 109/L Lymphocytes 60 20-40 % Potassium 5.5 3.5-5.1 mmol/L Phosphate, inorganic 1.48 0.82-1.51 mmol/L Creatinine 139 44-115 mol/L Uric acid 620 200-410 umol/L (Male) 140-360 mol/L (Female) Which of the following electrolyte abnormality is associated with the above condition?
k: TLS = three highs and one low: Hyperkalemia (arrhythmia risk); Hyperphosphatemia; Hyperuricemia (urate nephropathy, AKI)
r: Calcium is the one value that falls in TLS; a high calcium option is the trap.
n: Printed answer A. Hypocalcimia tagged (MG); embedded inset of the same version prints Answer: A. TLS causes hypocalcemia.

q: A 55-year-old male with a hematological malignancy developed tumor lysis syndrome (TLS) following chemotherapy. He subsequently developed oliguria and acute kidney injury, with laboratory findings suggesting obstructive nephropathy. Laboratory investigations: Urea: 24 mmol/L Creatinine: 320 umol/L Uric acid: 14 mg/dL Potassium: 6.1 mmol/L Phosphate: 6.5 mg/dL Calcium: 7.2 mg/dL What is the most likely cause of his acute kidney injury?
k: AKI in TLS is mainly intratubular crystal deposition: Uric acid crystals: acute uric acid nephropathy (the classic answer); Calcium phosphate crystals: from hyperphosphatemia; Prevention: hydration to keep high urine flow, plus allopurinol or rasburicase
r: Crystal obstruction inside the tubules is the TLS kidney lesion, not ATN or interstitial nephritis.
n: Printed answer A. Acute uric acid nephropathy (obstructive uric acid crystal nephropathy in TLS).

q: Patient recently treated for tumor lysis syndrome (TLS) is being evaluated for resumption of chemotherapy. Laboratory values show: Uric acid: 460 umol/L Creatinine: 135 umol/L Blood pH: 7.2 Which of the following criteria best indicate readiness to resume chemotherapy?
k: Recalled restart criteria after TLS: Uric acid < 475 umol/L (about 8 mg/dL); Creatinine < 141 umol/L; pH ≥ 7
r: Apply the patient's numbers to each option; the right set is the one his labs already satisfy.
n: Embedded inset: version with lab values and 3 options; printed answer B. Compiler: restart chemo when uric acid is 480 and Cr is 140. Compiler aside: the patient developed decreased urine output and was given allopurinol + sodium bicarb + hydration, not Lasix

q: A. patient in his 20s came to clinic for follow up regarding his HTN, he is complaining of fatigue and proximal muscle weakness 4/5. He is on two antihypertensive medications. BMI: 18 BP: 151/90 mmHg Potassium: 3.2 mmol/L Which investigation help to diagnose this patient?
k: Secondary hypertension screens: Resistant HTN or HTN + low K: aldosterone:renin ratio (Conn); Paroxysmal headache, sweating, palpitations: plasma or urine metanephrines (pheochromocytoma); Cushingoid features: 24 h urine free cortisol or dexamethasone suppression
