q: A patient presents with dull chest pain that is not related to activity. The pain is more prominent after spicy meals or emotional stress and increases with lying flat. How to establish the diagnosis?
k: GERD diagnostic approach.
r: Dysphagia to liquids more than solids points to motility, so barium swallow then manometry; burning pain worse lying flat points to reflux, so pH monitoring.
n: GERD picture; the word Ambulatory is emphasized in bold in option C. Other version of this recall in Part 3: SWR-2636 → C. Ambulatory pH monitoring

q: Patient has symptoms suggestive of heart failure. Which test would help guide the diagnosis?
k: Suspected heart failure: BNP or NT-proBNP, then echocardiography.
r: A raised BNP in an elderly patient with CKD or COPD may not mean left ventricular failure; obesity can falsely lower it.
n: Printed answer A (BNP).

q: A 35-year-old woman presents to the clinic with a 5-month history of fatigue. She takes no medication. Physical examination is unremarkable. Laboratory results reveal dyslipidemia with elevated LDL and total cholesterol, along with elevated TSH and low free T4. What is the most appropriate treatment for this patient's dyslipidemia?
k: Before treating dyslipidaemia, exclude secondary causes.
r: Fatigue plus dyslipidaemia should prompt a TSH before any lipid drug.
n: Printed answer D (secondary dyslipidemia from hypothyroidism: treat with thyroxine first).

q: A patient has chest pain. Examination found a mid-systolic click followed by a late systolic murmur heard at the apex, more prominent with standing and decreased with handgrip. What is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Click plus late systolic murmur = MVP.
r: MVP and HOCM are the two murmurs that get louder on standing; the click points to MVP.
n: Mid-systolic click with late systolic murmur that increases with standing and decreases with handgrip is mitral valve prolapse. Other version of this recall in Part 1: SWR-0069 → D. Mitral valve prolapse (MVP)

q: A 40-year-old man is admitted with palpitations of 4-hour duration. He had similar attack a month ago but did not seek medical advice. His initial electrocardiogram showed atrial fibrillation with controlled ventricular rate. He subsequently converted to sinus rhythm. Which of the following drugs is the most appropriate to maintain sinus rhythm?
k: AF management: Unstable: synchronized electrical cardioversion; Stable: rate control first (beta blocker, CCB, digoxin; digoxin if heart failure); Rhythm control / maintaining sinus rhythm: antiarrhythmic such as amiodarone
r: "Control the rate" = beta blocker/CCB/digoxin; "maintain sinus rhythm" = antiarrhythmic.
n: Rhythm control (maintaining sinus rhythm) uses an antiarrhythmic such as amiodarone; the other options are rate control agents.

q: infective endocarditis prophylaxis due to dental procedure
k: IE prophylaxis = high-risk HEART plus high-risk PROCEDURE.
r: Benzathine penicillin = rheumatic fever prevention; amoxicillin or ampicillin = endocarditis prophylaxis.
n: D (benzathine penicillin) is used to prevent recurrent ARF, not for IE prophylaxis. Recaller: Recaller (Arabic): 'there was a question on' IE prophylaxis; wrote 'I think' before option d.

q: 53 Year-Old Male Patient With Significant Past Medical History Of Ischemic Heart Disease Came To ER With History Of Severe Shortness Of Breath Started Suddenly. Other Past Medical History Is Unremarkable. Upon Examination, The Patient Is Conscious, Oriented And In Distress With Respiratory Rate Of 31, Pulse Is 112, And SpO2 Of 88. Creatinine Clearance 27. His BMI Is 41. What Do You Give Him?
k: VTE prophylaxis choice: renal function picks the drug, body weight picks the dose.
r: Low CrCl alone points to UFH; low CrCl plus BMI over 40 points to the higher-dose UFH option, not 5000 twice daily.
n: Printed answer: UFH 7500 every 8 hours (CrCl below 30 and BMI 41 favour higher-dose UFH thromboprophylaxis).

q: An obese woman provided her waist measurement (125 cm) and hip measurement 108cm . Laboratory results show normal HDL and elevated LDL (4.3 mmol/L). Among the following options, Which of the following is the most significant biochemical indicator of health risk?
k: Match the option to the category in the lead-in.
r: Drop the word 'biochemical' and the answer flips from LDL to waist-hip ratio.
n: The word 'biochemical' (red) decides it: High LDL is the only biochemical option. If the stem did not say biochemical, answer would be C (waist-hip ratio).

q: 25 year old woman with DM1 went hiking. 3 days later presented to the ER with severe dyspnea. Physical Exam showered s3 gallop and basal crepitations ECG showed widespread concave St segment changes what is the organism most likely
k: Acute viral myocarditis. Most common cause: Coxsackie B; others adenovirus, parvovirus B19, HHV-6; Picture: young patient, recent viral illness, chest pain or new heart failure, arrhythmias; ECG: diffuse concave ST elevation (pericardial involvement), nonspecific ST-T changes
r: Diffuse concave ST elevation plus heart failure signs = myocarditis (Coxsackie B), not pericarditis alone.

q: 48 years old male patient known with hyperlipidemia with recurrent history of acute pancreatitis presented with vomiting with hemoptysis 1 day ago, all labs are normal, and on examination, the patient had splenomegaly, on radiological examination, there were normal portal veins with enlarged pyloric varicose veins. What is the diagnosis?
k: Isolated gastric varices + normal portal vein + pancreatitis = splenic vein thrombosis.
r: Gastric varices with a normal liver and normal portal vein = splenic vein thrombosis, and the cure is splenectomy, not band ligation.

q: Patient (not remember age) come comatose by ambulance Na K8
k: Severe hyperkalemia ladder (the same question in Part 1 is keyed to IV calcium gluconate): 1. Stabilize the myocardium: IV calcium gluconate; 2. Shift K into cells: insulin with dextrose, nebulized salbutamol, bicarbonate if acidotic; 3. Remove K: loop diuretic, potassium binders, dialysis if refrac
r: Calcium does not lower the potassium level; it buys time, so shifting and removal must follow.
n: ↑ Same question as Part 1 card SWR-0265, where the answer was: B. IV calcium gluconate. Part 2 gives: (no answer marked).

q: A man in his 40s falls while playing tennis and develops garbled speech and right-sided weakness. Blood pressure is very high.
k: Acute focal deficit: non-contrast CT first, then decide.
r: Never thrombolyse a stroke before a non-contrast CT has excluded haemorrhage.

q: Patient known case of reduced ejection INFARCTION heart failure Denies any hx of dyspnia, orthopnia, PND, ECG: sinus tachycardia
k: HFrEF conventional sequencing: start with ACE inhibitor.
r: The word 'rate control' or AF on the ECG flips the answer to digoxin; sinus rhythm in stable HFrEF keeps it on the ACE inhibitor.
n: Printed answer D (ACE). If they ask SPECIFICALLY about rate control -> A. Digoxin. Recaller: Recaller (Arabic): the exam literally wrote 'infarction', not 'fraction'.

q: patient did a PCI for a myocardial infarction and they're asking about the medication he should take following his discharge They put his labs and he had an LDL of 3.5
k: Four statin benefit groups: Clinical ASCVD (MI, ACS, PCI, stroke, PAD): high intensity statin; LDL ≥190 mg/dL: high intensity statin; Diabetes aged 40 to 75: moderate, or high if higher risk
r: After MI the LDL value does not decide whether to start a statin; it is always high intensity.
n: Post MI/PCI: high intensity statin regardless of LDL.

q: A 40-year-old man with paraplegia following a road traffic accident one year ago is brought to the Emergency Department because of sudden onset dyspnea and chest pain. On examination, he is in severe distress and cyanosed. He has a left parasternal heave and loud P2. Chest is clear to auscultation. Reports: Echocardiogram: Dilated right ventricle with pulmonary artery pressure of 55 mmHg. Venous Doppler: Confirmed DVT in the left leg extending to the thigh. Vital signs: Blood pressure: 80/55 mmHg Heart rate: 110/min Respiratory rate: 30/min Temperature: 36.6 C Oxygen saturation: 86% Lab results: HCO3: 22 mmol/L (22-28) PCO2: 4.2 kPa (4.7-6.0) pH: 7.40 (7.36-7.45) PO2: 8.6 kPa (10.6-14.2) Which of the following is the best line of management?
o: Alteplase infusion (or Streptokinase in the recall)
k: PE management is decided by hemodynamics: Stable PE: LMWH (or DOAC), then oral anticoagulation; Massive PE (systolic BP below 90 or shock): systemic thrombolysis (alteplase); Thrombolysis contraindicated or failed: surgical or catheter embolectomy
r: Same PE with BP 125/70 = anticoagulate only; hypotension is the trigger for thrombolysis.
n: Handwritten red B: massive PE with hypotension and RV dilatation -> thrombolysis.

q: Case KC of heart failure came with dyspnea, Given on 0.2 NE And Currently his BP 85/50, What do Now? (Case as cardiogenic shock)
k: Match the drug to the shock physiology.
r: Pump problem = add an inotrope (dobutamine); vessel problem = add or increase a vasopressor.
n: Handwritten 'B, Confirmed'; compiler boxed 'cardiogenic shock' in the stem.

q: Pt known hypertension on losartan and amlodipine What to add?
k: Hypertension ladder: A or C, then A + C (or + D), then A + C + D, then resistant hypertension options.
r: On ARB + CCB, the missing letter is D: add a thiazide like diuretic.
n: Handwritten D; no further compiler commentary.

q: Patient with HFrEF on BB presented with Cardiogenic shock
o: Continue BB and add IV dobutamine
IV glucagon as antidote of BB
k: Beta blocker in HF: chronic = continue and uptitrate; shock = stop.
r: Do not stop the beta blocker for ordinary HF decompensation; stop it only when there is shock or hypoperfusion.
n: Compiler's handwritten answer B: stop the beta blocker in cardiogenic shock.

q: 50 years old man presented completely asymptomatic. Incidentally, they found a pansystolic ejection murmur. When they did echo, it was severe mitral regurgitation with dilatation of the left atrium I guess But the ejection fraction is normal. The management:
o: Give anti-heart failure medication (diuretics and lisinopril?)
k: Chronic severe MR: operate when one of these appears.
r: In MR, an EF of 55 to 60% already signals LV dysfunction because the leaking valve flatters the EF.
n: Indications for surgery in chronic MR: symptoms, EF <60%, pulmonary HTN (PASP 50, mPAP >20), atrial fibrillation. LA dilation is NOT an indication for surgery (some LV/LA enlargement is expected in severe chronic MR). Answer A as long as no pulmonary HTN and n

q: Patient came with typical chest pain and sweating. ECG shows sinus tachycardia with LBBB. Previous ECG is normal Started on aspirin, atorvastatin, Nitroglycerin , Beta blocker and morphine. Cardiac enzyme is pending. What is the next step?
k: New LBBB + ischemic symptoms = manage as STEMI.
r: If angiography/PCI is not among the options (or the setting has no cath lab), the answer becomes thrombolysis.
n: Compiler's handwritten answer C: coronary angiography (new LBBB with typical chest pain treated as STEMI equivalent, primary PCI).

q: A patient with mitral valve and aortic valve problems is undergoing a dental procedure Which of the following prophylactic should she take?
k: Prophylaxis only for high risk heart plus high risk procedure.
r: Add the words 'prosthetic' or 'previous endocarditis' and the answer flips to amoxicillin or ampicillin.

q: 71-year-old male, no diabetes, non-smoker. BP 171/90, total cholesterol 6.1, HDL 1. Calculate cardiovascular risk based on the risk chart (see image).
k: Using a cardiovascular risk chart (cholesterol ratio version): pick the panel, then the cell.
r: Calculate the TC:HDL ratio first; reading total cholesterol 6.1 straight onto a ratio axis only works here because HDL is 1.
n: Risk chart screenshot (cholesterol/HDL ratio chart, male 75 years nondiabetic nonsmoker) shown; answer >30%.

q: 2-A 40-year-old male, 5-pack-year smoker presents to the Emergency Room with a sudden onset of retrosternal chest pain radiating to the neck. His blood pressure is 150/92 ECG: ST-segment depression in II, III, and aVF. Which of the following is the most considerable risk factor?
k: Coronary risk factors: modifiable versus non-modifiable.
r: A single raised BP during acute chest pain is not a diagnosis of hypertension; watch how the stem frames the BP.

q: Elderly man DM HTN was admitted to the ward due to acute abdomen, during laparotomy surgical team found necrotic bowel and wanted to exclude cardiac causes, his ECG showed sinus rhythm, Echo was normal. What should you do next?
k: Embolic event + sinus rhythm on ECG = look for paroxysmal AF.
r: Normal resting ECG never excludes paroxysmal AF; prolonged monitoring does.
n: Mesenteric ischemia with possible embolic source: Holter to detect paroxysmal AF when ECG shows sinus rhythm and echo is normal. Recaller: Option D missing.

q: 3m Post mi , asymptomatic controlled by diet and exercise Total cholesterol high BP high 130 approximately Advice?
k: Secondary prevention after MI: lifestyle plus drugs for all.
r: After an MI, a statin is never optional: 'controlled by diet' is the trap.
n: Commentator: 'I go with B, start cholesterol lowering medication'. Textbook excerpt: all patients should receive statin therapy after acute coronary syndrome regardless of serum cholesterol concentration. Recaller: Recaller: it was a man post MI on lifestyle m

q: 58-YO man. Diabetic hypertensive and dyslipidemia, 2 day cough fever vomiting Admitted to the ICU and right heart catheter showed, Low CVP PCWP and cardiac output, High SVR and low venous saturation? Temp. 38 BP. 128/89 HR. 120 RR. 18 Hg 132 Wbc 19 Platelets.. Creatinine 60 Crp 120 What type of shock?
k: Shock type by catheter numbers.
r: Fever and leukocytosis tempt 'septic', but low CO with high SVR and low filling pressures is volume loss.
n: Compiler highlights in red: low CVP/PCWP/cardiac output, high SVR, low venous saturation (and WBC 19); printed answer D (hypovolemic), the hemodynamic profile driving the answer despite fever and leukocytosis. Other version of this recall in Part 4: SWR-3438 →

q: Harsh crescendo-decrescendo systolic ejection murmur Radiates to the carotids?
k: Aortic stenosis vs sclerosis.
r: Same murmur shape in both: carotid radiation, a slow rising pulse or a soft S2 means stenosis.
n: Compiler highlights sclerosis vs stenosis in red as the discriminator; radiation to the carotids points to aortic stenosis.

q: A patient known to have diabetes mellitus and hypertension presented with chest pain and shortness of breath for 3 hours. Vital signs were approximately stable, although I think he was tachycardic. On auscultation, there was a systolic murmur radiating to the axilla. An ECG was provided and showed STEMI. What is the diagnosis/complication?
k: New murmur after MI: name the mechanical complication.
r: If "papillary muscle rupture" or "acute mitral regurgitation" is offered, it beats cardiogenic shock, which is only the hemodynamic state.
n: The murmur suggests post-MI mitral regurgitation, but there is no mitral regurgitation option, so cardiogenic shock is chosen. Compiler marks 'tachycardic' in red.

q: Pt with eng stage kidney disease. Long case but at the end Echo shows moderate pericardial effusion and was unstable.
k: Pericardial effusion: stable versus unstable decides.
r: Same ESRD effusion but stable: the answer flips to hemodialysis.
n: Compiler highlights 'unstable' in red: hemodynamic instability with pericardial effusion in ESRD calls for pericardiocentesis rather than dialysis. Recaller: Long case, only the end remembered.

q: A patient with chronic hepatitis C presents with ascites and mild abdominal discomfort. Ascitic fluid analysis shows a PMN count of 300 cells/mm? What is the most appropriate management?
k: SBP = ascitic neutrophils ≥250 cells/mm³ in cirrhotic ascites.
r: Abdominal pain in any cirrhotic with ascites = tap the ascites; the neutrophil count, not the fever, makes the diagnosis.
n: Ascitic PMN count of 300 (above 250) indicates spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, treated with systemic antibiotics.

q: A i do not know the age is evaluated in the clinic for newly diagnosed hypertension that is not well controlled with lifestyle modifications. His systemic examinations are unremarkable (see lab results). Which of the following is the most appropriate management for this patient's hypertension?
k: First antihypertensive after failed lifestyle change: pick by age, ethnicity and comorbidity.
r: If the real paper gives a stage 2 BP and offers ACEi + CCB, the combination may be the intended answer; with no BP and no combination option, the ACE inhibitor is the safe pick.
n: Compiler: B. Lisinopril by gut feeling (all are first line unless diabetic and renal disease, where ACEi is preferred; the matter has a long detailed explanation). 'See Below' points to the related recall on the next page where the patient is diabetic (answer

q: A 50-year-old man is evaluated in the clinic for newly diagnosed hypertension that is not well controlled with lifestyle modifications. He is diabetic. Which of the following is the most appropriate management for this patient's hypertension?
k: Diabetes + hypertension = ACE inhibitor (ARB if ACEi not tolerated).
r: Once the stem says diabetic, age and ethnicity no longer change the first choice: start an ACE inhibitor or ARB.
n: Numbered recall 37: diabetic hypertensive patient, so ACE inhibitor (lisinopril). Shown as the related version of the page 26 recall. Other versions of this recall in this deck: SWR-2133 → B. Lisinopril

q: A 24 years old female, presented with blood pressure of 156-85 (around that), that was confirmed on multiple visits and home reading, she does not take any over the counter medication nor supplements, she does not complain of any medical condition other than obesity, examination revealed a right sided abdominal bruit Which of the following have the highest diagnostic test:
o: CT of the kidney (written like that, no mention of contrast)
k: Secondary hypertension in a young woman with an abdominal bruit = renal artery stenosis (fibromuscular dysplasia).
r: Plain US and plain CT see the kidney, not the renal artery; renovascular disease needs a vascular study (Doppler or angiography).
n: Printed B (CT of the kidney), but compiler says A is as wrong as B: it should be Doppler US, not plain US. Endorsed answer (Doppler US) is not among the recalled options. Recaller: CT option written like that, no mention of contrast

q: patient with HFrEF [STATED IN THE STEM] presents with palpitations. He denies dyspnea, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, or lower limb edema. ECG shows atrial fibrillation. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment?
k: AF management has three arms: rate, rhythm, anticoagulation.
r: Ivabradine is a trap: it is an HFrEF drug but works only in sinus rhythm; propranolol is a trap too, as it is not an HFrEF beta blocker.
n: Printed answer digoxin for rate control of AF in HFrEF (HFrEF and AF highlighted in red).

q: A patient with leukemia who is 3 days post-chemotherapy collapses on the ward. What is the most likely cause?
k: Collapse within the first days after chemotherapy for leukemia or lymphoma = think tumour lysis syndrome and arrhythmia.
r: Same patient but 10 days after chemotherapy with fever = neutropenic sepsis; it is the timing that flips the answer.
n: Printed answer arrhythmia; compiler notes he did not choose C (sepsis), and that option D was Stroke.

q: Case aortic stenosis what is highest diagnostic value ?
k: Valve disease = echo. TTE: first step for any new murmur or suspected valve lesion; TEE: best image quality (e.g. prosthetic valves, endocarditis, poor TTE window); Echo in AS gives severity and LV ejection fraction
r: Cardiac catheterization is only for discordant echo findings or to assess coronaries before surgery; ECG and CXR are supportive only.
n: Printed answer B. Echo.

q: 61-year-old man comes to the clinic with a 2-day history of dyspnoea on exertion. He has a long standing hypertension and a 30-pack-year smoking history. Physical examination is unremarkable except for rare crackles at the bases of the lungs. Which of the following ( something like most specific most helpful in diagnosing )
k: Pick the biomarker by the question being asked.
r: Dyspnea plus crackles without chest pain = think heart failure → BNP; switch to troponin only if the stem describes ischemic chest pain.
n: Printed answer A. BNP (suspected heart failure).

q: old male with a significant history of cardiovascular disease, currently on long-term (Aspirin or NSAIDs, or anticoagulations I dont remember wallah ) presents with bloody diarrhea What possible diagnosis ?
o: Diverticular disease ( not itis or osis )
k: Lower GI bleeding in the elderly: decide by stool form, pain and clues.
r: Bloody DIARRHEA = colitis (ischemic in the old vasculopath); bloody stool alone without diarrhea in the old = diverticulosis.
n: Compiler: answer is ischemic colitis, not among the recalled options (in his channel note he said that in its absence the best of these would be C). A recall found by an examinee had ischemic colitis as option B, the correct answer. Bloody diarrhea in a patien

q: An older patient with dementia is taking 10 concurrent medications, including Quetiapine prescribed for agitation. The patient has no history of cardiovascular disease. Which of the following medications is most appropriate to consider stopping?
k: In polypharmacy, stop first the drug with the highest harm and weakest indication.
r: Antipsychotic prescribed for agitation in dementia = the classic deprescribing target; the statin is the tempting but lower priority choice.

q: 5- A 68-year-old man, 5 days post-inferior myocardial infarction, develops sudden-onset dyspnea and hypotension. On cardiac auscultation, a new, harsh pansystolic murmur is heard, loudest at the right sternal border. What is the most likely explanation for this finding?
k: Post MI new murmur: site of the murmur separates the two ruptures.
r: Inferior MI tempts you to papillary muscle rupture; the sternal border location flips it to septal rupture.
n: Handwritten check mark and B: ventricular septal rupture. Recaller: 100% sure it was right sided

q: There was a female patient who had valve prolapse and a murmur, regurgitation to be specific. I don't remember which type of valve it was, (but I am very sure there was no valve replacement or prosthetic) . She only had valve prolapse and murmur. They were asking about prophylaxis for endocarditis, and they also mentioned in the question that she didn't have endocarditis previously. What is the prophylaxis?
o: Ampicillin dose was mentioned but I don't remember
k: IE prophylaxis = high-risk HEART + high-risk PROCEDURE (mainly dental work involving gingiva or periapical region).
r: A murmur or regurgitation alone does not qualify; only prosthetic material, prior IE, cyanotic CHD or transplant valvulopathy flip the answer to giving antibiotics.
n: Printed answer: No Antibiotic. Valve prolapse with regurgitation, no prosthetic valve and no previous endocarditis does not need endocarditis prophylaxis.

q: A 61-year-old man with a history of hypertension and diabetes mellitus presents with shortness of breath and chest pain suggestive of myocardial ischemia. On examination, an S4 gallop is heard. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment?
k: Suspected ACS: antiplatelets first, then reperfusion decided by ECG.
r: Thrombolysis needs ST elevation or a STEMI equivalent (new LBBB, posterior MI); never give it for NSTE-ACS.
n: Printed answer A. Compiler: DAPT should be given as soon as ACS is suspected.

q: An elderly woman presents with dyspnea and lower limp edema and Bilateral Basal crackles with other symptoms suggestive of heart failure for 6 months. She is a known diabetic and has chronic kidney disease (CKD), currently on medications for hypertension and diabetes. What is the best secondary prevention strategy for this patient?
o: Early treatment of heart failure symptoms
Glucose Control to prevent kidney disease
Encourage weight loss to prevent heart failure
k: Levels of prevention are defined by the disease stage.
r: The word "prevent" in an option does not make it primary; ask whether the disease already exists.
n: Printed answer A. Secondary prevention (red) means early detection and treatment of established disease, here heart failure.

q: Signs of heart failure and HR is 59. What to give
k: Bradycardia algorithm: decide stable vs unstable, then treat.
r: Classic algorithm threshold is HR below 50; with HR 59 the answer rests on the heart failure signs and the MI context.
n: Printed answer A. Compiler: it was a case of MI and the stem asked for the NEXT step, so atropine comes before saline.

q: Patient came with SOB and fatigue. He was stable. ECG: showed bradycardia (same pic, Dx not written). Next step in the management? With the same pic
k: Bradycardia: identify the rhythm, decide stability, then treat.
r: Cardioversion is for fast rhythms; slow rhythms get atropine, then pacing.
n: Printed answer: atropine for symptomatic bradycardia shown on ECG.

q: 71 years male no DM no medication not smoking BP 171/90 Cholesterol 6.1 HDL 1 Calculate cardiovascular risk based on picture :
k: Reading a cardiovascular risk chart: pick the panel, then the cell, then read the colour band.
r: Do not read total cholesterol (6.1) straight off the chart: divide by HDL to get the ratio, then locate the cell.
n: No commentary; printed answer >30. The risk chart picture is not shown.

q: Patient with stage 3 CKD or ESRD Found to have atrial fibrillation What to give?
k: AF anticoagulant in kidney disease: least renally cleared wins.
r: If the stem adds a mechanical valve or mitral stenosis, the answer becomes warfarin regardless of kidney function.
n: Apixaban is the DOAC of choice in advanced CKD/ESRD with AF.

q: A patient presents with a 2-hour history of hematemesis and has been passing bloody stools for the past 2 days. He has bilateral arthritis and complains of indigestion. His blood urea nitrogen (BUN) level is mildly elevated ( i think was only 2 points above the normal range) What is the most appropriate diagnostic test?
k: Hematemesis or raised urea with GI bleeding = upper source = EGD (after resuscitation).
r: Isolated high urea with normal creatinine in a bleeding patient points UPSTAIRS: even heavy red stools can come from an upper source.
n: Hematemesis with elevated BUN (and likely NSAID use for arthritis) points to an upper GI source -> EGD.

q: Female with history of comorbidity? (I forgot perhaps hx of rheumatic fever) came for annual follow-up. Everything normal (can't remember specifically) except for BP 157/70 and on auscultation there was diastolic blowing crescendo murmur What is the best advice for future prevention/maintenance health promotion?
k: Rule: a new murmur (especially diastolic) needs an echo now; TTE first, TEE for best detail.
r: 'Health maintenance' wording tempts dental prophylaxis; native rheumatic valve disease alone does not need it, get the echo.
n: No answer line under this version; the fuller sibling version on the same page is answered 'Echo immediately', mapped here to A. Echo now.

q: A 40 year old female presented to your clinic for routine checkup, asymptomatic, smoker 10 cigarettes daily for 15 years, her history significant for rheumatic fever 15 years ago On examination: AS murmur Vitals Bp 156/78 RR 18 What is the best advice for future preventive health maintenance?
k: Rule: a murmur in a patient with past rheumatic fever needs an echo now; TTE first, TEE for best detail.
r: New murmur + rheumatic history = echo first; smoking in the stem is a distractor toward CXR.
n: New murmur with rheumatic fever history: immediate echocardiography. Other version of this recall in Part 4: SWR-3682 → B. ECG immediately Other version of this recall in Part 4: SWR-4975 → B. ECG immediately

q: 40 years old famle came to follow up clinic , she was in good health 2 years old when examined Past medical hx of Rheumatic fever 15 years ago she smokes 10 cigarettes for 15 years On current examination she have good heart rhythm and blowing Diastolic decrescendo murmur at aortic area BP 154/56 HR 68 What the most appropriate advice for future preventive health mentinance ?
o: prophylaxis Abx before the dental procedure
k: Rule: a new murmur (especially diastolic) needs an echo now; TTE first, TEE for best detail.
r: Diastolic murmurs are never innocent: always echo.
n: Another version of the rheumatic fever plus new aortic regurgitation murmur recall: answer immediate echo (here option C).

q: A patient with known chronic kidney disease is being treated with gentamicin and furosemide. He is vitally stable. Echocardiography shows a moderate pericardial effusion. His creatinine is elevated, while his BUN is 11.8 mmol/L. What is the most appropriate next step?
k: Pericardial effusion in a renal patient: stability and cause decide.
r: Stable vitals take pericardiocentesis off the table; look for the reversible cause in the stem, here the gentamicin.
n: Printed D (stop the nephrotoxic aminoglycoside) in a stable patient. Compiler adds the rule: if cardiac tamponade -> B. Pericardiocentesis; if (uremic) pericarditis -> C. Urgent hemodialysis.

q: Patient ESRD on hemodialysis 3 times per weak. Developed pericardial effusion with BP 80/60 (I am sure about the systolic but not sure about the Diastolic) . What is next step: Had Muffled Heart Sounds). Echo: Pericardial effusion
k: Pericardial effusion: stability decides.
r: Same ESRD effusion stem: stable BP = dialysis, hypotension with muffled heart sounds = pericardiocentesis.
n: Printed pericardiocentesis: hypotension with muffled heart sounds and effusion means tamponade, which needs drainage rather than dialysis (contrast with the stable version where dialysis/stop the cause applies).

q: Diastolic murmur that radiates from apex to axilla?
k: First decide systolic vs diastolic, then use the radiation.
r: Radiation to the axilla means MR; an apical diastolic rumble that stays put means MS.
n: No printed answer; compiler questions the recall, thinks it is a mix-up and the murmur is actually SYSTOLIC, so answer A (MR). Rule: systolic radiating to axilla = MR; to carotids = AS; to sternal border = ventricular septal rupture.

q: Long case about patient with fever and tachycardia and BP??, with increased vascular resistance and CVP is( forgot if high or low).
k: Classify shock by SVR first, then by filling pressure (CVP/PCWP) and cardiac output.
r: Fever does not mean septic shock: if the SVR is high, the patient is vasoconstricted, so look at the filling pressure next.
n: Printed answer: cardiogenic shock (raised SVR).

q: A patient presents with an acute ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) and has a history of intracranial hemorrhage 10 years ago. The hospital does not have a cardiac catheterization laboratory. What is the most appropriate management?
o: Manage with aspirin, clopidogrel, and heparin
Transfer the patient to the nearest hospital with a cardiac catheterization laboratory for primary PCI
k: STEMI reperfusion: primary PCI preferred; fibrinolysis only if PCI delay is too long AND no contraindication.
r: Ischemic stroke has a time window (3 months); hemorrhagic stroke never expires as a contraindication to tPA.
n: Prior intracranial hemorrhage is an absolute contraindication to fibrinolysis, so transfer for primary PCI.

q: 75 yr old woman admitted because of palpitations. She's a known case of ckd, intermittent claudication. Irregular pulse is felt and ecg diagnoses Atrial fibrillation. Which of the following drugs is indicated to control the ventricular rate?
k: Pick the AF rate control drug by comorbidity (target HR below 100 at rest in the acute setting).
r: AF + claudication in exam recalls = diltiazem; AF + heart failure = digoxin.

q: A 46 year old woman presents with sudden onset facial weakness and inability to speak In her youth she had a history of fleeting joint pain, for which she required aspirin. Refer to the nearest center for primary PCI
k: STEMI in a non-PCI hospital: transfer for PCI vs lytics.
r: No PCI on site does not mean give lytics; a contraindication sends the patient to a PCI center.
n: Handwritten red circle on C (and underlining of 'ischemic stroke 2 months ago' and 'elevation'): recent ischemic stroke contraindicates fibrinolysis, so transfer for primary PCI.

q: Hypertensive pt came with chest pain BP :70/40 jvp elevated and hr 59 ecg shows st elevation in 2,3 and AVF What is the initial :
k: Inferior STEMI (II, III, aVF) = usually RCA, which supplies the SA and AV nodes and the right ventricle.
r: Inferior MI + hypotension + raised JVP: think RV infarct and avoid nitrates; true bradycardia (HR <50 or AV block) is what calls for atropine.
n: Printed answer A (IV atropine) for inferior STEMI with hypotension and bradycardia (HR 59).

q: Patient known case of hypertension presented with chest pain and syncope Bp: 70/40 HR: 59 JVP raised ECG: ST elevation in II, III, aVF What is the initial management?
k: Inferior STEMI (II, III, aVF) = usually RCA, which supplies the SA and AV nodes and the right ventricle.
r: Same stem as the IV atropine sibling: know the keyed answer, but recognize the RV infarct trap (raised JVP + hypotension).
n: Options printed unlettered (lettered by position). Printed answer IV Atropine for inferior STEMI with hypotension and bradycardia; BP 70/40 in red.

q: A 40-year-old male, 5-pack-year smoker presents to the Emergency Room with a sudden onset of retrosternal chest pain radiating to the neck. His blood pressure is 150/92 ECG: ST-segment depression in II, III, and aVF. Which of the following is the most considerable risk factor?

r: If the smoking history were heavy, smoking would replace hypertension as the key.
n: Printed answer is hypertension as the most considerable risk factor. 15-18 October update

k: Stroke history and lytics.

q: A 60-year-old man with hypertension presents to the emergency department with sudden-onset retrosternal chest pain, dyspnea, and palpitations lasting 2 hours. His medical history is significant for a non-hemorrhagic stroke 2 months ago. ECG shows ST-segment elevation in leads II, III, and aVF. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
k: STEMI localisation and reperfusion: II, III, aVF: inferior wall (usually RCA); V1 to V4: septal/anterior (LAD); I, aVL, V5 to V6: lateral (circumflex); Primary PCI first line
r: If the stroke were more than 3 months ago and no PCI were available, fibrinolysis would become acceptable.

q: CASE manifestation of marfan syndrome which investigation order detect complication choice
k: Marfan syndrome (fibrillin 1, autosomal dominant): Eye: ectopia lentis (upward), myopia; Skeletal: tall, long limbs, arachnodactyly, pectus, scoliosis; Heart: aortic root dilatation, dissection, AR, MVP
r: The question is about the aorta, so the answer is the test that sees the aortic root: echo.
n: Printed answer B (Echo) to detect aortic root/valvular complications of Marfan.

q: A 35-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Room with sudden onset of shortness of breath associated with pleuritic chest pain. Her past medical history is unremarkable. She is using oral contraceptives regularly. Physical examination is unremarkable. Imaging and laboratory tests are requested. Which of the following is the most appropriate investigation to establish the diagnosis?
k: Suspected PE work up. Low probability: D-dimer; negative rules out; High probability or positive D-dimer: CTPA to confirm; Contrast allergy or renal impairment: V/Q scan
r: Establish or confirm = CTPA; exclude in low probability = D-dimer.
n: Printed answer CTPA; embedded same-version inset (Q19) with red emphasis on 'most appropriate' and 'establish' also gives CTPA. CTPA establishes PE diagnosis.

q: Old patient with stable angina (chest pain relieved by rest) Ecg showed LBBB WHAT is the first next test in diagnosis?
k: Stable chest pain diagnostic algorithm: Resting ECG normal + can exercise → exercise ECG; Resting ECG abnormal (LBBB, paced, LVH, digoxin) → stress imaging (perfusion scan or stress echo); Cannot exercise → pharmacological stress (dipyridamole/adenosine or dobutamine) with imaging
r: LBBB on a resting ECG kills the exercise ECG; choose an imaging stress test.
n: Options numbered 1#/2#/3# lettered by position. Printed answer myocardial perfusion scan (LBBB makes exercise ECG uninterpretable, so imaging stress test). Recaller: Recaller chose myocardial perfusion scan.

q: Q82. A 58-year-old man presents with progressively worsening shortness of breath and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea. q: Patient with dilated cardiomyopathy on metoprolol develops cardiogenic shock. What is the most appropriate management?
k: Beta blockers in heart failure: start low and up-titrate when stable, hold in shock.
r: Shock = hold the beta blocker; overdose = glucagon. Do not mix up pump failure with poisoning.

k: Step 3 of hypertension treatment: ACEi or ARB + CCB + thiazide-like diuretic.
r: Already on an ARB is the trap: adding an ACE inhibitor is dual RAAS blockade (hyperkalemia, AKI) with no benefit.
n: Answer Diuretic. Embedded older recalls (losartan + amlodipine) also answer diuretic; already on ARB so don't add ACE.

q: Old patient in 60s with hypertension on combined therapy of losartan and amlodipine. Hypertension isn't controlled yet. With edema in examination and EF 60%. Creatinine is normal. What is the most appropriate management to add?
k: Step 3 of hypertension treatment: ACEi or ARB + CCB + thiazide-like diuretic.
r: Edema on amlodipine is often a CCB side effect (precapillary dilation), not fluid overload; EF 60% and normal creatinine argue against heart failure or CKD.
n: Why Lasix, 2 reasons: (1) he has lower limb edema; (2) any HTN regimen of at least 3 medications must include at least a diuretic.

q: A patient with a known history of hypertension is currently taking amlodipine and losartan. Despite adherence to both medications, the blood pressure remains uncontrolled. What is the most appropriate medication to add?
k: Step 3 of hypertension treatment: ACEi or ARB + CCB + thiazide-like diuretic.
r: Before escalating, check adherence and white coat effect; here adherence is stated, so go straight to the diuretic.
n: Printed answer C. Thiazide diuretic.

q: An elderly male patient is taking lisinopril, a statin, paracetamol as needed (PRN), and quetiapine for agitation. He has no other significant past medical history. As part of a geriatric medication review, which of the following medications should be discontinued?
k: Deprescribing in the elderly: stop drugs whose harm outweighs benefit (Beers criteria).
r: "For agitation" is the clue: an antipsychotic without a psychotic diagnosis in an elderly patient is the classic drug to stop.
n: Printed answer D. Quetiapine (antipsychotic in elderly, Beers list).

q: A 60-year-old man with diabetes, hypertension and dyslipidemia is admitted to the medical ward.His medications include amlodipine, losartan, metformin and a statin.he becomes agitated, pulls out his IV line and keeps shouting "Where am I?" o: Review his medications and doses, look for the underlying cause, and reassess
Keep the room dark and quiet
k: Delirium = acute fluctuating confusion with inattention; management = find and treat the cause.
r: Reorientation already failed is a distractor: the answer still is not sedation but searching for the cause.
n: Printed answer B (delirium: find and treat the underlying cause).

q: Patient presents with transient neurological symptoms lasting 20 minutes, suggestive of a transient ischemic attack (TIA). Her systolic blood pressure is 154–160 mmHg. Which antihypertensive medication is most appropriate?

r: BP is lowered gradually after a TIA; the acute permissive hypertension rule applies to acute ischemic stroke, not to established secondary prevention.
n: Printed answer B. Lisinopril.

q: A 60-year-old man known to have systemic hypertension, gout, and dyslipidemia presented to the Emergency Room 5 days ago with signs of heart failure and was diagnosed with congestive heart failure and new-onset diabetes mellitus. q: Patient presents with severe pneumonia and signs of sepsis. He was already started on antibiotics and vasopressors. (See lab results) Which of the following is the expected in his condition?

q: X-ray and Septic shock with high fever; typical haemodynamic parameter?
k: Shock profiles (CO / SVR / PCWP): Septic (early, warm): CO high, SVR low, PCWP low or normal.; Hypovolemic: CO low, SVR high, PCWP low.; Cardiogenic: CO low, SVR high, PCWP high.
r: Only septic (distributive) shock gives a HIGH cardiac output; everything else is low output.
n: Early (warm) septic shock is distributive: high cardiac output with low SVR.

k: Obstructive shock = extracardiac block to flow: CO low, CVP high, SVR high.
r: Raised CVP plus raised SVR with low output separates obstructive from hypovolemic shock (where CVP is low).
n: Printed answer C: obstructive shock has raised SVR.

q: A 58-YO man. q: Q21. A 65-year-old man with a known history of cardiovascular disease presents to the emergency department with fever, generalized weakness, and hypotension following a recent infection. On examination, he is febrile and tachycardic, with a blood pressure of 80/50 mmHg. Hemodynamic monitoring reveals the following findings: Parameter Finding Central venous pressure (CVP) Decreased Pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (PCWP) Decreased Cardiac output (CO) Decreased Systemic vascular resistance (SVR) Increased Mixed venous oxygen saturation (SvO2) Increased What is the most likely type of shock?
k: Shock type by hemodynamic profile: Hypovolemic: CO low, CVP/PCWP low, SVR high, SvO2 low; Cardiogenic: CO low, PCWP HIGH, SVR high, SvO2 low; Septic: CO HIGH, PCWP low, SVR LOW, SvO2 high
r: The infection history is a distractor: only a HIGH cardiac output with LOW SVR makes it septic.
n: Printed answer C: low CVP/PCWP with low cardiac output and high SVR is the hypovolemic pattern despite the infectious history (compiler highlights CO decreased and SVR increased in red).

q: 58-year-old male patient with a history of diabetes mellitus (DM) and hypertension (HTN) presents with fever, cough, and vomiting. Echocardiogram: Dilated right ventricle with pulmonary artery pressure of 55 mmH. Venous Doppler: Confirmed DVT in the left leg extending to the thigh. Blood pressure 80/55 mg Heart rate 110 /min Respiratory rate 30 /min Temperature 36.6 'C Oxygen saturation 86 % ABG HCO3- 22, PCO2 4.2 kPa, pH 7.4, PO2 8.6 kPa. Which of the following is the best line of management?
k: Massive PE = PE with hypotension (SBP below 90) = thrombolysis.

q: A 35-year-old woman with a history of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) was prescribed prednisone 60 mg daily and continued taking it for six weeks. She was told to taper the dose but did not. She was later found dead in the bathroom. What is the most likely cause of death?
k: Complications of prolonged high dose glucocorticoids: Cardiovascular: hypertension, fluid retention, accelerated atherosclerosis; Metabolic: hyperglycaemia, weight gain, hypokalaemia; Bone: osteoporosis, avascular necrosis
r: Here she did NOT stop the steroid, so the danger is excess (hypertension), not adrenal crisis from sudden withdrawal.
n: Answer B, marked Confirmed (embedded Telegram post says CONFIRMED / #Confirmed).

q: Lady with SLE was put on 60mg steroid dose and instead of tapering she took it daily for 6 weeks, she was later found dead in her bathtub. What is the likely cause of death?
k: Continuing high dose steroids = glucocorticoid excess; stopping abruptly = adrenal insufficiency.
r: She kept taking the full dose, so think steroid EXCESS (hypertension, bleed), not adrenal crisis from withdrawal.
n: Embedded inset: Telegram screenshot of an alternate wording with different options; answer B. Hypertensive intracerebral hemorrhage, labelled CONFIRMED. Printed again later in this file (p.6101).

q: SLE patient came with flare, was prescribed prednisone 60mg for 6 days (i think) but the patient mixed up and took it for 6 weeks. Later on she was found dead in her bathtub. What caused her death?
o: ischemic intestine (something like that) with perforation
k: Complications of prolonged high dose glucocorticoids: Cardiovascular: hypertension, fluid retention; Metabolic: hyperglycemia, hypokalemia; GI: peptic ulcer (mainly with NSAIDs), masked perforation
r: Sudden unexplained death in a patient on long high dose steroids: think of the hypertensive bleed, not a slow abdominal catastrophe.
n: Printed answer B (hypertensive brain hemorrhage) from prolonged high-dose steroid use. Embedded 1 September inset is the same version (Steroid 60mg daily for 6 weeks instead of tapering, found dead in bathtub) and also answers B. Hypertensive intracerebral hem

q: CT scan of the brain shows an intracerebral hemorrhage. The patient is hemodynamically stable. What is the target of blood pressure acceptable In The First 24-48 Hours?
k: BP targets in acute stroke differ by type.
r: Do not mix up ICH (around 140) with ischemic stroke thrombolysis (below 185/110, then below 180/105).
n: Older 1 September recall; printed answer C. 140-160 mmHg ('24-48' in red). ↻ Repeated recall (originally from 1 September). 19 October update

q: A 62-year-old male with a history of uncontrolled hypertension, presented with severe headache and altered mentation. A CT scan of the brain shows an intracerebral hemorrhage. The patient is hemodynamically stable. What is the target of Systolic blood pressure acceptable (Within First 24 Hours)?
k: Acute BP targets by stroke type: ICH: lower SBP toward about 140 mmHg, avoid below 130; Ischemic, no thrombolysis: treat only if above 220/120; Ischemic, thrombolysis candidate: below 185/110 before, below 180/105 after
r: If the CT shows blood, lower the BP; if it shows an infarct, permit it.
n: Older recall embedded inset; compiler: Still Same Answer C. Other versions of this recall in this deck: OCT-1112 → C. 140–160 mmHg 19 October update Other version of this recall in 19 October: OCT-1634 → C. ≤ 140/90.

q: A 74 years old male with history of uncontrolled hypertension and ischemic heart disease came to the emergency department with sudden onset of unresponsiveness , he is able to maintain airway and breathing and can open his eyes and move it up and down ( pinpoint on commands او شي زي كذا كان مكتوب) but he is unable to move his upper and lower limbs ( see report ). Vitals : sorry I don't remember but i think his BP was high CT : shows hemorrhage Where do you expect to see the hemorrhage?
k: Locked in syndrome: quadriplegia with preserved consciousness and vertical eye movements/blinking.
r: All four limbs paralysed but eyes move up and down on command = pons; one side paralysed = hemisphere or basal ganglia.
n: Answer A. pons (locked-in syndrome picture: quadriplegia with preserved vertical eye movements). Recaller: Recaller unsure of vitals, thinks BP was high.

q: 63-year-old man with poorly controlled hypertension, sitting with family, became unresponsive, only moves eyes vertically and does not move limbs bilaterally. Where is the lesion?"
k: Bilateral limb paralysis + only vertical eye movements = pons (locked-in).
r: "Unresponsive" in a locked-in patient is apparent only; test by asking him to look up or blink.
n: Answer A. Pons. Embedded inset is the same version (answer 'Pons').

q: A female patient returns from a trip to the cold mountains and develops chest pain lasting 3 days. ECG shows diffuse ST-segment elevation. What is the most likely etiologic agent?
k: Viral pericarditis / myocarditis = Coxsackie B.
r: Diffuse ST elevation = pericarditis; ST elevation in one territory with reciprocal depression = STEMI.
n: Viral pericarditis = Coxsackie. Embedded inset from 21-23 July is the same recall ('case pericarditis what virus Coxsackie', answer D. Coxsackie Virus).

q: 43 year old man came for a check up for job application, he is ASYMPTOMATIC. on examination, there was a heaving left apical impulse. ECG: left ventricular hypertrophy with left ventricular strain Which finding is most likely to be found?
o: respiratory rate of 35 (maybe 25 I forgot honestly)
k: LVH with strain = chronic pressure overload of the left ventricle.
r: LVH with strain is hypertensive target organ damage: in an asymptomatic adult the expected vital sign is a raised BP, not tachycardia, hypoxia or tachypnea.
n: LVH with strain in asymptomatic patient points to longstanding hypertension. Recaller: Respiratory rate value uncertain (35 or 25)

q: An asymptomatic patient undergoing employment screening, is found to have evidence of left ventricular hypertrophy with strain. Which additional finding is most likely to be seen in this patient?
k: Causes of LVH (pressure overload): Hypertension: most common; Aortic stenosis: ejection systolic murmur radiating to carotids; Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy: young, family history, asymmetric septal hypertrophy
r: An option that implies acute illness cannot belong to an asymptomatic screening patient.
n: Uncontrolled HTN is the most common cause of LVH. Embedded copy of same version answers A.

q: A woman in her 80s , presented to ER with Lt sided weakness of face , arm, and leg PE revealed Lt sided hemiplegia CT : age related changes with no hemorrhagic changes At which threshold should antihypertensives be initiated ?
k: Rule: acute ischemic stroke, no thrombolysis: permissive hypertension, treat only if BP >220/120.
r: If the stem says tPA is being given, the number flips to 185/110, not 220/120.
n: Printed answer C. 220/120. Compiler table: ischemic stroke with no tPA planned or contraindicated, treat if BP above 220/120; if tPA planned, initial below 185/110 then maintain below 180/105; intracranial hemorrhage target 140-160 systolic, at or below 140/90

q: A 40-year-old woman is under treatment for a recurrent helicobacter-associated duodenal ulcer. She noticed that her stool is turned non-tarry black (see lab result). Blood pressure 110/70 mmH Heart rate 70 /min Test Result Normal Values Hb 152 130-170 g/L (Male) 120-160 g/L (Female) What drug is likely to be the cause of the black stools?
k: Normal vitals + normal Hb + non-tarry black stool on ulcer treatment = bismuth effect, reassure.
r: If the stem gave tarry stool, tachycardia or a falling Hb, the answer would shift to rebleeding (melena), not a drug effect.
n: Embedded inset: 'See Similar' lookalike recall with ranitidine/aluminium hydroxide options; answer C. Bismuth subsalicylate (normal Hb, non-tarry stool). Other versions of this recall in this deck: OCT-9147 → D. Bismuth subsalicylate

q: A 40-year-old woman is under treatment for a recurrent Helicobacter pylori-associated duodenal ulcer. She notices that her stool has turned non-tarry black. Blood pressure is 110/70 mmHg and heart rate is 70/min. Hb is 152 g/L. Which drug is most likely to be the cause of the black stools?
k: Normal vitals + normal Hb + non-tarry black stool on ulcer treatment = bismuth effect, reassure.
r: If the stem gave tarry stool, tachycardia or a falling Hb, the answer would shift to rebleeding (melena), not a drug effect.
n: Embedded 11 Feb recall of the same version (options in different order) answers Bismuth subsalicylate. Other versions of this recall in this deck: OCT-9146 → C. Bismuth subsalicylate

q: A 34-year-old man patient a known case of ulcerative colitis on azathioprine 100mg/day and tapering dose of steroid presented to the clinic with 6-7 bloody bowel motions, lower abdomen pain and low grade fever. On abdominal examination, there is mild tenderness at left lower abdomen. Stool culture was negative. Stool for colostrum difficile toxins was positive (see lab results). Blood pressure 110/70 mmH, Heart rate 100 /min, Temperature 38.4 °C, Oxygen saturation 95 % Test Result Normal Values RBC 5 4.7-6.1 x 1012/L (Male) 4.2-5.4 x 1012/L (Female) Hb 11 130-170 g/L (Male) 120-160 g/L (Female) Platelets count 456 150-400 x 109/L WBC 16 4.5-10.5 x 109/L ESR 67 2-10 mm/h (Male) 3-15 mm/h (Female) Albumin 29 34-56 g/L Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
k: C. difficile: grade severity, then treat orally.
r: Vancomycin must be ORAL for C. difficile; IV vancomycin does not reach the colon.
n: Printed answer C, oral vancomycin, tagged (MG); embedded inset (same version) prints 'Answer: C'. Severe C. difficile (WBC >15, low albumin) -> oral vancomycin. Printed again later in this file (p.6523).

q: Patient came complain of heartburn and chest pain typical GERD symptoms without any red flags How to diagnose
k: GERD: typical symptoms without red flags = clinical diagnosis and treatment; pH monitoring is the objective confirmatory test.
r: If the options include clinical diagnosis or a PPI trial, those win for uncomplicated typical GERD; among investigations, pH monitoring is the diagnostic one.
n: Answer A, pH monitoring. 'See below' points to the next page lookalike: EGD cannot diagnose GERD unless reflux esophagitis is present (only ~30% of cases); EGD is for complications, excluding differentials, or alarm symptoms. Recaller: Recaller: typical GERD s

q: A 60-year-old man is found to have elevated blood pressure during a routine checkup. He has no symptoms, and physical examination is unremarkable. ECG, CBC, electrolytes, renal function tests, and urine analysis are normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next option in management?
o: Repeat office blood pressure measurement in 3 months
k: Elevated office BP without urgency: confirm before treating.
r: One high clinic reading is not hypertension: confirm with ambulatory monitoring first.
n: Printed answer C with source tag (GB); embedded 0069 copy of the same version prints Answer: C. Confirm hypertension out of office (ABPM) before treatment.

q: 23 yo female known case of SLE complaining of ll swelling and SOB. On exam she hs jugular venous distension, muffled heart sounds, prominent diastolic component, positive shifting dullness, and edema up to knees. Labs: - Creatinine 450 (high) - WBC: 3 (low) - ALT: 100 (high) - AST: 94 (high) -C3/C4: low Which SLE associated condition explains her symptoms?
k: Constrictive pericarditis.
r: Raised JVP + early diastolic knock + ascites = constriction; don't be pulled to liver or renal failure by the abnormal labs.

q: 45 k/c of HTN and 20 pack smoker, BMI 28 asymptomatic came for check up Best prevention? BP:150/95 Labs HDL 1.1 LDL4.5 Cholesterol: 6.5 Triglycerides: 2.1
o: Lifestyle modification and follow up in 3 months
k: Four statin benefit groups (age over 21), plus one screening rule: Clinical ASCVD: high intensity statin; LDL ≥190 mg/dL (about 4.9 mmol/L): high intensity statin; Diabetes, age 40 to 75, LDL 70 to 189: moderate intensity, high intensity if 10-year risk ≥7.5%
r: Asymptomatic plus multiple risk factors = statin for prevention, not a stress test; lifestyle only is for the low-risk patient.
n: Embedded inset: older lookalike recall labelled 'See Below (February 2026)' for the page 430 statin question; answer line '-High intensity statin'. Third option was left blank by the recaller. ↻ Repeated recall (originally from February 2026).

q: A patient presents with new-onset seizure; he seized 5 times without regaining consciousness between episodes. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
k: Status epilepticus: seizure lasting 5 minutes or more, or repeated seizures without recovery of consciousness in between.
r: Any ongoing seizure = benzodiazepine first; chronic antiepileptics (lamotrigine, carbamazepine) are never the acute answer.
n: Recurrent seizures without regaining consciousness = status epilepticus; first line is a benzodiazepine. Recaller: Other choices not remembered.

q: Pt with RT side weakness for 12 hrs after Ct there was occlusion in meddle to small artery What to do?

n: Thrombo-embolectomy should only be done for large/proximal vessels; medium/small vessel occlusions should not be offered thrombectomy. Compiler says he has explained this for 10 months and finally got the recall. See following recalls (proximal anterior/poster

q: An 18-year-old patient came with reduced level of consciousness and began to seize. While in the ambulance, he was in deep sleep and regained consciousness in the ER. He has HIV with questionable treatment adherence and drinks alcohol heavily. On examination, there is tooth clenching and a temperature of 37.9 C. What is the next step in management?
k: New seizure in HIV = image the brain first.
r: Immunocompromised + seizure: CT before LP, every time.
n: Answer CT (Athar). Screenshot: used to be solved as B (urine toxicology), but after revision it is C; CT brain is a priority since the patient has seizure (HIV patient, rule out mass lesion before LP).

q: Patient with meningitis asking how to protect house contacts?
k: Meningitis prevention for contacts: Who: household and close contacts of meningococcal or Hib meningitis (and staff with mouth-to-mouth or intubation exposure).; Meningococcus: single-dose ciprofloxacin or rifampicin for 2 days.; Hib: rifampicin (4 days) is the drug of choice.
r: Household contacts = prophylaxis; hospital staff and ward = isolation for the first 24 hours of antibiotics.
n: Compiler recalls the longer original (his own 13 August 2025 exam): patient admitted for isolation about 12-13 days after illness onset, so isolation no longer protects the family who already had enough contact; prophylaxis should be given, and the recall spec

q: patient presented with right sided weakness that started 12 hours ago .. proximal anterior circulation occlusion.. *small to moderate* size infarct core Management:
k: Acute ischemic stroke: time + vessel decide.
r: Beyond 4.5 hours, never tPA; a large vessel occlusion within 24 hours still earns thrombectomy.
n: Mechanical thrombectomy. It is the size of the vessel (proximal large vessel occlusion) that decides whether to intervene, NOT the size of the infarct.

q: Epilepsy patient on carbamazepine 600 mg BID (not sure since how long) she still have it 1-2 times per month what is the appropriate management?
k: Breakthrough seizures: check adherence, then dose up, then switch, then add.
r: If the stem says generalized or myoclonic seizures, the answer flips away from carbamazepine.
n: Option D was 'Switch to valproic' in a different recall. Compiler hopes future recalls state the seizure type (Davidson box: carbamazepine may worsen myoclonic seizures; valproate first line for generalized). For now answer is A (dose up carbamazepine), best w

q: Patient with 3 days hx of progressive lower limb weakness with urine retention. Also sensation at T10:
k: Myelopathy pattern: bilateral leg weakness + sensory level + bladder dysfunction = spinal cord lesion; urgent whole spine MRI.
r: A sensory LEVEL means the cord; areflexia and saddle anesthesia mean cauda equina or nerves.
n: Terse version of the same recall as the fuller version below; compiler's answer for the topic is cord compression, mapped by meaning to 'Spinal compression' here.

q: A patient presents with acute hemiparesis, facial droop, and aphasia. A non-contrast head CT shows no evidence of infarction or hemorrhage. What is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Acute stroke pathway: Point-of-care glucose first to exclude hypoglycaemia.; Urgent non-contrast CT to exclude hemorrhage (not to see the infarct).; Normal early CT plus focal deficit: ischaemic stroke; give thrombolysis if within the window and no contraindication.
r: A normal early CT does not exclude ischaemic stroke; it excludes hemorrhage.
n: Printed answer A. Ischemic stroke; compiler: ischemic stroke is abnormal on only about 30% of early CTs.

q: A woman developed sudden dizziness, blurred vision, and she keeps falling on the right side. (remember it being for 1 hour but not sure where it fits) She has horizontal/rotatory nystagmus, ptosis and miosis, impaired pain and temperature sensation on the right side of the face and ipsilateral extremities. What's the cause of her presentation?
k: Crossed signs (ipsilateral face, contralateral body) = brainstem lesion.
r: Horner plus pain and temperature loss on the face is the combination that points to the LATERAL medulla; motor weakness and tongue deviation point medial.
n: Compiler: this is lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome, answer should be D in theory. He questions 'ipsilateral' extremities; it should be right face plus left (contralateral) body loss of pain/temperature, so the examinee probably meant contralateral; reca

q: 38 years old woman has weakness of the right arm with neck extension, MRI brain done and reported normal, what is the most appropriate NEXT investigation?
k: Weakness triggered by neck movement = think cervical cord or root compression.
r: Neck extension as the trigger is the clue that moves the work up from the brain to the cervical spine.
n: Options B and C printed in red; answer line C. cervical spine MRI. Compiler remarks it is funny that options do not include CT.

q: Right arm weakness triggered by neck extension How to diagnose?
k: Positional arm weakness from the neck: image the cervical spine.
r: When the choice is CT versus MRI for the cord, discs or nerve roots, MRI wins; CT wins for bone and acute trauma.
n: Handwritten red 'B' on the page: MRI cervical. Same topic as preceding neck extension versions.

q: A patient presented with a generalized seizure lasting approximately 2-4 minutes. EEG showed generalized seizure activity. Laboratory investigations revealed hypocalcemia and hyponatremia, while the other electrolytes were normal. What is the most likely diagnosis/cause of the seizure?
k: Severity decides provoked vs unprovoked. The author leans to Generalized tonic-clonic epilepsy because the companion recall gave mild values (RBS 4, Ca 2.1, Na 134) and was keyed to idiopathic generalized seizure.
r: If the exam gives the actual values and they are mild, choose the epilepsy option; if they are severe, choose the electrolyte.
n: Compiler: it depends on the severity of hyponatremia and hypocalcemia (mild hypocalcemia and hyponatremia are unlikely to cause seizure). 'From future (1 day later): see below recall' points to the next recall (p664) with mild values (RBS 4, Ca 2.1, Na 134) an

q: case about a 70-year-old male with hypertension came presenting with a stroke. Calculate his CHADVASC2 score.
k: CHA2DS2-VASc (max 9): C: heart failure 1; H: hypertension 1; A2: age ≥75 = 2
r: Stroke/TIA and age ≥75 are the only 2-point items; age 70 earns just 1.
n: Examiner note: it was CHA2DS2-VASc, not CHADS2. Age 70 (1) + hypertension (1) + stroke (2) = 4.

q: Pt diagnosed by extradural haematoma before 4 week and treated successfully now present by weakness diagnosed by ischemic stroke, no atrial fib no DM or HTN What is cause of ischemia??
k: The recall is incomplete (option C wording is unclear), so decide by the clue pattern: young or risk factor free patient, recent head trauma, ischemic stroke = think traumatic arterial dissection (often with embolization).
r: Stroke without risk factors after trauma: look for dissection before blaming atherosclerosis.
n: Compiler tags it (Question) with no answer given. Recaller: Option C wording approximate (Arabic note: 'a word close to it').

q: Patient with jerky movement in one arm (myoclonic seizure) given valproic acid and failed, what to give?
k: Match the antiepileptic to the seizure type.
r: Sodium channel blockers (carbamazepine, phenytoin, and sometimes lamotrigine) can aggravate myoclonic and absence seizures.
n: Myoclonic seizure failing valproate: choose levetiracetam, even when lamotrigine is offered (options A and D shown in red as the competing choices). Other versions of this recall in this deck: SWR-1747 → A. Levetiracetam

q: Another scenario about meningitis, CSF finding were given and blood findings, when I calculated the CSF:Serum glucose it was 0.3 ratio, diagnosis?
k: Low CSF glucose = bacterial or TB; the cell type decides.
r: Low glucose with lymphocytes is TB; low glucose with neutrophils is bacterial. The stem here is incompletely recalled, so check the cell type on your paper.
n: Handwritten C (TB meningitis) for a CSF:serum glucose ratio of 0.3.

q: Weightlifter with worst headache of his life and vomiting. Most appropriate management.
k: Thunderclap headache: non contrast CT first, then LP if CT negative, then angiography to find the source.
r: Exertion (lifting, straining, bending, coitus) plus worst headache of life = SAH; first test is always plain CT, not angiography.
n: Handwritten B; no further compiler commentary. Recaller: Only two options recalled

q: Female 20 came with Right upper limb weakness and numbness since 1 week + left facial severe pain especially when she brushes her teeth Most appropriate
k: Young adult with neurological deficits separated in space or time = think MS; MRI with gadolinium is the key test.
r: Trigeminal neuralgia under 40 or with other neurological signs is MS until proven otherwise: MRI, not CT.
n: Handwritten D; no further compiler commentary.

q: A patient with known multiple sclerosis presents with diplopia. On examination, when asked to look to the right, the left eye fails to look to the right (adduct), while the right(not sure right or left) eye abducts with nystagmus. Where is the most likely lesion?
k: Horizontal gaze localisation.
r: Adduction failure with nystagmus in the OTHER eye = MLF; abduction failure of the same eye = 6th nerve.
n: Handwritten C (internuclear ophthalmoplegia from MLF lesion).

q: A young man developed a tonic-clonic seizure for the first time. The rest of the stem stated that the history and exam were negative for EVERYTHING (history went all the way back to birth, developmental, family). What is your next step?
k: First seizure approach: Step 1: history of the event (exclude syncope and non-epileptic events); Step 2: exclude provoked causes (glucose, sodium, calcium, drugs, alcohol, infection); Step 3: neuroimaging (CT in ED; MRI is the more sensitive elective study)
r: Febrile child aged 6 months to 6 years with a brief generalized seizure = febrile seizure, no CT and no EEG needed.

q: 68-year-old came to ER with 3 days history of bilateral leg weakness and brisk reflexes in both legs, with urinary retention, inability to walk, and a sensory level of T10. What is the diagnosis?
k: Sensory level + bilateral weakness + sphincter loss = spinal cord lesion; MRI now.
r: Brisk reflexes put the lesion in the cord; absent reflexes with saddle anaesthesia put it in the cauda equina.

q: 45- Pt with left-sided sensorineural hearing loss and left-sided facial weakness
k: Brainstem and cerebellar artery syndromes: ipsilateral cranial nerve signs plus contralateral body signs.
r: Facial palsy with hearing loss means AICA (pons, labyrinthine artery); hoarseness and dysphagia mean PICA.
n: AICA infarct gives ipsilateral SNHL and facial weakness. Athar: recalls are confusing; A should be 'Superior Cerebellar Artery' and C is 'cerebellar', not 'cerebral'. Recaller: Recaller: not the same question but the options looked the same; there was Anterior

q: A 52-year-old man presents to the emergency department with a sudden-onset severe headache described as "the worst headache. Which of the following is the best diagnostic test?
o: Non-contrast CT scan of the head
k: Thunderclap headache pathway.
r: 'Initial' or 'first' test = CT; 'confirm' after a negative CT = LP; 'find the source' = angiography.
n: Printed answer C (SAH is non-contrast CT) was crossed out and a handwritten 'A' (lumbar puncture) written; 'best diagnostic' is underlined. UpToDate excerpt shown: non-contrast head CT is the cornerstone of SAH diagnosis, sensitivity near 100% in first 6 hours

q: A 23-year-old woman is brought to the neurology clinic by her family due to episodes of altered behavior occurring for the past 3 months. During these episodes, she becomes unresponsive to her surroundings, stares blankly, and performs repetitive movements such as lip smacking and facial grimacing. Each episode lasts about 1-2 minutes, followed by brief confusion and then return to normal baseline. No history of generalized tonic-clonic seizures. Neurological exam normal. MRI shows hippocampal sclerosis. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Localize focal epilepsy by the semiology.
r: Staring with automatisms and postictal confusion = temporal lobe (focal impaired awareness); the same staring for seconds with no confusion = absence.

q: A 25-year-old woman with a known diagnosis of multiple sclerosis (MS) presents to the clinic for follow-up. She is in remission and on teriflunomide. She reports transient worsening of her symptoms when exposed to heat, such as during hot weather or after a warm shower. no neurological manifestations, no fever, and no other symptoms. What is the explanation for her symptoms?
k: Symptom worsening in known MS: real relapse or pseudorelapse?
r: Before calling a relapse, exclude heat and infection; both can bring back old symptoms without new disease activity.

q: A 38 yeara old right handed woman, 1 week post partum, presents with severe headache and generalized tonic clonic seizures. No fever and focal issues. The headache doesn't improve with paracetamol. Which of the following investigations has the highest diagnostic value?
k: Postpartum headache + seizure (with no hypertension or proteinuria) = think CVT; confirm with venography.
r: If MRI with MRV appears among the options, it beats CT venogram; if only plain CT and CT venogram are offered and the question asks for diagnostic value, pick the venogram.
n: Printed answer D (suspected cerebral venous thrombosis). However, if 'Brain MRI WITH MRV' is offered it would be the better answer: initial test in suspected CVT is brain CT + CTV or MRI + MRV, and MRI/MRV is probably more sensitive. Reference: Greenberg Neuro

q: Women came after 2 weak postpartm with headache and tonic-clonic seizure, and headache not relieved by paracetamol. What is the most appropriate next step
k: CVT workup: imaging of the venous system is what makes the diagnosis.
r: Read the lead-in: "initial" may justify plain CT, but "most definitive" or "highest diagnostic value" means the venogram.
n: Recall from 2025. Athar: B; likely cerebral venous sinus thrombosis, best would be MRV if among the options, otherwise B. Fay-Avengers: next should be plain CT as routine for new onset severe headache and seizure. Alhomrani: even if true, he would still choose

q: A 72-year-old man is brought to the clinic by his wife due to episodes where he suddenly stops speaking, develops a blank, staring look, and displays repetitive facial grimacing and lip-smacking after which he becomes agatated. What is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Staring + automatisms (lip-smacking, chewing, picking) + postictal confusion = temporal lobe (focal impaired awareness) seizure.
r: Postictal confusion separates focal impaired awareness (temporal) seizures from absence seizures, which have none.
n: Printed answer A. Temporal lobe seizure (automatisms such as lip-smacking with post-event agitation). No further commentary.

q: 70 years old Came to er after 12h complain of symptoms with rt side weakness. Ct showed: posterior artery occlusion with mild to moderate ischemic core Management?
k: Posterior stroke after the tPA window: decide by the vessel.
r: Time window kills tPA here; whether thrombectomy is right hinges entirely on basilar vs non-basilar occlusion.
n: Compiler: we need to know which posterior artery is affected; approach to posterior circulation stroke differs from anterior. Basilar stroke -> C. mechanical thrombectomy; non-basilar stroke -> B. observe. The stem does not specify, so no single answer.

q: Pt w chronic hep B, presented with inc fatigue and (flapping?) tremor, on exam he has shifting dullness Na 133 K 3.2 What to give?
k: Cirrhotic ascites: aldosterone antagonist first, loop diuretic as an add-on.
r: Hypokalemia precipitates hepatic encephalopathy, so a cirrhotic with low K and asterixis gets the potassium-sparing diuretic.
n: Spironolactone is preferred over furosemide in cirrhotic ascites (more effective), and the patient is hypokalemic, so spironolactone fits.

q: A patient diagnosed with MS developed weakness and hyperreflexia. MRI with gadolinum showed a new lesion on the spinal cord, what is the best management:
k: MS: treat the attack with steroids, prevent future attacks with disease-modifying therapy.
r: Disease-modifying drugs prevent relapses; they never treat the relapse in front of you.
n: Printed answer B: acute MS relapse is treated with high-dose IV methylprednisolone.

q: Patient with right sided weakness and when he tries to stand up he falls on the right side with horizontal nystagmus also there was other symptoms
k: Cerebellum = ipsilateral signs; brainstem = crossed signs (cranial nerve same side, limbs opposite side).
r: If the options include medulla and the stem adds dysphagia, hoarseness or crossed sensory loss, think lateral medullary syndrome rather than isolated cerebellar lesion.
n: Compiler asks whether medulla was an option; if not, then it is A (cerebellar lesions), since lateral medullary syndrome involves the cerebellum. Options were unlettered in source and lettered by position.

q: 19 year old known case of HIV non-compliant to meds and drinks alcohol has seizure (they describe the deatalis of tonic-clonic seizure) when arrived to ER he was awake and there are bruises and tongue bite? What is the best next step?

q: Female patient k/c of MS on teriflunomide and in remission, came complaining of worsening of symptoms when she gets out in the heat, no new symptoms, only the same one she gets, what is the explanation behind what is happening?

q: A case of a female with multiple sclerosis she is doing well. But sometimes her symptoms worsen with taking hot shawer. (Pain)

r: Heat = Uhthoff; neck flexion = Lhermitte.
n: Printed answer A: heat-induced transient worsening of MS symptoms is Uhthoff phenomenon.

q: A 30-year-old woman with a known history of multiple sclerosis presents to the neurology clinic for a routine follow-up. Her condition has been stable, with no recent relapses. However, she reports transient worsening of her neurological symptoms, including pain, particularly after taking a hot shower. Her symptoms improve after cooling down. Which of the following best explains this phenomenon?
k: MS symptom eponyms: Uhthoff: transient worsening with heat (shower, exercise, fever), reverses on cooling; Lhermitte: electric shock on neck flexion; Relapse: new deficit over 24 hours, no fever or infection
r: Heat in, symptoms up; cool down, symptoms gone = Uhthoff, not a relapse.
n: Heat-induced transient worsening of MS symptoms = Uhthoff's phenomenon. Same-version inset prints 'Answer: A'.

n: Fully resolved deficit with normal CT -> TIA.

Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

A 30-year-old woman with Sjogren's syndrome on hydroxychloroquine is evaluated in the clinic because of fatigue. Her physical examinations are unremarkable (see lab results). Which of the following renal tubular acidosis type is the most likely cause of her hypokalemia?

A 33-year-old woman known to have systemic sclerosis with normal kidney function, diagnosed 2 years ago, is on pantoprazole. She complains of drowsiness and visual changes, denies fever, cough, shortness of breath, chest pain, seizures, abdominal pain, or vomiting. Examination reveals an unwell patient with raised JVP, clear chest, and +3 lower limb edema (see lab result). Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

A 60-year-old man complaining of right knee pain for several years that has increased over the last few months. He also has noticed frequent knee clicks. A diagnosis of osteoarthritis is suspected. Which of the following is the most appropriate to confirm the diagnosis?

A 59-year-old woman admitted with an infected bedsore and had debridement 2 days ago. She suddenly developed mental confusion and poor response to commands. Which of the following is the most likely cause of her deterioration?

A 58-year-old woman presented to the medical clinic complaining of daily wheezing and breathlessness during allergy season. These episodes of wheezing have limited her activities several times a week. She has a long history of seasonal allergies in the form of itchy eyes and runny nose. No other medical history. Medications include loratadine as needed, and antihistamine eye drops. Examination revealed watery eyes with conjunctival irritation, expiratory wheezing, and normal cardiac examination (see reports). Chest radiograph: Unremarkable. Spirometry: FEV1 of 74% of predicted, which improved by 18% with a bronchodilator. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
o: Add a low-dose inhaled glucocorticoid and long-acting B2 agonist

q: A 33-year-old man presented with shortness of breath, fatigue, and nighttime cough. He has been working in a car repair shop for the past 1 year and notes that his symptoms began about 8 months ago. He believes his symptoms are associated with his workdays. He is being evaluated after several days off from work and currently has no symptoms or medical concerns. He has an unremarkable medical history and takes no medications. He has never smoked. Physical examination is unremarkable. A chest radiograph and spirometry results are normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

A 57-year-old man is evaluated for chronic cough, occasional wheezing, and exertional dyspnea while walking. Medical history includes an episode of bronchitis, for which he underwent outpatient treatment 8 months ago. He has a 20-pack-year smoking history. Examination revealed normal vital signs, mildly decreased breath sounds throughout both lungs, and scattered expiratory wheezes bilaterally. Spirometry shows an FEV1 of 75% of predicted and a post-bronchodilator FEV/FVC ratio of 68%. His modified Medical Research Council (mMRC) symptom score is 2. In addition to smoking cessation, which of the following is the most appropriate long-term management plan?
o: Combination inhaled glucocorticoid and a long-acting bronchodilator
Phosphodiesterase-4 inhibitor and combination inhaled glucocorticoid and long-acting bronchodilator
Short-acting bronchodilator as needed, a long-acting bronchodilator, and pulmonary rehabilitation
Short-acting bronchodilator as needed and an inhaled glucocorticoid

q: A 42-year-old woman presented to the clinic for follow-up of a 7-month history of chronic, nonproductive cough. She was recently diagnosed with cough-variant asthma after a methacholine challenge test. She was started on inhaled fluticasone and as-needed albuterol 2 months ago. Her cough initially improved; however, her symptoms have not fully resolved and are worsened at times, most notably when she lies down. She also noted that mild hoarseness occasionally accompanies her cough, especially when she wakes up in the morning. Examination revealed a dry cough with frequent throat clearing. The chest was clear with no wheezing. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

A 24-year-old woman is reviewed in the Asthma Clinic. She currently uses a salbutamol inhaler 100 mcg prn combined with a beclometasone dipropionate inhaler 400 mcg bd.
