q: A 60-year-old man with diabetes and hypertension presents to the Emergency Department with 3 hours of continuous retrosternal heaviness and profuse sweating. Examination shows tachycardia and an S4 gallop. He is started on aspirin, clopidogrel, metoprolol and a nitroglycerin infusion. ECG: sinus tachycardia with left bundle branch block; a previous ECG was normal. Cardiac enzymes are pending. [4 Nov examinee: PCI was not among the options.] Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: Wait for the results of cardiac enzymes
r: Ongoing ischaemic chest pain with a new LBBB (previous ECG normal) is managed as a STEMI equivalent: reperfusion must not wait for troponin, and with no PCI option, thrombolysis (door-to-needle <30 min) is the answer.
n: Why not D? Waiting for enzymes delays reperfusion; the decision is made on symptoms plus ECG, and troponin may still be normal in the first hours. Claude: If primary PCI (achievable within 120 min) appears in the options, it beats thrombolysis.

q: A 62-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes, hypertension, dyslipidaemia and an ischaemic stroke 1 month ago presents to the Emergency Room with central, stabbing, continuous chest pain for 3 hours. She denies dyspnoea, palpitations or change in consciousness. Medications: insulin, lisinopril, metoprolol, atorvastatin (Lipitor) and aspirin. She is in pain and is started on oxygen, morphine and sublingual nitroglycerin. [An ECG image was shown - presumably ST elevation.] Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
r: An ischaemic stroke within the last 3 months is an absolute contraindication to fibrinolysis, so reperfusion must be mechanical: urgent coronary angiography with primary PCI.
n: Why not D? thrombolysis would be right for a STEMI without contraindications, but a stroke 1 month ago carries an unacceptable intracranial-haemorrhage risk.

q: A 65-year-old man with diabetes and hypertension is admitted with an extensive anterior STEMI and has successful angioplasty and stenting of the left anterior descending artery. Aspirin, clopidogrel, bisoprolol and enalapril are started. Lipids: HDL 1.0 mmol/L (>1.03), LDL 3.36 mmol/L (<3.36), total cholesterol 5.0 mmol/L (<5.1), triglycerides 2.2 mmol/L (<2.16). Which of the following is recommended?
r: Every patient after an ACS needs a high-intensity statin (atorvastatin 40-80 mg) for secondary prevention regardless of baseline LDL; the LDL target (<1.4-1.8 mmol/L) is far below his 3.36. Fibrates and niacin add no mortality benefit and are reserved for very high triglycerides (>5.6 mmol/L).
n: Why not A? 'near-normal' lipids are irrelevant after an MI; statin benefit in established ASCVD does not depend on the starting LDL.

q: A patient with hypertension, diabetes and ischaemic heart disease presents with shortness of breath and fatigue. He is haemodynamically stable. The ECG (shown) shows bradycardia [rhythm not specified in the recall]. What is the next step in management?
r: Atropine 1 mg IV (repeat every 3–5 min, max 3 mg) is the first-line drug for symptomatic bradycardia (ACLS); if it fails, use transcutaneous pacing or dopamine/adrenaline infusion.
n: Why not A? Cardioversion treats unstable tachyarrhythmias; a slow rate that does not respond to atropine is paced, not shocked. Claude: in a stable patient with no symptoms, ACLS says monitor; his dyspnoea and fatigue are why atropine is the answer here. Claud

q: A 45-year-old man presents to the Emergency Room with palpitations. Initially he is conscious and oriented. After some time he becomes less responsive and his blood pressure drops to 80/45 mmHg. ECG: supraventricular tachycardia. Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate action?
r: Any tachyarrhythmia with instability (hypotension, altered consciousness, ischaemic chest pain, acute heart failure) is treated with immediate synchronised DC cardioversion.
n: Why not C? vagal manoeuvres, adenosine or AV-nodal blockers are for the stable patient; a beta-blocker would worsen his hypotension.

q: A woman presents with weakness. An ECG image is shown, and CT shows an infarction. Heart rate 300/min. What is the cause of the stroke?
r: AF is the commonest cause of cardioembolic stroke: loss of atrial contraction causes stasis and thrombus in the left atrial appendage.
n: Why not B? flutter also embolises but is far less common; choose it only if the ECG shows regular sawtooth flutter waves. Claude: '300/min' is the classic atrial rate of flutter, so read the ECG: irregularly irregular with no P waves = AF (key); regular sawtoo

q: A woman with a past history of fleeting (migratory) joint pains, previously treated with high-dose aspirin, now presents to hospital with weakness, and an embolic stroke is suspected. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause?
r: Migratory polyarthritis treated with high-dose aspirin = rheumatic fever; rheumatic mitral stenosis enlarges the left atrium, causing AF and left-atrial thrombus that embolises to the brain.
n: Why not A? flutter can also occur with a dilated atrium, but AF is the characteristic arrhythmia of rheumatic mitral disease and the commonest embolic source.

q: A patient has absent P waves, a narrow QRS complex and a ventricular rate of 220/min (no ECG picture provided). What is the most likely diagnosis?
r: A regular narrow-complex tachycardia at 150-250/min with no visible P waves (buried in the QRS) is SVT, most often AVNRT.
n: Why not A? flutter shows sawtooth F waves at ~300/min, usually with 2:1 block giving a ventricular rate near 150, not 220. Claude: The Untitled.pdf page also prints a related Medgard item (14-month-old, regular narrow complex at 250-300/min, absent P waves) ke

q: A patient with heart failure and atrial fibrillation complains of palpitations. What is the most appropriate management?
r: Beta-blockers (carvedilol, bisoprolol, metoprolol succinate) are first-line rate control in AF with HFrEF because they also lower heart-failure mortality; non-dihydropyridine CCBs (diltiazem) are negatively inotropic and avoided.
n: Why not C? digoxin controls the resting rate without a mortality benefit; it is an add-on, or used when the patient is hypotensive/decompensated.

q: A patient has heart failure with reduced ejection fraction due to dilated cardiomyopathy. He takes sacubitril/valsartan, metoprolol, spironolactone and furosemide, and his resting heart rate stays above 70 beats/min in sinus rhythm. Which medication should be added?
r: In HFrEF with sinus rhythm and resting HR ≥70/min despite a maximally tolerated beta-blocker plus ARNI and MRA, add ivabradine (If-channel blocker; the SHIFT trial showed fewer HF hospitalisations).
n: Why not C? bisoprolol is just another beta-blocker. He is already on metoprolol, so it adds nothing, and verapamil/diltiazem are harmful in HFrEF.

q: A 70-year-old woman with known chronic heart failure presents with severe shortness of breath, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea and orthopnoea [the 4 Nov post adds lower-limb oedema]. She looks unwell; JVP is raised, there are bilateral basal crackles and an S3 at the apex. BP 110/70 mmHg, HR 100/min, SpO2 88%. Which of the following is the best next step in management?
r: Acute decompensated HF with congestion and adequate BP ('warm and wet') is treated with an IV loop diuretic. Oxygen is titrated to SpO2 94–98% rather than given as fixed 100%, and the echo can wait until she is stable.
n: Why not A? She does need oxygen, but it is supportive and titrated to target; the treatment step being tested is IV furosemide.

q: A 73-year-old woman is brought to the emergency room by her family because of a change in her level of consciousness for 1 day. She has type 2 diabetes, hypertension, ischaemic heart disease and liver cirrhosis. Examination: drowsy, raised JVP, shifting dullness (ascites) and +2 lower-limb oedema. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
r: A raised JVP with ascites and oedema in a patient with cirrhosis and IHD means total-body volume overload, so a loop diuretic is indicated and every salt-containing fluid would worsen it.
n: Why not B? normal saline is for hypovolaemia (flat JVP, postural drop); with a raised JVP it worsens ascites, oedema and pulmonary congestion. Claude: drowsiness in cirrhosis also needs a search for hepatic encephalopathy precipitants and hyponatraemia; among

q: A patient has an ejection systolic murmur that increases with inspiration and a prominent a wave in the jugular venous pulse. What is the most likely diagnosis? [Options merged: the 4 Nov post recalled tricuspid stenosis vs pulmonary stenosis; the extract lists pulmonary stenosis, pulmonary regurgitation, mitral stenosis and aortic stenosis. Alhomrani's comment about TR suggests option A may have been tricuspid regurgitation.]
r: An ejection (crescendo–decrescendo) systolic murmur that gets louder on inspiration is right-sided (Carvallo's sign); add a giant a wave from the hypertrophied, stiff RV and the diagnosis is pulmonary stenosis.
n: Why not A? Tricuspid stenosis also gives a giant a wave and a murmur louder on inspiration, but the murmur is diastolic. TR is systolic but holosystolic, not ejection (Alhomrani).

q: A 76-year-old man known to have type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension and dyslipidaemia presents to the clinic with exertional shortness of breath for 1 year. He has to slow down his walk and stop after 10 metres. He denies syncope, chest pain or palpitations. Precordial examination reveals a forceful apex beat and a crescendo-decrescendo ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotids. What is the most likely diagnosis?
r: A crescendo-decrescendo ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotids with a forceful (pressure-loaded, heaving) apex and exertional dyspnoea in an elderly man with atherosclerotic risk factors = calcific aortic stenosis; dyspnoea, angina and syncope are its classic symptoms.
n: Why not D? aortic regurgitation also gives a forceful (hyperdynamic, displaced) apex, but its murmur is early DIASTOLIC at the left sternal edge, not ejection systolic to the carotids.

q: A 60-year-old man has a 6-month history of exertional shortness of breath. Examination shows a positive Corrigan's pulse, an early diastolic murmur at the left upper sternal border and bilateral fine basal crepitations. Echocardiogram: severe aortic regurgitation with ejection fraction 40%. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
r: Severe AR needs aortic valve replacement if it is symptomatic, or if asymptomatic with LVEF ≤50–55% or a dilated LV; this patient has both symptoms and EF 40%. Vasodilators and diuretics only relieve symptoms when surgery is not possible.
n: Why not D? ACE inhibitors reduce afterload and symptoms in patients who cannot have surgery, but symptomatic severe AR with LV dysfunction needs AVR.

q: A 60-year-old man has a blood pressure of 155/90 mmHg at a routine check-up. He has no symptoms; examination, ECG, CBC, electrolytes, renal function and urinalysis are normal. What is the next step?
r: A clinic BP between 140/90 and 179/119 must be confirmed out of the office before diagnosing hypertension: ABPM is the gold standard (home monitoring if not available) and excludes white-coat hypertension (NICE NG136). With no target-organ damage there is no need to treat immediately. (Alhomrani's S
n: Why not D? another office reading in 3 months delays the diagnosis and still does not exclude the white-coat effect; out-of-office confirmation is recommended now.

q: A 50-year-old man is evaluated in the clinic for newly diagnosed hypertension that is not well controlled with lifestyle modifications. He is diabetic. Which of the following is the most appropriate management for this patient's hypertension?
r: In diabetes an ACE inhibitor (or ARB) is the preferred first-line antihypertensive, especially with albuminuria, because it slows diabetic nephropathy.
n: Why not A? Amlodipine is first-line for general hypertension, but in a diabetic the ACE inhibitor is preferred for renal protection.

q: A 50-year-old man is evaluated for newly diagnosed hypertension. He has no diabetes. Blood pressure is 168/102 mmHg. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
r: BP ≥160/100 (stage 2, more than 20/10 above target) warrants starting two first-line agents, e.g. ACE inhibitor + CCB, rather than monotherapy.
n: Why not B? Lisinopril alone suits milder hypertension; at 168/102 one drug is unlikely to reach target.

q: A woman with blood pressure between 160/80 and 170/90 mmHg was previously diagnosed with hypertension but never treated. Which complication is she most likely to develop?
r: Chronic pressure overload causes left ventricular hypertrophy, then diastolic and later systolic dysfunction; hypertension is a leading cause of heart failure (alongside stroke and CKD).
n: Why not C? cardiac amyloidosis can mimic hypertensive LVH on echo, but it is an infiltrative disease, not a consequence of high blood pressure.

q: A 71-year-old man, not diabetic, on no medication and a non-smoker, has BP 171/90 mmHg, total cholesterol 6.1 mmol/L and HDL 1.0 mmol/L. Using the risk chart provided, what is his 10-year cardiovascular risk (%)?
r: Age over 70, systolic BP above 170 and a total cholesterol:HDL ratio of ~6 put a man in the top band of the chart (>30% 10-year risk) even without diabetes or smoking; age and systolic BP drive the score.
n: Why not C? 25–29% fits a younger man or a lower systolic BP; at 71 with SBP 171 and a ratio of ~6 the chart reads above 30%.

q: A 40-year-old patient with essential hypertension is counselled about the role of physical activity in reducing cardiovascular risk. Which physical activity is recommended?
o: 30 min brisk walking 5 times a week
10 min cycling most days of the week
r: Guidelines (WHO/AHA/ESC) recommend at least 150 min/week of moderate aerobic activity, such as 30 min of brisk walking on 5 or more days a week, which lowers BP by about 5-8 mmHg.
n: Why not D? 10 min cycling on most days adds up to only ~50-70 min/week, well below the 150-minute target.

q: A 50-year-old man is 6 days after an uneventful subtotal colectomy with ileocolic anastomosis when he develops sudden shortness of breath and one episode of haemoptysis. There are mildly decreased breath sounds at the left lung base, normal S1/S2, a soft abdomen with normal bowel sounds, and no leg oedema or tenderness. CXR: left basilar atelectasis. ECG: sinus tachycardia with a new right bundle branch block. What is the most appropriate test?
r: High pre-test probability of PE (post-op day 6, sudden dyspnoea, haemoptysis, tachycardia, new RBBB) → go straight to CTPA.
n: Why not A? D-dimer is almost always raised after major surgery and only excludes PE in low-probability patients — it cannot confirm it.

q: A 50-year-old man is 6 days after an uneventful subtotal colectomy with ileocolic anastomosis when he develops sudden shortness of breath and one episode of haemoptysis. Examination shows mildly decreased breath sounds at the left lung base, normal heart sounds, a soft abdomen with normal bowel sounds, and no leg oedema or tenderness. His serum creatinine is raised. Chest X-ray shows left basal atelectasis, and the ECG shows sinus tachycardia with a new right bundle branch block. Which of the following is the most appropriate test?
r: Sudden dyspnoea, haemoptysis, tachycardia and a new RBBB after surgery give a high pre-test probability of PE, so imaging is needed, not a D-dimer. The raised creatinine makes iodinated contrast for CTPA undesirable, so a V/Q scan is the test of choice.
n: Why not C? CTPA is the usual first-line test, but the raised creatinine (risk of contrast nephropathy) is the clue that switches the answer to V/Q. Claude: Extract status Review. Claude: agree. Basal atelectasis lowers V/Q accuracy a little, but renal impairme

q: A 57-year-old man who had a total knee replacement presents on the 7th postoperative day with shortness of breath and chest pain. Examination shows swelling and warmth of the left leg. What is the initial assessment?
r: In suspected PE with clinical DVT signs, compression (Doppler) ultrasound of the leg is a quick bedside first test: a proximal DVT confirms VTE and justifies anticoagulation without lung imaging. D-dimer is useless after recent surgery because it is always raised.
n: Why not D? with high pre-test probability, LMWH is started while waiting for imaging (Alhomrani's latest file keys LMWH), but the lead-in asks for an assessment, not a treatment. Claude: Debate: Alhomrani (latest, October Combined, 22 Oct Part 5 p. 6426 #482)

q: A 22-year-old man presents to the Emergency Room with left leg swelling and pain that started 2 days ago and is getting worse, involving the whole left leg. He also complains of chest tightness and shortness of breath. Examination: pitting oedema of the left lower limb extending to the thigh. ECG: sinus tachycardia. Which of the following is the most appropriate management at this time?
r: Proximal DVT with suspected PE needs immediate parenteral anticoagulation; of these options only UFH acts at once (bolus then infusion, titrated to the aPTT).
n: Why not C? warfarin takes about 5 days to work and is initially prothrombotic (protein C depletion), so it must start overlapped with heparin, never alone.

q: A 59-year-old man is evaluated in hospital for progressive shortness of breath and hypoxia 20 hours after surgery for colonic adenocarcinoma with known liver metastases. CT angiography shows a right lower-lobe pulmonary embolism. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment?
r: LMWH (enoxaparin 1 mg/kg twice daily) is the standard initial treatment of cancer-associated PE, especially with a GI cancer and in the early post-operative period; warfarin is inferior in cancer.
n: Why not C? rivaroxaban is an accepted option for cancer VTE, but a luminal GI cancer and a fresh bowel anastomosis raise DOAC-related GI bleeding, so LMWH is preferred.

q: A 53-year-old man with ischaemic heart disease presents with sudden severe shortness of breath. He is conscious and oriented but in distress. RR 31, pulse 112, SpO2 88%. Creatinine clearance 27 mL/min (significant renal impairment). BMI 41 (morbid obesity). The picture is consistent with pulmonary embolism. Which anticoagulant regimen is most appropriate? [another examinee recalled that the same case asked about the prophylactic choice]
r: With CrCl <30 mL/min, renally cleared LMWH and fondaparinux are avoided, so unfractionated heparin is used, and with a BMI of 40 or more the higher dose (7500 units SC every 8 hours) is needed.
n: Why not C? enoxaparin 40 mg twice daily is the obesity regimen only with normal renal function; at CrCl 27 it accumulates and raises bleeding risk. Claude: all the doses offered are prophylactic, so read it as 'VTE prophylaxis in morbid obesity with CrCl <30';

q: A patient with atrial fibrillation on warfarin has an INR of 7.0 and no bleeding. What is the most appropriate management?
o: Continue the current dose and repeat INR in 1 week
Reduce the weekly dose and repeat INR in 1 week
Hold warfarin and repeat INR the next day
r: At INR 7 without bleeding, omit warfarin and recheck promptly, then resume at a lower dose; a simple dose reduction is not enough once INR is above ~4.5–5.
n: Why not B? Dose reduction alone suits a mildly raised INR (<4.5–5); at 7 the drug must be held first. Claude: Bank options were dose changes (no reversal agents); the distractors here are reconstructed.

q: A 62-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation was started on warfarin. A few weeks later she falls and develops a subdural haematoma that requires evacuation. INR 3.9. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
o: Fresh frozen plasma and vitamin K
r: Life-threatening or intracranial bleeding on warfarin needs immediate replacement of clotting factors (4-factor PCC preferred, FFP if PCC is unavailable) plus IV vitamin K 5-10 mg to sustain the reversal.
n: Why not B? FFP alone reverses quickly but transiently (factor VII half-life ~6 h); without vitamin K the INR rebounds. Claude: PCC plus vitamin K would be the best answer if offered; recombinant factor VIIa is not recommended for warfarin reversal.

q: A 38-year-old physically active woman has had 3 unprovoked lower-limb DVTs over 2 years. She has migraine and is on warfarin. Examination shows skin rashes (livedo reticularis in the photo). Labs: BMI 29, platelets 100 ×10⁹/L, WBC 6, Hb 130 g/L, ANA negative. What is the cause of her recurrent DVT? [the slide also mentioned pregnancy loss]
r: Recurrent unprovoked thrombosis + livedo reticularis + migraine + mild thrombocytopenia (± pregnancy loss) = APS; ANA negative points to primary APS. Confirm with lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin and anti-β2-glycoprotein I positive twice ≥12 weeks apart; long-term warfarin (INR 2–3).
n: Why not B? Inherited protein S deficiency causes venous thrombosis but not livedo, migraine or thrombocytopenia.

q: A smoker (not stated whether already diagnosed with COPD) complains of dyspnoea. Which investigation is most appropriate?
r: Suspected COPD (smoker with dyspnoea) is confirmed by spirometry: post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC <0.70 (GOLD).
n: Why not A? a chest X-ray helps exclude other causes but cannot diagnose COPD; airflow limitation has to be measured.

q: A 60-year-old man has symptoms suggestive of COPD [not yet diagnosed]. He smoked for 40 years and stopped 5 years ago. What is the next step?
r: COPD has not been diagnosed yet, so it needs confirming. Spirometry would be the test but isn't offered, and HRCT can show emphysema or airway disease when spirometry isn't available. Alpha-1 antitrypsin testing comes after COPD is diagnosed.
n: Why not C? an AAT level is for a patient with DIAGNOSED COPD (WHO/GOLD advise screening such patients once); it doesn't establish COPD. Claude: post-bronchodilator spirometry (FEV1/FVC <0.7) is the real diagnostic test; choose it if it is offered.

q: A 60–69-year-old man with diagnosed COPD has had chronic cough with whitish sputum and progressive shortness of breath for 3–4 years, with no new complaint. Vitals are stable; WBC 3.8 ×10⁹/L, temperature 36.6 °C. [Lead-in not recalled. The extract gives age 69 and 3 years; the 4 Nov post gives age ~60 and 4 years.] What is the most appropriate next step?
r: WHO and GOLD recommend testing every patient with COPD once for alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, whatever the age or smoking history. A stable, afebrile patient with normal WBC and unchanged sputum has no indication for culture, bronchoscopy or HRCT.
n: Why not C? Sputum culture is for exacerbations or suspected infection; he is afebrile with a normal WBC and no change in his usual sputum. Claude: Key is 'by review' only. The examinee could not recall the lead-in.

q: A man in his 60s with known COPD controlled on bronchodilators comes for routine follow-up. He quit smoking 12 years ago. Oxygen saturation ranges from 89% to 91%. What is the most appropriate management?
r: All COPD patients should receive pneumococcal (and annual influenza) vaccination; long-term oxygen is indicated only for resting SpO2 88% or less / PaO2 55 mmHg or less (up to 59 mmHg with cor pulmonale or haematocrit >55%).
n: Why not C? a resting SpO2 of 89-91% does not meet LTOT criteria, and oxygen at this level gives no survival benefit (LOTT trial).

q: A patient with COPD comes to the ER with productive cough, shortness of breath and fever. Chest X-ray is clear. What do you give?
r: This is an infective exacerbation (productive sputum + fever, no pneumonia on CXR), so give a short-acting bronchodilator plus antibiotics. GOLD gives antibiotics when sputum purulence comes with more dyspnea or more sputum, or when ventilation is needed. (Alhomrani U2874; GOLD page U2876.)
n: Why not C? SABA + systemic steroids is the backbone of most exacerbations, but this stem stresses infection, so the pair that includes antibiotics is chosen. Claude: in practice all three are given (SABA, prednisolone 40 mg for 5 days, and an antibiotic if the

q: A patient with an acute COPD exacerbation has received nebulized SABA and SAMA and antibiotics, but no oxygen. He has no confusion or CNS symptoms, his gag reflex is present, and there is no other indication for intubation. ABG: pH 7.18, PaCO2 65, PaO2 55, SpO2 70%. What is the next step?
r: Acute hypercapnic respiratory acidosis (pH ≤7.35, PaCO2 >45) in AECOPD calls for non-invasive positive pressure ventilation (BiPAP). A pH <7.25 is not by itself an intubation criterion; it means NIV in ICU/HDU with a low threshold to intubate. Intubation is for NIV failure or intolerance, coma, arre
n: Why not D? the old file key used 'pH <7.25 = intubate' (GOLD 2006–2010 era); with the gag reflex present and no CNS signs, NIV comes first. Claude: Alhomrani (U2903): 'pH <7.25 an indication for intubation? In short: NO… BiPAP is correct, CPAP is wrong, PPV? I

q: A 54-year-old man presents to the Emergency Room with an acute exacerbation of COPD. Examination shows use of accessory muscles, a diminished gag reflex, and decreased breath sounds with wheeze throughout both lungs. Oxygen, glucocorticoids, antibiotics and nebulisers are started [laboratory panel not captured in the recall]. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: Close observation for the next 4-6 hours
Increase oxygen to 100% by non-rebreather mask
r: A diminished gag reflex means he cannot protect his airway, which contraindicates NIV, so he needs intubation and invasive ventilation.
n: Why not A? NIV is first-line for a hypercapnic COPD exacerbation (pH <7.35), but only in a patient who is alert and can protect the airway.

q: A 49-year-old woman is evaluated for a 4-month history of dry cough that began with paroxysmal, persistent coughing spells that make it difficult to carry on a conversation. She was initially diagnosed with allergic rhinitis and started on a glucocorticoid nasal spray, without improvement. History is otherwise unremarkable except for dust allergy. Vital signs are normal; there is slight nasal congestion and a dry cough; cardiovascular, pulmonary and abdominal examinations are normal. Chest radiograph: normal. Spirometry: slightly reduced FEV1/FVC ratio of 70%, which increased by 20% after bronchodilator. Which of the following is the most appropriate diagnostic test to perform next?
r: Chronic cough with a normal chest X-ray that does not respond to treatment of rhinitis suggests cough-variant asthma; bronchial provocation (methacholine challenge) demonstrates airway hyper-responsiveness and has a high negative predictive value.
n: Why not A? skin-prick testing identifies allergic triggers but does not diagnose asthma. Claude: if spirometry truly showed 20% bronchodilator reversibility, asthma is already proven; the classic version of this item has normal spirometry, which is when methac

q: A 24-year-old woman is reviewed in the asthma clinic. She uses salbutamol 100 mcg as needed plus beclometasone dipropionate 400 mcg twice daily. Despite this she has frequent exacerbations requiring repeated courses of prednisolone and three hospitalisations in the last 6 months. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
r: Uncontrolled on a medium-dose ICS (after checking adherence and inhaler technique), the next step is adding a LABA as ICS-LABA combination; a LABA is never used without an ICS.
n: Why not D? tiotropium is a later add-on (step 4-5) for patients still uncontrolled on ICS-LABA.

q: A 45-year-old man with type 2 diabetes who smokes presents to the ER with 3 days of fever and productive yellow sputum. There are decreased breath sounds and crackles at the right base, and CXR shows a right lower lobe infiltrate. What is the most appropriate management?
r: CURB-65 is 0, but his comorbidity (diabetes; smoking, per Alhomrani) makes an outpatient macrolide alone inadequate, so he needs a β-lactam plus a macrolide. With no outpatient dual-therapy option, ceftriaxone + azithromycin is the best available choice. (Alhomrani U2927.)
n: Why not D? cefuroxime alone lacks atypical cover; the dual option (cefuroxime + azithromycin) was only in the Gameboy copy.

q: A 45-year-old man with type 2 diabetes who smokes presents to the ER with 3 days of fever and productive yellow sputum. There are decreased breath sounds and crackles at the right base, and CXR shows a right lower lobe infiltrate. What is the most appropriate management?
r: CURB-65 of 0 allows outpatient treatment, and his comorbidity (diabetes) calls for combination therapy: an oral β-lactam (cefuroxime or amoxicillin-clavulanate) plus a macrolide (ATS/IDSA 2019).
n: Why not A? admission for IV therapy is unnecessary at CURB-65 of 0 when an adequate oral dual regimen is offered.

q: A diabetic patient in the ICU is being treated with azithromycin for severe community-acquired pneumonia. Which additional antibiotic is most appropriate?
r: Severe (ICU) CAP without MRSA or Pseudomonas risk factors: a β-lactam (ceftriaxone, cefotaxime or ampicillin-sulbactam) plus either a macrolide or a respiratory fluoroquinolone (ATS/IDSA 2019). The macrolide is already running, so add the β-lactam.
n: Why not B? Moxifloxacin can replace the macrolide in a β-lactam combination, but macrolide + fluoroquinolone leaves out the β-lactam backbone that severe CAP needs. Claude: The 4 Nov post recalled only two options: moxifloxacin and ceftriaxone.

q: A 52-year-old man recently returned from a holiday abroad was diagnosed with pneumonia and failed to respond to a course of amoxicillin. On admission he has cough, myalgia and abdominal pain; chest X-ray shows bilateral basal opacities. His GCS drops to 11. Temperature 38.5 °C, SpO2 91%, Na 118 mmol/L, creatinine 180 µmol/L. Which of the following is the cause?
r: Travel (hotel water systems), failure of a beta-lactam, GI symptoms, confusion, hyponatraemia and AKI are classic Legionella; diagnose with the urinary antigen and treat with a macrolide or fluoroquinolone.
n: Why not D? ANCA vasculitis gives a pulmonary-renal syndrome (haemoptysis, active urinary sediment), but not a travel-related pneumonia with confusion, abdominal pain and Na 118.

q: A 55-year-old woman is referred because of a 1 cm solitary nodule with sharp borders in the right lung, found on an abdominal CT done for abdominal pain. She has no respiratory complaints. She smoked 20 cigarettes per day for 10 years but stopped 20 years ago. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
r: A smooth solid nodule of ~1 cm in a low-to-intermediate-risk patient gets repeat CT at about 3 months (Fleischner: >8 mm → CT at 3 months, PET-CT or sampling); stability for 2 years means it is benign.
n: Why not D? Resection is for nodules with a high probability of malignancy (spiculated, growing, PET-avid); a sharp-bordered nodule in a remote ex-smoker gets surveillance first.

q: A 61-year-old woman is evaluated for a left pulmonary nodule discovered incidentally 2 months ago. She is asymptomatic (no dyspnoea, fever, chills, weight loss or night sweats), takes no medications and has never smoked. There is no cervical or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy and the lungs are clear. CT chest: 8 mm left lung nodule [a 4 Nov examinee recalled 0.5 cm]. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
r: A small (≤8 mm) solid nodule in a low-risk never-smoker is followed with CT (Fleischner: 6–8 mm, low risk → CT at 6–12 months then 18–24 months; <6 mm → no routine follow-up). PET is unreliable below ~8 mm.
n: Why not A? PET/CT is for solid nodules >8 mm at intermediate risk; at this size it is insensitive and not the next step.

q: A 70-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with increasing shortness of breath and a productive cough for 5 months. He has smoked for over 50 years. Over these 5 months he has had malaise, night sweats and fever, and he has lost 10 kg over the last 3 months. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
r: A heavy smoker aged 70 with months of cough, dyspnoea, constitutional symptoms and marked weight loss has lung cancer until proven otherwise (TB is the main differential and is not offered).
n: Why not B? pneumonia is an acute illness; a 5-month course with 10 kg weight loss points to malignancy (or a post-obstructive pneumonia caused by it).

q: A 63-year-old man is evaluated in the Emergency Room for 1 week of progressive shortness of breath and is found to have a right pleural effusion on chest X-ray. Aspiration yields clear transudative fluid. Which of the following is the most likely cause?
r: Heart failure is the commonest cause of a transudate (Light's criteria negative); its effusions are usually bilateral or right-sided.
n: Why not D? malignant effusions are exudates (often bloody), as are parapneumonic and pancreatic (left-sided, high amylase) effusions.

q: A patient presents with progressive dyspnoea for 3 months, with decreased tactile fremitus and decreased air entry on the right side (pleural effusion). He is vitally stable and liver enzymes are within normal limits. What is the cause?
r: A unilateral effusion developing over months in a stable patient with normal liver tests is most likely a tuberculous exudate (lymphocytic, high ADA), a very common cause in the region.
n: Why not C? heart-failure effusions are usually bilateral, with orthopnoea, raised JVP and oedema, none of which is described.

q: A 61-year-old obese man presents with daytime somnolence, poor concentration, nocturia and progressive shortness of breath. Examination shows an obese patient with bilateral lower-limb oedema and normal vesicular breath sounds. Which investigation is most appropriate to establish the diagnosis?
r: Obesity with daytime sleepiness, poor concentration and nocturia suggests obstructive sleep apnoea (with obesity hypoventilation and cor pulmonale explaining the oedema); overnight polysomnography is diagnostic.
n: Why not C? echocardiography would show the consequence (pulmonary hypertension, right heart strain) but not the underlying sleep-disordered breathing.

q: A 58-year-old man with diabetes, hypertension and dyslipidaemia presents with 2 days of cough, fever and vomiting. He is admitted to the ICU, and right-heart catheterisation shows low CVP, low PCWP, low cardiac output, high SVR and low mixed venous saturation. Temperature 38 °C, BP 128/89, HR 120, RR 18; Hb 132, WBC 19, platelets not recalled, creatinine 60, CRP 120. What type of shock is this?
r: Low preload (low CVP and PCWP) with low cardiac output, compensatory high SVR and low SvO2 is the hypovolaemic profile, here from vomiting and poor intake; cardiogenic shock has a high PCWP and obstructive shock a high CVP.
n: Why not C? fever, WBC 19 and CRP 120 tempt 'septic', but distributive shock has a low SVR with normal/high cardiac output and high SvO2, the opposite of these numbers.

q: A man is brought in after a road traffic accident with low blood pressure and a low heart rate, consistent with neurogenic shock. What should be given first?
r: Hypotension with bradycardia after trauma suggests neurogenic shock (loss of sympathetic tone). Give IV crystalloid first, after looking for haemorrhage, then vasopressors (e.g. norepinephrine) ± atropine if the patient does not respond.
n: Why not B? O-negative blood is for haemorrhagic shock, which causes tachycardia; bradycardia points away from blood loss as the cause. Claude: neurogenic shock is a diagnosis of exclusion in trauma, so still look for bleeding.

q: A 12-year-old patient presents with diarrhoea, vomiting, miosis, bronchoconstriction, sweating, lacrimation and excessive salivation. The breath has a garlic odour. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
r: Cholinergic toxidrome (SLUDGE/DUMBELS: salivation, lacrimation, urination, diarrhoea, emesis, bronchorrhoea, bradycardia, miosis) with a garlic odour = organophosphate poisoning; treat with atropine to dry the secretions plus pralidoxime.
n: Why not C? Cyanide smells of bitter almonds and causes lactic acidosis, seizures and collapse, without cholinergic secretions or miosis.

q: A 19-year-old woman presents with vomiting and dehydration. She is conscious but distressed and admits to methamphetamine overuse. Her sodium is low. Which known complication of her drug abuse is this? [one option not recalled]
r: Amphetamine-type stimulants (classically MDMA/ecstasy) cause hyponatraemia through ADH release and excessive water drinking, on top of losses from vomiting, so this acute presentation is an electrolyte disturbance. (Alhomrani's Sept page)
n: Why not B? stimulants can cause AKI (rhabdomyolysis, severe hypertension), but CKD is a chronic outcome and does not explain acute vomiting with low sodium.

q: A woman taking isotretinoin for acne wishes to conceive. What should the physician tell her about the appropriate timing?
o: She can conceive as soon as she stops isotretinoin
She can conceive while taking isotretinoin
She can conceive 3 months after stopping isotretinoin
She can conceive 1 month after stopping isotretinoin
r: Isotretinoin is highly teratogenic but cleared quickly, so contraception is required for 1 month before, during and 1 month after treatment (iPLEDGE, MHRA); conception is safe after that month.
n: Why not C? 3 months is not the isotretinoin rule; longer waits belong to other drugs (e.g. acitretin, 3 years). Claude: Recall file (SMLE_Questions.pdf Q158) ticked C (3 months).

q: A patient has typical GERD symptoms with mild improvement on antacids. Which lifestyle modification is most strongly recommended? [no symptom timing, e.g. nocturnal, was mentioned]
o: Avoid eating within 30 minutes before sleep
r: Alhomrani's quiz key is head-of-bed elevation; ACG 2022 lifestyle advice is weight loss if overweight, no meals 2-3 h before bed, and head-of-bed elevation for night-time symptoms.
n: Why not A? Avoiding lying down after eating is the bank answer when head elevation is not offered (twin q09118), but Alhomrani rates head-of-bed elevation as more strongly recommended. Claude: Recall gave only the question; options/key come from Alhomrani's N4

q: A patient has epigastric pain and burning (GERD). What lifestyle advice do you give?
r: Avoid lying down for 2-3 hours after meals, raise the head of the bed, lose weight and avoid late, large meals, so that gravity keeps acid in the stomach.
n: Why not C? fewer meals means larger meals that distend the stomach and promote reflux; small, frequent meals are advised.

q: A 38-year-old man with a 10-year history of gastro-oesophageal reflux disease on pantoprazole is evaluated in the clinic for a 4-month history of intermittent dysphagia to solids. What is the most appropriate next investigation?
r: Dysphagia is an alarm symptom in long-standing GERD (peptic stricture, eosinophilic oesophagitis, Barrett's/adenocarcinoma), so upper endoscopy with biopsy, which can also dilate a stricture, comes first.
n: Why not C? barium swallow is kept for suspected rings, complex strictures or motility disorders and cannot take a biopsy.

q: A patient has a positive test for Helicobacter pylori. Which of the following should be given?
r: Where clarithromycin resistance is high (as in Saudi Arabia), first-line eradication is bismuth quadruple therapy: PPI + bismuth + metronidazole + tetracycline for 14 days.
n: Why not D? a levofloxacin-based triple is a second-line/rescue regimen, and as written it lacks the PPI.

q: A 40-year-old woman is being treated for a recurrent Helicobacter pylori-associated duodenal ulcer. She notices that her stools have turned black but are not tarry. BP 110/70 mmHg, HR 70/min, Hb 152 g/L. Which drug is the likely cause of the black stools?
r: Bismuth (part of quadruple therapy for recurrent H. pylori) forms bismuth sulfide in the gut, turning stool and tongue black; non-tarry stool with normal Hb and vital signs separates it from melaena.
n: Why not D? aluminium hydroxide causes constipation (magnesium salts cause diarrhoea), not black stools.

q: A patient presents with sudden severe epigastric pain with vomiting and epigastric tenderness; no enzyme results are given. Which investigation confirms the diagnosis?
r: Lipase >3× the upper limit with typical pain confirms acute pancreatitis; it is more specific than amylase and stays elevated longer, so imaging is not needed for the diagnosis.
n: Why not B? CRP grades severity at 48 h; it cannot establish the diagnosis. Claude: Two bank look-alikes (q10743, q11021) share this wording.

q: A patient presents with sudden severe epigastric pain for 8 hours with nausea and vomiting. There is epigastric tenderness; amylase is 600. Which marker is most helpful to determine the severity of the disease?
r: CRP >150 mg/L at ~48 h is the standard single biochemical predictor of severe acute pancreatitis; amylase/lipase confirm the diagnosis but their level does not track severity.
n: Why not A? Procalcitonin helps flag infected necrosis, but it is not the routine severity marker. Claude: 2 Nov recall (#87979) options: procalcitonin / CRP / ESR / alkaline phosphatase.

q: A 30-year-old patient presents to the Emergency Department with 8 hours of severe upper abdominal pain not relieved by oral medication. He has had recurrent similar episodes over the last year, relieved by antispasmodics and anti-inflammatories. Examination: jaundiced, soft abdomen with marked right hypochondrial tenderness. BP 110/70, HR 110, RR 18, T 37.9 °C. Labs: WBC 16 ×10^9/L, indirect bilirubin 5, direct bilirubin 15, total bilirubin 20 µmol/L (3.5-16.5), ALP 400 IU/L (39-117), amylase 115 IU/L (24-151). Ultrasound: CBD 1.1 cm with dilated intrahepatic ducts. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
r: Charcot's triad (RUQ pain, fever/leucocytosis, jaundice) with a cholestatic picture (high ALP, conjugated bilirubin) and a dilated CBD = ascending cholangitis, usually from a CBD stone; treat with IV antibiotics and ERCP.
n: Why not D? acute cholecystitis gives RUQ pain, fever and Murphy's sign, but not obstructive jaundice with a dilated CBD and intrahepatic ducts.

q: A 45-year-old has 2 weeks of recurrent upper abdominal pain with fever. He is jaundiced with marked tenderness all over the abdomen. BP 90/60, HR 130, T 38 °C. Direct bilirubin 20, ALP 450, amylase 1400. US: CBD 1.4 cm with intrahepatic duct dilatation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
r: Abdullah's exam file keys, and the comment with 4 likes agreed: an amylase of 1400 (about 10× normal) defines acute (gallstone) pancreatitis, here with a stone obstructing the CBD.
n: Why not B? fever, jaundice and pain with a dilated CBD (Charcot's triad) plus shock also fits cholangitis; one comment argued for it. Claude: Clinically this looks like gallstone pancreatitis with ascending cholangitis; if the exam asks for the 'most urgent pr

q: A 28-year-old woman presents with intermittent diarrhoea, abdominal bloating, recurrent aphthous mouth ulcers and multiple joint pains (arthralgias). Laboratory tests show microcytic anaemia. What is the best INITIAL diagnostic test?
r: Bloating, diarrhoea, aphthous ulcers, arthralgia and iron deficiency in a young woman suggest coeliac disease; the initial test is IgA tTG (with total IgA, on a gluten-containing diet).
n: Why not D? duodenal biopsy is the confirmatory (gold-standard) test, done after positive serology, not the initial one. Claude: Alhomrani (23 Oct, post #1847) chose (colonoscopy with ileal biopsy, reading it as Crohn's); the extract and recall keep A. Claude:

q: What is the confirmatory test for coeliac disease?
r: Anti-tTG IgA (with total IgA) is the screening test; the diagnosis is confirmed by multiple duodenal biopsies on a gluten-containing diet showing villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia and intraepithelial lymphocytes. (comment.)
n: Why not B? tTG-IgA is the best initial/screening test, not the confirmatory one. Claude: Recall gave only the answer; the other options were added for practice.

q: A 44-year-old man has an abnormal blood test but is otherwise asymptomatic, with no family history of GI malignancy. Hb is low, MCV low and MCH low. What is the next step?
r: Unexplained (presumed iron-deficiency) microcytic anaemia in a man needs bidirectional endoscopy (OGD + colonoscopy) to exclude occult GI blood loss, mainly gastric or colorectal cancer; a negative family history does not remove that need.
n: Why not B? coeliac serology belongs in every IDA work-up (BSG), but it does not replace endoscopy in a man, in whom GI malignancy must be excluded. Claude: in practice ferritin/iron studies should confirm iron deficiency first; neither option offers it.

q: A 35-year-old man has chronic diarrhoea, steatorrhoea and weight loss. Endoscopic biopsy shows blunting of the villi (subtotal villous atrophy). What is the most likely diagnosis?
r: Malabsorption with villous blunting (subtotal villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, intra-epithelial lymphocytes) is the hallmark of celiac disease; confirm with anti-tTG IgA and the response to a gluten-free diet.
n: Why not B? Whipple's also causes steatorrhoea and weight loss, but its defining biopsy finding is PAS-positive foamy macrophages, usually with arthralgia, fever or neurological signs.

q: A patient has altered bowel habits and a rash over the elbows. What is the most likely diagnosis?
r: An itchy rash on the extensor elbows with bowel symptoms suggests dermatitis herpetiformis, the skin manifestation of celiac disease (IgA deposits in the dermal papillae; responds to a gluten-free diet and dapsone).
n: Why not B? Crohn's has skin manifestations too (erythema nodosum, pyoderma gangrenosum), but they are on the shins, not the elbows. Claude: Recall gave only the answer; the other options were added for practice.

q: A man travelled to Indonesia and Thailand 1 year ago and now complains of chronic, foul-smelling diarrhoea for 6 months without abdominal pain. CBC shows low Hb with high MCV (macrocytic anaemia). Tongue examination shows a thick, smooth tongue (glossitis) [as recalled]. What is the diagnosis?
r: Chronic malabsorptive diarrhoea that starts after time in the tropics (South-East Asia, India, Caribbean), with folate/B12-deficiency megaloblastic anaemia and glossitis, is tropical sprue; treat with tetracycline plus folic acid.
n: Why not C? coeliac disease also causes steatorrhoea, but it typically gives iron-deficiency (microcytic) anaemia and has no link to tropical travel.

q: A man in his early twenties presents with intermittent diarrhoea and abdominal pain. Colonoscopy with biopsy shows linear ulcers, segmental strictures and skip lesions, with inflamed areas alternating with normal mucosa. What is the most likely diagnosis?
r: Skip lesions, deep linear (serpiginous) ulcers and strictures reflect transmural, discontinuous inflammation, which is Crohn's disease.
n: Why not A? ulcerative colitis is continuous from the rectum and mucosal only, so it does not cause skip lesions or strictures.

q: A 67-year-old man with known HCV cirrhosis is admitted to the ER with massive haematemesis; variceal bleeding is suspected. He is drowsy with tense ascites. BP 110/70 mmHg, HR 86/min, SpO2 95%. Hb 8, INR 1.3. Which management option gives the greatest reduction in this patient's mortality? [Sept examinee's copy (#87965): the patient was unstable (tachycardia, hypotension); options ceftriaxone, PPI, octreotide, packed RBCs]
r: In cirrhotic upper GI bleeding, short-term antibiotic prophylaxis (IV ceftriaxone 1 g/day for up to 7 days) reduces bacterial infection, rebleeding and mortality, making it the intervention with proven survival benefit; vasoactive drugs and endoscopic banding control the bleed.
n: Why not A? octreotide is the first drug to control variceal bleeding and should be started, but its mortality benefit is weaker than that of antibiotic prophylaxis. Claude: Sept copy (#87965): unstable (tachycardic, hypotensive) patient with options ceftriaxon

q: A 55-year-old man with liver cirrhosis is admitted with massive upper gastrointestinal bleeding. In addition to volume restoration, which intravenous medication is recommended before upper GI endoscopy?
r: For suspected variceal bleeding, start a vasoactive drug (octreotide or terlipressin) and IV antibiotic prophylaxis (ceftriaxone) before endoscopy, then band ligation within 12 h.
n: Why not D? Vasopressin also lowers portal flow but causes coronary and mesenteric ischaemia, so octreotide or terlipressin replaced it; propranolol is for prophylaxis, never the acute bleed.

q: A man in his 50s with cirrhosis had hematemesis followed by altered consciousness. He is drowsy but arousable and hemodynamically unstable. What is the next step?
r: For a suspected variceal bleed with instability: resuscitate (large-bore access, cross-match, restrictive transfusion to Hb 7–8), then start a vasoactive drug (octreotide/terlipressin) plus ceftriaxone prophylaxis, with endoscopy within 12 h.
n: Why not D? intubation is for airway protection when consciousness is severely reduced or hematemesis is massive; a 'drowsy but arousable' patient doesn't need it yet, and lactulose isn't the urgent step.

q: A man in his 50s with liver cirrhosis has hematemesis, then becomes drowsy but arousable; he appears unstable. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: IV octreotide, blood grouping and cross-match
r: Abdullah's file keys D: an unstable variceal bleeder with a falling level of consciousness (hepatic encephalopathy) needs airway protection before endoscopy, plus lactulose.
n: Why not C? octreotide and cross-matching are essential too, but the airway comes first in a drowsy patient with hematemesis.

q: An alcoholic patient presents with haematemesis. What is the cause? [only two options recalled]
r: In a chronic alcoholic, haematemesis classically comes from oesophageal varices due to portal hypertension from cirrhosis; Budd–Chiari is hepatic vein thrombosis in prothrombotic states, not a complication of alcohol.
n: Why not B? Budd–Chiari also causes portal hypertension and varices, but it needs a prothrombotic state (myeloproliferative disease, OCP), not alcohol. Claude: If 'Mallory–Weiss tear' appears and the stem has retching before the bleed, choose it.

q: A patient with no past medical history presents with active, painless, bright-red rectal bleeding. Haemoglobin is below 7 g/dL and blood pressure is below 90/60 mmHg. What is the next step?
o: CT angiography to diagnose the cause
Nasogastric tube to rule out upper GI bleeding
r: A haemodynamically unstable bleed is resuscitated first, with transfusion for Hb <7 g/dL and shock; because ~10-15% of brisk haematochezia with shock comes from an upper source, an IV PPI is started pending endoscopy.
n: Why not A? CT angiography localises active bleeding, but only after resuscitation; a hypotensive patient with Hb <7 needs blood first. Claude: Recall file (SMLE_Questions.pdf Q190) printed 'D. Transfuse 2 units packed RBC and IV crystalloid' - different option

q: A 43-year-old medically free woman presents to the clinic after a single episode of maroon-coloured stool. She has had three previous episodes of gastrointestinal bleeding from an unknown source. She is vitally stable with no abdominal symptoms and no other complaints. What is the most appropriate next investigation?
r: Recurrent bleeding from an unidentified source is often from missed upper lesions (Cameron erosions, Dieulafoy lesion, angiodysplasia), and maroon stool can come from a brisk upper source, so the key starts with upper endoscopy.
n: Why not D? colonoscopy is the usual first test for maroon stool in a stable patient (the recall file's and Alhomrani's pick) and is done next if the upper endoscopy is negative. Claude: Recall file (Untitled.pdf p. 1) ticked D; Alhomrani (23 Oct, post #1294) a

q: A 43-year-old man with hepatitis B infection presents with fever and confusion. He is disoriented, with asterixis and shifting dullness. Ascitic fluid: SAAG 1.2 g/dL and 350 neutrophils/mm³ [4 Nov post: 400 polymorphs]; culture pending. Which of the following is the best management?
o: Oral lactulose and sedation with diazepam
High volume ascitic fluid aspiration and propranolol
r: Ascitic neutrophils ≥250/mm³ = spontaneous bacterial peritonitis: start an IV third-generation cephalosporin without waiting for culture (plus albumin). The asterixis and confusion are hepatic encephalopathy precipitated by the infection, so add lactulose.
n: Why not C? Lactulose treats the encephalopathy, but benzodiazepine sedation worsens it and the SBP goes untreated.

q: A patient with cirrhosis due to autoimmune hepatitis has hepatic encephalopathy. What should be avoided in the diet?
r: Dietary protein is the nitrogen source for gut-derived ammonia, so the traditional exam answer for hepatic encephalopathy is protein restriction.
n: Why not A? fat is limited for cholestatic steatorrhoea (see the twin), not for encephalopathy. Claude: current AASLD/EASL guidance does NOT restrict protein in HE (1.2-1.5 g/kg/day, vegetable/dairy protein preferred) because sarcopenia worsens HE; the exam sti

q: A 32-year-old obese diabetic has elevated liver enzymes (ALT/AST ~100 in the full recall), a large liver with many hypoechoic spots and a positive ANA. What is the treatment?
r: Obesity, diabetes and a mild transaminase rise = NAFLD/NASH; a low-titre ANA is common in NAFLD and doesn't mean autoimmune hepatitis. Treat with 7–10% weight loss plus a NASH drug such as vitamin E.
n: Why not A? steroids are for autoimmune hepatitis (high ALT and IgG, high-titre ANA, interface hepatitis on biopsy), which this is not. Claude: Alhomrani: 'we need numbers, not just high LFT'; the full Nov 2025 recall had ALT/AST ~100 and a clear NASH profile.

q: A 34-year-old woman with SLE on hydroxychloroquine has had jaundice for 2 months with pruritus and fatigue; she is obese with hepatomegaly. AST 654, ALT 734, ALP 129, GGT 60, glucose 7; US shows an enlarged liver with coarse echotexture; viral serology is negative; ANA 1:640; biopsy shows interface hepatitis with plasma cells. What is the next step?
r: Very high aminotransferases, a high-titre ANA and plasma-cell interface hepatitis = autoimmune hepatitis, treated with prednisolone (± azathioprine).
n: Why not C? obesity tempts NASH, but NASH doesn't produce ALT >700, ANA 1:640 and plasma-cell interface hepatitis.

q: An asymptomatic, well blood donor (blood transfusions 10 years ago) has normal LFTs (AST 20, ALT 22). Serology: HBsAg positive, anti-HBs negative, anti-HBc IgG positive, anti-HBc IgM negative, HBeAg positive, anti-HBe negative. Which is the most accurate interpretation?
r: HBsAg positive with IgG (not IgM) anti-HBc means ongoing chronic HBV infection; normal ALT in an asymptomatic carrier makes it the non-active phase among these options.
n: Why not C? immunity (vaccine or resolved infection) means anti-HBs positive with HBsAg negative, the exact opposite of this panel. Claude: Disputed: Alhomrani's 17 Sep slide printed 'immunisation from previous infection', which a positive HBsAg rules out. Clau

q: Serology: HBsAg positive, anti-HBc IgG positive, HBeAg positive. What does it indicate?
o: Chronic hepatitis B with active replication
r: HBsAg with IgG anti-HBc = chronic infection; HBeAg positive = high replication/infectivity (poster's answer).
n: Why not A? acute infection has IgM anti-HBc.

q: A 40-year-old with a blood transfusion 20 years ago is well. HBsAg +, anti-HBs −, anti-HBc IgG +, IgM −, HBeAg −, anti-HBe +, ALT/AST normal. What is the next step?
r: Inactive chronic carrier (HBeAg-negative, normal ALT) → monitor ALT and HBV DNA, no treatment.
n: Why not A? tenofovir is for active hepatitis (high DNA and ALT, or cirrhosis).

q: A man presents to the emergency department with icterus and jaundice. Serology: anti-HAV IgM positive, anti-HAV IgG positive; anti-HBs positive, HBsAg negative, anti-HBc negative, HBeAg negative. What is the diagnosis?
o: Acute hepatitis A with immunisation against hepatitis B
Acute hepatitis A with previous hepatitis B infection
r: IgM anti-HAV = acute hepatitis A; anti-HBs alone, with negative HBsAg and anti-HBc, is the pattern of hepatitis B vaccination.
n: Why not D? immunity from past HBV infection carries anti-HBc (IgG) as well as anti-HBs; a negative anti-HBc means the anti-HBs is vaccine-derived.

q: A patient with 8 months of fatigue has positive HCV with a viral load of 2 million IU/mL and a normal abdominal ultrasound. What is the next step in investigation?
o: Test for co-infection with hepatitis B
r: Before DAA therapy, every HCV patient needs HBV testing (HBsAg, anti-HBc) and HIV testing, because HBV can reactivate on DAAs, plus non-invasive fibrosis assessment (FibroScan). Alhomrani says A and C are equally correct (EASL grade 1A for both; AASLD 1A for FibroScan, 2B for HBV); A is the file key
n: Why not C? FibroScan is just as guideline-backed and Alhomrani accepts it ('8 months' may hint at chronicity and fibrosis), but HBV co-infection testing is the file's key. Claude: Alhomrani's final answer: 'I don't know, both HBV & FibroScan are EQUALLY correc

q: A patient with chronic hepatitis C infection and cirrhosis presents with a mildly elevated bilirubin and other mildly abnormal liver function tests. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: Direct-acting antiviral therapy for hepatitis C
Observation and repeat liver function tests
r: All patients with chronic HCV, cirrhotics most of all, should receive pangenotypic direct-acting antivirals (e.g. sofosbuvir/velpatasvir), which cure >95% and lower decompensation and HCC risk; HCC surveillance continues afterwards.
n: Why not C? mildly abnormal LFTs do not justify watchful waiting, because untreated HCV keeps driving fibrosis, decompensation and HCC.

q: A 60-year-old man presents with jaundice for 2 months. Examination reveals a nodular enlarged liver. CT: cirrhotic liver with two lesions in the right lobe measuring 4 × 5 cm (hepatocellular carcinoma). Which risk factor is most strongly associated with this condition?
r: Chronic hepatitis B is the strongest and commonest risk factor for HCC worldwide and in Saudi Arabia, and can cause HCC even without cirrhosis through viral DNA integration.
n: Why not A? aflatoxin (Aspergillus-contaminated grain) is a genuine carcinogen (p53 mutation), but it mainly acts as a co-factor that multiplies the HBV risk.

q: A 60-year-old man presents with jaundice for 2 months [otherwise asymptomatic; a very short stem]. Ultrasound shows liver cirrhosis with 2 lesions. What is the cause of his condition? [remaining options not recalled]
r: Focal lesions in a cirrhotic liver suggest hepatocellular carcinoma; aflatoxin B1 (from Aspergillus-contaminated grains and peanuts) is a classic HCC carcinogen (p53 mutation) and acts synergistically with hepatitis B. (comment on #88046)
n: Why not B? Lead poisoning causes anaemia with basophilic stippling, neuropathy and abdominal colic, not cirrhosis or liver tumours. Claude: If hepatitis B/C or alcohol appear among the options, the stem's exposure history decides.

q: What is the best screening tool for hepatocellular carcinoma in a cirrhotic patient?
r: HCC surveillance in cirrhosis is an abdominal ultrasound every 6 months (± AFP; AASLD/EASL); triphasic CT or MRI is the diagnostic test once a nodule ≥1 cm is found (arterial enhancement with washout). (Alhomrani's Sept page)
n: Why not B? AFP alone has poor sensitivity (~60%) and is only an add-on to ultrasound.

q: A patient with chronic hepatitis B cirrhosis, WITHOUT ascites and with a normal bilirubin, has a single 6-cm arterially enhancing hepatic mass; the portal and hepatic veins are patent. What is the most appropriate management?
r: With preserved liver function (no portal hypertension, normal bilirubin) and a single tumour without vascular invasion, the treatment is surgical resection. (Alhomrani U2923: 'if no ascites we choose surgery? Yes'.)
n: Why not B? TACE is for unresectable disease, or when portal hypertension or a high bilirubin rules out surgery. Claude: Twin built from Alhomrani's reply to the examiner (U2923), which he calls an 'over-simplified approach'.

q: A patient with chronic hepatitis B cirrhosis has ascites controlled on diuretics and is asymptomatic. During evaluation of a focal lesion, imaging shows a 6-cm hepatic mass with arterial-phase enhancement; the portal and hepatic veins are patent. INR 1.5, with low platelets and Hb (as recalled). What is the most appropriate management?
r: Ascites, low platelets and a raised INR mark portal hypertension and impaired liver function, which rule out resection. A single 6-cm tumour (beyond Milan) without vascular invasion is treated with TACE. (Alhomrani U2923.)
n: Why not A? resection is for HCC with no portal hypertension and a normal bilirubin, as in the look-alike without ascites.

q: A patient who recently travelled to India presents with jaundice; ultrasound shows a hepatic cyst [abscess]. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment for this amoebic liver abscess?
r: Amoebic liver abscess responds to metronidazole in >90% of cases, followed by a luminal agent (paromomycin) to clear gut cysts. Aspiration is reserved for no response after 3–5 days, very large or left-lobe abscesses, or diagnostic doubt.
n: Why not D? Percutaneous aspiration is for failure of medical therapy or impending rupture, not first-line.

q: A 27-year-old man has RUQ pain and fever for 10 days. ELISA is positive for Entamoeba histolytica, and CT shows a 10 × 15 cm septated abscess in the right lobe. What is the initial management?
r: Amoebic liver abscess of any size is treated with metronidazole, then a luminal agent (paromomycin); >90% respond within 72 h. Drainage or aspiration is an adjunct for diagnostic doubt, no response after 3–5 days or a high rupture risk (large, left lobe).
n: Why not D? aspiration may be considered for very large (>5–10 cm) abscesses, but only alongside metronidazole, never as the initial treatment.

q: A young man has RUQ pain, fever and positive E. histolytica serology. Ultrasound shows a 6-cm complex cystic liver lesion. What is the BEST management?
r: Metronidazole is the primary treatment. Cochrane found no benefit from adding needle aspiration in uncomplicated abscesses, and Harrison doesn't recommend drainage even up to 10 cm, so a 6-cm abscess without treatment failure or rupture risk needs drug therapy alone.
n: Why not C? Sabiston says 'consider aspiration >5 cm', but that is an adjunct for non-responders or rupture risk, not the best primary management. Claude: Alhomrani (U2863): 'Modified MG — size is less and stem is different. Does the answer change? Not clear… w

q: A 36-year-old man presents to the ER with right abdominal pain. He is febrile and toxic, with tenderness in the right upper quadrant and over the lower intercostal margins, plus anorexia and weight loss. Temperature ~37.9 °C, high WBC, elevated bilirubin. Ultrasound: a cystic lesion with a thick wall in the liver. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
r: A toxic patient with a thick-walled cystic liver lesion has a (presumed pyogenic) liver abscess. Treatment is IV antibiotics plus image-guided percutaneous drainage/aspiration for source control; open surgery is kept for failure, rupture or multiloculated abscesses.
n: Why not B? metronidazole alone is first-line only for an amoebic abscess (endemic exposure, positive E. histolytica serology), which is not suggested here.

q: A 28-year-old man who recently joined military service and underwent excessive training presents to the Emergency Department with light-headedness on standing, muscle cramps and fatigue. Examination shows postural hypotension and is otherwise unremarkable. Acute kidney injury due to hypovolaemia is diagnosed. Which of the following is the most expected laboratory abnormality?
o: Dysmorphic red blood cells and RBC casts
r: In prerenal AKI the tubules are intact and avidly reabsorb sodium, water and urea, giving a BUN:creatinine ratio >20:1, FENa <1%, urine osmolality >500 and urine Na <20 mmol/L.
n: Why not B? FENa >2% means damaged tubules that cannot conserve sodium, i.e. intrinsic AKI (ATN), not prerenal. Claude: if the stem added dark urine or a high CK after exertion, think rhabdomyolysis (dipstick blood-positive without RBCs).

q: An elderly patient on lisinopril has had several days of vomiting, diarrhoea and abdominal pain. Creatinine has risen from 60 to 160 µmol/L. Urine sodium 68 mmol/L, urine osmolality 220 mOsm/kg, specific gravity 1.009, urea 11. What is the diagnosis? [one option not recalled]
r: Damaged tubules cannot conserve sodium or concentrate urine: urine Na >40, urine osmolality <350 and a fixed SG ~1.010 (FENa >2%) = acute tubular necrosis, here ischaemic ATN after prolonged volume loss made worse by the ACE inhibitor. (Alhomrani's Sept page)
n: Why not A? the history (GI losses + ACE inhibitor) suggests prerenal AKI, but prerenal urine is concentrated: Na <20, osmolality >500, SG >1.020, FENa <1%.

q: A patient presents with cola-coloured urine; investigations show proteinuria. What is the next step? [rest of the stem not recalled]
r: The examinee answered renal biopsy: haematuria with significant proteinuria that does not fit classic post-streptococcal GN needs a biopsy to identify the glomerulonephritis.
n: Why not B? In a typical post-streptococcal picture (child, recent throat or skin infection), C3 and ASO come first and biopsy is not needed. Claude: Recall gave only the answer; the other options were added for practice. Claude: if the stem is classic PSGN in

q: A patient with hypertension for 10 years on amlodipine 5 mg presents for follow-up of chronic kidney disease. He was diagnosed with diabetes mellitus and dyslipidaemia 5 months ago. BP 170/? (diastolic not recalled). What is the cause of the CKD?
r: Ten years of poorly controlled hypertension causes hypertensive nephrosclerosis; diabetic nephropathy usually takes about 10 years of diabetes to develop, and his diabetes is only 5 months old.
n: Why not B? diabetes is the commonest cause of CKD overall, but 5 months of known disease is too short to explain established CKD.

q: A man in his 50s with a 10-year history of diabetes mellitus comes to the clinic for follow-up. History and examination are unremarkable and vital signs are normal. Labs: urea 5 (normal), creatinine 130, urinalysis glucose 2+ and protein 2+. Which of the following medications is most appropriate to slow the progression of his condition?
r: ACE inhibitors (or ARBs) lower intraglomerular pressure and proteinuria and slow diabetic nephropathy even in normotensive patients with albuminuria.
n: Why not A? dihydropyridine CCBs lower systemic BP but do not reduce proteinuria, because they dilate the afferent arteriole. Claude: SGLT2 inhibitors are now also recommended in diabetic CKD; among these options the ACE inhibitor is the answer.

q: A patient presents with symptoms of a urinary tract infection [details not recalled]. What is the initial investigation?
r: The first test for suspected UTI is urinalysis (dipstick/microscopy for leucocyte esterase, nitrite and pyuria). Culture confirms the infection and guides antibiotics; imaging is for complicated or recurrent cases. (21 Oct examinee in #87978: 'initial → urine analysis')
n: Why not B? urine culture is the confirmatory test and is sent alongside, but the initial bedside test is urinalysis. Claude: Recall gave only the answer; the other options were added for practice. 'Initial' → urinalysis; 'confirm/most accurate' → urine culture

q: A 20-year-old woman presents to the clinic with dysuria and suprapubic pain, without fever. A urine dipstick was done [results not captured in the recall]. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
o: Send culture and wait for results
r: Typical cystitis symptoms in a young, non-pregnant woman = uncomplicated UTI: treat empirically (nitrofurantoin for 5 days, single-dose fosfomycin or TMP-SMX for 3 days) without waiting for a culture.
n: Why not C? urine culture is needed for pyelonephritis, pregnancy, men, recurrence or treatment failure, not before treating simple cystitis.

q: An elderly woman has recurrent UTIs (frequency per year not stated). What is the best clinically proven way to prevent recurrent UTIs?
r: Drinking an extra ~1.5 L of water a day halved recurrent cystitis in an RCT (JAMA Intern Med 2018) and is the simplest evidence-based measure; clothing advice and post-coital voiding have no proven benefit.
n: Why not B? Cranberry products also have modest RCT support (Cochrane 2023), which is why this question is debated, but the key and the examinee chose hydration. Claude: Disputed: Alhomrani's latest October compilation (15–18 Oct) chose cranberry juice. Claude:

Alhomrani adds that post-coital v
n: Why not A? increased water intake also helped in one RCT (Hooton 2018), and some examinees chose it, but cranberry is the better-supported, more commonly keyed choice. Claude: hydration vs cranberry has long been debated for this recall; if 'prophylactic antib

q: A girl with recurrent urinary tract infections asks how to promote urinary health and prevent further infections. What is the best advice?
r: Drinking about 1.5 L of extra water a day roughly halved recurrent cystitis in premenopausal women in an RCT, making hydration the best-supported simple behavioural advice.
n: Why not C? cranberry products give at most a modest, inconsistent benefit, weaker than the hydration RCT; it was the recall file's tick. Claude: Recall file (SMLE_Questions.pdf Q88) ticked cranberry juice. Debated: Alhomrani's October Combined keyed cranberry

q: A 48-year-old woman admitted several days ago with pyelonephritis still has fever and left flank pain after 5 days of an appropriate antibiotic. There is left loin tenderness; the rest of the examination is unremarkable. Urine culture grew E. coli susceptible to the antibiotic already started. What is the most appropriate management?
r: Fever persisting >48–72 h on an antibiotic the organism is sensitive to suggests a complication — obstruction/pyonephrosis or a renal/perinephric abscess — so image the kidney (ultrasound or CT) and drain if needed.
n: Why not B? Changing the antibiotic is pointless when the isolate is already susceptible; the problem is anatomical (abscess/obstruction), not resistance.

q: A man of about 37 with depression on antidepressants presents to the ER with dysuria and inability to pass urine for 12 hours. The bladder is distended; on rectal examination the prostate is small, soft and TENDER. What is the most likely diagnosis?
r: A tender prostate on DRE in a man with dysuria ± retention is acute bacterial prostatitis (examine gently, no massage; treat with a fluoroquinolone or TMP-SMX and relieve retention). Anticholinergic antidepressants may add to retention but don't make the gland tender.
n: Why not A? BPH gives a smooth, enlarged, firm, NON-tender prostate in an older man — here the gland is small and tender. Claude: Extract options: UTI / prostatitis / BPH / none.

q: A patient prescribed amitriptyline presents with urinary retention. What is the most likely cause?
r: Tricyclics block muscarinic receptors, which weakens detrusor contraction and causes urinary retention (with dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision and confusion); they also block α1 and H1 receptors.
n: Why not A? TCAs do raise noradrenaline, but the classic, tested mechanism of retention is muscarinic blockade of the detrusor.

q: A woman presents with galactorrhoea and infertility. Her serum prolactin is 120. What is the most appropriate next step?
r: Hyperprolactinaemia suppresses GnRH and causes anovulation; once prolactin is confirmed high (pregnancy, hypothyroidism and drugs excluded) the pituitary is imaged with MRI, then a dopamine agonist (cabergoline) usually restores ovulation — no assisted reproduction needed.
n: Why not C? Clomiphene is for normoprolactinaemic anovulation (e.g., PCOS); hyperprolactinaemic anovulation is imaged and then treated with a dopamine agonist.

q: A patient has had Cushingoid features for 4 months. Laboratory investigations show HIGH cortisol and HIGH ACTH. What is the most likely cause? [2 Nov copy (#87973): cortisol ~800 at 4 pm and ~500 at 8 pm, ACTH 17 (reference 15)]
r: High cortisol with high (only mildly raised) ACTH = ACTH-dependent Cushing syndrome, and the commonest cause is a pituitary corticotroph adenoma (Cushing disease, ~70%); a modest ACTH rise fits pituitary rather than ectopic ACTH.
n: Why not D? ectopic ACTH (e.g. bronchial carcinoid) is also ACTH-dependent, but it is rarer and usually gives very high ACTH, hypokalaemia and rapid onset; adrenal adenoma and exogenous steroids suppress ACTH. Claude: 2 Nov copy: cortisol ~800 at 4 pm and ~500

q: A 17-year-old boy has had recurrent episodes of muscle cramps and fatigue for 6 months and presents with muscle weakness since the morning. His father was diagnosed with hypertension at 30 years of age. BP 162/102 mmHg, HR 70/min. Labs: Na 142, K 2.7, bicarbonate 34; serum renin low and serum aldosterone low (no numbers given). Genetic testing for SCNN1B and SCNN1G is requested. What is the most likely diagnosis? [examinee 100% sure of the labs]
r: Hypertension + hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis with BOTH renin and aldosterone low = a mineralocorticoid-like effect that is not caused by aldosterone; SCNN1B/SCNN1G encode the β/γ subunits of the collecting-duct ENaC, whose autosomal-dominant gain-of-function (father hypertensive at 30) is Liddle
n: Why not A? Conn syndrome gives the same hypertension with hypokalaemic alkalosis, but aldosterone is HIGH with suppressed renin; here aldosterone is low.

q: A patient has hyponatremia and normal potassium. What is the most likely diagnosis? [Alhomrani: the stem should probably read hypokalemia]
r: Bartter syndrome is a salt-wasting tubulopathy that acts like a loop diuretic, so sodium is normal to low and BP is normal or low. Liddle, Cushing and Conn all retain sodium (normal or high Na) and cause hypertension. A is chosen by exclusion; the classic Bartter picture is hypokalemic metabolic alk
n: Why not C? Cushing syndrome retains sodium and causes hypertension (hypokalemia if severe), not hyponatremia; 'C' in the file was a typo.

q: A patient has resistant hypertension associated with palpitations, sweating and headaches. What is the most definitive treatment?
r: Episodic headache, sweating and palpitations with resistant hypertension is phaeochromocytoma; definitive treatment is laparoscopic adrenalectomy after alpha-blockade (phenoxybenzamine) followed by beta-blockade.
n: Why not A? renal artery stenting treats renovascular hypertension (abdominal bruit, flash pulmonary oedema, creatinine rise on ACEi), which has no adrenergic paroxysms.

q: A woman who has had a mastectomy [for breast cancer] has a raised serum sodium and decreased urine osmolality. What is the most likely diagnosis?
r: High serum sodium with inappropriately dilute urine = diabetes insipidus — in a breast-cancer patient think central DI from pituitary (posterior lobe) metastasis. (comments: two 'DI' with reasoning vs one 'SIADH', 0 likes.)
n: Why not B? SIADH gives the opposite picture — LOW serum sodium with inappropriately concentrated urine.

q: A 65-year-old patient presents with a 3-day history of seizures. Labs: sodium 112 mmol/L (134–146), potassium 3.9 mmol/L (3.5–5.1), urea 3.4 mmol/L (2.75–7.4), serum osmolality 240 mmol/kg (280–300). Urine osmolality 860 mOsm/kg H2O (280–910). [The 4 Nov post recalled 3 seizures, Na 121, K 3.4, urine osmolality 840.] Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
r: Hypotonic hyponatraemia (serum osmolality <275) with inappropriately concentrated urine (>100 mOsm/kg), normal potassium and low-normal urea = SIADH.
n: Why not B? Addison's also gives hyponatraemia with concentrated urine, but expect hyperkalaemia, raised urea and hypotension; here K and urea are normal.

q: A 22-year-old woman presents with recurrent seizures and cognitive dysfunction and is subsequently diagnosed with glioblastoma multiforme. She is hyponatraemic [laboratory panel not captured in the recall]. Which of the following is the most likely cause of her hyponatraemia?
r: Intracranial lesions (tumour, trauma, infection, haemorrhage) commonly cause SIADH: euvolaemic hyponatraemia with low serum osmolality, inappropriately concentrated urine (>100 mOsm/kg) and urine Na >30 mmol/L.
n: Why not A? the CNS salt-wasting state is cerebral salt wasting (hypovolaemic, typically after SAH or neurosurgery); salt-wasting nephropathy is a primary renal disorder unrelated to a glioma.

q: A 28-year-old woman with no known medical illness complains of increased sleepiness, fatigue and constipation for the last few months. She eats a very healthy diet, does not smoke and does not drink alcohol. Examination: overweight, not in distress, no lymphadenopathy or masses [the lab panel was not captured]. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
r: Hypothyroid symptoms in a young woman in an iodine-sufficient setting are most often due to Hashimoto's (chronic autoimmune) thyroiditis; as the poster noted, Graves' and subacute thyroiditis present with thyrotoxicosis.
n: Why not B? Subacute thyroiditis can have a later hypothyroid phase, but it starts with a painful, tender thyroid and thyrotoxicosis after a viral illness.

q: A 32-year-old woman presents to the clinic with a 6-month history of mild fatigue. She has no other symptoms and is planning a pregnancy. Physical examination is unremarkable. TSH is 7 with normal T3 and T4. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
o: Proceed with pregnancy without any intervention
r: Subclinical hypothyroidism in a woman planning pregnancy is treated with levothyroxine before conception, aiming for TSH <2.5 mIU/L, because the fetus depends on maternal T4 in the first trimester.
n: Why not C? waiting until pregnancy is confirmed leaves the critical early weeks of fetal brain development under-replaced. Claude: Alhomrani's October Combined (22 Oct Part 5, #795) keyed. Claude: I agree with B (ATA 2017 advises treating a TSH above the refer

q: A 67-year-old man presents with insomnia, irritability and palpitations for 3 months. He has hypertension, depression and atrial fibrillation and takes amiodarone, fluoxetine and enalapril. Examination is unremarkable. BP 130/70 mmHg, HR 76/min, SpO2 95%. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
r: Amiodarone (37% iodine by weight) causes thyrotoxicosis or hypothyroidism in roughly 15-20% of users; new insomnia, irritability and palpitations call for TSH and free T4 before anything else.
n: Why not C? fluoxetine can cause insomnia and agitation, but swapping it before excluding amiodarone-induced thyrotoxicosis misses a treatable, dangerous cause.

q: A male patient has a 2 cm thyroid nodule classified as TI-RADS 4. Which of the following is an indication for surgery?
o: Increase of 10% in size over the last 6 months
r: FNA cytology drives management: Bethesda IV (follicular neoplasm, roughly 30% malignant) -> diagnostic lobectomy (or molecular testing); Bethesda V-VI -> surgery; Bethesda II -> follow-up.
n: Why not B? only significant growth (20% or more in two dimensions, or >50% in volume) warrants repeat FNA, not surgery; 10% is within measurement error.

q: A patient has a thyroid mass, and laboratory results show a markedly elevated serum calcitonin level. This finding is most consistent with which type of thyroid cancer?
