r: Medullary carcinoma arises from parafollicular C cells, which secrete calcitonin (and CEA), both used for diagnosis and follow-up; screen for RET/MEN2 and phaeochromocytoma.
n: Why not A? papillary carcinoma is the commonest thyroid cancer but arises from follicular cells; its marker after thyroidectomy is thyroglobulin, not calcitonin.

q: A patient with newly diagnosed diabetes has an HbA1c of 7.9% and a BMI of 34. What is the first-line treatment? [SGLT2 inhibitor not among the options]
r: Metformin with lifestyle change is first line for type 2 diabetes in obese and non-obese patients alike (weight-neutral, no hypoglycaemia, cheap); a GLP-1 receptor agonist such as liraglutide is added to or alongside metformin when weight loss or cardiovascular benefit is needed. (Alhomrani's Sept p
n: Why not B? liraglutide suits obesity, but it is an add-on after or with metformin, not the initial monotherapy at HbA1c 7.9%.

q: A 55-year-old man newly diagnosed with type 2 diabetes was started on metformin 1000 mg twice daily plus gliclazide (or glyburide). After 6 months of treatment: urea normal, fasting glucose 6.8 mmol/L (normal <6.5), HbA1c 5.8% (normal 4.7-5.6). What is the next step?
o: Inform him he is at high cardiovascular risk
r: An HbA1c of 5.8% and fasting glucose of 6.8 mmol/L are within diabetic targets (HbA1c <7%, fasting 4.4-7.2 mmol/L), so he is well controlled: reassure and continue.
n: Why not B? the values exceed the non-diabetic lab range, but intensifying a sulfonylurea at an HbA1c of 5.8% only adds hypoglycaemia risk. Claude: in practice an HbA1c this low on a sulfonylurea should prompt asking about hypoglycaemia and possibly reducing th

q: A diabetic patient admitted to hospital follows different diets from social media and asks for dietary advice. What is the most appropriate advice?
o: Follow diets shared on social media
Refer to a registered dietitian / diabetes educator
r: Individualised medical nutrition therapy delivered by a registered dietitian or diabetes educator is the evidence-based standard for diabetes diet advice and lowers HbA1c.
n: Why not A? a blanket ban on information is paternalistic and leaves him without guidance; the better approach is to direct him to a reliable expert source.

q: A 25-year-old man with type 1 diabetes on insulin is found in the clinic waiting area drowsy and sweating excessively. A quick blood glucose measurement is low. Which of the following is the most appropriate action?
r: A hypoglycaemic patient who is conscious and able to swallow gets 15-20 g of fast-acting oral carbohydrate (juice, glucose tablets) and a recheck after 15 minutes; 5% dextrose is too dilute to correct hypoglycaemia (10-20% is used IV).
n: Why not C? glucagon (IM/SC) is for patients who are unconscious or cannot swallow and have no IV access. Claude: if the stem says unconscious or unable to swallow, the answer flips to IV dextrose or glucagon.

q: A patient with diabetic ketoacidosis has a serum potassium of 4.2 mmol/L. What is the management? [IV fluids were not among the options]
o: Hold insulin until potassium is replaced
r: With K between 3.3 and 5.2 mmol/L, start the IV insulin infusion (0.1 U/kg/h) and add 20–30 mEq KCl to each litre of fluid to keep K at 4–5; hold insulin only if K is below 3.3.
n: Why not B? Insulin waits for potassium replacement only when K is below 3.3 mmol/L; at 4.2 it can start. Claude: Recall gave only the answer; the other options were added for practice. If IV 0.9% saline is offered, fluids come first.

q: A 60-year-old woman with asthma and alcoholism presents with bone pain that prevents her from performing her activities. BMI 31 kg/m2. Which of the following is an indication for osteoporosis screening in her?
r: In a postmenopausal woman under 65, DXA screening is indicated when clinical risk factors are present; alcohol intake of 3 or more units/day is a FRAX risk factor, whereas obesity is protective.
n: Why not D? glucocorticoids count only when 5 mg/day or more of prednisolone (or equivalent) is taken for 3 months or longer; short courses do not qualify.

q: A woman has a clear clinical and laboratory picture of microcytic (iron-deficiency) anaemia. What is the most DEFINITIVE test to diagnose the underlying condition?
r: A bone marrow aspirate with Prussian-blue iron stain (absent stores) is the gold-standard, definitive test for iron deficiency, though rarely done in practice. Alhomrani's rule (U2820): gold standard / definitive / highest diagnostic → bone marrow; confirmatory or highest diagnostic VALUE → ferritin
n: Why not B? ferritin is the best practical, confirmatory test (low ferritin is ~99% specific), but 'definitive' means bone marrow. Claude: #88044 comments were split (♥5 bone marrow vs ♥3 ferritin).

q: A woman has symptoms of iron-deficiency anaemia with a microcytic picture. Which investigation BEST CONFIRMS the diagnosis (or: has the highest diagnostic VALUE)? [rebuilt from the bank look-alike line]
r: Serum ferritin is the single most useful test for iron deficiency: below 15 µg/L it is ~99% specific, so it confirms IDA without a marrow. Alhomrani's rule: confirmatory → ferritin.
n: Why not D? bone marrow iron staining is the gold standard but has no practical value; choose it only when the stem says definitive, gold standard or highest diagnostic. Claude: Alhomrani put some individual 'best confirms'/'highest diagnostic value' recalls on

q: A patient has microcytic anemia. What is the highest diagnostic test to diagnose the underlying disease?
r: Absent stainable iron on a bone marrow iron stain is the gold-standard (definitive) test for iron deficiency, so 'highest diagnostic test' = bone marrow. Alhomrani's rule: gold standard, definitive or highest diagnostic → bone marrow; any other wording → ferritin / iron profile. (Alhomrani U2820.)
n: Why not B? ferritin is the best practical test (a low value is ~99% specific) and wins for 'highest diagnostic VALUE' or 'confirm', but not for the plain 'highest diagnostic' (gold-standard) wording.

q: A woman with symptoms of iron deficiency anemia has frequent menses. Which test has the highest diagnostic VALUE?
r: Serum ferritin is the single most useful test: a low ferritin (<15 ng/mL; some use <30) proves iron deficiency with ~99% specificity, while bone marrow has no practical role. Alhomrani's own rule (U2820) maps 'highest diagnostic VALUE' to ferritin.
n: Why not C? bone marrow is the gold standard ('highest diagnostic') but invasive and of no practical value; the word VALUE flips the answer to ferritin. Claude: Alhomrani (U2821): 'Okay GG, now I saw one… I have no answer for now', although in U2820 he had said

q: A woman is suspected of having iron deficiency anemia. Which investigation BEST CONFIRMS the diagnosis (most specific)?
r: A low serum ferritin confirms iron deficiency (~99% specific); bone marrow is kept for 'gold standard' or 'definitive' wording. Alhomrani's modified approach (U2820) says confirmatory → ferritin / iron profile. (Claude, applying his rule; he put this copy on hold.)
n: Why not C? a bone marrow iron stain is the gold standard, but his rule maps 'confirm' to ferritin. Pick bone marrow only if the stem says gold standard, definitive or highest diagnostic. Claude: Alhomrani (U2822): 'Okay, this is new… on hold for now (no answer

q: A patient has iron deficiency anemia. Which finding is the most specific to establish the diagnosis?
r: Serum iron falls with any inflammation and varies through the day, and TIBC is only moderately specific. Low ferritin is the most specific laboratory marker of depleted iron stores.
n: Why not C? a raised TIBC supports iron deficiency but is less specific, and it can be normal or low when inflammation coexists.

q: A young, medically free woman presents with palpitations and fatigue and is found to have symptomatic iron deficiency anaemia; the haemoglobin drop is not severe. What is the management? [Recall vague: ferritin level and the remaining options were not remembered.]
r: Oral iron (ferrous sulfate/fumarate, ideally alternate-day dosing) is first-line even when symptomatic, as long as she is haemodynamically stable.
n: Why not B? IV iron is reserved for failure or intolerance of oral iron, malabsorption (coeliac, IBD, bariatric surgery), CKD on dialysis or the need for rapid repletion (late pregnancy). Claude: Transfusion only for haemodynamic instability or severe anaemia w

q: A patient has had symptoms of iron deficiency anemia for the past 6 months. What is the most appropriate management? [the recall gave a hemoglobin level, which decides oral vs IV iron]
r: Symptomatic iron deficiency needs iron replacement, because diet alone cannot refill stores. Oral ferrous sulfate is first line; IV iron is for intolerance, malabsorption, ongoing losses or a very low Hb late in pregnancy. (News comment ♥2 on N435: 'for a long time (months) diet alone is not enough'
n: Why not A? dietary advice is only an adjunct; it supplies too little absorbable iron to correct an established deficiency.

q: A woman [with constipation and a urinary problem — the stem was poorly recalled] has Hb 9 g/dL. Which type of hemoglobin is NOT found on electrophoresis?
r: 'Hb B' does not exist: β is a globin chain, not a hemoglobin, so it can never appear on electrophoresis. HbA, HbF (<1% in adults) and the variant HbC are all real bands that electrophoresis detects. (Claude, agreeing with the examiner.)
n: Why not D? HbC is absent in a normal adult, but it is a genuine variant seen on electrophoresis in HbC trait or disease; it was Alhomrani's original key. Claude: Alhomrani (U2881): his file said Hb C. On the examiner's argument: 'You actually have a strong & v

q: A patient with SLE presents with fatigue. Labs: low haemoglobin, high reticulocyte count (7%), LDH raised (400 or 600 - examinee unsure) [the recall page adds low haptoglobin]. What type of anaemia is this?
r: Reticulocytosis with raised LDH (and low haptoglobin) means peripheral red-cell destruction; in SLE this is a warm (IgG) autoimmune haemolytic anaemia, confirmed by a positive direct Coombs test.
n: Why not A? anaemia of chronic disease is the commonest anaemia in SLE, but it is hypoproliferative (low reticulocytes) with a normal LDH.

q: A young (30-year-old) woman presents with an acute illness of 1 week and jaundice. There is no family history of a similar condition. Labs: low haemoglobin, raised reticulocyte count, raised indirect bilirubin, low haptoglobin, normal platelets. [No Coombs test, blood film, gallstone/cholecystectomy history or recent infection was given.] Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
r: Haemolysis of recent onset in an adult with no family history points to acquired autoimmune haemolytic anaemia (next test: direct Coombs). Hereditary spherocytosis is autosomal dominant and usually shows up in childhood with a family history, splenomegaly and gallstones.
n: Why not B? HS is a lifelong inherited haemolysis, so a negative family history and a 1-week illness in an adult make it the less likely choice. Claude: Extract key is 'by review' only (not verified).

q: A man in his forties presents with easy bleeding and gum bleeding on brushing his teeth. Labs: Hb 12.5 (12.9 in other recalls - mildly low), platelets 5 ×10^9/L, WBC 7.6. What is the cause?
r: Isolated severe thrombocytopenia with mucocutaneous bleeding and otherwise normal counts in a well adult = immune thrombocytopenia (a diagnosis of exclusion; the smear shows large platelets).
n: Why not B? aplastic anaemia causes pancytopenia, so Hb and WBC would also be low.

q: A 38-year-old woman has had fever and headache for 2 days. Examination shows scattered petechiae over her body. A peripheral smear is shown. Temperature 38.6 °C. Labs: Hb 112 g/L (F 120-160), reticulocytes 5.6% (0.2-1.2), platelets 32 ×10^9/L (150-400), indirect bilirubin 48 µmol/L (3.2-12.1), total bilirubin 76 µmol/L (3.5-16.5), LDH 690 IU/L (60-160), APTT 33 s (30-40), INR 1.0, PT 10 s (10-13). Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
r: Thrombocytopenia plus microangiopathic haemolysis (reticulocytosis, high LDH and indirect bilirubin, schistocytes) with normal PT/APTT, fever and neurological symptoms = TTP; urgent plasma exchange cuts mortality from ~90% to ~10-20%. Platelet transfusion is avoided because it fuels microthrombi.
n: Why not A? IVIG plus steroids is ITP treatment and ITP has no haemolysis; in TTP steroids are only an adjunct to plasma exchange.

q: A patient with sickle cell disease presents with acute chest syndrome. While you are transfusing blood, he develops fever and chills. What should you do immediately?
r: Fever, chills, hypotension or dyspnoea during a transfusion means stopping the transfusion first, keeping the line open with saline, re-checking patient and unit identity, and sending samples to exclude an acute haemolytic reaction or bacterial contamination.
n: Why not C? IV hydration supports renal function in a haemolytic reaction, but only after the offending unit has been stopped.

q: An 18-year-old boy receiving chemotherapy for acute lymphoblastic leukaemia develops fever on day 17 of chemotherapy, with no focus of infection. HR 110/min, temperature 38.9 °C. Platelets 25 (low), WBC 0.6 (very low), neutrophils 60%, lymphocytes 20%. What is the most appropriate management?
o: Send blood, urine, sputum cultures and start paracetamol
Send blood, urine, sputum cultures and start oral broad spectrum antibiotics
Send blood, urine, sputum cultures and start intravenous broad spectrum antibiotics
r: Febrile neutropenia (T ≥38.3 °C; ANC ≈ 0.6 × 60% = 0.36 ×10⁹/L) is an emergency: take cultures and start empirical IV broad-spectrum anti-pseudomonal beta-lactam (piperacillin-tazobactam or cefepime) within 1 hour.
n: Why not C? oral antibiotics are only for low-risk adults (MASCC ≥21); a tachycardic patient with profound post-chemotherapy neutropenia from leukaemia is high risk and needs IV therapy.

q: A 55-year-old man with acute myeloid leukaemia on chemotherapy presents to the Emergency Room with a 1-day history of fever. Physical examination is unremarkable; chest radiograph and urinalysis are normal. Blood and urine cultures are taken [laboratory panel not captured in the recall]. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
r: Fever in a neutropenic patient on chemotherapy is an emergency: start an empiric IV broad-spectrum antipseudomonal beta-lactam (piperacillin-tazobactam or cefepime) within 1 hour of presentation.
n: Why not D? oral therapy is only for low-risk patients (MASCC score 21 or more, usually solid tumours); AML on chemotherapy is high-risk, and antifungals are added only if fever persists for 4-7 days.

q: A young adult with AML M5 (bone-marrow biopsy) is admitted to isolation and develops a fever of 38.9 °C one day before starting chemotherapy; other vital signs are normal. Haemoglobin, platelets, WBC and PMN count are all low (neutropenia). Which antibiotic should be started?
r: Fever with neutropenia is febrile neutropenia: start empirical IV anti-pseudomonal β-lactam monotherapy within 1 hour — piperacillin-tazobactam (extended-spectrum penicillin), cefepime or a carbapenem.
n: Why not D? Usual 3rd-generation cephalosporins (ceftriaxone, cefotaxime) don't cover Pseudomonas; only ceftazidime does, and it is no longer preferred.

q: A patient with sickle cell disease after bone marrow transplantation has febrile neutropenia on ceftazidime with no improvement after 72 hours. There is no pneumonia and no hypotension. What should be added?
r: Neutropenic fever that persists on broad-spectrum antipseudomonal therapy in a high-risk (post-HSCT) patient calls for an empiric mould-active antifungal (voriconazole, or an echinocandin or amphotericin). Vancomycin is added only for specific triggers: instability, pneumonia, catheter or skin infec
n: Why not D? persistent fever alone is not an IDSA indication for vancomycin, and none of its triggers is present. Claude: IDSA starts empiric antifungals after 4–7 days of persistent fever; 72 h is early, but the logic is the same.

q: A woman presents with a painless neck mass, weight loss and fever for 3 months [the 4 Nov post: a patient with Burkitt lymphoma]. Labs: high creatinine, low albumin, high potassium, high uric acid, high magnesium [as recalled; classically phosphate] and low calcium. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
r: TLS = hyperuricaemia, hyperkalaemia and hyperphosphataemia with secondary hypocalcaemia and AKI, typically in high-grade lymphoma (Burkitt), at the start of treatment or spontaneously. Prevent with IV hydration plus allopurinol or rasburicase.
n: Why not C? Sarcoidosis gives lymphadenopathy with HYPERcalcaemia, the opposite of the low calcium here.

q: A patient with non-Hodgkin lymphoma, uncontrolled type 2 diabetes for 20 years and hypertension dies BEFORE chemotherapy is started. Labs showed high uric acid and high potassium (and a high creatinine). What is the most likely cause of death?
r: High-turnover lymphomas can lyse spontaneously: hyperuricaemia + hyperkalaemia (+ hyperphosphataemia, hypocalcaemia) with a rising creatinine meets the Cairo-Bishop criteria for TLS, and hyperkalaemic arrhythmia is its main cause of death; TLS does not need chemotherapy to occur. (Alhomrani's 15–16
n: Why not C? 20 years of diabetes and hypertension could cause undiagnosed CKD, but CKD does not explain a marked uric-acid rise in a patient with lymphoma. Claude: The same page has a vaguer version (cancer not yet on chemo, DM, HTN, 'may take a K-sparing diure

q: A patient with Burkitt lymphoma starts chemotherapy and then presents with deteriorating renal function. Labs: calcium 2.1 mmol/L (low), potassium 5.8 mmol/L, uric acid high. What is the cause of the renal deterioration?
r: Chemotherapy of a bulky, rapidly dividing tumour (Burkitt) causes tumour lysis syndrome; the AKI comes from uric acid (and calcium phosphate) crystals precipitating in the renal tubules, prevented by hydration plus allopurinol or rasburicase.
n: Why not B? hyperkalaemia is a consequence of the cell lysis and the AKI, not the cause of the renal failure. Claude: Recall file (SMLE_Questions.pdf Q1) ticked 'D. Tumour lysis syndrome', an option this version does not keep; pick TLS whenever it is offered, s

q: A patient with spinal metastases presents with rapidly progressive paraparesis and faecal incontinence (thoracic level); MRI shows cord compression. His symptoms continue to worsen despite medical management. What is the most appropriate next step in management? [extract wording: 'most appropriate initial management']
r: Malignant cord compression: give high-dose dexamethasone at once, then definitive treatment within 24 h. Deficits progressing despite steroids, spinal instability or a radioresistant tumour mean urgent surgical decompression (± radiotherapy).
n: Why not B? Steroids come first, but he is already worsening on medical therapy, and a higher dose does not decompress the cord. Claude: Extract flags a key conflict: a version without 'worsening despite medical management' was keyed corticosteroids.

q: A patient has recurrent infections. Labs show absent T cells and low serum immunoglobulins, with recurrent fungal infections and diarrhoea. What is the diagnosis?
r: Absent T cells plus low immunoglobulins (combined T- and B-cell failure), with candidiasis, chronic diarrhoea and failure to thrive in infancy, is SCID. The definitive treatment is haematopoietic stem cell transplant.
n: Why not B? Wiskott-Aldrich gives the triad eczema + thrombocytopenia with small platelets + recurrent infections, with low IgM and initially normal T-cell numbers.

q: A man presents to the emergency department with fever, rigors and chills. He also reports back pain and gives a history of drinking unpasteurised milk. Which of the following is the most appropriate laboratory test?
r: Fever with back pain (sacroiliitis/spondylitis) after raw milk = brucellosis; confirm with Brucella serology (standard agglutination titre of 1:160 or more) and blood cultures.
n: Why not B? MRI shows spondylodiscitis but not its cause, and it is not a laboratory test; serology confirms Brucella.

q: Brucellosis is suspected [scenario not recalled]. Which test is used to make the diagnosis?
r: Serology — a standard tube agglutination titre ≥1:160 (or a rising titre) — is the most widely used test to diagnose brucellosis; culture is definitive but slow and often negative.
n: Why not B? Blood culture is the gold standard to confirm (bone marrow culture is even more sensitive), but it is slow and insensitive — pick it only when the question asks 'gold standard/confirm'. Claude: Recall gave only the answer; the other options were add

q: A 28-year-old woman has 3 weeks of fatigability, malaise, arthralgia, back pain and fever; she drinks raw milk. There is mild hepatosplenomegaly. Hb 10.5, platelets 120. Blood culture grows gram-negative coccobacilli. What is the optimal duration of therapy? [no MRI findings given]
r: Uncomplicated brucellosis (no spondylitis, endocarditis or neurobrucellosis) is treated for 6 weeks: doxycycline plus rifampicin for 6 weeks, or doxycycline with streptomycin/gentamicin for the first 2–3 weeks; back pain alone without imaging evidence of spondylitis does not extend it.
n: Why not C? 12 weeks is for brucella spondylitis proven on MRI; the back pain tempts it, but no spondylitis is shown.

q: A 28-year-old woman who drinks raw milk has 3 weeks of fever, malaise, arthralgia and back pain with mild hepatosplenomegaly; blood culture grows gram-negative coccobacilli. MRI of the spine shows spondylitis. What is the optimal duration of therapy?
r: Brucella spondylitis is a focal complication and needs at least 12 weeks (3 months) of doxycycline + rifampicin (± an aminoglycoside at the start), longer if there is an abscess. (Alhomrani's Sept page note: 'if MRI shows spondylitis → 12 weeks')
n: Why not B? 6 weeks is enough only for uncomplicated brucellosis without focal disease. Claude: Twin built from Alhomrani's page note (the original Medgard version had MRI findings), not a separate November recall.

q: A patient presents with neuropsychiatric symptoms; examination shows hepatosplenomegaly. What is the most likely diagnosis?
r: Brucellosis (raw milk or livestock contact; endemic in Saudi Arabia) causes fever, arthralgia and hepatosplenomegaly, and neurobrucellosis can present with neuropsychiatric features (depression, psychosis, meningoencephalitis).
n: Why not B? Wilson disease also combines neuropsychiatric and liver disease, but it is a young patient with hepatitis or cirrhosis and Kayser–Fleischer rings, without a systemic febrile illness. Claude: Recall gave only the answer; the other options were added

q: A young patient presents with jaundice and yellow discoloration at the sclero-conjunctival (corneoscleral) junction [probably a Kayser-Fleischer ring]. ALT and AST are over 1000 and bilirubin is 28. What do you expect to find?
r: A young patient with acute hepatitis and a golden-brown ring at the corneal limbus (Kayser-Fleischer) has Wilson disease, in which serum ceruloplasmin is low (<20 mg/dL) with high 24-hour urinary copper.
n: Why not B? hepatocyte necrosis on biopsy is a non-specific finding in any severe acute hepatitis (e.g. paracetamol) and is not needed when a specific serum marker exists. Claude: Alhomrani (23 Oct, post #1138) chose (necrosis, reading it as paracetamol-type hy

q: A patient has high fever, arthralgia and an erythematous rash after multiple mosquito bites; there is no abdominal pain. What is the management? [options as recalled]
o: Supportive treatment with good oral hydration
r: Dengue (or chikungunya) without warning signs is managed with oral fluids, paracetamol and daily review of platelets and haematocrit; IV fluids are for warning signs (abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, mucosal bleeding, rising haematocrit with falling platelets) or shock.
n: Why not A? NSAIDs and aspirin are avoided in dengue because, with thrombocytopenia and platelet dysfunction, they raise bleeding risk; use paracetamol.

q: A 35-year-old Indian man presents to the Emergency Department with lethargy, weight loss and headache for 3 months. He had contact with a tuberculosis patient several years ago. Neurological and ophthalmological examinations are unremarkable. CSF PCR is positive for Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
o: Isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide, ethambutol and diuretics
Isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide, ethambutol and acyclovir
Isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide, ethambutol and dexamethasone
r: TB meningitis is treated with RIPE (extended to 9-12 months) plus adjunctive dexamethasone, which reduces death and disability.
n: Why not A? RIPE alone treats the infection, but in CNS TB omitting adjunctive corticosteroids increases mortality.

q: A 45-year-old man with pulmonary tuberculosis was started on 4 anti-tuberculous drugs 2 months ago. Routine follow-up blood work shows hyperuricaemia: uric acid 600 µmol/L (male 200-410). Which anti-TB drug is responsible for this finding?
r: Pyrazinamide (through its metabolite pyrazinoic acid) inhibits renal urate excretion, causing hyperuricaemia and sometimes gout; it is also hepatotoxic.
n: Why not C? ethambutol can raise uric acid modestly, but its signature toxicity is optic neuritis (red-green colour loss); pyrazinamide is the classic cause.

q: A 40-year-old man presents to the emergency department with fever, severe headache, neck stiffness and photophobia for 2 days (suspected meningitis). On examination, passive flexion of his neck causes involuntary flexion of the hips and knees. Which clinical sign is demonstrated?
r: Brudzinski (neck) sign: passive neck flexion produces involuntary hip and knee flexion, a sign of meningeal irritation.
n: Why not A? Kernig sign is pain or resistance on extending the knee with the hip flexed to 90 degrees; the manoeuvre starts at the leg, not the neck.

q: A 20-year-old woman is brought to the Emergency Room with a 2-day history of headache, fever, photosensitivity, lethargy and a skin eruption. She is drowsy with neck rigidity but no focal neurological findings, and has a purpuric rash over her extremities [laboratory panel not captured in the recall]. Which investigation is most appropriate to establish the diagnosis?
r: CSF analysis by lumbar puncture (cell count, glucose, protein, Gram stain, culture/PCR) establishes bacterial meningitis; antibiotics must not be delayed while it is arranged.
n: Why not B? blood cultures are drawn first and are often positive in meningococcaemia, but they do not establish meningitis; CSF does. Claude: IDSA advises CT before LP when consciousness is impaired, and LP is deferred with extensive purpura, shock or coagulop

q: A patient is admitted with meningococcal meningitis. The family asks what should be done to protect the household contacts who live with the patient. Which of the following is the most appropriate action?
r: Close and household contacts of meningococcal disease get chemoprophylaxis as soon as possible (single-dose ciprofloxacin, rifampicin for 2 days, or IM ceftriaxone in pregnancy).
n: Why not A? droplet isolation for the first 24 h of effective therapy protects others from now on, but household contacts are already exposed and need prophylaxis.

q: A 70-year-old has had right-sided weakness that started 12 hours ago. Vital signs are normal, and coagulation profile and platelets are normal. Imaging shows a proximal anterior-circulation occlusion with a small-to-moderate infarct core. What is the next step? [October recalls described a 'posterior artery' occlusion]
r: IV thrombolysis is not given beyond 4.5 hours, but a large/proximal vessel occlusion with a persistent deficit, a small core and salvageable tissue qualifies for mechanical thrombectomy up to 24 hours (DAWN/DEFUSE-3); the decision rests on a proximal large vessel, not on infarct size alone.
n: Why not D? tPA + thrombectomy (bridging) is standard only within 4.5 hours; at 12 hours tPA is out of its window, so thrombectomy alone. Claude: The extract marks it disputed (an August recall carried a different key); the October copies recalled a 'posterior'

q: An elderly man had an episode of left-sided limb weakness with facial drooping. The symptoms resolved completely after 10 minutes. CT shows a small infarct in the middle cerebral artery territory. What is the diagnosis?
r: A focal deficit lasting 10 minutes with full recovery is clinically a TIA; an acute infarct is not visible on CT within minutes, so the CT infarct is read as old and the current event stays a TIA.
n: Why not A? by the tissue-based definition an acute infarct on imaging (usually DWI-MRI) makes it a stroke, which is why the recall file and Alhomrani chose A. Claude: Recall file (SMLE_Questions.pdf Q52) ticked ischaemic stroke; Alhomrani's October Combined (2

q: A patient with carotid stenosis has had 3 transient ischaemic attacks while taking aspirin and now has another episode. What is the best action?
o: Stop aspirin and start an alternative antiplatelet
r: Recurrent TIAs on aspirin are managed by intensifying antiplatelet therapy: aspirin plus clopidogrel (short-term DAPT) lowers early recurrence after minor stroke or high-risk TIA (CHANCE/POINT).
n: Why not A? switching to a single alternative antiplatelet is a long-term option, but in the acute recurrent phase dual therapy is preferred. Claude: symptomatic carotid stenosis of 50-70% or more also needs carotid endarterectomy within 2 weeks, so pick it if

q: A patient with chronic hypertension suddenly develops contralateral hemiplegia. Imaging shows an intracerebral haemorrhage. Which location is the most common site of hypertensive intracerebral haemorrhage?
r: Hypertensive ICH comes from lipohyalinosis and Charcot-Bouchard microaneurysms of small penetrating arteries. The commonest site is the putamen/basal ganglia (~50%), then the thalamus, pons and cerebellum.
n: Why not B? lobar (occipital/frontal) haemorrhage in an elderly patient suggests cerebral amyloid angiopathy, not hypertension.

q: Imaging shows a haemorrhagic stroke. The patient can move his eyes, but the pupils are pinpoint and he cannot speak or move his body. Where is the lesion?
r: Pontine haemorrhage causes pinpoint (but reactive) pupils from sympathetic disruption and a locked-in state: quadriplegia and anarthria with preserved vertical eye movements.
n: Why not C? putaminal (basal ganglia) bleeds, the commonest hypertensive site, give contralateral hemiplegia and gaze deviation with normal pupils, not pinpoint pupils with quadriplegia.

q: A 63-year-old man with poorly controlled hypertension becomes unresponsive; he can only move his eyes vertically and cannot move his limbs on either side. Where is the lesion?
r: Quadriplegia with preserved consciousness and only vertical eye movements/blinking = locked-in syndrome from a ventral pontine infarct or haemorrhage (basilar territory): the corticospinal and corticobulbar tracts are destroyed, while the reticular formation and the midbrain vertical-gaze centres ar
n: Why not C? the vertical-gaze centre is in the midbrain, which is exactly why vertical gaze is SPARED; a midbrain lesion would impair vertical gaze (Parinaud) and consciousness.

q: A known epileptic who is not compliant with medication [extract: 23-year-old woman] has had repeated tonic–clonic seizures — 4 attacks over the past 3 hours [2 Nov recall: more than 4 hours] — without regaining consciousness. What is the first-line management?
r: Seizures lasting ≥5 min or recurring without recovery = status epilepticus: first IV lorazepam/diazepam (or IM/buccal midazolam), then a second-line IV agent (levetiracetam, fosphenytoin/phenytoin, valproate), then anaesthesia (propofol, midazolam) if refractory.
n: Why not C? Phenytoin is the second-line drug, given after benzodiazepines fail (or with them to prevent recurrence) — not first. Claude: 1–5 Nov copy: it was not stated whether any drug had already been given; if the full stem says benzodiazepine and phenytoin

q: A 30-year-old man has seizure episodes in which he stares with a blank face, lip-smacks, grimaces and shows automatisms. He has labile emotions and now has sudden episodes of aggression. What is the most likely diagnosis? [question ask not recalled]
r: Focal impaired-awareness seizures with oral automatisms (lip smacking), staring and affective or behavioural change localise to the temporal lobe (often mesial temporal sclerosis).
n: Why not B? absence seizures also cause staring, but they last seconds, occur in children, have no aura or postictal confusion and show 3-Hz spike-and-wave.

q: A 72-year-old man is brought by his wife because of episodes in which he suddenly stops speaking, stares blankly, and shows repetitive facial grimacing and lip-smacking. Each episode lasts 1-2 minutes and is followed by temporary confusion. What is the most likely diagnosis?
r: Episodes of 1-2 min with behavioural arrest, staring and oral automatisms (lip-smacking, grimacing), followed by post-ictal confusion, are focal impaired-awareness (complex partial) seizures of temporal-lobe origin.
n: Why not B? typical absences last seconds, start and end abruptly with no post-ictal confusion, and almost always begin in childhood.

q: A patient presents with numbness, and MRI of the brain shows white-matter demyelinating lesions. Which of the following will support the diagnosis of multiple sclerosis?
r: CSF-specific oligoclonal IgG bands (present in >90% of MS) support the diagnosis and, under the 2017 McDonald criteria, can substitute for dissemination in time.
n: Why not B? nerve conduction studies assess peripheral nerves (e.g. GBS); the supportive electrophysiology for MS is visual evoked potentials.

q: An elderly woman in the ICU wakes and becomes agitated, posing a danger to herself and staff; all physical (non-drug) measures have failed. What is the most appropriate medication?
r: Hyperactive delirium that endangers the patient or staff after failed non-drug measures is treated with a short course of an antipsychotic, and a combative patient needs a parenteral route: IV/IM haloperidol.
n: Why not B? olanzapine is an acceptable antipsychotic for delirium, but an oral dose is unreliable in a combative patient who may refuse or aspirate it. Claude: 5 mg is a high starting dose for an elderly patient (usually 0.5-1 mg, titrated); the exam point is

q: An elderly woman with cancer receiving palliative care becomes agitated and confused. Despite repeated attempts by the healthcare team to settle her, she remains agitated. How should she be managed?
r: Agitated delirium at the end of life is treated first with an antipsychotic — haloperidol (0.5–1 mg PO/SC/IV) — once non-drug measures fail; benzodiazepines are added only for refractory agitation or palliative sedation.
n: Why not B? Benzodiazepines alone can worsen delirium (paradoxical agitation); they are reserved for refractory cases, alcohol/benzodiazepine withdrawal or terminal sedation on top of an antipsychotic. Claude: Extract version: end-stage metastatic cancer, aggre

q: A 46-year-old right-handed woman complains of sausage digits (dactylitis) in the left hand and nail pitting. What else would you expect to find in the history?
r: Dactylitis plus nail pitting = psoriatic arthritis; skin psoriasis (look at the scalp, umbilicus, natal cleft) comes before the arthritis in most patients, so ask about skin disease.
n: Why not C? Lung involvement (ILD, nodules) is an extra-articular feature of RA; dactylitis with nail pits points to psoriatic disease.

q: A 40-year-old man with recurrent painful attacks in the right big toe was diagnosed with gout and started on allopurinol. He has also had psoriasis for several years. He now presents with recurrent pain in the right big toe, left ankle and both knees despite taking allopurinol regularly as prescribed. Examination shows active arthritis of the left ankle and both knees [laboratory panel not captured in the recall]. Which of the following is the most likely cause of his joint pain?
r: A patient with psoriasis who develops an asymmetric oligoarthritis of large joints while adherent to urate-lowering therapy most likely has psoriatic arthritis (psoriasis also raises urate, so it mimics gout).
n: Why not B? active gout fits only if uric acid is still high or crystals are found; with regular allopurinol and no stated hyperuricaemia, the new pattern points to PsA. Claude: The lab panel was not captured; if it showed a raised uric acid the answer flips to

q: A man with gout on allopurinol who also has long-standing psoriasis presents with recurrent pain in the right big toe, left ankle and both knees. Laboratory tests show an elevated serum uric acid level. What is the most likely cause of his joint pain?
r: A persistently high serum urate despite allopurinol means inadequate urate lowering, so recurrent podagra and ankle/knee attacks are active gout.
n: Why not C? psoriasis does predispose to PsA, but the stated hyperuricaemia gives a direct explanation; PsA wins only when urate data are absent (the 22 Oct version).

q: A patient presents with arthritis and a facial rash. What is the most likely diagnosis?
r: Non-erosive arthritis with a malar (butterfly) rash that spares the nasolabial folds is classic SLE; confirm with ANA and anti-dsDNA.
n: Why not D? Dermatomyositis has a facial (heliotrope) rash, but its hallmark is proximal muscle weakness with Gottron papules; arthritis is minor. Claude: Recall gave only the answer; the other options were added for practice.

q: A child has a heliotrope rash (and Gottron papules over the knuckles). What is the most likely diagnosis?
r: Heliotrope rash + Gottron papules + proximal weakness = juvenile dermatomyositis.
n: Why not A? SLE causes a malar rash sparing the nasolabial folds.

q: A 23-year-old woman with SLE presents with a 3-month history of lower-limb swelling and shortness of breath, without chest pain, palpitations or fever. Examination: jugular venous distension that increases with inspiration, distant heart sounds and a prominent early diastolic sound without murmurs or gallops; breath sounds are normal; shifting dullness; pitting oedema to the knees. BP 110/70, HR 95, RR 25, T 36.6 °C, SpO2 90%. Labs: Hb 90 g/L, platelets 450, WBC 3, creatinine 150 µmol/L, albumin 28 g/L, C3 0.5 g/L (0.7-1.5), C4 0.1 g/L (0.15-0.45), AST 100, ALT 94. Which SLE association most likely explains the current condition?
r: A JVP that rises on inspiration (Kussmaul sign), distant heart sounds and an early diastolic pericardial knock with ascites and oedema = constrictive pericarditis, a recognised sequel of lupus serositis; congestive hepatopathy explains the raised AST/ALT.
n: Why not D? low complements, creatinine 150 and albumin 28 suggest lupus nephritis, but renal disease does not cause Kussmaul's sign or a pericardial knock.

q: A patient with SLE (long stem with many investigations) has a 3-month history of shortness of breath, raised JVP, lower-limb oedema and crepitations. What is the diagnosis? [poor recall: no labs and no answer; the examinee doubted it matched the known Medgard SLE question]
r: The known Medgard version (SLE; JVP that rises on inspiration, i.e. Kussmaul sign; distant heart sounds with an early diastolic pericardial knock; ascites and oedema) is keyed constrictive pericarditis. Pericarditis is the commonest cardiac manifestation of SLE, and a raised JVP points to the heart,
n: Why not C? lupus nephritis with fluid overload can also give oedema, crackles and a raised JVP. Pick renal failure only if the stem stresses heavy proteinuria, rising creatinine and pulmonary congestion without pericardial signs. Claude: answered by analogy wi

q: A patient has back pain that is worse in the morning and improves within an hour with movement, with a positive Schober test. What examination should be done next?
r: Inflammatory back pain with reduced lumbar flexion (Schober) = ankylosing spondylitis; acute anterior uveitis is its commonest extra-articular feature (~25-40%) and needs urgent treatment.
n: Why not C? the cardiac lesion of AS is aortic regurgitation (aortitis), not mitral regurgitation, and it is much rarer than uveitis.

q: A patient comes to the clinic requesting sick leave because of back pain felt on waking from sleep. Yesterday he played football, with no injury or trauma. Examination shows localized tenderness and no limitation of flexion. What is the most appropriate management? [fourth option not recalled]
o: Give him sick leave for 3 days
Give analgesia and avoid (long or bed) rest
r: Acute non-specific mechanical back pain without red flags needs no imaging: give simple analgesia (NSAID or paracetamol) and advise him to stay active, because bed rest slows recovery. (comment on #88046)
n: Why not B? Rest is not therapeutic; guidelines advise continuing normal activity, and nothing here justifies time off work. Claude: Another 22 Oct recall (extract Q244) listed steroid / sick leave + strict bed rest / anti-inflammatory + muscle relaxant, keyed

q: A teenage footballer presents with low back pain that started this morning, the day after a football game, with no trauma, and asks for a sick leave. Examination shows lumbar tenderness. What should be done?
r: Acute mechanical back pain with no red flags needs only conservative care (superficial heat, simple analgesia, staying active); imaging and referral are not indicated.
n: Why not B? MRI is reserved for red flags (neurological deficit, cauda equina symptoms, fever, cancer, major trauma) or pain persisting beyond 6 weeks.

q: An adult presents with pain in the knee, wrist and ankle on one side for about 5 weeks. He had an upper respiratory tract infection a few weeks before the symptoms began. The knee is swollen. Laboratory studies and synovial fluid analysis are normal. What is the diagnosis?
r: A self-limiting, sterile synovitis after a viral URTI with normal labs and normal synovial fluid fits a post-infectious (transient) synovitis, the only recalled option that matches.
n: Why not A? septic arthritis has purulent synovial fluid (WBC >50,000, positive Gram stain/culture), fever and a raised CRP, all absent here. Claude: 'transient synovitis' is classically a childhood hip diagnosis; in an adult this picture is better called react

q: A patient presents with active bleeding [context not recalled]. What is the first thing to do?
o: Send blood for group and cross-match
r: Stopping ongoing haemorrhage comes first — direct pressure/tourniquet for external bleeding (<C>ABC); fluids and blood only buy time while the source keeps bleeding.
n: Why not B? Large-bore access is part of circulation management, but it does not stop the loss — haemorrhage control comes first. Claude: Recall gave only the answer; the other options were added for practice.

q: A patient has an open-book pelvic fracture [recalled as 'open pelvic fracture']. Which fluid should be used for resuscitation?
r: ATLS: start with 1 L of warmed isotonic crystalloid (Ringer's lactate preferred), move early to blood products (1:1:1) if bleeding continues, and apply a pelvic binder.
n: Why not A? Colloids such as albumin give no survival benefit over crystalloid in trauma and are not used for initial resuscitation.

q: An 18-year-old is hypotensive after an MVA. Which IV fluid is most appropriate for initial resuscitation?
r: ATLS recommends warm isotonic crystalloid, with Ringer's lactate preferred (1 L in adults), followed early by blood products.
n: Why not B? normal saline is acceptable, but large volumes cause hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis.

q: A trauma patient with chest and femur injuries is hypotensive (haemorrhagic shock); no CBC result is given. What should be given first? [rebuilt from the bank look-alike line]
r: Haemorrhagic shock from chest and femur injuries (a femoral fracture alone can lose 1-1.5 L) needs early blood. Until cross-matched blood is available, give uncross-matched O-negative blood; no CBC is needed to start.
n: Why not A? large crystalloid volumes dilute clotting factors and worsen the lethal triad; ATLS limits crystalloid to about 1 L before blood in haemorrhagic shock.

q: A patient involved in a road traffic accident presents to the emergency department with hypotension and tachycardia. What is the most likely diagnosis?
r: In trauma, hypotension with tachycardia is haemorrhagic (hypovolaemic) shock until proven otherwise. Neurogenic shock causes hypotension with bradycardia and warm peripheries after a cervical or high thoracic cord injury.
n: Why not A? Neurogenic shock causes hypotension with bradycardia (loss of sympathetic tone), not tachycardia.

q: A patient presents after a motorbike accident with only a large leg wound (laceration). His blood pressure is manually undetectable and haemoglobin is 6–7 g/dL; there is mild tachypnoea and O2 saturation is good. What would you most likely find in this patient?
r: Class III–IV haemorrhagic shock produces compensatory tachycardia (HR >120–140) with a thready pulse; the undetectable BP is already the hypotension, so the 'other' finding is tachycardia.
n: Why not D? Hypotension is already given (undetectable BP) — the question asks what else you would find.

q: A 21-year-old driver is involved in a head-on collision. He is severely tachypnoeic and hypotensive (BP 80/60). His trachea is deviated to the left, with palpable subcutaneous emphysema and reduced air entry over the right hemithorax. What is the most appropriate management?
o: Arterial puncture to measure blood gases
r: Tracheal deviation away from the side with reduced air entry, plus hypotension, is a tension pneumothorax. It is a clinical diagnosis, treated at once with needle (or finger) decompression and then a chest tube; never wait for an X-ray.
n: Why not C? intubating and starting positive-pressure ventilation before decompression makes a tension pneumothorax worse and can cause arrest.

q: A 27-year-old previously healthy man is brought to the ED after a motor vehicle accident. He is conscious and oriented. BP 80/70 mmHg, HR 98/min. He has distended neck veins and muffled heart sounds; there is no tracheal deviation. What is the most definitive treatment? [only the answer option was recalled]
r: Beck's triad (hypotension, distended neck veins, muffled heart sounds) with a central trachea and a narrow pulse pressure is cardiac tamponade. Of these choices, only pericardial decompression treats it.
n: Why not B? needle decompression treats tension pneumothorax, which would show tracheal deviation and absent breath sounds rather than muffled heart sounds. Claude: Recall gave only the answer; the other options were added for practice. Claude: ATLS calls peric

q: After a motor-vehicle accident in which the car swerved off the road and crashed, imaging shows a widened mediastinum and a pleural effusion. What is the most likely diagnosis?
r: Rapid deceleration tears the aorta at the isthmus (ligamentum arteriosum); the chest X-ray clues are a widened mediastinum (>8 cm), left haemothorax/apical cap, an obscured aortic knob and deviation of the trachea/NG tube to the right. Confirm with CT angiography. (Alhomrani's Sept page)
n: Why not C? tamponade gives Beck's triad (hypotension, raised JVP, muffled heart sounds) and a globular heart, not a widened mediastinum with haemothorax.

q: A 25-year-old after an MVA has dullness to percussion over one hemithorax, is drowsy, and is hypotensive (~80/64 mmHg) with HR >100. What is the most appropriate INITIAL step? [4th option not recalled]
r: Dullness with shock = massive hemothorax, which needs a chest tube to decompress it and measure blood loss (≥1500 mL, or >200 mL/h → thoracotomy). The drowsiness comes from hypoperfusion, and fluids are kept to a minimum at SBP ~80 (permissive hypotension: 80–90 per Schwartz, 70–90 per Bailey & Love
n: Why not C? intubation wins only when the drowsiness is due to hypoxia or airway compromise (e.g., SpO2 80%), as in the look-alike recall. Claude: in ATLS an unprotected airway always comes first; if the stem gives GCS ≤8 or an inability to protect the airway,

q: A trauma patient after an MVA has dullness over one hemithorax and hypotension, and is drowsy with SpO2 80%. What is the most appropriate initial step?
r: Drowsiness caused by hypoxia (SpO2 80%) means the airway and breathing are failing, so secure the airway by intubation first (A before B in ATLS), then insert the chest tube. (Alhomrani U2841: 'O2 80 + drowsiness = obviously intubation'.)
n: Why not B? a chest tube treats the hemothorax but doesn't immediately protect the airway of a hypoxic, obtunded patient. Claude: A new recall reported to Alhomrani; the other details are assumed to match the hemothorax recall.

q: A man has progressive shortness of breath for 5 days; he was in a traffic accident 2 weeks ago. Breath sounds are absent on the right. The chest X-ray (shown) has a homogeneous white opacity at the right lung base, looking like a haemothorax. RR 24/min, SpO2 90%, other vitals normal. What is the most appropriate management?
r: A significant traumatic haemothorax causing hypoxia is drained with a large-bore tube thoracostomy (5th intercostal space, mid-axillary line). Thoracotomy is reserved for massive haemothorax (>1500 mL at insertion or >200 mL/h for 2–4 h).
n: Why not D? Thoracic surgery is for massive or ongoing bleeding, or for clot retained after drainage; a stable patient gets a chest tube first.

q: A man with chest trauma complains of severe chest pain. There is severe chest-wall tenderness with multiple bruises over the right chest. On primary survey the airway is patent and clear, and he is alert and conscious, but his chest wall moves paradoxically (unstable) when he moves or breathes deeply. Air entry is present and clear bilaterally. Vital signs are normal apart from SpO2 86%. What is the most appropriate management?
r: Flail chest with underlying pulmonary contusion is treated with oxygen and strong analgesia (IV opioids, epidural or intercostal blocks) so he can breathe and clear secretions. Equal breath sounds exclude a pneumothorax or haemothorax needing a tube. Ventilation is only for respiratory failure despi
n: Why not B? Mechanical ventilation is for respiratory failure that persists despite oxygen and adequate analgesia. He is alert and protecting his airway, and his hypoxia is driven by pain and contusion. Claude: Extract status Review. Claude: oxygen is given alo

q: A patient is brought to the ED after a motor vehicle accident. He is oriented; vital signs are not given. Air entry is normal, and the chest X-ray shows a flail chest (ribs 2-6) with lung contusion. What is the next step?
r: Flail chest with contusion in an oriented, adequately ventilating patient is managed with oxygen and good analgesia (IV opioids, epidural or regional block) so he can breathe deeply and cough, plus careful fluids. Intubation is only for respiratory failure.
n: Why not B? intubation and ventilation are for hypoxia or respiratory failure despite analgesia; they are not routine in flail chest.

q: After a motor-vehicle accident, a patient has a 2 × 1.5 cm open wound on the left chest with a sucking-air sound, left chest pain, reduced breath sounds and a resonant percussion note. What is the most appropriate management?
r: Open (sucking) pneumothorax: close the defect at once with an occlusive dressing taped on three sides so that it acts as a flutter valve, then insert a chest tube away from the wound and close the wound surgically later (ATLS).
n: Why not C? A chest tube is the definitive next step, but the wound must be sealed with the 3-sided dressing first.

q: A patient is brought to the ED after a motor vehicle accident with a cervical collar in place. Part of the car penetrated his chest, and there is a bubbling wound on the right side of the chest. What is the most appropriate next step in management? [consciousness and vital signs not recalled]
r: A bubbling (sucking) chest wound is an open pneumothorax, which is a Breathing problem: cover it with a three-sided occlusive dressing, support ventilation, then insert a chest tube away from the wound. With no stated airway compromise, assisted ventilation is the next step.
n: Why not B? a definitive airway comes first only if the airway is threatened (unconscious, GCS ≤8, falling SpO2), as in the fuller 18 Oct copy. Claude: Disputed: the fuller 18 Oct copy (unconscious, shallow breathing, SpO2 89%) is keyed 'establish a definitive

q: A 27-year-old motorcyclist hit by a car was briefly unconscious, then regained consciousness in the ER with labored breathing. He has a penetrating chest wound from glass with air bubbling from the wound. BP 90/59, SpO2 89%. What is the next step?
r: Air bubbling from the wound means an open (sucking) pneumothorax, a Breathing problem: cover with a three-sided occlusive dressing and support ventilation, then chest tube. Alhomrani: open pneumothorax 'can' be ventilated.
n: Why not A? he is conscious and talking, so his airway is patent; a definitive airway is for GCS ≤8 or a threatened airway.

q: A 27-year-old motorcyclist was rendered unconscious after being hit by a car and arrives with labored breathing. He has a penetrating chest wound from glass with air bubbling from the wound. BP 90/59, SpO2 89%. The stem does NOT say that he regained consciousness. What is the next step?
r: Alhomrani (21:57, '100% sure'): if the stem doesn't mention that he regained consciousness, he is still unconscious and can't protect his airway, so A comes first. If the stem says he regained consciousness, the answer is C (support ventilation and seal the open pneumothorax).
n: Why not C? correct only in the 'regained consciousness' version, where the airway is already patent. Claude: The previous 20 October file (Q1) had the 'regained consciousness' version, keyed. Silent comments on this post were split between A and C.

q: After a motor vehicle crash a patient was unconscious; he now has shallow breathing, SpO2 89% and BP 100/70, with a penetrating (bubbling) chest wound. What is the most appropriate next step? [18 Oct copy, from the extract's 'other answer' line]
r: ABCDE order: an unconscious, hypoxic patient with shallow breathing cannot protect or maintain his airway, so a definitive airway (RSI with in-line c-spine stabilisation) comes before breathing support and IV access.
n: Why not C? ventilatory support treats the open pneumothorax but does not work without a secured airway in an unconscious, hypoxic patient. Claude: Made from the extract's 'Other answer' line (the fuller 18 Oct copy), not from a Lookalike line.

q: A patient comes to the ER with a stab wound to the central abdomen. BP 116/58, SpO2 92%. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
r: A haemodynamically stable patient with an anterior abdominal stab wound and no peritonitis or evisceration can be evaluated with CT (plus serial examinations or local wound exploration). Laparotomy is for shock, peritonitis or evisceration.
n: Why not B? FAST is quick but insensitive in penetrating injury (it misses hollow-viscus, diaphragm and retroperitoneal injuries), so a negative FAST does not clear a stab wound. Claude: SpO2 92% hints at an associated chest injury, so get a chest X-ray as well

q: A patient involved in a motor vehicle accident presents shouting, with anterior chest pain. His blood pressure is 90/60 mmHg and his heart rate is 110/min. What is the next step?
r: He is shouting, so airway and breathing are intact. With hypotension the priority is to find the bleeding source fast, and bedside FAST (pericardium, abdomen) is the rapid adjunct in an unstable patient; CT is only for stable patients.
n: Why not D? IV access belongs to the C step and is done at the same time by the team; the key wanted the step that finds the source. Claude: Disputed: the 22 Oct examinee (SMLE_Questions.pdf Q179) ticked 'Establish IV access', and the extract records D as an al

q: A man in his 20s involved in an MVA is alert, with abdominal distension. BP 85/54; FAST shows free intra-abdominal fluid. What is the appropriate NEXT management? [another copy asks 'appropriate management' — same answer]
r: Unstable blunt trauma with a positive FAST means intra-abdominal hemorrhage, so he needs immediate laparotomy. Stopping the bleed is the priority, and blood (MTP) runs during transfer to theatre (permissive hypotension, SBP ~80–90). (Alhomrani U2837: both 'next' and 'appropriate' → laparotomy.)
n: Why not B? MTP is started alongside, but transfusion can't stop ongoing bleeding; THE management is surgical source control.

q: A 55-year-old man sustained blunt abdominal trauma in an MVA. BP 90/63, HR 104, and he is NOT responding to fluids. FAST is negative for fluid in the pericardium, chest and abdomen. What is the next best step?
r: A patient who doesn't respond to fluids is unstable and must not go to CT. With a negative FAST, DPL (or aspiration) is the bedside test to exclude intraperitoneal bleeding before deciding on laparotomy. (Alhomrani U2928: DPL only because 'not responding to fluid' is written in the stem.)
n: Why not B? CT is only for hemodynamically stable patients, and a fluid non-responder can't leave the resuscitation bay. Claude: Alhomrani: if 'not responding to fluid' was NOT written, CT vs DPL is unclear ('I don't know'). A shock index >1 predicts the need f

q: A trauma patient has evidence of active internal bleeding and hypotension (BP 88/55 mmHg). What is the most appropriate management? [assumed NOT pelvic]
r: Ongoing intra-abdominal hemorrhage with hypotension needs surgical control (damage-control laparotomy), with transfusion given at the same time.
n: Why not A? transfusion supports the patient but doesn't stop the bleeding; it was the answer only for the copy that said internal PELVIC bleeding. Claude: Alhomrani: the full recall said 'internal PELVIC bleed', so this may be a poorly recalled copy or a diffe

q: A trauma patient has active internal PELVIC bleeding and hypotension (BP 88/55 mmHg). What is the most appropriate management?
r: Laparotomy doesn't control pelvic (retroperitoneal) bleeding, and opening the abdomen can release the tamponade. Treat with blood products (MTP) and a pelvic binder, then angioembolization or preperitoneal packing. (Alhomrani U2896: the full recall said 'internal pelvic bleed', which is why laparoto
n: Why not B? laparotomy is for intraperitoneal bleeding; it doesn't control pelvic venous or arterial bleeding. Claude: Alhomrani implied A for the pelvic version rather than stating it outright.

q: A patient involved in a motor vehicle accident is undergoing laparotomy for abdominal bleeding and is haemodynamically unstable. Intraoperatively, the surgeon finds multiple liver lacerations. What is the best next step in management?
r: An unstable patient with multiple liver lacerations needs damage-control surgery. Perihepatic packing (with a Pringle manoeuvre if needed) tamponades the bleeding, followed by ICU resuscitation and a planned second look. Resection and ligation are avoided while the patient has the lethal triad (hypo
n: Why not C? Individual vessel ligation suits a stable patient with an isolated bleeder. With multiple lacerations in an unstable patient it wastes time and worsens coagulopathy.

q: A young man presents after a motorcycle accident. There is blood at the urethral meatus and pelvic X-ray shows a pelvic fracture. Blood pressure is 110/70 mmHg. What is the initial investigation?
r: Blood at the meatus (± high-riding prostate, perineal/scrotal haematoma) with a pelvic fracture means urethral injury until proven otherwise: perform a retrograde urethrogram before any urethral catheter.
n: Why not B? Contrast CT is the work-up of a stable pelvic-trauma patient, but the urethra must first be cleared by RUG when there is meatal blood.

q: A patient with a pelvic fracture has a scrotal haematoma and blood at the urethral meatus. What is the next investigation?
r: Meatal blood plus scrotal/perineal haematoma after a pelvic fracture signals urethral disruption → retrograde urethrogram before any catheterisation.
n: Why not A? CT does not reliably show urethral disruption, and blind catheterisation before RUG can convert a partial tear to a complete one.

q: A 25-year-old man presents after a motorcycle accident with generalized body pain. He looks anxious, breathing normally, with no external bleeding. Pelvic examination shows an unstable pelvic fracture and no blood at the external meatus; the bladder was drained by suprapubic aspiration. BP 110/80, temperature 36.6 °C, RR 16. X-ray shows unstable pelvic rami fractures. Which is the initial imaging?
r: A haemodynamically stable patient with a pelvic fracture and no urethral signs (bladder already drained suprapubically) needs contrast CT of the abdomen/pelvis (with delayed/cystographic phase) to define the fractures, bleeding and bladder injury.
n: Why not B? RUG is indicated only with signs of urethral injury (meatal blood, high-riding prostate, perineal haematoma) — none here, and a suprapubic catheter is already in. Claude: Extract version: 'pelvic trauma without urethral bleeding', with 'CT urography

q: A 26-year-old man complains of pelvic pain after a motorcycle collision. Physical and radiological examination confirm a pelvic fracture. Urological work-up shows a normal urethrogram and an extraperitoneal bladder injury. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment for his bladder injury?
o: Placement of a permanent suprapubic tube
Catheter drainage followed by definitive repair after 2 weeks
Catheter drainage for 2 weeks followed by repeat imaging
r: Uncomplicated extraperitoneal bladder rupture is managed with urethral catheter drainage for about 10-14 days, then a cystogram to confirm healing. Intraperitoneal rupture, bladder-neck injury, bone fragments in the bladder or a concurrent laparotomy need surgical repair.
n: Why not A? Immediate repair is for intraperitoneal rupture or complicated extraperitoneal injuries, not this one.

q: A man has a head injury in an MVA with a temporal bone fracture. Paramedics report a lucid interval (initially unresponsive but arousable), and he then becomes unconscious again in hospital. What is the most likely diagnosis?
r: A temporal (pterion) fracture tears the middle meningeal artery, giving an arterial extradural haematoma: brief LOC, lucid interval, then rapid decline with an ipsilateral blown pupil. CT shows a biconvex hyperdensity that does not cross sutures → urgent craniotomy.
n: Why not B? Subdural haematoma is venous (bridging veins), crescent-shaped, and usually causes a slower decline in elderly or alcoholic patients without the classic temporal-fracture lucid interval. Claude: The 4 Nov recall listed only subdural vs extradural; o

q: An elderly patient has a subdural haematoma with lateralising signs and a 13 mm midline shift; GCS 7/15. He has been intubated and resuscitated. What is the next step?
o: Elevate the head of the bed
r: An acute SDH with midline shift >5 mm or thickness >10 mm needs urgent surgical evacuation whatever the GCS (Brain Trauma Foundation); with GCS ≤8 and lateralising signs, craniotomy is the definitive step once the airway is secured. (Alhomrani's Sept page, Q28)
n: Why not A? mannitol (like head elevation and brief hyperventilation) only buys time on the way to theatre; it does not remove the clot.

q: A patient presents with an open femur fracture with a 5-cm wound. What is the first step in management?
o: IV antibiotics within the first hour
r: In open fractures, IV antibiotics (e.g. cefazolin, plus gentamicin for Gustilo III) and tetanus prophylaxis should be given as early as possible, ideally within 1 hour. Formal debridement and stabilisation follow in theatre within 24 hours.
n: Why not A? Debridement is essential but comes after early antibiotics. Delay in antibiotics, more than delay in debridement, drives infection risk. Claude: The 22 Oct examinee ticked 'debridement and stabilisation' (option D in his copy); the extract key is ke

q: An adult in a motor-vehicle collision has a Gustilo IIIa open, contaminated wound with a comminuted, displaced mid-shaft femur fracture. What is the most appropriate management?
o: Intramedullary fixation with primary wound closure
Debridement, external fixation and delayed wound closure
r: Open fractures need IV antibiotics and tetanus cover, urgent debridement and irrigation, skeletal stabilisation and DELAYED closure of a contaminated wound; with no 'debridement + IM nail' option, damage-control external fixation is the safe choice. (Alhomrani's Sept page: 'no option with debridemen
n: Why not B? IM nailing is the definitive fixation for femoral shaft fractures, but closing a contaminated IIIa wound primarily without debridement invites deep infection. Claude: The fourth option was nonsense (e.g. cast) and is omitted.

q: A 30-year-old man [age recalled as '300'] presents 6 hours after an assault with an open scalp wound, within the window for primary closure. What is the appropriate wound management?
o: Leave it to heal by granulation
r: The scalp's rich blood supply allows primary closure after irrigation and debridement even beyond the usual 6–8 h window (up to ~24 h); a clean early wound is closed primarily.
n: Why not A? Delayed or secondary closure is for heavily contaminated, infected or late wounds (e.g., bites, >24 h) — not a 6-hour scalp wound.

q: An adult who does not remember when he last received a tetanus vaccine presents with a dirty wound. What is the best preventive method?
o: Irrigation and cleaning of the wound
r: With an unknown tetanus history and a dirty (tetanus-prone) wound, give a tetanus-toxoid vaccine (Td/Tdap in adults) plus tetanus immunoglobulin, alongside wound cleaning and debridement. Cleaning alone gives no immunity.
n: Why not A? Irrigation and debridement are needed for every wound, but they do not provide the immunisation that an unknown vaccine history requires. Claude: adults receive Td/Tdap (DTaP is the paediatric form), TIG is also indicated here, and antibiotics are n

q: After appendicectomy, the patient's wound shows mild erythema and exudate. Which type of dressing is most appropriate?
r: Hydrocolloid dressings suit wounds with low to moderate exudate and keep the wound moist. Alginates are for moderate to heavy exudate, and VAC is for large, deep or complex wounds.
n: Why not B? Alginate absorbs moderate to heavy exudate; the examinee's copy read 'moderate', which is why he chose it, but 'mild' fits hydrocolloid. Claude: Disputed: the 22 Oct examinee (whose copy read MODERATE erythema and exudate) ticked B, Alginate. Claude

q: A diabetic patient has a plantar ulcer with exudate. Which dressing should be used?
r: Alginate (calcium alginate from seaweed) forms a gel with exudate and absorbs many times its weight. It is the classic choice for moderately to heavily exuding (and bleeding) wounds, including diabetic foot ulcers.
n: Why not B? hydrofiber (CMC) is also highly absorbent, but the standard exam answer is alginate; hydrocolloid and film are occlusive dressings for dry or low-exudate wounds and are avoided in infected diabetic ulcers.

q: A 35-year-old woman with appendicitis is scheduled for laparoscopic appendectomy. She has asthma with no recent exacerbation and a fever above 38 °C. Which of the following will improve surgical safety?
o: Site marking and preparation of surgical equipment
Pre-op IV antibiotics to accelerate the process
Omit consent because it is minor surgery
r: The WHO Surgical Safety Checklist (site marking, equipment check, sign-in/time-out/sign-out) is the intervention proven to reduce surgical complications and wrong-site errors.
n: Why not B? prophylactic antibiotics within 60 minutes of incision reduce surgical-site infection, but their purpose is not to 'accelerate the process', so the option's rationale is wrong. Claude: Twin trap (Alhomrani U2895, wrong-site knee surgery): a site-mar

q: A 27-year-old woman has 3 days of colicky abdominal pain, vomiting and constipation. She had an appendectomy 5 years ago. Her abdomen is distended with high-pitched bowel sounds. A CT abdomen with IV contrast is planned. Which investigation is most important before the CT?
r: Adhesive small-bowel obstruction is likely; before any ionising imaging in a woman of reproductive age, pregnancy must be excluded with beta-hCG, because it changes both imaging and management.
n: Why not B? renal function is checked before IV contrast, but in a young healthy woman the must-do test before a CT is the pregnancy test.

q: A patient diagnosed with acute (uncomplicated) appendicitis asks how long she will receive antibiotics. What is the most appropriate regimen? [Sept examinee's copy (#88013): all options began 'one dose preoperative' and differed only in postoperative days]
o: Preoperative and continue for 3 days after surgery
r: For uncomplicated (non-perforated) appendicitis, a single prophylactic dose within 60 minutes before incision (e.g. cefoxitin, or cefazolin + metronidazole) is enough. Postoperative courses are only for complicated or perforated appendicitis.
n: Why not B? about 3 days of postoperative antibiotics fits complicated (perforated or gangrenous) appendicitis, not an uncomplicated case.

q: A patient on post-operative day 5 after sigmoidectomy has fever (38.5 °C) only; the surgical site is not described [extract version: 4th post-op day]. What is the most important initial next step?
r: Fever on day 5–7 after bowel surgery is wound infection or anastomotic leak until proven otherwise, so examine the surgical site first; drug review comes only once the wound is known to be clean.
n: Why not D? Medication review (drug fever) is a diagnosis of exclusion, chosen only when the stem already says the wound is clean. Claude: Disputed: this examinee chose 'review drugs'.

q: A 45-year-old woman on day 5 after hysterectomy has fever. She has no complaints and the wound is clean. What is the next step?
r: When a post-op patient is well, with a clean wound and no localising symptoms, the keyed next step is to review the drug chart for drug fever (antibiotics, heparin, anticonvulsants).
n: Why not B? UTI is a classic day-3–5 cause and was the original key, but with no urinary symptoms and a well patient the confirmed answer is medication review. Claude: Extract key changed 4 Oct B→D (confirmed by a 100% scorer).

q: A 25-year-old man underwent an open appendicectomy for a perforated appendix and was discharged on the 2nd postoperative day. He returns on the 8th postoperative day with pain and redness around the wound. There is purulent discharge from the wound site. The abdomen is soft, with tenderness over the wound only. Digital rectal examination is unremarkable. BP 110/70 mmHg, HR 110/min, RR 18/min, temperature 38 °C. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
r: A superficial surgical-site infection with pus is treated by opening and draining the wound, with dressings. The soft abdomen and normal DRE make a deep or pelvic collection unlikely. Antibiotics are an adjunct for cellulitis or systemic features.
n: Why not A? Antibiotics alone do not treat a collection of pus; source control by opening the wound is the key step.

q: A patient develops abdominal pain and distension after colonic surgery. He is vitally stable. There is fresh blood and coffee-ground aspirate from the NG tube. What is the diagnostic modality of choice?
r: Fresh blood and coffee-ground NG aspirate localise bleeding to the upper GI tract (e.g. post-operative stress ulceration); upper endoscopy is both diagnostic and therapeutic, ideally within 24 hours.
n: Why not D? CT suits post-operative leaks, collections or obstruction, but a bloody NG aspirate is an upper-GI bleed that needs endoscopy.

q: A man with rheumatoid arthritis on NSAIDs presents with severe epigastric pain, vomiting and abdominal distension. What is the initial investigation?
r: NSAID use with sudden severe epigastric pain suggests a perforated peptic ulcer; an erect chest X-ray showing free air under the diaphragm is the quick initial test, and endoscopy is contraindicated when perforation is suspected.
n: Why not D? CT is more sensitive and is done if the erect film is negative but suspicion remains; it is not the initial test.

q: A diabetic patient with rheumatoid arthritis who takes NSAIDs presents with sudden-onset severe abdominal pain with guarding and rigidity. Amylase is mildly raised and an erect chest X-ray (shown) has free air under the diaphragm. What is the most likely diagnosis?
r: NSAID use + sudden severe pain + board-like rigidity + pneumoperitoneum = perforated peptic ulcer. Amylase can be mildly raised after a perforation, but pancreatitis does not put free air under the diaphragm.
n: Why not C? The raised amylase tempts toward pancreatitis, but free subdiaphragmatic air means a perforated viscus.

q: A known peptic ulcer patient presents with severe epigastric pain, and the erect X-ray shows free air under the diaphragm. What is the management?
o: Conservative management with IV PPI and nasogastric suction
r: Perforated peptic ulcer with pneumoperitoneum and peritonitis is a surgical emergency: resuscitate, give IV PPI and antibiotics, then operate (laparotomy or laparoscopy) with an omental (Graham) patch repair.
n: Why not B? Non-operative (Taylor) management is only for a sealed perforation in a stable patient without peritonitis, confirmed by water-soluble contrast. Claude: Recall gave only the answer; the other options were added for practice.

q: A 67-year-old man has had sudden severe left lower abdominal pain for 8 hours with vomiting and fever, and has passed no gas or stool since yesterday. No previous abdominal surgery or recent weight loss. Venous lactate 2.5, CRP 18, WBC 17. X-ray shows air under the diaphragm. What is the diagnosis?
r: An older patient with acute LLQ pain, fever, leucocytosis and pneumoperitoneum, without weight loss, has perforated sigmoid diverticulitis (Hinchey III/IV); the sigmoid is the commonest site. Management is resuscitation, antibiotics and surgery (Hartmann's or resection with anastomosis).
n: Why not C? perforated colon cancer is possible at 67, but the lack of weight loss or change in bowel habit and the acute febrile LLQ onset favour diverticulitis.

q: A boy has periumbilical pain that has shifted to the right iliac fossa, with vomiting, RIF tenderness and leucocytosis. How should the diagnosis be confirmed?
r: Pain migrating to the RIF + vomiting + tenderness + leucocytosis = acute appendicitis (high Alvarado score), and imaging confirms it: ultrasound first in children (no radiation), CT if the US is equivocal. (Alhomrani's Sept page, Q20)
n: Why not B? IV fluids with active observation suit equivocal, low-risk cases; with this classic picture the next step is confirmation and surgery, not waiting.

q: A 24-year-old has RLQ pain, nausea and vomiting. Examination shows a right iliac fossa mass. CT shows a 10 × 12 periappendicular abscess with a faecolith, extending to the right flank. What is the most appropriate management?
r: A large (>3–4 cm) walled-off appendiceal abscess in a stable patient → image-guided percutaneous drainage + IV antibiotics, with interval appendectomy considered later (especially with a faecolith); operating into the inflammatory mass risks ileocaecal resection.
n: Why not B? Laparoscopic appendectomy suits uncomplicated appendicitis or a small abscess; for a large mature abscess with a drain option, drainage comes first. Claude: Alhomrani (U1775) answered laparoscopic appendectomy for the extract's wording, whose option

q: A 24-year-old complains of RLQ pain; examination shows a right iliac fossa mass. CT shows a 10 × 12 periappendicular abscess. What is the most appropriate management?
r: When percutaneous drainage is not offered, laparoscopic appendectomy with drainage of the collection (WSES: safe in experienced hands, shorter stay) beats open surgical incision and drainage or open appendectomy. (Alhomrani U1775.)
n: Why not D? Open surgical incision and drainage is a more morbid operation that leaves the appendix in place; it is not percutaneous drainage. Claude: Extract key for this wording was D (incision and drainage, past recall). Pairing inferred from the extract, wh

q: A 29-year-old man presents to the ER with suspected acute appendicitis: RLQ pain and tenderness around the umbilicus. At appendicectomy through a gridiron incision the appendix is found to be normal. What should the surgeon do?
o: Do a midline incision and remove the appendix
Remove the appendix and close the abdomen
r: When the appendix is normal at operation, the surgeon must look for another cause of RLQ pain. The main one is Meckel's diverticulum (inspect about 60 cm of terminal ileum); others are mesenteric adenitis, Crohn's ileitis and, in women, adnexal pathology. The appendix is usually removed as well.
n: Why not D? Removing the appendix and closing without exploring misses the real pathology. Appendicectomy is done in addition to the search, not instead of it.

q: A patient underwent appendectomy for acute appendicitis. One week later, histopathology revealed an appendiceal carcinoid tumour. Which of the following is the most appropriate management? [tumour size and site were not recalled]
r: Further surgical excision (right hemicolectomy) is indicated for an appendiceal NET >2 cm, at the base/caecal margin, with mesoappendiceal invasion >3 mm or lymphovascular invasion; the ✓ answer assumed a tumour at the base.
n: Why not C? Observation (appendectomy alone is curative) is right only for a tumour <1 cm at the tip with clear margins and no adverse features. Claude: without size/site in the stem, most incidental carcinoids are <1 cm at the tip, where observation (C) is cor

q: A 44-year-old woman has epigastric pain after eating a fatty meal that resolves within 2 hours. What is the diagnosis?
r: Pain in the epigastrium or RUQ after a fatty meal that settles within a few hours, with no fever or jaundice, is biliary colic from a stone transiently blocking the cystic duct. Pain lasting more than 6 hours with fever suggests cholecystitis.
n: Why not B? Pancreatitis gives severe, persistent epigastric pain radiating to the back with raised lipase. It does not settle within 2 hours.

q: A 45-year-old woman has postprandial right upper quadrant pain, nausea and emesis for a few days that became persistent over the last 20 hours. BP 110/70 mmHg, HR 87/min, T 37.2 °C. WBC 11 ×10⁹/L, direct bilirubin 9.5 µmol/L (1.5–6.5), total bilirubin 18.5 µmol/L (3.5–16.5), ALP 463 IU/L (39–117). Ultrasound: cholelithiasis, gallbladder wall thickening and a common bile duct of 12 mm. Which of the following is the most appropriate management? [The 4 Nov examinee's own recall was shorter: a woman with RUQ pain 2 days ago, ultrasound showing a very dilated CBD, asking for the initial management, with options ERCP, MRCP and lap chole. The photo matched it to this fuller version.]
r: Gallstones with a dilated CBD (12 mm) and cholestatic LFTs are read as choledocholithiasis: clear the duct by ERCP, then do laparoscopic cholecystectomy in the same admission.
n: Why not B? MRCP is the test when the likelihood of CBD stones is intermediate; with a 12 mm duct and obstructive LFTs the keys go straight to therapeutic ERCP. Claude: strictly by ASGE criteria (no stone seen, bilirubin only ~1.1 mg/dL) this is intermediate ri
