q: A patient was diagnosed with ulcerative colitis 6 years ago. When should screening colonoscopy for colon cancer be done?
r: Surveillance colonoscopy for colitis (UC beyond the rectum, or Crohn's colitis involving ≥1/3 of the colon) starts 8–10 years after symptom onset and is repeated every 1–3 years. The exception is UC with PSC: surveillance starts at diagnosis and is annual.
n: Why not C? Starting at diagnosis applies only to UC with primary sclerosing cholangitis.

q: A patient with schizophrenia on medication presents with chronic constipation and abdominal pain. CT shows massive colonic dilatation of about 10 cm with no mechanical obstruction. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Colonoscopic decompression with a rectal tube
r: Massive colonic dilatation without mechanical obstruction, here from antipsychotic or anticholinergic drugs, is managed without surgery. Stop the offending drugs, correct electrolytes, then use neostigmine or colonoscopic decompression with a decompression tube. Surgery is only for perforation, isch
n: Why not B? Total colectomy is reserved for perforation, ischaemia or failure of decompression. It is not the first step for a non-obstructed dilated colon. Claude: Extract status Review. Claude: neostigmine usually comes before colonoscopic decompression, but

q: A 28-year-old woman has on-and-off painless rectal bleeding and an anal swelling that reduces spontaneously. Anoscopy shows haemorrhoids at 3, 7 and 11 o'clock with active bleeding. Haemoglobin is 8.8 g/dL. What is the most appropriate management? [the 2 Nov fragment (#88000) asked for the 'definitive' treatment, Hb 8]
r: Haemorrhoids that have bled enough to cause significant anaemia are treated definitively by excisional haemorrhoidectomy; banding suits uncomplicated grade I–II disease without anaemia.
n: Why not C? Rubber band ligation is first-line for grade I–II internal haemorrhoids (spontaneously reducing = grade II), but not once they have caused anaemia (Hb 8.8). Claude: Extract key changed 6 Nov C→D (the extract editor's ruling). Another copy is the 2 N

q: A 45-year-old woman comes to the clinic complaining of blood in her stool. On examination she has grade III haemorrhoids at the 6 and 9 o'clock positions with active bleeding. Her blood pressure is 126/75 mmHg, heart rate 120 bpm and haemoglobin 105 g/L. What is the most appropriate next management?
r: In a 45-year-old with rectal bleeding and anaemia, haemorrhoids seen on examination must not be assumed to be the only source. Colonoscopy is needed to exclude a proximal lesion or colorectal cancer before definitive haemorrhoid treatment.
n: Why not A? Haemorrhoidectomy is the definitive treatment for grade III-IV disease, but the next step is to exclude another bleeding source with colonoscopy. Claude: Extract status Review (one source). Claude: with HR 120, resuscitate first in practice.

q: A 47-year-old woman with iron-deficiency anaemia has third-degree haemorrhoids. What is the most appropriate next step?
r: Iron-deficiency anaemia must not be blamed on haemorrhoids in a patient over ~40–45 until colonoscopy has excluded colorectal (especially right-sided) cancer.
n: Why not B? Haemorrhoidectomy treats grade III piles but would miss a colonic cancer causing the anaemia.

q: A 30-year-old man has bleeding per rectum. Anoscopy shows swellings at the 3 and 7 o'clock positions. Injection of a sclerosing agent is planned. Which lesion is the best indication for sclerotherapy?
r: Injection sclerotherapy (e.g. phenol in almond oil, injected above the dentate line where the mucosa is insensate) is used for small bleeding first- and second-degree internal haemorrhoids.
n: Why not C? prolapsed (third/fourth-degree) haemorrhoids respond poorly to sclerotherapy and need banding or haemorrhoidectomy; external and thrombosed piles lie below the dentate line and are painful to inject.

q: A 70-year-old woman presents with rectal pain and passage of mucus. A clinical photograph is shown. What is the diagnosis?
r: Full-thickness rectal prolapse typically affects elderly women. It appears as a mucus-covered mass with concentric circular mucosal folds protruding through the anus, with mucus discharge, soiling and discomfort.
n: Why not A? Prolapsed haemorrhoids are discrete cushions with radial folds and usually present with bright red bleeding, not a concentric mucus-covered mass. Claude: Picture-based question; the photograph was not captured in the recall.

q: A patient presents with a chronic anal fissure. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
r: First-line treatment for a chronic anal fissure is topical 'chemical sphincterotomy' with diltiazem 2% (a CCB) or GTN, plus fibre and sitz baths. Botulinum toxin is second-line, and lateral internal sphincterotomy is for failed medical therapy.
n: Why not C? Lateral internal sphincterotomy is the most effective (definitive) treatment but is reserved for fissures that fail 6-8 weeks of topical therapy. Claude: Extract status Review (one source).

q: A patient has a perianal fistula with an external opening at the 7 o'clock position. Where is the internal opening most likely to be?
r: Goodsall's rule: external openings behind the transverse anal line (the 3-9 o'clock line through 6) follow a curved tract to the posterior midline (6 o'clock). Anterior openings within ~3 cm of the anus run straight (radially) into the canal. 7 o'clock is posterior, so the tract goes to the posterio
n: Why not A? a short straight radial tract is the rule only for anterior openings; posterior ones curve to the posterior midline.

q: A patient has perianal pain, pruritus and a fluctuant perianal mass, with fever and a high WBC count (size not given). What is the appropriate next step?
r: A fluctuant perianal abscess needs prompt incision and drainage. Antibiotics are added AFTER drainage when there is cellulitis, systemic signs, immunosuppression or valve disease. (Alhomrani U2892: final B.)
n: Why not A? fever doesn't change the order, because antibiotics can't penetrate an undrained abscess.

q: A 32-year-old man at a routine check-up has had an inguinal hernia for 3 years. It is asymptomatic and reducible, and the deep-ring occlusion test is positive. What is the best next step?
r: A positive deep-ring occlusion test (hernia controlled) = indirect inguinal hernia. A young, surgically fit man is offered elective tension-free mesh repair (Lichtenstein or laparoscopic), because most watched hernias need surgery within 5–7 years. (Alhomrani U2879, citing Bailey & Love 27th ed. and
n: Why not C? watchful waiting is acceptable mainly for elderly men with small asymptomatic hernias or high surgical risk, not for a fit 32-year-old. Claude: Alhomrani's add-ons: incisional hernia — small and asymptomatic is 50/50, large or symptomatic → repair.

q: A 68-year-old otherwise healthy man has been advised to have surgery for a reducible left inguinal hernia. What is the most appropriate treatment? [photo page: 72-year-old with moderate pain; poster: 'option B was repair with mesh']
r: Tension-free open mesh (Lichtenstein) repair is the standard for a primary unilateral inguinal hernia: lower recurrence than suture repair, and it can be done under local anaesthesia in older men.
n: Why not C? Laparoscopic (TEP/TAPP) repair is favoured for bilateral or recurrent-after-open hernias and needs general anaesthesia; the keyed answer for a primary unilateral hernia is open mesh. Claude: HerniaSurge 2018 also accepts laparo-endoscopic repair for

q: A 28-year-old man has a 2-year history of a reducible right inguinal hernia that has become painful over the last 16 hours, with progressive abdominal distension and vomiting. Examination shows a distended abdomen, exaggerated bowel sounds and a tender right inguinal swelling with red discoloration of the overlying skin. WBC 9.8 x10^9/L (4.5-10.5). Erect abdominal X-ray: multiple air-fluid levels. Which of the following is the most likely hernia complication?
r: A painful hernia with bowel obstruction (distension, vomiting, air-fluid levels) plus tenderness and redness of the overlying skin means the blood supply is compromised: strangulation. A normal WBC does not exclude it.
n: Why not B? 'Obstructed' explains the distension and air-fluid levels, but red, tender skin over the sac signals ischaemia, i.e. strangulation.

q: A patient has intestinal obstruction from an incarcerated hernia, with guarding and rigidity (signs of strangulation/peritonism). What is the management?
o: Urgent exploratory surgery for the hernia
r: An incarcerated hernia with obstruction and peritonism is strangulated until proven otherwise. Resuscitate and take the patient to theatre urgently to reduce and repair the hernia and resect non-viable bowel; imaging must not delay surgery.
n: Why not C? adhesions are the commonest cause of small-bowel obstruction overall, but here the obstruction has an obvious cause, the incarcerated hernia, and that is what must be explored.

q: A patient with a previously reducible hernia now has signs suggesting strangulation. No surgical option is offered. What is the next step? [rebuilt from the bank look-alike line]
r: When surgery is not among the options, the best choice is CT abdomen/pelvis. It confirms bowel within the hernia and shows obstruction or ischaemia to plan the operation.
n: Why not A? ultrasound can show hernia contents but is operator-dependent and poor at judging obstruction and bowel ischaemia; observation is unsafe.

q: A middle-aged man with chronic liver disease and ascites has a large REDUCIBLE umbilical hernia with abdominal distension, thinning of the overlying skin and dilated veins. What is the most appropriate management?
o: Delay repair until ascites is controlled
r: In cirrhosis, elective umbilical hernia repair waits until ascites is medically controlled (diuretics, paracentesis, TIPS); repair with tense ascites leads to recurrence, leaks and infection. Transplant candidates have it repaired at transplant, and complicated hernias are repaired now. (Alhomrani U
n: Why not D? paracentesis with immediate open repair is for urgent or complicated hernias, and this one is reducible. Claude: thinning skin signals impending rupture, so some surgeons would expedite repair once ascites is controlled; if the stem shows ulceration

q: A patient with cirrhosis and ascites has a reducible but uncomfortable umbilical hernia, and repair is planned. What is the next step?
o: Delay repair until ascites is controlled
r: With no stated indication for transplantation, the rule is to control the ascites first and then repair electively. Referral 'for transplantation' (as opposed to transplant EVALUATION) isn't justified by this stem. (Alhomrani's simplified approach U2871, from Sleisenger; AASLD U2872.)
n: Why not C? correct only if worded 'refer for transplant EVALUATION' (every cirrhotic is evaluated) or if the patient already has a transplant indication, in which case repair is done at transplant. Claude: Alhomrani flagged this copy for revision (U2869); this

q: A 61-year-old woman complains of bloody nipple discharge; examination of the right breast is normal. What is the next step?
r: Pathological (bloody, unilateral, spontaneous) nipple discharge in a woman over 30–40 is evaluated first with diagnostic mammography plus retroareolar ultrasound; intraductal papilloma is the commonest cause, but cancer must be excluded.
n: Why not A? Ultrasound alone leads under age 30 (and was the answer in a recall worded 'initial investigation'); at 61 mammography comes first. Claude: Extract version: 45-year-old with right breast pain and bloody discharge, normal exam, 'most appropriate inve

q: An elderly woman has bloody nipple discharge, and imaging shows 'suspicious atypical proliferation'. What is the next step?
r: With no MRI option, ductography (galactography) localises the intraductal lesion for targeted duct excision and histology.
n: Why not A? Repeating mammography later only delays the diagnosis of a suspicious lesion.

q: An older woman's mammogram shows a BI-RADS 4 lesion [with a skin finding the examinee could not remember]. What is the management?
r: BI-RADS 4 (suspicious, 2–95% malignancy) and BI-RADS 5 lesions need tissue diagnosis by image-guided core needle biopsy; MRI does not replace the biopsy.
n: Why not A? MRI is for high-risk screening or staging the extent of disease; it cannot replace biopsy of a suspicious lesion.

q: A 40-year-old woman underwent breast cancer screening because of a positive family history [the relative's age and degree were not mentioned]. Bilateral mammography shows dense tissue with no lesions. What do you advise?
r: Dense breasts reduce mammographic sensitivity, and ACR (2023) recommends supplemental annual breast MRI for women with dense breasts and for those at elevated risk, so MRI is the key. (Alhomrani U2933: 'MRI, confirmed — ACR guidelines'.)
n: Why not A? the examiner argued for routine mammography (by USPSTF/UpToDate, density alone isn't an MRI indication unless lifetime risk is >20%), but Alhomrani's confirmed key follows ACR. Claude: Examiner X (U2934) chose MRI and got 80 in Surgery.

q: A postpartum lactating woman complains of breast tenderness and erythema with a 2 x 3 cm mass. Ultrasound shows a 3 x 4 cm collection of thick fluid; the differential includes breast abscess. What is the most appropriate management?
r: A lactational breast abscess is treated first with ultrasound-guided needle aspiration (repeated as needed) plus antibiotics, and breastfeeding or expressing continues. Incision and drainage is kept for large or multiloculated abscesses, failed aspiration or thinned, necrotic skin.
n: Why not C? Incision and drainage is second-line, used after repeated aspiration fails or when the overlying skin is compromised. It leaves a worse scar and risks a milk fistula.

q: A breastfeeding woman has breast erythema, warmth, purulent discharge and a palpable breast MASS. What is the next step?
r: A palpable mass with purulent discharge in a lactating breast = breast abscess, which needs drainage plus antibiotics. US-guided needle aspiration is first line; incision and drainage is the drainage option offered here (and is used for large or multiloculated abscesses or thinned skin). She should
n: Why not B? antibiotics alone treat lactational mastitis (no mass); an abscess won't resolve without drainage. Claude: The file key was B (vague stem). Alhomrani (U2935): 'I honestly don't know… maybe you're correct (no answer from my side)'.

q: A postpartum woman presents with a painful breast. Ultrasound shows an ill-defined mass with internal septations. What is the most likely diagnosis and appropriate management?
r: A septated or loculated collection in a postpartum breast is an abscess. It needs drainage (aspiration, or incision and drainage if multiloculated) plus antibiotics; antibiotics alone are for mastitis without a collection.
n: Why not B? Mastitis shows no collection on ultrasound. Once a septated mass is seen, antibiotics alone will fail. Claude: The bank question had only two combined options; the second is rebuilt from the parent's options.

q: A 25-year-old man has had bilateral breast enlargement since age 18. It makes him uncomfortable and he avoids swimming and the gym. He has grade 4 gynaecomastia. What is the most appropriate management?
r: Gynaecomastia starting at puberty that persists more than 2 years becomes fibrotic and will not regress; with severe (grade 4) bilateral disease and psychosocial impact, surgery (subcutaneous mastectomy ± liposuction) is the treatment. (Alhomrani's Sept page)
n: Why not D? an endocrine/liver/drug work-up is for recent-onset, painful or rapidly enlarging gynaecomastia; 7 years of stable bilateral enlargement since puberty needs definitive surgery.

q: A 14-year-old has a painless midline neck swelling that moves with swallowing. What is the management?
r: A thyroglossal duct cyst is excised with the middle third of the hyoid bone (Sistrunk procedure) to prevent recurrence.
n: Why not B? thyroidectomy is not indicated; confirm normal thyroid tissue elsewhere first.

q: A woman comes to the clinic with a right-sided thyroid nodule; multiple thyroid nodules measuring 3 cm were recently detected. There are no other remarkable clinical findings. Thyroid function tests (T3, T4, TSH) are normal, but CEA is markedly elevated. What is the most likely diagnosis?
r: Medullary carcinoma arises from parafollicular C cells and secretes calcitonin and CEA, both used as tumour markers; it is the only thyroid cancer with a raised CEA. About 25% are familial (RET, MEN2), so exclude phaeochromocytoma before surgery. (comment ♥0: B)
n: Why not A? papillary carcinoma is the commonest thyroid cancer, but it comes from follicular cells and does not raise CEA (its post-thyroidectomy marker is thyroglobulin).

q: A 28-year-old woman with a history of neck irradiation presents with a neck swelling. Ultrasound shows a 3 x 4 cm lesion in the left thyroid lobe, confirmed as papillary thyroid cancer. Which of the following is the best management?
r: Previous neck irradiation raises the risk of multifocal, bilateral disease, and a tumour of about 4 cm sits at the size limit. Either one calls for total thyroidectomy, which also allows radioiodine and thyroglobulin follow-up. Lobectomy is only for low-risk, unifocal 1-4 cm tumours without risk fac
n: Why not B? Lobectomy with isthmusectomy suits low-risk unifocal 1-4 cm PTC with no radiation history; radiation exposure tips the choice to total thyroidectomy. Claude: Extract status Review.

q: A 50-year-old patient underwent a total thyroidectomy 5 hours ago. He has developed a large neck swelling with stridor and shortness of breath. BP 165/90 mmHg, HR 130/min, RR 24/min, temperature 37 °C. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
r: A neck haematoma with stridor after thyroidectomy is an airway emergency. Open the skin and strap-muscle sutures at the bedside to evacuate the clot and decompress the trachea, then return to theatre for haemostasis.
n: Why not A? A surgical airway is not first. The airway is being compressed by the clot, so evacuating it at the bedside relieves the obstruction fastest.

q: A 60-year-old man is recovering from thyroidectomy. One day after surgery he develops perioral tingling and a positive Chvostek sign, with no other symptoms. Total calcium 1.7 mmol/L, ionized calcium 1.2 (normal), Mg 0.5 mmol/L; albumin not given. What is the NEXT step?
r: Post-thyroidectomy hypoparathyroidism with only mild symptoms (perioral tingling, Chvostek) is treated with oral calcium ± calcitriol (ATA/AAES). IV calcium is kept for severe symptoms (tetany, Trousseau/carpopedal spasm, seizures, arrhythmia, laryngospasm) or failure of oral therapy. Mg 0.5 mmol/L
n: Why not C? IV Mg is for severe hypomagnesemia (≤0.4 mmol/L or life-threatening symptoms), and even then IV calcium comes first for tetany. Claude: Alhomrani admits >10 references would give IV calcium for a corrected Ca <1.9 mmol/L; he follows the symptom-base

q: A patient is being prepared for LEFT adrenalectomy. What is needed postoperatively? [indication not recalled]
r: After unilateral adrenalectomy for a cortisol-secreting adenoma (overt or subclinical Cushing), the other adrenal is suppressed, so give perioperative stress-dose hydrocortisone and taper it slowly over months until the HPA axis recovers. (Alhomrani's 12–13 Sep page; another recall: 'stress dose and
n: Why not A? lifelong glucocorticoid (plus fludrocortisone) is for BILATERAL adrenalectomy; a single remaining adrenal recovers with time. Claude: The recall lost the indication; after removal of an aldosteronoma or phaeochromocytoma with a normal HPA axis, no s

q: A patient with a clear history of aortic dissection has BP 85/55 mmHg. What is the best NEXT step? [4th option not recalled]
o: IV labetalol to decrease aortic shear
IV fluids to maintain blood pressure
r: Hypotension in dissection signals rupture, tamponade (type A) or severe AR, so the patient needs emergency surgery. Beta-blockers are only for hypertensive or normotensive patients (target HR <60, SBP 100–120), and fluids are limited (permissive hypotension, SBP ~80–90). (Alhomrani U2838.)
n: Why not B? large-volume fluids worsen the bleeding; give only minimal resuscitation (permissive hypotension) while the patient goes to theatre.

q: A 78-year-old man with hypertension who smokes presents with sudden-onset severe chest pain radiating to the back. FAST is positive. HR 130/min, BP 85/55 mmHg. What is the most appropriate DEFINITIVE management?
o: CT angiography to confirm the diagnosis
IV labetalol to reduce aortic wall stress
IV fluid resuscitation to maintain systolic BP above 100 mmHg
Prepare for emergency open surgical repair
r: Tearing chest-to-back pain with shock and a positive FAST (hemopericardium or rupture) = complicated, likely type A dissection, which needs emergency open repair. An unstable patient goes straight to theatre (TEE there) instead of CT.
n: Why not A? CTA is for stable patients; in shock with a positive FAST, imaging delays definitive repair. Claude: Alhomrani: the target in option C is also wrong — permissive hypotension aims for SBP 80–90, not >100.

q: A patient with a suspected ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm is hypotensive. What is the next step?
o: Aggressive IV fluids to normalize BP
r: A known or suspected AAA with hypotension is a rupture until proven otherwise, so the patient goes straight to theatre with permissive hypotension (SBP ~70–90). CT is done only if the patient is stable enough.
n: Why not B? CT delays surgery in an unstable patient; it is used when the patient is stable enough and EVAR is being considered. Claude: Recall gave only the answer; the other options were added for practice. Alhomrani asked whether BP was >80 or <80, whether E

q: A patient with a known abdominal aortic aneurysm is haemodynamically unstable. After eating he developed severe abdominal pain despite analgesia, and in hospital he became confused and then unconscious. Examination shows a tender pulsatile abdominal mass and low BP. What is the most appropriate management?
o: Persistent ductus arteriosus [garbled option as recalled]
r: Known AAA + abdominal pain + tender pulsatile mass + shock = ruptured AAA. Go straight to theatre for emergency open repair, with permissive hypotension meanwhile; imaging is only for stable patients.
n: Why not B? CT is right for a haemodynamically stable suspected rupture (to plan EVAR), but an unstable, unconscious patient must not go to the scanner. Claude: On a similar 'suspected AAA rupture with hypotension' recall, Alhomrani (N437) asked whether BP was

q: A 70-year-old man presents with abdominal pain. Examination reveals a pulsatile abdominal mass on deep palpation with mild tenderness just above the umbilicus. BP 110/70 mmHg, HR 76, RR 14, T 36.6 °C, SpO2 99%. Labs: RBC 6.0, Hb 135 g/L, HCT 0.42, platelets 155, WBC 13.5 ×10^9/L (4.5-10.5), Na 136, K 4, HCO3 25. Upright chest X-ray: no air under the diaphragm. Which is the most appropriate lab investigation to order next?
r: Epigastric pain with a tender pulsatile mass and leucocytosis must be separated from acute pancreatitis, its main mimic (a swollen pancreas can transmit aortic pulsation); serum amylase/lipase is the discriminating lab test.
n: Why not D? an ABG (lactate, acidosis) helps in shock or mesenteric ischaemia, but he is haemodynamically stable with a normal bicarbonate. Claude: the decisive test for a tender pulsatile mass is imaging (bedside ultrasound or CT angiography for a symptomatic

q: A 47-year-old woman in the CCU 3 days after an acute MI with arrhythmia develops sudden pain and numbness of the right leg for 2 hours. The femoral pulse is palpable but distal pulses are absent. What is the next step?
r: Sudden onset after an MI with arrhythmia (cardiac source), a palpable femoral pulse with absent distal pulses, and numbness = acute embolic occlusion with a threatened limb. Give IV heparin and do an urgent Fogarty embolectomy. (Alhomrani U2844 full recall; the short copy '852' was corrected from C
n: Why not C? angiography is for suspected thrombosis in situ or an unclear diagnosis; with a clear embolus and sensory loss it only delays revascularization (angiography is done on the table). Claude: Alhomrani's order: embolus → heparin, Doppler, embolectomy; t

q: A 67-year-old woman with diabetes sustained a mild laceration of her leg and then developed pain out of proportion to the examination findings. Distal pulses are preserved. Her white blood cell count is 22 x10^9/L. How should she be managed?
r: Pain out of proportion after minor trauma in a diabetic with marked leukocytosis suggests necrotising fasciitis. It is a surgical emergency: urgent exploration and debridement (positive finger test: fascia separates easily, 'dishwater' fluid, no bleeding) with broad-spectrum IV antibiotics.
n: Why not A? CT angiography looks for arterial ischaemia, but the pulses are preserved, and imaging must not delay exploration when necrotising infection is suspected.

q: A patient presents with an ulcer over the medial side of the leg [38 years old in a 1 Nov version]. What is the expected risk factor for this condition?
r: An ulcer over the medial malleolus/gaiter area is a venous ulcer caused by chronic venous hypertension (incompetent valves, previous DVT). Arterial ulcers sit on the toes, lateral foot and pressure points; neuropathic ulcers on the sole.
n: Why not B? Arterial ulcers are punched-out, painful and distal (toes, lateral malleolus), not in the medial gaiter area.

q: A 38-year-old man has an ulcer on the medial aspect of the FOOT. What is the most likely cause?
r: Venous ulcers sit in the gaiter area of the LEG (above the medial malleolus), not on the foot. A foot ulcer over a pressure point in a young man is most likely diabetic (neuropathic).
n: Why not D? venous ulcers are on the medial lower leg or malleolus, and the word 'foot' excludes them.

q: A 44-year-old man presents with painless haematuria only; physical examination is normal. What is the next step? [urinalysis was not among the options]
o: Follow-up and repeat urinalysis after 2 weeks
r: Painless haematuria in an adult over ~35–40 is urothelial cancer until proven otherwise: cystoscopy for the bladder plus CT urography for the upper tracts; urine cytology adds sensitivity for high-grade tumours. (comment ♥4.)
n: Why not B? Non-contrast CT is the stone protocol for painful haematuria; the cancer work-up needs CT urography with contrast plus cystoscopy.

q: A stable patient with a 30 pack-year smoking history has painless gross hematuria. What is the next step? [in the full recall option C was NON-contrast CT]
o: Observation and repeat urinalysis in 2 weeks
r: Painless gross hematuria in a smoker is bladder cancer until proven otherwise, so evaluate with cystoscopy (± cytology) plus upper-tract imaging by CT urography. A non-contrast (stone-protocol) CT can't assess the urothelium, so it is wrong here. (Alhomrani U2929.)
n: Why not C? CT urography would be a valid next step, but a NON-contrast CT doesn't show the urothelium. Claude: Alhomrani: CTU shows the whole urinary tract, not only the kidneys; with 'most useful' wording the answer is cystoscopy even if CTU is offered.

q: A 50-year-old man presents with painless haematuria. What is the most appropriate next investigation?
r: Painless haematuria in a man of 50 is urothelial (bladder) cancer until proven otherwise. Full evaluation is cystoscopy for the bladder plus CT urography for the upper tracts, with cytology.
n: Why not A? Urinalysis with microscopy confirms true haematuria and excludes infection, which matters mainly when haematuria was found only on dipstick. Claude: Live debate: the 22 Oct examinee ticked Urinalysis, and Alhomrani's October Combined (latest) also g

q: A 65-year-old man has painless hematuria. He is a 45 pack-year smoker with a small prostate; urinalysis shows 100 RBC/hpf, and a previous ultrasound was normal. What is the most useful diagnostic test?
r: Cystoscopy looks directly at the bladder urothelium (the most likely source in a heavy smoker), and retrograde pyelography images the upper tracts; 'CT kidneys' is not CT urography.
n: Why not E? a CT of the kidneys misses the bladder and ureteric urothelium; only CT urography images the whole tract.

q: A 52-year-old medically free man has had red urine for 2 days with right flank pain, without dysuria or fever. There is right flank tenderness. Urine culture is negative; urinalysis shows RBCs, negative nitrite and no WBCs. What is the next investigation?
r: Visible haematuria with loin pain and no infection points to an upper-tract cause (stone, or renal tumour at 52); non-contrast CT-KUB is the investigation of choice for suspected urolithiasis, with CT urography for the haematuria work-up if no stone is found. (Alhomrani's 15–16 Sep page, 'likely B')
n: Why not D? cystoscopy is needed for PAINLESS visible haematuria over 40 (bladder cancer), but flank pain sends the first investigation to the kidney and ureter. Claude: The page marks B as 'likely'.

q: An elderly man with known BPH presents to the OPD with difficult urination, frequency, urgency and a feeling of incomplete bladder emptying. He has taken an alpha-blocker for 2 years with persistent symptoms. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: Adjust the dose of the alpha-blocker
r: Persistent bothersome LUTS after 2 years on an alpha-blocker means medical therapy has failed, and the standard next step is surgery: TURP. Adding a 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor for a large prostate is the other option but is not offered.
n: Why not A? alpha-blockers show little dose-response beyond the standard dose, so 'adjusting' after 2 years of failure only delays definitive treatment.

q: A man has had BPH for 2 years on an alpha-blocker, and for 2 weeks has urgency and frequency and is unable to void. What is the management?
r: Urinary retention despite medical treatment is an indication for TURP (comment key).
n: Why not B? CIC is for neurogenic bladder or unfit patients.

q: An elderly man with known prostate cancer presents with sudden inability to void. Attempts to insert a urethral catheter have failed. There is mild abdominal distension and mild suprapubic tenderness. Ultrasound shows urethral compression and bladder trabeculation. What is the most appropriate initial management?
o: Retrograde urethrogram with guided catheter insertion
r: Acute urinary retention with a failed urethral catheter, here from malignant compression of the prostatic urethra, needs immediate bladder drainage by suprapubic catheter. Definitive treatment of the obstruction comes later.
n: Why not B? A retrograde urethrogram is for suspected urethral trauma (blood at the meatus, pelvic fracture). In malignant compression it only delays draining a painful, full bladder.

q: A 30-year-old woman presents with chronic pelvic pain and urinary urgency that is relieved by voiding. Diagnostic laparoscopy to rule out endometriosis was normal. What is the next best step in management?
r: Pelvic pain with urgency or frequency that is relieved by voiding, after a negative laparoscopy, suggests interstitial cystitis (bladder pain syndrome). Refer to urology for cystoscopy (Hunner lesions, glomerulations).
n: Why not C? Amitriptyline is used in bladder pain syndrome, but only after a urologist has made the diagnosis. Claude: Extract status Review.

q: A 3-year-old boy presents with a unilateral undescended testis and an empty, underdeveloped hemiscrotum on the affected side. Which of the following is an associated finding? [examinee noted this appeared in the surgery/medicine part, not paediatrics]
r: Cryptorchidism is associated with a patent processus vaginalis in most cases, so an indirect inguinal hernia is the commonest associated finding; it is repaired at orchidopexy.
n: Why not A? Hypospadias is linked to cryptorchidism (together they suggest a disorder of sex development), but it is the answer only when the question asks about sexual-development associations. Claude: Extract status Review.

q: A 3-year-old boy presents with a unilateral undescended testis and an empty hemiscrotum on the affected side. Which of the following associated findings is related to sexual development?
r: Hypospadias is the genital (sexual-development) anomaly that accompanies cryptorchidism; the combination should prompt evaluation for a disorder of sex development.
n: Why not B? Inguinal hernia is the commonest association overall, but it is not a sexual-development anomaly.

q: A preterm newborn now has respiratory distress. What is the most likely cause?
r: In a preterm infant, respiratory distress is most often hyaline membrane disease (RDS) from surfactant deficiency: onset within hours, grunting and retractions, and a ground-glass CXR with air bronchograms.
n: Why not C? transient tachypnoea of the newborn is typical of term/late-preterm babies born by caesarean; it is mild and resolves in 24-72 h.

q: A term baby delivered by caesarean section becomes tachypnoeic with nasal flaring and expiratory grunting. Chest X-ray shows fluid in the horizontal fissure. BP 60/35 mmHg, HR 140/min, RR 65/min, T 36.6 C, SpO2 92%. What is the most likely diagnosis?
r: Term + caesarean (no labour, delayed lung-fluid clearance) + early tachypnoea with fluid in the fissures/perihilar streaking = TTN, which resolves within 24-72 h with supportive care and oxygen.
n: Why not C? RDS is surfactant deficiency of preterm infants, with a low-volume ground-glass film and air bronchograms - not fissure fluid in a term baby.

q: A newborn delivered at 37 weeks by cesarean section develops respiratory distress. A congenital heart problem was found before birth, and the CXR shows cardiomegaly. What is the most likely explanation?
o: Congestive heart failure from the congenital heart disease
r: Known congenital heart disease plus cardiomegaly with respiratory distress = heart failure. Posted in a comment without a key.
n: Why not D? TTN gives fissure fluid and hyperinflation with a normal heart size.

q: A newborn (gestational age not stated) delivered by caesarean section presents on day 2 with grunting and respiratory distress. The mother is not diabetic [the recaller notes this, as in other recalls]. What is the most important next step?
r: A neonate with respiratory distress needs a chest X-ray to separate TTN, RDS, pneumonia, pneumothorax and meconium aspiration and to direct management; with no maternal diabetes, hypoglycaemia is not the driver here.
n: Why not B? Glucose is checked routinely in a sick neonate, but the stem removes the diabetic-mother clue, so the decisive next step is imaging the chest.

q: A preterm baby born at 33 weeks to a diabetic mother presents with grunting and respiratory distress. The chest radiograph shows a ground-glass appearance with air bronchograms. What is the most appropriate management?
r: Prematurity, maternal diabetes (hyperinsulinaemia delays surfactant production) and ground-glass lungs with air bronchograms = respiratory distress syndrome; treat with CPAP and intratracheal surfactant.
n: Why not B? GBS pneumonia can look like RDS, so antibiotics are often started alongside, but surfactant is the specific treatment for RDS. Claude: Extract notes an Alhomrani News answer (relayed in a 20 Oct compilation) of IV antibiotics ('sepsis first') for a

q: A 33-week preterm baby of a diabetic mother has grunting, chest retraction and respiratory distress; CXR shows a ground-glass appearance. What is the next step?
r: Alhomrani: until proven otherwise, any preterm with respiratory distress is neonatal sepsis → IV antibiotics, because CXR can't separate RDS from pneumonia.
n: Why not D? surfactant treats RDS (the older Silent key was D) but doesn't cover sepsis/pneumonia. Claude: The older recall answer was D (surfactant). Alhomrani now chooses B; pick D if the stem clearly excludes infection.

q: A preterm infant delivered at 34 weeks' gestation with bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD) fails weaning from mechanical ventilation. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Increase tidal volume [and inspiratory pressure — option only partly recalled]
r: Systemic dexamethasone is used to help extubate ventilator-dependent infants with evolving BPD; the most-liked comment (♥2) chose the high-dose option — but see note: guidelines favour a low-dose short course. (comment ♥2.)
n: Why not B? Low-dose short-course dexamethasone is what the extract key and the other four comments chose; it loses here only on the like-count rule (see note). Claude: I'd pick B — the DART low-dose short course (~0.89 mg/kg over 10 days) is standard; high-dos

q: A baby delivered at 37 weeks has a heart rate below 100/min, blue extremities, a weak cry with grimace, and little flexion. What is the most accurate APGAR score?
r: Score each sign 0-2: HR <100 = 1, blue extremities (acrocyanosis) = 1, grimace = 1, some flexion = 1, weak cry/slow irregular breathing = 1, so the total is 5.
n: Why not A? a score of 4 would need one sign at 0 (no heart rate, limp, apnoeic or no response), and none is described.

q: A newborn is evaluated for perioral cyanosis; he stops breathing for 15 seconds several times per hour. What type of apnoea is this? [garbled recall]
r: Cyanosis during the pauses rules out benign periodic breathing (short 5-10 s pauses without colour change). With no mention of airway obstruction or continued chest-wall effort, the bank keys central apnoea: absent respiratory effort from an immature brainstem respiratory centre.
n: Why not C? mixed (central + obstructive) apnoea is the commonest type in preterm infants, and Alhomrani's October Combined file keys it, but it needs evidence of an obstructive component. Claude: Debate: Alhomrani (latest, October Combined, 19 Oct p. 2177) ans

q: A term newborn with intrauterine growth restriction is admitted to the NICU for close monitoring because of the risk of complications. Which complication is most likely?
r: Growth-restricted newborns are prone to hypoglycaemia (low glycogen stores), hypothermia, polycythaemia and hypocalcaemia (often with perinatal asphyxia); of the options, only hypocalcaemia fits.
n: Why not D? IUGR babies tend towards polycythaemia (chronic hypoxia drives erythropoietin), not anaemia, and towards hypo-, not hyperglycaemia.

q: A 4-day-old baby presents to the clinic with slight yellow discoloration of the body. He is feeding well. What is the cause of his jaundice?
r: Mild jaundice appearing after 24 h in a well, feeding baby is benign; haemolytic causes present within 24 h or with pallor and rapidly rising bilirubin. Of the options, only breast milk jaundice is a benign cause.
n: Why not C? G6PD deficiency (common in Saudi Arabia) causes haemolytic jaundice - early, rapidly rising or severe, often after a trigger - not mild jaundice in a thriving baby. Claude: Extract status [Review]. Claude: strictly, mild day-4 jaundice is physiologi

q: By which age does a baby no longer have the stepping reflex?
r: The stepping (walking) reflex is present at birth and disappears by about 2 months.
n: Why not B? 4 months is the age for the rooting reflex; stepping fades earlier.

q: A 6-month-old child is brought for a well-child visit. He was born at term after a normal pregnancy and spontaneous vaginal delivery. Linear growth and weight gain over the past 6 months are both appropriate. His mother began pureed baby foods about 1 month ago while continuing breastfeeding. He has been well since birth and the physical examination is normal for age. Developmental screening is performed. Which gross motor skill is most appropriate for his age?
r: With these options the 6-month gross-motor skill is sitting without support; standing while holding on is ~9 months, rolling prone-to-supine ~4 months, and palmar grasp is a fine-motor skill.
n: Why not C? Rolling prone-to-supine is achieved by ~4 months, so it is not the skill that characterises 6 months. Claude: The Untitled.pdf copy (options sits / rolls prone-to-supine / pincer grasp / walks with support) had its key changed 31 Oct from B to A by

q: A 6-month-old child is brought for a well-child visit. He was born at term after a normal pregnancy and spontaneous vaginal delivery. Linear growth and weight gain over the past 6 months are both appropriate. His mother began pureed baby foods about 1 month ago while continuing breastfeeding. He has been well since birth and the physical examination is normal for age. Developmental screening is performed. Which gross motor skill is most appropriate for his age?
r: Rolling from supine to prone (back to tummy) is secure by about 5-6 months and is what the bank keys when it is offered; steady independent sitting follows at ~6-8 months.
n: Why not A? Independent sitting is only emerging at 6 months, so when 'rolls supine to prone' is available the bank prefers it.

q: A 6-month-old infant is brought for a routine check-up. The mother is worried because the child cannot sit independently and needs support to stay sitting. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Reassure the mother and advise routine follow-up
r: Sitting with support (tripod) is normal at 6 months; independent sitting is expected by 7-9 months, and not sitting unsupported by 9 months is the red flag.
n: Why not B? neurology referral is for true red flags: no unsupported sitting by 9 months, hypotonia or asymmetry, or loss of skills.

q: A mother is concerned that her baby cannot sit unsupported at 9 months of age. The baby was born prematurely at 28 weeks with no complications after birth. What is the next step?
o: Reassure, as the baby's corrected age is 6 months
r: Corrected age = chronological age minus weeks born early (40 - 28 = 12 weeks, ~3 months), so this 9-month-old is developmentally 6 months, when unsupported sitting is not yet expected. Correct for prematurity until about 2 years.
n: Why not B? Developmental referral is needed only if milestones are delayed for corrected age or there are red flags (asymmetry, abnormal tone, regression).

q: A child is brought by his mother for developmental assessment. He can walk backwards and follow simple commands, has started using a spoon and points to things he is interested in. What is the expected age in months? [examinee: 12 may have been an option instead of 48]
r: Walking well (even backwards), following simple commands, starting to use a spoon and pointing to show wants fit ~15 months (Nelson/Denver); by 18 months the child runs, feeds himself with a spoon, has ~10 words and points to body parts. (comment 'walk backwards = 15', 0 likes.)
n: Why not A? 18 months is where the CDC 2022 checklist places 'points to show interest' and 'tries to use a spoon' — a real competitor; the comment chose 15. Claude: Single 0-like comment; milestone tables differ between 15 and 18 months for these items. Conflic

q: A 12-month-old child is brought by his mother, who is worried about autism because his cousin has it. What advice will you give her?
o: Screening for autism starts at 18-24 months
r: The AAP recommends universal autism-specific screening (M-CHAT-R/F) at 18 and 24 months, with developmental surveillance at every visit. A cousin with autism does not justify formal screening at 12 months if development is normal.
n: Why not B? Plain reassurance ignores the need for ongoing surveillance and the planned 18-24-month screen.

q: A mother notices that her child is withdrawn and does not mix with other children [age not recalled]. What is the most appropriate next step?
r: Poor social interaction with peers is a core red flag for autism spectrum disorder — screen with a validated tool (M-CHAT-R/F at 18–24 months) and refer for formal developmental assessment.
n: Why not C? A hearing test is the first step for isolated speech delay (and is part of the ASD work-up), but social withdrawal calls for autism screening. Claude: Recall gave only the answer; the other options were added for practice.

q: A mother brings her daughter for a pre-school follow-up visit. She is concerned because her daughter is less physically active, tires easily during outdoor play and spends a lot of time watching TV. The child's weight is within the expected range and there are no other concerning symptoms. Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation to improve her energy and activity levels?
o: Give multivitamin supplements to increase energy
Encourage increased physical activity and limit screen time
r: With normal weight and no red flags, fatigue and low activity in a child who watches a lot of TV are best addressed with lifestyle advice: at least 60 minutes of activity a day and screen time limited to about 1 hour a day at pre-school age.
n: Why not A? Multivitamins have no proven benefit for energy in a well-nourished child who is growing normally. Claude: Extract status Review.

q: A 14-year-old boy with ADHD started methylphenidate 10 mg twice daily 4 weeks ago. His mother now reports loss of appetite, weight loss and difficulty falling asleep. Examination shows a 2-kg weight loss and nothing else, and laboratory tests are unremarkable. Which of the following best explains his symptoms?
o: Common side effects of the drug
Poor eating habits leading to weight loss
r: Reduced appetite, weight loss and insomnia are the commonest side effects of stimulants such as methylphenidate, typically early in treatment. Manage by dosing after meals, avoiding late doses and monitoring growth.
n: Why not B? Hyperthyroidism could explain weight loss and insomnia, but normal labs, no other findings and onset right after starting the stimulant point to the drug.

q: A newborn is below the 3rd percentile for weight. The family is poor and dilutes the formula milk. What is the next most appropriate step?
o: Advise the family how to prepare formula
r: Admission criteria for growth faltering include severe undernutrition and home circumstances that make outpatient care unsafe. A newborn below the 3rd centile on diluted formula (ongoing starvation, risk of hyponatremia) qualifies.
n: Why not C? teaching formula preparation is part of care, but advice alone won't fix poverty-driven dilution in an already severely underweight newborn. Claude: the 7 Nov photo copy (#88056) carries the same key, but Alhomrani wrote on that page that he was unh

q: An 8-year-old is referred with MODERATE failure to thrive. His parents are divorced, and he lives with his mother, who has social and financial problems, takes antidepressants and works 6 days a week. What is the next step?
r: Moderate, mainly psychosocial FTT is managed as an outpatient by a multidisciplinary team (pediatrician, dietitian, social worker, psychologist) that addresses both feeding and the family's stressors. (Alhomrani U2890.)
n: Why not B? extra calories alone ignore the psychosocial cause and will fail. Claude: Another copy gave the 10th percentile; watch for changes in severity.

q: A 3-year-old girl found during a health campaign in a poor area has generalized oedema, severe wasting, hyperkeratosis, a distended abdomen and sparse hair. BP 85/45 mmHg, HR 80/min, RR 25/min, T 36.0 °C. Na 132 mmol/L, K 3.2 mmol/L, Mg 0.4 mmol/L, glucose 3.1 mmol/L, albumin 20 g/L (36–52). Which of the following contributes to the finding?
r: Oedema with hypoalbuminaemia, skin changes and sparse hair is kwashiorkor (marasmic kwashiorkor with the wasting), caused by severe protein deficiency relative to energy intake.
n: Why not D? Pure energy deficiency (marasmus) causes severe wasting without oedema; the oedema and an albumin of 20 point to protein deficiency.

q: A 9-month-old baby is mainly breastfed, and the mother is introducing solids slowly. What is the best nutritional advice?
r: Breast milk is low in iron and term iron stores run out by 4–6 months, so a mainly breastfed infant who gets little iron-rich food needs iron supplements (~1 mg/kg/day) to prevent iron-deficiency anaemia and its neurodevelopmental harm. (Alhomrani's 15–16 Sep page)
n: Why not B? vitamin D 400 IU is also advised for all breastfed infants from birth, but the clue in the stem (solids introduced slowly at 9 months) points to iron depletion.

q: How should a vitamin D dose be written?
r: Error-prone abbreviations must be avoided: 'U' (misread as 0 or 4) and 'OD' (read as 'right eye'); write 'unit' and 'daily' in full - only C avoids both.
n: Why not B? 'units' is written correctly, but 'OD' for daily is a banned/error-prone abbreviation.

q: A 1-year-old infant presents to the vaccination clinic with a normal examination and growth. What are the recommended vaccines according to the national (Saudi) program?
r: Keyed by the 4 Nov poster ('MOVP') and the extract (Medgard): OPV, MMR, varicella and the PCV booster. It is the only option containing OPV + MMR + PCV, the core of the 12-month visit.
n: Why not A? hepatitis A is not a 12-month vaccine in the Saudi schedule (it is given at 18 months). Claude: the current MOH schedule lists 12 months = OPV, MMR, PCV and MCV4 (meningococcal conjugate), with varicella and hepatitis A at 18 months. If an option wi

q: A healthy 12-month-old has had all vaccines on time. According to the Saudi schedule, which vaccines are due today?
r: Saudi MOH schedule at 12 months: MMR (first dose), OPV, PCV booster and MCV4. Varicella is given at 18 months. Keyed A in the 21 October recall file and by several examinees today.
n: Why not C? varicella belongs to the 18-month visit. Claude: This changes Q76 of the 20 October Part 1 file, which was keyed 'OPV, MMR, varicella, PCV'.

q: An 18-month-old child is brought by his mother to the well-baby clinic for MMR vaccination. He has an upper respiratory tract infection, a fever of 38.9 °C and a congested throat. On examination he appears slightly ill. Regarding vaccination, what is the best option?
o: Postpone vaccination until the child recovers
Give the MMR vaccine without the rubella component
The second dose should be given at 4 years
r: Mild illness such as a URTI, even with fever, is not a contraindication. Only moderate or severe acute illness (with or without fever) is a reason to defer, so a 'slightly ill' child should be vaccinated now to avoid a missed opportunity.
n: Why not B? Postponing is only for moderate to severe acute illness; deferring for a mild URTI is a classic missed-opportunity error. Claude: Debated: the extract records a different key in the August recall. 38.9 °C is high, but 'slightly ill' marks this as mi

q: A baby is brought for the 9-month vaccination. Which of the following is a contraindication to vaccination?
o: Recent exposure to an infectious disease
r: Moderate or severe acute illness, with or without fever, is a reason to defer vaccination until recovery. Antibiotic therapy, penicillin allergy, recent exposure to infection and mild illness are not reasons to delay.
n: Why not D? Recent exposure to an infectious disease is a common false contraindication and does not delay vaccination.

q: A 5-year-old child is due to receive the pre-school vaccines. What do you need to know before giving the vaccine?
r: The 4-6-year pre-school vaccines include live MMR and varicella. Antibody-containing products (IVIG, blood) received in the previous months neutralise live vaccines, so MMR and varicella must be delayed (about 3-11 months depending on the dose).
n: Why not A? Egg allergy is no longer a contraindication to MMR; the vaccine is grown in chick fibroblast culture with negligible egg protein.

q: An 18-month-old child is brought to the clinic for a regular check-up. The doctor finds that he has not received any of his scheduled vaccines. When asked why, the mother says: 'Vaccines will make my son retarded!' What is the appropriate action?
o: Refer the mother for psychiatric assessment
Explain the benefits of vaccines to the mother
r: Vaccine hesitancy is addressed first with respectful education: explain the benefits and risks, correct misinformation (vaccines do not cause intellectual disability or autism) and document. Refusal alone is not neglect requiring CPS.
n: Why not B? Child protective services are not the first step for parental vaccine refusal; education and repeated counselling come first.

q: A fully vaccinated 6-year-old child presents with an injury from a rusty nail. What is the most appropriate management in addition to antibiotics? [recalled as 'additional to ab']
r: A child who has completed the DTaP series (last dose <5 years ago) needs no tetanus vaccine or immunoglobulin even for a dirty wound, so management is thorough cleaning/irrigation (± debridement). (Alhomrani U2138: irrigation, no tetanus vaccine; ✓ comment ♥2.)
n: Why not B? DTaP is for a child <7 years whose series is incomplete/unknown or whose last dose was >5 years before a dirty wound — 'fully vaccinated' removes that need. Claude: Extract key was DTaP [Review, disputed] for a version where irrigation was already d

q: A child was bitten by a cat. What is the most appropriate management?
r: In a rabies-endemic setting, a cat bite that breaks the skin is a WHO category III exposure. Wash and irrigate the wound for 15 minutes, then give rabies vaccine plus rabies immunoglobulin infiltrated into the wound, with tetanus cover and amoxicillin-clavulanate.
n: Why not A? irrigation is essential, but on its own it leaves a category III exposure unprotected.

q: A child on treatment for leukemia is exposed to chickenpox and has no symptoms. What is the most appropriate management?
r: Immunocompromised, non-immune contacts should receive VZIG as soon as possible (ideally within 96 h, up to 10 days); acyclovir is an alternative if VZIG isn't available. (Alhomrani U2894; 'IVIG' belonged to a different recall — a typo.)
n: Why not B? IVIG is only a fallback when VZIG is unavailable; 'B' in the file was a typo carried over from another recall.

q: A 6-year-old, asymptomatic, was exposed to another child with chickenpox. What is the most appropriate management?
r: A healthy, susceptible child exposed to varicella should get the vaccine within 3–5 days of exposure (post-exposure prophylaxis).
n: Why not A? immunoglobulin (VZIG) is for immunocompromised children, pregnant women and neonates.

q: A former 29-week preterm infant is now healthy and off oxygen. The mother asks about preventing bronchiolitis. What do you advise?
r: AAP (2014) limits palivizumab to infants born <29+0 weeks in their first RSV season, or with chronic lung disease of prematurity or hemodynamically significant CHD. A healthy ex-29-week infant off oxygen doesn't qualify, so reassure and advise hand hygiene, avoiding smoke and sick contacts, and brea
n: Why not B? palivizumab is for <29 weeks or CLD/CHD, and a healthy 29-week infant is just outside the criteria. Claude: since 2023 CDC/AAP also recommend nirsevimab for all infants <8 months entering their first RSV season; it isn't among these options.

q: A paediatric patient has symptoms of meningitis (or encephalitis). How do you prevent risk to his family? [one option not recalled]
r: Close household contacts of bacterial (meningococcal or Hib) meningitis need chemoprophylaxis as soon as possible (rifampicin, single-dose ciprofloxacin or ceftriaxone); treating the index case does not clear carriage in the contacts.
n: Why not A? Treating the patient alone leaves the contacts at risk; they need prophylaxis. Claude: A commenter recalls a similar 13 Aug 2025 item in which the child was admitted for isolation 2–3 days after symptom onset. Claude: if the stem is clearly viral en

q: A child is diagnosed with meningococcal meningitis. His brother and sister, who live in the same household, are asymptomatic. Which chemoprophylaxis regimen is appropriate for these close contacts? [3 Nov copy (#88022/#88023) had 'Ceftriaxone IM 3 doses' as an option]
r: Household contacts of invasive meningococcal disease receive a single dose of ciprofloxacin (UKHSA: any age), or rifampicin for 2 days, or a single IM dose of ceftriaxone (preferred in pregnancy). Penicillin does not clear nasopharyngeal carriage.
n: Why not D? ceftriaxone is a correct drug but is given as ONE IM dose, not four.

q: A child has (meningococcal) meningitis. Which prophylaxis should his household contacts receive? [only two options recalled]
r: Household contacts of meningococcal disease need chemoprophylaxis within 24 h: single-dose IM ceftriaxone, single-dose ciprofloxacin or rifampicin for 2 days (archive: a 21 Oct examinee's comment, 3 likes, lists exactly these three).
n: Why not B? Rifampicin alone is valid prophylaxis, but doxycycline + rifampicin is the treatment for brucellosis, not meningitis prophylaxis. Claude: If ciprofloxacin single dose or rifampicin for 2 days appear among the options, they are also correct; ceftriax

q: A child has been in contact with a patient with tuberculosis [screening results not recalled]. What should be given?
r: A child contact with latent infection, once active disease is excluded, gets isoniazid monotherapy for 6-9 months. Isoniazid alone for 3 months is not a recognised regimen; 3-month regimens pair INH with rifampicin or rifapentine.
n: Why not B? 3 months is valid only for INH + rifampicin (3HR) or INH + rifapentine (3HP), not for isoniazid alone.

q: A child's mother had TB a year ago. The child now has signs and symptoms of TB and the chest X-ray is positive. What is the management?
o: Isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide and ethambutol for 2 months, then isoniazid and rifampin for 4 months
r: Symptoms with an abnormal chest X-ray = active pulmonary TB, treated with the standard 6-month regimen: an intensive phase of isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide (± ethambutol) for 2 months, then isoniazid + rifampicin for 4 months. (Alhomrani's Sept page, 1 Nov album)
n: Why not B? one- or two-drug regimens treat only LATENT infection (asymptomatic, normal CXR); using them for active disease breeds resistance.

q: A 3-month-old boy presents to the Emergency Room with paroxysmal episodes of cough followed by a whooping sound at the end of each episode, associated with perioral cyanosis and post-tussive vomiting. There is no diarrhoea. The illness was preceded by a runny nose a few days earlier. He has not yet received his 2-month vaccines. On examination he looks unwell and tachypnoeic. What is the most likely diagnosis?
r: A catarrhal coryza followed by paroxysmal cough with inspiratory whoop, cyanosis and post-tussive vomiting in an unvaccinated infant is pertussis; treat with azithromycin (also for close contacts).
n: Why not D? Chlamydia pneumonia also occurs at 1-3 months but gives a staccato cough after neonatal conjunctivitis, with eosinophilia and no whoop.

q: A 3-month-old boy presents to the Emergency Room with a staccato cough and tachypnoea. The illness was preceded by conjunctivitis. Examination reveals crackles, and the blood count shows elevated eosinophils. What is the most likely diagnosis?
r: Afebrile pneumonitis at 1-3 months with a staccato cough, preceding conjunctivitis, crackles and eosinophilia is Chlamydia trachomatis pneumonia; treat with oral azithromycin.
n: Why not A? Pertussis gives paroxysms with a whoop and post-tussive vomiting and a lymphocytosis rather than eosinophilia, without preceding conjunctivitis.

q: A full-term infant developed bilateral conjunctivitis at 2 weeks of age, followed by a severe cough; the infant remained afebrile. At 4 weeks, a chest X-ray shows bilateral symmetrical interstitial infiltrates. Labs: WBC 14 x10^9/L (4.5-10.5); neutrophils 32% (40-60); lymphocytes 15% (20-40); monocytes 2% (2-8); eosinophils 4% (1-4); IgG 30 g/L (7.5-19); IgA 8 g/L (1-4); IgM 3.5 g/L (0.52-1.52). What is the most probable infectious agent?
r: Neonatal conjunctivitis (5-14 days) followed at 1-3 months by an afebrile staccato cough, bilateral interstitial infiltrates, eosinophilia and raised immunoglobulins is Chlamydia trachomatis pneumonia; treat with oral azithromycin.
n: Why not D? Adenovirus can cause conjunctivitis plus pneumonia, but with fever and an acutely ill child, not afebrile pneumonitis with eosinophilia and high IgM weeks after the eye infection.

q: An unvaccinated child develops high-grade fever, cough, coryza, conjunctivitis and a maculopapular rash that started behind the ears and spread downward to the trunk. Small grey-white spots on an erythematous base (Koplik spots) are seen on the buccal mucosa. What is the most appropriate management?
o: Supportive and conservative care (fluids and antipyretics)
r: Measles is treated supportively (fluids, antipyretics, isolation) plus vitamin A (WHO: every child with measles); antivirals and antibiotics have no role unless there is bacterial superinfection.
n: Why not C? Measles vaccine is post-exposure prophylaxis for contacts within 72 h - it does not treat established disease.

q: A child presents with lymphadenopathy. The father reports that the child drank unpasteurised milk during a farm trip. What is the most diagnostic investigation?
r: Suspected brucellosis (raw milk, farm exposure, lymphadenopathy ± fever, hepatosplenomegaly) is confirmed by serum agglutination titre (≥1:160) or by blood culture, which is the gold standard but slow; among these options, serology.
n: Why not D? FNA of a node shows non-specific granulomas and is not the diagnostic test for brucellosis.

q: A fully vaccinated child (13 months in the examinee's recall; 18 months on the study page) has an upper respiratory tract infection and crepitations over the right lower lung. What is the most likely causative organism?
r: S. pneumoniae remains the commonest bacterial cause of focal (lobar) pneumonia beyond the neonatal period, even after PCV; Hib is rare in fully vaccinated children.
n: Why not B? Mycoplasma is typical of school-age children (>5 years) with atypical, often bilateral findings, not a toddler with focal crepitations. Claude: Extract status [Review]. Viruses are the commonest cause overall at this age, but no viral option was giv

q: A 14-year-old girl presents with a productive cough and a low-grade fever. Her chest X-ray shows bilateral infiltrates [4 Nov post: 'bilateral consolidation']. Which of the following organisms is most likely responsible?
r: In school-age children and adolescents, a subacute illness with low-grade fever and bilateral or interstitial infiltrates is typical of Mycoplasma ('walking' pneumonia); treat with a macrolide.
n: Why not A? S. pneumoniae is the commonest bacterial cause overall, but it usually gives high fever and lobar consolidation.

q: A 3-year-old child is seen in the clinic with fever and cough for 5 days following a flu-like prodrome. Examination: decreased air entry and crackles over the right middle zone; chest X-ray done (image). BP 90/64 mmHg, HR 110/min, RR 20/min, temperature 36.6 °C, SpO2 97%. Labs: Hb 12 g/dL, platelets 328 ×10⁹/L, WBC 22 ×10⁹/L with neutrophils 80–84% and lymphocytes 15%. What is the most appropriate management?
r: Focal crackles with a neutrophilic leucocytosis = bacterial (likely pneumococcal) pneumonia; a well child with SpO2 >92%, no respiratory distress and able to take orals is treated at home with high-dose oral amoxicillin.
n: Why not C? Admission/IV antibiotics are for hypoxia (SpO2 <92%), respiratory distress, dehydration or inability to take orals, toxic appearance or complications such as empyema — none present.

q: A child [age not recalled] presents with cough, fever, moderate respiratory distress, crepitations and expiratory wheeze. What is the diagnosis?
r: Cough, usually low-grade fever and respiratory distress with diffuse crackles and expiratory wheeze in an infant is bronchiolitis (usually RSV). Pneumonia gives focal crackles without wheeze, and asthma is not diagnosed from a first feverish wheezy episode in infancy.
n: Why not A? Pneumonia causes fever and crackles, but they are usually focal and lack the widespread wheeze of bronchiolitis. Claude: Age not recalled; bronchiolitis applies to children under 2 years.

q: A 3-4-month-old infant presents to the ED after 3 days of coryza and flu-like symptoms and develops severe respiratory distress, with bilaterally reduced air entry, diffuse crackles, and subcostal and intercostal retractions. The extremities are pale with weak peripheral pulses. SpO2 stays at 80% despite 100% oxygen via a non-rebreather mask. [fever uncertain in the recall] What is the most appropriate next step?
r: SpO2 of 80% despite 100% oxygen via non-rebreather, with severe distress and poor perfusion, is respiratory failure with shock. Intubate and ventilate first, then support the circulation.
n: Why not D? a saline bolus addresses the poor perfusion, but the immediate threat is refractory hypoxaemia, so airway and breathing come first (and diffuse crackles warn against large fluid volumes).

q: A 3-year-old boy has a fever of 39 °C, a muffled voice and drooling. He looks acutely ill and sits on his mother's lap with his neck extended. What is the next step?
r: A toxic child with drooling, a muffled ('hot potato') voice and the sniffing/tripod posture has acute epiglottitis: secure the airway first, by intubation in the OR by the most experienced anaesthetist with ENT ready for tracheostomy, keeping the child calm on the parent's lap and not examining the
n: Why not D? IV ceftriaxone is essential but comes AFTER the airway is secured; delaying intubation risks complete obstruction. Claude: Second album version: 'difficulty swallowing, congested throat, febrile, no cough, ill, sitting silently on mother's lap with

q: A 3-month-old infant is brought by his mother because of noisy breathing since birth. The noise changes with position: it is more obvious when supine and disappears when prone. It worsens during feeding and improves during sleep. Physical examination and growth parameters are completely normal. What is the most appropriate management?
o: Immediate rigid bronchoscopy and urgent ENT referral
Reassurance and advice that the condition typically resolves spontaneously
Initiate continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) therapy
Prescribe systemic corticosteroids and broad-spectrum antibiotics
r: Positional inspiratory noise from birth, worse supine and with feeding and better prone, in a thriving infant is classic laryngomalacia; mild disease needs only reassurance because it usually resolves by 12-24 months.
n: Why not A? Bronchoscopy/urgent ENT referral is reserved for red flags (faltering growth, apnoea, cyanosis, aspiration with feeds, severe retractions) - none are present.

q: A baby of about 2 months has had a barking cough since 4 weeks of age that worsens when lying supine and during feeding. Examination reveals a bilateral monophasic expiratory wheeze. What is the most likely diagnosis?
r: Early-onset barking (brassy) cough with a central monophasic expiratory wheeze, worse with feeding, crying and lying supine, is tracheomalacia (intrathoracic airway collapse on expiration).
n: Why not A? Laryngomalacia shares the worsening when supine and with feeds, but it produces inspiratory stridor, not an expiratory wheeze. Claude: Extract status [Review].

q: A 3-year-old boy presents with a barking cough, appears cyanotic, and has breath-holding spells. Auscultation reveals a monophasic wheeze; there is no inspiratory stridor. What is the most likely diagnosis?
r: Tracheomalacia (dynamic collapse of the intrathoracic trachea on expiration) gives a barking/brassy cough, a central low-pitched monophasic expiratory wheeze and, when severe, cyanotic 'dying spells'.
n: Why not C? Laryngomalacia produces inspiratory stridor (absent here) that improves prone, not an expiratory monophasic wheeze.

q: An infant a few months old is brought because of cyanosis during crying and poor weight gain; growth is below the 3rd centile. He is admitted as a case of tracheomalacia. What is the next best step in management?
r: Most tracheomalacia is mild and resolves by 1-2 years. Severe disease, with cyanotic spells and failure to thrive, needs surgical referral (aortopexy, tracheal stenting or tracheostomy).
n: Why not B? home oxygen treats hypoxaemia but not the dynamic airway collapse behind the spells and the growth failure.

q: A child has had shortness of breath for 1 day. Salbutamol was given and was not effective. Examination shows localised wheezing and absent breath sounds on one side. What is the initial investigation?
r: Sudden unilateral wheeze/absent breath sounds unresponsive to bronchodilators suggests an inhaled foreign body; the initial investigation is a chest X-ray (AP and lateral, ideally inspiratory/expiratory or decubitus to show air trapping), while rigid bronchoscopy is diagnostic and therapeutic.
n: Why not B? Rigid bronchoscopy is the definitive diagnostic and therapeutic procedure - the 'most appropriate/definitive' answer, not the initial investigation. Claude: Extract status [Review]; the extract places it in the 22 Oct sitting via older post #49289.

q: A 3–5-year-old child is brought to the Emergency Department after choking on cereal; back slaps restored his breathing. There is a right lower-lobe wheeze, and the chest X-ray shows hyperinflation of the right lung. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
r: A choking episode, unilateral wheeze and obstructive (ball-valve) hyperinflation = bronchial foreign body; rigid bronchoscopy under general anaesthesia both diagnoses and removes it.
n: Why not B? Flexible laryngoscopy sees only the upper airway and cannot retrieve a bronchial foreign body.

q: A 5-month-old infant has been admitted many times with pneumonia (recurrent, in the same area) and now has a cough and a fixed monophonic expiratory wheeze. Which is the diagnostic test?
r: Recurrent pneumonia in the same lobe with a fixed, monophonic wheeze points to a localised airway lesion (foreign body, bronchomalacia, external compression, congenital malformation), which is best diagnosed by flexible bronchoscopy.
n: Why not A? A chest X-ray shows the recurrent consolidation but cannot define the endobronchial or structural cause; bronchoscopy is diagnostic.

q: A child with asthma was prescribed an inhaler but isn't using it, missing it 2–3 times per week. The family has cats at home. How should you manage this patient? [4th option not recalled]
o: Tell them to remove the cats from the environment
r: Before stepping up, check adherence, technique and triggers. With no ICS option, removing the identified allergen trigger (cats) is the right step; a LABA is never added without an ICS, and oral steroids are for exacerbations. (Alhomrani U2907.)
n: Why not B? escalating to a LABA ignores the poor adherence and trigger, and LABA monotherapy is unsafe in asthma.

q: A 10-year-old with severe uncontrolled asthma has night cough almost every night. His room is ventilated and sunny; the family has 2 cats. He misses his inhaler 1–2 days a week. What is the most important step?
r: Uncontrolled persistent asthma needs a regular inhaled corticosteroid (with adherence counselling); most archive comments chose ICS.
n: Why not A? removing the cats helps and one comment chose it, but controller therapy is the priority in severe uncontrolled asthma.

q: A child has severe uncontrolled asthma with frequent use of the reliever inhaler and misses it 1–2 times. How should you manage?
r: Uncontrolled asthma with frequent reliever use needs regular controller therapy, and ICS is the cornerstone. Then address triggers, then escalate (ICS-LABA). (Alhomrani U2907: second recall → ICS.)
n: Why not B? avoiding triggers matters, but it comes after starting an ICS when an ICS is offered.

q: A 5-year-old has bronchial asthma that is well controlled on inhalers (responded to inhalers; no history of eczema or allergy). The mother is worried about adulthood. What is the most likely prognosis?
o: Childhood asthma will disappear by adulthood
r: Most children with mild, well-controlled, non-atopic asthma outgrow it. Persistence into adulthood is predicted by poor control, frequent exacerbations, atopy or allergic sensitization (eczema), female sex and abnormal lung function. (Alhomrani News N434.)
n: Why not C? persistence is the answer only when the stem gives poor control, frequent exacerbations or co-existing atopy.

q: A 5-year-old has poorly controlled asthma with frequent exacerbations and co-existing eczema and allergies. The mother asks about adulthood. What is the most likely prognosis?
o: Childhood asthma will disappear by adulthood
r: Poor control, frequent exacerbations and atopy (eczema, allergic sensitization) are the main predictors of asthma persisting into adulthood. (Alhomrani News N434.)
n: Why not B? remission is expected only in mild, well-controlled, non-atopic childhood asthma. Claude: Twin built from Alhomrani's rule (N434); not a verbatim recall.

q: A 4-year-old with asthma is responding to inhaled therapy. What is the most appropriate test to CONFIRM the diagnosis?
r: Asthma is confirmed objectively by spirometry showing reversible airflow obstruction (FEV1 rises ≥12% after bronchodilator). UpToDate notes that many children can do it from ~3–5 years, and Nelson uses PEF from 4 years. (Alhomrani U2850; references U2851–U2852.)
n: Why not B? in under-5s a trial of ICS supports the diagnosis (GINA), but it is a treatment, not a confirmatory test. Claude: GINA says spirometry is often unreliable under 5 years; there the diagnosis rests on the symptom pattern and the response to a controll

q: A child presents with asthma symptoms that worsen at night. He has a personal history of atopic dermatitis and a family history of asthma. After a bronchodilator, his symptoms improve. Which of the following is the strongest indicator of asthma in this patient?
r: Objective evidence of reversible airflow obstruction, an FEV1 rise of 12% or more after a bronchodilator, is the strongest support for asthma. Night symptoms, atopy and family history only raise the probability.
n: Why not C? Night-time symptoms are typical but nonspecific (also seen in GERD and postnasal drip); objective reversibility is stronger evidence. Claude: Extract status Review.

q: A school-aged child with asthma presents to the ER with an acute exacerbation. SpO2 95%, peak flow 60% of best, able to complete full sentences, mild wheeze on auscultation. He took two puffs of salbutamol at home. Which is the most appropriate management?
o: Give salbutamol by spacer, then reassess
r: SpO2 of 92% or more, full sentences and PEF of 50% or more make this a mild to moderate exacerbation. Give a SABA by spacer (2-10 puffs, repeated every 20 minutes) and reassess; oral prednisolone is commonly added, but admission and ipratropium are for severe attacks or a poor response.
n: Why not C? Ipratropium is added for severe or life-threatening attacks or a poor response to the first SABA, not first-line in a mild to moderate exacerbation. Claude: The key was changed from C to D before 8 Sep (the source's key was corrected).

q: A child with asthma has persistent foul-smelling stools. What is the next investigation?
r: Recurrent respiratory symptoms plus steatorrhea suggest cystic fibrosis; the sweat chloride test confirms it (≥60 mmol/L). Closest wrong answer: Stool elastase shows pancreatic insufficiency but doesn't diagnose CF.

q: A child has a positive sweat chloride test. What is the most frequent complication of this disease?
r: In cystic fibrosis thick secretions and chronic infection (S. aureus, Pseudomonas) cause progressive bronchiectasis in nearly all patients; respiratory failure is the main cause of death. (comment, 0 likes.)
n: Why not A? GI-tract cancer risk is raised in adult CF survivors, but it is uncommon — not the most frequent complication. Claude: A third (pulmonary) option was not recalled. Fuller version (1–5 Nov extract Q180): child with poorly controlled 'asthma' and foul

q: A child with cystic fibrosis presents with an increasing cough and greenish sputum. Vital signs are within normal limits apart from a mild fever of 37.8 C. Sputum culture grows methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus. What is the most appropriate management?
r: A mild CF pulmonary exacerbation with MSSA is treated with an oral anti-staphylococcal antibiotic (amoxicillin-clavulanate, flucloxacillin or cephalexin), usually for 2 weeks; IV therapy is for severe exacerbations or Pseudomonas.
n: Why not D? In CF, new S. aureus growth with increased symptoms is always treated - observing risks progressive bronchiectatic lung damage.

q: A boy under 10 years has fatigue, dyspnoea and palpitations during physical activity. His physical examination is normal. His older brother had a sudden cardiac death. What is the most likely diagnosis?
r: Exertional symptoms + a family history of sudden cardiac death (autosomal dominant) = HCM, the commonest cause of SCD in young athletes; the murmur may be absent at rest. Screen with ECG and echocardiography before allowing sport.
n: Why not A? PDA gives a continuous machinery murmur and bounding pulses, not a normal exam with familial sudden death. Claude: Extract (Medgard) version: 15-year-old with no murmur and equal pulses at a sports check, 'which condition must be excluded before spo

q: A patient has arachnodactyly (suspected Marfan syndrome). What is the most important investigation to check for a life-threatening complication?
r: The life-threatening complication in Marfan syndrome is aortic root dilatation leading to dissection or rupture (plus mitral valve prolapse). Echocardiography at diagnosis and then yearly measures the aortic root.
n: Why not B? an ECG cannot measure aortic root size or show valve structure.

q: A child has migratory arthritis (starting in the knee, resolving, then moving to the Achilles and other joints), a rash that appears after a warm shower (erythema marginatum), and a history of recurrent streptococcal sore throat. What is the most likely diagnosis?
r: Recent GAS infection plus major Jones criteria - migratory polyarthritis and erythema marginatum (evanescent, heat-accentuated) - is acute rheumatic fever.
n: Why not A? Systemic JIA has daily spiking fever with a salmon-pink evanescent rash and persistent (not migratory) arthritis, without a streptococcal link.

q: A boy presents with fever and a sore throat. Examination shows a congested throat without follicles and tender bilateral cervical lymph nodes of 0.5-1.5 cm. A throat culture swab is positive for group A streptococcus. Which of the following decreases the complications of this condition?
o: Completing a 10-day course of penicillin V
r: A full 10-day course of oral penicillin V (or amoxicillin) eradicates GAS and prevents acute rheumatic fever and suppurative complications if started within 9 days; it does not reliably prevent post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis.
n: Why not B? Influenza vaccination prevents influenza, not streptococcal complications such as rheumatic fever. Claude: Extract status [Review].

q: A child presents with fever, conjunctival injection, dry cracked lips, cervical lymphadenopathy and a skin rash. What is the most likely diagnosis?
r: Fever ≥5 days plus ≥4 of: bilateral non-exudative conjunctivitis, oral changes (cracked lips, strawberry tongue), cervical lymphadenopathy, polymorphous rash and extremity changes = Kawasaki disease; give IVIG + aspirin to prevent coronary aneurysms.
n: Why not B? Scarlet fever shares the strawberry tongue and rash, but it has a sandpaper rash and exudative pharyngitis, and no conjunctivitis.
