q: A woman at 32 weeks of pregnancy has BP 160/110 mmHg, headache and blurred vision, with no proteinuria. What is the management?
r: BP of 160/110 or more is a hypertensive emergency in pregnancy and must be lowered within 30-60 minutes with IV hydralazine or labetalol (or oral nifedipine). Headache and blurred vision make this pre-eclampsia with severe features even without proteinuria.
n: Why not C? MgSO4 is also indicated for seizure prophylaxis, but it does not lower BP, and severe-range BP is the immediate threat (stroke). Claude: The extract records a conflicting answer in the September register. Claude: both drugs are given; 'to prevent se

q: A twin pregnancy is scanned. Ultrasound shows a lambda (twin-peak) sign and a thick dividing membrane between the sacs. What type of twin pregnancy is this?
r: The lambda (twin-peak) sign, where chorionic tissue extends into the base of a thick membrane between the twins, means dichorionic diamniotic twins. A T-sign with a thin membrane means monochorionic diamniotic. Chorionicity is best assigned at 11-14 weeks. (extract key, Picture File (Almakrami))
n: Why not C? Mono-Di twins show the T-sign with a thin membrane, not a lambda sign. Claude: Recalled on 5 Nov by a 22 Oct examinee (#88049), with the options in a different order.

q: A 30-year-old woman in her first pregnancy has an ultrasound confirming dichorionic diamniotic twins. What was the time interval between ovulation and cleavage?
r: Splitting within 0-3 days (before the chorion forms) gives dichorionic diamniotic twins; 4-8 days gives monochorionic diamniotic, 9-12 days monochorionic monoamniotic, and after 12 days conjoined twins. Dizygotic twins are always DCDA.
n: Why not B? Splitting at 4-8 days (after the chorion forms, before the amnion) gives monochorionic diamniotic twins.

q: A 30-year-old woman in her first pregnancy has an ultrasound confirming monochorionic diamniotic twins. What was the time interval between ovulation and cleavage?
r: Monochorionic diamniotic twins arise when the embryo splits at days 4-8 (blastocyst stage), after the chorion has formed but before the amnion.
n: Why not C? Splitting at 9-12 days, after the amnion has formed, gives monoamniotic twins.

q: A 30-year-old woman in her first pregnancy has an ultrasound confirming monochorionic monoamniotic twins. What was the time interval between ovulation and cleavage?
r: Splitting at days 9-12, after both the chorion and amnion have formed, gives monochorionic monoamniotic twins.
n: Why not D? Division after day 12-13 is incomplete and produces conjoined twins.

q: A woman with a dichorionic diamniotic twin pregnancy is seen at 12 weeks. Which intervention decreases the risk to the mother and fetuses? [options partially recalled]
r: Twin pregnancies carry higher risks of pre-eclampsia, preterm birth, FGR and anaemia, so care is by a specialist team with increased antenatal surveillance; DCDA twins have growth scans about every 4 weeks from 20 weeks.
n: Why not A? Iron supplementation addresses the higher risk of anaemia but is only one part of care; increased surveillance reduces risk to mother and fetuses. Claude: Extract status Review.

q: A woman 12 weeks pregnant with monochorionic twins complicated by twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome presents with exertional dyspnoea. What is the next step?
r: Fetoscopic laser ablation of the placental anastomoses is used only from about 16 to 26 weeks; before 16 weeks laser is not possible, so symptomatic polyhydramnios (maternal dyspnoea) is relieved by amnioreduction. (Alhomrani's Sept page; his final word over Athar's 'laser regardless of week': <16 w
n: Why not C? laser photocoagulation is the definitive TTTS treatment, but only from 16 weeks; at 12 weeks it is not technically feasible.

q: A woman at 20 weeks with monochorionic diamniotic twins has severe twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome (polyhydramnios in one sac, oligohydramnios in the other). What is the most appropriate management?
r: Between 16 and 26 weeks, fetoscopic laser photocoagulation of the vascular anastomoses is the treatment of choice for stage II+ TTTS; it gives better survival and neurological outcome than serial amnioreduction. (Alhomrani's rule on the Sept page: >16 weeks → laser)
n: Why not D? amnioreduction only relieves the polyhydramnios temporarily and is the fallback before 16 weeks or when laser is not available. Claude: Twin built from Alhomrani's rule on the page, not a separate recall.

q: A pregnant woman has a fetus with hydrops [recalled as 'fetal hydrobe']. Which artery is used to detect fetal anaemia?
r: Middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity >1.5 MoM is the non-invasive test for fetal anaemia (thinner anaemic blood flows faster); confirm by cordocentesis.
n: Why not C? Umbilical artery Doppler assesses placental resistance in growth restriction (absent/reversed end-diastolic flow), not fetal anaemia. Claude: Extract version: 'best artery to diagnose anaemia in a 24-week fetus'.

q: A 23-year-old pregnant woman is at 28 weeks of gestation. Ultrasound shows fetal hydrops with a middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity above 1.8 MoM on Doppler. Which of the following is the most likely cause?
r: An MCA peak systolic velocity above 1.5 MoM indicates fetal anaemia. With hydrops, red-cell alloimmunisation is the classic cause, and anti-Kell causes particularly severe anaemia because it also suppresses fetal red-cell production.
n: Why not A? Aneuploidy causes non-immune hydrops without fetal anaemia, so the MCA velocity would not be raised.

q: A postpartum woman is Rh-negative and her newborn is also Rh-negative. What is the appropriate management?
o: No dose of anti-D is required
Administer anti-D only if the mother develops symptoms
r: Postpartum anti-D is needed only when the baby is RhD-positive, given within 72 hours. If the newborn is RhD-negative, there is no risk of sensitisation.
n: Why not A? Anti-D is given routinely at 28 weeks, but after delivery only if the baby is D-positive, and this baby is negative.

q: A 26-year-old average-sized woman delivered a baby boy within the last 24 hours. On the postnatal ward round it is found that her blood group is B negative, her husband is O positive and her son is A positive. A 300-microgram dose of anti-D immunoglobulin is prescribed. What volume of fetal blood will the prescribed dose protect against?
r: A standard 300-microgram (1500 IU) dose of anti-D neutralises about 30 mL of fetal whole blood, equal to about 15 mL of fetal red cells. Larger bleeds, measured by Kleihauer-Betke testing, need extra doses.
n: Why not D? 30 mL is the whole-blood figure; in red cells the dose covers only about 15 mL. Claude: the ABO groups as recalled (mother B, father O, baby A) are biologically inconsistent; ignore them for the dose question.

q: A 23-year-old primigravida presents at 31 weeks of gestation in preterm labour. The uterus is contracting and the cervix is closed. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
r: Between 24 and 34 weeks, antenatal corticosteroids are the single most beneficial step in threatened preterm labour, reducing RDS, IVH, NEC and neonatal death. Tocolytics (nifedipine first-line) are given only to buy 48 hours for the steroid course.
n: Why not A? Nifedipine is the first-line tocolytic, but tocolysis improves no neonatal outcome by itself; its role is to let the steroids act. Claude: Extract status Review.

q: A 23-year-old primigravida is admitted with threatened preterm labour at 30 weeks' gestation and has received antenatal corticosteroids. Which of the following is the rationale behind corticosteroid administration in this case?
r: Antenatal betamethasone or dexamethasone (24-34 weeks) speeds fetal lung maturation through surfactant production and reduces respiratory distress syndrome; it also lowers IVH, NEC and neonatal death.
n: Why not C? Steroids do not prevent neonatal hypoglycaemia; late-preterm courses actually increase it.

q: A 23-year-old G2P1 at 40 weeks presents to the ER with painful uterine contractions. Vaginal examination shows the cervix 3 cm dilated and 60% effaced. On admission to the labour room she has a gush of clear fluid. What is the most likely diagnosis?
r: Rupture of membranes after labour has begun (here at 40 weeks, contracting and 3 cm dilated) is spontaneous rupture of membranes. PROM means rupture BEFORE labour starts.
n: Why not B? premature (prelabour) rupture of membranes requires no labour at the time of rupture, but she was already contracting and 3 cm dilated.

q: A 30-year-old woman, G2 P1 L1, presented 3 days ago at 30 weeks' gestation with preterm prelabour rupture of membranes and was managed expectantly. Today she has developed fever and abdominal pain. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
r: Fever with abdominal pain or uterine tenderness during expectant management of PPROM is chorioamnionitis (intra-amniotic infection) until proven otherwise; it is the main risk of expectant management. It requires antibiotics and delivery.
n: Why not C? Abruption presents with painful vaginal bleeding and a tense, tender uterus, not fever.

q: A 26-year-old G4P3 at 31 weeks presents with labour pains. She had preterm prelabour rupture of membranes 4 weeks ago. Today the cervix is 3 cm dilated with clear liquor. [The question comes with a CTG showing fetal tachycardia.] What is the most appropriate next step?
o: High vaginal swab for bacterial culture and sensitivity
r: Prolonged PPROM (4 weeks) with labour and fetal tachycardia raises suspicion of chorioamnionitis: take a high vaginal swab for culture and sensitivity, start broad-spectrum IV antibiotics and allow labour to progress; infection alone is not an indication for caesarean.
n: Why not C? chorioamnionitis is a reason to expedite delivery, but vaginal delivery is preferred; caesarean is only for obstetric indications or fetal compromise, and she is already 3 cm.

q: A woman with PPROM at 31 weeks of gestation is managed conservatively. At 35 weeks she develops contractions. What is the most likely fetal complication?
r: After a long latency (4 weeks) from PPROM, ascending infection is the main risk, so neonatal sepsis is the most likely complication. At 35 weeks, especially after steroids, the risk of RDS is low.
n: Why not A? RDS is the main risk when PPROM delivers early (before 32-34 weeks); at 35 weeks after prolonged rupture, infection outweighs lung immaturity. Claude: Extract status Review.

q: A woman at 41 weeks has a closed, long cervix. What is the most appropriate cervical ripening agent?
r: An unfavourable cervix needs a ripening agent, not oxytocin. Misoprostol (PGE1) and dinoprostone (PGE2) work about equally well, with misoprostol slightly ahead (ACOG, CURRENT), so Alhomrani picks misoprostol; prostaglandins are avoided after a prior C-section. (Alhomrani U2913.)
n: Why not B? PGE2 isn't wrong, and it is the answer when misoprostol isn't offered (Gameboy copy); Alhomrani prefers misoprostol when both appear. Claude: Alhomrani's list of PGE2 contraindications: asthma, prior C-section, glaucoma, heart disease.

q: A woman at 41 weeks has a closed, long cervix. What is the most appropriate cervical ripening agent? [Gameboy copy — misoprostol not among the options]
r: A closed, long cervix (low Bishop score) needs ripening before oxytocin, and PGE2 (dinoprostone) is the prostaglandin offered.
n: Why not A? oxytocin brings on contractions but doesn't ripen an unfavourable cervix; it is used after ripening or with a favourable Bishop score. Claude: Only these two options were stated for the Gameboy copy.

q: A 35-year-old G3P2 diabetic woman at 38 weeks is planned for induction of labour. She has no abdominal or pelvic pain and no vaginal loss; the uterus corresponds to dates and is soft and non-tender; the cervix is closed and uneffaced. A CTG is shown (baseline ~140 bpm, normal variability). What is the most likely diagnosis?
r: Baseline 110–160 bpm, variability 5–25 bpm, accelerations and no decelerations = a normal (reassuring) CTG; a woman who is not contracting cannot show early or late decelerations, which are defined relative to contractions.
n: Why not A? late decelerations (uteroplacental insufficiency) are the feared pattern in diabetic pregnancy, but they need contractions and a delayed nadir, and none are shown.

q: A woman at 38 weeks' gestation is admitted to the labour ward with 4 cm cervical dilatation and a fetus in complete breech presentation. The CTG is reactive. On reassessment there is no change. What is the most appropriate next step?
r: A breech in labour that fails to progress (no cervical change on reassessment) should be delivered by caesarean section. Oxytocin augmentation of breech labour is discouraged, and ECV is contraindicated in established labour.
n: Why not B? Oxytocin augmentation for slow progress is avoided in breech labour, because arrest may signal disproportion and risks head entrapment.

q: A patient underwent caesarean section in the second stage of labour and presented 2 days later with continuous leakage of clear fluid from the vagina. What is the cause? [no other type of fistula was among the options]
r: Continuous painless leakage of urine from the vagina after a second-stage caesarean = vesicovaginal fistula from bladder injury at the lower segment; confirm with a methylene blue dye test.
n: Why not D? Ureteric injury can cause a ureterovaginal fistula, but at a second-stage CS the bladder is the organ at risk; with a ureteric fistula the patient also still voids normally.

q: A 34-year-old pregnant woman at 36 weeks of gestation presents with acute painful vaginal bleeding associated with uterine tenderness. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
r: Painful third-trimester bleeding with a tender, often hard ('woody') uterus = placental abruption. Placenta previa bleeds painlessly from a soft, non-tender uterus.
n: Why not C? Uterine rupture also gives pain and bleeding, but it needs a scarred uterus or labour and presents with loss of fetal station, palpable fetal parts and sudden fetal distress.

q: What is the most common risk factor for placental abruption?
r: Hypertension (chronic or pre-eclampsia) is the commonest risk factor for placental abruption. Others are a previous abruption, trauma, cocaine or smoking, PPROM, sudden decompression of polyhydramnios and multiple pregnancy.
n: Why not D? PPROM is a recognised risk factor, but much less common than hypertension.

q: A medical student is preparing to examine a pregnant woman who is a known case of low-lying placenta. The student plans to perform a digital vaginal examination. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Perform the digital vaginal examination under supervision
Perform the digital vaginal examination after obtaining the patient's consent
Digital vaginal examination is not allowed unless placenta praevia/low-lying placenta has been ruled out
Perform the examination only after consulting the obstetrician
r: Digital vaginal examination is contraindicated with antepartum bleeding or a known low-lying placenta until ultrasound has excluded placenta praevia, because it can provoke torrential haemorrhage. Supervision or consent does not make it safe.
n: Why not A? Supervision does not remove the risk; the examination itself is contraindicated until the placenta is confirmed clear of the os. Claude: The 22 Oct recall ('22 October .pdf' Q8) worded its answer as 'he may examine under supervision after confirming

q: A patient presents at 32 weeks of gestation with sudden vaginal bleeding of 700 mL. Which of the following describes this type of bleeding?
r: Antepartum haemorrhage is bleeding from the genital tract after 24 weeks and before delivery, when the patient is not in labour; at 32 weeks with no labour described, this is APH.
n: Why not C? Intrapartum haemorrhage needs bleeding during established labour (e.g. cervix 7 cm), and no labour is described here.

q: A patient at 32 weeks of gestation who is 7 cm dilated has sudden vaginal bleeding of 700 mL. Which of the following describes this type of bleeding?
r: Bleeding during established labour (cervix 7 cm) is intrapartum haemorrhage, even at 32 weeks.
n: Why not D? It would be antepartum only if bleeding started before labour; 7-cm dilatation means active labour.

q: A patient has sudden vaginal bleeding of 700 mL 10 hours after a vaginal delivery. Which of the following describes this type of bleeding?
r: Primary (early) PPH is blood loss of 500 mL or more within 24 hours of delivery, so bleeding at 10 hours qualifies.
n: Why not B? Late (secondary) PPH occurs from 24 hours up to 12 weeks after delivery.

q: A 40-year-old woman comes in labour with her seventh child. Following delivery she develops postpartum haemorrhage because the placenta fails to deliver (retained placenta). What is the type of postpartum haemorrhage?
r: Primary PPH is blood loss ≥500 mL within 24 hours of delivery; bleeding from a retained placenta straight after birth is therefore primary ('Tissue' of the 4 Ts: Tone, Trauma, Tissue, Thrombin). There is no 'tertiary' PPH.
n: Why not B? secondary PPH is abnormal bleeding from 24 hours to 12 weeks postpartum (classically retained products or endometritis); retained tissue causes it only when the bleeding starts after the first day.

q: A patient has sudden vaginal bleeding of 700 mL 3 weeks after a vaginal delivery. Which of the following describes this type of bleeding?
r: Secondary (late) PPH is abnormal bleeding between 24 hours and 12 weeks postpartum, commonly from retained products or endometritis; 3 weeks fits.
n: Why not A? Early (primary) PPH is limited to the first 24 hours after delivery.

q: A 32-year-old woman, G4 P3 L2, had normal deliveries with no prenatal or postnatal complications. She had an uneventful pregnancy and had a spontaneous vaginal delivery after 16 hours of labour of a healthy 3000 g boy. After delivery of the placenta she started to bleed heavily. Which of the following was her risk factor for postpartum haemorrhage? [the 1 Nov recall (#87957) said 'twins, 4 kg, prolonged labour 16 h']
r: 16 hours of labour in a multiparous woman is prolonged, and a fatigued myometrium predisposes to atony. P3 is not grand multiparity (≥5), and 3000 g is not macrosomia (≥4000–4500 g).
n: Why not A? Grand multiparity means ≥5 previous births; she is P3. Claude: The 1 Nov recall said twins (4 kg); a commenter asked 'why not multiple pregnancy?'. If the stem truly has twins, multiple gestation competes; the bank wording is a singleton of 3000 g.

q: A 31-year-old woman, G2 P1, had normal deliveries with no prenatal or postnatal complications. She had an uneventful pregnancy and delivered a 3000 g boy after only 2 hours of labour, just making it to the hospital. After delivery of the placenta she started to bleed heavily. Which of the following was her risk factor for postpartum haemorrhage?
r: Precipitous labour (<3 hours from onset to delivery) causes genital-tract trauma and uterine atony.
n: Why not B? It is the opposite — 2 hours is precipitous, not prolonged.

q: A 36-year-old woman, G4 P3 L2, had normal deliveries with no prenatal or postnatal complications. She had an uneventful pregnancy and delivered twins weighing 2800 g and 2900 g after only 5 hours of labour. After delivery of the placenta she started to bleed heavily. Which of the following was her risk factor for postpartum haemorrhage?
r: Twins overdistend the uterus and cause atony; 5 hours is a normal labour, P3 is not grand parity, and neither twin is macrosomic.
n: Why not B? 5 hours of labour is not prolonged.

q: A woman delivered twins (birth weight recalled as 4 kg) after a prolonged labour of 16 hours [and had postpartum haemorrhage — the outcome asked about was not clearly recalled]. What is the most likely cause?
r: Twin pregnancy overdistends the uterus and is a classic major risk factor for atonic postpartum haemorrhage.
n: Why not B? Prolonged labour also causes uterine atony — it was the poster's stated answer (apparently the bank key); the commenters found it odd with twins in the stem. Claude: Recall gave only the answer ('prolonged labour'); the options were added for practi

q: A 32-year-old woman, G4 P3 L2, had normal deliveries with no prenatal or postnatal complications. She had an uneventful pregnancy and had a vaginal delivery after 5 hours of labour of a 4600 g baby. After delivery of the placenta she started to bleed heavily. Which of the following was her risk factor for postpartum haemorrhage?
r: A birth weight ≥4000–4500 g overdistends the uterus and raises the risk of atony and genital-tract trauma.
n: Why not B? 5 hours is a normal labour length.

q: A woman, G7 P6 L6, had normal deliveries with no prenatal or postnatal complications. She had an uneventful pregnancy and had a vaginal delivery after 7 hours of labour. After delivery of the placenta she started to bleed heavily. Which of the following was her risk factor for postpartum haemorrhage?
r: Grand multiparity (≥5 births) leaves an overstretched myometrium prone to atony; 7 hours is a normal labour.
n: Why not D? 7 hours is not precipitous (<3 hours).

q: A 30-year-old G2P1 with a past history of postpartum haemorrhage now has a singleton pregnancy. What is her risk factor for PPH in the current pregnancy?
r: A previous PPH is one of the strongest predictors of PPH (recurrence roughly 10–15%), so she needs active management of the third stage and IV access with cross-matched blood. She is para 1, singleton and 30, so the other options do not apply. (Alhomrani's Sept page)
n: Why not C? grand multiparity (≥5 previous births) predisposes to atony, but she is only para 1.

q: What is the most common cause of postpartum haemorrhage?
r: Uterine atony causes ~70–80% of PPH (the 4 Ts: Tone > Trauma > Tissue > Thrombin); first steps are uterine massage and oxytocin.
n: Why not C? Genital-tract trauma is the second commonest cause, and the likeliest one when bleeding continues despite a well-contracted uterus.

q: A 38-year-old woman known to have a low-lying placenta had a normal vaginal delivery. One hour after delivery she has a postpartum haemorrhage. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
r: Uterine atony causes about 70-80% of PPH, and a low-lying placenta adds to it because the lower uterine segment contracts poorly over the placental bed.
n: Why not D? Genital tract trauma is the second commonest cause; suspect it when bleeding continues despite a firm, well-contracted uterus.

q: A 24-year-old primigravida has an uneventful vaginal delivery. After delivery of the placenta she bleeds 1000 mL. She is alert and stable, and the uterus is FIRM. What is the most common cause?
r: Atony is the commonest cause of PPH overall, but a well-contracted (firm) uterus excludes it; bleeding with a firm uterus after a first vaginal delivery is genital-tract trauma (cervical, vaginal or perineal tears) until proven otherwise, so examine under good light and repair. (Alhomrani's Sept pag
n: Why not A? uterine atony is the most common cause of PPH in general, but the FIRM uterus in the stem rules it out.

q: A postpartum woman develops disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC). What is the most common cause?
r: Placental abruption is the commonest obstetric cause of DIC: the retroplacental clot releases tissue thromboplastin into the maternal circulation (worst with large abruption and fetal death). Other causes are amniotic fluid embolism, severe pre-eclampsia/HELLP, sepsis and a long-retained dead fetus.
n: Why not C? uterine atony is the commonest cause of postpartum HAEMORRHAGE, but the question asks about DIC, and atony causes coagulopathy only secondarily (dilution/consumption). Claude: Other copies offered amniotic fluid embolism, severe pre-eclampsia/HELLP,

q: A woman in labour required oxytocin for augmentation. How should postpartum haemorrhage be prevented?
o: Active management of the third stage of labour
r: Oxytocin augmentation (receptor desensitisation, longer labour) increases the risk of atony; active management of the third stage (prophylactic uterotonic such as oxytocin 10 IU IM at delivery, controlled cord traction, checking uterine tone) cuts PPH by about 60% and is recommended for every birth.
n: Why not A? monitoring detects atony once it has happened; it does not prevent it, which the prophylactic uterotonic of active management does.

q: After a spontaneous vaginal delivery, a P2 woman has primary postpartum haemorrhage due to uterine atony. Which of the following is the standard of care?
r: Oxytocin (IV infusion or IM), with uterine massage, is first-line for both preventing and treating atonic PPH; ergometrine, carboprost and misoprostol are second-line.
n: Why not B? ergometrine is the usual second agent and is contraindicated in hypertension/preeclampsia.

q: An asthmatic woman delivered after an IUFD and now has postpartum hemorrhage from uterine atony that isn't responding to oxytocin. What is the next medication? [misoprostol not among the options]
r: After oxytocin, the next uterotonic is methylergonovine (contraindicated in hypertension/preeclampsia). Carboprost (PGF2α) is contraindicated in asthma because it causes bronchospasm. ACOG and the California (CMQCC) protocol place TXA after these uterotonics. (Alhomrani U2847: final B.)
n: Why not C? TXA is an adjunct given within 3 h, but ACOG/CMQCC sequencing puts it after methylergonovine and carboprost; Alhomrani advises avoiding the newer 2022–24 'TXA early' approach in the exam.

q: A 23-year-old woman with known idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura delivered at 39 weeks, and the delivery was complicated by postpartum haemorrhage. What is the most appropriate management?
r: PPH in a thrombocytopenic woman with ITP is treated with platelet transfusion (plus IVIG/steroids as needed) alongside uterotonics. FFP and cryoprecipitate replace clotting factors, which are normal in ITP.
n: Why not C? packed red cells replace lost blood but do not correct the platelet deficit that is causing the bleeding.

q: A 24-year-old single woman presents with (progressive) dysmenorrhoea and a feeling of pelvic heaviness. Pelvic examination shows a firm, palpable pelvic mass. What is the most likely diagnosis? [1 Nov copy (#87926): options were ovarian/uterine cyst, uterine leiomyoma, PID and an irrelevant fourth]
r: Pelvic heaviness/pressure, dysmenorrhoea and a firm uterine mass point to a leiomyoma, the commonest pelvic tumour in women.
n: Why not A? an ovarian cyst gives an adnexal, often cystic mass and does not typically cause dysmenorrhoea.

q: A woman presents with heavy menstrual bleeding and pelvic pressure. Examination shows a symmetrically enlarged, tender uterus. What is the most likely diagnosis?
r: A diffusely, symmetrically enlarged ('globular'), tender uterus with heavy bleeding ± dysmenorrhoea is adenomyosis (endometrial tissue within the myometrium).
n: Why not A? Endometriosis causes dysmenorrhoea, dyspareunia and a fixed retroverted uterus or adnexal masses, but does not enlarge the uterus itself.

q: A 42-year-old P4+2 presents with severe, progressive secondary dysmenorrhoea and menorrhagia. Pelvic examination shows a tender, diffusely enlarged uterus. Endometrial biopsy: normal endometrium. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
r: Adenomyosis typically affects multiparous women aged 40-50. It causes progressive secondary dysmenorrhoea and heavy periods with a uniformly enlarged, tender, globular ('boggy') uterus; a normal biopsy excludes hyperplasia or cancer.
n: Why not B? Endometriosis causes dysmenorrhoea and dyspareunia, usually with a normal-sized, often fixed retroverted uterus and adnexal or uterosacral nodularity rather than a diffusely enlarged uterus.

q: A 35-year-old woman has a uterine leiomyoma with heavy menstrual bleeding [an image and lab results were shown; the key implies anaemia]. What is the most appropriate next management step?
r: With fibroids, heavy bleeding and anaemia, first correct the anaemia (iron ± transfusion; GnRH agonists can stop bleeding and raise Hb) before any definitive procedure.
n: Why not A? myomectomy is the definitive fertility-sparing option, but operating on an anaemic patient adds risk; optimise Hb first.

q: A woman who wants to become pregnant is found to have a 2-cm asymptomatic fibroid and is worried about its effect on pregnancy. What is the appropriate action?
r: Small (under 4-5 cm) asymptomatic fibroids that do not distort the cavity rarely affect fertility or pregnancy, so reassure and follow up.
n: Why not B? myomectomy is for submucosal fibroids distorting the cavity, or large symptomatic fibroids with infertility or recurrent loss, not for a 2-cm asymptomatic one.

q: A female patient's imaging shows a fibroid distorting the endometrial cavity [recalled as 'subserosal'; a cavity-distorting fibroid is normally submucosal or intramural]. What is the recommended next step?
r: A fibroid that distorts the endometrial cavity (causing bleeding or infertility) is removed by myomectomy, preserving the uterus: hysteroscopic for submucosal fibroids, laparoscopic or open for intramural or subserosal ones.
n: Why not A? GnRH analogues are only a temporary pre-operative measure to shrink fibroids and correct anaemia; they are not the definitive step. Claude: Extract status Review. The fourth option was not recalled.

q: A 25-year-old woman has been trying to conceive for 3 years and has had 2 unsuccessful IVF cycles. Pelvic ultrasound: multiple uterine fibroids of variable sizes. Which of the following will most likely increase her chance of a successful pregnancy?
o: GnRH injection to reduce the size of the fibroids
r: Fibroids, especially submucosal or cavity-distorting ones, impair implantation. With failed IVF and a wish for pregnancy, myomectomy is the treatment that improves the chance of conceiving; UAE and long-term hormonal therapy are avoided in women who want pregnancy.
n: Why not D? GnRH agonists shrink fibroids only temporarily (as a pre-operative measure) and prevent conception while used; the fibroids regrow when they are stopped.

q: A woman in her 40s has progressively worsening abnormal uterine bleeding [the 4 Nov post: from fibroids]. She has completed her family and does not desire future fertility. What is the most appropriate definitive management?
o: Referral to a pain clinic or pain management
r: Hysterectomy is the only definitive cure for symptomatic fibroids or AUB and is appropriate once childbearing is complete; GnRH agonists and progestins only buy time.
n: Why not A? GnRH agonists shrink fibroids and stop bleeding only while they are given (usually up to 6 months because of bone loss), so they are not definitive.

q: A 45-year-old P5+3 presents with abnormal uterine bleeding for the last 3 months. Her periods are regular, every 30 days, lasting 5 days, with blood clots and pain not relieved by simple analgesia. She had a myomectomy 12 years ago and 3 surgical evacuations for incomplete miscarriage. The uterus is not palpable abdominally, but on pelvic examination it is bulky and tender with no adnexal mass. BMI 40 kg/m2. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for her presentation?
r: Age 40-50, multiparity and previous uterine surgery (myomectomy, repeated evacuations that breach the endometrial-myometrial junction) are classic risk factors. Heavy, painful, regular periods with a bulky tender uterus mean adenomyosis.
n: Why not C? Fibroids can recur after myomectomy, but they give an irregular, non-tender enlarged uterus; a uniformly bulky, tender uterus with dysmenorrhoea is adenomyosis.

q: A 50-year-old P2+3 with diabetes, hypertension and polycystic ovarian syndrome presents with abnormal uterine bleeding for 8 months. The uterus is normal-sized. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for her presentation?
r: Chronic anovulation (PCOS) plus metabolic risk (diabetes, hypertension) means prolonged unopposed oestrogen, leading to endometrial hyperplasia. It presents as months of AUB with a normal-sized uterus.
n: Why not A? Adenomyosis gives a bulky, tender uterus with painful heavy periods, but this uterus is normal-sized. Claude: The look-alike line says only that endometrial hyperplasia was offered; the other options are rebuilt from the parent.

q: A 60-year-old woman with diabetes and hypertension presents with postmenopausal bleeding for 8 months. BMI 42 kg/m2. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for her presentation?
r: Postmenopausal bleeding in an obese, diabetic, hypertensive woman (the unopposed-oestrogen risk triad) is endometrial cancer until proven otherwise; assess with TVUS endometrial thickness and then endometrial biopsy.
n: Why not B? Fibroids shrink after menopause and rarely cause new postmenopausal bleeding. Claude: Adenomyosis was not offered in this version; options are rebuilt from the parent's options.

q: A 45-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Room complaining that her period has not stopped for the past 15 days. She feels drowsy, gets easily fatigued and sometimes faints. Laboratory results are provided [values not recalled; they implied significant anaemia]. Which of the following is the most appropriate next management step?
r: Once labs confirm significant anaemia in a symptomatic patient (drowsiness, fainting), stabilising her with a blood transfusion comes before working up the cause of the bleeding.
n: Why not B? A pregnancy test belongs in the work-up, but a symptomatic, severely anaemic patient must be stabilised first.

q: A 25-year-old woman has crampy lower abdominal pain that starts on the first day of her menses and usually improves by the third day. Her periods are regular, and clinical assessment and pelvic ultrasound are normal. What most likely explains her presentation?
r: Crampy pain beginning with menses and settling within 2-3 days, regular cycles, and a normal pelvic exam and ultrasound in a young woman are primary (prostaglandin-mediated) dysmenorrhoea, treated with NSAIDs ± COCP.
n: Why not B? endometriosis causes secondary dysmenorrhoea that often starts before the period, worsens over time, and comes with dyspareunia, infertility or a pelvic finding.

q: A 23-year-old woman complains of severe pain starting the day before menses and lasting 2 days. The pain is so severe that she misses work. Which of the following is the most appropriate to control her pain so that she can go to work?
r: Primary dysmenorrhoea is treated with NSAIDs and/or combined hormonal contraception, which suppresses ovulation and endometrial prostaglandins. With no NSAID offered, the combined pill is the most effective option.
n: Why not B? Paracetamol is a weak analgesic that does not block uterine prostaglandins as NSAIDs and the COC do, so it is inadequate for pain severe enough to miss work.

q: A woman has a history of increasing pelvic pain that is cyclic and intensifies just before menses. Which is the acceptable method for diagnosing endometriosis?
r: Laparoscopy with direct visualisation (± biopsy) of the lesions remains the gold-standard diagnosis of endometriosis; transvaginal US/MRI show endometriomas and deep disease but cannot exclude superficial peritoneal disease.
n: Why not D? transvaginal ultrasound is the first-line imaging and finds endometriomas, but a normal scan does not rule out endometriosis, so it is not the diagnostic standard.

q: A patient has endometriosis. What is the most definitive management?
r: Definitive treatment of severe endometriosis, once the family is complete, is total hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy and excision of visible lesions; removing the ovaries removes the oestrogen drive.
n: Why not B? Endometrial ablation destroys only the lining of the uterine cavity, while endometriotic lesions are outside the uterus.

q: A 45-year-old woman with 3 children who has completed her family had an endometriotic cyst removed from the right ovary in the past. She now has dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia and chronic pelvic pain, and a new endometriotic cyst is found on the left ovary. What is the most appropriate management?
o: Remove the cyst only when it exceeds 10 mm
Laparoscopic cystectomy and ablation of endometriotic tissue
r: In a 45-year-old with a completed family and recurrent symptomatic endometriosis (a new endometrioma after a previous cystectomy), definitive surgery is best: hysterectomy with BSO and excision of disease. Removing the ovaries lowers recurrence. (Alhomrani U2925, referring to Updates #2048.)
n: Why not D? laparoscopic cystectomy with ablation is the conservative option for women who want fertility or to keep their ovaries, and recurrence is common; an MG look-alike keyed D, so check what differs (age, wish for fertility). Claude: Alhomrani pointed to

q: A young woman has breast tenderness, irritability and fatigue that start before her period and resolve by the second day of menses. Breast imaging, prolactin and TSH are all normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
r: Physical and mild mood symptoms in the luteal phase that resolve in the first days of menses, without marked functional impairment, are premenstrual syndrome.
n: Why not B? PMDD (DSM-5) needs 5 or more symptoms, including at least one prominent mood symptom (marked depression, anxiety, irritability or lability), with significant dysfunction.

q: A patient with severe PMS has failed initial medical management. What is the next line?
r: SSRIs are used for PMS, not only PMDD, when the severe symptoms include mood change or functional impairment. Combined OCPs (drospirenone) are preferred for severe NON-mood (physical) symptoms or when contraception is wanted. (Alhomrani U2900; UpToDate U2901.)
n: Why not B? OCPs win only when the severe symptoms are physical (e.g., dysmenorrhea, bloating) without mood symptoms.

q: A woman has severe premenstrual symptoms that are mainly physical (dysmenorrhea, bloating, breast tenderness) without mood symptoms, and initial treatment has failed. What is the next line?
r: Suppressing ovulation with a combined OCP is preferred for severe premenstrual symptoms that are mainly physical, or when contraception is also wanted. (Alhomrani U2900.)
n: Why not A? SSRIs target the mood and irritability component, which is absent here. Claude: Twin built from Alhomrani's rule (U2900); not a verbatim recall.

q: A 14-year-old girl [19-year-old in the extract version] presents with amenorrhoea and no secondary sexual characteristics. FSH and LH are low. What is the next step?
o: Brain MRI to assess the pituitary and hypothalamus
r: Absent puberty with LOW FSH/LH = hypogonadotropic (central) hypogonadism, so the hypothalamus–pituitary is imaged with MRI to exclude a mass (e.g., craniopharyngioma, prolactinoma) before diagnosing constitutional delay or Kallmann syndrome.
n: Why not A? Pelvic US is the step when breasts are present (to check for a uterus); with low gonadotropins and no puberty the problem is central.

q: A 15-year-old girl is brought by her mother because of primary amenorrhoea. Breast development is good, but she has no axillary or pubic hair. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
r: Normal breasts (from aromatised testosterone) with absent pubic and axillary hair (androgen resistance) in primary amenorrhoea is complete androgen insensitivity: 46,XY, blind vagina, no uterus, testes in the abdomen or groin.
n: Why not B? MRKH also has normal breasts and primary amenorrhoea, but pubic and axillary hair is normal because the ovaries and androgen response are intact.

q: A 28-year-old woman presents with a 6-month history of amenorrhoea. Her prolactin and TSH are normal, but her FSH is elevated. What is the most likely diagnosis?
r: Amenorrhoea for ≥4 months before age 40 with raised FSH (>25 IU/L on two samples ≥4 weeks apart) = premature ovarian insufficiency. Hypothalamic amenorrhoea has low or normal FSH.
n: Why not B? PCOS causes oligo-amenorrhoea, but FSH is normal (often with high LH and androgens), not raised.

q: A woman with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) presents with hirsutism and irregular menstrual cycles. Local cosmetic treatments have not helped. What is the most appropriate management?
r: Combined OCPs are first-line drug treatment for PCOS-related hirsutism: they raise SHBG and suppress ovarian androgens, and they also regulate the cycle. Anti-androgens (spironolactone, cyproterone, finasteride) are added after 6 months if the response is inadequate, with contraception.
n: Why not C? Cyproterone acetate is an anti-androgen added after about 6 months of an inadequate response to the COC, not first-line on its own.

q: A 50-year-old woman complains of hot flushes and insomnia. Which of the following is the most appropriate first-line management?
r: First-line management of vasomotor symptoms is lifestyle change: layered clothing, a cool room, avoiding triggers (caffeine, alcohol, spicy food), weight loss, exercise and sleep hygiene. Systemic HRT is the most effective treatment when symptoms are moderate to severe or lifestyle fails.
n: Why not D? Systemic HRT is the most effective treatment, but the question asks for first-line management, which is lifestyle.

q: An infertile woman's hysterosalpingography shows bilateral tubal blockage; no laparoscopy has been done. What is the most appropriate next step? [partial bank recall; only one option seen]
r: Blockage seen only on HSG is confirmed by laparoscopy and dye test before IVF is offered, the same rule as the 21-year-old twin.
n: Why not B? IVF follows bilateral blockage confirmed at laparoscopy, as in the 4 Nov version.

q: A woman with primary infertility has a normal hormonal profile and a normal partner semen analysis. She has completed a 3-month trial of clomiphene without conceiving, and no tubal patency testing has been done. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
r: Tubal patency must be assessed before treatment is escalated; after a failed clomiphene trial with no tubal test, the next step is diagnostic laparoscopy (with dye).
n: Why not B? IVF is chosen once tubal disease is proven; going to IVF without assessing the tubes is premature.

q: A 26-year-old woman with primary infertility for 4 years has a normal hormonal profile and a normal partner semen analysis. Hysterosalpingography and laparoscopy with dye test show only the right fallopian tube is blocked; the left tube is patent. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
r: With one patent tube, normal semen and normal hormones, natural conception is still possible; the bank keys ovulation stimulation with clomiphene before IVF.
n: Why not B? IVF is for bilateral blockage or failure of simpler measures; one patent tube allows a trial of ovulation induction first.

q: A 26-year-old woman with primary infertility for the last 4 years presents for follow-up. Her hormonal profile is normal and her husband's semen analysis is normal. Hysterosalpingography and diagnostic laparoscopy with dye test confirmed bilateral tubal blockage. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
r: Confirmed bilateral tubal occlusion can only be bypassed by IVF; ovulation induction and IUI both need at least one patent tube.
n: Why not C? IUI puts sperm in the uterus, but fertilisation still needs a patent tube, so it fails with bilateral blockage.

q: A 21-year-old woman with primary infertility for 4 years is seen for follow-up. Her hormonal profile is normal and her husband's semen analysis is normal. Hysterosalpingogram shows bilateral proximal tubal blockage. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
r: Proximal tubal blockage on HSG is often a false positive (tubal spasm or mucus plugs). Confirm it with laparoscopy and dye (chromotubation), the gold standard, before committing to IVF.
n: Why not A? IVF is the treatment for confirmed bilateral tubal blockage, and it becomes the answer once laparoscopy and dye has confirmed it (the look-alike).

q: A 30-year-old woman has a single PAINLESS ulcer on the left labium majus with a ragged edge and a necrotic base, and palpable left inguinal adenopathy. What is the most likely diagnosis?
r: The bank keys a painless genital ulcer with inguinal nodes as primary syphilis — painlessness outweighs the edge description; confirm with dark-field microscopy/serology and treat with benzathine penicillin G 2.4 MU IM.
n: Why not B? Chancroid ulcers are characteristically painful, so 'painless' rules it out.

q: A 30-year-old woman presents with whitish vaginal discharge that has a fishy odour and is associated with vaginal itching. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
r: Thin white-grey discharge with a fishy odour (positive whiff test, pH >4.5, clue cells) = bacterial vaginosis; treat with metronidazole.
n: Why not B? Trichomoniasis can smell fishy too, but it gives a frothy yellow-green discharge with a strawberry cervix and marked irritation.

q: A 30-year-old woman presents with whitish vaginal discharge and vaginal itching for 3 days. There is no fishy odour. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
r: An itchy, white, curd-like discharge with no odour and normal pH (<4.5) = vulvovaginal candidiasis; treat with an azole.
n: Why not A? The defining feature of BV is the fishy odour, and it causes little itching.

q: A woman [about 40 — examinee unsure of age] presents with lower abdominal pain without vaginal bleeding. The pregnancy test is negative. On examination there is cervical motion tenderness and the cervix is closed. What is the diagnosis?
r: Lower abdominal pain with cervical motion (or uterine/adnexal) tenderness in a sexually active woman, once pregnancy is excluded, meets the CDC minimum criteria for PID — treat empirically.
n: Why not B? UTI/cystitis causes dysuria, frequency and suprapubic tenderness, not cervical motion tenderness. Claude: 4th option forgotten (examinee says it was not ectopic). Extract version: woman with multiple sexual partners and cervical motion tenderness; o

q: A newly married woman, 1 week into her honeymoon, complains of dysuria and frequency. How will you manage?
r: Uncomplicated ('honeymoon') cystitis is treated with first-line nitrofurantoin for 5 days (alternatives: TMP-SMX, fosfomycin); fluoroquinolones are held back because of resistance and adverse effects.
n: Why not C? Ciprofloxacin works, but it is not first-line for simple cystitis; keep it for pyelonephritis or complicated infection.

q: A 28-year-old woman known to have an ovarian cyst comes to your clinic asking about contraception. Which of the following methods is most appropriate for her?
r: Combined OCPs suppress ovulation, so they reduce new functional ovarian cysts while providing contraception. Progestogen-only methods do not reliably suppress ovulation and are linked to persistent functional cysts.
n: Why not C? The vaginal ring is also combined hormonal contraception and suppresses ovulation, but the OCP is the standard first-line answer.

q: A patient with ovarian cancer asks about the best form of contraception. Which is the most appropriate?
r: Ovarian cancer is not a contraindication to hormonal contraception: the combined pill is UK/US MEC category 1 (and it lowers ovarian cancer risk), so an effective hormonal method is appropriate. (Alhomrani's Sept page, citing Eithar/Avengers: 'OCP category 1 in ovarian cancer')
n: Why not B? condoms are 'safe' but much less effective, and there is no reason to avoid hormones in ovarian cancer; the non-hormonal answer belongs to current BREAST cancer (combined pill MEC 4). Claude: the vaginal ring is also a combined hormonal method in th

q: A sexually active woman, not on oral contraceptives, comes to the clinic worried about an unintended pregnancy. What is the primary preventive measure for her?
o: Refer her to a sexual behaviour programme [garbled in the recall]
r: Primary prevention stops a problem before it happens; for fear of unintended pregnancy, that means contraceptive counselling and education (plus emergency contraception after recent unprotected intercourse).
n: Why not B? STD screening is secondary prevention (early detection) and does nothing to prevent pregnancy.

q: A 20-year-old woman presents to the clinic with lower abdominal pain for 3 months [stem also said 'asymptomatic']. Ultrasound: a multiloculated, solid, right adnexal complex mass of 6 cm. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
r: A 6-cm complex (solid, multiloculated) adnexal mass in a young woman is most often a benign germ-cell tumour (dermoid). It needs surgical removal by ovarian cystectomy, preserving the ovary for fertility, not aspiration or observation.
n: Why not B? Oophorectomy removes healthy ovarian tissue unnecessarily in a 20-year-old; ovary-sparing cystectomy is preferred for a presumed benign mass.

q: A 76-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Room with lower abdominal pain for 1 week. Ultrasound: a multiloculated, solid, right adnexal complex mass of 6 cm. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
r: A solid or complex adnexal mass in a postmenopausal woman is suspicious for ovarian cancer (calculate the RMI with CA-125). It should be managed by a gynaecologic oncologist, who performs the staging surgery.
n: Why not B? Oophorectomy alone is inadequate if the mass is malignant; staging or debulking by a gynaecologic oncologist improves survival.

q: A 61-year-old woman has progressive abdominal distension, early satiety and weight loss, and her CA-125 is very high. Biopsy shows high-grade epithelial ovarian cancer with extensive metastatic spread in the abdomen. What is the next step?
o: TAH-BSO with excision of all visible metastases (cytoreductive surgery)
r: Advanced epithelial ovarian cancer is treated with primary cytoreductive (debulking) surgery aiming for no residual disease, followed by platinum–taxane chemotherapy, even when spread in the abdomen is extensive. (Alhomrani U2891: unchanged.)
n: Why not B? neoadjuvant chemotherapy with interval debulking is for women unfit for surgery or whose disease is unlikely to be fully resected; choose it only if the stem gives such a clue.

q: A para 3 woman diagnosed with ovarian cancer is scheduled for chemotherapy. She requests oocyte cryopreservation [exact wording not remembered]. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Tell her it is possible only for nulliparous women
Proceed after counselling her about the process and that it may not succeed
r: Fertility preservation should be offered to any woman of reproductive age before gonadotoxic chemotherapy, whatever her parity. Respect her autonomy and proceed after counselling on the process, the treatment delay, the risks and the limited success rate.
n: Why not A? Parity is not a criterion for fertility preservation, so refusing on that basis is wrong.

q: A 45-year-old woman complains of postcoital bleeding. Pelvic examination shows a 2 × 1 cm cervical mass. What is the most appropriate next step?
r: A visible cervical lesion must be biopsied directly (punch or colposcopic biopsy). Cytology is a screening test for normal-looking cervices and can be falsely negative in invasive cancer.
n: Why not A? a Pap test is for screening; a gross 2 × 1 cm mass with postcoital bleeding needs histology.

q: A 49-year-old woman had colposcopy, which shows CIN 3. What is the most appropriate management?
r: CIN 2–3 is treated by excision (LEEP/LLETZ or cold-knife conization), which also excludes occult invasion; hysterectomy is not first-line treatment for CIN.
n: Why not B? Hysterectomy is not primary therapy for CIN 3; an excisional procedure must come first to rule out invasive cancer.

q: A 32-year-old woman has choriocarcinoma with lung metastases (FIGO stage III) and a WHO prognostic score of 10. What is the treatment? [one option not recalled]
r: A FIGO/WHO risk score ≥7 means high-risk GTN, treated with multi-agent chemotherapy (EMA-CO); a score ≤6 is low-risk and gets single-agent methotrexate. Chemotherapy, not surgery, is primary and cures most patients even with lung metastases.
n: Why not B? Methotrexate monotherapy is for low-risk disease (score ≤6); a score of 10 needs combination chemotherapy.

q: A patient has a breast mass with nipple retraction and features suggestive of malignancy (BI-RADS 5). Which of the following is the best biopsy method?
r: Core-needle (Tru-cut) biopsy is the standard for a suspicious breast mass: it gives histology, invasion status and receptors (ER/PR/HER2) before definitive surgery. FNA gives cytology only.
n: Why not B? Excisional biopsy is for a non-diagnostic or discordant core result; doing it first compromises planning of the definitive operation.

q: A 50-year-old woman has been managed conservatively for 6 months for grade 3 posterior vaginal wall prolapse with mild to moderate pelvic discomfort. Examination today shows similar findings with no progression or improvement. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in her management?
r: A symptomatic advanced (grade 3) prolapse that has not improved after 6 months of conservative treatment (pelvic floor training or pessary) warrants counselling about surgical repair (posterior colporrhaphy).
n: Why not A? Continuing reassurance ignores persistent symptoms after an adequate trial; the discussion should now move to surgery (or a pessary if she declines). Claude: Extract status Review.

q: A pregnant woman in labour is told that vaginal delivery is dangerous for the fetus and a C-section is necessary. She understands the risks but refuses surgery and insists on vaginal delivery. What should the doctor do?
o: Refer her to the psychiatric department
Sedate her and perform the C-section
r: A competent woman may refuse a caesarean even when the fetus is at risk; respect her decision, document it, and keep offering CS and support.
n: Why not D? The husband's consent is irrelevant for a competent adult woman - only her own consent or refusal counts.

q: A patient cannot deliver vaginally and the fetus is in distress. The doctor wants to perform a caesarean section, but the patient refuses and wants a second opinion. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Try to persuade her against her will
Document refusal of medical advice with consent from the patient and her husband
r: A competent patient's request for a second opinion is her right and should be facilitated promptly; she cannot be coerced and the husband's consent has no role.
n: Why not D? Documenting refusal is appropriate, but requiring the husband's consent is wrong - a competent woman's decision needs no husband. Claude: Key changed 16 Sep from D to C. Claude: arrange the second opinion urgently given fetal distress.

q: A fetus is diagnosed with anencephaly and the doctor advises termination. The mother agrees but the father refuses. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Take consent from both the mother and the father
r: In Saudi practice, termination for a lethal fetal anomaly needs a medical-committee report and the written consent of both parents; when they disagree the doctor keeps counselling and does not act on one parent's consent or decide alone.
n: Why not B? the mother consents for most procedures on her own body, but termination of pregnancy is a joint decision in Saudi practice, so her agreement alone is not enough.

q: A multiparous woman who has had six caesarean deliveries wants her seventh baby by caesarean section. The doctors recommend tubal ligation to prevent serious complications in future pregnancies. What is the best action?
o: Take consent from her and her husband
Take consent from her and tell her to inform her husband
r: Sterilisation is permanent and affects the couple's reproduction, so Saudi practice requires consent from both wife and husband (outside a life-threatening emergency).
n: Why not C? the patient's own consent is enough for most procedures, but for permanent sterilisation the husband's consent is expected too, not just informing him.

q: A patient with colorectal cancer does not wish to have surgery; his wife and son disagree with him. He then develops a decreased level of consciousness, and the family requests the surgery. What is the most appropriate management?
o: Do the surgery if there is written consent
Refuse the surgery as the patient wishes
Do the surgery if there is benefit for life
r: A competent patient's informed refusal remains valid after he loses capacity; family members cannot override his known prior wish.
n: Why not D? An ethics consult is for genuine uncertainty about wishes or capacity - here his competent refusal is known and must be respected.

q: A pregnant woman in the delivery room tells the nurse she does not want a blood transfusion. During the procedure she bleeds and starts to faint. What is the appropriate action?
o: Take consent from her before she faints
Call her husband and ask him for consent
Press on the wound until the ethics committee is contacted
r: The key treats a remark to the nurse - not an informed, documented refusal made to the physician - as non-binding in a life-threatening haemorrhage, so transfusion proceeds under emergency implied consent.
n: Why not B? A husband cannot consent for (or refuse on behalf of) a competent adult, and calling him wastes critical time. Claude: Also seen in the 17/19 Sep sittings with the same key. Claude: if the stem says she signed an informed refusal (e.g., a documented

q: A woman comes to the clinic requesting oral contraceptive pills. She refuses a pelvic examination, Pap smear and screening for sexually transmitted diseases. What should be done regarding the OCPs?
o: Educate her about the benefits/harms of the examination; if she still refuses, document and give the OCP
r: Pelvic examination, cervical cytology and STI screening are not prerequisites for starting hormonal contraception (CDC/WHO): counsel, respect her autonomy, document the refusal and prescribe (blood pressure is the only essential check before combined pills).
n: Why not B? Referring her elsewhere just passes on a request you can safely meet; declining optional screening is no reason to withhold contraception. Claude: Second 2 Nov copy (#87968): options refuse / refer / 'tell her the importance of screening and give he

q: You are a GP and a mother refuses vaccination for her children because she thinks it may harm them. What should you do?
o: Report to the Ministry of Health
r: Address vaccine hesitancy first by exploring her concerns and explaining benefits and risks respectfully; if she still refuses, document the informed refusal. Reporting or coercion is not the first step.
n: Why not A? Reporting to the authorities is not the first response to parental hesitancy; counselling comes first.

q: A woman with a strong family history of breast cancer undergoes BRCA genetic testing. Three days later her sister comes to the clinic asking for the results of all the genetic tests she had. What is the most appropriate action by the physician?
o: Refuse to disclose the results to protect patient confidentiality
Give the results to the sister as she shares a genetic risk
Refer the sister to the patient affairs department to sign a release form
Contact the patient immediately while the sister is in the clinic to get verbal consent
r: Genetic results belong to the patient and are released only to her or with her explicit consent; a relative's shared risk does not override confidentiality — encourage the patient herself to share relevant results with family.
n: Why not D? Consent must come from the patient through proper, unpressured channels — phoning her on the spot while the sister waits is not the right response; decline and advise the sister to ask the patient. Claude: 2 Nov copy (#87968) options: refuse / tell

q: A woman with a strong family history of breast cancer undergoes BRCA testing. Her employer requests the results. As a physician, what do you do?
o: Tell the patient to send a request to the ethics committee
Tell the patient to give it to the employer if it is positive
Tell the employer to contact the ethics committee
r: Genetic results are confidential and are released to third parties (employer, relatives) only with the patient's explicit consent; no legal or public-safety exception applies, so refuse.
n: Why not D? Sending the employer to the ethics committee implies the request might be legitimate - it is not; refuse without the patient's consent. Claude: #87968 (2 Nov) recalls the same question with her sister asking instead of the employer; answer still Ref

q: A woman presents to the emergency department with multiple physical injuries after being beaten by her husband. What is the appropriate action for the physician?
r: Under the Saudi Protection from Abuse Law, healthcare workers must report suspected domestic abuse (through the hospital's family-safety/social services to the authorities) after treating her injuries and securing her safety.
n: Why not B? Confronting the husband can escalate violence and breaches her confidentiality; it is not the physician's role. Claude: One option was not recalled. Debate: Alhomrani's October Combined (21 Oct p. 3280) keys 'tell the husband'; Athar/SMLE Brain chos

q: A 13-month-old child of smoking parents has many problems (tachycardia, tachypnea, failure to thrive). Another consultant suggests a DNR order. What is the next step?
o: Ask the opinion of 3 trustworthy consultants
Inform the parents and discuss the DNR
Do not discuss it with the parents
Ask the opinion of another consultant AND 3 referral physicians
r: Saudi DNR policy: the decision is made by THREE physicians, one attending consultant plus two who are at least specialists. When that exact combination isn't offered, '3 consultants' is the closest correct option, while D adds up to FOUR doctors. (Alhomrani U2826, policy page U2830.)
n: Why not D? one consultant + three physicians = four doctors, not the three required; it only looks like the '1 consultant + 2 specialists' rule.

q: A 13-month-old child of smoking parents has many problems (tachycardia, tachypnea, failure to thrive), and a DNR order is being considered. What is the next step in the DNR order?
o: No need for the parents' opinion
Needs 1 trustworthy consultant and 2 trustworthy specialists
r: This copy offers the exact Saudi Health Council wording: three physicians, one consultant plus two who are at least specialists. That beats '3 consultants'. (Alhomrani U2827, policy page U2830.)
n: Why not A? '3 consultants' is only the fallback when the '1 consultant + 2 specialists' option is absent.

q: A critically ill ICU patient is being considered for a DNR order. Which statement is true?
o: DNR is decided by 3 trustworthy (qualified) doctors
DNR must be discussed with the patient
DNR must be discussed with the family
DNR is decided by a consultant AND three specialists
r: Saudi policy requires three physicians (one consultant plus two who are at least specialists). The patient and family are informed, but their approval isn't required. Option D totals four doctors, so A is the true statement.
n: Why not D? a consultant plus THREE specialists is four doctors — the wrong number. Claude: There are four copies of this recall (Alhomrani U2826).

q: Regarding a Do-Not-Resuscitate (DNR) order from another hospital, which statement is correct? [3 Nov copy (#88022): a 5-month-old with brain disease transferred from a private to a tertiary hospital; after CPR the team finds a signed DNR]
o: A DNR must be from the same hospital
A DNR from another hospital is valid for 24 hours
The family must verify the DNR
Any member of the medical team can verify the DNR
r: Under the Saudi DNR policy, a DNR from another facility is honoured for 24 hours after transfer. During that time the receiving team must reassess and write its own order, signed by three physicians: one consultant plus two others of at least specialist rank.
n: Why not A? the outside order is not void; it stays valid for 24 hours while the new team re-evaluates.

q: A child with white matter disease, global developmental delay and permanent brain damage has a DNR order that was agreed and signed. What is the next step by the physician regarding this DNR order?
o: DNR is reviewed based on the patient's condition
DNR is reviewed by the primary consultant annually
DNR should be reviewed every 3 months for the paediatric age group
r: A DNR order is not permanent: it must be reviewed whenever the patient's condition changes (and on each admission), rather than only on a fixed calendar.
n: Why not C? Some bank siblings (q09854, q08852) key 'reviewed annually', but a fixed annual review ignores the core rule that any change in condition triggers review. Claude: Disputed: bank siblings conflict (q10127 'based on condition' vs q09854/q08852 'annual

q: A surgeon was about to perform knee surgery on the wrong side. The nurse hesitated to speak up, and another team member checked the chart. What is the best way to prevent this error?
o: Surgical-site marking and team verification during the TIME-OUT
Assign a single nurse to inform the surgeon
Rely on the surgeon's final confirmation
r: The Universal Protocol fixes wrong-site surgery and hierarchy-driven silence: pre-procedure verification, site marking, and a team time-out just before incision in which anyone can speak up.
n: Why not C? chart review alone is only one step, and it fails without marking and the team time-out.

q: Two patients with cataracts are scheduled for surgery on the same day. They have the same name but cataracts in different eyes. How can the error of operating on the wrong eye be prevented?
o: Surgeon checks the consent form before incision
r: Same-name patients are a classic identification hazard: use a standardised protocol with at least two identifiers (full name plus medical record number/date of birth), with site marking and a time-out (Universal Protocol).
n: Why not B? One surgeon checking one document relies on a single person and cannot reliably distinguish two patients with the same name. Claude: Options only partly recalled (the examinee's answer was option C in the file).

q: A hypertensive patient is prescribed hydralazine, but the nurse administers hydroxyzine. Which strategy would best prevent this error?
o: Using brand names instead of generic names
r: Hydralazine/hydroxyzine is a classic look-alike, sound-alike (LASA) pair; Tall Man lettering (hydrALAZINE vs hydrOXYzine) highlights the letters that differ on labels, orders and screens and is the ISMP/FDA-recommended fix.
n: Why not B? verbal orders add sound-alike errors and are discouraged except in emergencies; they do not fix a reading/selection mix-up.

q: A hypertensive patient was given a wrong prescription by the doctor by mistake. The pharmacist noticed it but assumed the doctor was aware. The patient then developed a severe drop in blood pressure. What would best prevent this type of error?
o: Patient reviews medications before leaving hospital
Computerized physician order entry with alerts
r: System-level fixes beat reliance on human vigilance. Computerised physician order entry with decision-support alerts catches wrong-drug and wrong-dose errors at the point of prescribing.
n: Why not A? a nurse double-check is just another human layer that can fail in the same way the pharmacist's check did.

q: A patient with sickle cell disease (vaso-occlusive crisis) is requesting analgesia. The nurse called the on-call doctor, who ordered the analgesia by phone. What is next?
o: Write the full order in the file
Do not give the order by phone
Ask another nurse to approve the order
r: The key holds that an analgesic (opioid) order should not be acted on from a phone instruction alone - the doctor must attend or write the order.
n: Why not B? Writing the order down with read-back and later co-signature is how many hospitals accept telephone orders - the main rival answer, ticked by the examinee. Claude: Disputed; the examinee ticked '(give and) write the order in the file'. Claude: I'd l

q: A child with sickle cell disease has a vaso-occlusive crisis; the nurse calls the doctor, who orders analgesics over the phone. What should be done?
o: Write the full order in the file (read back and document)
You can't give it over the phone
r: Telephone/verbal orders are allowed in urgent situations if the nurse writes them down in full, reads them back and the doctor co-signs later.
n: Why not C? verbal orders aren't banned; they need documentation and read-back.

q: A surgeon asks a nurse to give IV adrenaline to a child. The nurse repeats 'give IV adrenaline', and the surgeon says 'that's right'. What kind of communication is this?
r: Closed-loop communication is the full cycle: sender gives the order, receiver repeats it back, sender confirms - exactly what happens here.
n: Why not A? Check-back (TeamSTEPPS) names the repeat-back tool used within this loop; once the surgeon confirms, the exchange as a whole is closed-loop communication, which the key prefers.

q: A road-traffic-accident trauma patient is in the operating room. The surgeon says, 'Charge nurse, hang a blood unit.' The nurse responds, 'One unit of blood,' and then hangs it. Which communication technique is being used?
r: In closed-loop communication the sender gives a clear, directed order, and the receiver repeats it back and carries it out, with the sender confirming. (Athar: B for the copy without option D; Alhomrani: closed loop for the copy with check-back, U2897.)
n: Why not D? 'check-back' is TeamSTEPPS' name for the same repeat-back step, so it is close to a synonym; Alhomrani still chose closed loop but says he isn't sure. Claude: One copy had no option D. Alhomrani: 'I don't know, but I think it's closed loop… could be

q: A patient did not stop warfarin despite clear instructions. The nurse in the OR noticed this and informed the surgeon, who postponed the operation. How is this event classified?
r: A near miss is an error or hazard caught before it reaches or harms the patient - operating on an anticoagulated patient was prevented by the nurse.
n: Why not A? An adverse event requires harm (the incident reaching the patient); the operation never went ahead.

q: An asthmatic patient is prescribed an inhaler for the first time, but the doctor is too busy to refer him to the education clinic. What is the most likely consequence?
r: Without education on inhaler technique, patients use the device wrongly (poor technique, overuse of relievers, underuse of controllers), which leads to poor control, exacerbations and medication-related adverse events, a patient-safety outcome. (Alhomrani's Sept page)
n: Why not A? confidence may drop, but the consequence examined is harm: adverse events from incorrect use.

q: A 60-year-old patient with controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus has missed his last two scheduled appointments at the diabetes clinic. Which IOM domain of quality will help the patient adhere to his appointments?
r: Patient-centred care - respecting the patient's preferences, needs and values and involving him in scheduling and decisions - is the IOM domain that improves engagement and adherence. (Extract key, SMLE First Aid bank.) Why not B/C? Timeliness (reducing waits and delays) and efficiency (avoiding was
n: Claude: The examinee ticked C (Efficiency) in 22 October .pdf; the extract key is kept.

q: An orthopaedic surgeon completed a fellowship in spinal surgery on time and is now requesting clinical privileges to perform complex spinal surgeries in the hospital. As the body granting privileges, what should you do? [stem wording uncertain in the recall]
o: Grant privileges based on his years of experience
Approve privileges based solely on completion of the certificate
Do not grant privileges until he completes at least 2 years of on-site clinical practice
Assess the competency of his performance before certification [22 October .pdf: 'after certification']
r: Privileging rests on verified current competence: the certificate (credential) is necessary but not sufficient, so the hospital assesses his performance (e.g., focused evaluation/proctoring) before granting specific privileges.
n: Why not B? A fellowship certificate verifies training (credentialing), but privileges for complex procedures need demonstrated competence, not the certificate alone.

q: A woman with a history of anxiety disorder presents with lethargy and fatigue and asks for some days off. She says she is going through a stressful time, but no physical illness is found. What is the ethically appropriate response?
o: Refer to stress management and don't give sick leave
r: A sick-leave certificate must reflect genuine medical incapacity; without it, decline the leave but address the underlying stress/anxiety by referral to stress management - honesty plus beneficence.
n: Why not B? Refusing is right about the certificate, but stopping there neglects her evident psychological need; C adds the appropriate care. Claude: Extract status [Review].

q: A medical intern asks his physician for sick leave because he has an exam and did not study well while caring for his sick mother. He hands you a paper confirming his mother's condition and appointment. What will you do?
o: Refuse and tell him he should have studied earlier
Call the hospital to confirm his mother's condition
Give him the sick leave to save his future
Refer him to another physician who you know does not give sick leave easily
r: A leave certificate must reflect a genuine, verified reason, so first verify his documents with the treating hospital. Caring for a sick first-degree relative can justify a companion leave, but a certificate must never be issued just to help him pass an exam.
n: Why not C? granting leave 'to save his future' without verification means issuing a certificate on non-medical grounds, which is unprofessional and potentially fraudulent.

q: An oncologist is sponsored by a company and offered 2,000 to present a lecture. What should he do?
o: Accept if he will disclose the financial relationship
r: Reasonable payment for genuine educational work (a lecture) is acceptable provided the financial relationship is disclosed to the audience and the content stays independent of the sponsor.
n: Why not B? Refusing is unnecessary - fair payment for real work is allowed; what is prohibited is payment tied to prescribing or undisclosed influence. Claude: Key changed 23 Oct from B to C (compiler's typo); the older Untitled.pdf page printed B, which Alhom

q: During a study, a patient developed bleeding (a complication). The surgeon decided to remove this case from the research report to make the results look better. Which ethical principle did the surgeon violate?
r: Deliberately omitting unfavourable data is falsification - research misconduct that violates research integrity (honest, complete reporting).
n: Why not D? Non-maleficence concerns harming participants; the wrong here is dishonest reporting, not the complication itself.

q: Researchers studying childhood smoking contact randomly selected people by phone and invite them to participate. Which ethical principle applies? [poorly recalled]
r: Researchers who phone participants know who they are, so anonymity can't be promised; what they must guarantee is that the data collected stay confidential.
n: Why not A? anonymity means even the researcher can't link the data to a person, which is impossible when people are recruited by phone. Claude: Alhomrani doesn't correct ethics; this key is Athar's.

q: A couple presented with primary infertility. After successful IVF, a quantity of cryopreserved sperm remains. What should be done with it?
o: Keep it for use for an indefinite time
It is prohibited ethically and religiously
Keep it for a specific time frame then ethically discard it
Keep it in a governmental authorized fertility center
r: Saudi IVF rules allow a husband's cryopreserved sperm to be stored for a defined period, for use by the same married couple only, and then discarded; it is never donated or used after the marriage ends.
n: Why not D? Storage must be in a licensed centre anyway, but the decisive rule is a defined storage period followed by ethical disposal, which only C states. Claude: Untitled.pdf: excess sperm is not the same as a fertilised embryo.

q: A 50-year-old man, medically and surgically free with no family history, comes for cancer screening. Which screening should be done?
r: Average-risk adults are screened for colorectal cancer from 45-50 years (FIT or colonoscopy); prostate screening is shared decision-making only, and lung screening needs a heavy smoking history (>=20 pack-years, age 50-80).
n: Why not B? PSA screening (55-69 years) is an individual shared decision, not a routine test that 'should be done'.

q: A 47-year-old woman [extract: sexually active; the 2 Nov examinee's copy did not say so] with hypertension for 5 years on medication and BMI 37, no family history, attends a preventive clinic. What is the highest recommended screening test?
r: Adults aged 35–70 who are overweight or obese should be screened for prediabetes/type 2 diabetes (USPSTF); with BMI 37 and hypertension, fasting glucose is the highest-yield test.
n: Why not B? Pap is also due if she isn't up to date, but Alhomrani corrected B to D for this fasting-glucose version; Pap wins only when the glucose option is 'random' (see twin). Claude: Extract 'other answer': Alhomrani's 15–18 Oct compilation keyed — the #88

q: A 47-year-old sexually active woman with hypertension and BMI 37 asks which screening can be done at this visit.
r: The Alhomrani file screenshot posted in Silent (17 Jul and 15–18 Oct versions) keys Pap smear. The AI-explained 21 October file chose blood glucose.
n: Why not C? diabetes screening is also indicated (hypertension + obesity), which is why the question is debated. Claude: Q331 of the 20 October Part 1 file was keyed (fasting glucose). If the stem says her cervical screening is up to date, choose glucose.

q: A 47-year-old sexually active woman with hypertension for 5 years on medication and BMI 37 attends a preventive clinic. Which screening is most recommended?
r: A random glucose is not an accepted screening test for diabetes, so the valid screen due for this sexually active woman is cervical cytology (Pap every 3 years at 30–65).
n: Why not D? Random glucose diagnoses diabetes only when ≥11.1 mmol/L with symptoms; screening uses fasting glucose, HbA1c or OGTT. Claude: annual FOBT/FIT is also guideline-due from 45 (USPSTF 2021); older keys predate that.

q: A 33-year-old woman with a BRCA mutation and a family history of breast cancer (sister/mother diagnosed at 43) attends a screening clinic; imaging shows heterogeneously dense breast tissue with microcalcification. What is the most appropriate screening/next step? [the examinee was unsure of the exact ages and options]
r: BRCA carriers need annual breast MRI from age 25–30 (with annual mammography added from 30); MRI is far more sensitive than mammography in young, dense breasts.
n: Why not D? Mammography is insensitive in the dense breasts of young women; surveillance of high-risk (BRCA) women relies on MRI. Claude: if the stem truly shows suspicious microcalcifications, stereotactic biopsy would come next; as recalled, the screening ans

q: A man attends a smoking cessation clinic. He acknowledges the risks of smoking, is willing to quit, and has already BOUGHT nicotine patches. Which stage of change is he in?
r: Preparation = he intends to quit within the next month and has taken a concrete step (bought patches, set a date).
