n: Why not A? the action stage starts only once he has actually stopped smoking.

q: A man at a smoking cessation clinic acknowledges the risks of smoking and is willing to quit, but only AFTER he buys nicotine patches (he hasn't bought them yet). Which stage of change is he in?
r: He is aware of the problem and intends to change but hasn't taken a concrete step yet, which is contemplation. (Alhomrani U2924: 'he did NOT buy it → contemplation'.)
n: Why not B? preparation requires a step already taken toward quitting (e.g., patches bought). Claude: Alhomrani calls this a linguistic disagreement in a poorly worded ethics recall; this is how the examiner read the stem.

q: An explosion occurs at an industrial facility and you are exposed to radioactive material. What is the first thing you should do? [wording approximate]
r: After a wide-area release of radiation, first get yourself out of the contaminated area (distance, shielding, isolate the area), then decontaminate by removing clothes and washing. (Alhomrani U2916.)
n: Why not C? taking off clothes is the first decontamination step only once you are out of the contaminated area, or when only your clothing is contaminated.

q: A man working in industry is exposed to radioactive liquid over his whole body. What is your next step?
o: Tell him to shower with warm water
Wash him with lots of soap
Stay away from the incident location
r: When radioactive material contaminates the area, the first step is to leave or isolate the scene (time, distance, shielding). Then decontaminate: remove clothing (~80–90% of the contamination) and wash with lukewarm water and mild soap.
n: Why not A? removing clothes comes first when the contamination is confined to the person's clothes and the area is clean (REMM); Alhomrani isn't sure which scenario this copy describes. Claude: Alhomrani (U2916): 'not sure if poor recall or different recall' —

q: A worker in industry comes to the Emergency Department 1 hour after radioactive liquid was spilled all over his body. What is the FIRST thing to do?
o: Stay away from the incident site
r: Make the site safe and protect healthcare workers first (PPE, isolate the area), then decontaminate the patient: removing clothing removes most contamination, followed by washing with soap and water.
n: Why not A? Removing clothing is the first decontamination step for the patient, but it comes only after the scene and staff are safe. Claude: The 4 Nov examinee (unsure) chose 'get away from the area'. Alhomrani's earlier October Combined answer was 'stay away

q: Radioactive liquid splashes onto a worker's clothes only; the surrounding area is not contaminated. What is the first step?
o: Stay away from the incident location
r: With personal contamination only, remove the contaminated clothing immediately (removes ~80–90% of external contamination), then wash the skin with lukewarm water and mild soap. (Alhomrani rule U2916; spill-procedure references U2920–U2921.)
n: Why not D? leaving the area is the first step only when the spill contaminates the room or building. Claude: Twin built from Alhomrani's rule (U2916); not a verbatim recall.

q: A patient presents with an infection. Which of the following diseases must be reported to the Ministry of Health?
r: Chlamydia is a notifiable sexually transmitted infection (it needs contact tracing and partner treatment); BV, ordinary pneumonia and EBV mononucleosis are not notifiable.
n: Why not C? Pneumonia is notifiable only when caused by a specific notifiable organism (e.g. Legionella, TB).

q: Which mosquito should be used in the surveillance of malaria?
r: Malaria (Plasmodium) is transmitted only by female Anopheles mosquitoes, so vector surveillance targets Anopheles (in Saudi Arabia mainly An. arabiensis in the south-west).
n: Why not C? Aedes aegypti is the dengue vector (the surveillance mosquito for dengue in Jeddah/Makkah), not malaria.

q: A worker with 15 years in a chemical factory wants to be screened for cancer. What is the most sensitive test?
r: The Ames test (Salmonella reverse-mutation assay) is the most widely used and most sensitive short-term screen for mutagenic chemical carcinogens; most known carcinogens test positive.
n: Why not D? Cytogenetic assays (chromosomal aberrations, micronuclei) are used to biomonitor exposed workers but are less sensitive screens of carcinogenic potential. Claude: strictly, Ames screens chemicals rather than people; keep the bank key.

q: A researcher studies students reading books at schools. Results: 4, 6, 7, 5, 5, 3, 7, 5, 5, 6, 5, 5, 6, 5, 5, 5, 4, 6, 4, 5. What is the mode? [the 4 Nov recall listed options 3 / 4 / 5 / 6]
r: The mode is the most frequent value: 5 occurs 10 times (6 four times, 4 three times, 7 twice, 3 once).
n: Why not C? 6 is only the second most frequent value (4 times). Claude: Another copy (posted 4 Nov, probably from the 3 Nov sitting) recalled only the options 3/4/5/6 without the data set and may also have asked the study type.

q: 150 children were on a cruise trip and 30 of them developed gastroenteritis (food poisoning). What is the attack rate?
r: Attack rate = new cases ÷ population at risk during the outbreak = 30/150 = 20%; it is the cumulative incidence used for outbreaks.
n: Why not C? 25% is 30/120, which divides by the unaffected children instead of the whole population at risk.

q: In a population of 10,000 people, 500 new cases of a disease are diagnosed. What is the incidence rate?
r: Incidence = new cases / population at risk = 500/10,000 = 0.05 = 50 per 1,000 over the period.
n: Why not A? 5 per 1,000 would require only 50 new cases - a misplaced decimal. Claude: Extract status [Review].

q: A country's study of maternal mortality found 450 maternal deaths due to complications of pregnancy and childbirth, and 200,000 live births in the same year. Which of the following represents the maternal mortality rate?
r: Maternal mortality ratio = maternal deaths / live births x 100,000 = 450/200,000 x 100,000 = 225 per 100,000 live births.
n: Why not C? 450 per 200,000 is the same proportion but not expressed per the standard 100,000 live births.

q: A researcher wants to assess the relationship between birth weight and cognitive function and finds r = +0.8. What is the interpretation of the correlation coefficient? [examinee 100% sure of r]
o: Increased birth weight causes cognitive function to be lower
Increased birth weight increases cognitive development
r: r = +0.8 is a strong positive correlation: higher birth weight goes with higher cognitive scores. Correlation shows association, not causation - C wins only as the sole positive-direction option.
n: Why not A? An inverse relation needs a negative r; the + sign means both variables rise together.

q: A 20-year-old college student presents with a 1-month history of low mood, severe anhedonia, poor concentration and early-morning awakening. Over the past 10 days he has developed persecutory delusions (he believes one of his friends is plotting to harm him) and auditory hallucinations. What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Major depressive disorder with psychotic features
r: The depressive syndrome came first and the delusions/hallucinations appeared only inside that mood episode, which is MDD with psychotic features. Psychosis confined to a mood episode never counts as schizophrenia.
n: Why not B? schizophrenia needs psychosis that isn't explained by a mood episode (≥6 months of disturbance). B is the key only for the look-alike with NO depressive features.

q: A 20-year-old college student presents with persecutory delusions (he believes a friend is plotting to harm him) and auditory hallucinations. There are NO depressive features. What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Major depressive disorder with psychotic features
r: Delusions plus hallucinations with no mood episode point to the schizophrenia spectrum (brief psychotic disorder, then schizophreniform, then schizophrenia, by duration). (Alhomrani U2814: the look-alike without depressive features = B.)
n: Why not D? delusional disorder allows no prominent hallucinations; auditory hallucinations push it into the schizophrenia spectrum. Claude: Rebuilt from Alhomrani's description of the look-alike; its exact stem and duration were not given.

q: A young patient presents with social isolation and odd, bizarre behaviour. He also has visual hallucinations and a delusion that his roommate is spying on him. What is the most likely diagnosis?
r: Delusions, hallucinations and bizarre behaviour with negative symptoms (social withdrawal) and no primary mood episode fit a schizophrenia-spectrum disorder; duration then separates schizophreniform from schizophrenia.
n: Why not C? Psychotic depression needs a major depressive episode with psychosis occurring only within it - no low mood is described.

q: A 25-year-old woman with known bipolar disorder, on no medication, has had 2 weeks of elevated mood with reduced sleeping hours. On examination she is hyperactive. What is the most appropriate pharmacological intervention?
o: Olanzapine to control her manic episode
SSRI to address her depressive symptoms
r: For an acute manic episode in a patient not on treatment, a second-generation antipsychotic such as olanzapine controls symptoms fastest (NICE first-line); lithium is the long-term mood stabiliser for relapse prevention.
n: Why not A? Lithium works but is slow to act and needs level monitoring - it is the answer when the question asks to prevent mania (maintenance). Claude: Key changed 5 Oct from A to B (confirmed by a 100% scorer).

q: A 25-year-old woman with known bipolar disorder, on no medication, has had 2 weeks of elevated mood with reduced sleeping hours. On examination she is hyperactive. What is the most appropriate pharmacological intervention TO PREVENT MANIA?
o: Olanzapine to control her manic episode
SSRI to address her depressive symptoms
r: Preventing further manic episodes (maintenance) is the role of lithium, the best-evidenced mood stabiliser for relapse prevention, with serum level monitoring (~0.6-0.8 mmol/L).
n: Why not B? Olanzapine controls the acute episode quickly, but the lead-in asks for prevention, where lithium is the gold standard.

q: An 8-year-old boy is easily distracted, does not listen, is restless and talks excessively. What is the most appropriate PREVENTIVE method? [original recall: 'has 4 features of ADHD']
o: Avoiding prenatal exposure to addictive substances
Limiting TV and rapid video games
r: Prenatal exposure to tobacco, alcohol and drugs is an established modifiable risk factor for ADHD, so avoiding it in pregnancy is the true (primary) preventive measure; school screening is early detection, not prevention. (Alhomrani's 14 Sep page)
n: Why not D? limiting screen time is popular advice, but there is no good evidence that it prevents ADHD; it is a management tip, not prevention.

q: An 80-year-old man is brought by his family with worsening forgetfulness; he forgets places that were familiar to him and struggles to manage his finances. How should this patient be evaluated? [poster: the stem asked how to diagnose, not 'next' or 'most appropriate']
r: Suspected dementia is first evaluated with a structured cognitive assessment (MMSE/MoCA) plus an informant history and reversible-cause labs (B12, TSH); neuroimaging follows to exclude structural causes.
n: Why not A? CT (or MRI) belongs to the work-up after cognitive impairment is confirmed; it does not establish dementia. Claude: Extract version: 70-year-old woman with memory problems, 'next step', options cognitive assessment / brain CT / brain MRI / EEG — sam

q: An elderly man in his 70s with hypertension is brought by his son. He forgets recent events but remembers old ones, forgets names, misplaces items and cannot find them, and has withdrawn from social activities through lack of interest. The mini-mental state examination score is low. MRI shows cortical atrophy. What medication should be started?
r: Progressive recent-memory loss with preserved remote memory, a low MMSE and cortical atrophy = Alzheimer dementia; start an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor (donepezil, rivastigmine or galantamine) for mild-moderate disease.
n: Why not B? Apathy and social withdrawal are common in dementia; without depressed mood, an antidepressant does not treat the cognitive decline.

q: A daughter is caring for her 80-year-old mother, who has had dementia for 10 years that is getting worse. She asks how to deal with her mother's constant questioning (for example, asking 'Where am I?' five times). What is the most appropriate advice?
o: Answer her questions until she understands
r: Repetitive questions stem from anxiety and lost short-term memory; carers should answer calmly and patiently, reorienting and reassuring each time, never ignoring or restraining.
n: Why not C? Distraction is a useful add-on, but the confirmed key is to answer and reorient calmly - the question asks how to deal with the questioning itself. Claude: Key changed 5 Oct from C to D (confirmed by a 100% scorer).

q: A 28-year-old with asthma and a history of alcohol use presents after a motor vehicle accident. Some days later he develops tremors, sweating and agitation consistent with alcohol withdrawal. What is the most appropriate initial treatment?
r: Alcohol withdrawal is treated with benzodiazepines, and thiamine must be given (before any glucose) to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy, so the combined option is the complete initial treatment.
n: Why not B? Chlordiazepoxide is a correct benzodiazepine, but without thiamine the treatment is incomplete.

q: A 40-year-old woman with anorexia nervosa was admitted to start nutrition. After feeding began, blood tests showed hypophosphataemia, hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia. What is the most likely cause of these laboratory findings?
r: Feeding a starved patient triggers insulin release and an intracellular shift of phosphate, potassium and magnesium; hypophosphataemia is the hallmark. Prevent with slow calorie build-up (NICE: ~10 kcal/kg/day in high risk), thiamine and electrolyte replacement.
n: Why not A? A too-rapid regimen can precipitate it, but the clinical syndrome behind these labs is refeeding syndrome, which occurs even with correct protocols in high-risk patients.

q: An 11-year-old boy presents to the family physician with bilateral red eyes and yellow discharge (duration recalled as either 12 hours or 2 days); no eye pain is mentioned. What is the most appropriate action?
r: Acute conjunctivitis without pain, photophobia or visual loss is usually self-limiting, so reassurance with saline cleansing is acceptable; this is the answer in Alhomrani's file.
n: Why not D? ophthalmology referral is for red flags (pain, photophobia, reduced vision); with pain, the confirmed answer becomes D.

q: A 6-year-old has a red eye with yellow (purulent) discharge in one eye, and the eyelids are stuck together on waking. What is the most appropriate treatment? [rebuilt from the bank look-alike line; topical antibiotic offered]
r: Bacterial conjunctivitis (purulent discharge, lids glued in the morning) is treated with topical antibiotic drops or ointment, which shorten the illness and allow an earlier return to school; oral antibiotics are not needed.
n: Why not A? saline and reassurance are acceptable for mild cases, but when a topical antibiotic is offered for clearly bacterial conjunctivitis, the bank keys it.

q: An 11-year-old boy has bilateral red eyes with yellow discharge and eye PAIN. What should you do?
o: Reassure and give normal saline eye drops
r: Pain is a red flag in a red eye (keratitis, uveitis, acute glaucoma, orbital involvement). Simple conjunctivitis causes grittiness, not pain, so refer for a slit-lamp and fundus exam. (The examiner's copy had PAIN and he chose; Alhomrani marked it #Confirmed, U2815.)
n: Why not A? reassurance and saline are only for painless conjunctivitis; pain takes the case out of the 'simple' category.

q: A hypertensive man presents with a bright red spot in his eye. He denies pain or visual changes, and there are no signs of infection. What is the most likely diagnosis?
r: A painless, well-demarcated bright-red patch with normal vision - often in hypertensive or anticoagulated patients or after straining - is a subconjunctival haemorrhage; reassure (clears in 1-3 weeks) and check BP/INR.
n: Why not C? Episcleritis is also benign and near-painless, but it is sectoral dilated vessels (blanching with phenylephrine), not a flat bright-red blood patch.

q: A patient sustains an eye injury from a wooden stick involving the sclera, with bleeding, inability to move the eye and severe pain. There is a teardrop-shaped pupil and a cloudy anterior chamber. What type of injury is this? [another recall: a metallic object]
r: A full-thickness wound of the eye wall (sclera) with a teardrop/peaked pupil (iris drawn toward the wound) and a cloudy/bloody anterior chamber = open globe injury. Shield the eye without pressure, no drops, keep NPO, give IV antibiotics and tetanus cover, and arrange urgent surgical repair. (Alhomr
n: Why not A? a corneal laceration counts as open globe only if full thickness, and this wound involves the sclera with a peaked pupil, so 'open globe injury' is the correct category.

q: A mother brings her 2-month-old baby with a squint (no mention of sudden onset or trauma). What is the next assessment?
r: Intermittent misalignment is normal up to 4–6 months, so at 2 months assess with the corneal light reflex (Hirschberg), which Alhomrani ranks above the red reflex, and refer if it is abnormal. Referral indications: constant squint at any age, intermittent squint beyond 4–6 months, or an abnormal cor
n: Why not B? the cover test needs steady fixation and cooperation, so it suits older infants and children; at 2 months the corneal reflex comes first.

q: A mother brings her 2-month-old because she is concerned the baby may have a squint. What is the most appropriate assessment?
r: In a young infant, the red reflex test screens for cataract and retinoblastoma behind an apparent squint.
n: Why not A? the cover test needs a cooperative child with fixation and is more useful later.

q: The mother of a 2-month-old baby is concerned about a SUDDEN squint. What is the most appropriate step?
r: A sudden squint is a red flag (cranial nerve palsy, raised ICP, intraocular tumour such as retinoblastoma). Alhomrani's rule is MRI/CT to exclude a space-occupying lesion; with no imaging option, urgent referral is the safe answer. (Claude, applying Alhomrani's rule from N442.)
n: Why not C? a red reflex test is quick and screens for retinoblastoma, but it can't replace urgent specialist assessment and imaging of a sudden squint. Claude: This examinee recall was posted as a News comment (d52) with '????'; no key was given.

q: A 6-month-old has had left esotropia since birth with an ABSENT red reflex, and the left eye does not move on cover/uncover testing. What is the next step?
r: Constant strabismus at any age, or any abnormal red reflex, needs urgent paediatric ophthalmology referral: an absent red reflex raises cataract or retinoblastoma, and an untreated deviation causes amblyopia.
n: Why not D? patching the good eye treats amblyopia, but only after an ophthalmologist has excluded an organic cause such as cataract or retinoblastoma.

q: A 6-week-old has an absent red reflex in the left eye (leukocoria) but is developing normally. What is the most likely diagnosis?
r: Leukocoria at 6 weeks in a well, normally developing infant is most often congenital cataract, the commonest cause of leukocoria in early infancy; retinoblastoma usually presents later (median ~1-2 years).
n: Why not B? retinoblastoma is the must-not-miss cause and a classic exam answer, but it usually presents around 1-2 years, often with strabismus. Claude: The 21 Oct examinee answered retinoblastoma (docx); the key was changed 30 Oct B→C.

q: A child has atopic dermatitis on the elbow that isn't responding to a MILD topical steroid. What is the best next step? [4th option not recalled]
r: Without a 'higher-potency steroid' option, step up to a topical calcineurin inhibitor. Oral antihistamines don't treat eczema (they only sedate for itch), and systemic steroids are avoided. (Alhomrani News N443–N444.)
